Moscow plans to link two of its main rail terminals under a vast glass canopy. Preservationists fear Yaroslavsky Station’s Soviet architecture could disappear in the process.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:41:38 UTC
04:41:38 KST

Moscow plans to link two of its main rail terminals under a vast glass canopy. Preservationists fear Yaroslavsky Station’s Soviet architecture could disappear in the process.
Reconstruction of Moscow’s Yaroslavsky Station will begin in December 2026. A wave-shaped glass canopy will connect it to neighboring Leningradsky Station, allowing passengers to transfer between the two without going outdoors. Work will continue until 2028. The station’s appearance has changed many times over the years: the building designed by Fyodor Schechtel that Muscovites know today came much later. Architecture journalist Asya Zolnikova traces the station’s history and explains why preservation advocates are concerned about the upcoming reconstruction.
What’s happening?
Moscow plans to reconstruct Yaroslavsky Station, one of the city’s busiest transportation hubs. It handles more commuter rail passengers than most stations in Europe. On August 25, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said reconstruction would begin this year. It is scheduled to finish by the end of 2028.
What does the plan look like?
The design is still being developed, and few details are available. The most conspicuous change will be wave-shaped glass canopies covering 12,800 square meters (about 138,000 square feet). They will be built between the platforms of Yaroslavsky and neighboring Leningradsky Station. The canopies over the platforms themselves will also be updated.
Inside the building, plans call for new entrances and exits connecting to Komsomolskaya metro station, new utility systems, and additional passenger halls. Vladimir Yefimov, Moscow’s deputy mayor for urban development and construction, said every part of the design allows for growth in passenger numbers and trips. The station is already considered the country’s busiest for commuter rail services: 80,000 people use its commuter trains on a normal workday, and that number will exceed 100,000 by 2035.
Moscow’s urban development and construction authorities say the building will regain its “historic architectural appearance.” Officials have not specified which period they mean, however: Yaroslavsky Station has been rebuilt many times over the past century and a half.
How did the station come about? And what is it known for besides being busy?
The first station on the site was built in 1862. Both the station and the railway running from it were called Troitsky (from the Russian word for “Trinity”) because the tracks led to Sergiyev Posad and the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius. Natalya Shashkova, a specialist in railway architecture and director of Moscow’s Shchusev Museum of Architecture, said that despite the route’s economic advantages, ideology played a central role in the project. The railways were mired in “financial misconduct,” prompting a proposal to improve their reputation with a line “built by Russian engineers, from Russia’s ancient capital to its principal shrine.”
The original plan was to build the station on 1st Meshchanskaya Street, along a direct route to the monastery. A plot in the Apothecary Garden was selected, but Moscow State University, which owned the garden, managed to keep the land. Construction was then moved to Kalanchevskaya Square (renamed Komsomolskaya Square in 1932 and also known as Three Stations Square), where Nikolayevsky Station, later renamed Leningradsky, already stood. Its neoclassical architecture was a model for Troitsky Station.
The station received its current name in 1870, when the tracks reached Yaroslavl. They were later extended to Arkhangelsk. Many branch lines were connected to the main railway, including routes to Ivanovo, Shuya, and Vologda.
At the time, the station and railway belonged to a joint-stock company headed by industrialist and arts patron Savva Mamontov. In the 1890s, he decided to rebuild and expand the station, but while construction was underway, he was accused of defrauding shareholders. The railway was placed under state management, and the authorities commissioned a new design. The resulting building, erected in 1902–1904 and designed by architect Fyodor Schechtel, is the one for which the station is best known.
By the end of Nicholas II’s reign, Moscow had become a major transportation hub for travel to the country’s east. During the Soviet period, Yaroslavsky Station came to be recognized as the Trans-Siberian Railway’s “kilometer zero.” A monument beside the tracks has marked this status since 2001. Trains to Vladivostok still depart from here. Alexander Solzhenitsyn also arrived at Yaroslavsky Station in July 1994, returning to his homeland along the Trans-Siberian Railway.
How much of Schechtel’s work remains today? And what survives from other architects?
Despite many reconstructions and repairs, much of Schechtel’s work remains at the station. He designed the main building facing Komsomolskaya Square, an example of the neo-Russian style, a national romantic strand of Russian Art Nouveau.
This explains its many references to Russia’s North: facade patterns reminiscent of Pomor ornamentation; images of pine branches, walruses, deer, and other animals at the bases of engaged columns; and cool, muted colors. Above the windows and entrances are majolica panels depicting landscapes and fortresses in Russia’s northern regions, while a frieze above the main entrance depicts pale lilac wild strawberry stems. The ceramics were produced at the Abramtsevo ceramics factory, also owned by the Mamontov family. The majolica panels were based on drawings by Schechtel and artist Konstantin Korovin and fired using a technique developed by Mikhail Vrubel and ceramicist Pyotr Vaulin.
Schechtel did not design the building from scratch; he worked with the existing structure. In the mid-19th century, when the station was called Troitsky, it was built to an austere neo-Renaissance design by Roman Kuzmin. Under Mamontov, the side wings were expanded, and a gallery with columns of labradorite, an iridescent rock, was added beside the platform. The architect behind that reconstruction was Lev Kekushev, another celebrated figure of Moscow Art Nouveau.
Schechtel retained the eastern wing and the platform colonnade but added new halls and transformed a building with a symmetrical floor plan into a series of varied architectural forms. This tripled the station’s size. Art historians compare it to merchants’ ornate terem houses, a “ship”-style church, or even the maw of a fantastical sea creature.
Beyond its general northern motifs, much of Yaroslavsky Station recalls Schechtel’s earlier projects. According to Moscow Art Nouveau scholar Natalya Nashchokina, the station’s “folk-print quality and grotesquerie” echo the Russian Empire’s pavilion at the Glasgow International Exhibition, which was also inspired by northern architecture. Schechtel worked on that project in 1901 and considered it his finest building. Yaroslavsky Station also clearly resembles his Levenson dacha in Peredelkino.
What was added after Schechtel?
During the Soviet period, the facade remained virtually unchanged apart from a few details: the coats of arms of the Russian Empire, Moscow, Arkhangelsk, and Yaroslavl were replaced with the hammer and sickle, and Soviet stars were added. In 1946–1947, Schechtel’s halls were partly rebuilt in the style of Stalinist neoclassicism to a design by Alexey Dushkin. The station was expanded again in 1965, when Mosgiprotrans architects Alexander Kulagin and Galina Matokhina designed glass-walled modernist buildings housing ticket offices and a waiting hall.
The station has undergone several renovations in the 21st century. In the early 2000s, it was restored using plans drawn up by Timur Bashkayev’s firm, reinstating some of Schechtel’s details that had been plastered over or altered during the Soviet period. The floor was also lowered by 15 centimeters (about six inches) to expose the bases of the late-19th-century columns and restore their original proportions. The hammer and sickle remained in the wrought-iron roof crest in place of the imperial double-headed eagle, however, as did the Soviet coat of arms above the entrance. These and other Soviet features were later included on a list of the building’s legally protected features, approved on May 26, 2020.
That explains the facades. What about the interior?
The station’s interior is much less consistent in style than its facades. Almost nothing recalls Kuzmin’s original building. Kekushev’s colonnaded arcade is still in place, but during Kulagin and Matokhina’s reconstruction in the 1960s, it became part of a new waiting hall with vaulted ceilings built between the station’s side wings.
Schechtel’s interiors survive only in part: the Stalin-era reconstruction changed them substantially. That was when Ivan Yefimov, a sculptor known for his animal subjects, added decorative plasterwork and openwork reliefs depicting hunting, fishing, and factories. Earlier, in the 1930s, the wooden paneling, benches, kiosks, light fixtures, and wrought-iron “Glasgow roses” had been removed. The roses are a motif associated with Scottish Art Nouveau and the architecture of Charles Rennie Mackintosh. Schechtel evidently saw these works during the Glasgow International Exhibition and later used the motif in several of his buildings. Some of these elements were recreated during restorations in the 2000s.
After the revolution, Konstantin Korovin’s paintings, including “Fishing in the Murmansk Sea,” “Northern Lights,” and “Walrus Hunting,” disappeared from the building. The artist brought them back from a trip sponsored by Mamontov, aiming to use the paintings to raise money to build railway lines to the North. They were first exhibited in the “Far North” pavilion at the 1896 industrial exhibition in Nizhny Novgorod, after which most were hung in the station.
After the revolution, the paintings were taken down and stored in a utility room at the station itself. In the 1960s, art historian Mikhail Kiselyov found them badly damaged. They were then transferred to the Tretyakov Gallery’s storage facilities, where they remain today. Only some have been restored, and with great difficulty. Copies hung in the 2000s now occupy their places at the station.
What do people think of the latest reconstruction plan? Are the new canopies a good idea?
From a transportation standpoint, the reconstruction is necessary. Experts say doubling the waiting area would clearly make passengers more comfortable, while the canopies would let them move between trains, the metro, and other forms of transportation without going outdoors or getting their feet wet.
“Maybe they’ll even manage to introduce a single platform numbering system and stop tormenting passengers,” wrote urbanist Arkady Gershman. In his view, the best thing about the renderings is that they show no “security gizmos” — checkpoints with walk-through scanners and metal detectors (though that does not mean there won’t be any in practice). But images, Gershman said, are always “rendered from a flattering angle to ‘sell’ the idea.” Perhaps “it’ll all just come down to installing 101 screens and a million cameras.”
The plans for the historic parts of the station raise more questions. Museum of Architecture director Natalya Shashkova said the last major reconstruction, in 2005, sought to preserve every historical layer of the building. Now the Soviet additions are at risk: unlike Schechtel’s main station building, they have no heritage protection. She said:
This [Soviet, modernist] part of the building is as vivid and important a record of its time as the elements from the 19th and 20th centuries. It reflects the spirit of the generation that left Yaroslavsky Station to build the Baikal–Amur Mainline. It would be a great shame to lose the Soviet chapter of Yaroslavsky Station’s history, as happened at Leningradsky Station.
A statement by Pavel Ivankin, president of the National Research Center for Transportation and Infrastructure, also indirectly points to the risks facing the modernist part of the building: he says the restoration will be modeled on the one at Leningradsky Station.
What happened at Leningradsky Station?
Leningradsky Station is Moscow’s oldest. It was built in 1849, and its latest reconstruction was completed in May 2026. Work lasted almost two years, beginning in August 2024. The facades and proportions survive from the original design by Konstantin Thon, the architect of the Cathedral of Christ the Savior and the Grand Kremlin Palace. Everything else was added later, mostly during the Soviet period, including work by Dushkin, who, as at Yaroslavsky Station, renovated the interiors in the late 1940s.
In the 1970s, the building was expanded on the side facing the tracks to accommodate a waiting hall. The reconstruction followed a design by Lengiprotrans. This part of the building, like virtually everything apart from Thon’s facades and floor plans, was left off the list of protected features in 2020. As a result, the Soviet part of the building was substantially altered during the recent reconstruction: two mosaic panels depicting Moscow and St. Petersburg, covering more than 800 square meters (about 8,600 square feet), were added to the side walls. If the same approach is taken at Yaroslavsky Station, the interior of its modernist section could also be radically rebuilt.
Why did the square need three stations? Couldn’t they have built one big station?
No one ever planned a single station. In the Russian Empire, railways were built by different companies, both private and state-owned. Each served its own route and built its own terminal station.
Moscow’s three stations ended up beside one another because land was available. The city’s first railway connected it to St. Petersburg, and Thon designed the stations in both cities. The buildings are very similar: the main difference is the St. Petersburg station’s wider wings, while their central sections and train sheds were originally identical. Kalanchevskoye Field, then on Moscow’s outskirts, was chosen as the construction site.
Beside Nikolayevsky Station, later renamed Leningradsky, stood a customs house, freight warehouses, and other transportation infrastructure. Most importantly, railcars could be transferred from there to other routes. For these reasons, Yaroslavsky Station was built nearby first, and construction of Ryazansky Station, later renamed Kazansky, began in 1913. Schechtel also entered the competition to design that building, but Alexey Shchusev won. Komsomolskaya metro station on the Circle Line was later built to Shchusev’s design as well.
Such clusters are not unique. In imperial-era St. Petersburg, Baltiysky and Varshavsky stations stood side by side; the latter is no longer in operation and has been turned into a public space. In London, two masterpieces of Victorian architecture, King’s Cross and St. Pancras, stand right beside each other along Euston Road, with a third station, Euston, a few hundred meters (several hundred yards) away. Paris’s Gare de Lyon and Gare de Bercy are one block apart and share surrounding rail infrastructure.
Modern transportation complexes take a fundamentally different approach: they are much larger and more interconnected, designed as hubs linking different forms of transportation. All forms of transportation are brought together in a single megastructure, and passengers transfer through underground and covered passageways.

'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing

'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
Hundreds of thousands of students and their supporters took part in nationwide protests across France on Tuesday after weeks of student barricades protesting school conditions.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
If the French government was hoping to drive its protesting high schoolers back into their classrooms with a whiff of tear gas, it hasn’t worked.
Hundreds of thousands of students and their supporters took part in nationwide demonstrations, barricading school entrances and marching through France's major cities.
The interior ministry estimated that a quarter of a million people took part on Tuesday; organisers maintain it was almost twice that.
High schoolers have been blocking access to hundreds of schools across the country since mid-September, protesting what they say is a lack of teaching staff, harsh timetables and run-down buildings ill-equipped to deal with the worsening heatwaves that now stifle the country each summer.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Accusing the movement of descending into "urban violence" as some demonstrators set fire to school buildings and allegedly assaulted staff, the government told the police last week not to hold back from using all the "intermediary" (non-lethal) weapons at their disposal to re-open the schools.
The ensuing crackdown has been severe. Widely circulated footage has shown a 14-year-old boy set upon by three police officers, with one of whom firing a tear gas grenade point-blank into his face, knocking most of his teeth out and fracturing his jaw.
A 15-year-old boy in the northern town of Lens had his hand blown off up to the elbow by a sting-ball grenade; while a 16-year-old in Tours lost the use of his right eye to what the local prosecutor said was likely a projectile fired by riot police.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that 215 students and 85 teaching staff had been wounded in the protests, as well as 715 police officers. More than 5,000 people have been arrested since the movement began – the overwhelming majority of them minors.
Read moreFrench student protests fuel political clash ahead of 2027 presidential vote
A number of France's trade unions have called for members to throw their support behind the protesting students Tuesday to shield them from possible police violence.
True to their word, members of the left-wing Confédération Générale du Travail (CGT) formed a human chain between riot police and high schoolers barricading the Lycée Hélène Boucher on the eastern edge of Paris. It was one of dozens of occupations that students had planned for the day – marking "Act III" of a movement that shows no signs of slowing.
Class struggle
At the Lycée Sophie Germain in Paris’s winding Marais district, students choked off one end of the narrow street with a blockade of upturned bins, steel railings and chain-link fences.
Students crowded the front doors of the high school, cardboard signs held high. A portable speaker passes from hand to hand – the students are singing, rapping, dancing as one body.
Between songs, they chant well-worn slogans – “Siamo tutti antifascisti” (We are all anti-fascists), “Aux armes!” (To arms!) and “La jeunesse emmerde le Front National!” (a somewhat vulgar attack on the far right – it's probably best if you Google this one).
Unlike at other barricades piling up in front of high schools across France, there’s not a police officer in sight.
Bachir, 17, said the people who organised the barricade had come to an understanding with the authorities.
“The police said that as long as there aren’t any problems with fires, or firework-launchers or anything like that – as long as it’s peaceful – they won’t do anything,” he said.
It seems a shaky truce. At one point, a police van crawls up the main avenue, coming to a halt in front of the chain-link barricade. A few of the apparent organisers hurry down to conduct a quick negotiation through the van’s rolled-down window. The van keeps moving.
The ivy-draped walls of the Marais couldn’t feel further away from the working-class outer suburbs of Paris where the school protests first took root in mid-September.
Like many of the students barricading their schools across the capital, Bachir said he wanted to help draw attention to the widening socio-economic gulf between Paris and its sprawling banlieues.
“Conditions are terrible in the suburbs,” he said. “There aren’t enough resources, there aren’t enough teachers, and the class sizes are too large. Most high school buildings date back to the 1970s, but only 14 percent have been renovated or rebuilt” in the past 10 years, he highlighted.
“We’re talking about young people’s education, about the future – we just can’t leave education in this state,” he added.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Léa, a student from Lycée Lamartine in Paris’s 9th arrondissement (district), said she was hoping that the growing movement would put pressure on the government to rethink its funding priorities.
“That they put more money into education rather than funding military operations or Bastille Day parades that no one gives a stuff about,” she said. “It would be a lot more beneficial for the students, and also for the teachers. There’s one teacher for 40 students in some classes, and it’s not okay – especially when it’s 40 degrees (104°F).”
Watch moreFrench unrest: Are we witnessing a new 'Yellow Vests' movement?
Like many of the high schoolers and their supporters who poured into the streets of Paris on Tuesday, she was incensed by the severity with which the police had responded to the protests.
“I find it completely unacceptable. One guy lost his hand, another lost an eye, another his teeth – and no one has been [held accountable] for any of it,” she said. “Even if it was the students who insulted them or threw a couple of punches first, they’re still 14, 15, 16-years-old up against trained police officers in their 40s armed with batons. It’s not OK.”
But Bachir said he had not been surprised by the heavy-handedness of the police response.
“The police, they’re happy – they’re just there to have a bit of a scrap,” he said. “I know the police very well – they lose their tempers quickly. My old high school was in the suburbs, and the police – they were really just looking for a fight.”
A long march
At the Lycée Hélène Boucher, the human chain has been broken. Police have cleared the barricade from the school doors, and a line of armed and armoured riot police have herded the die-hard remnants into the middle of the avenue between lines of rusting chestnut trees.
They advance in stages, driving the stragglers back into the city. When they’ve pushed them back to Place de la Nation, they pile into their vans and pull away.
So begins the long march to Place de la République. A few dozen demonstrators take to the middle of the street, making their slow way along to Père Lachaise cemetery and curving around towards the city centre.
As they go, they are joined by students who have drifted away from other barricades across the city. They raise their hands, and chant, and clap, and the passing drivers sound their horns to the beat of their hands.
Towards the back, a few marchers stop from time to time to drag a bin into the street and upend it. Passersby step in, and the bins are back on the pavement before the march has moved ten metres.
A young teenager stops to set the corner of a discarded board of plywood on fire, to general derision. It smoulders, catches, and is doused by a man who hurries up with half a bottle of water.
The pace quickens as they draw closer to Place de la République – someone has spotted the lines of riot police forming behind them, cutting off their retreat with a wall of reinforced plastic shields. In the street ahead, a line of police officers are searching people's bags before they let them pass.
Probably not by coincidence, the march takes a sharp left turn down a side street. A police squad takes off after them, pushing an unlucky few up against the wall to go through their backpacks.
They confiscate a few plastic vials of saline solution – used by demonstrators to flush tear gas from their eyes – and the mood turns ugly.
A heavily armoured officer snaps at one of the demonstrators: "Go on, get lost, gauchiasse," – a pejorative word for people with left-wing views.
'Taking up the cause'
At Place de la République, the mood could not be more different. Avenue Voltaire is heaving with high schoolers, university students, teachers, parents, trade unionists. The march had started half an hour earlier, and more students are still pouring into the square.
Gilles, a secondary school teacher in the suburb of Saint-Denis, said that France's high schools were not the only part of the education system to suffer from a lack of funding.
"There's an overall lack of staff, of education assistants, of medical and social services staff in secondary schools," he said. "Some of the buildings are run-down – and it's the same across all levels, from primary school onward."
He said he was delighted to see so many young people speaking out about school conditions.
"It's great. We went on a lot of demonstrations in 2023, 2024, for the 93 Emergency Plan, which highlighted the staff shortage," he said. "And it’s great that the demands of teachers and educational staff are now being echoed by high school students. It’s fantastic that they’re taking up the cause."
Thibault, a secondary teacher working in Versailles west of Paris, said he had gone on strike to support the student movement.
"We're fed up, everyone is tired, the students can't take it anymore," he said. "High schoolers are at school from eight in the morning to six o'clock at night with just half an hour for a break – you can't even do that under French labour law."
But while he was proud to see so many students taking to the streets, he didn't think it had much chance of bringing about the changes he thought were needed.
"To be honest? I don't expect anything anymore, because the government will never listen to us," he said. "Instead, they take advantage of the fact that there are two or three people breaking things to say, 'See? This movement isn't legitimate.'"

Google was ordered to halt the construction of data centers in Finland over environmental concerns

Google was ordered to halt the construction of data centers in Finland over environmental concerns
Kyiv • UNN
Google was ordered to suspend work in Muhos and Kajaani due to the absence of an environmental impact assessment. In Muhos, 330 hectares of forest were cleared.
Google was ordered to temporarily suspend work at two sites for the construction of data centers in Finland because the company had not conducted the required environmental impact assessment, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
The planned data centers in the municipalities of Muhos and Kajaani are part of a €13 billion large-scale project by the technology company, covering several locations in northern Finland and being implemented against the backdrop of huge demand for capacity to host online infrastructure.
The decision was made after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, which represents Google’s interests, had cleared 330 hectares of forest in Muhos without conducting an environmental impact assessment (EIA).
Google Fined €403 Million in Ireland for Tracking Users’ Geolocation21.09.26, 13:52 • 6104 views
It is reported that in Kajaani, the company also cleared an area of just under 200 hectares of forest.
The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been turned into "sand" and explained the violations by the situation in the "overheated" market for new data centers.
Additionally
On Tuesday, the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) announced that it had ordered the company to "immediately suspend" — no later than October 23 — "preparatory measures that significantly alter the environment" at both sites until the environmental impact assessment is completed. Google has until next Wednesday to provide a written explanation.
The EIA process is ongoing and is expected to be completed later this year. However, according to the LVV, Google has already begun "extensive preparatory measures," including felling trees, removing topsoil, and building access roads.
Tommy Muilu, head of environmental protection at the LVV, said: "In our view, the measures in question will alter the environment and cause impacts whose identification and assessment are among the key tasks of the EIA procedure."
The LVV said that if the requirements are not met, it will consider applying enforcement measures and imposing a fine.
In response, Google issued a statement saying that it "understands the concerns" and acknowledges that it "did not meet its own high standards." The company added: "We will review the LVV’s findings and follow its recommendations. We acted in good faith in accordance with the Forestry Act: we conducted environmental studies and took measures to protect areas of high value. As we continue our long-term operations in the region, we are implementing plans to restore the sites and preserve biodiversity, including planting trees across 130 hectares (321 acres) in Muhos."
Tapani Väistölä, chief operating officer of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said that the violations identified at the two sites indicated a "systemic problem." According to him, the site in Muhos "is no longer a forest — it is a sandy area."
He cited the huge demand for data center construction in Finland as one of the reasons, forcing companies to work as quickly as possible and placing excessive pressure on small municipalities.
"The main reason is an overheated market that is forcing companies to accelerate processes considerably. The lack of relevant experience in municipalities is also a factor."

Facing mounting pressure to get the protests under control, the French Education Ministry launched a national consultation for students on Monday. Open until Oct. 23, the portal is intended to provide a safe space for young people to express their concerns regarding France’s lycée system, the final three years of high school education.
“It is essential for us to hear from all high school students and to take into account the diversity of their educational experiences,” said Education Minister Édouard Geffray.

Yemen forces run armored vehicles over Houthi soldiers as fighting escalates

Video posted by government forces in Yemen showed them driving armored cars over opposing fighters as they recaptured areas around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Iran-backed Houthis on Monday in a deadly new phase of the fragmented country's war.
The videos give a glimpse into the brutal closing stages of a pitched battle for control of territory near the strait that the Houthis had captured last month. The Houthi advance sent shockwaves through the oil market and pushed up petrol and diesel prices worldwide.
Fighting continued near Bab el-Mandeb on Tuesday as Saudi-backed government forces battled to consolidate Monday's counter-attack, besieging Houthi fighters at a military camp near the strait and pushing into hills to the east, Yemeni military sources said.
The videos, verified by Reuters and filmed from inside the armored vehicles, showed them striking fighters with their vehicle. Some were armed and some were walking or running. However, others were unarmed and some were sitting, lying or crouching on the sandy shore and made no move to evade the oncoming vehicle as they were run over.
At one point, a vehicle hits a man, running and unarmed, and another crouching on the ground. It then loops back to drive over two men, both with their hands up and unarmed. Shooting can be heard during the video and at one point the vehicle's windscreen is cracked by a gunshot.
A Houthi statement decried the videos as proof of war crimes, saying they showed "the true nature of the Saudi regime and the forces it has mobilized from extremist factions."
The Saudi-led coalition backing the government forces in Yemen did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the videos or the Houthi accusations of war crimes.
A spokesperson for the Giants Brigade — the main Yemeni government force involved in the fighting at Bab el-Mandeb this week — did not immediately comment in response to a Reuters request.
The Homeland Shield Forces, a significant formation in the Yemeni government's military coalition, did not comment directly on the videos but issued a directive on Tuesday urging troops to treat prisoners well and adhere to religious, ethical and legal standards.
Rights groups have previously accused the Houthis of war crimes, including sniper and shelling attacks on civilian targets, seizures of aid, abuse of prisoners and use of child soldiers. The group has denied war crimes.
'Turning point'
Reuters has not been able to independently verify the extent of government gains and the Houthis denied they had lost ground, saying the government claims of advances were baseless.
Intense fighting meanwhile continued around Yemen's third-largest city of Taiz, where Houthi gains in a mountain district have in recent days cut off a main road to Aden, leaving government forces encircled.
Yemen's civil war pits the Houthis against an uneasy coalition of sometimes rival military forces under the internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies.
The renewed clashes have added a new front to the Iran-US conflict, with the US rebuffing Saudi requests for military help to reverse Houthi gains on the Red Sea coast near Bab el-Mandeb last month and end the group's missile and drone attacks on their territory.
"The operation itself is significant because it's a turning point in the trajectory of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group.
"The biggest test will be when they move towards the mountains," he added.
Religious and regional faultlines
The Giants Brigade is a southern military formation originally formed by students at ultra-conservative Sunni Muslim religious colleges. That background gives both a religious and regional edge to their enmity with the Houthis, who originate in north Yemen and belong to the Zaydi school of Shi'ite Islam.
The Giants have themselves fractured this year, splitting between factions backed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, illustrating the internal divisions that have long beset the Yemeni government's efforts to fight the Houthis.
As well as further squeezing global trade routes after Iran's disruption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the conflagration in Yemen has poured new fire onto Saudi Arabia, a US ally.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports, oil refineries and pipelines. Residents of the Saudi capital Riyadh reported hearing booms overnight and two of the kingdom's southern airports were targeted.
Saudi Arabia's intervention in the latest wave of fighting included intense air strikes on Houthi forces on Monday as the Giants Brigade advanced along the flat coastal strip towards Bab el-Mandeb.

AI generated
PARIS - Mass protests over decrepit conditions at France’s high schools descended into sporadic violence on Oct 6, leading to nearly 500 arrests and prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call an emergency meeting.
The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.
US President Donald Trump weighed in on Oct 6 to blame the unrest in France on “mass migration” and Islam, as he pushed his global right-wing narrative ahead of tough midterm elections at home.
In France, parents, teachers and union workers joined the high school students’ movement in the capital Paris and other cities.
The interior ministry said 256,000 people protested nationwide, while union organisers put the figure at 450,000.
Macron was expected to meet top officials late on Oct 6, including Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, in response to the unrest, a government source said.
At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were wounded on Oct 6, the interior ministry announced.
‘Wants to be heard’
Rights groups, unions and the students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force.
A teenager lost a hand on Oct 5 after police fired a stun grenade.
A 14-year-old student in north-west Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged on Oct 6 over that incident.
“Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard,” 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped Macron would listen.
At Paris’ Place de la Republique, protesters gathered beneath banners demanding better-funded schools, including one reading “Neglected schools, sacrificed youth”.
An AFP reporter described the Paris march as largely peaceful, but tensions flared near its endpoint in the east of the capital as police fired tear gas and some demonstrators threw rocks at a line of officers carrying riot shields.
Police officials said that “300 hostile individuals” attempted to confront officers.
Yanis, 16, said students felt ignored until the demonstrations turned violent. “It makes us feel like everything gets solved through violence,” he said.
The unrest comes ahead of a 2027 election to choose Macron’s successor, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters, or clashed with riot police.
Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned violence linked to the protests, telling lawmakers the violence would not be tolerated.
“Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings,” he told Parliament, rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.
He also said that high schools across the country would be closed for a half-day between Oct 7 and 9, to permit “internal democracy” in the establishments.
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
The government has sought to address the students’ grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Thousands of arrests
Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.
“We just want better conditions for studying,” he told AFP.
Teachers and parents joined demonstrations across France.
In Lyon, parents organised to support the youngsters, while teacher Rindala Younes said she wanted to help students “convey their message peacefully”.
“The high school students’ demands are legitimate,” she said.
In neighbouring Belgium, students have started a similar protest movement in the city of Liege. On Oct 6, several of them were arrested after what police said were clashes and vandalism on the sidelines of a demonstration.
Amnesty International on Oct 5 said the French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests”.
Nunez said police had opened 10 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.
More than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested. The prime minister’s office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured. AFP

Cornell hires ex-Justice Dept official Yates to review rape claims response
Oct 6 - Cornell University has hired a top former US Justice Department lawyer for an internal investigation of how it handled a student's allegations that she was gang-raped, a case that has brought mounting scrutiny and triggered student protests at the Ivy League school.
Sally Yates, who served as deputy US attorney general from 2015 to 2017, will conduct an independent review of how Cornell prevents and responds to sexual assault claims, university officials said on Tuesday.
The investigation by Yates, now a partner at law firm King & Spalding, will include a “detailed review” of Cornell’s response to the student's claims that she was sexually assaulted by multiple men during a fraternity party in October 2024.
The student, referred to as Jane Doe in a lawsuit she filed against Cornell and seven fraternity members, has said the Ithaca, New York university failed to adequately investigate and punish the fraternity members involved.
Other Cornell students staged a mass rally on Monday voicing solidarity with Jane Doe and demanding that the school take firmer action against sexual violence on campus.
A newly formed Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees said Yates will have “full independence” to conduct her review.
A lawyer for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about the investigation.
Yates was previously hired by the US Soccer Federation to investigate allegations of sexual abuse and misconduct within the National Women's Soccer League.
'DEFINING MOMENT'
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff on October 3 called the alleged sexual assault case a “defining moment” and said the university "must do better."
In her lawsuit, filed last month, Jane Doe said she was plied with drugs and alcohol and then sexually assaulted by several members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after she had become incapacitated.
She had reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges.
Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members involved, including expulsions and other sanctions. REUTERS

President Volodymyr Zelensky denied Ukraine’s responsibility for the strikes on two Bulgarian civilian vessels in the Black Sea, instead pinning the blame on Russia.
In his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, Zelensky said that the Ukrainian Navy had been in contact with its Bulgarian counterparts. According to him, they established that the ships were hit in a combined Russian strike using maritime and aerial drones. However, Ukrainian intelligence and special services were still gathering additional details.

“The Ukrainian Defense Forces conducted no operations in this part of the sea,” Zelensky said. “This latest tragedy involving civilian vessels is part of Russia’s ongoing attempt to make the western Black Sea completely unsuitable for navigation.”
The President has ordered the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), the Defense Ministry, intelligence services and other relevant agencies to cooperate as closely as possible with partners, so that both Ukraine and its allies are better able to defend themselves against such attacks.
Radev: Drones ‘either Russian or Ukrainian’
Zelensky’s statement came hours after Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Sofia had not yet determined who launched the drones.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday afternoon, Radev said the vessels were struck by both a maritime and an aerial drone, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) reported.
“We have yet to try to establish where the attack came from, but it is clear: they are either Russian or Ukrainian,” he said, adding that the situation is “extremely worrying.”
Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
According to him, the ship that was moving north was the one that sank, and for which Bulgarian authorities did not have further information on what it had onboard at the time of the report.
The other ship that was damaged was traveling south, carrying wheat, he said.
Although it struck Bulgarian vessels, the attack could not be grounds for triggering NATO’s Article 4, which allows allies to request consultations; or 5, which invokes the alliance’s collective defense.
“We have much more serious attacks inside territorial waters. Keep in mind that this is 130 km [roughly 81 miles] from our coast; it falls within our exclusive economic zone, but these are considered neutral waters,” Radev said.
Still, the prime minister warned of a broader pattern, noting that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea. “This is hardly the most serious incident,” he said. “But it is serious as a trend because, as I said, when a war is not stopped in time, it expands its geographic reach.”
Crew still missing
Earlier on Tuesday, the vessels were identified as the Able and the Alfa Watan.
Vessel-tracking data from VesselFinder showed the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan heading toward Romania’s port of Sulina. Its last known position was about 70 nautical miles off the Bulgarian coast, shortly after 2 a.m. local time.
The Able caught fire, and all 18 people aboard abandoned it, according to Rumen Nikolov, who leads rescue operations in Varna, as cited by Bulgarian public radio BNR.
The Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria picked up the crew, some of whom were reportedly hurt.
Euronews described the strike as the first such attack inside the economic zone of a NATO member state.
The incident is the latest in a widening campaign against commercial shipping. Moscow has increasingly targeted merchant vessels in retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities and tankers.
On Monday, Oct. 5, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying grain caught fire and sank after a drone struck it in the Black Sea.
On Tuesday, Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper said a Russian drone hit a Marshall Islands-flagged ship loaded with rapeseed oil. One person was killed and seven were injured.
Radev, a former president seen as pro-Russian, won in the April 2026 parliamentary election, which ended a stretch of seven national votes in four years.
His government has since said it would halt all weapons deliveries to Ukraine, after Bulgaria had been a key supplier of Soviet-standard artillery shells to the country.
The strikes follow increasing drone incursions, sabotage campaigns and cyberattacks conducted by Russia, which Ukraine’s Western allies say may be intended to test NATO’s collective resolve.

Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:27:59 UTC
04:27:59 KST

John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.
The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.
Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.
Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.
If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.
The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.
He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.
Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.
But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.
As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.
The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.
Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.
Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.
Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.
She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?
“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”
Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.
Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.
Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.
“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”
A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.
Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.
An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.
The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.
Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”
He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”
Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.
“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

Italy deported two foreign nationals suspected of attacking Milan Chabad emissary Rabbi Tzemach Mizrahi, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi announced on Monday.
Piantedosi said the two men had been returned to their countries of origin. The minister said, "There is no place in our country for hatred and violence, and no antisemitic act will be tolerated."
The attack took place on September 16 at a bus stop in Piazzale Bande Nere in western Milan, near an area with a large Jewish population.
The three men surrounded 51-year-old Mizrahi, rabbi of the city's central Chabad synagogue on Via Soderini, as he waited for a bus. They shouted at him in Arabic, grabbed his hat, put it on, and mocked him.
When Mizrahi began filming them on his phone, one of the men kicked him from behind and pushed him off the sidewalk into the road. The three then left the scene.
Mizrahi: Nobody at bus stop intervened in antisemitic attack
Mizrahi said about 20 people were waiting at the bus stop at the time, but none intervened.
According to Milan's Jewish community, footage recorded by Mizrahi helped authorities locate the three suspects shortly afterward.
One of those deported was a Moroccan national whose name was not released. The other was 21-year-old Tunisian national Battar Zahani, who was deported to Tunisia.
The third suspect, Zahani's 20-year-old brother, Ilyes Zahani, remains in Italy under restrictive conditions while awaiting trial.
Walker Meghnagi, head of Milan's Jewish community, welcomed the deportations, calling the move "wonderful news."
In an interview after the attack, Mizrahi said he would not stop wearing his rabbinic clothing or conceal his Jewish identity, but added that he would not allow his children to walk the streets alone.

Progressive Jews embracing ‘craziest’ ideologies are ‘no longer our friends,’ Israeli scholar says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:59 UTC
04:26:59 KST

Israeli historian and political commentator Gadi Taub sharply criticized progressive Jews abroad on Tuesday, saying those who embrace what he called the “craziest progressive ideologies” are “no longer our friends” and warning that Israel was losing political support on both the Western Left and Right.
Taub made the comments at NatCon Jerusalem, a three-day gathering of conservative politicians, intellectuals, journalists and activists from Israel, the United States and Europe. The National Conservatism movement emphasizes national sovereignty, traditional institutions and the nation-state, and has become increasingly influential within parts of the American and European Right.
Taub, who holds a doctorate in American history from Rutgers University and has written extensively about Zionism, nationalism and liberalism, was speaking during a panel titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement.” His address was titled “Immigration and the Undermining of Democracy.”
During the discussion, Taub departed briefly from the central subject of his remarks to address the role of progressive Jews outside Israel.
“We, the Jews of Israel, have a great problem with progressive Jews abroad promoting immigration,” he said. “And we should start calling them out before the antisemites do.”
Taub did not identify specific Jewish organizations or individuals, nor did he limit his criticism to a particular Diaspora community.
Taub: Issue connected to Israel's loss of support amongst political Left, Right
He then connected the issue to what he described as Israel’s increasingly difficult political position in the West.
“We have lost the left, not due to Netanyahu or any fault of our own, because the Left has been indoctrinated by Edward Said for 40 years now,” Taub said. “It’s not something new. But we are also losing the Right.”
Edward Said, the Palestinian-American academic and literary theorist who died in 2003, was one of the most influential figures in the development of postcolonial studies. His work, particularly his critique of Western representations of the Middle East, shaped generations of academics and political activists.
Taub argued that parts of the Western Left had adopted an intellectual framework increasingly hostile to Zionism, while warning that Israel and Jews were now facing a separate challenge from elements of the political Right.
His strongest criticism was directed at progressive Jews themselves.
“Progressive Jews who think they will grovel at the feet of anti-Semites by agreeing to the craziest progressive ideologies are no longer our friends,” Taub said. “And we should be clear about it.”
Earlier in the discussion, Taub argued that Western societies had become vulnerable to Islamist movements because of what he described as a loss of confidence in their own civilization.
“There’s a perfect balance between imperialistic Islamic philosophies like the Muslim Brotherhood and the West’s loss of confidence in itself, or I would call it its autoimmune disease,” he said.
He argued that Islamist movements had learned to use Western debates over multiculturalism, racism and minority rights to shield themselves from criticism, saying forces that presented themselves as opposing racism could end up “cooperating in promoting a new form of racism.”
Antisemitism and the American Right
Taub’s warning that Israel was “also losing the Right” comes amid a growing debate within the conservative movement itself over antisemitism, Israel and the direction of the younger American Right.
Yoram Hazony, the Israeli political theorist who founded the National Conservatism movement and chairs the Edmund Burke Foundation, has repeatedly raised concerns about antisemitism gaining influence in parts of the American conservative movement.
Hazony to 'Post': Carlson significantly influenced young conservative political conversation
In a recent interview with The Jerusalem Post ahead of the Jerusalem conference, Hazony singled out Tucker Carlson, arguing that the former Fox News host had significantly influenced the political conversation among younger conservatives.
“In the last two years, his show is the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America,” Hazony said.
Hazony said polling he had seen suggested Carlson enjoyed a positive image among a large majority of young Republican men, although he did not identify the poll. He stressed that support for Carlson should not itself be taken as evidence that those voters shared antisemitic views.
Earlier this year, Hazony warned more broadly about what could happen to American Jewish life if antisemitic ideas became entrenched across both major political camps. After arguing that antisemitism had become increasingly tolerated in parts of the political Left, he said that if Republicans followed the same course, “it’s not clear what would be left of Jewish life in America.”

'Three years without my Asaf': Mother of soldier killed on Oct. 7 pleads for truth - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:41 UTC
04:26:41 KST

Three years, my Asaf.
My beloved son.
Three years have passed – yet I wake up this morning as if time had stood still.
I return to that terrible morning, minute by minute.
To the rockets piercing the sky, to the sirens shattering the silence, and to your calming voice – a voice that was also that of a leader, a steady, clear commander’s voice – leading even in moments of truth and in the direst times, taking responsibility, and showing the way.
And above all, to your voice, my beloved son, Col. Asaf Hamami, commander of the Southern Brigade.
I hear you again over the radio: “Scramble the emergency standby squads, tanks, and vehicles. Shift to full combat footing. We are at war.” That was the moment you realized the country was at war. And I am going through it all with you, with Tomer and Kiril, your command team, minute by minute. Hearing your orders.
The attempt to mobilize forces, the speed with which you grasped that this event was far greater than anything we had ever known.
You leave the base with your team, heading into battle. A few against many. A commander and heroic fighters facing down dozens of terrorists.
Right up to the moment you were critically wounded. Up to the moment you fell – alongside Tomer and Kiril – and were abducted to Gaza.
You “returned” home wrapped in the Israeli flag, after 758 days, back to the homeland you loved so dearly.
My beloved, beautiful son, Assaf. In your final moments... I was not there.
I was not by your side like a mother lioness.
I could not cradle you in my arms, hold you tight, rest your head against my heart, and whisper with a mother’s warmth: “Mommy is here, my Asaf. Everything is fine; I’m with you.”
And I cannot stop asking myself: What did you feel in those moments? What were you thinking about?
Who were you thinking of?
Did you see me and Dad? Did you see your younger brother, Eitan, whom you loved so dearly and always worried about?
Did you think of the warm home you built, the woman you loved, and your children, beloved Ella, Alon, and Arbel, of whom you spoke with a face lit up by a wide, happy smile? Alon – who was with you just hours earlier on the holiday eve, and who stayed behind in the room at the base when you went off to fight – did you think of him in those moments?
What images flashed through your mind in those final moments?
And what passed through your heart the moment your beautiful eyes closed forever?
No one can give me the answers to these questions anymore.
But one thing I know: Your smile didn’t stop at that moment. The smile that always lit up your beautiful face lives on within us.
It continues to be with me, with Dad, with your children, with the family, with your friends, and with everyone who had the privilege of knowing you.
I can no longer meet your beautiful, radiant eyes, but the light within them can never be extinguished.
SINCE LAST week, I have been wandering aimlessly.
My stomach churns. My heart knows this day is coming.
Dad and I needed to be close to you. We drove to visit you at your new home, your permanent home at Kiryat Shaul. We bought flowers, washed and cleaned the site, and lit a candle.
A new home, one I never imagined would be the place where we’d be with you. The longing tears at my heart all over again.
I open your WhatsApp messages and read them once more:
“Come visit us at home.”
“Come over for dinner.”
“Love you.”
My heart and mind still refuse to accept this new reality.
How is it possible that your last messages spoke of home, of a visit, of dinner, yet the only visits left for us with you are at Kiryat Shaul?
I stand before you, cradling your beautiful head against the headstone, imagining the tight hugs I used to shower you with whenever we met. For a mother keeps hugging her son even when her hands can no longer touch him.
On Simchat Torah, Ella, Alon, and Arbel, your children and our beloved grandchildren, joined us for dinner, and my heart couldn’t help drifting back exactly three years.
On October 6, 2023, the eve of Simchat Torah, Alon was with you at the base.
I can picture it in my mind.
You, a father overjoyed, and Alon, your son, who so wanted to spend time with you at the base, playing soccer.
Alon is wearing you out, and you are absolutely delighted. Smiling. Beaming with happiness.
The simple happiness of father and son, just the two of you, moments you shared before the rest of the family was set to join you the next day.
And today, I look at your three children and think of how proud you would have been of them.
How much more you would have wanted to see. How many more moments you were meant to share. How much life still lay ahead of you.
There is something unfathomable about this intersection of holidays and joy with pain and bereavement.
How does Simchat Torah, a festival of joy, of Torah, of home, of family, become mingled with the memory of the day that terrible disaster befell us?
How can one process the magnitude of this tragedy, day after day, year after year, without pausing for a moment to ask: What happened to us?
And not just: What happened at the border fence?
Not just: What happened that morning?
What happened to us as a society? What happened to us as a people?
How did we reach a point where the hatred among us became so deep? In the months leading up to October 7, we witnessed a fractured society – arguments turning into battles, words into vitriol, and disagreements into hatred.
And then came that morning.
In an instant, our disputes paled in comparison to an enemy intent on killing, abducting, and destroying.
Thousands of bloodthirsty terrorists breached the border.
Communities were attacked. Civilians were massacred. Soldiers fell.
And you, my Asaf, went out to defend.
You didn’t ask who was Right or Left. You didn’t ask who was for or against. You went out to defend human beings. To defend the residents of the Gaza border area. To defend the country.
Three years later, I believe we owe ourselves one thing above all else: The truth.
Not the truth of the coalition.
Not the truth of the opposition.
The truth of a people.
I hear the debate over which committee will conduct the inquiry, who will appoint it, who will head it, and who its members will be.
AND I SAY: Enough arguing. Just start the investigation.
A state commission of inquiry, a national commission, or any other mechanism – the main thing is that it be established and be independent, professional, and, above all, accepted by everyone – or at least by the broadest possible segments of the public.
It is important to me that there be a commission in which this wounded nation can place its trust. One that bereaved families can trust, knowing it was not set up to shield any particular side. One that investigates everyone; that asks all the questions; that reaches every corner, even those places no one wants to go.
Who knew? Who didn’t know? Who raised the alarm? Who didn’t listen? What failed? Who bore the responsibility?
And above all, what must we, as a society, change so that such a disaster can never happen again?
We do not seek revenge. We seek the truth.
We do not ask for a committee that serves a faction. We ask for one that serves the state.
Because we deserve answers; not for the sake of revenge; not to single out culprits in advance, simply to understand.
And when someone is found responsible, let that responsibility be examined through the proper mechanisms of a well-functioning state, in accordance with the law.
Because without truth, there is no healing.
And without healing, the wound remains open.
I do not want us to remain a country where every disaster immediately turns into yet another war among ourselves.
I want us to finally learn to listen to one another. To argue without hating. To criticize without humiliating. To disagree without tearing each other apart.
To be strong without losing our humanity.
Perhaps this is one of the things you, my Asaf, would have asked of us.
Because you believed in people.
You saw what others did not see.
You listened.
You gave.
You took action.
Throughout your life, you taught – even without grand speeches – that one can be a great person without needing to be greater than others. And today, three years later, perhaps this is our greatest test:
Not only to defeat the enemy from without but to succeed in remaining one people from within.
For in the end – after all the arguments, all the factions, and all the headlines – we are left with one another. And if, after the heavy and terrible price we have paid, we do not understand this: When will we?
MY DEAR Asaf,
Three years.
Three years that you have been so deeply missed, yet so present in our lives.
Today, I no longer ask how one goes on living without you. I know.
We go on with you.
In every child who knows your story. In every value we pass on. In every person we truly see. In every act of giving.
Every time we choose unity over hatred. Every time we take action instead of just talking.
Your path was cut short in battle on that cursed day, but your path did not end.
We will carry it forward.
And I promise you, my beloved son: We will do everything to ensure that life in this country is worthy of the price you – and so many of our sons and daughters – paid for it.
YOU ARE NOT merely a story of October 7.
You are a person. You are a son. You are a father. You are a commander. You are a brother. You are a friend. You are loved.
And above all, you are my Asaf.
Three years. I miss you with every breath. And yet, amid all the pain, I see your smile. That same beautiful, warm, mischievous, radiant smile.
And today, your handsome face and the name Asaf Hamami are with us all across the country – on stickers, flags, walls, signs, classrooms, and in so many places where people have chosen to keep your presence and your path alive.
Your smile continues to be with me, and it is no longer just mine.
It is everywhere in the country.
It accompanies people who never had the chance to know you.
There is something captivating about it, just like your quiet leadership:
Less talking, more action. At eye level.
With a hug full of meaning, and with a goodness that was always directed toward others.
So simple. So genuine. So you.
But home is where we still meet. Your photo is on the fridge; you are waiting for me every morning. We “meet” in the kitchen over the morning coffee you loved so much.
And at the front door, as we leave, we are met by your smiling face and your blessing for the journey ahead.
And when we return, I say – as if you were here: “Asaf, we’re home.”
For even within our home, you are still a part of our lives.
Your eyes have closed forever, but your smile stays with us, and your presence walks beside us.
And I promise you, my beautiful, beloved boy, Mom is here. Just as I always was. And you will always be here with us because there is no love in the world like a mother’s love.
The writer is the mother of Col. Asaf Hamami, the highest-ranked IDF soldier killed on October 7, 2023.

Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:27 UTC
04:26:27 KST

Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
Russia denies plague cases after laboratory technician’s death; US demands ‘transparency’ as WHO monitors situation.
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case which has drawn international scrutiny.
Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague on Friday.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among staff who had come into contact with the laboratory worker for the past 10 days.
“This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests,” the watchdog said.
The institute said in a statement that extensive testing during an autopsy on the woman’s body found no microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute.
It said results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.
Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said no “dangerous diagnosis” had been confirmed.
She added that 60 percent of those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released.
Local media said about 200 people had previously been quarantined.
‘Transparency’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information on Friday.
“Anytime you hear there is a disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago in 2020 and 2021 when we saw that happen. That said, it would be irresponsible for me to sit here and speculate,” Rubio said.
The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk.
It was unclear if this meant that the laboratory technician’s death was unrelated to plague infection.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO.

Israel blocks Palestinian election officials as vote faces fresh delay

19:18:09 UTC
04:18:09 KST

Israel has refused to allow Palestinian election officials to enter Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem to prepare for upcoming legislative elections, raising fresh fears that the long-delayed vote could once again be postponed, Palestinian officials said on Tuesday.
The Palestinian Central Elections Commission is due to oversee preparations for legislative polls scheduled for November 28. But the reported restrictions threaten to complicate efforts to hold a vote across all Palestinian territories and revive concerns over Israel’s role in obstructing Palestinian political participation.
Wafa, the official Palestinian news agency, reported that Israel had denied the commission access to Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem, citing a Palestinian official.
Israel’s defence ministry and COGAT, the Israeli body responsible for civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territories, did not respond to AFP requests for comment.
Palestinian election commission vows to continue
Despite the restrictions, Palestinian election officials say preparations will continue.
Farid Taamallah, spokesperson for the Central Elections Commission, said that the body could still hold the elections, saying its employees in Gaza had already been trained and were present on the ground.
“The Commission is continuing to organise the electoral process despite the Israeli decision,” Taamallah said.
The European Union has also stepped up its support for the vote.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was “ready to deploy” election observers, stressing that Palestinians have the right to choose their representatives through elections that are “credible, inclusive and transparent.”
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh called for European backing to overcome obstacles to elections and ensure participation by Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, occupied East Jerusalem and Gaza.
A vote two decades overdue
The November election would be the first Palestinian legislative vote since 2006, when Hamas secured victory over Fatah. 
The Palestinian Legislative Council has not met since 2007, when political divisions between the rival factions deepened.
The election was previously scheduled for 2021 but was postponed indefinitely, with President Mahmoud Abbas citing Israel’s refusal to allow voting in occupied East Jerusalem.
Abbas, whose presidential term expired in 2009, won the last Palestinian presidential election in 2005 and has governed largely by decree since then.
Fears of another delay
The prospect of another postponement has already grown.
In September, senior Palestinian official Jibril Rajoub said the legislative election would not take place on schedule and suggested holding presidential elections first.
An August poll by the Jerusalem Media and Communication Center found that only 29 percent of Palestinians expected the November vote to proceed as planned.
With Palestinians having gone nearly two decades without legislative elections, the reported Israeli restrictions add another major obstacle to a process already burdened by occupation and repeated delays.

In September 2026, the Ukrainian Defense Forces intensified their strikes on targets deep within Russian rear areas and set a record for the number of air defense systems and radar stations destroyed since the inception of the e-Points (e-Baly) program.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
By the end of September, 33,087 invaders had been confirmed killed — a figure surpassed only in March and April 2026.
A notable achievement in September was the highest number of Russian air defense systems, particularly radar stations, destroyed since the program’s inception. The destruction of one Russian air defense system at a distance of 552 km was also recorded.
In September, the number of confirmed target strikes at distances exceeding 20 km from the front line exceeded 11,000 for the first time.
The number of strikes at a depth of over 50 km also set a record. A significant portion of these attacks targeted the Mariupol-Crimea logistics route, which Russian troops use to supply their forces in southern Ukraine.
The program’s results indicate a gradual shift in combat operations from the immediate front lines to the enemy’s rear areas.
Every result within the program is recorded on video in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
The e-Points system works as follows: confirmed strikes are uploaded to DELTA, after that units receive points that they can spend on equipment on the Brave1 Market. Since March, military personnel have also been allowed to exchange e-Points for equipment components.
The overall trend toward an increase in Ukrainian strikes behind enemy lines is clearly evident in individual operations as well. In September, the Unmanned Systems Forces, in particular, struck dozens of energy facilities in the occupied territories.
To systematize such operations, Militarnyi launched the Deep Strike map in September, which tracks strikes on military, industrial, energy, and other targets in Russia and the occupied territories.
Another notable development in September was the increased effectiveness of Ukrainian air defense against attack drones.
Despite Russia’s increased use of jet-powered UAVs, Ukrainian units shot down 28% more Shahed-type drones in September than in the previous month.
At the same time, specialized interceptor drones are playing an increasingly important role in combating such targets. In May, the share of Shaheds shot down by these drones reached 40%. Since the beginning of September, the Defense Forces have neutralized about 55% of Russian Geran jet-powered drones.
