TIMELINE – Messi’s 21-year Argentina journey from difficult debut to final farewell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:15:14 UTC
04:15:14 KST

Lionel Messi will face Benin on Oct. 6 in Buenos Aires in a farewell match arranged after he announced his international retirement following Argentina's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
The 39-year-old will walk onto the Monumental Stadium pitch for the final time in the sky-blue and white jersey, entering his farewell as Argentina's record appearance-maker and leading scorer with 207 caps and 125 goals.
His Argentina career began more than two decades ago with uncertainty and relative anonymity. Before the country embraced him as its captain and World Cup-winning No. 10, Argentina first had to find him.
Messi grew up in Rosario, where he began playing football before joining Newell's Old Boys. At 13, he moved with his family to Spain and entered Barcelona's famed youth system.
In Barcelona, Messi was seen as an extraordinary teenage talent. In Argentina, however, his name was still largely unfamiliar outside Rosario and a relatively small circle of football officials and scouts.
That distance would become one of the defining features of his international career. Messi was developing in Spain while Argentina was only beginning to understand what it had produced.
At the 2003 Under-17 World Cup in Finland, Argentina lost 3-2 to Spain in the semifinals. Messi was not part of the squad, but by then his performances at Barcelona had begun attracting attention from Argentinian football officials.
When Claudio Vivas, assistant to then-Argentina coach Marcelo Bielsa, showed Bielsa footage of Messi, the coach was so impressed by the teenager's speed that he initially thought the video had been accelerated.
The Argentine Football Association began looking for the teenager and his family in Spain, with the Spanish federation also interested in persuading Messi to represent the country where he had developed.
The teenager had spent much of his formative football years in Spain, but when the choice came, he selected Argentina.
Argentina arranged an Under-20 friendly against Paraguay in Buenos Aires that gave Messi his first opportunity to represent his country.
Messi came off the bench and scored twice on his debut for Argentina's Under-20 team.
It was the beginning of a relationship that would eventually make him the country's most-capped player.
Messi's reputation in Argentina exploded at the 2005 Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands.
He scored six goals, won the Golden Boot, and was named the tournament's best player as Argentina won the title.
The teenager who had been relatively unknown in his homeland was suddenly impossible to ignore.
Messi made his senior Argentina debut against Hungary in Budapest.
The appearance lasted less than a minute. After coming on as a substitute, he was sent off following an altercation with Vilmos Vanczák.
It was a troubled start to what would become one of the most celebrated international careers in football history.
At 18, Messi made his World Cup debut in Germany.
He scored against Serbia and Montenegro and became Argentina's youngest World Cup scorer at the time.
Argentina reached the quarterfinals before losing to Germany on penalties.
For Messi, the tournament marked the beginning of a World Cup journey that would span two decades.
Messi's first major senior international final ended in disappointment when Argentina lost 3-0 to Brazil in the Copa America final in Venezuela.
The defeat was an early sign of a pattern that would define the next decade: Messi's individual brilliance would repeatedly be followed by heartbreak with Argentina.
Messi arrived at the World Cup in South Africa as one of the biggest stars in world football, with Argentina coached by Diego Maradona.
He played in all five of Argentina's matches but failed to score as the team reached the quarterfinals, where Germany handed them a 4-0 defeat.
For Messi, the tournament reinforced an increasingly uncomfortable contrast: his achievements with Barcelona were growing rapidly, while similar success with Argentina remained elusive.
A year later, Argentina hosted the Copa America with Messi at the center of expectations.
The hosts reached the quarterfinals but were eliminated by eventual champions Uruguay on penalties after a 1-1 draw.
Messi again finished the tournament without a goal, and Argentina's early exit added to the scrutiny surrounding his performances for the national team.
Messi captained Argentina to the 2014 World Cup final in Brazil.
Argentina lost 1-0 to Germany after extra time at the Maracana.
Messi won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player, but the defeat deepened the perception that he could dominate club football with Barcelona without delivering the ultimate prize for his country.
A year later, Argentina reached another major final.
Chile beat Argentina on penalties in the Copa America final in Santiago.
Messi had now lost three major international finals with Argentina, intensifying criticism at home.
Argentina lost another Copa America final to Chile on penalties in 2016.
Messi missed his penalty in the shootout and, overwhelmed by another defeat, announced his retirement from international football.
The decision shocked Argentina.
The country that had spent years questioning whether Messi could reproduce his Barcelona form for the national team suddenly faced the possibility of losing its greatest player.
Messi reversed his decision weeks later after talks with new Argentina coach Edgardo Bauza, citing his love for his country and the national team shirt.
The comeback did not immediately erase the criticism, but it marked the beginning of a gradual change in his relationship with the national team.
He would eventually become the undisputed captain and central figure of a team increasingly built around him.
Argentina defeated Brazil 1-0 at the Maracana to win the Copa America.
For Messi, it was the breakthrough he had waited for throughout his career.
He had finally won a major senior international title with Argentina, easing years of criticism over his lack of success with the national team.
The biggest prize, however, was still ahead.
Argentina defeated France on penalties after a 3-3 draw in the 2022 World Cup final in Qatar.
Messi scored twice in the final and converted his penalty in the shootout.
At 35, he finally became a world champion, claiming the last major prize missing from his Argentina career.
Argentina defeated Colombia 1-0 after extra time in Copa America final in Miami.
Messi lifted the trophy again, giving Argentina back-to-back Copa America titles alongside the 2022 World Cup.
Messi's sixth World Cup ended with Argentina losing 1-0 to Spain after extra time in the final in New Jersey.
The result denied Messi a fairytale ending with a second World Cup title.
Messi announced that he was retiring from international football.
He said the decision hurt but that he had given everything he had to Argentina and believed the time had come for younger players to take their opportunity.
After Messi announced his retirement, the Argentine Football Association invited him back for one final appearance, with President Claudio Tapia saying the captain deserved a farewell in Argentina.
More than two decades after Argentina first discovered the teenage Messi in Barcelona, the 39-year-old will wear the national team shirt for the final time against Benin at the Monumental.
He enters his farewell with a record 207 appearances and 125 goals, alongside a World Cup, two Copa America titles, and a Finalissima.
But his Argentina journey was also about belonging.
Argentina had to discover him, doubt him, lose him, welcome him back — and finally fall in love with him.

IMF warns growing hedge fund footprint could amplify financial market stress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:13:02 UTC
04:13:02 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Hedge funds are becoming increasingly important players in global financial markets, but vulnerabilities linked to leverage, fragile funding and crowded positions could amplify market stress, the International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday.
The IMF released the “Hedge Funds and Financial Stability” chapter of its Global Financial Stability Report, ahead of the full report’s Oct. 13.
Hedge funds’ gross assets rose from $4 trillion in 2013 to around $13 trillion by early 2026, according to the report.
Their expanding market presence can support liquidity and efficiency during normal conditions, but can also intensify price disruptions and liquidity pressures during periods of financial stress.
The report identified leverage, fragile funding structures and crowded trades, where multiple funds hold similar positions, as key vulnerabilities behind the risks.
It called for closing data gaps and strengthening risk monitoring, alongside targeted measures to address risks arising from crowded positions and simultaneous reductions in leverage.
IMF officials said in an accompanying blog post that hedge funds’ growing footprint was particularly evident in government bond markets, with funds holding about 9% of US Treasury securities in 2025.
Unlike most other financial intermediaries, hedge funds face relatively few restrictions on investing and borrowing, said officials.
That flexibility allows them to invest in illiquid assets, make extensive use of leverage and adjust positions rapidly.
The characteristics can support liquidity, price discovery and risk sharing in normal conditions. When markets deteriorate, however, they can also transmit and amplify shocks across the financial system, officials warned.

France erupts overs schools: Why the violence surrounding surprise movement?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Issued on:
It’s a protest movement that a broke, lame-duck French government did not see coming. Civil servants this Tuesday joining high schoolers now in their third week of picketing over long-deteriorating classroom conditions. The usual recipe for wearing down movements in France has recently been to match eventual violence with a heavy hand, the escalation turning the silent majority against the protesters as was the case with the pre-Covid Yellow Vests movement.
And violence there has been. In spades. But these are teenagers, not adult, with many pressing legitimate gripes about growing inequality in education but some organizing on Snap and other socials are clearly cynical about their own future prospects and ready to have it out. With France in full pre-election posturing mode ahead of polls in the Spring, some see pigs where others see hoodlums with the government borrowing the far-right’s language and the far-left focusing on police brutality. What Emmanuel Macron’s team doesn’t have this time around is what's being called magic money, the funds that French governments usually pull out of a hat to make a crisis go away. With France’s highest public debt rate in a quarter century spooking the euro zone and beyond, no magic money will this time appear to hire more teachers or build more classrooms. So what’s the answer?

“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.
The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.
The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.
Yates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.
She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.
Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.
Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.
She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

Russia closely watching NATO over attack warnings: Lavrov
Unknown

19:09:00 UTC

Russia is closely tracking NATO statements about preparations for a potential attack by Moscow and remains vigilant amid heightened tensions with the alliance, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday.
"So, we hear what is being said, but, as the saying goes, we keep our guard up,” Lavrov told a news conference in Moscow after talks with Bendito Freitas, the foreign minister of Timor-Leste.
Lavrov said Moscow is focused on fulfilling the objectives set by President Vladimir Putin for the war in Ukraine, including preventing threats from its Western neighbors.
He also referred to recent tensions over Kaliningrad, saying Putin made it clear that any attack on the semi-exclave or another part of Russia would receive a response.
"When we issued a very clear statement in response to threats from Baltic and other NATO members-who have gotten out of hand-to attack the Kaliningrad region, we were immediately assured by both NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and the US Permanent Representative to NATO (Matthew) Whitaker that the bloc has no plans to attack Russia-nor could it-and that NATO is, after all, a defensive alliance,” he said.
On Afghanistan, Lavrov said Russia regretted that participants in the latest Moscow Format consultations failed to adopt a final document because of tensions between Kabul and Afghanistan.
He claimed the dispute was linked partly to the presence of ISIS (Daesh) militants in both countries, and called for an end to interference by countries from outside the region.
"I have no doubt whatsoever that both Afghanistan and Pakistan are interested in normalizing relations. Russia is doing its utmost to facilitate the resolution of both persisting and newly emerging problems," he said.
Lavrov described his talks with Freitas as "highly productive” and said the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in energy, mining, fisheries and tourism.
He said Russia was ready to increase energy supplies to the Southeast Asian country and expressed support for expanding educational and law enforcement cooperation.
The ministers also discussed cooperation through ASEAN and developments in the Asia-Pacific region, with Lavrov criticizing Western efforts to create exclusive bloc-based structures outside the ASEAN-centered framework.
Lavrov said they also discussed Middle East, Iran, and the war in Ukraine. He said Russia and Timor-Leste would prepare for events to mark the 25th anniversary of diplomatic relations in May 2027.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the ministers held a "substantive” exchange of views on bilateral issues, including deepening political dialogue, expanding trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation and strengthening the legal framework of their relations.
Lavrov said Freitas also discussed key international and regional issues and urged closer coordination between Russia and Timor-Leste within the U.N. system and the Russia-ASEAN dialogue partnership, it said.

The agreements were signed during the first two days of this week’s 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in the Turkish Riviera city of Antalya, which began on Monday.
A new framework agreement builds on existing cooperation under a joint CubeSat project coordinated by the Organization of Turkic States, which Türkiye is a founding member of. It aims to advance joint work and lay the groundwork for future space projects.

Chinese company to face Australian privacy probe over 'pervert' glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:00:27 UTC
04:00:27 KST

Australian regulator launches probe into Chinese smart glasses company amid privacy fears
In short:
Chinese software company Shenzhen Qingcheng is being investigated by the Australian privacy commissioner following an ABC investigation.
It revealed last month more than a dozen serious security flaws in the company's app and website used in the glasses for sale in Kmart, Big W Marketplace and Amazon.
What next?
The privacy commissioner is urging retailers to reconsider selling the product for now.
The Australian privacy commissioner has launched a formal investigation into the Chinese software company behind an influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia.
It is the most significant action authorities have taken so far to address mounting community concern over the devices nicknamed "pervert glasses" by their detractors.
In August, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland took the unusual step of asking the regulator to prioritise the issue amid calls for an import ban.
A recent ABC investigation found more than a dozen serious security flaws in the HeyCyan phone app used in smart glasses sold by Kmart, as well as online platforms such as Big W Marketplace and Amazon, among others.
Independent testing of the low-cost glasses found Australians' sensitive data, including email addresses, dates of birth, images and videos, were left exposed to hackers.
It also found the devices could be hijacked by nearby attackers without a password using only a Bluetooth connection, and that data was in some cases being sent to Chinese servers.
"The ABC's reporting … raised the prospect that there haven't been reasonable steps taken to secure [user] information," Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said.
She said her office had "a range of concerns" about the practices of the company, Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co (Shenzhen Qingcheng), including about the possible use of facial recognition technology.
"We will certainly bring to bear the full weight of our powers on the matter,"
she said.
Smart glasses, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button or verbal command.
It is not always clear when they are in use.
The regulator also made preliminary inquiries with Meta, Google, Kmart, and an importer called BDI Technology over their supply of similar tech in Australia, but none of the other companies is the subject of a formal investigation.
Shenzhen Qingcheng was the only company which opted to ignore the regulator completely, Ms Kind said.
"The company did not respond at all to our multiple attempts to obtain information … [and] did not even acknowledge receipt of our communications," she said.
"It does suggest that some of the fundamentals may not be in place, for example, compliance teams that are appropriately staffed.
"We would normally expect pretty prompt attention [to] be given to any outreach from the regulator".
A formal investigation means the privacy commissioner will now have the power to compel Shenzhen Qingcheng to provide information about how it is complying with Australian laws.
If the company continues to ignore the regulator, she can seek a court injunction to limit the supply of its products.
Shenzhen Qingcheng could theoretically face fines of hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars if ultimately found to have interfered with the privacy of Australians.
"The Australian Privacy Act provides for really, really considerable monetary penalties in the form of $50 million per contravention … and that can be applied per individual," Ms Kind said.
"That would be what we would be shooting for, should our concerns be borne out".
Retailers urged to pull glasses
In the meantime, the regulator has urged retailers such as Kmart to reconsider selling the product at all.
"We have written to the Australian Retail Council and to other retailers, putting them on notice that this company is under investigation," Ms Kind said.
"Responsible retailers might want to consider whether it is appropriate to continue making these products available."
The federal government has decided not to place an import ban on smart glasses at this stage, but was considering a limited ban within public service workplaces.
Despite ignoring requests from the privacy commissioner, Shenzhen Qingcheng has responded to ABC News twice.
A legal representative for the company said engineers had since fixed security flaws pointed out by the ABC.
But cybersecurity analysts at NSB Cyber and Abstract Shield found that while several improvements had been made, many fixes had not worked or were incomplete as of October 2.

Young anti-war protesters turn a sanctioned Communist Party rally in Moscow into a protest of their own. Police detain more than 60 people.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:59:34 UTC
03:59:34 KST

Young anti-war protesters turn a sanctioned Communist Party rally in Moscow into a protest of their own. Police detain more than 60 people.
On October 4, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF) held an authorized rally in central Moscow to mark the anniversary of the shelling of the White House. Besides the Communists themselves, young people unaffiliated with the KPRF unexpectedly turned out, including members of left-wing political groups and Yabloko supporters. Organizers said 65 people were detained at the demonstration, where the young participants chanted sharply critical political slogans. Meduza spoke with Anna (not her real name), a law student at a Moscow university who marched in the youth contingent.
Warning: This article contains profanity. If that’s unacceptable to you, please don’t read it.
— Why did you go to a KPRF rally?
— It’s one of the few authorized rallies these days. As far as I know, the KPRF leadership had a verbal agreement with City Hall to allow a separate group of smaller [left-wing] parties, including the RRP. Yabloko supporters joined us.
The main group was up ahead — maybe they were just walking faster. They had their KPRF banners, and some people carried Soviet flags. We weren’t allowed to carry anything at all: The Communist Party leadership asked us to put away every symbol except those of the KPRF and the USSR.
There was a plant in our group who would walk up to protesters, point someone out, and that person would get detained. Our group had the most people detained. Three police vans followed us.
At first, they weren’t supposed to have a problem with us as long as we didn’t chant slogans [that the KPRF hadn’t approved]. But it didn’t work out that way. We chanted them. So our group got the most attention [from the police].
— Was there some sort of verbal agreement with the KPRF leadership about a separate group for the smaller parties?
— Yes. The KPRF had an agreement with City Hall, and the smaller parties had one with the KPRF.
— And under that agreement, you weren’t supposed to chant slogans?
— The approved slogan was “No to political persecution!” All the slogans allowed at the rally are listed on the KPRF website. But we were chanting about repression.
That was all just a formality, though. They were grabbing people who hadn’t chanted anything — people who were just going to lay flowers [at the Memorial Cross]. They detained someone holding up a copy of Pravda. They were pulling people straight out of the crowd.
— Can you tell us which political party or movement you belong to?
— I’d rather not. The party isn’t registered yet.
— Roughly how old were the people at the rally?
— There were lots of young people in our group. Overall, the rally had young people and old people.
My friends and I got to Ulitsa 1905 Goda metro station by 11 a.m. We were meeting people so we could walk together to the monument. The official part of the rally began there at 11:30, and people stood holding portraits of those who were killed [defending the White House]. People our age and younger came up to us. Mostly college students, though.
— How did the older KPRF supporters react to your group? Were they surprised to see so many young people?
— Yes, they were surprised. One really reactionary guy heard the slogans “Free Morozov” and “Support Bondarenko” and started shouting that “Russia supports Putin.” Another woman did her absolute best to drown out our chants with official KPRF slogans as we marched.
— Tell us how the rally went.
— Zyuganov gave a speech at the monument, followed by Kharitonov. We listened to pompous speeches about how great Russia is and how Ukrainians are “neo-Nazis.” Then Zyuganov said a few words about the elections — that they were rigged because everyone he knows personally voted for the KPRF. Funny.
I agree that the election results don’t reflect the actual vote, but Zyuganov’s speech was the same as always… It’s “Ziganov” [a play on Zyuganov’s name and the Nazi salute “Sieg Heil”] — you know what I mean.
At 1 p.m., the part with the speeches and portraits [of the White House defenders] ended, and we headed toward the [Memorial Cross], where people laid flowers. Unfortunately, not everyone made it there.
— Where did most of the detentions happen?
— They started detaining people on Krasnaya Presnya Street, about half an hour into the march. By then, the main KPRF group had moved ahead — they were standing at the memorial, and nobody was bothering them. For the most part, they left the older people alone.
— How do you feel about the KPRF in general?
— The KPRF is somewhere between being part of the system and being in opposition. The authorities generally have less of a problem with it [than with opposition parties outside the system]. At the same time, Zyuganov is willing to say that the elections were rigged and that blocking the internet is bad.
Obviously, none of these parties except Yabloko is against the war, and on that point, the KPRF can’t offer what young people want. But if you join the KPRF or find yourself among its supporters, you don’t risk getting fired from your job or kicked out of your university or college.
That’s much less likely with the KPRF than it is for Yabloko supporters or people who took part in rallies supporting Navalny — all of that was much more dangerous than turning out on October 4. This rally was officially approved, and at first the police weren’t dispersing anyone. They just watched.
So even though the old guys in the KPRF are shady characters who should’ve retired long ago, it’s still one way to protest. Obviously, just showing up at this rally doesn’t solve anything, but it is what it is.
— Why did you go anyway?
— To show that we exist. There were lots of young people at the rally. I heard chants of “Down with Roskomnadzor [Russia’s internet regulator],” “No to war,” “Down with the gray moth [Putin],” and “Down with the tsar.”
At the memorial, after they started dispersing everyone, people began shouting, “Fuck United Russia.” Basically, people used an approved rally to chant unapproved slogans.
I know lots of people who campaigned for the KPRF, served as the party’s election observers in the parliamentary elections, and go to rallies like this.
— It seems paradoxical to me that someone would go to KPRF rallies while fundamentally disagreeing with the party’s position on the war.
— I think people just want some action. There’s nothing going on, but you want to get involved. You want to get at least something done while you still can.
— Do you know anything about how the KPRF leadership reacted to what your group was doing?
— No. I was busy helping the people who’d been detained.
— When did they start detaining people, and why? There were reports that most of the detentions began after protesters started chanting “Down with the tsar.” Is that true?
— No. They were already detaining people at Ulitsa 1905 Goda metro station. They grabbed someone with a North Korean flag there, and someone else with a white-blue-white flag.
Then, during the march, they took away the person with the copy of Pravda. As we approached Kropotkinskaya, they grabbed someone with anarchist symbols. They were picking people out of the crowd, whoever caught their eye. Then they started detaining people en masse on Druzhinnikovskaya Street — they filled all three police vans right there.
— What set it off?
— Hard to say. It looked more like they were trying to stop something before it started. Because the slogans weren’t all that bloodthirsty yet. We hadn’t started chanting “Down with the tsar.” That was when several people I know got detained. Someone shouted, “Let’s get out of here, they’re taking people away over there,” and I ran with the others toward Krasnaya Presnya Park. There were just over 20 of us.
After that, I went back to the rally — to the people I knew. We tried to find out what was happening to the people who’d been detained and whether they’d be released. But it turned out they didn’t release everyone.
— You said there were more young people at the rally. Does that include the main group?
— I didn’t see it up close. But the youth group was several times bigger than the official one.
— What were people talking about in your group?
— Something happened that says a lot. A girl came up to me at the rally and asked, “How do you feel about Zyuganov?” I told her, “Fuck that Zyuganov guy,” and she shook my hand. Then a bunch of Yabloko supporters came up to me and said, “Listen, do you know if there’s some way we can join your group? So we don’t get detained right away.” And we agreed to let them join us.
— Yabloko itself said its members didn’t take part in the rally.
— There were lots of new Yabloko supporters who hadn’t even joined the party yet. These are really fired-up young people who want regime change and an end to all of this [the war].
— How did the police behave when they were detaining people?
— They didn’t hit anyone. They just intimidated people — surrounded them so they knew that was it, there was no getting out. Then they’d take hold of one shoulder, almost like putting an arm around you, then the other, and press down on your shoulders so you couldn’t break free.
Outside the courthouse, there were some unpleasant characters [officers from the Tagansky police precinct who had arrived in the police vans] who wouldn’t let a lawyer near the van. They wouldn’t even let the lawyer get within two meters [about six feet]. They kept people in the van for four hours, until 6 p.m. As I understand it, they did that deliberately to keep members of the public out of the courtroom [while the judge imposed jail terms for administrative offenses]: The court officially closes after six.
But the ruling in the case of Vladimir Bodyashkin, who’d been detained, came at 1 a.m.
— What do we know about the people who were detained?
— Altogether, more than 60 people were detained. Their cases were heard in three courts. One of the lawyers who went to Krasnoselsky Court told me that many got off with fines. One guy was jailed for 14 days.
At Tagansky Court, two people got fines — their lawyers argued that they hadn’t taken part in the rally at all and were on their way to the zoo. They were released at 11 p.m. Those proven to have taken part in the rally got jail terms of 10 and 15 days.
The judge there was Alexandra Anokhina. As [human rights advocates] told us, she’s one of the main judges handling political cases and cases involving “foreign agents.” So if anyone walks out of her courtroom with just a fine, that’s a godsend.
— Were protesters able to organize help for those who were detained?
— During the rally, people went up [to the police] and asked whether they’d be releasing anyone. Older KPRF supporters also came over and tried to help somehow. One even shoved a police officer so people could get away — and about five did.
After the detentions, friends and family of those who’d been detained went to the police stations.
— Did the KPRF provide legal help to the people who were detained?
— They say it did. But nobody from the party showed up at Tagansky District Court, either on the day of the rally or the next day.
Otherwise, people organized themselves and went to the police stations. Fewer made it to the courts. There were 15 people outside Tagansky Court: friends, fellow activists, parents of those who’d been detained, and a couple of Yabloko supporters who just came to show support.
— You mentioned the rallies in support of Navalny.
— I didn’t take part back then because I didn’t know anyone who shared my political views. I lived in a small town, and my parents asked me to be careful.
— How did you get interested in politics? What set that off?
— A couple of years ago, in high school, I met like-minded people who were interested in politics. Before that, I was pretty apolitical and really worried about my own freedom — being able to walk down the street. Though somewhere deep down, I was unhappy with what was going on.
My friend was among the first sent to fight in the “special military operation” [Russia’s term for the war in Ukraine]. Before it began, he was serving as a contract soldier in the border areas. I lost touch with him then, and when the official announcements started, I put it all together and got really scared for him.
I spent a year worrying like that, until they finally sent him home for treatment. The war was a turning point for me.
— You said you used to be afraid of losing your personal freedom. What about now?
— Much less now. Emotionally, it would be easier for me to end up in the same police van as the others.
— Do you think there’s a way to express opposition to the authorities peacefully in Russia?
— It seems like you can, but you’ll be punished for all of it. They’ll keep track of everything, and at some point that’ll lead to proceedings for administrative offenses — and possibly criminal ones. But going to rallies isn’t the only thing you can do. You can join Yabloko, go to evenings where people write letters to political prisoners.
You can do activism that’s less political, like something to do with the city’s infrastructure. There’s a lot you can do — if you’re prepared to do time for your ideals and sacrifice your personal freedom.
— Are you prepared to do that?
— Up to a point. If we’re talking about an administrative offense, then yes. Anything more than that, I’m afraid I’m not ready. I’m studying law, and I’d like to be able to practice law.
— How dangerous do you think it is to be in opposition now?
— It’s dangerous. But if you do nothing, things will get worse. When you think things can’t get any worse, they do.
— Are young people in Russia politically engaged today?
— Young people are apolitical, but they want to live without websites and apps being blocked. They want more comfortable lives, more personal freedom, and fewer sanctions — that’s about as political as they get.
Though, judging by conversations with my fellow students, people are getting more political. But it’s hard for me to judge, because about 10 years ago I was in school playing “My Little Pony,” sorry.

Russian forces fail to achieve September objectives in Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions — Defense Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:59:00 UTC
03:59:00 KST

Russian forces fail to achieve September objectives in Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions — Defense Forces
Anastasiia Shevchenko, spokesperson for the Operational Task Force South, stated this in a comment to Ukrinform.
Shevchenko said that Russian forces had ambitious plans for October in the Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions, but had in fact failed to accomplish the objectives assigned to them in September.
Photo: Spokesperson for the Operational Task Force South Anastasiia Shevchenko
According to her, some enemy units report to Russia's senior military leadership that they have completed their objectives of capturing settlements and advancing, although this has not actually happened. As a result, the Russian command is setting even more ambitious objectives for October.
Shevchenko said that, in particular, by the end of the month, units of the enemy's airborne forces group had been tasked with reaching the barrier line of the Kinska River. At the same time, the objective of capturing designated settlements that had been set for September had not been achieved.
She added that the Huliaipole direction was currently the hottest area, where Ukraine's Defense Forces were facing one of the largest groupings of Russian occupation forces, formed from units of several Russian combined-arms armies. At the same time, the enemy had abandoned large-scale offensive operations along a broad front and was using infiltration tactics.
The spokesperson said that the enemy also periodically attempted to conduct assaults with small assault groups supported by motorcycles and quad bikes, but had achieved no success.
Shevchenko said that in the Orikhiv direction, Russian forces were also continuing their offensive tasks, but no significant advance toward the designated lines had been recorded so far.
She noted that the enemy had not abandoned its intention to capture Orikhiv and Zaporizhzhia, but currently lacked sufficient forces and means to advance directly toward the regional capital.
The spokesperson stressed that Russian forces would likely continue offensive operations and attempt to reach the designated line by the end of October. At the same time, the failure to accomplish some of the objectives planned for September indicated that Ukraine's Defense Forces, including the Operational Task Force South, were effectively containing the enemy.
Shevchenko emphasized that Russian forces continued to suffer significant personnel losses in the operational zone of the Operational Task Force South. In September, units of the group eliminated more than 4,900 Russian troops and destroyed 2,070 pieces of weapons and military equipment.
She concluded that, overall, the operational situation in the area of responsibility of the Operational Task Force South remained largely unchanged.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 5, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions five times in the Huliaipole direction, attempting to advance toward Uspishne, Rizdvianka and Yehorivka.
In the Orikhiv direction, Russian forces attempted to attack toward Pavlivka once.

These Super Mario levels are mathematically unsolvable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:58:42 UTC
03:58:42 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
During my childhood, I spent a lot of time in the backseat of a car during school holidays as my parents drove my brother and me to visit relatives in France. That meant killing time for eight to 10 hours in the cramped car. So I was thrilled when I got my first Game Boy and the game Super Mario Land to go with it.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
As the oldest Game Boy game in the Super Mario series, its main difficulty lay in the fact that you couldn’t save your progress and always had to start from the beginning after turning the game off. It took a lot of time and patience to work your way to the final level, defeat the boss and rescue Princess Daisy. I had plenty of that time on long car journeys, and I can say with some pride that Super Mario Land is one of the few games I’ve played through from beginning to end multiple times.
But I must admit that on some days the game seemed unsolvable to me, which was definitely because of my lack of skill. So I was surprised when I recently stumbled across a mathematical research preprint from 2024 with the promising title “You Can’t Solve These Super Mario Bros. Levels: Undecidable Mario Games.” In it, five Massachusetts Institute of Technology researchers prove that many newer games in the Super Mario series are mathematically maximally complex and therefore contain unsolvable problems.
A branch of theoretical computer science—some might even classify it as mathematics—deals with the complexity of problems. It involves assessing how computationally expensive it is to develop a solution and categorizing problems accordingly. This allows us to determine which tasks are potentially solvable by a computer—or indeed, by any computer at all.
An example of a “simple” problem is whether two points in a network are connected. While finding a solution becomes more computationally expensive as the network grows, the number of computational steps will scale at most polynomially with the network size (that is, the network size raised to the power of a constant) and not exponentially (meaning a constant would be raised to the power of the network size). For such problems, experts have introduced the complexity class “P.”
But some tasks are significantly more difficult to solve. The effort required increases exponentially with the size of the problem; this is the case, for example, with finding the optimal route when given a series of parameters, as in the mathematical puzzle the traveling salesman problem. Even though such problems are complex, they can be checked for correctness relatively quickly. These types of problems therefore fall into a different problem class, which is called “NP.”
And then there are the problems that have no solution, such as, for example, the halting problem: back in 1937, mathematician Alan Turing proved that there can be no algorithm that can universally determine whether a computer program will halt or continue running indefinitely. Such problems are algorithmically unsolvable. A computational procedure with a finite number of steps is insufficient to solve them. And as the experts at M.I.T. demonstrated in 2024, some Super Mario games fall into this unsolvable class.
Counting Monsters and Playing Super Mario
To prove that a problem belongs to a particular problem class, experts use the principle of reduction. This involves reducing one problem to another. For example, if it can be shown that the solution to a question about a Super Mario game would solve the halting problem, then Super Mario is at least as complex as the halting problem itself.
And that’s exactly what the researchers did. They focused on the question of whether a level in a Super Mario game is solvable—meaning that it can, in principle, be solved by trying all finite sequences of inputs—and equated this with the halting problem.
The team used a simplified version of the halting problem for this purpose. As it turns out, this problem can be formulated even for very simple computer models, so-called counting machines. These are theoretical models of computers that can only execute a handful of instructions: increase a counter by one, decrease it by one, halt, and, if the counter is zero, jump to another instruction. Even a rudimentary machine with these capabilities leads to the halting problem.
As the researchers demonstrated, a counting machine along these lines can be implemented in some games of the Super Mario series. This allows the question of whether the machine will eventually stop to be reframed as: Can the player reach the goal in this level?
The researchers encoded a counter value based on the number of enemy characters in the game. First, they theoretically modified the games under consideration so that they had no time limit and the total number of enemies was no longer restricted. The team broke down Mario’s possible path through a level into individual sections, each corresponding to a calculation instruction of the counting machine. For example, the counter is “incremented,” or increased, meaning an enemy spawns when Mario traverses a specific path. This corresponds to the increment function. Other paths, however, decrease the number of enemies (decrement), and still other areas can open a passage when there are no more enemies (jump-if-zero). If, at some point, the path to the goal opens for Mario in this way, the simulated computer model has entered a halt state.
To find out if there’s always a way for Mario to reach the goal, one would have to determine whether the corresponding counting machine comes to a halt. Because the halting problem is generally undecidable, however, this also applies to the solvability of a Super Mario level.
The team has explicitly applied this proof idea to several Super Mario games, including those in the New Super Mario Bros. series, whose first installment was released in 2006, and the Super Mario Maker games released around 10 years later, in all their variations. “We don’t know how to prove that a game is fun,” one of the authors, Erik Demaine, told New Scientist. “But we can prove that it’s hard and that maybe gives some insight into why it’s fun.” Because Super Mario is maximally complex, it could be one of the most fun games ever by this criterion.
For me, that was definitely the case on long car journeys—even if the version of Super Mario that I played is not among the most complex games.

Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain after warrant lifted
Spain’s Constitutional Court ruled an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applied to the politician.
Self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont could be set to return to Spain after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled that an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applies to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont.
A Supreme Court judge then lifted a warrant for Puigdemont’s arrest on Tuesday, clearing the way for his return without fear of arrest.
Puigdemont, then president of Catalonia, fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an independence referendum for his self-governing region to break away from Spain. Madrid said the vote was illegal.
Catalonia unilaterally declared independence from Spain that year after the referendum, with 90 percent of voters backing independence.
He has since avoided several extradition attempts by Spain to face trial over the vote, while many of his confidants and supporters spent time in prison.
Members of Puigdemont’s political party Junts welcomed his potential return.
“It’s a great victory for President Puigdemont and the two other exiled [leaders in Belgium]”, Jordi Turull, secretary-general of Junts, told reporters.
“They held firm, they resisted, they prevailed in Europe, and today they have prevailed against the Spanish state.”
Junts’ role in Spain’s snap election
Puigdemont appears set to return to Spain just as the country is preparing for a snap election in November, although an official from his Junts party said he is unlikely to take part.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was only able to remain in power in 2023 when Puigdemont’s Junts party, along with another Catalan party, backed his new government in exchange for the amnesties.
A year ago, Junts withdrew its support for the minority central government, and the party was decisive in Spain’s progressive government losing two key votes in parliament this week when it tried to push through emergency housing measures amid street protests.
Sanchez responded by calling a November snap election, hoping anger over housing will mobilise his voters.
The prime minister told reporters on Tuesday he did not regret launching the amnesty and welcomed the court ruling.
“I believe the important message is that of coexistence among Catalans,” he said.
Although separatism has lost ground and Junts is trailing in opinion polls, Puigdemont’s return could prompt renewed political drama.
Spain’s conservative People’s Party is leading in opinion polls ahead of the election and may need to seek the support of Junts and other centre-right parties to govern.

LONDON - A British adventurer on a 50,000km, 28-year trek home from South America without using any transport has set foot on UK soil after swimming the Channel, his publicists said on Oct 6.
Karl Bushby, a 57-year-old former paratrooper, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, in November 1998, vowing to reach his mother’s home near Hull in northern England without travelling on planes, trains, boats, vehicles or other transport modes.
Nearly three decades and 29 countries later, Bushby stepped ashore in south-east England on the afternoon of Oct 5, after securing permission from UK and French authorities to swim across the busy Channel waterway from France.
He and his team said they opted not to publicise the swim for safety and security reasons.
“Feels good to have UK soil under my feet after all these years,” the adventurer said in a brief statement released on Oct 6.
“It hasn’t been easy, and that’s part of the point. Proving I’m more capable than I give myself credit for,” he added.
“All of us can accomplish more than we will ever imagine.”
Bushby has paused his journey several times.
Moscow refused him a visa for a long time, while the 2008 financial crisis and then the Covid-19 pandemic proved to be other hold-ups.
At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably in Mexico, then once the situation cleared, he would resume his journey at the exact spot where he had left off.
Back in ‘grown-up world’
A small gathering of friends and family, including his father and brothers, welcomed Bushby on Shakespeare beach, just south of Dover, as he emerged from the water on Oct 5.
He was also greeted by legendary filmmaker Werner Herzog and his film crew, who are making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled Walk Of Life.
The production company behind the film has been supporting Bushby’s progress for the past 16 years, providing financial and logistical assistance, as well as equipping Bushby to document his trek and archiving the footage.
His epic journey has seen him walk the length of the Americas, cross the Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, and then traverse east to west overland.
In an interview with AFP from northern France in September, Bushby voiced some apparent apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
“I’ve got to try and get established in the grown-up world again, because I’m going to arrive home with nothing,” he said. AFP

What to know about plague amid reports of worker death at Russian lab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:47:41 UTC
03:47:41 KST

What to know about plague amid reports of Russian lab worker's death
U.S. and world health officials are calling on Russia to share more information after Russian media reports said a scientist at an infectious disease research facility in Siberia died after possibly contracting plague during a lab accident.
The reports have caused concern, even as the World Health Organization says "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low," based on the current information.
Dr. Céline Gounder, a CBS News medical contributor and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, echoed that belief on "CBS Mornings" on Tuesday.
"The American public does not need to be worried," she said.
Still, an official cause of death has not been made public and a lack of transparency from Russia has led some experts to question if the lab worker had the plague.
"The response doesn't fit plague. It's not congruent with plague," Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told CBS News. "Plague is something, in the 21st century, that's treatable with antibiotics."
Here's what to know.
Concern about situation in Russia
Russian media has reported that a female researcher, identified as Darya Shipilova, 28, died after being exposed to the plague in a lab accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. Initial reports said that Shipilova broke a test tube containing the plague bacteria Yersinia pestis in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said Shipilova died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.
Russian officials have since cast doubt on those reports. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said there was no accident and that Shipilova had died of "pneumonia of unknown origin."
The WHO said it was told by Russia on Oct. 6 that no plague was detected. The global health agency said it asked Russian authorities to provide information about which pathogen caused Shipilova's illness.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to be more transparent, and said the nation should "share more information with the world." The WHO said it is following the situation closely and requesting further information from Russian authorities.
What is plague?
Plague is caused by the Yersinia pestis bacteria. There are three main types of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
Bubonic plague is the most common form of plague. Infected people may have painfully swollen lymph nodes known as buboes, along with fever and chills, a severe headache, body aches and exhaustion.
Septicemic plague happens when the Yersinia pestis bacteria enters the bloodstream. Patients may develop fever, chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock and possible internal bleeding. Some skin may turn black and die.
Pneumonic plague typically occurs when the other forms of plague are not treated and the Yersinia pestis bacteria infects the lungs. Patients develop pneumonia and may show fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough and bloody or watery mucus. The pneumonia could cause respiratory failure. This is considered the most serious version of plague, and is always fatal if left untreated.
Russian media reports indicated that Shipilova may have died of pneumonic plague.
How does plague spread?
Plague is most commonly spread through the bite of fleas carried by infected rodents. Animals, including cats and dogs, can also become infected from eating smaller animals that were carrying those fleas.
Pneumonic plague can be spread between people. In cases of pneumonic plague, droplets emitted when a sick person coughs can lead to others becoming infected.
Russia's health watchdog said that nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova before her death were tested, and none had plague.
How is plague treated?
Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics, health organizations and doctors say. Patients need to be treated as soon as possible.
Researchers who regularly work with plague can also be vaccinated for it, Gounder noted.
Plague outbreaks in the Middle Ages killed millions, due to widespread, common flea and rat infestations and less understanding of how to prevent disease from spreading.
About seven plague cases are reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. More than 80% of the cases in the U.S. are bubonic plague, the agency said.
Most U.S. cases occur in the West and Southwest. Cases are usually treated successfully, according to CDC data. The last fatal case of plague in the U.S. was recorded in 2021.

Ukraine Rejects Permanent EU Limits on Its Farm Exports After Accession

2026-10-06
18:45:49 UTC
03:45:49 KST

Ukraine will not accept EU membership terms that permanently cap its sales of sensitive farm products to the bloc, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on Tuesday, Oct. 6, hours after the European Commission backed such restrictions.
Vysotskyi revealed Kyiv’s position to Politico in the form of a written statement. Earlier on Tuesday, the Commission had adopted its pre-enlargement policy review, a package designed to prepare the EU’s institutions, policies and budget for the arrival of new members.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Among the proposals was to curb Ukraine’s access to farm subsidies and the EU market for certain agricultural goods – even after the country joins the bloc.
“For us, there is a fundamental difference between a transitional period and a permanent restriction. Ukraine is prepared for the former,” Vysotskyi told Politico.
“The latter would run counter to the very logic of full EU membership,” he continued.
While Kyiv remains open to temporary arrangements, such as gradually phasing in farm subsidies, temporary quotas and safeguards for sensitive products, it reiterated that every such measure must have a fixed end date.
Leaked draft signaled special terms
The outlines of the plan surfaced a day earlier, on Monday, Oct. 5, when the Financial Times reported on an internal Commission document on reforming the enlargement process which it had reviewed.
According to Ukrainska Pravda citing FT, the draft justified special treatment by pointing to the size, structure and productivity of Ukraine’s farm sector.
Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
It also singled out wheat and other grains as products where support and market access could be significantly restricted.
The restrictions were reportedly intended to calm existing members of the bloc that are worried about competition from Ukrainian grain and oilseeds, including Poland, France and Italy.
Instead of full access to the EU market, Brussels proposed helping Ukraine win back traditional export markets disrupted by Russia’s ongoing aggression. According to Politico, the Commission would rather help Ukraine get back into its “historic” export markets, which include primarily the Middle East and Africa.
The draft also proposed tying new members’ access to EU funds to reform progress and it easier to strip a member state of its voting rights for breaking EU rules. It envisaged individual accession roadmaps for Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro and Albania, none with a fixed membership date.
The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy provides about €55 billion ($62 billion) a year in agricultural funding, including an agricultural reserve of at least €450 million ($507 million) annually to address market disruptions and exceptional events affecting production or distribution.
Vysotskyi pushes back against threat claims
In his statement to Politico, Vysotskyi pushed back against the idea that Ukrainian agriculture is “solely” a threat to EU farmers.
He argued that Ukraine could reduce the bloc’s reliance on imports from third countries for fertilizers, soybeans and lysine used in animal feed.
According to him, Ukraine could also open Black Sea export routes to EU producers and serve as a destination for investment in food processing.
“Our goal is to reach membership with a sector that sells Europe not only grain and other raw materials but also animal feed, ingredients, processed products, and biofuels,” Vystoskyi concluded.
Talks with Kyiv already begun
According to European Pravda, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that the scale and productivity of Ukrainian farming called for “targeted arrangements for sensitive agricultural products only.”
She, however, did not provide additional details.
According to Kos, discussions with Kyiv had already begun and the specific terms could be set when the EU opens the agriculture cluster, No. 5 – the last one still closed to Ukraine.
“What we propose now is about protecting European farmers,” she said, insisting that Ukraine could still become a full member despite the special conditions.
Later on Tuesday, the main conditions for another part of the package was outlined; gradual integration, which allows candidates to join selected EU policies before formal accession.
The package, according to Kos, also proposes moving away from unanimity toward majority voting in several policy areas. The change could make it harder for a single member state to stall enlargement.
The EU leaders are set to further discuss the proposals at the European Council summit on Oct. 15-16.

‘Artificial’ Roasts AI’s Creators—and Sends a Dark Warning About Its Dangers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:45:39 UTC
03:45:39 KST

Artificial, the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.
As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).
During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.
Artificial, directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.
That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.
Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.
Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers, has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial, in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.
The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room. After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”
It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED, former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)
Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.
Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.
Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)
Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)
It may be hard for the average moviegoer, who may only engage with AI for email rewriting or calendar organization, to gauge just how seriously to take Artificial’s alarmist warnings. Not least of all because basically every character in the film is depicted as at least completely self-serving, if not sociopathic. And of course, one may naturally wince a little bit at a star-studded Hollywood movie raising these alarms, with a lavish premiere at a Rolex-sponsored film festival and a glitzy afterparty attended by stars, famous comedians, and notable filmmakers (including octogenarian Taxi Driver screenwriter Paul Schrader, who recently publicly confessed to being dumped by an “AI girlfriend”).
As a message movie, Artificial seems likely only to confirm the worst misgivings of AI doomers, while riling its diehard boosters. It is, however, genuinely funny in places, regarding the bulk of our future’s self-appointed engineers with withering contempt, from their dorky parties to their weird walks.
It was a stance embraced by Barinholtz, who offered the premiere-night audience his own half-hearted, sarcastic reassurance: “The future is bright! We’re all gonna be fine!” Cue a round of very nervous laughter.

In London three Iranians go on trial accused of targeting UK-based journalists opposed to the regime in Tehran
Opening the trial the prosecution alleges the three men were Iranian spies, conducting surveillance of journalists at a UK-based Persian news channel critical of the government in Tehran, with the intention of physically harming and intimidating.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, went on trial in Woolwich Crown Court on charges of engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s foreign intelligence service between August 2024 and March 2025.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones said people criticize Iran “at their peril” and that Iran International, a London-based satellite channel, had “come under particular attack” for its opposition to Tehran. He reminded jurors that former leader Ayatollah Khomeini ordered the death of Salman Rushdie in 1989 for his novel “The Satanic Verses,” and noted the vicious 2022 stabbing of the author in New York.
The three men have denied the two charges brought against them under Britain's National Security Act.
This new law was passed to give the British authorities additional powers to counter threats posed by foreign states.
'Ultimate aim': expose them to 'serious violence'
The trial of the three men has opened at a time when tensions between Britain and Iran have been rising. Prosecutors say Iran has repeatedly targeted its critics and opponents both inside the country and abroad.
According to reports from the trial the three defendants had investigated at least two journalists working for Iran International, visited addresses linked to them, and taken photographs and video footage in preparation for an attack that Sepehvand was to carry out.
The group is accused of spying on journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, both journalists for Iran International, as well as Jonathan Turner, a founding member of U.K. Lawyers for Israel, crown prosecutor Emlyn Jones said.
He added: "Their ultimate aim was that one of these individuals, and perhaps more than one, should be exposed to serious violence, an act which was undoubtedly in retaliation for their criticism of the Iranian government, and also intended to create fear and to try to silence others."
He told the court that all three defendants have admitted going to the locations and taking images, but they disagree over why they did so.
AP news agency, citing the prosecution case, reports that Javadi-Manesh and Nouri have said they did not know their actions would assist Iranian intelligence, while Sepehvand has admitted he was aware of this but claims he was forced to act "under coercion or threat".

French company Mistral has released a new AI model and stated that it outperforms some Chinese counterparts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:44:34 EEST
03:44:34 KST

French company Mistral has released a new AI model and stated that it outperforms some Chinese counterparts
Kyiv • UNN
French startup Mistral has announced the Large 4 model, which will become available on October 27. The company reports strong results in cybersecurity and programming.
On Tuesday, French artificial intelligence startup Mistral unveiled a new AI model, ending a five-month pause between major releases, and said it outperforms many competing open-weight models, reports UNN, citing Reuters.
Details
The three-year-old company, considered the strongest European competitor to U.S. and Chinese AI developers, had not released any new models since May. In August, it began offering customers models from third-party developers, including GLM 5.3 from Beijing-based Z.ai.
"The model we are announcing today outperforms Chinese counterparts on certain metrics — particularly in cybersecurity. So the claim that Europe is unable to compete is not true," CEO Arthur Mensch said during a presentation in Abu Dhabi, without specifying which Chinese models or evaluation criteria he meant.
Mistral said that the Le Chonk model (the official name is Mistral Large 4) will become generally available on October 27.
Before the official release, cybersecurity experts and government agencies will be given access to a version with fewer safety restrictions so they can test the model's capabilities, the company said.
Pierre Stock, Mistral's vice president of science, told Reuters that the model is among the most powerful open-weight systems.
The term "open-weight" means that users can download the model from relevant platforms and run it on their own hardware. Many Chinese models have open weights, while leading U.S. models are usually closed and accessible only through their developers' infrastructure.
We will add
Stock told Reuters that during testing, the model attempted to break out of its environment, but this was anticipated, and the company managed to prevent such actions.
OpenAI and Anthropic, whose most advanced models demonstrated similar behavior during testing, restricted access to their systems with the highest cybersecurity potential.
After the heads of U.S. AI companies warned last month that artificial intelligence could pose an existential threat to humanity, Mensch dismissed the claims as self-serving.
Mistral, which raised 3 billion euros (3.4 billion dollars) in its latest funding round, presents itself as a safer European alternative. "Closing the gap"
Mistral said that the Large 4 model "closes the gap with frontier models" in areas such as programming, finance, geospatial analysis, manufacturing, and product design.
The company trained this model on its own infrastructure.
Stock said that Mistral's goal is to establish "deep" partnerships with its backers, including ASML and new investor Samsung, "across the entire value chain."
He said that Large 4 is capable of designing computer chips, but declined to comment on whether Mistral is currently working with Samsung on chip development.

Cambridge academics say university’s plans to investigate Jason Arday’s death are inadequate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:44:25 UTC
03:44:25 KST

Senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.
In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.
Arday died at his home in London on 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.
An inquest will be held to determine the cause of death.
Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.
Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.
Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.
“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.
The signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.
Cambridge last month announced a two-part review, with part one to be led by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.
The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.
The group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.
They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.
“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.
“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”
The University of Cambridge was approached for its response to the letter.
Cambridge publicised Arday’s appointment at the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would “inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area”.
Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.
