Tuareg rebels withdraw from strategic town of Kidal in northern Mali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:46:52 UTC
02:46:52 KST

Tuareg rebels withdraw from strategic town of Kidal in northern Mali
The Azawad Liberation Front said sustained air strikes by Malian troops and Russian allies forced its tactical retreat.
Mali’s Tuareg rebels have announced they are withdrawing from the strategic town of Kidal, in the north of the country.
The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), a coalition formed in 2024 uniting Tuareg and northern separatist factions, said in a statement on Tuesday that it had decided to carry out a “controlled withdrawal” from Kidal six months after capturing the town and amid fresh air strikes by Mali’s military backed by Russian fighters.
“The FLA specifies that this is a temporary operational measure, also intended to preserve its human and logistical capabilities intact. This methodical withdrawal from the area took place without any direct combat having yet pitted its forces against the enemy,” the statement said.
Earlier on Tuesday, Mali’s military said it had launched large-scale air and ground operations in the region around Kidal.
The goals of the operations included “tracking down and neutralizing” armed groups in the area, destroying their supply networks, and restoring “lasting security” and free movement for people and goods, a Malian military statement said.
Pro-government fighters, including Russian paramilitaries, re-entered Kidal on Tuesday afternoon, a security source said.
Mali has been gripped by conflict since 2012, when a Tuareg separatist rebellion in the north was overtaken by al-Qaeda-linked Islamist militants, who later consolidated under Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in 2017.
While the FLA presents itself as a secular nationalist movement seeking independence for Mali’s Azawad region and JNIM is an al-Qaeda-affiliated group, the two sides have set ideological differences aside to confront the Malian government.
The FLA says it remains committed to independence for Azawad, the name separatists use for northern Mali, while JNIM says it is fighting to “liberate” Mali and overthrow the government.
The military has ruled the country since a 2021 coup, pledging to restore order and unity.
JNIM has gained in strength since the Malian soldiers who seized power expelled French forces and some 15,000 United Nations peacekeepers, and turned to Russian paramilitaries for defence support.
Since the FLA and JNIM launched a joint offensive in April, the conflict has escalated with increasing attacks on the military-backed government forces.
The Malian government says it is working to restore state authority and dismantle what it calls a “terrorist alliance” between the FLA and JNIM.

5,236 amendments submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — Parliament says it is a record
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:45:28 EEST
02:45:28 KST

5,236 amendments submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — Parliament says it is a record
Kyiv • UNN
5,236 amendments were submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — 1.5 times more than last year. Two-thirds were called legislative spam.
A record 5,236 amendments were submitted to the draft law "On the State Budget of Ukraine for 2027," which is 1.5 times more than last year. This was reported by MP Roksolana Pidlasa, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budgetary Matters, UNN reports.
Members of Parliament submitted 5,236 amendments to the 2027 budget bill. This is 1.5 times more than last year and a record for at least 24 years (statistics have generally been kept since the 2003 budget)
According to her, two-thirds of these amendments are so-called "legislative spam," submitted in order to speak for hours in the plenary hall or to demand that desired amendments be taken into account.
If at least 90 seconds are spent on each amendment, their consideration will take more than 16 full working days. Clearly, amendments to draft laws are necessary, but there must be common sense in everything. Alongside the budget, the Rada must also vote on other laws that are critical for receiving international funding
Additional information
On Tuesday, September 15, the Cabinet of Ministers submitted to the Verkhovna Rada the draft State Budget for 2027. This draft budget allocates UAH 4 trillion 885 billion for defense alone, amounting to almost 44% of GDP.
On September 16, the draft law was presented in the Verkhovna Rada chamber. In accordance with the procedure, by October 1, MPs, committees, and factions study the document and submit their proposals to the Committee on Budgetary Matters. The Accounting Chamber prepares its expert opinion.
The Accounting Chamber stated that the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external borrowing, but potential creditors have not yet been identified.
After that, the Verkhovna Rada considers the draft law on the State Budget of Ukraine for the following year in the first reading no later than October 20. However, according to MPs, consideration of the draft law is not planned for the nearest plenary session, which is to take place from October 12 to 16.
"It will be brought forward for October 26–30; Monday the 26th has already also been declared a plenary day to begin consideration of the amendments," MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported.
Adoption of the draft law in the first reading means approval of the Conclusions and Proposals concerning the draft law, which become binding for the Cabinet of Ministers to revise. Within 14 days after the draft law is adopted in the first reading, the government revises the draft budget, taking into account the Budget Conclusions of the Verkhovna Rada, and submits it to parliament for the second reading.
Consideration in the second reading must take place by November 20. The following are adopted in the second reading:
-  the maximum amount of the annual state budget deficit (surplus), the maximum amount of public debt, and the maximum amount of state guarantees to be provided; 
-  the total amount of state budget revenues, expenditures, and lending;  
-  the minimum wage for the relevant budget period, the subsistence minimum for the relevant budget period calculated per month per person, as well as separately for the main social and demographic groups of the population, and the level of subsistence minimum provision for the relevant budget period; 
-  budget allocations for intergovernmental transfers and other provisions necessary for the preparation of local budgets. 
By December 1, the Verkhovna Rada votes on the bill in the third reading and adopts the document as a whole.

France’s Mistral unveils ‘Le Chonk’, its latest model in sovereign AI push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:44:58 UTC
02:44:58 KST

France’s Mistral unveils ‘Le Chonk’, its latest model in sovereign AI push
- - Mistral launched “Le Chonk”, its biggest open-weight model, to give enterprises and governments more control over data, compute and AI operations.
- - The model can be downloaded or used on Mistral’s servers, and the company says it offers stronger security and lower costs than closed models.
- - Built on 4,000 Nvidia chips in Europe, Chonk is aimed at private, sovereign AI use and supports more than 160 languages.
AI generated
PARIS - French AI startup Mistral announced on Oct 6 its biggest open-weight model, dubbed “Le Chonk”, claiming enhanced performance and security capabilities for clients seeking to keep their data private instead of relying on closed models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.
The new model lets users download and customise the parameters, or “weights”, that determine how it computes to their own servers.
It is Mistral’s first major product launch since it raised €3 billion (S$4.3 billion) in September in Europe’s biggest technology fund-raising ever.
The company is betting that companies and governments will increasingly want total control over their AI deployments, as opposed to using proprietary models that require handing over data to third parties and can be much more expensive.
“Enterprises across financial services, manufacturing and the public sector can govern the intelligence, data, compute and operations underpinning their critical infrastructure... without exposing their most valuable knowledge to anyone outside their own walls,” the company said in a statement.
“That one took some groundwork,” Mistral’s chief executive Arthur Mensch posted on X.
“Trained and served on our own compute, and RL shows no sign of saturation,” he wrote, referring to reinforcement learning to further develop AI models, and the possibility that adding further data starts to produce diminishing performance returns.
Open-weight models are also touted as more secure, a growing concern after several incidents of AI agents going rogue by hacking databases or otherwise doing things they were not supposed to do.
“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral’s chief scientist Guillaume Lample said in the statement.
Data ‘under their control’
Mistral, considered Europe’s leading AI developer, was valued at over €21 billion in September’s funding round – far below the valuations for US giants like OpenAI or the AI operations of Google, Meta and SpaceX.
Anthropic is reportedly preparing an initial public share offering in the coming weeks that could see it valued at US$2 trillion.
But their so-called closed models that currently dominate the market are facing growing competition from open-weight models, largely from Chinese developers including DeepSeek and Moonshot.
These AI versions can be fine-tuned by clients for specific needs on in-house infrastructure, and used at a fraction of the cost.
Mistral’s new model also comes as a US open-weight rival, Reflection AI, announced its own widely anticipated Beam model on Oct 5, also promising cheaper operating costs.
Mistral said Chonk’s scores on performance benchmarks so far make it one of the best open-weight models available, and “by far the best in Europe and the US”.
It said the model, which is still being refined, was built on 4,000 Nvidia chips over two months at its own data centres in Europe.
Customers can either download the model to their own servers, or access it via Mistral’s infrastructure, including in “our European sovereign region where data stays under EU jurisdiction to ensure data remains under their control”.
Mistral said the model was trained on more than 160 languages, and can answer prompts and questions in each one natively. AFP

UN Human Rights Council adopts Poland's resolution on artificial intelligence in public administration
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:44:30 CEST
02:44:30 KST

UN Human Rights Council adopts Poland's resolution on artificial intelligence in public administration
06.10.2026
On 6 October 2026, the UN Human Rights Council adopted without a vote the resolution on good governance prepared by Poland. For the first time in the Council's history, a document of this kind sets out principles for the responsible use of artificial intelligence by public institutions with full respect for human rights.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in public offices, the judiciary and public services around the world. These technologies make institutions more effective, but if used improperly they may lead to erroneous or discriminatory decisions.
The resolution calls on States to assess the impact of such systems before deploying them, to ensure transparency and human oversight of decisions, and to guarantee the right to challenge them. It also underlines the need to preserve access to public services for people who do not use digital channels.
The resolution provides for the UN to develop practical guidance for public administrations on the responsible use of artificial intelligence. It will support all countries, including those still developing their digital public services.
Poland initiated the resolution on good governance in 2008 and has led work on it in the Council ever since. This year’s text was prepared together with Australia, Chile, the Republic of Korea and South Africa, and co-sponsored by 58 countries from all regions of the world. Its adoption without a vote confirms the effectiveness of Polish diplomacy in building agreement across divides and Poland’s role in shaping international standards for new technologies.
The Human Rights Council, composed of 47 States elected by the UN General Assembly, is the foremost United Nations forum for the protection of human rights worldwide – and Poland is seeking a seat on it for the 2029–2031 term.

A 28-year-old plague researcher died in Russia. Authorities have imposed a quarantine but deny any threat of plague, and locals are struggling to make sense of it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:41:31 UTC
02:41:31 KST

A 28-year-old plague researcher died in Russia. Authorities have imposed a quarantine but deny any threat of plague, and locals are struggling to make sense of it.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of a plague research institute, died overnight on October 1–2 in Shelekhov, a city just outside Irkutsk. Authorities then isolated about 200 people who had been in contact with her and imposed quarantine restrictions at the hospital where she had been admitted a couple of days before her death. Around the same time, media outlets and social media users began circulating reports that she had died of pneumonic plague after contracting it at her institute. Almost immediately, however, pro-government outlets deleted these reports from their websites, and authorities began denying that plague was involved, saying Shipilova had died of pneumonia.
The news outlet People of Baikal traveled to Irkutsk and Shelekhov to investigate whether negligence could have caused Shipilova’s death and whether local residents believed there was a threat of plague. Meduza is translating its report in full.
“The smell was unbearable, really acrid,” a resident of the building, a woman around 40, tells People of Baikal. She thinks it was a strong disinfectant. Residents opened the doors to the stairwell because “you could barely breathe.”
The people who arrived told residents that “Rospotrebnadzor sent us,” referring to Russia’s consumer protection and public health agency. “We asked what happened. They told us some young woman had died from a deadly virus,” the woman told People of Baikal. “They didn’t know anything else. They said, ‘We came to work, they told us to go disinfect the place, so we came and disinfected it.’”
Residents did not yet know that their neighbor, 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, had died at Shelekhov District Hospital overnight on October 1–2. She worked at the Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Immediately after her death, reports spread across the Irkutsk region that she had died of pneumonic plague.
Since then, the building where Darya lived has been disinfected twice more. None of the workers mentioned a “deadly virus” again. They still wore gas masks while disinfecting the building, but this time they were in white protective suits.
“The second time, a woman from their team knocked on our door and asked for water to mix the solution,” Shipilova’s neighbor recalled. “I said, ‘What are you spraying for?’ By then I knew everything [about the plague rumors]. She goes, ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t have any cockroaches in our building. Then I see her packing her little [protective] suit into a bag. I’m like, ‘Well, that explains it.’”
‘A woman who may have died of plague’
An employee of the plague institute, speaking anonymously, told People of Baikal that Darya Shipilova developed cold symptoms at work. “She didn’t have a fever, but then she got worse and developed swelling.”
Shipilova was hospitalized on September 29 and died at Shelekhov Hospital overnight on October 1–2. Officials have not explained why she was taken there. Most likely, it was because the inpatient facility had previously been used as a COVID hospital.
Immediately after Shipilova’s death, Shelekhov Hospital was placed under quarantine. Governor Igor Kobzev said the reason was “a particularly dangerous infection.” Official statements did not mention the word “plague.”
That same day, October 2, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and Russia’s chief public health officer, flew to Irkutsk. She attended an emergency meeting of the regional commission responsible for public health and epidemic prevention. Officials, doctors, and law enforcement and security personnel approved an “emergency action plan” at the meeting.
People who had been in contact with Darya were isolated and placed under medical observation. Authorities did not disclose the exact number. The television channel REN TV reported that there were about 200, but deleted its posts that same day. The people who had been in contact with Shipilova were housed in at least two hospitals in Irkutsk and Shelekhov.
People of Baikal’s sources in law enforcement and security agencies said her contacts were taken away in ambulances escorted by the Federal Security Service, or FSB.
An Irkutsk resident told People of Baikal that her friend, a nurse at Shelekhov Hospital, had been quarantined. “Everyone there was worried. The bosses were freaking out, and that means things are bad,” she said, quoting her friend.
Employees of the plague institute were isolated inside the institute itself. One employee told People of Baikal: “They quarantined 200 of us. Kept us there for three days, took swabs twice a day. But they did feed us. We slept on chairs, and those who didn’t have a spot slept on their jackets. I slept on my jacket. We didn’t sign any documents. They let us go on Sunday.”
There was no official information about what had happened to Darya. On the afternoon of October 2, Irkutsk journalist Pavel Stepanov wrote that, according to his information, Shipilova had “broken a test tube with a pneumonic plague sample in it” and “concealed what happened.” This account spread widely but has yet to be confirmed. Rumors that Darya had visited Buryatia shortly before her death also circulated online.
On Friday evening, October 2, Buryatia’s leader, Alexey Tsydenov, denied that she had visited the region. More significantly, he became the first official to mention plague, saying that the “woman who died of plague in the Irkutsk region” had not visited Buryatia. That same day, however, Tsydenov edited his post to read “a woman who may have died of plague.”
‘She was very afraid of infecting anyone’
Darya Shipilova was born and raised in Irkutsk. In high school, she decided to become a doctor. A former classmate tells People of Baikal she was “smart, honest, and responsible.” Others who spoke to the outlet, including her colleagues, also call Darya “responsible.”
“Dasha was really anxious about infecting anyone if something went wrong. You could tell from how often she disinfected her hands, even outside work,” says a colleague at the plague institute.
In the summer of 2022, Darya graduated from Irkutsk State Medical University with a degree in medical biochemistry. That same year, she joined the Irkutsk Plague Institute, where she had previously interned. She initially worked as a laboratory assistant and became a researcher a year and a half later.
Darya continued her studies, entering a residency program in clinical laboratory diagnostics. The plague institute paid for her training. Shipilova completed her residency with honors in 2024. She worked in the plague microbiology department until at least January 2025.
In the spring, Shipilova and her colleagues from the institute spoke at the annual All-Russian Congress on Infectious Diseases in Moscow. She gave a presentation titled “Studying the Antibiotic Susceptibility of Yersinia pestis from Natural Plague Foci in Siberia.”
Darya’s interests extended beyond science. At 17, she graduated from music school. In 2025, she and other institute employees took part in the “Songs of Victory” competition for employees of the regional Rospotrebnadzor office. They performed the song “Maisky vals” (“May Waltz”). A year later, Shipilova and her colleagues won the “Musical Entertainment ABC” quiz. In August 2026, Shipilova took part in drills for public health emergency rapid response teams.
“Dasha was really smart,” says an Irkutsk resident who studied in the same department as Shipilova. “Not many people from our department get jobs at the plague institute. I did an internship there. It’s a serious facility. They take everything seriously, and it’s safe.”
Darya lived in a two-story brick building in an outlying neighborhood of Irkutsk. The neighborhood is considered rough. The building is surrounded by old wooden barracks-style housing, and many of the buildings are 60 to 70 years old.
Neighbors call Shipilova “calm” and her parents, who visited their daughter often, “quiet people who don’t drink.” Darya had a dachshund in her apartment, and her father often walked it.
Darya was very close to her mother. Like her daughter, Svetlana Shipilova works in health care. Rumors have spread among Darya’s neighbors that Svetlana “couldn’t bear her daughter’s death and died of a heart attack.” That is not true: Her mother, like other family members, is still quarantined at a hospital in the city.
How pro-government outlets published and deleted reports
On October 2, the pro-government newspaper Izvestia reported that following Darya Shipilova’s death, authorities in Irkutsk had opened a criminal investigation under Part 2 of Article 236 of the Criminal Code — “Violation of public health and epidemic prevention rules resulting in a person’s death through negligence.” Izvestia soon deleted the report, along with other articles about a possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk.
The Kazan branch of Argumenty i Fakty deleted a report on the death of the Irkutsk laboratory assistant that it had published on October 2. The article remained in the Yandex search engine’s cache. The Kuzbass edition of Moskovsky Komsomolets deleted a report that Rospotrebnadzor had denied Irkutsk hospitals were being placed under quarantine. That article also remained in Yandex’s cache.
Government agencies also deleted information. On the morning of October 3, the Baikalsk administration recommended that residents temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov, citing “unofficial information” that plague had been detected there. Two hours later, city authorities deleted the post.
That same day, management at the Irkutsk Aluminum Smelter, Shelekhov’s main employer, introduced a mask requirement on its premises. “Contradictory information about the plague situation is circulating in Shelekhov,” director Artyom Fominykh said. A day later, Fominykh said in another post that “the mask requirement at IrkAZ is unrelated to the quarantine at Shelekhov Hospital” and was prompted by respiratory illnesses.
“All our employees know this isn’t the first time. We bring back mask requirements from time to time during cold and flu season,” the plant’s director wrote, urging people “not to spread rumors.”
Throughout Saturday, October 3, authorities issued no official statements. Governor Kobzev posted on his Telegram channel about a forum for young workers and a meeting with the head of Russia’s health care regulator, Roszdravnadzor. There was not a word about the suspected plague that the whole city was discussing.
Meanwhile, several municipal hospitals in Irkutsk introduced quarantines. These included City Clinical Hospitals No. 1, 3, and 10, as well as the city’s Ivano-Matreninskaya Children’s Clinical Hospital.
Irkutsk Regional Clinical Hospital stopped admitting visitors on October 3, according to a patient. “The sister of a seriously ill patient in my room used to visit her. Since Saturday, staff have been bringing everyone’s care packages up, and they brought mine right to the room. Today I went downstairs for a food delivery. They wouldn’t let the delivery driver past the security desk.”
Over the weekend, residents bought up antibiotics at pharmacies in Irkutsk and Shelekhov. “There were fights at some pharmacies on Saturday,” an employee of the plague institute tells People of Baikal. “They cleaned the pharmacies out of antibiotics! Even the really, really old ones. People were panicking because everywhere you heard the words ‘plague’ and ‘pneumonic.’”
‘Listen, the situation is completely under control’
Rospotrebnadzor did not comment officially until Sunday afternoon, October 4. The agency told TASS that the plague institute employee had suffered from “pneumonia of unknown cause.” It also said no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms had occurred at the institute. Rospotrebnadzor did not publish any statements on its own platforms.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, institute employees had not sought medical care for infectious diseases. Among those who had been in contact with Darya, two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection were detected.
“Pneumonia of unknown cause” means that a patient had inflammation of the lungs, but doctors could not identify the specific microorganism that caused it: a bacterium, virus, or fungus. Rospotrebnadzor did not explain this in its statement or address why hundreds of people had been quarantined over pneumonia.
On the evening of October 4, Governor Kobzev repeated Rospotrebnadzor’s statement on his Telegram channel. The next day, he said that “the public health situation in Irkutsk and Shelekhov District is currently stable.”
On Monday, October 5, Kobzev said in a video statement: “Listen, the situation is completely under control. It’s unpleasant, of course, but the doctors and Rospotrebnadzor have done everything possible to make sure all of them [people who had contact with Shipilova] are under observation. Life goes on in the city, and life goes on in Shelekhov.”
That same day, Vladimir Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people to listen only to Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements, rather than trust rumors and speculation about plague online.
“Rospotrebnadzor is staffed by highly qualified professionals in this field. Let’s listen to their official statements,” the Kremlin spokesman said.
Residents of the Irkutsk region bought up antibiotics and protective masks over the weekend
On October 5, U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States was ready to help Russia following reports of suspected pneumonic plague. Trump said that in Russia, “they call it pneumonia.”
On October 6, the Shelekhov district administration responded to Trump’s offer. Deputy Mayor Yelena Sofyina said: “Let me answer directly. We can handle this ourselves. The situation is completely under control.”
‘They went into quarantine just in case’
Authorities insist there is no plague in the region and that hospitals are operating as usual, but quarantine measures remain in place. On October 5, People of Baikal learned of restrictions at a psychiatric clinic in Irkutsk. A source told the outlet it was “something like a quarantine”: “They say they introduced it just in case.” The clinic had made no official announcement of the restrictions or posted any notices. A patient learned of them from a security guard when he tried to go to a store.
The Irkutsk Perinatal Center also introduced access restrictions. Blogger Ulyana Gavryunina reported them on social media and confirmed them to People of Baikal. On October 5, she arrived for a checkup. Her mother, who accompanied her, was not allowed into the maternity hospital. Since Friday, the center has admitted only pregnant patients.
“[At the hospital] they explained that there’s still unconfirmed information about a virus that might even be worse than coronavirus, and they don’t yet know what kind of virus it is or how to handle it, with the babies being so little. That’s why they introduced the quarantine. And no one knows how long it’ll last,” Ulyana told People of Baikal.
At the entrance, staff took Ulyana’s temperature and asked her to show her tongue. They gave her two health checklists to fill out. One was titled “Checklist for a suspected particularly dangerous infection: ‘Plague.’”
The checklist asked how the pregnant patient felt, whether she had been in contact with anyone who had arrived from abroad or was ill, and whether she had a fever or a stuffy nose.
The center barred partners from attending births during the quarantine. Ulyana had chosen to pay to give birth there so she could have someone with her. Now she is considering canceling her contract and wants to give birth in Angarsk, where she lives, because in Irkutsk “things feel unsettled, it’s really inconvenient and stressful, and there’s no point anymore.” In Angarsk, “everything is calm,” both in the city and at the maternity hospital.
An employee of the Irkutsk Plague Institute believes the city’s hospitals went into quarantine “just in case.” “Our scientists are working around the clock now. Samples just keep coming in. That’s because everyone admitted to a hospital with any signs of a cold is swabbed [for plague] and tested. That goes for absolutely every hospital.”
‘There are still no final findings on her death’
The Irkutsk Plague Institute is not commenting officially. An employee does not believe Darya broke a test tube in the laboratory: “That doesn’t happen here. But even if she had broken one, you’re working in a sealed containment cabinet, in sealed protective gear. Nothing would happen at all.”
A former university classmate of Shipilova’s who interned at the plague institute agrees: “Besides the strict safety measures, everyone there gets vaccinated against plague — even students who come for internships.” The medical professional says: “I can’t even imagine what could have happened there, even in theory.”
The plague institute’s employees have now been released from quarantine. “They took swabs from everyone for three days in a row, but everyone is completely healthy. Today is a normal workday for us,” one of Shipilova’s colleagues told People of Baikal on Monday, October 5. “Things are calm.”
Speaking anonymously, she said several times that “there are still no final findings [on the causes of Darya’s death].” “Tests are still being done, and there are no results at all yet. They’re still trying to determine the cause of death. Everything will settle down in a week, when the results are ready.”
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
‘The theory that there was no outbreak is unconvincing’
A Russian physician, who asked to remain anonymous, tells People of Baikal that he sees two possible explanations for what happened. Either Darya Shipilova was indeed found to have plague (or another particularly dangerous infection), but officials “contained it and decided not to talk about it publicly.” Or authorities and doctors still do not know exactly what happened, are “conducting an epidemiological and laboratory investigation,” and fear “panic and being held responsible.”
The physician finds the theory that there was no outbreak unconvincing. “A young employee of a plague institute suddenly develops a severe infection and quickly dies. Afterward, the hospital is closed, and the institute’s employees and her relatives are isolated. And an epidemiological investigation is conducted. That doesn’t prove it was plague, but it gives journalists sufficient grounds to investigate that possibility.”
The doctor suspects that “some potentially significant epidemiological event” did occur at the plague institute. He says the internal investigation and the isolation of a large number of employees point to this. Darya may not have realized that she had been at risk of exposure. Or she may have known about an incident but underestimated its seriousness.
The physician is skeptical of Rospotrebnadzor’s statement that Shipilova’s illness was “unrelated to her work.” Definitive laboratory confirmation takes up to 10 days. That time is needed to test blood, sputum, tissue, and other samples from Shipilova’s body.
“You can’t definitively identify the pathogen in a single day after the autopsy,” the physician said.
A former university classmate of Darya Shipilova’s who interned at the plague institute and now works at an Irkutsk hospital told People of Baikal the same thing. She called Rospotrebnadzor’s official reference to “extensive laboratory testing” in Shipilova’s case “rather vague wording.”
“It all depends on the testing method. And nowhere have they said exactly which test they performed.”
‘I’ve saved patients like that, but they let my daughter die’
Darya’s mother, 64-year-old Svetlana Shipilova, was still quarantined at an Irkutsk hospital on October 5. She told the outlet Glubina that samples and swabs were being taken from her every day. “They’re testing for something, looking for something. Maybe they’re worried about some other infection, so we don’t catch COVID or something in here.”
Shipilova said that as of October 5, she still had not received an official report on her daughter’s death. “I’m waiting for something official,” she said. “Not just something in the media, but from Rospotrebnadzor. It has to be an official document.”
Svetlana says she is “having a very hard time” and does not want to “read nasty things about my child”: “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid people I know who believed all this. The smart ones didn’t believe it, of course. Even some medical professionals don’t understand that it’s impossible to break that test tube. Even if you fling it against a wall. Only someone who doesn’t know what they’re talking about could say that. Even hypothetically, you simply can’t spill what’s inside or break the tube. They’re that well protected.”
People who knew Darya also do not believe she could have broken a test tube. “They dragged her name through the mud without even finding out what happened,” a former schoolmate says. A friend tells People of Baikal: “I can’t square this whole story with the Dasha I knew. It’s like they’re talking about someone else. Knowing how hardworking and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”
Svetlana Shipilova calls her daughter “a hard worker”: “Such a pure, pure soul. Her boss is taking it hard because she knew Dasha and knew why she hired her. It’s really hard to get a job at the plague institute. She saw how Dasha worked when she was interning there. She realized what a pure soul she was, such a workaholic,” she says. “I’ve saved more than one patient like that, but they didn’t save my daughter. They just let my daughter die.”
Darya has not been buried, and it’s not clear when the funeral will be. “Who’s going to bury her when we’re locked up in here?” her mother says.
Darya’s neighbors are worried that “no swabs at all” have been taken from them. “The clinic has called me every day since Friday to ask how I’m feeling. They say if I develop symptoms, I have to see a doctor. But no one tells us anything — what the illness was, what’s going on at all. It’s like we don’t exist. We’re shocked they haven’t quarantined us. We’ve all been in contact with her. We probably shouldn’t be going to work. We should be staying home.”
A notice at the building’s entrance asks residents who were not home during the disinfection to call the phone numbers listed “due to a sharp increase in illness in your building.” Among them is the number for the internal medicine department at Irkutsk City Hospital No. 10.
The residents who spoke to People of Baikal’s reporters say they feel well and have no symptoms.
‘There’s no panic in Shelekhov’
There is “no panic” in Shelekhov, where Darya Shipilova died, one resident tells People of Baikal. We arrived on a weekday, after the governor’s statements that the situation was stable. Mothers were walking with their children in the city park, and teenagers were riding bicycles. In stores, the shopping center, the local café, and the park, no one was wearing a mask. A few people wore them on buses — mainly older women and children.
The local café is busy at lunchtime. The word “plague” drifts over from just one table, where two women are eating and talking quietly. Everyone else is talking about other things.
The registration area at the Shelekhov outpatient clinic is packed with visitors. The clinic is operating as usual. Receptionists sit at desks, with visitors across from them and no protective glass screens between them. The electronic appointment system malfunctions: The terminals freeze, then print out stacks of tickets, slowing down registration. Only sample collection has been suspended since October 2. A notice still hangs on the procedure room door: “No blood samples will be taken due to quarantine,” followed by five exclamation points. The receptionists do not know when collection will resume.
The inpatient facility, a four-story brick building on the hospital campus, is closed for now and expected to remain so until the end of the week, the receptionists say.
A colorful banner on the inpatient building reads: “Doctors serving in the special military operation,” the Kremlin’s term for the war in Ukraine.
The plastic-framed windows are open, but no patients are visible near them. The door is wide open too. A trash can on the threshold and a mop handle across the doorway are meant to stop visitors from walking in. There are no quarantine notices, only a notice about access restrictions.
A female security guard in a black uniform came out to meet us. Her only protective gear was an ordinary face mask from a pharmacy.
“Is it really plague?” the journalist asks her.
“Who’s going to tell us? We only read about it online. A particularly dangerous infection — that’s all,” she replies.
There is a pharmacy at the hospital. The journalist asks for antibiotics and says plainly: “I want to keep some at home in case of a plague epidemic.” The pharmacist is not surprised. She initially offers a drug costing 680 rubles, but then sells the cheapest one, for 100 rubles. Antibiotics are available, and there is no rush to buy them.
At a pharmacy on the other side of town, another pack of inexpensive antibiotics is sold without anyone asking for a prescription. A mask requirement notice is posted on the door, but the pharmacist is not wearing a mask. The notice has been there since 2020, she says, laughing conspiratorially: “But I didn’t wear a mask back then either.”
At the entrance to the Irkutsk Aluminum Smelter (IrkAZ), however, even the groundskeepers sweeping up leaves are wearing masks. This is Shelekhov’s main employer. Its director introduced a mask requirement on October 3, and it remains in place.
When the shift ended, all the workers filed toward the gate. All were wearing masks and took them off only once they were past the gate.

‘Mike Rogers Is Watching You’: New Ad Blitz From Abdul El-Sayed Attacks Surveillance Support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:39:48 UTC
02:39:48 KST

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Michigan race for the US Senate, launched a new ad blitz on Tuesday attacking his opponent Mike Rogers for helping expand the government’s mass surveillance powers while he was in Congress.
The paid digital video and billboard ads mark a final-stretch effort ahead of the midterm elections to pin bipartisan voter anxieties about privacy concerns, recently spurred by Flock cameras, onto Rogers.
The video from the El-Sayed campaign intersperses clips of Rogers praising the Patriot Act of 2001, which, in addition to expanding law enforcement powers, also allowed the collection of Americans' telephone data without a warrant after the September 11 terrorist attacks.
Rogers’ career is dotted with support for government surveillance over the years, including in 2011, when Rogers introduced a bill that would have allowed companies to share emails with the National Security Agency. (In 2014, however, Rogers introduced a bill that would have ended “bulk collection of metadata,” though it never made it to a vote.)
“You can’t have your privacy violated if you don’t know your privacy is violated,” the ad repeatedly quotes Rogers as saying in 2013, when he served as chair of the House Intelligence committee.
The video also includes Rogers’ remarks extolling surveillance by companies like Google.
In addition to the video, the El-Sayed campaign will run billboards with the tagline “Mike Rogers is watching you” in parts of Michigan, according to the El-Sayed campaign.
In tying Rogers to surveillance concerns, El-Sayed is leaning into one of the major technology-related complaints from voters this cycle as he battles in a Senate race rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.
Among other privacy concerns surrounding AI, voters have increasingly voiced skepticism of law enforcement surveillance products like those of Flock cameras, which have begun to rapidly proliferate across the nation. While police agencies argue Flock has helped reduce crime, recent cases of abuse by individual officers to stalk ex-girlfriends and incidents of suspects being misidentified have sparked growing public opposition.
A spokesperson for Rogers’ campaign has previously said Rogers “vehemently opposes unchecked use of Flock cameras to track law-abiding citizens” and noted he left Congress before the technology was founded in 2017.
But the new slate of ads underscores the El-Sayed campaign's unrelenting effort to draw a line from Rogers’ legislative record to current voter anxieties.
This kind of strategy appears to have proven effective in other close Senate races, like in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown cast incumbent Republican Jon Husted as “the face of data centers” in the state, according to a recent GOP memo.
El-Sayed’s race against Rogers has remained close, and most paths to Democrats taking the majority in the Senate rely on El-Sayed keeping the Michigan Senate seat in his party's hands.
As part of a blitz to rebuild the Democratic coalition fragmented by the primary, where El-Sayed has weathered attacks of antisemitism after he called the war in Gaza a genocide and pushed for an end to US military aid to Israel, El-Sayed announced on Monday he will rally with former president Barack Obama in late October.
El-Sayed is also expected to launch an extended campaign swing through the state in the final weeks before the midterms with progressive allies, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a source familiar with the matter said.

Focus must now be on taking digital literacy, financial literacy to every citizen: Uttarakhand CM
Dehradun (Uttarakhand) [India], October 6 (ANI): Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami participated in a programme organised at the Mukhya Sevak Sadan at the Chief Minister's Camp Office on Tuesday to mark Uttarakhand becoming a fully literate state.On the occasion, the Chief Minister felicitated neo-literates who successfully cleared the examination conducted by the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS).The Chief Minister said the achievement was the result of the hard work and collective participation of teachers, students, neo-literates, volunteers and everyone associated with the campaign while congratulating the people of Uttarakhand on the state becoming the sixth fully literate state in the country.He said achieving the goal of full literacy in Uttarakhand, with its challenging geographical terrain and remote areas, reflected the strong determination and collective strength of the people of the state.The Chief Minister said Uttarakhand had achieved the distinction of becoming a fully literate state under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the ULLAS-Nav Bharat Saaksharta Programme."After Mizoram, Goa, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim, Uttarakhand has become the sixth fully literate state in the country," he said.
He said the achievement would further strengthen the state's resolve to emerge as a leader in education and other sectors.Congratulating the neo-literates, the Chief Minister said they had demonstrated that there is no age limit for learning and that it is never too late to move forward."Education not only instils confidence in individuals but also opens up new opportunities in their lives," he said.He said literacy is no longer limited to reading, writing or signing one's name. "In the changing times, awareness of rights and duties, digital and financial literacy, and life skills are also important components of literacy."The Chief Minister said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, continuous efforts are being made to make education more inclusive and modern across the country. He said that the Prime Minister's vision is to ensure that no person remains deprived of education and an educated person not only transforms their own life but also contributes significantly to the progress of their family, society and nation.He said the state government was focusing on improving the quality of education as well as the overall development of students."Under the Nanda Gaura Yojana, eligible girl students are being provided financial assistance. Virtual classrooms and a central studio are being established in 500 schools across the state to ensure that students in remote areas also have access to quality education. As many as 189 Atal Utkrisht Schools are being operated in the state. Under the Mukhyamantri Balashray Yojana, free education is being ensured for orphaned children. Work is also underway to develop modern laboratories in 100 schools each at the high school and intermediate levels," CM Dhami said.The Chief Minister said the achievement of full literacy should not be viewed as a destination but as a new beginning."The focus must now be on taking digital literacy, financial literacy, health awareness and life skills to every citizen. Continuous efforts will be made to ensure that every citizen of the state keeps pace with changing technology and is able to use it to improve their quality of life," he said.Education Minister Dhan Singh Rawat said Uttarakhand had achieved the significant milestone of becoming a fully literate state under the leadership of Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami. He said around 25,000 volunteers had made an important contribution to the success of the campaign.
"The state has now set a target of achieving 100 per cent literacy over the next six months".He said the National Education Policy 2020 has set a national target of increasing the Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education to 50 per cent by 2035, and Uttarakhand is moving rapidly towards achieving this target this year itself.The Education Minister said the state government was committed to ensuring access to education for every child. He added that no school would be closed in a village as long as even a single child in that village is enrolled as a student. (ANI)

'Israelis had no warning': Biden aide Brett McGurk reveals how October 7 shook the White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:37:45 UTC
02:37:45 KST

On the morning of October 7, 2023, former White House coordinator for the Middle East Brett McGurk walked into the Oval Office and immediately understood that something unprecedented was happening. The full scale of the Hamas attack was not yet known, and the White House was struggling to establish what exactly had happened.
Former president Joe Biden looked pale. "He was just like, this is the last thing he expected and wanted,” McGurk recalls in an interview with The Jerusalem Post, discussing his new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, which chronicles the Biden administration’s handling of the hostage crisis.
Biden had been preparing for a very different morning. A special prosecutor was expected to question him about classified documents found in his Delaware garage. "I just told the president, ‘This is unprecedented, but we don’t know exactly what we’re dealing with.’”
That uncertainty would soon give way to the defining crisis of Biden’s presidency.
McGurk’s account of October 7, detailed in Brink and discussed in his interview with the Post, begins not on the morning of the massacre but the evening before. On October 6, McGurk had been working toward one of the Biden administration’s biggest diplomatic ambitions: a normalization agreement between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
"I had the Saudis in my office,” he recalls. Saudi Ambassador Princess Reema bint Bandar was there, and the administration hoped to conclude the agreement by the end of the year. "We’re planning on trying to close out that Israel-Saudi deal by the end of the year and rolling it out in the first quarter of 2024,” McGurk said. Secretary of State Antony Blinken was preparing to travel to the region.
Then, after putting his child to bed, McGurk began receiving messages from the White House Situation Room. "We had rockets fired from Gaza.” The following hours transformed everything. "I’m also hearing from Israel’s ambassador here in Washington, Mike Herzog, as this unfolded,” he said. “It was about after midnight, when he said, ‘This is war. We’re at war.’”
The words captured the extraordinary transformation.
Just hours earlier, senior American officials had been discussing peace and normalization. Now they were confronting a war whose dimensions they could barely comprehend.
Was there a warning?
One of the most politically sensitive questions surrounding October 7 has been whether Israel had received advance intelligence indicating that Hamas was preparing a major attack. McGurk said the American intelligence community did not.
The Americans subsequently reviewed their intelligence. "We looked through, in the aftermath, all of our intelligence information,” McGurk said. “Had no warnings or indicators. I say in the book, we had no warning, and the Israelis had no warning from what they told us.”
But that does not mean there was nothing to investigate. "Whenever something like this happens on this scale, there’s always something in the system that should’ve been seen or somebody that knew something and the information didn’t get up,” he said.
For McGurk, Israel needs to conduct the same kind of institutional reckoning that the United States undertook after 9/11. "We reformed our intelligence community. We reformed how intelligence is briefed and categorized,” he said. Israel, he argues, needs “a commission of inquiry of some kind” to determine “what was missed and to make the reforms necessary so that nothing ever gets missed again.”
Biden to McGurk: 'Do anything we can to get these hostages out'
As the scale of the massacre became clearer, McGurk’s mission changed. He was now tasked with helping bring the hostages home. One of the most painful scenes in Brink took place in the Oval Office. Biden met with families of missing Americans and other hostages via a large screen. "It was one of the most gut-wrenching meetings I’ve been in in the Oval Office,” McGurk said.
Then something happened that he said he will never forget. "One woman left the screen, and when she came back, she learned that her loved one was actually confirmed dead.” She began “wailing into the screen” at the president. "Do something. Help us.”
The meeting affected Biden deeply. The president told McGurk that he had worked on hostage deals with Iran before.
"Few things are more difficult in the line of work of diplomacy,” Biden said. Then came the instruction that would define McGurk’s next year. "Do anything we can to get these hostages out.”
The first hostage deal
McGurk began working with CIA Director William Burns and negotiators in Israel, Egypt and Qatar. The negotiations were anything but straightforward. Israel initially believed there were around 75 hostages who might fit the category being discussed. Eventually, the terrorist organization offered to release 20. Israel rejected the proposal.
McGurk traveled to Jerusalem and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Maybe we should just take… Let’s try to get 30 so we can get a process started,” McGurk suggested.
Netanyahu refused. "I have to have at least 50 guaranteed, otherwise Hamas is gonna hold hostages back,’” McGurk recalls the prime minister as saying. Eventually, however, the negotiations succeeded. The first hostage deal was implemented on November 24, 2023.
An eight-day ceasefire followed, and hostages began returning home. Among them was Abigail Edan, the young American-Israeli girl whose parents had been murdered on October 7.
On the eighth day, Hamas refused to release the younger women. Many had been kidnapped from the Nova music festival or from their homes on October 7. McGurk remembers the dilemma. "You know, there’s no real right answer", he said. "The cease-fire had worked. The hostage releases were continuing". But Hamas was refusing to release young women who had been among the most vulnerable hostages. "I kind of want to keep it going,” McGurk said of the cease-fire. But Israel took a different view.
“The Israeli side was unanimous,” he said. “We cannot skip over the younger women, basically potentially signing their death sentences.” The war resumed. "I did not anticipate in that moment,” McGurk said, “that it would take 14 months to get back to that deal.”
McGurk on Hersh Goldberg-Polin: 'We failed that family'
For months, the Americans, Israelis, Egyptians and Qataris continued trying to reach another agreement. McGurk said Israel repeatedly agreed to proposals while Hamas resisted.
In May 2024, one proposal was put on the table and then, on August 16, 2024, another proposal was put forward, backed by Qatar and Egypt. "It went further in the direction of Hamas,” McGurk said. “It was a much better deal for Hamas than what they have today.”
But once again, the negotiators waited. "Again, waiting on Hamas, which I think was very much, unfortunately, the common course.” Then came the news that six hostages had been found dead in a tunnel under Rafah. One of them was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a dual Israeli-US citizen.
McGurk had been expecting potentially good news. Instead, he received a call from Burns.
"I just felt your kind of guts rip out of your body; [your] heart drops,” he said. Then came the emotion that perhaps best captures McGurk’s description of the hostage negotiations. "I felt like a complete failure. Whatever you can say in this process, we failed that family.”
The discovery of the six murdered hostages changed McGurk’s thinking. He concluded that as long as Yahya Sinwar remained in control of the hostage negotiations, a deal was unlikely. "So long as Yahya Sinwar was the one holding the keys to the hostages, we were not going to get a deal,” McGurk said in situation room meeting on August 1 with president Biden. "Sinwar had to be removed from the scene.”
The morning Israel almost struck Hezbollah
Another extraordinary episode in Brink occurred only days after October 7. On October 11, Israeli officials believed Hezbollah was preparing to open a major northern front, and the Israelis were preparing a strike against Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, his senior lieutenants and Iranian advisers.
The stakes were enormous. A strike could potentially trigger a full-scale war with Hezbollah and Iran at a moment when Israel was already fighting Hamas in Gaza.
Then Ron Dermer called Jake Sullivan’s office, then-president Biden's national security advisor. "Ron tells us that the attack has started,” McGurk recalls. “Hezbollah has started its attack with paragliders, very similar to the October 7th attack from Hamas.”
The Israelis were preparing to strike. "We kind of said, ‘Hey, let’s slow down, see what’s going on.’”
Then came an extraordinary back-channel message. A Norwegian intermediary delivered a message from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard: Hezbollah would not launch a new ground front as long as Israel did not do so first. "I don’t trust anything the Iranians tell me,” McGurk emphasizes. But the message mattered. McGurk believes the United States and Israel were not prepared for the consequences of an Israeli strike. "My judgment, we were not set. We were not prepared".
The strike was ultimately called off. The decision remains controversial in Israel. McGurk acknowledges the debate. "I know some [say] maybe they should have done the strike,” he said. But his own conclusion is clear: the timing was wrong.
The confrontation over Iran
The relationship between Biden and Netanyahu became increasingly tense as the war continued. One of the most dramatic confrontations followed the Israeli strike on senior Iranian commanders in Damascus in April 2024. At the same time, Washington and Jerusalem were already deeply divided over the war in Gaza, the planned Israeli operation in Rafah and the World Central Kitchen strike, in which seven aid workers were killed. McGurk describes the atmosphere as a “boiling point.” It was just frustration,” he said.
But another crisis was unfolding behind the scenes. American intelligence was detecting preparations for a direct Iranian attack on Israel. The scale was unprecedented. "We’re seeing the intelligence that Iran is preparing this unbelievable missile and drone attack directly against Israel,” McGurk said.
The United States therefore faced two simultaneous challenges: preventing a regional escalation while preparing to defend Israel. Israeli officials threatened a massive cyber attack against Iran if Israeli would be killed. Biden’s message was effectively: defend Israel, but do not turn the Iranian attack into a wider war. Then came Biden next objective: Let’s try to get back to that hostage and ceasefire process.”
The Iranian attack ultimately involved hundreds of missiles and drones. The joint Israeli-American and regional defensive effort largely succeeded. McGurk sees that episode as a critical turning point. Take the win,” Biden told Netanyahu, according to McGurk’s account. Let’s try to contain this, and let’s get back to that process.
The Haniyeh assassination
The killing of Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran in July 2024 triggered another confrontation. Inside the White House, officials feared that the assassination would destroy the hostage talks. McGurk said Biden believed the killing had put the negotiations at risk and was frustrated with Netanyahu. Netanyahu disagreed.
"The opportunity to kill Haniyeh had been unique," Netanyahu argued in a phone call with president Biden, and added the operation was unrelated to the negotiations. "It could even strengthen Israel’s position"
Biden pressed him to compromise. Netanyahu responded that Biden was not reading the regional map correctly. Biden’s answer was blunt: "This may be the last chance for a deal.”
The disagreement reflected the fundamental problem at the heart of every negotiation. As McGurk puts it: "Hamas’s core demand [was] we stay in power. We go back to October 6th status quo.” "I don’t think any Israeli government could have accepted that.”
"Trying to bridge that is what the story of this book is about," McGurk said.
Witkoff enters the picture
By late 2024, the strategic landscape had changed dramatically. Sinwar had been eliminated. Nasrallah had been eliminated. Israel and Hezbollah had reached a cease-fire. Israel had struck Iran. And Donald Trump had won the presidential election.
McGurk began working closely with Trump’s incoming envoy, Steve Witkoff.
"I worked very closely with Steve Witkoff,” McGurk said. "And without that cooperation, which I think is quite unique in today’s Washington, without that cooperation, we would not have gotten that done.”
The negotiations intensified. Eventually, they reached another hostage deal. But even then, the agreement nearly collapsed. Trump had already announced the deal publicly, while Netanyahu had not yet formally approved it. McGurk described entering the room as Mossad Director David Barnea spoke to Netanyahu.
"What’s going on?” McGurk asked. He was told Netanyahu still needed time. McGurk could hardly believe it. "But we have a deal.” Then Witkoff intervened. His message to the Israelis was explosive: If the deal collapsed, he would publicly say that the Israelis did not want an agreement. Barnea warned that Witkoff had crossed a red line. Witkoff reportedly reached for his phone.
The Israelis asked for more time. Witkoff gave them 3 minutes. Eventually, the problem was resolved. The second agreement went forward. 33 were freed.
Closing the circle
For McGurk, the eventual release of the hostages was deeply personal. Three young women whom Hamas had refused to release in the first hostage agreement – Romi Gonen, Doron Steinbrecher and Emily Damari – finally returned to Israel in January 2025.
It happened on Biden’s final day as president. "It kind of connects this story,” McGurk said. He was in the green room preparing to appear on Face the Nation when he received the news. "I actually got the news of Romi, Doron, and Emily in Israeli hands – the 3 that weren't released in the first deal,” he recalls. He broke the news on television. But even in that moment of relief, McGurk could not forget the months that had passed. "They should have come out in November,” he said.
And perhaps that is the central message of Brink. For McGurk, the story of the hostage negotiations is not one of a single diplomatic breakthrough. It is a story of repeated failure and persistence, of moments when a deal appeared close and then collapsed, of pressure applied behind closed doors and of decisions that could mean life or death for people being held underground.
Looking back, McGurk describes the final agreement with one word: "Relief.” But there is also regret. "I just wish it had… I wish we were able to get there sooner, honestly.” That sentence may ultimately say more about the year after October 7 than any diplomatic victory.
For 24 months, Washington, Jerusalem, Doha and Cairo tried to bridge two fundamentally incompatible demands: Hamas’s insistence on survival and Israel’s insistence that October 7 could never happen again.
In Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, and in his interview with the Post, McGurk offers an unusually intimate view of that struggle – the Oval Office meetings, the midnight calls, the intelligence warnings, the arguments with Netanyahu, the pressure on Hamas and the moments when negotiators wondered whether the process had finally failed. It is a story of diplomacy conducted at the edge of catastrophe.

Russian-made Oxygen Forensics software was used to extract data from Hunter Biden’s laptop, RFE/RL reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:37:12 UTC
02:37:12 KST

Oxygen Forensic Detective, whose Russian version is marketed as “Mobilny Kriminalist,” was used to examine the laptop of Hunter Biden, according to a report by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. In the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the younger Biden faced allegations of corruption and conflicts of interest, including claims based on files taken from his computer.
Former U.S. Secret Service agent Konstantinos “Gus” Dimitrelos discussed his work on the laptop investigation during a presentation in Alexandria, Virginia, in October 2024. RFE/RLobtained video of the event from a former Oxygen Forensics employee.
The Washington Examiner had commissioned Dimitrelos to conduct the analysis and published its findings in May and June 2022. When speaking about that work in 2024, Dimitrelos said:
“Oxygen is my number one tool. It's the only tool that I use. It's the only tool that I teach. I love it.”
Dimitrelos added that he had recovered over 160,000 deleted files, more than any other investigators had found.
Oxygen software has been used by the U.S. Department of Defense, FBI, and Department of Homeland Security, among others. The U.S. Secret Service terminated a five-year contract with the company in February, citing “security risks,” but the State Department nevertheless signed a new contract with Oxygen Forensics in late August.
The same software, sold in Russia under the name “Mobilny Kriminalist,” is supplied to the Federal Security Service (FSB) by Russian company MCO Systems and has been used in politically motivated cases in Russia. On Sept. 23, the U.S. Justice Department charged Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Chief Technology Officer Oleg Davydov of concealing that Russian citizens effectively controlled the company through a Cyprus offshore entity. Reiber was released on bail in Idaho, while Davydov is awaiting extradition to the United States after being detained at London’s Heathrow Airport.
According to prosecutors, the company’s shareholders discussed possible cooperation with the Russian state in early 2023, as evidenced by a document titled “General Staff, Citadel.”
The Insider previously reported that the FSB used “Mobilny Kriminalist” to gain access to the iPhone of RFE/RL journalist Alsu Kurmasheva, who in July 2024 was sentenced to 6.5 years in prison for “spreading false information” about the Russian armed forces. Kurmasheva was subsequently released alongside former U.S. Marine Paul Whelan, Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, and multiple others in a 26-person prisoner exchange between Russia and the West on Aug. 1, 2024.
On Oct. 1 of this year, The Telegraph reported that the London Metropolitan police had used Oxygen software at least 40 times over the previous year to access suspects’ phones. Law enforcement agencies in several European countries have stopped using the company’s software after the reports emerged about the company’s secret Russian owners.

Ex-Ukrainian Lawmaker Sent to Trial Over $1.3 Million Fraud Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:37:00 UTC
02:37:00 KST

Reported by
Ukrainian anti-corruption authorities have sent a case to trial charging former lawmaker Heorhii Lohvynskyi and five others with misappropriating 54.18 million hryvnias (about $1.3 million) in state funds and laundering the proceeds.
Investigators allege that between 2013 and 2016, Lohvynskyi organized a scheme involving Golden Mandarin Oil LLC and a debt dispute with energy company Kyivenergo. The group allegedly used a fraudulent "friendly settlement" at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) to trick the Ukrainian government into paying off a private corporate debt with public money.
According to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), a representative of Golden Mandarin Oil applied to the ECHR seeking payment from the state over a debt Kyivenergo allegedly owed under a 2009 domestic court ruling. Investigators say the company concealed from the ECHR that the legal right to claim the debt had already been transferred to a third party.
NABU alleges that Lohvynskyi colluded with senior Justice Ministry officials to secure the friendly settlement before the European court and trigger the payout from the state budget. The funds were then transferred to a company controlled by members of the scheme and laundered through illicit financial clearing fronts.
The investigation was completed in January.
Among the defendants is Borys Babin, who served as Ukraine’s government representative before the ECHR. Babin denied wrongdoing in a written response to OCCRP.
“I do not admit the charges brought against me and believe that my innocence will be established by the court through due process,” he said.
Babin added that he intends to challenge the prosecution’s claims in court and personally participate in the proceedings. Maintaining the position he has held throughout the inquiry, Babin said that on Oct. 5 he asked the High Anti-Corruption Court to transfer the case to another jurisdiction.
Former First Deputy Justice Minister Nataliia Bernatska also denied wrongdoing. In a statement provided to OCCRP by her lawyer, Denys Shkarovsky, she maintained that she acted strictly within her legal authority and never made unlawful decisions or pressured other officials. Bernatska said she did not approve the settlement with Golden Mandarin Oil, stating that the decision rested solely with the government’s ECHR representative acting within his own powers.
She added that the state payout was a lawful consequence of Ukraine’s obligation to enforce ECHR rulings. Describing the nearly decade-long prosecution as baseless, Bernatska noted that investigating judges at the High Anti-Corruption Court had already rejected several prosecution arguments against her. She said she is seeking a “swift and open” trial and has lodged a complaint with the ECHR alleging human rights violations during the criminal proceedings.
The investigation was launched in 2017. Lohvynskyi was identified as the key organizer and formally notified of suspicion in 2023. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.
Representatives for Heorhii Lohvynskyi, Feliks Kozakov, and Liudmyla Trubchaninova did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.

For Israel’s Olympic hopefuls, the road to the podium comes with a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:36:04 UTC
02:36:04 KST

For an athlete chasing the Olympics, a few thousand dollars can separate a missed opportunity from a breakthrough.
Israeli judoka Izhak Ashpiz learned that in 2025, when he was still trying to establish himself on the senior international circuit. His earlier results had fallen short of the Israel Judo Association’s funding criteria, leaving him without financing for the Grand Prix in Lima, Peru.
The trip would cost about 12,000 shekels ($4,000), a significant sum for a young athlete still trying to prove he belonged among the world’s best.
The Paltchik Foundation paid for the trip.
Ashpiz went to Lima and won gold — his first senior international medal. His world ranking jumped 333 places.
It proved to be the start of something much bigger.
Over the following season, Ashpiz won Grand Slam gold medals in Tbilisi and Budapest, bronze medals in Paris and Ulaanbaatar and a bronze medal at the senior European Championships. By Sept. 19, 2026, he was ranked No. 2 in the world in the under-60-kilogram category.
He also became Israel’s youngest judoka to win senior Grand Prix gold and its youngest senior Grand Slam champion. He was the youngest male judoka in the world to win a Grand Slam since Japan’s Hifumi Abe, who went on to become a two-time Olympic champion.
There is no way to know whether Ashpiz’s career would have followed the same trajectory had he stayed home from Lima. But his experience illustrates a problem familiar to many young elite athletes: Long before the medals, sponsorships and Olympic spotlight arrive, someone has to pay for the journey.
The expensive years before the Olympics
Israel’s leading young athletes can spend years training full time, traveling to international competitions and structuring their lives around their sport. Yet those who have not reached the required rankings or results for significant institutional funding can find themselves caught in an awkward stage: expected to compete like professionals without the financial security of established professionals.
Some rely heavily on their families. Others take on part-time work. In some cases, the expense of competing abroad can determine whether an athlete gets the chance to advance at all.
It is a predicament Peter Paltchik knows firsthand.
Before becoming one of Israel’s most successful judokas, Paltchik worked temporary jobs and, at times, slept in his car while trying to finance his athletic career.
He eventually became a two-time Olympic medalist, world bronze medalist and European champion. After experiencing the financial uncertainty of elite sport himself, he established the Paltchik Foundation in 2024 to help younger athletes through the same period.
Now in its second year, the foundation supports 10 Israeli athletes in judo, gymnastics and swimming.
Each receives a monthly scholarship of 4,500 shekels, or 54,000 shekels a year. For athletes whose days revolve around training, recovery and competition, the money is intended to reduce the need for outside work and help cover the basic costs of pursuing an international career. The foundation also helps athletes access training, equipment and medical support through outside partners.
Paltchik and the foundation’s board serve on a voluntary basis, with no salaried positions or administrative overhead.
“The foundation helped me at the beginning of my journey,” Ashpiz said. “Whenever I needed help or someone to listen, I knew I had someone to turn to. I know they are always there for me.”
Betting on athletes before they become household names
Ashpiz is the foundation’s most dramatic success story so far, but its roster reflects a broader strategy: supporting athletes while they are still emerging rather than waiting until they have already established themselves internationally.
Among those receiving support are World Cup gymnastics medalists Yahli Shoshani and Noam Berkovitz, World Championships swimming finalist Daniel Krichevsky, world No. 11 judoka Yuli Mishiner and youth world judo medalist Tom Simchaiv.
For Mishiner, the value of the program is not limited to paying expenses.
“An Olympic campaign means dedicating myself completely to judo,” she said. “The foundation gives me confidence that someone sees the entire journey, believes in me and has chosen to become a partner in my greatest goals.”
Galit Shoshani, the mother of gymnast Yahli Shoshani, said her daughter’s selection gave her a significant boost in confidence.
“It was much more than financial support,” she said. “It was an expression of belief that helped her believe in herself and in her ability to fulfill her dreams.”
That belief can matter in sports where careers are often determined by narrow margins. A single competition can change an athlete’s ranking, qualification prospects and access to future funding. Conversely, missing an event because of its cost can mean losing an opportunity that may not return.
Looking beyond Los Angeles
The foundation is now changing the way it decides how long to support athletes.
Beginning in 2027, it plans to continue assisting selected athletes through their first Olympic Games rather than ending its support once they qualify for an official Olympic funding program.
The idea is to provide continuity during the years when an athlete is making the transition from promising prospect to Olympic competitor.
Its planning also extends beyond the next Games. The foundation says it intends to work two Olympic cycles ahead, currently focusing on athletes who could compete at Los Angeles 2028 and Brisbane 2032. After the Los Angeles Games, its horizon will shift toward Brisbane and the 2036 Olympics.
According to its projections, athletes currently supported by the program could eventually account for roughly 10% of Israel’s delegation to the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
For Paltchik, the effort is also a way of translating his own Olympic career into something that lasts beyond his medals.
“My medals represent what I achieved as an athlete,” he said. “The foundation represents what I want to leave behind. My legacy will be measured by the athletes who reached the world stage because someone believed in them when they needed it most.”
There is also a broader Israeli dimension to the project. International sporting events are among the relatively few places where athletes compete visibly under the national flag before large global audiences. For Israelis and many Jewish communities abroad, a medal ceremony featuring the Israeli flag and the national anthem can carry significance well beyond the result itself.
But those moments begin years earlier, far from packed arenas and television cameras, with training sessions, plane tickets and competitions that few people are watching.
For Ashpiz, one of those competitions was in Lima.
It cost 12,000 shekels to get him there.
He came home with a gold medal — and a career that suddenly looked very different.
The Paltchik Foundation accepts tax-deductible donations in the United States through JNF-USA. More information is available at PaltchikFoundation.org
