Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian border, announces $26 billion civil defense plan
Poland will station Patriot air defense batteries in its Lublin region, bordering Ukraine, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Oct. 5, according to Polish Radio. The same day, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced his government will adopt a civil defense program worth 102.4 billion zlotys ($26.4 billion).
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Patriot batteries are meant to reassure the residents of the Lublin region and protect Lublin airport and its air traffic, Polish Radio reported. Amid rising tensions between Russia and Poland, Russia has repeatedly violated Polish airspace.
The defense minister also announced that new military formations, including unmanned systems forces, will be created in the region, Polish Radio said.
Tusk announced his government will adopt a draft resolution for the Population Protection and Civil Defence Programme for 2027-2031, Polish state news agency Pap wrote.
"Five years of full funding for the program, we are talking about very large sums guaranteed for the protection of civilians and civil defense. It will be mainly investments," Tusk said.
While previous programs only paid for emergency purchases such as generators, local governments had pushed for a longer, better-funded program, Tusk said.
The money will be spent on shelters, equipment, rescue bases, stockpiles, and securing water and energy supplies during natural disasters and wartime, the prime minister said. Additionally, funding will go toward warning systems and ICT security, Tusk said. Of this money, 30 billion zlotys (about $7.7 billion) will be allocated to the regional authorities, according to him.
"Local governments will decide, so that they have a voice co-deciding what type of investment, whether it's a shelter, whether it's a firehouse, whether it's a matter of telecommunications - what is most needed," Tusk said.
On Sept. 13, Tusk warned that Russian escalation could increase in the upcoming months, following Russian strikes on a Polish-Ukrainian border crossing and a passenger train.
"The escalation of actions of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact and its examples are getting closer and closer to our borders," Tusk said in a briefing with defense officials. "What can be expected is that the next weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions from the Russian side. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."

EU offers 1-year flexibility on methane rules amid energy crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:50:49 UTC
01:50:49 KST

Melike Pala
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday that the European Union will give fossil fuel exporters an additional year of flexibility on methane requirements as the bloc seeks to ease energy costs amid a wider energy crisis.
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the measure would help reduce costs for exporters amid heightened pressure on Europe's energy markets.
"We will give flexibility to exporters for one more year on methane," she said, adding that the measure would "save additional costs at a moment of crisis."
The EU's methane regulation is designed to reduce methane emissions from the energy sector and covers fossil fuels produced within the bloc as well as imported oil, natural gas and coal.
Under the regulation's current implementation timeline, importers were due to begin demonstrating from Jan. 1, 2027 that methane emissions linked to the production of fossil fuels covered by relevant contracts had been monitored, reported and independently verified in line with standards equivalent to those applied under EU rules.
She said gas prices have risen 140% since the end of February, while diesel prices have doubled, adding that imported fossil fuels had cost Europe an additional €100 billion ($112 billion) without providing additional energy.
"Families and industries are paying the cost of a crisis far beyond our borders... Businesses are under high pressure. People struggle to pay their bills. And this could intensify as we head into winter," von der Leyen said.
The EU executive is also planning a strategic dialogue on European refineries and a new task force to aggregate energy demand and facilitate joint procurement, von der Leyen said.
She stressed, however, that the bloc's longer-term response must focus on reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.
"As long as Europe depends on oil and gas, our prosperity remains exposed to events beyond our control. When we import fossil fuels, we import the shocks and crisis that come with them," von der Leyen warned.
Von der Leyen said Europe should therefore replace fossil fuels with clean electricity generated within Europe.

Greek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:50:19 UTC
01:50:19 KST

The Greek prime minister has vowed to “ramp up” his country’s claims to get back the Parthenon marbles from the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.
“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the fifth-century BC marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.
“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”
It was the first time Mitsotakis had conceded that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of its chair, George Osborne, had failed to make headway.
Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected to Burnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire, more than 200 years ago.
“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.
“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe.”
The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.
Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with Greek officials seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of finally ending the row.
In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”
“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”
The British Museum has been home to about 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.
Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, said on Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.
There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens allowing gems that had never been seen outside Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.
“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”

Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conference | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:49:03 UTC
01:49:03 KST

Just another day in Crapland. It’s amazing what you can get used to. You can’t say the Tories haven’t put a lot of thought into their party conference. It takes some programming skill to make every day even more dismal than the last. You come expecting very little and get even less.
Schopenhauer would be in dreamland. The very act of being has never felt so inconsequential. Yet there’s something very comforting about this. You leave the Birmingham theme park attraction feeling better about yourself than when you arrived. Who knew abject failure could be so much fun? You find yourself congratulating some members on being able to dress themselves. A curious hybrid of an endangered species and care in the community?
You might find yourself wondering if you are being gaslit. Small pockets of people roaming around aimlessly with a smile on their face, insisting that it is very heaven in this dawn to be alive and repeatedly crossing themselves before images of the beatific Kemi Badenoch. But then you realise that the people the Tories are really gaslighting are themselves. It’s almost painful to watch. Almost. But mostly it’s like a remake of The Truman Show. Everyone waking up each day and believing they are engaged in something meaningful. When the reality is nothing is happening. They are living in a Potemkin village. A series of distractions designed to look like a party conference.
The breakout star is, of course, Kemi. She is the Tories’ chosen one. KULT KEMI. The leader who has rescued them from one black hole and is plunging them straight back into another. I’ve come to realise I’ve got Kemi wrong. Sure, she’s short-tempered and can’t tolerate dissent. But she’s actually a supremely gifted entertainer. A comedy genius. A woman whose one-liners often get mistaken for serious comment. A female Jack Dee. She would be far more successful taking her show to the Edinburgh fringe than Birmingham.
Kemi’s act on the morning media round was one of her best yet. No one does improv better. Understandably, every interviewer wanted to ask her about the Tories’ overnight announcement of a £10bn Iron Dome to rival the Israelis’ that would protect the UK from any kind of drone or missile attack. Like, how did she imagine she was going to build the Iron Dome for about a tenth of the money that all the experts said it would cost? And wasn’t this just some bullshit nonsense designed to make the front pages of the Tory press that wouldn’t stand contact with reality?
“Stop calling it an Iron Dome,” Kemi dead-panned. She really is a comedy pro. Even at 8.10am she’s still in role. “It isn’t an Iron Dome. I’ve never called it an Iron Dome. It’s a Britannia Shield.” Genius. She couldn’t think for the life of her why everyone was calling it an Iron Dome. Mmm. It might have been something to do with the Tory press office releasing a statement calling it an Iron Dome? And the opinion piece in the Sun, written by Kemi herself, calling it an Iron Dome? There are clearly a lot of replicant Kemis rushing around pretending to be the real one.
OK, OK, we’ll call it a Britannia Shield, said the radio and TV presenters. Sometimes it’s easier to humour a guest. So when was it going to be operational, what would it look like and how much of the UK would it cover? Kemi laughed. She hadn’t a clue. She was just the one with the ideas. The details she left for others. But it definitely would be up and running before Penny Mordaunt returned to parliament to reprise her role in Sky’s The War Game. As for the shield itself, that would be a few Sopwith Camel biplanes and barrage balloons that could be diverted to Scotland at a fortnight’s notice if required.
Are you really just a one-woman band? Anna Foster asked on the Today programme. Your personal polls are higher than your party’s. A polite way of saying the Tories are tanking in third place. Not at all, Kemi ad-libbed. Even Jeffrey Archer would have struggled to lie quite so shamelessly. Everyone knows who my shadow cabinet is. Er. I’m not sure I could name them all. I’m not even sure the shadow cabinet could. Just an array of nodding dogs on a dashboard. But maybe we’ve underestimated the public. They do know exactly who the shadow cabinet is. And that’s why the Tories are still bottom-lining.
Back in the conference centre, those members who were still alive were struggling to find something to do. The morning’s entertainment was centred around the “Main Hall”, AKA the converted cupboard. For Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, there were about 15 people in the room. The rest of the audience had disguised themselves as seats again. Still, not all bad news. Eight people were watching online. A figure that soon went down to one. For a while I wondered who this one poor sod was. Then I realised it was me.
Laura looked close to tears by the time the session was over. She was met beside the stage by someone who I hope was a therapist. Quite where everyone else had got to was a mystery. There was also no one to hear Rebecca Paul – me neither – talk about £50k handbags with a woman called Plum. Self-selecting, I guess. Maybe there’s a separate hall for those experiencing extreme catatonia.
By the afternoon we lucky few were stretched out into the much-reduced Symphony Hall to prepare for war with a Shahed drone hanging above our heads. First up was the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, a man who has sold his one-nation soul for a job in Kemi’s Kabinet. “I am coming back to serve,” SuperTug announced, matching the oratory skills of Andrew Griffith. He is a man who wakes up every day, and seems disappointed not to find himself at war. He rather died on his arse.
Then we got the special guest. The rightwing historian Niall Ferguson. A more swivel-eyed, deranged Dr Strangelove. He had come to tell everyone that he too fancied a war, even if you didn’t want one. “A world war is coming,” he said, trying not to show if he had become sexually aroused. “And there is nothing we can do about it.” All of which made the later speeches of Kemi-come-latelies Helen Whately and James Cartlidge somewhat redundant. There’s no need to starve benefits claimants or build an Iron Dome when the apocalypse is upon us.
Suddenly the Tory conference made sense. It wasn’t just a place where hope came to die. It was a place where we all came to die.

France’s conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:49:00 UTC
01:49:00 KST

France's conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
October 6, 2026
France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.
At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.
On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.
Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.
On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.
Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.
A signal to the markets
Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.
"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.
No majority in sight for the budget
The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.
Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.
More money for schools — and more protests
The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.
For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.
Financing education is getting more costly
The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."
Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.
Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.
Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.
Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns
In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.
From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.
A French problem with a European dimension
France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.
In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.
This article was originally published in German.

Ovechkin retires: The NHL record-breaker who never turned his back on Russia (PHOTOS, VIDEOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:48:33 UTC
01:48:33 KST

Ovechkin retires: The NHL record-breaker who never turned his back on Russia (PHOTOS, VIDEOS)
One of the world’s most recognizable and beloved athletes, Washington Capitals captain Alexander Ovechkin, has announced he will retire at the end of the current NHL season, closing out a record-breaking career spanning more than two decades.
The 41-year-old Russian legend, who is entering his 22nd and final NHL season, broke the news to his teammates on Monday, saying it was hard to tell them he would leaving after this season, but “it is what it is.” He urged the team to “enjoy the moment” and “do some special things this year.”
The timing was poignant: Monday marked exactly 21 years since Ovechkin made his NHL debut with the Capitals.
For more than two decades, the man known as ‘the Great Eight’ (he has worn the number 8 throughout his NHL career) has been far more than a celebrated athlete. Known affectionately as Ovi, he became the face of a franchise, an icon in both Russia and the US, and the most prolific goalscorer in NHL history. Through it all, he remained proudly Russian, even as political pressure on Russian athletes reached a boiling point.
So who is the man behind the records?
How Ovi came to hockey
Ovechkin was born into a sports family in Moscow. His mother, Tatyana, was a two-time Olympic basketball champion, and his father, Mikhail, played professional football. But it was hockey that captured their son’s imagination.
He came through the famed Dynamo Moscow system and made his professional debut in the Russian Superleague at just 16. Powerful, fast, and relentlessly physical, Ovechkin combined brute force with a devastating shot – qualities that quickly made him one of the game’s most exciting young talents.
The Washington Capitals selected him first overall in the 2004 NHL Draft, although the 2004-2005 lockout delayed his arrival in North America by a year. When he finally stepped onto NHL ice in October 2005, he scored twice on his debut and went on to win the Calder Trophy as the league’s top rookie.
Ovechkin’s spectacular goals and bruising style soon helped turn the Capitals into one of the NHL’s biggest attractions. In January 2010, he became the 14th captain in franchise history – a role he has held ever since, making him the Capitals’ longest-serving captain.
Trophies and records
Ovechkin’s trophy cabinet is difficult to match. He is a three-time world champion with Russia, a three-time Hart Trophy winner as NHL MVP, and an eight-time First All-Star Team selection. In 2007-08, he won the Art Ross Trophy after recording 112 points, including 65 goals.
Washington reached the playoffs in 16 of Ovechkin’s 21 seasons and won three Presidents’ Trophies (given to the team with the best overall record). But the big prize that had eluded him for many years finally came in 2018, when he captained the Capitals to their first and only Stanley Cup, scoring a league-leading 15 playoff goals.
Then came the record once thought untouchable. On April 6, 2025, Ovechkin scored his 895th regular-season goal, passing Wayne Gretzky’s 894 to become the NHL’s all-time leading regular-season goalscorer.
ALEX OVECHKIN. FROM HIS OFFICE. BECAUSE OF COURSE. #ALLCAPS https://t.co/SMWk89x5Ys
— NHL News (@PuckReportNHL) April 6, 2025
He went on to become the first player to reach 900, pushing the record to 929 at the time of writing.

Behind many of those goals was an Ovechkin trademark: His devastating one-timer from the left faceoff circle. The spot became known as ‘Ovi’s office’.
His name sits atop numerous other lists: He holds NHL records for power-play goals (331), game-winning goals (141), overtime goals (27), empty-net goals (72), and 30-goal seasons (20). His nine 50-goal seasons tie Gretzky and Mike Bossy. Gretzky still holds the records for career points, playoff goals, as well as combined regular-season and playoff goals – but Ovechkin still has plenty of time to pass ‘the Great One’ in combined regular-season and playoff goals.
The quirks behind the Great Eight
For all the discipline required to stay at the top for more than two decades, Ovechkin has never exactly been a sports nutritionist’s dream. Teammates have spoken of his fondness for spicy Italian sandwiches, hot Cheetos, and Coca-Cola – which he has been known to drink on the bench.
His celebrations have been equally memorable. After Washington’s 2018 Stanley Cup triumph, Ovechkin famously performed a headstand over the Cup in a Georgetown fountain. The stunt was later recreated on ‘The Tonight Show’, with Ovechkin holding Jimmy Fallon upside down as the host drank from the Cup.
4 years ago today, Alex Ovechkin and the Washington Capitals showed the world how to do a proper Stanley cup stand. It was just part of an unforgettable 3 day party in Washington DC! 🏆🍺❤️ #ALLCAPS @Capitals https://t.co/HN9SgDptHq
— LoyalCaps 🇺🇸🏒🥅 (@dmddusseau) June 8, 2022
His legendary slapshot has even reached space, at least in name. In 2014, an asteroid was officially named 257261 Ovechkin in honor of the player whose slapshot has been clocked at more than 160 kph.
One of his best-known rituals carries a far more personal meaning. After scoring, Ovechkin kisses his finger and points to the sky in memory of his older brother Sergey, who died in a car accident when Ovechkin was ten.
A different kind of legacy
Away from the rink, Ovechkin has spent years supporting children, cancer research, and accessible hockey in both North America and Russia. His Ovi’s 8’s program, launched in 2006, has provided more than 6,000 game tickets to underserved children and families. In Russia, he has supported children’s charities, orphanages, and adaptive sports, including para hockey.
One memorable episode came at the 2015 NHL All-Star Draft, when Ovechkin famously campaigned to be picked last so he could win a new Honda – not for himself, but to donate to a hockey program for children with developmental disabilities, inspired by 10-year-old fan Ann Schaab, who had Down syndrome. He missed out, but Honda later gave him a car anyway – and Ovechkin kept his promise.
More recently, he turned his pursuit of Gretzky’s record into a fundraising drive. His ‘GR8 CHASE’ campaign has raised more than $256,000 for pediatric cancer research, with Ovechkin donating for every goal he scores and Monumental Sports & Entertainment matching his contributions. His farewell season will also feature a new charitable effort announced on the eighth of each month, the team announced on Monday.
Unapologetically Russian
For all the affection Ovechkin has earned in Washington, he has never tried to hide his love for his homeland. Through more than two decades in the US – and amid tensions between Washington and Moscow – he has continued to describe himself first and foremost as Russian.
That refusal to distance himself from his homeland has made him a target of criticism from supporters of Ukraine, particularly since the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022. While Ovechkin has publicly called for peace, he has repeatedly resisted pressure to denounce Russia. Among his fiercest critics is former Czech goaltender Dominik Hasek, who has called for Russian NHL players’ contracts to be suspended and accused the league of facilitating Russian propaganda by continuing to showcase Ovechkin.
The pressure has extended beyond criticism. Ukraine imposed sanctions on Ovechkin in 2022, and he was later added to Kiev’s controversial state-linked ‘Mirotvorets’ database, which lists people it considers enemies of the country, and has been described by critics as a ‘kill list’ after several people named on it were killed or died under suspicious circumstances.
Ovechkin once again attracted criticism after appearing in a campaign video for Russia’s ruling United Russia party last month. Latvia subsequently banned him from entering the country, while the Ukrainian Canadian Congress called for him to be sanctioned and barred from Canada. Commenting on the ad, Ovechkin said: “I’m Russian, and I support my country.”
The controversies have done little to diminish Ovechkin’s standing with hockey fans, with his milestones celebrated in North America and around the world. US President Donald Trump earlier this year described him as “a great hockey player, a great gentleman.”

How Ovi’s news was received
The announcement prompted tributes from teammates, rivals, and some of hockey’s biggest names.
Zach Leonsis, the president of Capitals owner Monumental Sports & Entertainment, who has known Ovechkin for more than 21 years, said, “I know this season will be emotional,” urging fans to “cherish every game and every moment.”
Capitals coach Spencer Carbery pointed to Ovechkin’s reach far beyond Washington, recalling his amazement at seeing thousands of his jerseys at away games. For younger players, he said, Ovechkin’s 22 seasons carry a simple lesson: “It goes by in a flash… Make sure you make the most of it.”

Gretzky said the farewell season will be “great for the NHL... I’m happy for him.” Fellow Russian star Evgeny Malkin, who entered the NHL a year after Ovechkin and went from bitter rival to close friend, was similarly reflective. “He’s a legend. Fans love him,” Malkin said, wishing Ovechkin a healthy final season.
Columbus coach Rick Bowness recalled Ovechkin’s famous falling-down goal against Phoenix during his rookie season, saying his defenseman and goalie did everything perfectly, but the puck still went in. “I knew right there, ‘Wow, this kid’s special.’” More than 20 years later, he said it’s been “a real pleasure to coach against him his whole career.”
What’s next, Ovi?
When Ovechkin told his teammates he is retiring, he did not specify whether he meant the NHL or professional hockey as a whole, briefly leaving open the possibility of a return to Russia’s KHL. Speaking to reporters later on Monday, however, he indicated that this would likely be his final season as a professional player.
“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision… I’m not 20 years old,” he said. “I want to play with my kids when they’re growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff.”
Ovechkin has revealed few other retirement plans, but several projects offer clues.
Earlier this year, he completed the preliminary defense of a 145-page dissertation on hockey training methods as part of his pursuit of a candidate of sciences degree in pedagogical sciences – roughly equivalent to a Western PhD. He is also closely involved in the Alexander Ovechkin International Hockey Academy, a 43,000-square-meter complex under construction in Moscow. Ovechkin owns a 35% stake in the academy, which aims to develop young Russian talent and could give the Great Eight a new role in hockey after retirement.
Last month, Ovechkin made it clear where he expects to settle once hockey is over.
“I’m Russian, so when I’m done playing hockey, probably I’m gonna stay there,” he said. For now, though, Ovechkin has one season left and a characteristically simple priority: “I’m gonna focus on my game.”

Reframing Spanish Language Teaching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:47:24 UTC
01:47:24 KST

Walk into almost any high school or university world language department and you will face a curious contradiction. On the posters lining the hallways, bilingualism is celebrated as a superpower and marketed to students as an asset that can open many doors. Traditional second-language (L2) learners who are studying Spanish for the first time are often showered with praise as they memorize vocabulary lists and struggle through unfamiliar conjugation charts.But when a heritage speaker (HS), typically a child of immigrants who grew up speaking Spanish at home, walks into that same department, the temperature seems to change. For one, the knowledge they bring to the classroom is rarely viewed as an asset, at least not in the same way. More often than not, their linguistic practices are seen as a collection of “bad habits” that need to be broken so they can eventually be replaced by “better” or “proper” versions. Many instructors fall into this trap because they genuinely believe that they are acting in their students’ best interests. Their intentions are good, but they rarely pause to consider the invisible harm of this linguistic policing.
This double standard directly shapes how HS students perceive themselves. When an educational institution tells a young person that the language they use to connect with family is flawed or inappropriate, it does not motivate them to learn the standard dialect. When the textbooks used in the classroom perpetuate the misconception that Spanish is a foreign language in the US, it does not inspire them to embrace their heritage with pride. And when local Spanish varieties that have developed organically in places like Miami or Orlando are routinely dismissed by instructors and labeled as lazy, sloppy, or ungrammatical, it does not make them want to read classic Spanish literature. All this does is inflict a form of linguistic trauma that invalidates their already vulnerable lived experiences and transforms their cultural and linguistic capital into a perceived academic problem that needs to be corrected. We must also look at the lesson this double standard teaches the L2 students in the room. When they watch their instructor claim to show appreciation of different cultures and values,yet stop a classroom discussion to correct a HS for saying troca or aplicar instead of camioneta or solicitar, it teaches them that local US Spanish varieties are not legitimate (and by extension their speakers aren’t legitimate either). This reinforces the false but unfortunately long-held belief that bilingualism is only acceptable when it is learned in formal environments and that knowledge of grammar rules is more important than authentic communication. Over time, this creates a ripple effect that extends beyond the classroom walls. When we condition students to view US Spanish as inferior, we are participating in a subtle yet serious form of discrimination.
To be sure, the educational landscape looks very different today than it did twenty years ago. With HS students now present in virtually every Spanish class across the country, teachers and administrators areleft to improvise without a clear blueprint. But adopting a new textbook or opening a dedicated heritage section to follow current trends is not the same as knowing what to do once students show up on the first day of class. Because most educators have not had the opportunity to receive the specialized training that this kind of teaching requires, they often default to the same prescriptive ways we have been trying to move past for decades.
The Path Forward
Defenders of the status quo feel very strongly about upholding the norm. They behave as if the integrity of the Spanish language would collapse if they lowered their guard. To these linguistic gatekeepers, not teaching “pure” and “correct” Spanish is a disservice to their students and to their academic duty. In their mission to maintain the perceived “purity” of the language, many instructors claim a moral high ground but do not realize that they are drowning in a sea of contradictions. For example, they police modern US Spanish innovations but seem to forget that the standard they are defending is itself a patchwork of foreign borrowings and simplified vulgar Latin. They forget that the very accent and syntax they use to lecture their classes today would have been branded as lazy and incorrect not too long ago.
Any meaningful shift toward a socially responsible pedagogy must necessarily begin with self-reflection. We ought to be willing to look critically within ourselves and question why we remain so content to treat language as a dead textbook abstraction while fearing it as the living organism that it is. For most, this process will be uncomfortable, mainly because we are simply not used to facing our (linguistic) ideologies. But without taking this step, not only will we not have a clear grasp of what our true purpose in the classroom is, we will also remain blind to the ways that we may continue to perpetuate our biases under the guise of instruction.
Until we stop treating HS students as deficient projects who need constant fixing and start recognizing them as legitimate bilinguals with inherent cultural and linguistic capital, our teaching will remain hollow. To be clear, this does not mean that we should give up on teaching grammar or on correcting students altogether, but rather that we’ve got to break out of the comfort zone that misrepresents language as a neatly bound abstraction and completely ignores the messy ways real people actually talk outside the classroom walls.
We’ve got to break out of the comfort zone that misrepresents language as a neatly bound abstraction and completely ignores the messy ways real people actually talk.
To be honest, I am not sure what the magic formula is, but this much is clear to me: being mindful must be part of it. Mindful of the inherent power dynamics that dictate whose speech carries authority and respect and whose does not. Mindful of the idealized standards we blindly enforce. And last, but not least, mindful of the heavy baggage that lurks behind our red ink. Only when this happens can we transform Spanish language education from a tool of assimilation into a pathway for true bilingualism.
Diego Pascual y Cabo directs the Spanish Heritage Language Program at the University of Florida. His work examines heritage speaker bilingualism through theoretical and applied lenses. Dedicated to raising critical language awareness, he seeks to dismantle negative ideologies and to champion the linguistic practices of minoritized bilinguals.

Reopening channels to bypass sanctions through Russian banking system
In an editorial, Kayhan discussed the reopening of channels for bypassing financial sanctions through Russia's banking system. Iran's Central Bank has so far transferred more than $1.5 billion of its funds through the Russian banking network, thereby utilizing the Russian route to circumvent US financial sanctions.
Available information indicates that, in addition to China, Russia's banking infrastructure can be used to settle trade with countries such as India, Brazil, African nations, etc. However, despite the effect of sanctions and external pressure, exchange-rate increases cannot be explained solely by outside factors. Therefore, one of the government's most important tasks under current conditions is to manage foreign pressure while simultaneously abandoning and revising its economic adjustment policies.
Shargh: Diplomacy backed by strength and readiness for defense
In its analysis of Araghchi's meeting with foreign ambassadors, heads of diplomatic missions, and representatives of international organizations in Tehran, Shargh argued that Iran's foreign minister sought to present a clear picture of Tehran's evolving foreign policy. The central message was that the door to diplomacy remains open, but it is now supported by a stronger readiness for defense. The core message of Araghchi's remarks is neither negotiation alone nor resistance alone, but rather the simultaneous pursuit of both. Viewed from this perspective, Araghchi's recent statements can be seen as an effort to define Iran's foreign policy at a stage when war, negotiations, the Strait of Hormuz, and regional relations have become more interconnected than ever.
Jam-e-Jam: It was the enemies, not Iran, that chose war
In a commentary, Jam-e-Jam highlighted Iran's ethical outlook and its approach to international engagement. While Western governments accused the Islamic Republic of warmongering and alleged that Iran sought to eliminate certain regional countries and resolve disputes through military force, Iran consistently stated that it preferred understanding and negotiation in dealing with contentious foreign-policy issues, including the nuclear question. The newspaper pointed to numerous rounds of negotiations and serious dialogue with global powers and neighboring countries as evidence that Iran favors engagement over confrontation. In particular, over the past year and several months, Iran repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to negotiate on nuclear matters by accepting proposals for talks. Nevertheless, Iran's adversaries chose the path of conflict and imposed two, or arguably three, wars on the country during the past 18 months. Iran's ethical and humanitarian view of power was once again distinguished from what it characterized as the aggressive and inhumane approach of its opponents.
Khorasan: Iran is fully prepared
In an article examining current Iranian and American policies, Khorasan argued that Iran's foes have entered a phase of "operational patience," seeking to select the most effective and least costly option from among various scenarios. However, this patience stems not from caution but from weakness, and Trump knows that losing one or both chambers of Congress would significantly complicate his position. Military limitations continue to constrain any potential action by the US military. While Iran's opponents may view the situation as static, realities on the ground remain dynamic and subject to change. Under these circumstances, it predicted that war could eventually begin. However, it emphasized that Iran remains committed to serious negotiations, though not in a manner that would imply surrender or deception. The article concluded that Iran is preparing for the worst-case scenarios, harbors no optimism regarding future developments, possesses a broad range of response options, and regards maintaining public calm as the most crucial element of national security.
Ettelaat: Escalating crisis in the region
Ettelaat discussed that indirect communication between Tehran and Washington is continuing, but even more significant are the military and political signs suggesting a growing possibility of a new conflict. According to the paper, Iran says it has received the US response to Tehran's seven-day trust-building proposal concerning the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and is currently reviewing it. At the same time, Washington is reinforcing its forces in the region and Donald Trump has spoken of a decision regarding Iran that could proceed through either an "easy path" or a "hard path." Meanwhile, Iranian military and political officials have spoken of greater readiness for any future conflict and of improving missile capabilities. The newspaper noted that the principal disagreement between the two sides remains clear: Iran views the reopening of Hormuz, an end to pressure on shipping, and sanctions relief as the main pillars of negotiations, whereas the United States continues to place the nuclear issue at the center of its proposals.  According to the article, this disagreement, combined with the growing US military posture in the region, has created a situation in which diplomacy has not entirely collapsed, yet discussions about the possibility of political pressures evolving into a new confrontation are becoming increasingly frequent.

Malian army enters strategic northern city of Kidal

The Malian army said it had entered the strategic northern city of Kidal after Tuareg-led separatists announced the withdrawal of their forces as the military advanced.
Two Malian military officers told AFP on Tuesday that government forces had entered the city without encountering resistance.
A military convoy left the town of Anefis earlier in the day and “entered Kidal shortly before 1:00 pm,” one officer said.
“We encountered no resistance. We are on the ground,” he added.
Another officer said government forces had “arrived in Kidal ahead of schedule”.
The advance came shortly after Mali’s armed forces announced “large-scale air-ground operations” across the wider Kidal region alongside Russia’s Africa Corps.
The Tuareg separatist FLA group said earlier on Tuesday that it had decided to carry out a “strategic and controlled withdrawal” from Kidal.
The group said the move was intended to preserve lives and protect its personnel and logistical capabilities, describing the withdrawal as temporary.
The FLA blamed what it described as the disproportionate use of air power by the Malian military and Russia’s Africa Corps for its decision to leave the city.
A resident who left Kidal with six family members on Monday told AFP that most civilians had already fled, saying fewer than 100 people had remained in the city for some time.
Fighting in northern Mali
Kidal was captured earlier this year by Tuareg-led separatists and members of the Al Qaeda-linked JNIM terror group during a series of attacks against Mali’s military government.
The offensive, launched in late April, targeted government forces across northern Mali and included the seizure of Kidal.
A Malian military officer in Gao said troops had been operating across the Kidal region for several days with the aim of securing the area and fighting armed groups.
Mali has faced a prolonged security crisis since 2012, involving terror groups linked to Al Qaeda and Daesh, separatist movements and criminal networks.
The country has been ruled by a military government following coups in 2020 and 2021.
Since taking power, Mali’s military authorities have reduced longstanding security ties with former colonial power France and strengthened political and military cooperation with Russia.

What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:46:06 UTC
01:46:06 KST

What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed?
Territorial gains alone will not be enough to change the trajectory of the war.
Two days after the announced counter-offensive by the internationally recognised Yemeni government, the operation named Dawn of Yemen has already made significant advances. Its forces recaptured territory from the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, along the Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Saudi-led coalition backing the government has deployed 100 fighter jets, flying round-the-clock to help secure the strait. In response, the Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi territory.
This is the most consequential escalation in the Yemen war since the UN-brokered truce of 2022. For four years, the war was managed as a frozen conflict. Now, both sides are trying to redraw the map.
In the coming days, the success of the offensive will be determined not only by gains along three different fronts, but also by the ability of the forces loyal to the Yemeni government to maintain cohesion and force the Houthis to change their cost of conflict calculus.
Keeping the Houthis overstretched
The western coast is where the campaign will be won or lost, and the reason lies beyond Yemen. With Iran disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become the Gulf’s strategic lifeline. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline to Yanbu is its main route around Hormuz, yet crude shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets must still pass through Bab al-Mandeb.
A Houthi grip on the strait’s Yemeni shore turns that bypass into a hostage. The Arabian Peninsula would then be squeezed at both ends simultaneously, a scenario that no Gulf capital, and few oil importing economies, can tolerate for long.
There is also a counterintuitive point here. The Houthis’ greatest gain of the year – the territories near Bab al-Mandeb – may also be their most exposed position. Their traditional strength lies in the mountains of the north, where terrain, tribal networks and short supply lines favour defence.
The Tihama coast is the opposite: a flat plain, far from their highland base, with long and vulnerable supply routes and little cover from sustained airpower.
If the government can win decisively anywhere, it is here. The immediate aim need not be to defeat the Houthis outright, but to push them back from the strait, retake the islands and deny them the ability to convert geography into regional leverage.
The second decisive front is Taiz. The city is the hinge between the Houthi-held north, the government-held south and the western coastal theatre. If the Houthis keep the Aden road severed, any broader offensive is split in two. If government forces reopen it, they gain territorial continuity between Aden, Taiz and the coast.
The third is Marib governorate, where fighting has escalated on the Raghwan front, and potentially al-Jawf.
Despite sweeping rhetoric from the Yemeni government, an early march on Sanaa remains unlikely. The more plausible strategy is cumulative pressure: if the coast, Taiz and Marib are pressed at the same time, the Houthis will struggle to concentrate manpower, missiles, drones and logistics on any single axis. The government does not need breakthroughs everywhere; it needs to keep the Houthis overstretched.
Support is not the problem, cohesion is
The government has rarely lacked external backers. Its recurring failure has been converting that support into coherent Yemeni military power. Saudi Arabia remains decisive, and its incentives are now direct rather than abstract: Aramco facilities are under fire, Saudi-linked shipping has been declared a target and the main route circumventing the Strait of Hormuz is exposed.
The commitment of 100 aircraft signals that Riyadh is willing to invest heavily.
Airpower can destroy positions, cut supply lines and break concentrations of force, but it cannot hold territory. That requires Yemeni forces to fight under a unified chain of command, support functioning local administration and maintain political agreement that prevents infighting between factions.
Here the anti-Houthi camp is arguably weaker than at any point in the war. The Southern Transitional Council, which launched its own offensive across the south in December 2025, was dissolved in January after a Saudi-backed counteroffensive, and its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, left the country. The southern units that fought under its banner remain armed and capable, but without a political roof, and their loyalty to the Yemeni government is conditional.
Alongside them, Tareq Saleh’s National Resistance on the coast, the Southern Giants Brigades, and units aligned with the Islah Party in Taiz and Marib each answer to different leaderships, regional priorities and external patrons.
The Houthis, by contrast, possess a centralised political and military command.
This asymmetry is the offensive’s greatest vulnerability. If it is fought through fragmented chains of command, gains will be temporary: rival forces will compete over captured territory, revenues and authority, and the Houthis will regroup and counterattack.
Recognising this reality, the Yemeni government has started preparing to hand out salary payments and undertake reconstruction in recovered areas. That is the right instinct. A town taken by airstrikes but left unpaid and ungoverned will not stay taken. This effort needs to be maintained.
A turning point?
The offensive should not be judged by whether it captures Sanaa. That benchmark is maximalist and almost guarantees a verdict of failure. The better question is whether it makes the conflict ripe for resolution.
In the language of conflict studies, parties negotiate seriously when they perceive a mutually hurting impasse. Since 2022, the deadlock has hurt the Yemeni people, the government, Saudi Arabia and global shipping, but not the Houthis, who have had every reason to believe that time works in their favour. The purpose of Dawn of Yemen, properly understood, is not total victory, but a change in the Houthis’ assessment of the costs of continued confrontation.
There is a complication. The Houthis’ calculus is no longer purely Yemeni. Their decisions are now entangled with Tehran’s war and its bargaining with Washington. Even significant battlefield losses may not produce flexibility in the group if its leadership believes concessions should be traded within a wider regional deal. A specifically Yemeni settlement may therefore depend partly on movement in a negotiation that Yemenis do not control.
Over the coming weeks, four indicators will tell us which way the war is turning: whether government forces retake and hold the coast and the strait islands; whether the Taiz-Aden road is reopened; whether the Houthis are forced to pull forces from Taiz to defend the coast and Marib; and whether recovered areas come under a single command and receive salaries and services.
If most of these happen, the strategic geometry of the war may shift. If government forces advance only marginally, suffer heavy losses or turn on one another, the Houthis will claim to have survived yet another externally backed campaign, and that narrative will harden their conviction that they can outlast their opponents.
All of this unfolds amid a deepening humanitarian catastrophe. The World Health Organization has recorded more than 5,000 casualties since early August, while nearly 200,000 people have been displaced and suspected cholera cases have tripled. A campaign that ignores this will exhaust international patience quickly, as happened with the operation to recapture Hodeidah in 2018, when government forces were pressured to stop to avert a humanitarian disaster.
The offensive then is not the turning point itself. It is the opening of a test. The Yemeni government must do what it has struggled to do throughout this war: convert external support into unified political authority and sustainable military power. If it fails, the Houthis will emerge from another round more convinced than ever that time remains on their side.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Carney to make first bilateral visit by a Canadian PM to Turkey
OTTAWA, Oct 6 - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to Ankara and Istanbul from October 21 to 23, his office said on Tuesday, in what will be the first dedicated bilateral visit to NATO ally Turkey by a Canadian leader.
The visit, which was first reported by Reuters, would mark Carney's latest break with Canadian diplomatic convention as he seeks to reduce the country's reliance on the United States, by far its biggest trading partner, after a collapse in trade talks in August.
Carney will meet with Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara and work toward bolstering bilateral relations in areas including energy and mining, climate, and defence and security, the prime minister's office said in a statement.
He will meet with Turkish business leaders and investors in Istanbul and tout Canada as an attractive destination for trade and investment.
"The Prime Minister will emphasize opportunities to expand that growing trade relationship in priority sectors, including energy, aerospace, advanced technologies, and mining and critical minerals," Carney's office said.
Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-US trade over the next decade and has rushed to establish ties with a host of countries, including China and India, with which it had past strains.
Carney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement at the NATO leaders' summit in July. Turkey has agreed to join Canada's Defence Security and Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of Carney's multilateral "middle powers" bank. REUTERS

Iran calls on France to respect human rights
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has called on France to respect human rights and the right to peaceful protest, criticizing 'contradictory approaches by French officials toward demonstrations in Iran and France.'
In a post on his X account on Tuesday, Baqaei recalled that France had called on Iran in January 2026 to guarantee the right to peaceful protest without fear of reprisals and had urged restraint in dealing with demonstrations.
He noted that, despite calls for revolt from abroad and reports of armed attacks against facilities and security forces in Iran, France’s foreign minister had characterized the unrest at the time as a peaceful revolt.
Baqaei contrasted that position with the French government’s current response to protests by high school students, saying demonstrations in France were now being described as “urban violence.” He also pointed to the French interior minister’s calls for rapid intervention and the use of force to restore public order.
The Iranian spokesman noted that French officials had also cited political manipulation and the role of far-left movements in the protests.
Baqaei stressed that violence against police, arson and damage to public property could not be justified and acknowledged the state’s responsibility to maintain and restore public order.
He argued, however, that the central issue was the differing standards applied to protests depending on where they take place.
The Iranian spokesman questioned why similar conduct was assessed differently when the protesters were in Iran rather than France, emphasizing that the right to peaceful protest and respect for human rights should be upheld consistently.
“If human rights and the right to protest are universal principles, their definition should not change based on the geographical location of the protester,” Baqaei’s remarks underscored.

China plans to join the race for the leadership position at the WHO and has already chosen a candidate
Kyiv • UNN
Beijing plans to nominate Sun Li for the position of WHO Director-General at a late stage. China seeks to strengthen its influence after the United States' withdrawal from the organization.
China plans to put forward its candidate for the post of head of the World Health Organization (WHO) at a late stage of the process. This will give Beijing an opportunity to expand its influence after the United States leaves the organization. Reuters reports this, citing four diplomats and a knowledgeable source, as reported by UNN.
Details
Beijing has long sought to play a more active role in UN institutions and other multilateral organizations, while the United States, during Donald Trump’s presidency, reduced its participation in the work of the UN and some of its agencies.
The WHO leads international efforts to combat diseases and health crises, such as the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the recent COVID-19 pandemic.
Sources said that China plans to nominate Song Li — a senior health official with 20 years of experience working on maternal and child health policy and international cooperation — to replace the current Director-General, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
It should be added
A diplomatic source noted that the planned nomination is clear evidence of China’s desire to fill the vacuum created by the US withdrawal.
Having lost its largest donor, the UN health agency was forced to carry out a major restructuring: scale back its operations, eliminate senior management positions and cut thousands of jobs.
The Trump administration repeatedly criticized the WHO’s actions during the pandemic and accused the organization of bias toward China — the country where COVID-19 originated (the WHO rejects the accusation).
China announced additional funding for the WHO, but these funds cannot fully make up for the deficit that emerged after the United States’ withdrawal.
The WHO will publish the full list of candidates after the regional committee meetings are completed, which are expected in early November.
However, six candidates representing Saudi Arabia, Belgium, Qatar, Botswana, Indonesia and Spain have already decided to publish their names on the WHO website.
Song Li’s candidacy may come under close scrutiny amid longstanding tensions over relations between the WHO and China during the pandemic. In 2020, she was the lead editor of a document containing recommendations on preventing and combating COVID-19 for women in China, intended to establish national standards for maternal and child health care during the pandemic.
If elected, she will become the second representative of China to head the WHO after Margaret Chan.

Mamdani's $7.4m. antisemitism strategy funds groups critical of Israel, financial filings indicate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

Millions of dollars in New York City funding earmarked for Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new antisemitism strategy could flow to organizations with records of anti-Israel advocacy, financial filings indicate.
Last week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled what he described as the first municipal strategy of its kind in the United States to combat antisemitism, announcing investments in hate-crime prevention, security coordination and Jewish cultural institutions.
The strategy outlines a $7.4 million package of measures to combat antisemitism, including $6.4m. in grants for hate-crime prevention and survivor support, $1m. for security upgrades at synagogues and other houses of worship, expanded Holocaust education, investment in Jewish cultural and historical institutions, and renewed coordination between city agencies and Jewish institutions.
However, the 30-page strategy does not adopt a formal definition of antisemitism, saying that New York City can combat antisemitism without adopting a single definition.
The omission has drawn criticism from Jewish organizations, which say that the strategy also fails to address the relationship between anti-Zionism and antisemitism or the forms of anti-Jewish hostility Jewish New Yorkers are currently encountering.
The words Zionism, Zionist, or even anti-Zionist do not appear even once in the entire document. Israel is only mentioned a couple of times.
Breaking down the funding of Mamdani's plan
Part of the strategy involves doubling funding for Partners Against the Hate (PATH) grants to community-based organizations aligned to the prevention framework with a renewed focus on countering online hate speech, data collection, restorative justice and survivor support. This is now set at $6.4m.
One of the top advocacy groups involved in PATH is the Arab American Association of New York, an anti-Israel organization previously run by pro-Palestine activist Linda Sarsour.
According to the Arab American Association of New York’s (AAANY) 2025 Form 990, the association gave a grant of $57,779 to Council on American-Islamic Relations, New York (CAIR-NY) as part of PATH, and a $58,084 grant to Jews For Racial and Economic Justice (JFREJ), also as part of PATH.
In fact, AAANY has given over $223,000 to CAIR-NY since 2021.
CAIR was founded 30 years ago as an organization dedicated to fighting anti-Muslim hate. It has, however, become known for its extreme anti-Israel and antisemitic messaging.
CAIR co-founders scrutinized for terrorist ties
Co-founders of CAIR, Omar Ahmad, Nihad Awad, and Rafiq Jaber have all faced government scrutiny over their ties to Islamist terrorism.
Ahmad, according to the FBI, led a pro-Hamas conference in Philadelphia in 1993, where he and the Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development and Islamic Association of Palestine members discussed how to best support Hamas while concealing their true beliefs, such as support for Hamas conquering all of Israel, from the US.
Recently, the New Jersey branch of CAIR came into the headlines for teaching students that the 9/11 terror attacks were due to “America’s support of Israel” and said, “terrorism is defined differently by different groups of people.”
CAIR has not been designated as a terrorist organization by the US federal government, but it has faced state-level terrorist designations by Republican governors in Texas and Florida.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott designated CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist organizations in 2025, and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet voted to designate CAIR as a domestic terrorist group in September 2026.
JFREJ is a progressive Jewish organization that strongly opposes the adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism. It deems Israel’s actions “occupation and apartheid.”
Figures online such as David Kelsey have noted the irony of city anti-hate money being passed through AAANY to groups like CAIR.
It is also relevant as CAIR was one of the largest backers of Zohran Mamdani’s winning mayoral campaign.
In the lead-up to the November New York City mayoral election, the Washington Free Beacon reported that Mamdani’s campaign received $100,000 from a CAIR-affiliated PAC.
CEO and Director of the National Jewish Advocacy Center Mark Goldfeder pointed out on X/Twitter that most of Mamdani’s “first-ever” antisemitism strategy is just the plan of his predecessor, former mayor Eric Adams’ plan “but with every page that touches Israel torn out.”
And the funding designed to combat hate will likely end up bolstering the very organizations fueling it.
The Jerusalem Post reached out to CAIR for comment.

Nearly half of Israelis equally blame government, IDF for October 7 failures, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:42:09 UTC
01:42:09 KST

Almost half of respondents to an N12 News poll believe that both the government and IDF are equally responsible for the failures of the October 7 massacre, the Israeli news outlet's survey found on Monday.
Of those polled, 47% held this view, compared with 25% who placed responsibility on the government but not the IDF; 17% blamed the IDF but not the government; and 11% were unsure.
The poll also asked to what extent respondents believe that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu bears personal responsibility for the failures.
Almost two-thirds of respondents (65%) said the prime minister bears "a great deal of responsibility," while 22% said he bears "some" responsibility, 6% said he bears no responsibility, and 7% were unsure.
The poll also broke down the political alignment of the 65% who said he bore "a great deal of responsibility," with 91% of opposition bloc voters holding this view, as compared with 27% of coalition voters.
Do Israelis want a state commission of inquiry into October 7?
N12 News also surveyed public opinion on establishing an October 7 State Commission of Inquiry. Of those surveyed, 66% supported this, 21% opposed it, and 13% were unsure. The results also broke down by political alignment: 93% of opposition bloc voters, 37% of coalition voters, and 80% of Arab party voters supported establishing a commission.
The survey also explored how the October 7 massacre, Israel's failures, and its consequences affected how people intend to vote in the upcoming Knesset election.
Overall, about half of respondents said it affected their decision. Of these, 15% said it affected their decision "to a very great extent," 18% "to a great extent," and 22% "to a small extent."
Additionally, 41% of respondents said it did not affect their decision at all, while 4% were unsure whether it had any effect.
Opposition bloc leads coalition 54-49, latest N12 News Knesset elections poll shows
The poll also directly queried which political parties Israelis intend to vote for in the Knesset election, slated for October 27.
The poll forecasted that Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party would be the largest single party, with 23 seats, ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, which polled at 21 seats.
The Knesset has 120 seats, divided proportionally among all parties that pass the 3% electoral threshold.
In total, the opposition bloc received 54 seats, the coalition received 49, Arab parties received 13, and the Reservists-Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, received four seats.
Additionally, Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad received 13 seats, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu and Yair Golan's The Democrats received nine seats each.
The Joint List of Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad received eight seats, as did Ashkenazi haredi (ultra-Orthodox) party United Torah Judaism. The Sephardi haredi party, Shas, received seven seats, as did Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, the poll found.
The alliance between Religious Zionist Party and Zehut, headed by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, won six seats, and Mansour Abbas's Ra'am won five seats.
Ofer Winter's People of Israel party did not pass the electoral threshold in the latest poll, receiving 1.5% of the predicted votes.
Poll queries Israelis' preferred prime ministerial candidate, pairing Netanyahu against Bennett, Eisenkot, Liberman, respectively
The poll also queried who would be the best candidate for prime minister. When choosing between Netanyahu and Bennett, Netanyahu took the lead, with 41% of respondents backing the incumbent compared with 37% backing Bennett.
Additionally, 16% said neither is suitable, while 6% said they were unsure.
The results of this question vary widely based on political alignment, the poll found. Among coalition voters, 90% supported Netanyahu as compared to 3% who backed Bennett, while 70% of opposition voters backed Bennett while 11% supported Netanyahu.
In a contest for prime minister between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, the latter takes the lead with 41% support, compared to 38% for Netanyahu. Meanwhile, 13% said neither is suitable, and 8% were unsure.
Support also varied sharply by political alignment: 77% of coalition voters supported Netanyahu, compared with 6% for Eisenkot. However, 85% of opposition voters supported Eisenkot, while 9% supported Netanyahu. Additionally, Eisenkot led Arab party voters with 43% support, compared to Netanyahu's 37%.
Further, the poll queried suitability for prime minister between Netanyahu and Liberman, with Netanyahu taking a larger lead at 43% support, compared to 26% for Liberman. Additionally, 26% said neither of them would be suitable as prime minister, while 5% were unsure.
Among coalition voters, Netanyahu has 90% support, compared with 4% for Liberman; among opposition voters, Liberman leads with 50% support, compared with Netanyahu's 14%.
Among Arab party voters, neither Netanyahu nor Liberman would be popular as prime minister, with 59% choosing neither as their preferred candidate, while 22% backed Liberman and 5% backed Netanyahu.

Israeli watchdogs demand state inquiry into flight security failures following flydubai attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

The Movement for Quality Government in Israel called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Transportation Minister Miri Regev, and Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara to establish a government inquiry headed by a retired judge and grant it investigative powers to examine failures in the security screening of foreign flights entering Israel.
The demand followed the attempted terrorist attack on a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, amid reports of persistent gaps in the screening of flight crews and the transfer of information between state authorities.
In its appeal, the Movement for Quality Government presented information indicating that the details of the flight's crew members, including the co-pilot's personal information and citizenship, had been transferred before takeoff to the Tax Authority's National Passenger Data Analysis Center. However, the Transportation Ministry claimed that it had not received the crew list.
According to reports cited in the appeal, data on crew members aboard foreign flights had not been retrieved or checked for approximately two years. The movement therefore demanded an investigation into how information already held by the state failed to result in security screening that could have identified the risk.
The appeal also pointed to warnings issued before the incident that called for changes to the way security screening of foreign flights was conducted. As early as 2024, the State Comptroller recommended regulating responsibility for aviation security and allocating the necessary resources for the task.
Movement for Quality Government says NSC review insufficient
The appeal cited reports showing that the responsibility for securing foreign flights remained with the Transportation Ministry despite a separate recommendation by the National Security Council, and even though personnel in the ministry's security division had warned that they lacked the intelligence tools required to carry out the mission.
The Movement for Quality Government argued that the National Security Council review ordered by the prime minister was insufficient given the severity of the failures and the fact that the NSC had previously examined the issue.
The movement demanded that a government inquiry be established under Section 8A of the Government Law, led by a retired judge, and that the panel be granted investigative powers. The committee should examine how previous warnings were handled, how information about flight crews was used, coordination with intelligence agencies, and the individual and institutional responsibility for any failures identified, the movement said.
Demands establishment of committee immediate action
Alongside the establishment of the committee, the movement demanded immediate action to close the security gaps. It called for a binding procedure governing the transfer, review, and cross-checking of information, as well as an interim arrangement ensuring that an authorized security body actually carries out intelligence screening, with a clear division of responsibility among the relevant agencies.
"The security of passengers must not depend on the bravery of those sitting next to them on the plane," said attorney Dr. Eliad Shraga, chairman of the Movement for Quality Government in Israel.
"The reports paint a grave picture of warnings that went unanswered and information that was in the state's possession but was not examined as required. The public deserves to know who was responsible, what was not done, and how the next disaster will be prevented. A commission of inquiry with investigative powers is required, alongside the immediate correction of the security gaps. We must not wait for a disaster before taking action."
