Mudbrick houses: The heritage of traditional Iranian architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:35:29 UTC
01:35:29 KST

Mudbrick houses: The heritage of traditional Iranian architecture
TEHRAN - Across Iran’s deserts, dry plains and mountain valleys, houses built from earth form some of the country’s most distinctive architectural landscapes. Their rounded roofs, thick walls, shaded courtyards and, in places, tall windcatchers are more than picturesque features. They are the result of centuries of experience in building with local materials and adapting everyday life to a difficult climate.
Mudbrick, or adobe, is among the oldest building traditions in the ancient country. Archaeological evidence shows that sun-dried mud bricks were being used in the Iranian plateau as early as the late 9th or early 8th millennium BCE. At Tepe Ganj Dareh in present-day Kermanshah province, early walls were built with shaped, sun-dried mud bricks. This means that the history of earthen construction in Iran is far older than the Achaemenid, Sasanian or Islamic periods.
Over thousands of years, Iranian builders refined the use of earth into a sophisticated architectural tradition. Mud was readily available, relatively inexpensive and particularly suitable for many of Iran’s dry regions. It could be shaped into bricks, packed into walls or used in other forms of earthen construction. Straw and chaff were commonly mixed with the earth, while walls could be protected with mud, lime or other plasters.
For visitors, the appeal of these buildings lies not only in their age. Traditional earthen architecture offers a way to understand how Iranian communities once responded to heat, cold, limited water and scarce building materials without relying on modern mechanical systems.
Architecture shaped by climate
Much of central and southeastern Iran has hot, dry summers, strong sunlight and limited rainfall. Traditional houses developed in response to these conditions.
One of the most important features is the thick earthen wall. Such walls slow the transfer of heat, helping interiors remain relatively cooler during the day and retaining warmth when temperatures fall at night. The effect is reinforced by courtyards, shaded passages, underground spaces and carefully positioned openings.
In Yazd, perhaps the best-known surviving example of this approach, the relationship between architecture and climate can be seen throughout the historic city. UNESCO describes Yazd as a living example of the intelligent use of limited resources in a desert environment. Its traditional buildings use earth for walls and roofs, while courtyards, thick walls and windcatchers help create a more comfortable microclimate.
The result is an urban landscape that can appear almost monochromatic from a distance. Up close, however, its surfaces reveal different textures and shades of earth, plaster and brick. Narrow lanes often provide shade, while partially covered passages known as Sa’bats protect pedestrians from the intense sun.
For a traveler walking through Yazd’s old quarters, these details make the city feel less like an open-air museum and more like a functioning architectural system. The buildings, streets, water infrastructure and public spaces were designed as parts of the same environment.
The courtyard at the heart of the home
The traditional Iranian house was not simply a collection of rooms surrounded by walls. In many regions, the courtyard was the center of domestic life.
Rooms were arranged around an enclosed open space, creating privacy and providing a protected environment for family life. In desert cities such as Yazd, courtyards could also be positioned below street level. UNESCO notes that traditional houses in Yazd include sunken courtyards and underground areas, which helped improve the local microclimate.
This inward-looking design was also connected to cultural ideas about privacy. Unlike many modern houses, which open toward streets and public spaces, traditional Iranian homes often turned their main living spaces toward the courtyard.
The courtyard could contain trees, plants and sometimes a pool or water feature. These elements were not merely decorative. Shade and vegetation helped soften the heat, while water contributed to a sense of coolness and comfort.
The house therefore became a small climate-controlled world, achieved through architectural planning rather than machinery.
Windcatchers: an ingenious response to heat
Few elements of Iranian architecture are more recognizable than the Badgir, or windcatcher.
These tall towers rise above many traditional houses and other buildings in central Iran. Their function is simple but effective: they capture air and direct it into the building. Depending on their design and the prevailing conditions, windcatchers can help circulate air through rooms and other parts of a house.
Yazd’s skyline is particularly famous for them. UNESCO identifies windcatchers, courtyards and thick earthen walls as important elements of the city’s traditional climate-adapted architecture.
A Badgir also demonstrates an important characteristic of vernacular architecture: local builders did not necessarily need sophisticated modern technology to solve environmental problems. They observed wind, temperature, sunlight and seasonal changes, then incorporated that knowledge into the buildings themselves.
For tourists, climbing to a rooftop in the historic quarters of Yazd offers one of the best ways to appreciate this relationship. From above, windcatchers, domes and earthen roofs appear as a continuous architectural landscape, with modern development often disappearing behind the old city’s dense fabric.
From bricks to domes and vaults
Mudbrick was only one part of Iran’s earthen-building tradition. Builders also developed sophisticated methods for constructing arches, vaults and domes.
The advantage was both practical and structural. Curved roofs could span spaces without requiring the large quantities of timber that were difficult to obtain in many arid regions.
The technique can be seen on a monumental scale at Bam in Kerman province. The UNESCO-listed Bam and its Cultural Landscape contains the remains of a fortified settlement constructed with mud layers, known as Chineh, sun-dried mud bricks or Khesht, as well as vaulted and domed structures. The origins of Bam can be traced to the Achaemenid period, while the citadel reached its height between the seventh and 11th centuries.
Bam is particularly important because its architecture cannot be separated from the oasis that supported it. Underground irrigation channels, or Qanats, brought water into the settlement and allowed agriculture and urban life to develop in an otherwise arid environment. UNESCO considers the relationship between the earthen settlement and its water system an outstanding example of the interaction between people and their environment.
The earthquake of 2003 severely damaged the historic citadel, but conservation work has preserved and restored important parts of its traditional fabric. The site remains one of Iran’s most powerful places for understanding earthen architecture on a large scale.
An architectural tradition across Iran
Yazd and Bam are perhaps the best-known destinations, but earthen construction is not confined to these two places.
Traditional earth architecture can be encountered across large parts of central, eastern and southeastern Iran. Historic settlements and houses in areas around Kerman, Kashan, South Khorasan and Sistan reflect different versions of the same broad knowledge: use what the land provides and design buildings according to local climate and resources.
The materials and construction methods were not identical everywhere. Iran’s architectural traditions developed according to local soil, climate, available vegetation, water resources and building customs.
This regional diversity is one reason it is misleading to think of “mudbrick architecture” as a single architectural style. A house in Yazd may look quite different from an earthen building in Kerman or South Khorasan. What connects them is the use of earth and a long tradition of adapting architecture to place.
The archaeological record also shows that the use of mudbrick continued through different historical periods. Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that sun-dried mud bricks were predominant in Iran until the end of the Achaemenid period, while later periods saw increasing use of fired brick in important buildings.
This combination of continuity and change is visible across Iran’s historic towns. Earthen construction did not disappear when fired brick, stone and other materials became available. Instead, different materials were often used according to function, location and status.
Why mudbrick matters today
Traditional mudbrick houses are increasingly vulnerable to neglect, abandonment, urban expansion and the replacement of traditional materials with modern construction. Yet the knowledge embodied in them has gained new relevance at a time when architects around the world are looking for ways to reduce energy consumption and respond to climate change.
The historic city of Yazd has become an important reference point in this discussion. UNESCO describes its earthen architecture as a source of inspiration for contemporary architecture facing sustainability challenges.
The lesson is not that modern buildings should simply copy old houses. Rather, traditional architecture demonstrates how much can be achieved through passive design: orientation, shade, thermal mass, natural ventilation, compact urban form and the careful use of local resources.
One contemporary initiative is the Esfahk Mud Center in the historic village of Esfahk in South Khorasan province. Founded in 2015, the center focuses on education and the revival of traditional earthen construction techniques. Research on Esfahk has documented courses and practical work involving traditional building methods, including the construction of vaults.
For visitors interested in architecture, Esfahk offers a different experience from the major heritage cities. It provides an opportunity to see traditional techniques not simply as archaeological remains, but as knowledge that is still being studied, taught and tested.
A different way to experience Iran
The best way to understand Iran’s mudbrick heritage is to walk through it.
In Yazd, travelers can explore historic neighborhoods where earthen houses, windcatchers, domes, covered lanes and traditional water systems remain part of the urban landscape. UNESCO inscribed the Historic City of Yazd on the World Heritage List in 2017, recognizing its exceptional earthen architecture and its adaptation to the desert environment.
In Bam, the scale changes. The citadel reveals how earth could be used not only for individual houses but for an entire fortified settlement. Its walls, towers, courtyards, vaulted spaces and relationship with the oasis show how architecture, trade, water management and security were woven together.
Elsewhere, smaller villages and historic neighborhoods offer a quieter encounter with the same tradition. Their value often lies precisely in their simplicity: an earthen wall, a shaded alley, a courtyard, an arched roof or a weathered brick surface can reveal centuries of practical knowledge.
Iran’s mudbrick houses are therefore more than remnants of a pre-industrial past. They are evidence of how generations of builders learned to live with their environment. The earth beneath their feet became walls and roofs; scarce water shaped their settlements; the desert sun influenced the orientation of their homes; and the wind was turned into a natural source of ventilation.
For travelers, these buildings offer an architectural journey into that accumulated knowledge. For architects and conservationists, they offer lessons that remain relevant. And for local communities, preserving them means protecting not only old buildings but a part of the knowledge, identity and landscape that made life possible in some of Iran’s harshest environments.

Lithuania Moves to Lift Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Weapons on Its Territory
Lithuania’s parliament has backed a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s ban on weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, being stationed on Lithuanian territory, LRT reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed amendment would remove part of Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from being located on the country’s territory. The proposal under consideration concerns the provision on weapons of mass destruction.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said removing the restriction would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities while eliminating legal differences between Lithuania and other EU and NATO members.
Opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, who supported the amendment, said Lithuania’s existing restrictions prevent allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country for deterrence purposes.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans. Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas also supported the change, linking the initiative to the security environment created by Russia’s war against Ukraine and the presence of strategic weapons in Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression. If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today,” Kaunas said.
The debate over Lithuania’s constitutional restrictions also follows recent Russian nuclear threats involving Kaliningrad, the heavily militarized Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania. On September 30, Reuters reported that Moscow had privately warned NATO it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance sought to isolate the region.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Russia accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that posed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”

The Chinese Electronics Trail Behind Russia’s Kurier Combat Robot
Unknown

- Category

The Chinese Electronics Trail Behind Russia’s Kurier Combat Robot
The company behind Russia’s Kurier unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) has repeatedly filed documents covering Chinese-made electronics, batteries, radio equipment, and other components.
The findings were revealed in an investigation by the international intelligence community InformNapalm published on October 4.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
InformNapalm examined Russian corporate and conformity records linked to NRTK KAPS LLC, a Moscow-based company headed and solely owned by Zorikto Gombozhapov, who is connected to the development of the Kurier military robot.
The investigation identified dozens of Russian declarations from 2025 and 2026 in which NRTK KAPS was listed as the applicant and Shenzhen-based HD LED TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. as the manufacturer.
The equipment covered by the records included radio modules and modems, chargers, batteries, IP cameras, power supplies, and other electronics.
One declaration dated July 30, 2025, covered 4,200 WTX-2S6 batteries and 8,400 WTX-2A2DC batteries—a total of 12,600 units.
InformNapalm stressed that declarations of conformity are not customs records and do not prove that all of the listed equipment was actually imported into Russia or installed in Kurier systems. The documents instead demonstrate the scale of Chinese-origin equipment covered by declarations filed by a company directly linked to the robot’s developer.
The investigation also raised questions about the role of HD LED TECHNOLOGY. In one Russian declaration, the Chinese company was listed as the manufacturer of a JY-ME02-CAN encoder. However, an independent 2025 technical paper identified the same model as a product of Shenzhen-based WIT Motion.
InformNapalm said the available evidence does not establish the precise relationship between the companies, which could involve contract manufacturing, OEM production, consolidation, or resale.
Gombozhapov’s business links to China also predate the NRTK KAPS declarations. Another company he heads, Eychdi LLC, filed declarations in 2024 covering products from Chinese manufacturers SHENZHEN DICOLOR GROUP CO., LTD. and Unilumin Group Co., Ltd.
Corporate records examined by InformNapalm also showed that Gombozhapov previously co-owned Moscow-based NIHAO LLC with Chinese citizen Du Tianzhu, with each holding a 25% stake.
Kurier is a Russian remotely operated tracked UGV designed for logistics and combat missions, including ammunition transport, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, mine-laying, and weapons carriage. Configurations have been shown carrying PKTM 7.62 mm machine guns, NSVT or Kord heavy machine guns, and AGS-17 and AGS-30 automatic grenade launchers.
On October 2, Russian Airborne Forces also conducted their first reported airdrop of Kurier UGVs from an Il-76 transport aircraft during the Center-2026 exercise. The systems were dropped from an altitude of roughly 600 meters before being used to support an assault unit.

Pezeshkian calls for broader engagement with EU, Asia

President urges new envoys to advance national interests
At a separate ceremony to bid farewell to Iran’s newly appointed ambassadors to the United Arab Emirates, Greece, Italy, Uganda and Senegal, Pezeshkian instructed the envoys to advance Iran’s national interests, expand multilateral relations and strengthen economic engagement with their host countries.

U.S. Army robot mule contest gets BLADE’s Hunter WOLF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:33:18 UTC
01:33:18 KST

- BLADE, formerly HDT, submitted its Hunter WOLF robotic vehicle for the U.S. Army's Infantry Last Tactical Mile resupply and casualty evacuation initiative.
- The U.S. Army selected six vendors in August and plans an operational assessment with an Army unit in early 2027 to inform production.
BLADE, the robotics company formerly known as HDT, said it has submitted its Hunter WOLF unmanned ground vehicle for the U.S. Army’s Infantry Last Tactical Mile initiative, a prototype effort to use robotic vehicles for resupply and casualty evacuation near the front line.
The company was one of six vendors the U.S. Army selected for the program in August. BLADE confirmed on Oct. 6 that the Hunter WOLF, a six-wheeled diesel-electric hybrid robot built for light and dismounted infantry, is the vehicle it will field. The company did not disclose the value of its agreement or how many vehicles it will provide.
The program, known as ILTM, focuses on the most exposed stretch of ground between rear support units and the forward line of own troops, where soldiers moving ammunition and supplies forward, or carrying wounded back, are most likely to come under fire. The U.S. Army chose the six vendors through prototype Other Transaction Agreements. The others are Maren-Go, Overland AI, Forterra, Hendrick’s Motorsports and American Rheinmetall.
According to the U.S. Army, the vendors will deliver production-ready prototypes that go through a series of demonstrations and assessments, ending with an operational assessment alongside an Army unit in early 2027. Feedback from that rotation is meant to inform a production decision on the Army’s next generation of autonomous infantry systems.
BLADE says the Hunter WOLF can carry 2,800 pounds (1,270 kg) autonomously, drive through dense forest, climb 60 percent grades and cross 40 percent side slopes. It can also supply electrical power to other equipment and accept different payloads depending on the mission, from cargo to casualty evacuation. The company describes the vehicle as production-ready and at Technology Readiness Level 9, the highest rating on the U.S. military’s scale, which indicates a system proven in actual operations.
“The Hunter WOLF is engineered, manufactured, field-proven and ready to support warfighters in challenging contested environments,” said Tom Van Doren, president of robotics at BLADE.
“It is battle-tested and field-proven to be the Army’s solution for the most dangerous and logistically complex segment of the battlefield,” Van Doren said.
The Hunter WOLF has been in service since 2017 and received upgrades in 2025. BLADE has run a string of evaluations with U.S. Army units this year, including the 10th Mountain Division and the 101st Airborne Division, and an August event with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Polk, Louisiana. The company has said the vehicle has supported the U.S. Marine Corps, Australian forces and the Ukrainian army and has been used in more than 60 field exercises.
In May, the company delivered Hunter WOLF vehicles to the 10th Mountain Division at Fort Polk under the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport effort, training soldiers to operate and maintain them across several mission configurations.

INTERVIEW - 'We'll be up and operational' before ISS retires: Axiom Space CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:31:40 UTC
01:31:40 KST

- 'I believe there is a race to create a space economy,' Cirtain tells Anadolu
US firm Axiom Space will have its commercial space station operating before the International Space Station (ISS) is retired in 2030, the company's CEO said Tuesday.
"We're waiting on a solicitation from the US government, from NASA, for the procurement of the services for that replacement to the ISS. But meanwhile, we've been using our own capital to build our space station," Jonathan Cirtain told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
"We have two vehicles that we are in the process of completing the manufacture of, and we'll launch in 2028 and 2029 those first two modules," he said. "The International Space Station is not set to retire until 2030. So, we'll be up and operational in advance of the ISS being decommissioned."
Rather than build its own replacement for the ISS, NASA plans to buy services from privately owned and operated space stations. The agency put out a draft call for proposals in July. Its schedule targets contract awards in spring 2027.
Axiom, a Houston-based company, has flown four private astronaut missions to the ISS. It is also developing the spacesuits NASA astronauts are set to wear on the Moon. Cirtain, a physicist, became CEO in October 2025.
 
'Race to create a space economy'
Asked whether the world is entering a race to build the next space station, Cirtain said the competition is broader.
"I believe there is a race to create a space economy," he said. "Now that the ISS has done 25 years of research and development to demonstrate the uses of microgravity ... it's time to use those capabilities for the benefit of humans back here on Earth."
He also pointed to a separate competition over the Moon.
"I also think that there's a geopolitical race between the United States, Europe, and its allies, Japan, Canada, for exploration of the Moon and what resources are available there," he said.
Scientists believe the Moon's south pole contains water ice. That ice could one day supply astronauts with drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.
"The United States, its allies, and separately, China, are all seeking to explore and find out what those resources are," Cirtain said. "Whether it's a space race or something else ... what an exciting time it is to be in space."
As an example of what research in orbit can offer, he cited the cancer drug Keytruda. Its maker, Merck, has run crystal-growth experiments on the ISS since 2014. The research helped Merck develop an injectable version of the drug, which US regulators approved in 2025.
"There's a whole set of reasons why crystals grown in space are better than crystals grown on Earth," Cirtain said. He argued that commercial stations are now needed to turn such research into actual products.
 
Managing a more crowded orbit
Last month, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the US has weapons in orbit capable of defending its forces against hostile action. It was the most direct acknowledgment by a US official that such systems exist.
Asked how a commercial station could stay a neutral international laboratory amid such developments, Cirtain said: "I think the US government and what it might be doing for its defensive posture is kind of independent of how Axiom Station is meant to operate."
As for how he sees the future of the peaceful use of outer space, he said: "I think that is the purpose of Axiom Space. For the peaceful, purposeful use of space for the benefit of humans back here on Earth."
He said the ISS has gained extensive experience tracking and managing space debris and natural hazards such as micrometeorites. He warned, however, that growing traffic in low Earth orbit will demand more care.
"As more spacecraft are deployed, we're going to have to become more sophisticated about how we manage the use of low Earth orbit," he said. "I really hope that we are clever about the way in which we use that resource and don't saturate that resource."
Overcrowding, he added, could lead to more collisions and more maneuvers by spacecraft to avoid them.
On artificial intelligence, Cirtain acknowledged concerns over security. "I think there's a lot of interest in understanding how security around the use of AI should be considered," he said.
"But I also think that there's a lot of opportunity," he added. He said AI tools beyond the large frontier models could help operate spacecraft and make better use of data collected in orbit. "There are other types of artificial intelligence tools that I do believe benefit us."
 
Cooperation with Türkiye
Axiom Space and the Turkish Space Agency signed an agreement in January 2025 to explore how Türkiye's space industry could contribute to Axiom Station.
"This is an expansion of a relationship that's already existing," Cirtain said. He recalled that Axiom worked with Turkish industry and a university on a science payload for its Ax-3 mission in 2024. Alper Gezeravci, Türkiye's first astronaut, flew on that mission.
Axiom has since established a university alliance that includes Turkish institutions. Through the alliance, the company helps universities turn ground-based experiments into payloads that can fly in space.
"We see this as an ongoing relationship, and as the space ecosystem in Türkiye expands, we just see there even more opportunities for collaboration between Axiom Space and industry here in Türkiye," he said.
The congress runs through Friday.

BAE wins F-35 electronic warfare order for Lots 20-22
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:29:35 UTC
01:29:35 KST

- BAE Systems received a Lockheed Martin contract to deliver AN/ASQ-239 electronic warfare systems for F-35 Lots 20 through 22 and retrofits for older aircraft.
- The company has delivered more than 1,500 F-35 electronic warfare systems and did not disclose the new contract's value.
BAE Systems will build electronic warfare systems for three more production lots of the F-35 Lightning II under a new contract from Lockheed Martin, the company said on Oct. 6.
The contract covers AN/ASQ-239 systems for F-35 Lots 20 through 22, along with systems to retrofit and modernize older aircraft already in service. BAE Systems did not disclose the value of the contract or how many systems it will deliver.
The AN/ASQ-239, the F-35’s built-in electronic warfare suite, listens for radar and other signals around the aircraft, identifies threats and warns the pilot, and supports both self-protection and offensive electronic attack. BAE Systems says the system’s passive, long-range sensing lets pilots detect threats without giving away their own position, and that it is designed to help the jet operate against enemy fighters, missiles, drones and modern integrated air defense networks.
According to BAE Systems, much of that capability is software-based, so operators can update the system quickly to respond to new threats without waiting for hardware changes.
“We’ve been a trusted contributor since the origin of the Joint Strike Fighter program, and we’ve continuously evolved our EW hardware and software to maintain our warfighters’ decisive battlespace advantage,” said Amber Dolan, vice president of F-35 Solutions at BAE Systems. “We’re laser-focused on scaling production and delivering software-based capabilities to meet the rapid pace of conflict.”
BAE Systems, which has supplied the electronic warfare suite for every F-35 built, says it has now delivered more than 1,500 systems, up from the roughly 800 it had delivered in 2021, when it received its Lot 16 order. The systems are designed and built at BAE Systems facilities in Nashua, Manchester and Merrimack in New Hampshire, and in Austin, Texas.
To keep up with F-35 production, the company said it is using more automation, newer system designs and a broader supply chain, and has invested in its facilities to build and support more systems faster.
The new order follows years of work on an upgraded version of the suite. In December 2021, Lockheed Martin awarded BAE Systems a $493 million contract modification to develop new core hardware for the AN/ASQ-239 as part of the F-35’s Block 4 modernization, which is meant to improve the jet’s ability to detect hard-to-see threats and handle more threats at once.
The F-35 is flown by the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, as well as a growing list of allied air forces, and BAE Systems said the contract supports the global F-35 fleet.

Six-volume “1001 Questions on Resistance” unveiled in Tehran
TEHRAN- The six-volume book “1001 Questions on Resistance,” based on three decades of conversations with the late Hezbollah leader Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah, was unveiled Monday at the Sarcheshmeh Cultural Center in Tehran during a gathering examining his thought and legacy.
The ceremony was attended by Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Qomi, head of Iran's Islamic Ideology Dissemination Organization; Mohammad-Hossein Saffar-Harandi, a member of the Expediency Discernment Council; Hojjatoleslam Asad Qasir, a cleric and director of the Center for Authentic Islam; Hojatoleslam Ahmad Rahdar, a faculty member at Baqer al-Olum University; Abbas Khamehyar, a former Iranian cultural attaché in Lebanon; Mehdi Afraz, author of the book; and a number of religious, academic and cultural figures.
Speaking at the ceremony, Afraz described resistance as one of the most significant human ideas of the contemporary era, saying that important questions about its intellectual and social dimensions remain unanswered despite extensive discussion of the concept.
He said the six-volume collection was compiled to address some of the ambiguities surrounding resistance in public discourse and social life.
“After extensive research, we selected the personality and views of martyr Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah as the main source, because his entire life and actions were closely intertwined with the issue of resistance, while his words offer strategic guidance for Muslim societies,” Afraz said.
He described Nasrallah as a strategic architect of resistance, adding that the collection covers six major areas: the theology of resistance, political thought of resistance, resistance society, strategic equations of resistance, the resistance bloc, and resistance in Lebanon.
According to Afraz, the collection presents Nasrallah’s statements in the form of 1,001 questions and answers, with two principal objectives: fostering an emotional and spiritual connection with him that can contribute to media and artistic productions, and enabling readers to engage more directly with his ideas.
Addressing the ceremony, Qomi described “1001 Questions on Resistance” as an example of the effort to clarify and accurately narrate the history and ideas of resistance.
He said Nasrallah’s legacy should not be reduced to his military role, stressing that the late Hezbollah leader had presented resistance as a path toward progress and dignity for the oppressed, supported by rational, innate and religious arguments.
“We all feel a debt toward Sayyed Hassan, and there is much that needs to be done,” Qomi said, emphasizing that the task today is not merely to recall his character, conduct and courage, but to explain the path of resistance that he placed before humanity.
Khamehyar, a West Asia researcher and former Iranian cultural attaché in Lebanon, called for greater attention to the different dimensions of Nasrallah’s thought and the values he established in Lebanon.
He said Iranian media and public platforms had largely focused on Nasrallah’s military role over the past two years, arguing that this approach overlooks other aspects of his legacy.
“We must address the diverse values that Sayyed Hassan established in Lebanon and which later spread to other Arab and Islamic countries,” Khamehyar said.
Referring to the concept of the “School of Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah,” he called for its less-explored dimensions to be studied and highlighted.
He said understanding the resistance movement in Lebanon requires examining Nasrallah’s managerial abilities, rationality, realism, ethical conduct and emphasis on educating a new generation.
“Sayyed Hassan held classes more than he delivered speeches,” he said, noting that Nasrallah regularly held sessions for the families of martyrs and young people and devoted considerable attention to educating and developing cadres.
Saffar-Harandi said Nasrallah filled a vacuum for a hero in the Muslim world by establishing a new standard for political leadership.
He said Nasrallah represented a victorious model of resistance, creating expectations among his contemporaries and subsequent generations that would not easily be reversed.
Saffar-Harandi highlighted Nasrallah’s deep religious convictions, close connection with the people and courage in difficult circumstances. He also pointed to his understanding of Lebanon’s diverse social fabric, saying that despite leading a Shiite movement, he gained support among Sunnis, Maronites and other Christian communities.
He also described Nasrallah as a bridge between the Islamic Revolution in Iran and the Arab world, including Iraq, Yemen, Palestine and Syria.
Rahdar called for the compilation and publication of Nasrallah’s collected speeches in a volume similar to “Sahifeh-ye Nour,” the collection of the late Imam Khomeini’s speeches and writings.
He described Nasrallah as an “allameh” in the full sense of the word, saying it would take time for the different dimensions of his personality and thought to be fully understood.
He said the wisdom evident in Nasrallah’s speeches was not merely the product of theoretical study, but had developed through years of practical and ethical struggle.
“1001 Questions on Resistance” is published in six volumes covering the theology of resistance, political thought, society, strategic equations, the resistance bloc and the Lebanese resistance, offering a thematic presentation of Nasrallah’s views through 1,001 questions and answers.
Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah became secretary-general of Hezbollah in 1992, following the assassination of his predecessor, Sayyed Abbas al-Musawi. He led the movement for more than three decades, during a period that included the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and the 2006 war between Hezbollah and Israel. Under his leadership, Hezbollah developed into a major political and military force in Lebanon and assumed a broader role in regional affairs.
Nasrallah was also widely known for his televised speeches, through which he addressed supporters and commented on major developments in Lebanon and the wider region. Born and raised in Beirut, he came from a family with roots in Bazouriyeh in southern Lebanon. While his public life was closely followed across the region, his personal and family life largely remained outside the spotlight.
He was tragically killed at the age of 64 during a series of intense Israeli airstrikes in southern Beirut on September 27, 2024.
The attack that claimed Nasrallah’s life was carried out by Israeli fighter jets targeting Hezbollah’s main headquarters, resulting in the martyrdom of several senior Hezbollah commanders and prominent Iranian Revolutionary Guards Lieutenant General Abbas Nilforoushan, who was present at the scene.
Under Nasrallah's leadership, whose name means "victory through God," Hezbollah evolved from a grassroots armed movement into the largest political party in Lebanon's recent history. Renowned for his captivating speeches, Nasrallah garnered attention throughout the West Asia and beyond, establishing himself as a significant figure within the Axis of Resistance, which includes Hezbollah, the Palestinian groups Hamas and Islamic Jihad, the Houthi movement in Yemen, and various Iraqi paramilitary factions.

The US signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland in late September that will allow Washington to establish two new military bases there, drawing the autonomous Danish territory further into US orbit.
Rubio said at a news conference that Iceland had long served as “a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behaviour and deterring our adversaries”.
He arrived in Reykjavik on Oct 5 and has held talks with Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir and top diplomat Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir.
They covered topics including geothermal energy, data centres and the pharmaceutical industry.
With competition on the rise in the Arctic, Iceland has regained status as a strategic player, even as the island continues to rely heavily on the US for security.
“For decades this nation, Iceland, has occupied a critical strategic position for our collective security and that remains true today more than ever before,” Rubio said.

In response, Reykjavik summoned the US ambassador and called the image “wholly inappropriate”.

Breadcrumb
Israel demolishes Jerusalem building, forcibly displacing dozens of Palestinians
Israeli bulldozers on Tuesday demolished a five-storey residential building in annexed East Jerusalem, displacing its 70 residents in a move the local Palestinian authority said was aimed at "forcible transfer".
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who gleefully oversaw the demolition, claimed the building had been constructed without a permit.
"I love hearing this noise. We demolish what is illegal," Ben Gvir said in a video posted on X, which showed him inside the cab of one of the bulldozers.
Densely populated East Jerusalem faces a severe housing crisis, with thousands of homes built without permits, which its Palestinian residents say are near impossible to obtain from Israeli authorities.
The Jerusalem Governorate, the Palestinian local authority for the area, condemned Tuesday's demolition which it said was "a dangerous escalation in the policy of home demolitions and forcible transfer... and the imposition of a new demographic and urban reality".
Hanine Hreibat, a teacher and mother of four who was renting one of the 10 apartments in the building, said a large Israeli police force arrived in the At-Tur neighbourhood in the early hours of the morning, accompanied by three bulldozers.
They stormed the apartments and gave residents 10 minutes to leave, she said.
Hreibat told AFP she had woken up to the sound of her husband shouting at the police, asking them not to enter the bedroom where she was, adding she had endured "five minutes of terror, with weapons pointed at our heads".
She said police officers had allowed her to take only medicine, money, her handbag and ID card.
Among the rubble, residents collected gas cylinders and filled plastic bags with clothes they had managed to pull out from the huge mound of debris.
Hreibat said she had nowhere to go following the demolition.
"We'll look for a second home. Today we're at my in-laws' and tomorrow at my parents'," she said.
Residents confirmed to AFP that they had received a demolition notice on Monday, but did not know when it would be carried out.
Israel regularly carries out demolitions of what it says are illegal structures built by Palestinians in East Jerusalem and the occupied West Bank.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967, later annexing it and declaring it part of its undivided capital, a move not recognised by the UN or most of the international community.
More than 360,000 Palestinians live in East Jerusalem as well as some 230,000 Israelis.
Palestinians aspire to make it the capital of a future Palestinian state, while Israel regards the entire city as its "unified and indivisible" capital.

'Our doors and hearts are always open to Iran': Malaysia's chargé d'affaires tells the Tehran Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:26:17 UTC
01:26:17 KST

'Our doors and hearts are always open to Iran': Malaysia's chargé d'affaires tells the Tehran Times
TEHRAN - Dato' Wan Aznainizam Yusri bin Wan Abdul Rashid arrived in Tehran in late August to take up the post of Chargé d'Affaires and Head of Mission at the Embassy of Malaysia. He will be elevated to Ambassador upon the formal presentation of his credentials.
In his first exclusive interview in Iran, granted to the Tehran Times, he talks about his first month in the country, Malaysia's firm stance on U.S.-Israeli aggression, the state of trade between the two countries, and the cultural and educational ties that keep Malaysians and Iranians connected.
He also shares what he hopes to achieve during his time here, and has a simple message for the people of Iran.
 
Below is the full text of the interview:
You have been in Tehran for a month now. What have your first impressions been of the country and its people?
My first impression of Iran is one of profound admiration and warmth. Upon arriving, one is immediately struck by the deep cultural heritage and historical ties that Malaysia and Iran have shared for centuries. Our nations are bound by a rich tapestry of mutual respect, intellectual exchange, and civilizational links that continue to strengthen our modern diplomatic relations.
What stands out most, however, is the remarkable resilience of the Iranian people. To witness how this nation has consistently overcome immense challenges, including decades of economic sanctions since 1980, is truly inspiring. The ingenuity, self-reliance, and strength they display in navigating these difficulties speak volumes about their character. And honestly, seeing how the country stood firm and successfully defended its capital during the onslaught of aerial attacks by Israel and the U.S. was truly remarkable. It showed the world a profound level of resolve and courage.
Above all, I have been deeply moved by the incredible warmth and hospitality of the Iranians. From my very first interactions, the generosity and welcoming nature of the people have made me feel entirely at home. I look forward to working closely with our Iranian friends to further deepen the bonds of friendship and cooperation between Malaysia and Iran.
The most important issue in Iran today is the U.S.-Israeli aggression, which has both a military and an economic dimension. Malaysia was one of the most outspoken countries in Southeast Asia in condemning the military phase of the war. What drove Malaysia to take that stance when many Muslim countries hesitated to explicitly condemn the U.S. and Israel?
Malaysia's strong stance against U.S.-Israeli military aggression is driven by a deeply ingrained, bipartisan foreign policy that prioritises international law, national sovereignty, and an absolute rejection of geopolitical double standards.
When people look at Malaysia's vocal position today, they shouldn't see it as a sudden political shift. It is actually the continuation of a long-standing, deeply rooted principle. For decades, Malaysia has held a firm, institutional stance against illegal warfare, unprovoked aggression, and the violation of any nation's sovereignty. We do not choose our principles based on political convenience or who the aggressor happens to be.
My Prime Minister, Dato' Seri Anwar Ibrahim, has been very clear on this at the global stage. Following the military strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Anwar immediately issued a statement condemning the attack. He had also made it clear to the world that we can no longer swallow lectures on human rights and democracy from Western powers when such double standards are playing out in real time. Under his leadership, Malaysia has consistently reaffirmed Iran's internationally recognized right to defend its own sovereignty under international law, while also calling for a peaceful resolution to the conflict.
This outspokenness is a legacy passed down through our leadership. Past Prime Ministers, including Tun Dr. Mahathir Mohamad, spent decades challenging Western hegemony and calling out global superpowers for using military and economic coercion against developing nations. Because this position is deeply embedded in our national identity, Malaysia's Parliament is entirely united on this issue, bridging all political parties to unanimously condemn these acts.
This is exactly why, at the recent UN General Assembly, our Foreign Minister, Datuk Seri Utama Mohamad Hasan, explicitly called out the global governance system. He stated plainly that Malaysia is sick of seeing the collective will of the General Assembly silenced by the Security Council's veto power. He demanded that to ensure true peace and global stability, the veto power must be challenged and ultimately abolished, especially when it paralyses action against crimes against humanity. Expanding membership is pointless if the veto remains an asymmetric tool for superpowers to shield aggression.
While other nations might hesitate due to pressure or strategic ties, Malaysia believes that staying silent makes one complicit. We speak out because true global stability cannot be built on deception, and a nation's right to exist in peace should never be compromised for another's tactical advantage.
How does Malaysia view Iran's role in regional security in West Asia?
Malaysia views Iran as an indispensable, sovereign pillar of regional security in West Asia, and our perspective is rooted in a clear recognition of interconnected global realities. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan have consistently underscored three fundamental parameters.
First, absolute support for sovereignty and stability. Malaysia respects Iran's territorial integrity and sovereign right to defend itself under international law. We have openly condemned external aggression against Iran, viewing unilateral attacks as grave violations of state sovereignty. For true peace to return to West Asia, all parties must decisively reduce tensions, halt escalations, and allow diplomacy to replace military hostility.
Second, an interconnected, self-reliant security architecture. Malaysia firmly believes that the security of West Asia is an interconnected whole. History has proven that the region cannot rely on external players, be it the United States or Israel, to engineer a manufactured or asymmetric stability. True, sustainable security can only be achieved when regional nations work together, manage their own borders, and determine their own future without foreign interference.
Lastly, deep appreciation for strategic cooperation. On a practical level, Malaysia deeply appreciates Iran's constructive role and cooperation in ensuring maritime safety. During periods of intense regional conflict and disruptions, Tehran actively facilitated the safe passage of Malaysian-owned merchant vessels through the critical chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz. This concrete gesture is a testament to the trust between our nations and highlights Iran's capability to act as a responsible guardian of vital global trade routes.
Ultimately, Malaysia looks at Iran not through a lens of isolation, but as a key partner with whom we must engage to cultivate lasting, self-determined stability in the region.
How would you describe the current state of economic ties between Iran and Malaysia? Is it growing at all, given the difficulties caused by sanctions and the war?
The current state of economic ties between Malaysia and Iran is resilient and demonstrating growth, despite navigating a highly challenging landscape shaped by long-standing unilateral sanctions and recent regional volatility. While external geo-economic pressures and maritime instability present undeniable hurdles, both nations remain firmly committed to expanding their commercial relationship, driven by mutual economic interests and a shared vision of a self-reliant Islamic world.
Recent data demonstrates that commercial ties are not stagnant but are actively expanding where permitted. Total bilateral trade between Malaysia and Iran reached RM2.45 billion, with Malaysian exports driving the bulk of this volume at RM2.17 billion. Malaysia's exports are anchored heavily by palm oil and palm-based products, while primary imports from Iran consist of essential pharmaceutical products, edible fruits, and nuts, alongside permitted oil and gas derivatives. While this represents a fraction of Malaysia's total global trade, the baseline shows a clear upward trend. In historic periods of engagement, bilateral trade has scaled past RM3.68 billion. The institutional intent from both capitals is to use current frameworks to return to and exceed those levels.
The expansion of these economic links faces explicit operational constraints that both governments are actively trying to bypass. Malaysia strictly enforces United Nations-mandated sanctions. However, navigating unilateral secondary sanctions imposed by Western powers creates severe compliance and banking hurdles, making standard international trade settlements exceptionally difficult. Geopolitical tensions in West Asia, particularly conflict disruptions impacting shipping through critical maritime channels like the Strait of Hormuz, have also introduced high freight costs, logistical uncertainties, and supply chain bottlenecks for merchants on both sides.
During the recent BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim engaged in vital bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Malaysia reaffirmed its stance to pursue economic linkages guided by national interest and respect for state sovereignty. Among the high-potential sectors identified are food security and agriculture, where we can deepen the supply chain for Malaysian palm oil while collaborating on broad food security initiatives to counter global economic shocks. The halal economy also offers opportunities, leveraging Malaysia's global leadership in halal certification alongside Iran's robust domestic market to create a strong alternative trading network. We are also exploring permitted collaborative frameworks in energy distribution and technological exchange, as well as promoting joint academic ventures, research opportunities, and technical training between Malaysian and Iranian institutions to foster organic, long-term economic integration.
Our leaders also discussed how both nations can leverage the BRICS platform to bypass traditional geo-economic hurdles. The BRICS platform provides Malaysia and Iran with a powerful institutional framework to re-engineer our commercial relationship. For too long, developing nations have been vulnerable to unilateral secondary sanctions because the global financial architecture relies so heavily on a single currency. Through BRICS, we are actively working to change that.
At the global summit, Prime Minister Anwar advocated for a fairer global financing system that reduces our vulnerability to external economic pressures. For Malaysia and Iran, the most actionable path forward lies in Local Currency Settlement Mechanisms and de-dollarization. Malaysia has already successfully proven the value of local currency trading with regional neighbours like China and Indonesia; BRICS gives us the platform to expand that exact blueprint to a larger pool of Global South nations, including Iran.
Of course, we manage this path with clear institutional caution. Malaysia's trade strategy remains fiercely independent and balanced. We are not creating an anti-Western front, but rather building practical economic alternatives that protect our national interests. For Iran and Malaysia, the BRICS platform turns our shared desire for economic sovereignty into a technical, workable reality.
Ultimately, Malaysia views its trade relationship with Iran as a sovereign right. By utilizing joint commissions and exploring alternative investment channels, both nations are actively working to translate diplomatic goodwill into durable, practical economic partnerships.
Beyond politics and trade, how do you assess cultural and people-to-people ties between Iran and Malaysia?
While trade data and geopolitical alignments dominate headlines, the true heartbeat of the Malaysia-Iran relationship lies in our cultural and people-to-people ties. These connections are organic, deeply felt, and entirely insulated from external political pressures.
When we look beyond politics, what we find is a profound shared cultural heritage. Malaysia and Iran are bound by centuries of civilizational links and an overlapping tapestry of Islamic and Eastern values. At the core of both our societies are the sacred principles of hospitality, mutual respect, and genuine brotherhood. When a Malaysian visits Iran, or an Iranian arrives in Malaysia, I believe they do not feel like strangers in a foreign land. They instantly recognize a familiar warmth, a shared emphasis on family values, and a culture of welcoming the traveler with open arms.
A vital pillar of this contemporary relationship is our incredible alumni network. Over the past few decades, thousands of Iranian students have chosen Malaysia for their higher education. In my recent engagements with these Iranian alumni of Malaysian universities, I have been deeply inspired by how fondly they speak of their time in our country. Today, these individuals are professionals and entrepreneurs thriving right here in Iran. They serve as an irreplaceable human bridge between our nations, carrying a piece of Malaysian culture back with them and acting as organic ambassadors of our friendship. The same can also be said about the alumni of our very own Malaysian Technical Cooperation Programme, which has trained 419 Iranian officials in both the public and private sectors.
To harness this incredible energy, we are actively driving an initiative to establish the Malaysia-Iran Friendship Group. This group is designed to move beyond formal diplomacy, creating a lifelong network of collaboration. It will serve as a structured platform to deepen grassroots cultural ties, foster direct academic exchange between our universities, and create joint research initiatives. We want to ensure that the next generation of Malaysian and Iranian thinkers, artists, and professionals have a continuous, institutional framework to collaborate and innovate together.
Finally, we are aggressively building on this momentum through targeted tourism promotion. We want more Iranians to experience the multicultural beauty of our country firsthand. My team and I here in Tehran are focused on promoting Malaysia as the premier destination for leisure, family travel, and world-class higher education. This effort is perfectly timed with our global Tourism Malaysia push under the Visit Malaysia 2026-2027 campaign. We are showcasing Malaysia's renowned Muslim-friendly tourism offerings, diverse ecosystems, and modern infrastructure to the Iranian public.
Governments can sign treaties and businesses can exchange commodities, but it is the students, tourists, and cultural exchanges that weave the permanent fabric of our relationship. Malaysia and Iran will continue to nurture these bonds, ensuring our people remain closer than ever.
Are there concrete plans to expand exchanges in education, science, culture and tourism, for example scholarships, university partnerships, cultural weeks, or direct flight and tourism promotion?
Yes, there are concrete, active plans and freshly implemented initiatives to significantly expand our exchanges in education, science, culture, and tourism. Public statements and high-level diplomatic efforts from both Malaysian and Iranian leaders confirm that rather than just discussing potential frameworks, both nations have put definitive actions into motion to deepen grassroots connectivity.
Our academic cooperation has entered a highly practical phase, moving past generic agreements into targeted scientific collaboration. In high-level consultations, Malaysia's Minister of Higher Education, Datuk Seri Dr. Zambry Abdul Kadir, and Iran's Minister of Science, Research, and Technology, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, explicitly committed to expanding university partnerships. They have underscored the need to bolster joint scientific research, share technologies, and establish specialized working groups. I have mentioned the MTCP earlier. Malaysia continues to leverage the flagship MTCP as a bridge to share our knowledge and expertise with our partners including Iran. This state-sponsored initiative by Malaysia had already provided direct training and knowledge-sharing for 419 Iranian professionals in tech, economics, and agriculture.
Cultural exchange is being institutionalized to create continuous, lifelong linkages between our thinkers and artists. During our official dialogue with the vibrant network of Iranian alumni who graduated from Malaysian institutions, we proposed a formal Malaysia-Iran Friendship Group. This group will serve as a permanent, non-political framework dedicated to fostering ongoing academic exchanges, cultural weeks, and continuous collaboration. On a broader civilizational level, both capitals have continuously supported the cross-pollination of our national identities. This includes establishing reciprocal language programs, such as Persian teaching courses in Malaysia and the promotion of Malay studies in Iran, alongside high-profile translations of classic Persian and Malay literature to deepen mutual understanding.
In a monumental boost to our people-to-people connectivity, direct flights between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur officially resumed following years of absence. We now have a weekly direct flight operated by Iran Air Tour since last August and soon Iran Air and Mahan Air. This direct aerial link drastically reduces travel hurdles and provides the necessary transport infrastructure to support a massive influx of tourists and students. To fully capitalize on this direct flight path, the Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran has launched the Malaysia Tourism Connect initiative. We are actively engaging with top Iranian tour operators and travel agencies to aggressively promote Malaysia's diverse, family-friendly, and world-class halal tourism environment. This forms a core component of our global Visit Malaysia 2026-2027 campaign, positioning Malaysia as the premier destination of choice for Iranian travelers.
By the end of your time here, what would you most like to have achieved in the Malaysia–Iran relationship, politically, economically, and in terms of people-to-people ties?
When my time here comes to an end, I want to look back and know that we didn't just maintain a diplomatic friendship. We built an unshakeable, self-reliant partnership that truly changes lives.
Politically, my goal is to leave our relationship completely integrated on the global stage. Based on the aspiration of both my Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, I want Malaysia and Iran to stand shoulder-to-shoulder as independent voices, defending state sovereignty, calling out international double standards, and pushing to reform a broken UN system. I also hope that there will be more exchanges of high-level visits from both Tehran and Putrajaya.
Economically, I want to turn our shared vision into everyday reality. By fully leveraging the BRICS platform, I hope that we will witness an increase in bilateral trade and investments between our two countries. We must find ways to bypass external financial pressures to comfortably push our bilateral trade past historic highs.
In terms of people-to-people ties, this is deeply personal to me. With direct flights finally restored, I want to see a massive surge in families, tourists, and students crossing borders under our Visit Malaysia campaign. By launching our formal Friendship Group, I want to ensure that our brilliant university alumni and researchers have a permanent, lifelong bridge to collaborate on the sciences of the future.
Ultimately, I want to leave behind a resilient network that protects our sovereignty and keeps the people of Malaysia and Iran permanently connected.
If you could say just one sentence to the people of Iran, what would that sentence be?
Choosing just one sentence is always difficult for a diplomat, because when you give a microphone to an ambassador, he will talk without being stopped. You know, we are just like singers. But if I were to have one simple sentence for the people of Iran, for my brothers and sisters in Iran, it would be this: please rest assured that our doors and hearts are always open to you all, because to know Malaysia is to love Malaysia, a country that is in every sense truly Asia.

Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:24:58 UTC
01:24:58 KST

Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
In Tehran, discussions about Iran’s potential withdrawal from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) are growing increasingly urgent. Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has recently acknowledged that the issue is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. His statements lend significant political weight to the discourse around Iran’s potential withdrawal from the NPT: One can no longer downplay it as something proposed by hardliners or fringe groups. While Baghaei also reaffirmed Iran’s commitment to its membership in the NPT and the associated obligations, he made it clear that the possibility of exiting the treaty is being considered.
This situation has been triggered by Tehran’s mounting frustration. Iran finds it increasingly difficult to justify why participation in the NPT demands constant concessions from it, while the country’s rights remain negotiable. Despite Iran’s regular affirmation of the peaceful nature of its nuclear program, disputes persist and external pressure continues to mount. This gives Iran reason to question the practical value of the agreement. The Iranian leadership is signaling that its willingness to remain a member of the NPT cannot be viewed as unconditional.
The NPT was designed to maintain balance: Non-nuclear states refrain from developing nuclear weapons and receive international guarantees, while their right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy is recognized by the treaty; nuclear powers, meanwhile, pursue negotiations toward nuclear disarmament. For Tehran, the critical issue lies in the balance of rights and responsibilities. Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear technology does not exclude the international monitoring of its nuclear program. But there is a difference between inspections and demands to relinquish nuclear technologies, and Iran believes that this line is increasingly being blurred.
A pivotal aspect of the NPT is the so-called ‘nuclear deal’ signed in 2015. Iran agreed to impose significant limitations on its nuclear program and accepted extensive international oversight in exchange for relief from sanctions. In 2016, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed that Iran had implemented the necessary measures to put the agreement into effect. However, in 2018, the US withdrew from the deal and reinstated sanctions. This unfortunate experience casts a shadow on how Tehran views any potential future compromises. Iran accepted the restrictions, but the change in Washington’s policy undermined many of the anticipated benefits of the deal.
Strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities have further compounded the crisis of trust, raising concerns over physical security. The IAEA reported attacks on several Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025; this shows that even with international guarantees, the facilities remain vulnerable. It’s true that the NPT does not offer military protection or immunity from attacks. However, the main problem for Iranian political circles is that the international oversight of Iran’s nuclear program has failed to ensure a diplomatic settlement of disagreements.
This raises a poignant question for Tehran. If cooperation with international institutions does not prevent sanctions and strikes against Iran, then what argument can the supporters of the treaty bring up in favor of remaining a party to the NPT? The treaty’s supporters outline its theoretical benefits, but the country assesses its results. As the costs of external pressure rise, it becomes increasingly hard to convince anyone that further concessions will enhance security. Instead, there’s a growing perception that new compromises simply lead to new demands. This sense of injustice largely explains Iran’s current irritation.
Another factor is the unequal standing of the countries in the region. Israel is not a party to the NPT and does not face the same comprehensive oversight that Iran does. While Tehran is constantly questioned about its nuclear program, no one raises concerns about Israel. This situation strikes Tehran as fundamentally unfair; its participation in the treaty imposes restrictions that Israel does not have to deal with. From Iran’s perspective, Israel, which is not bound by the treaty, enjoys greater freedom, while Iran’s membership comes with constraints and threats. Consequently, the treaty’s opponents have a strong argument in favor of withdrawing.
One cannot dismiss the fact that the IAEA has grounds to question Iran’s compliance. The IAEA faces multiple restrictions in Iran when it comes to inspections, nuclear material tracking, access to facilities, and so on. The Iranian Foreign Ministry emphasizes that it remains committed to the NPT and expects respect for its rights under the treaty, noting that disagreements with the IAEA should be resolved through dialogue and inspections, not through threats or attacks on Iranian facilities.
The heightened public attention to Iran’s potential exit from the NPT is also tied to ongoing negotiations. The prospect of Iran’s withdrawal raises the stakes for the US and increases the cost of failing to reach an agreement. As long as Iran remains a party to the NPT, there are legal grounds for international oversight and the possibility of engaging in meaningful discussions about its nuclear program. Exiting the treaty would complicate this process and increase uncertainty. Tehran is signaling that maintaining the current negotiations framework requires political effort. If this framework is systematically undermined, there are no guarantees that it will exist indefinitely.
At the same time, Iran is raising the stakes. As long as Iran’s opponents believe that it will remain in the NPT despite pressure, the threat of withdrawal can be dismissed as mere rhetoric. Baghaei’s statements make it clear that the option of leaving the NPT is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. However, Tehran is in no rush to actually exit the treaty. The Foreign Ministry has reaffirmed Iran’s existing obligations while leaving the final decision to the country’s leadership and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
By openly discussing the possibility of withdrawing from the NPT, Tehran can analyze the reaction of Russia, China, the EU, its neighbors in the region, and also its own populace. This will help assess the potential support for such a move and see whether other parties are willing to offer conditions that might persuade Iran to remain a party to the agreement. The Foreign Ministry’s statement is most likely driven by several factors, including a strategic calculation in negotiations, internal disagreements within the leadership, and a growing dissatisfaction with external pressure.
Moreover, Tehran understands that withdrawing from the NPT could further escalate tensions in the region. Türkiye and Saudi Arabia may believe that Iran is about to develop nuclear weapons, prompting them to consider their own nuclear capabilities. Their argument would be straightforward: If Iran no longer feels bound by the prohibition against acquiring nuclear weapons, why should its neighbors refrain from doing the same? Although withdrawing from the treaty doesn’t confer a legal right to nuclear arms, this detail could easily be overlooked in political debates. Tehran faces a serious risk: In its quest to enhance national security, it may inadvertently push its neighbors toward a nuclear arms race, and ultimately have to confront new threats. Therefore, we can neither be confident of Iran’s inevitable exit from the treaty nor reduce the situation to mere bluffing.
Iran’s reaction to Russia’s proposal regarding the export of its enriched uranium should be considered in this light. Baghaei confirmed that Tehran is considering Moscow’s offer and will act in accordance with its national interests. This keeps the door open for negotiations. Before taking such a step, Tehran seeks clarity on what it will gain in return and how this will affect its nuclear program moving forward. While Russia’s proposal could facilitate an agreement, Iran wants to be sure that the potential transfer of enriched uranium is accompanied by a genuine reduction in external pressure. Trust in Moscow plays an important part in this, but Iran needs assurances that all the other parties will uphold their end of the deal.
The main takeaway from the statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry is that Iran no longer wishes to view its participation in the NPT as grounds for America’s endless, unfounded demands. Tehran insists on discussing its rights, the predictability of its partners’ commitments, and the potential for peaceful development. For now, this demand is articulated through diplomatic language, allowing room for negotiation. However, it is rooted in a profound crisis of trust. If the NPT continues to be perceived in Iran as a source of restrictions without practical benefits (an outlook that appears increasingly likely), then the arguments in favor of remaining a party to the treaty will become weaker. At some point, it may cease to be an issue that raises the stakes in negotiations and may become a matter requiring practical resolution.

Google ordered to halt data centre works in Finland over environmental concerns
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:24:52 EEST
01:24:52 KST

Finnish authorities have ordered Google subsidiary Tuike Finland to halt work affecting the environment at planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani until environmental impact assessments are completed.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency, LVV, issued the request on Tuesday. Tuike Finland must stop the specified work immediately and no later than 23 October.
The order covers tree removal, excavation, blasting, crushing, soil removal, drainage work and the construction of site roads and storage areas.
Planning, measurements, soil surveys and work that has limited environmental effects and is easy to reverse remain permitted.
LVV said investigations available to the agency indicate that work has already changed both sites. This includes tree clearance, removal of topsoil, construction of roads and storage areas, changes to ditches and culverts and stormwater work.
“Our assessment is that these measures change the environment and cause impacts whose identification and assessment are among the central objectives of the environmental impact assessment procedure,” Tommi Muilu, head of LVV’s environmental department, said in the agency’s statement.
Environmental impact assessment procedures for both projects remain unfinished. They are expected to conclude during 2026.
Tuike Finland has until 14 October to submit a written response to LVV and state whether it intends to follow the request. Google has since said it will comply.
“We understand the concern caused by the situation. In this case, we did not meet the high standards we set ourselves,” Sondre Ronander, Google’s communications manager for Finland and Norway, said in a company statement.
Ronander said Google had acted in good faith under Finland’s Forest Act, conducted nature surveys and taken measures to protect sites with environmental value. He said Google plans to plant trees across 130 hectares in Muhos.
The dispute had already drawn scrutiny in September. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said more than 300 hectares of forest had been cleared at the planned data centre site in Leppiniemi, Muhos, while environmental impact assessment procedures were still incomplete.
The organisation argued that permanent land-use conversion on that scale should have been preceded by an environmental impact assessment. It also raised concerns about work at Google’s Otanmäki project in Kajaani.
The projects are a part of Google’s €13 billion data centre investment in Finland.
LVV said environmental assessments are intended to identify significant effects before decisions and major preparatory work take place. Large-scale changes made before the process ends risk limiting the assessment of alternatives and measures designed to reduce environmental harm.
If Tuike Finland fails to comply, LVV said it will consider administrative enforcement under environmental assessment legislation or other applicable laws. Such proceedings could include a conditional fine.
Google’s decision to comply means such enforcement is not required at this stage.

Paramount completes takeover of Warner Bros, creating media behemoth Skydance
Paramount completed its acquisition of Warner Bros Discover on Tuesday, after a bidding war against Netflix. The deal closed following federal approval of a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that tried to block the transaction on antitrust grounds. Opponents in the movie industry warned of job cuts, while media groups said Warner-owned CNN's independence could be compromised.
Paramount completed on Tuesday its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, uniting two of Hollywood's most storied studios in a media empire spanning television, news and cinema under the control of David Ellison.
The combined company – renamed Skydance – brings together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures, the CBS News and CNN networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands.
Ellison plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services over time.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump.
Skydance shares began trading Tuesday on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker "SKYD," while Warner Bros Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share in cash.
Read moreParamount settles with US states, clearing path for Warner Bros. merger
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.
Paramount won a bidding war against Netflix in February for Warner Bros Discovery, and the Trump administration approved the deal – one of the largest-ever media mergers – in June, without demanding a change to its business.

In response to the UN Human Rights Council’s vote today adopting the resolution that renews the mandate of the Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela, as well as of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, for another two years, Amnesty International’s Americas director, Ana Piquer, said:

Extending the Mission’s crucial work for the next two years reinforces the international community’s interest in justice and accountability for gross human rights violations in the country, including crimes against humanity. This is a clear sign of recognition that the government’s repressive apparatus is still in place while opacity and impunity remain the norm.”
We welcome this decision to continue the scrutiny over the ongoing human rights crisis in Venezuela. Extending the Mission’s crucial work for the next two years reinforces the international community’s interest in justice and accountability for gross human rights violations in the country, including crimes against humanity. ”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas director.
“Renewing UN scrutiny and investigations into the situation in Venezuela speaks to the seriousness of the continuing crisis in the country and of the repressive structures and practices still in place. The Mission’s investigation, reporting, and evidence-based recommendations are a key tool for scrutinizing the government’s long-standing policy of repression. Its victim and justice-centred mandate can play a crucial role in finding solutions for accountability and the non-repetition of the suffering that people have endured for long over a decade.”
“We remind the Venezuelan authorities and the international community that victims’ rights to truth, justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence must be front and centre in all efforts to ensure a future where the rule of law and human rights are fully respected in Venezuela. We also continue calling for the immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained for political reasons, for all repressive laws and regulations to be repealed, for the end to political persecution, and the full dismantling of the state’s policy of repression.”
“Victims’ rights to truth, justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence must be front and centre in all efforts to ensure a future where the rule of law and human rights are fully respected in Venezuela.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas director.
Background information
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela (FFM) is a mechanism created by the UN in 2019 to exercise scrutiny and investigate gross human rights violations in Venezuela. Its work has been highly regarded, and its continuity deemed necessary, so its mandate has been renewed in 2020, 2022, and 2024 for two-year periods. Since 2024, the states that lead this effort are Argentina, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, Guatemala, Paraguay, and Uruguay.
