How a playwright transformed a sister’s loss into art for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:48:29 UTC
00:48:29 KST

For Yuval Naim, the grief of losing her younger sister, Agam, in the Gaza conflict is not a static sorrow but a shifting landscape.
To process this new reality, the 28-year-old Jaffa resident has turned to the stage, channeling her family’s heartbreak into a children’s play titled Out of Three, One is Missing (Mishalosh Yotzet Achat), which premiered last week. Through a whimsical narrative about a hive of bees, Naim explores a heavy truth: There is no single, correct way to mourn.
“It was hard for me to cope with the grief. I told my psychologist I didn’t know what to do. She replied, ‘You’re a creator – so create,’” Naim said. “It made me realize that if I found it difficult to talk about Agam for the time being, I could express what I was going through through my art.”
Naim is the eldest of three sisters who grew up in the quiet settings of Pardes Hanna before moving to Kibbutz Mishmarot. Her sisters, Peleg and Agam, followed.
“Agam was driven to excel in everything she touched,” Naim recalled, sketching a portrait of a vibrant, deeply loved young woman. “She had so many different circles of friends – from her pre-military service year at the Edenim youth village to her intensive training as a combat paramedic. Even now, her friends still come to visit us. So many people loved her; she meant the world to so many.”
Agam Naim deployed in Gaza Strip for seven months
St.-Sgt. Agam Naim spent seven months deployed with combat forces in Gaza. She had fulfilled her frontline duties and was scheduled to transition to a safe, prestigious instructional role – commanding and training the next generation of paramedics. She was never supposed to re-enter the conflict zone. Yet, driven by fierce duty and loyalty to her peers, she insisted on going back one final time.
“Mom would tell her that the difference between a score of 90 and 95 didn’t really matter anymore,” Naim said, “but Agam would reply that she was going to be treating people, so it was important.
“She wasn’t supposed to go back into Gaza anymore, but she insisted on entering one last time just to say goodbye to her people and to be with them,” Naim said.
First female IDF soldier killed in Gaza during September 2024 operation
During this final entry, Agam fell. On September 17, 2024, at just 20 years old, Agam was killed alongside four other combat soldiers when an explosive device detonated in Rafah’s Tel Sultan neighborhood. She became the first female soldier killed in action during the ground operation in the Gaza Strip.
The tragedy in Out of Three, One is Missing is filtered through a metaphor children can understand. The story follows three busy bees. When the third bee suddenly disappears, the remaining two must navigate the hive alone.
“Each of the two remaining bees copes with the disappearance of the third bee in a completely different way,” the playwright explained, detailing the invisible friction that can fracture a grieving family.
“One desperately wants to hold a ceremony, while the other does not. One wants to speak about the missing bee, but the other isn’t ready to talk about her yet. One really wants to use laughter as a way to cope, while the other feels completely differently about it.”
Despite the underlying gravity, Naim deliberately keeps the texture of the play light and comedic. Much of the action centers on a competitive nectar-gathering tournament.
“While the play certainly deals with the different ways we cope with loss, for the most part, it is light and funny,” Naim said. “The bees are entirely caught up in a nectar-collecting competition that they are determined to win. They just aren’t used to being only two yet, and that brings its own set of challenges.”
The play ultimately serves as a lesson in empathy and radical patience. “The show demonstrates that you have to be patient with another person’s distinct way of coping,” Naim explained.
By translating her family’s private pain into a universal fable, she hopes to give children the tools to understand their own emotional worlds. “The play seeks to provide children with a safe space to see themselves, to recognize the ways they navigate different hardships, and to understand that all coping mechanisms are legitimate,” she explained.
As she moved through final rehearsals with her cast, Naim kept her eyes on the project's broader future.
“I want as many children as possible to see this play,” she said. “My aspiration is to bring it to one of the major children’s theaters and to take it on the road to regional councils and schools.”
In doing so, she ensures that while the family trio can never be whole again, Agam’s spirit continues to teach, protect, and heal. Yet away from the theater lights, the personal journey of grief remains a daily, quiet battle for the older sister left behind.
“Sometimes,” Naim reflected, “I still feel like my subconscious is just waiting for her to come back.”

UK seeks to keep East Jerusalem consulate open as it declines to comment on reported diplomat expulsions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:48:25 UTC
00:48:25 KST

Aysu Bicer
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The United Kingdom has reportedly warned Israel that it could expel 27 Israeli diplomats if Israel proceeds with plans to close the British Consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, according to Israeli media reports, in a diplomatic standoff that has pushed bilateral relations to a historic low.
The reported warning, first published by Israeli outlet Ynet on Monday, allegedly came from British Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters, who was said to have conveyed to Israeli officials that London would respond to the closure on a one-for-one basis.
According to the reports, such a move could effectively paralyze Israel’s diplomatic mission in London, which has already been operating without a permanent ambassador for more than a year.
The British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), however, did not confirm the reported threat when approached by Anadolu.
“I would steer you away from rumours. We would not comment on speculation or live discussions,” a spokesperson said.
The reported dispute follows Israel’s decision to order the closure of the nearly 200-year-old British Consulate in East Jerusalem within 30 days.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the closure after Britain imposed economic sanctions and a trade ban on goods originating from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The Israeli government has described Britain’s measures as unjustified. Sa’ar called the UK’s trade restrictions a “moral distortion” and accused the Labour government of adopting a hostile approach toward Israel, according to Israeli media reports.
Ynet reported that Israeli diplomatic sources had indicated that Israel would respond to any British action against its diplomats.
The outlet quoted the sources as saying: “Israel has shown in the past that it will respond in kind to every step taken against it, and it will show it again.”
 
Quiet diplomatic efforts
The escalation has also prompted behind-the-scenes diplomatic efforts to prevent the closure of the British Consulate in East Jerusalem.
Reuters reported that UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made a quiet visit to Israel last week in an effort to resolve the dispute and keep the consulate open.
According to the report, the diplomatic effort did not produce an agreement.
British officials have reportedly been particularly angered by Israel’s decision to give London only 30 days to close the consulate.
The British government has maintained that the consulate plays an important role in its engagement with Palestinians and that its closure would undermine longstanding diplomatic and humanitarian work.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in September, referring to the Israeli government’s response to Britain’s sanctions measures: “I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I’m proud of what we did and it was the right thing to do.”
He also previously rejected speculation about possible British retaliation over the consulate, saying: “I do not want to speculate on this, but we do not want this to happen. It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities. The consulate has been there for nearly 200 years. And this is a long-standing position that we have had. And so, you know, this is a conversation we continue to have, but we do not want this to happen.”
The confrontation marks a significant deterioration in relations between London and Israel, following Britain’s decision to impose measures targeting goods originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The British government has defended its sanctions policy as part of its response to developments in the occupied Palestinian territory and the broader conflict.
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid has meanwhile criticized the government’s decision to close the British consulate, warning of the diplomatic consequences.
“Fighting with the world is not a policy. This effectively means closing our embassy in London. What benefit does this have for Israel?” Lapid said.
With the Oct. 8 deadline approaching for the reported closure of the British Consulate in East Jerusalem, the dispute remains focused on whether a diplomatic channel can prevent further escalation.

Unidentified drones attacked two merchant ships off Bulgaria’s coast, the country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said.

rotating octagonal forms marked with community voices shape queens landmark
Unknown

rotating octagonal forms marked with community voices shape queens landmark
developed in collaboration with astoria houses residents, revolving voices combines interactive structures with etched poetry to create a public space that shifts between everyday gathering and community storytelling.
Community voices inform waterfront Public landmark in Queens
Revolving Voices by The Urban Conga and local poet Tamra Cosby is a permanent public artwork and gathering space at Astoria Houses, a New York City public housing development in Queens. Located beside the Astoria waterfront and ferry dock, the installation brings community stories, memories, poetry, and imagery into a sculptural and interactive structure.
The project was developed through community engagement sessions with Cosby as part of From Roots to Arts: Celebrating NYCHA’s Cultural Heritage, an artist-in-residence program created by the Public Housing Community Fund and NYCHA. Residents shared memories, experiences, and ideas that informed both the physical design and the imagery and text embedded in the installation.
Revolving Voices features four rotating octagonal structures | all images ©Urban Conga
Rotating megaphone forms compose a changing public space
Taking the form of a megaphone, Revolving Voices by studio Urban Conga and poet Tamra Cosby consists of four large-scale octagonal structures arranged along the curve of a performance space and gradually decreasing in size. Their perforated metal exteriors depict people, activities, and stories from the Astoria Houses community, while the interiors feature etched messages, memories, and poetry by Cosby and other residents.
Each component can be manually rotated, changing the installation’s orientation and the views it frames. The structures can face outward toward the waterfront or turn inward toward Astoria Houses, creating different relationships between the artwork, its surroundings, and the community. The rotating forms also allow the installation to function as a set of portals, seating areas, and gathering spaces.
Revolving Voices serves not just as a visual work but as a functional gathering space for residents
Playable public artwork for everyday use and community events
Designed for both everyday use and community events, Revolving Voices supports sitting, climbing, exploring, performance, poetry, music, conversation, and reflection. By combining interactive structures with community-generated imagery and writing, the project turns a waterfront public space into a setting for gathering and storytelling.
inspired by the form of a megaphone, the octagonal structures metaphorically amplify and project the voices of the Astoria Houses community
‘By centering the voices, memories, and continued participation of residents, the work creates a place that feels rooted in the community and invites people to gather, engage, and connect,’ shares Ryan Swanson, Principal of Urban Conga.‘This piece reflects the idea that our voices may change over time, but they remain connected,’ adds artist Tamra Cosby.
the exterior perforated imagery celebrates the people, talents, and stories that make up the Astoria Houses community
‘The Connected Communities program places residents at the heart of the design process, ensuring that the art in our developments directly reflects the people who live there,’ says NYCHA Chief Executive Officer Lisa Bova-Hiatt. ‘Revolving Voices reflects the stories and lived experiences of residents living at Astoria Houses, and tells the history of the community in a fun, interactive way,’ comments Alex Zablocki, Executive Director of the Public Housing Community Fund.
the interior panels feature powerful messages, stories, and poetry from Tamra Cosby and other community members, created through community workshops
each unit rotates to be reoriented for different experiences within the space
a group of kids regulates and relaxes within the artwork
the movement of the artwork allows the community to make it theirs and adjust it as they want it to be set up
during community events, Revolving Voices creates as a backdrop for performance, music, conversation, and shared expression
the words in the artwork are cut out to create a textural moment, allowing people to literally feel the words within the work
Revolving Voices sits at Hallet’s Cove overlooking the Manhattan skyline

56 Ukrainians Still Missing in Nepal After Flood as Search and Identification Efforts Continue
The fate of 56 Ukrainian citizens missing after the devastating floods in Nepal remains unknown, even after the government formally ended its 40-day active search-and-rescue operation, Suspilne reported on October 6.
“Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, they have still not been found among either the dead or the injured,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The Nepalese government’s announcement that the 40-day active search-and-rescue operation has ended does not mean that the search or efforts to establish the circumstances of people’s disappearances have stopped. Rescue services continue searching for and identifying remains,” the ministry continued.
According to data the ministry provided to Suspilne, 5,285 people are currently listed as missing in Nepal, including 261 foreign tourists. Of those, 56 are Ukrainian citizens.
Suspilne reported that the Ukrainian Embassy in India contacted Nepalese authorities again after the country began legally recognizing some missing people as deceased. Diplomats requested clarification on how deaths are officially documented when remains cannot be located or identified.
“The National Police of Ukraine continues the pretrial investigation and is completing the formation of a database of relatives’ DNA profiles for subsequent transfer to the foreign side,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry told Suspilne. “The case remains under special supervision of the Foreign Ministry, the Consular Service Department, and Ukraine’s embassies in India and China.”
Suspilne noted that Nepal formally ended the active search-and-rescue operation on October 5. Authorities reported that at least 1,455 people had died, while 13,795 people were rescued.
When the floods first struck Nepal in late August, Ukrainian authorities initially lost contact with an organized tour group of 46 citizens. The number of Ukrainians reported missing later rose to 53 as additional relatives contacted the Foreign Ministry’s emergency hotline.

Germany Arrests Former Intelligence Chief Accused of Passing Secrets to Foreign Spy Services
Germany has arrested former Federal Intelligence Service (BND) chief August Hanning on suspicion of espionage and treason, accusing him of using classified information in contacts with foreign intelligence services.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office on October 6, Hanning and former BND employee Manfred D. were detained under warrants issued by the Federal Court of Justice. Authorities also searched properties linked to the suspects in Bavaria, North Rhine-Westphalia, and Berlin.
Prosecutors allege that Manfred D. supplied Hanning with around 2,000 BND documents over several years in exchange for payment. Many contained classified information intended exclusively for internal intelligence use, including material prepared for briefings of senior German officials.
Hanning allegedly used some of the information in his private consulting work. Prosecutors said that on one occasion he used classified intelligence “to draft an analysis” for an officer of a foreign intelligence service. Authorities have not disclosed which foreign country was involved or whether the material reached its intended recipient.
Investigators also allege that Hanning maintained close contact for several years with a representative of another foreign intelligence service and passed political information partly based on material obtained from Manfred D.
Hanning headed the BND, Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, from 1998 to 2005. According to the BBC on October 6, the investigation emerged after authorities discovered classified BND documents on an electronic storage device during a separate investigation in 2025.
The arrest comes a day after current BND chief Martin Jäger warned that Germany has become an increasingly important target for foreign intelligence operations, sabotage, and political interference, particularly from Russia.
Speaking before the Bundestag on October 5, Jäger said Moscow was waging an undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and warned of further attempts at intimidation and interference.

Europe is learning the wrong lesson from Russia's drone war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:44:08 UTC
00:44:08 KST

Europe is learning the wrong lesson from Russia's drone war
A sign reading "No drone zone" at Brussels Airport in Zaventem, Belgium, on Nov. 5, 2025. (Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images)
Megi Benia
Founder and Director of the Strategic Security Initiative
European governments are preparing for a form of confrontation that their current investments do not fully match.
While Russian-linked sabotage usually uses drones, logistics networks, criminal intermediaries, and deniable proxies against European cities, official policies and national strategies remain focused on detecting and intercepting each incident as it arises.
This approach treats only the instrument of attack, leaving the vulnerability it exploits mainly overlooked.
That vulnerability is clear: Europe's security architecture remains slow, fragmented, and expensive to mobilize across agencies and national boundaries.
In this environment, drone incursions become just separate incidents, while the problem of long, inefficient responses remains unaddressed. The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 with a quadcopter carrying plastic explosives that went unnoticed by security systems and landed near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft without detonating, belongs to a wider pattern of Russian sabotage activities against European cities, especially those targeting the major airports across the continent.
Each case, whether or not an attack was intended or completed, leaves the same residue of uncertainty, and that uncertainty is what makes cheap, deniable activity so effective against institutions that are otherwise highly capable.
A drone flying near or above an airport can disrupt the normal performance of critical civilian infrastructure by forcing the immediate closure of airports, overloading the work of police and intelligence services, and occupying resources even if no attack follows.
Democratic governments have legitimate reasons to take ambiguous threats seriously, but that very prudence can hand Moscow and its proxies an operational advantage, since an attacker capable of creating enough doubt to interrupt normal activity has no need to defeat an air-defense system at all.
Thus, the strategic value of such operations is their ability to force the defender to spend time, resources, and political capital determining whether an attack is actually taking place.
Under these conditions, Europe may win individual tactical engagements while losing the broader struggle over resources, resilience, and tempo.
More importantly, Europe's reading of Russia's drone campaign in Ukraine has focused attention on counter-drone technology, sensors, and interception systems, all of which are necessary for protecting infrastructure but cannot compensate for the institutional fragmentation that an adversary is actively exploiting.
In fact, Ukraine's experience demonstrates the importance of an organizational approach.
Against years-long Russian drone attacks, Ukraine has progressively connected battlefield reporting, air-surveillance data, acoustic and other sensor inputs, drone feeds, and intelligence into increasingly integrated situational-awareness and command systems, including the DELTA platform, allowing information from different sources to be brought together and distributed to those responsible for action.
It has also adapted its response architecture by combining centralized information with distributed defensive capabilities, enabling units and mobile teams to respond to threats without waiting for every decision to move through a complicated process of hierarchy.
As a result, Ukraine streamlined the process of detection, identification, decision, and action. This is a useful model that Europe should explore.
Attribution is another problem, because deniable sabotage is designed to take advantage of the interval between an incident and a verdict.
When investigators need weeks to establish responsibility, as it was during the Leipzig incident, where German authorities took around four weeks to publicly assign responsibility to Russia, attribution becomes a retrospective exercise and no longer functions as an indispensable aspect of deterrence and defense.
Indeed, public attribution requires credible evidence, and obtaining one might take a long time before authorities establish rock-solid data. .
However, when a citizen is suddenly stranded at an airport due to a drone-related disruption, the consequences of delayed decision-making are immediate and tangible.
To effectively address these challenges, Europe needs to organize counter-sabotage efforts that would incorporate connections, allowing aviation authorities, law enforcement, intelligence services, and armed forces to share information across institutional and national boundaries before an incident becomes a crisis.
In this process, applying lessons from the Ukrainian experience is essential because Ukraine has been forced to solve the problem Europe now faces, and it has learned to turn fragmented information into a usable operational picture and then convert that picture into action before an adversary can weaponize the gap.
Intercepting a drone can prevent an incident, but it cannot address the broader system behind it, leaving the entire process supporting a single drone operation largely intact.
Herewith, success should not be measured by the number of intercepted drones, as it reflects little about the capabilities of the entire system.
The decisive advantage is ensuring that Russia, not Europe, is forced to react, robbed of initiative, denied the ability to dictate the tempo, and made to confront operational costs and risks. Because only by reclaiming the initiative can Europe shift from a posture of reaction to one of control and force its adversaries onto the defensive.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

The EU will postpone the introduction of methane emissions rules by one year, but no more — European Commissioner
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:43:25 EEST
00:43:25 KST

The EU will postpone the introduction of methane emissions rules by one year, but no more — European Commissioner
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission is considering a one-year postponement of methane emissions control rules for oil and gas imports. Czechia and Italy are demanding three years.
The European Union plans to postpone the introduction of methane-emissions rules for oil and gas imports by one year, but no longer, despite calls from some member states for a longer delay. European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen said this on Tuesday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that these rules, which are due to enter into force on January 1, 2027, require foreign oil and gas suppliers to the EU to track and report methane emissions — a potent greenhouse gas. Jørgensen said the European Commission was considering a one-year postponement.
Methane is the second-largest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide. The EU’s methane law — the first of its kind in the world — was designed to tackle such emissions, but has faced growing political pressure after the conflict involving Iran disrupted global energy supplies and heightened concerns about fuel availability this winter.
"I have decided to instruct my services to consider postponing various rules concerning the import component of this regulation," Jørgensen said in the European Parliament.
"We do not envisage this lasting longer than a year," he said, adding that EU governments would need to ensure readiness to comply with these rules once the postponement period ends.
We would add
The Commission has not yet confirmed exactly when it will propose changes to the law, although some EU officials expect this to happen next week. Any changes would require approval from both EU member states and the European Parliament before entering into force.
Last month, French President Emmanuel Macron called for a one-year postponement, arguing that the rules could create legal risks for importers amid constrained energy supplies.
Around a dozen other EU countries, as well as the United States — the largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe — have called on the bloc to suspend the law or abandon it. Some countries, including the Czech Republic and Italy, are insisting on a three-year postponement.
Supporters of the postponement argue that companies are not ready to meet the requirements and may divert LNG cargoes to other regions rather than Europe to avoid the risk of penalties. However, some EU officials told Reuters that assessing the impact of these rules on oil and gas contracts had proved difficult, as the details of such agreements are usually not made public.

Ireland’s 2027 budget offers tax break to help people invest savings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:42:28 UTC
00:42:28 KST

DUBLIN — Ireland will create a new national savings system to spur tax-free investments in stocks and bonds, the government announced Tuesday as the centerpiece of its next tax-cutting budget.
The measure is designed to woo at least some of the more than €170 billion currently resting in Irish savers’ bank accounts, most of which is earning paltry rates of interest, into riskier investments with much higher potential returns.
The move represents Ireland’s national riposte to pressure from several other European Union countries to boost consumer investment in stocks and bonds on a union-wide basis. Ireland is among the EU members resistant to creating a proposed “Savings and Investments Union” regulated from Brussels, not Dublin.
Advertisement
Presenting his 2027 budget, Finance Minister Simon Harris told lawmakers that residents would be able to open Irish Investment Accounts starting in July. He said individuals could use those accounts to invest in stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), many of which are listed on the Dublin stock exchange, via a list of state-approved banks and brokers.
The first €50,000 in each account would not be taxed, while any balances above that would be charged 1% on the excess amount, he said. This means a fund valued at €100,000, for example, would face an annual tax liability of €500.
Under the plan, most investors would take a few years to grow their accounts to the €50,000 threshold. Annual contributions to each account would be capped at €12,000, Harris said, underscoring the center-right government’s aim to spur investment by middle-class savers, not the wealthy.
This approach, he said, “strikes a balance between encouraging small-scale investment, while ensuring that those with greater means continue to make a fair contribution.”
Investment firms offered a muted welcome, noting that Harris’ regime retained significant disincentives.
“Today was the government’s chance to get Ireland investing, and it has missed it,” said Michael Healy, chief executive of online trading and investment platform IG Consumer.
Healy dismissed Ireland’s plans as “fundamentally flawed,” as they will tax all balances above €50,000, regardless of whether they have recorded any gains that year. “Someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value — effectively paying tax on losses,” he said.

Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death after patient returns from DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:41:44 UTC
00:41:44 KST

Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death after patient returns from DR Congo
Kenya on Tuesday reported its first-ever Ebola death after a Kenyan national who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) died after returning to the country. Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern DR Congo in mid-May.
A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend became Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak, authorities said Tuesday, sparking urgent contact-tracing efforts to try to contain the spread of the virus.
The man had been residing in Congo for the past seven years and fell ill about a month ago. He was treated at various hospitals before travelling by road to Kampala, Uganda, where he boarded a flight to the Kenyan capital, arriving on Saturday afternoon, Health Minister Aden Duale said.
Health authorities in Kenya have placed the country’s border points on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases.
Duale said that the man had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for the Ebola virus and died late Monday.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing.
The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, months after it had been spreading in a remote part of eastern Congo. At least 8,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,000 deaths, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history.
Kenya has never had an outbreak of Ebola, according to the Kenya Medical Research Institute.
The country hosts a United States-funded isolation center for American citizens exposed to Ebola to quarantine for 21 days before travelling back to the US. The isolation facility faced legal battles and deadly protests by locals who feared it was exposing them to the virus.
Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda has recorded 20 cases and France, one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August.
Duale said that 28 contacts of the man who had returned on Saturday – including family members and health workers who cared for the patient – had been identified. Another 23 passengers on the flight and four crew members, who travelled on the same plane from Uganda, were being traced.
The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released after testing negative for the virus, said the ministry’s director-general, Dr. Patrick Amoth.
After the man arrived in Nairobi, his relatives later took him in a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated. He will be buried within 24 hours in accordance with recommended public safety protocols.
The minister said that Kenya had tested 267 samples at five laboratories across the country since May before this first case was detected.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday commended the “rapid identification, isolation and testing of the patient” and said a high-level team had been dispatched to Kenya to offer support.
In Congo, where the outbreak has spread to seven provinces, conditions are difficult. Responders have faced attacks on health teams, misinformation about the virus, a failure by locals to report symptoms and rebel violence that has limited access to treatment centres.
While cases have slowed in Ituri province, the epicentre, the outbreak is spreading in emerging hot spots in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
“It is like fighting a megafire. Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations,” Stéphanie Hoffmann with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said in a statement.
The World Health Organisation has warned that it could surpass the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, which erupted more than a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people in West Africa.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:38:58 UTC
00:38:58 KST

Alternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war.
Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast.
Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy.
The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency, won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month, dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU).
Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained.
The AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority. Five politicians from the BSW, a small leftwing party that echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration, had already said they would vote for Rausch. Tuesday’s result means that four other MPs voted for the 35-year-old in the secret ballot.
The willingness of politicians to break the “firewall” – a moral agreement among other parties to shun the AfD – gives the party a chance of being able to form a government in the state – a feat it had looked unlikely to pull off. This would be even more of a historical watershed in postwar Germany.
The BSW’s support for Rausch came after the party’s founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, declared it was time to do away with “firewall idiocy”. The party’s deputy leader, Christian Leye, said the “firewall is not working” and the votes of nearly 44% of electors could not be ignored.
“We need an intelligent way of dealing with the AfD and that means dealing with the content of their programme instead of a firewall,” Leye told German media.
It was not immediately clear who was behind Tillschneider’s election because the BSW had said it would refuse to vote for him. He received 44 votes.
As the architect of the AfD’s “radical” manifesto, he is lined up to become culture and science minister in the state. He has referred to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as “a real man with a sound set of values” and accused immigrants of “streaming in here in masses … wanting to squander our money”.
Tillschneider is a scholar of Islamic studies who has described Islam as a “fungus” growing on the “German oak”. His family emigrated from Romania to Germany in the 1980s.
In his acceptance speech, Rausch promised to represent all voices and “take different opinions seriously and to try to take decisions in a transparent way”. He was applauded by his own parliamentary group and the ranks of the BSW. The other MPs did not respond.
Rausch was one of the key figures in a nepotism scandal over AfD MPs employing family members in parliament. He denied claims that several of his siblings and a brother-in-law were working in the state parliament but confirmed he was employing several players from the football club where he is a member.
He is a close ally and confidant of Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, who is positioning himself to take over as leader of Saxony-Anhalt. He has yet to say which parties or politicians have agreed to cooperate with the AfD, only that “negotiations are going well”. The AfD claims to be courting members of the CDU to break the firewall, a claim CDU leaders deny.
The BSW says it will support an AfD-led parliament only if a nonpartisan figure is appointed to lead it, a position the AfD rejects. Siegmund has until December to form a government.
Opposition MPs raised alarm over the breaching of the firewall. “Whoever has invested a representative of extremist and anti-constitutional party with this office will bear responsibility for the consequences,” said Green MP Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, to loud applause.
The result of the Saxony-Anhalt poll, along with two other regional elections in September, has piled huge pressure on Merz, who pledged on taking office in 2025 that he would halve the AfD’s support by boosting the economy and reducing immigration. Instead, the CDU’s support has more or less halved and that of the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls.
Before the vote, Eva von Angern of the leftwing Die Linke party and the longest-serving member of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament, drew parallels between Rausch’s election to the post of speaker, and Hermann Göring’s use of that role in the Reichstag in the 1930s to facilitate Adolf Hitler’s rise to power.
She claimed that the negative consequences of the AfD’s win in the state were already being felt in lower tourist numbers and teachers withdrawing job applications.

Israeli settlers beat AFP photographer covering West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:38:10 UTC
00:38:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers beat AFP photographer covering West Bank
Israeli settlers on Tuesday beat an AFP photographer and fired guns in the direction of him and a colleague as they covered ongoing violence by settlers against West Bank olive farmers.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, a veteran photographer for the international news agency in the Palestinian territory, suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken by ambulance to a hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.
Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba where they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.
A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of the hill and a man from it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.
At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with guns.
"I could hear his screams," said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint.
Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, is conscious and under 24-hour supervision at a hospital in Nablus, where he will undergo X-rays, said his son, Zain Jaafar.
The assailants also took his camera equipment, Wessels said.
The violence took place despite the presence of at least a dozen fully equipped Israeli soldiers around 500 metres away, according to Wessels.
The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.
AFP has reached out to the Israeli military for comment.
"We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene," said Phil Chetwynd, AFP's global news director.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by extremist settlers against Palestinians.
There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.
Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol.
Some 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel captured in 1967, among three million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.
Media rights groups say that Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.
Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel by Gaza-based Hamas, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.
(AFP)

Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:37:29 UTC
00:37:29 KST

Seven tankers made 14 trips from South Korea to Russia's Far East in July and August, carrying more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, most of it diesel, the Guardian found in a 6 October analysis of port records and ship-tracking data. The UK and EU have sanctioned three of the ships, and one loaded its fuel from another tanker at sea off South Korea instead of at a terminal.
Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia's fuel output as Moscow scrambles for supplies, while fuel loaded at South Korean ports has flowed to Russia. Loadings began to surge in July, the same month South Korean President Lee Jae-myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine's reconstruction, the Guardian reported. That creates a tension in Seoul's policy toward the war: South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian and non-lethal aid but ruled out sending weapons directly, while the fuel trade appears legal under South Korean law even though three of the tankers are under UK and EU sanctions.
Russia imported 368,000 metric tons of oil products by sea in August, 112,000 of them from South Korea, according to Kpler data analyzed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and cited by the Guardian. CREA's own August report gives 172,000 metric tons in total, including 18,000 from South Korea. Neither explains the gap.
Where the tankers said they were going
The Layla, a tanker under UK and EU sanctions, made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a total of 57,000 metric tons of diesel. It left South Korea on 19 July and 10 August. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities it was bound for Vladivostok; on the second, it declared Niigata, Japan, but sailed to Vladivostok again.
The Astoria, a Russian-flagged tanker under UK, EU, and Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 metric tons of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August. It declared Japan as its destination but sailed to Vladivostok.
The Chongchon did not berth at a South Korean port. Instead, it took about 26,000 metric tons of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in early August. It declared Singapore as its destination but headed to Vladivostok. The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to the Guardian's requests for comment.
Why Russia needs the fuel
Ukrainian drone strikes have severely disrupted Russia's refining capacity, the Guardian reported. In July, Ukraine's General Staff said the strikes had knocked out 42% of Russia's refining capacity, costing the industry billions of dollars.
Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% from a year earlier, the International Energy Agency said, according to the Guardian.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, extending its diesel export ban until the end of October; on 2 October, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow could consider partially lifting the ban if there was overproduction, according to the Moscow Times.
Responses to the shipments
Seoul's non-lethal aid has included helmets, body armor, and demining vehicles, and in 2023 it pledged $2.3 billion in support, mostly in loans.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at CREA, told the Guardian:
"It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia. This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea's support for Ukraine."
South Korea's Foreign Ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said the government supports international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery. The ministry said it was strictly enforcing its export controls and had expanded them to cover 1,402 non-strategic items with high potential for diversion to military use. The UK Foreign Office did not answer the Guardian's questions about UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, saying only that it remains committed to monitoring its sanctions.
Ties between Kyiv and Seoul are also strained over Ukraine's disclosure of its transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul said should have remained private.

Photo: Alexandra Astakhova / Mediazona
Russian authorities have dropped the criminal case alleging the spread of “fake news about the army” against Lida Moniava, the prominent director of the Lighthouse (“Dom s Mayakom”) children’s hospice, her defence team announced. She was arrested and charged in early September over a social media post marking the anniversary of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, prompting crowds of supporters to gather outside the courthouse.
Today, an investigator informed defence lawyer Mikhail Biryukov that the case had been formally terminated due to the absence of the body of the crime. The official decree has been sent by post.
“This is a miracle of miracles. But it did not happen on its own—you made it happen,” Moniava’s support group wrote in a statement on Telegram. “Thank you to everyone who came to the court! A special thank you to the heroic patients of the Lighthouse who came to support Lida in wheelchairs and on mechanical ventilators. Thank you to everyone who wrote official letters in Lida’s defence and posted messages of support! Thank you to the journalists! Big thanks to everyone who prayed.”
This is an extremely rare reversal by the Russian investigative apparatus, especially against the record of near-total conviction rates in wartime censorship cases since the February 2022 invasion.
Investigators had initially charged Moniava under Paragraph “d”, Part 2 of Article 207.3 of the Criminal Code (spreading “fake news about the military” motivated by “political hatred”), an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to ten years.
Moniava’s Telegram post in question was published on February 24, 2023, the first anniversary of the full-scale invasion. In it, Moniava recounted the deaths of Ukrainian civilians killed in Russian strikes, including children and medical workers.
Moniava, who co-founded the Lighthouse children’s hospice and pioneered paediatric palliative care in Russia, had pleaded not guilty during interrogation.

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. Tea Next, a fiber optic communication line linking western and eastern borders of Russia, was launched in six years after the project implementation start, the press service of Russian telecom company Rostelecom said.
Rostelecom calls this project a "super-speed digital mainline" and the largest infrastructural projects in the field of communications in Russia over the past years. Tea Next also has breakouts on the borders with Mongolia and China. Capital investments into the communication line totaled 17.6 bln rubles ($206.1 mln).
According to the press service, the data transmission speed over the cable varies from 384 Tbps to more than 1 Pbps. Such difference is due to differences in DWDM technologies used for the line. The estimate service life of cables in Tea Next is 25 years at the least.

Russia Drops Criminal Case Against Children’s Hospice Founder Lida Moniava
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:36:37 UTC
00:36:37 KST

Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against Lida Moniava, a prominent advocate for critically ill children’s care, after finding no grounds for prosecution, her supporters said Tuesday, citing her lawyer.
Moniava was arrested on Sept. 2 and charged with spreading “false information” about Russia’s military over a social media post about Ukrainian civilians killed in Russian attacks. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Her support group said lawyer Mikhail Biryukov had confirmed the decision and that an official notice closing the case had been sent by mail.
“This is a miracle. But it didn’t happen on its own. You made it happen,” the group wrote, thanking those who attended her court hearing, wrote letters in her defense and publicly supported her.
The group gave special thanks to hospice patients who came to court, some of whom were in wheelchairs or using ventilators.
Moniava is the founder of the Moscow-based charity Lighthouse, which operates hospices for seriously ill children and young adults in the Russian capital and surrounding region.
Her case had prompted an outpouring of support from families whose children had received care from the charity.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moniava created a foundation that provided shelter, medical supplies and food to people fleeing from the war. That foundation suspended operations in 2025 due to the dwindling number of refugees arriving in Moscow and the Moscow region.
Following her Sept. 2 arrest, Moniava announced that she was stepping down as Lighthouse’s director and leaving its board but said she intended to stay in Russia.
The dismissal of her case marks a rare outcome in Russia’s crackdown on anti-war speech. In a February 2025 report, rights group OVD-Info said it knew of just over 20 instances in which anti-war criminal cases had been dropped at various stages since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

====================================================================================================

Hunting for cannon fodder: How Russia&#039;s private recruitment market for the war in Ukraine really works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:34:38 UTC
00:34:38 KST

The prosecutor's office in the Russian city of Nizhny Tagil proposed scrapping payments to recruiters who sign up contract soldiers for the war in Ukraine, citing a rise in fraud cases. Amid a shortage of willing volunteers, Russia has developed a vast state-backed intermediary recruitment market, with multilayered networks of middlemen, “ready-made creatives,” and region-specific rates. The Insider examined several of the schemes and traced how money from regional budgets reaches private headhunters. Spending on recruitment alone, excluding payments to contract soldiers, may run into billions of rubles a month, and private recruiters can receive up to 1.25 million rubles (almost $15,000) for bringing in a single soldier.
In the fifth year of Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, the Russian army continues to lose tens of thousands of soldiers every month. As of Aug. 28, 2026, Mediazona and the BBC had confirmed by name the deaths of 242,747 Russian servicemen — and these are only the deaths that have become publicly known. Actual monthly losses of killed and wounded exceed 30,000, and direct recruitment of contract soldiers is no longer enough to replace them.
The state now separately funds organizations that seek out and recruit people for the war in Ukraine. The Insider examined court records, NGO reports, procurement requests, and internal materials from recruitment agencies, reconstructing the chain through which some of this money flows – from regional budgets to intermediaries and ultimately to the individuals who bring recruits directly to military enlistment offices.
A million rubles per head: the cannon-fodder market
As recently as 2024, Ivanovo’s Center for Creative Solutions was engaged in activities that had little to do with military recruitment. For example, the organization ran a quiz called “Favorite Ivanovo Region” at polling stations during the presidential election, with prizes including tickets to sporting events and a car. Another of its projects, “Urban Treasures: A Family Quest,” received a regional grant of almost 1 million rubles (almost $12,000).
On July 4, 2025, Ivanovo businessman Dmitry Gruzdev took over as head of the organization. That same month, the regional budget allocated funds for an entirely different purpose: “financing costs associated with providing services to attract and select candidates for military service under contract.” The Center for Creative Solutions was among the recipients of this funding.
The Insider found that a November 2025 order by the regional government awarded the center a 260 million ruble ($3.1 million) subsidy specifically for recruiting and selecting prospective contract soldiers. The sums it received were on an entirely different scale from its previous earnings from civilian quizzes.
In 2025, the organization received 1.06 billion rubles ($12.5 million), and a similar amount under the same budget line was awarded by the Moscow Region government to the non-profit Dobryye Dela (Good Deeds), which then passed the money on to its contractor, Russia's Agency for Communication Strategies.
As is often the case, the Center for Creative Solutions and Dobryye Dela appear to be the main distributors of budget funds to a long chain of other organizations. They outsource most of the work to private contractors, who in turn often subcontract it.
One such subcontractor emerged through an ordinary commercial dispute. In February 2026, Nizhny Novgorod businessman Alexander Kondratyev sued the center in the Nizhny Novgorod Region Arbitration Court, seeking 24.78 million rubles ($297,000) in unpaid debt. Court documents identify the contract as being for the “provision of services to attract and select candidates for military service under contract.” In March, the parties reached a settlement, with the Center for Creative Solutions acknowledging the full amount of the debt.
The court documents make it possible to determine how much the recruiter earned per contract soldier, as the debt was the result of two certificates of completed work. Kondratyev was owed 12.98 million rubles ($153,000) for November and another 11.8 million ($139,000) for the first half of December.
Both sums divide evenly by 590,000 rubles: the first amounts to 22 such payments and the second to 20. In other words, Kondratyev appears to have been paid 590,000 rubles (just under $7,000) for each contract recruit, with the two certificates covering 42 people.
In virtually all similar schemes in different regions examined by The Insider, recruiters are paid only after a candidate signs a contract, and the commission varies considerably. For example, at the previously mentioned Agency for Communication Strategies, one of the largest recruitment organizations, a recruiter gets 1.25 million rubles ($14,700) for a person who signs a contract through Moscow. Through Orenburg, the rate is 850,000 rubles ($10,000) “per head”; through Voronezh, 680,000 ($8,000); and through Balashikha, 530,000 ($6,250). In other areas, the rates ranged from 150,000 to 450,000 rubles ($1,750 to $5,300).
Debtors, addicts, bankrupts: recruiters target the vulnerable
Instructions for recruiters from the Agency for Communication Strategies (ACS) reveal who makes up the main pool of prospective contract soldiers. Its “target audiences” include former prisoners and Wagner PMC members, bankrupts, clients of microfinance organizations, residents of economically depressed regions, 18- and 19-year-olds with limited educational prospects, people with gambling or substance addictions, and “socially vulnerable groups.” They also include people who face legal trouble, particularly if they have not yet been convicted.
ACS advises recruiters to seek potential targets through advertising platforms and by buying ads in social media communities.
A recruit’s suitability directly affects the payment: if a prospective soldier fails a stricter medical examination in one region, he can simply be sent to another. An internal ACS information sheet divides medical commissions into “strict,” “moderate,” “lenient,” and “very lenient.”
Moscow, for example, is listed as having a strict commission. Voronezh, on the other hand, is described as “very lenient,” accepting recruits people with hepatitis A, B, or C, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval that would disqualify them in other regions.”
“Very lenient” Voronezh accepts people with hepatitis A, B, or C, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval”
Ufa’s commission is also described as “very lenient”: candidates with hepatitis, psoriasis, HIV, and “serious medical conditions subject to approval” may be accepted there. Orenburg and Cheboksary, meanwhile, are designated as merely “lenient.”
Under certain conditions, candidates with a Group III disability, diabetes, hypertension, missing organs, blindness in one eye, psychiatric or addiction records, signs of self-harm, or a history of tuberculosis may still be eligible to sign a contract.
Bonuses for recruiters
Although organizations like the Center for Creative Solutions and the Agency for Communication Strategies do not recruit soldiers themselves, they do provide smaller private businesses with the infrastructure for recruitment: up to 400,000 rubles ($4,700) per recruit, along with “ready-made creatives,” CRM, scripts, and training for new recruiters. The service works with candidates for contract military service from across Russia and attempts to maximize the number of contracts signed through Moscow, where bonus payments are higher.
For people looking to sign a contract, the organization can select a destination, arrange travel, meet them on arrival, and help with accommodation, food, medical examinations, and paperwork.
The page for prospective recruiters states the job’s purpose plainly: “The partner’s task is to get the candidate to sign a contract.” Payment is tied to that outcome – “for one signed contract.” The site promises that earnings are “unlimited.”
The Contract Call service is run by sole proprietor Fyodor Shchepetov, whose main business is “other personnel recruitment.” Public sources identify Shchepetov as a political consultant, conflict-resolution specialist, and internet technologist. He also serves on the public council of Rosprirodnadzor, Russia’s environmental regulator.
The demand for personnel in military recruitment is clearly substantial. Recent job postings offer “military recruiters” up to 300,000 rubles ($3,550) for each contract recruit they bring in, with no experience required and training provided. The job involves handling incoming inquiries, conducting initial interviews, “working with objections,” and managing candidates in Bitrix24 through to the final result.
“Military recruiters” are offered up to 300,000 rubles per contract recruit, with no experience required
The Agency for Communication Strategies has also launched a referral program called “Bring a Colleague.” Partners are promised an additional 100,000 rubles ($1,200) if a recruiter they refer brings in someone who signs a contract through Moscow, and 50,000 rubles ($600) if the contract is signed through another region.
In short, the agency pays not only for new contract soldiers but also for new recruiters who supply them. According to ACS itself, more than 250 “partners” work with the organization, and it has helped arrange more than 6,000 contracts.
How much does it cost the state to recruit one soldier?
There is no fixed price per recruit in this market, as payments vary widely from region to region. Much also depends on the numerous intermediaries involved. In the schemes examined by The Insider, recruiters who directly bring candidates to the point of signing a contract can receive the ruble equivalent on more than $10,000, but a substantial share of the money is absorbed by the intermediary organizations participating in the process.
Adding only the recruiter’s fee and the contract soldier’s enlistment bonus, the total can be much higher. For example, for a contract signed through St. Petersburg, ACS promises the soldier 4.5 million rubles ($53,000) and the recruiter 150,000 ($1,750). According to Re:Russia’s calculations, by mid-May 2026 the average “effective” bonus in the regions where a large share of contracts are signed had reached about 2.74 million rubles ($32,300).
In some schemes, the two visible payments – to the contract soldier and the recruiter – already total 4.65 million rubles per person
The scale of the spending becomes even more evident when these sums are compared with the rate at which the army is being replenished. CSIS estimates that in 2026 Russia has been recruiting an average of 27,000 new service members a month. Applying Re:Russia’s estimate of an average effective bonus of 2.74 million rubles, one-time payments to new contract soldiers alone would amount to about 74 billion rubles a month ($872.4 million).
As for recruiters, even using 300,000 rubles ($3,550) per contract soldier as a rough benchmark would put direct payments to the middlemen at more than 8 billion rubles ($94.3 million) a month.
After four years of war, Russia has built a system in which the army’s need for manpower has created a rapidly growing market fueled by public money. A region allocates the funds, an intermediary gets the contract, a recruiter searches for “leads,” and a person placed at the disposal of the Russian military machine.
As long as the Russian army continues to suffer losses, this market will persist. The state may even increase its funding, and professional recruitment agencies will devise ever more “creative” approaches to get their share of the outlays.

A discussion Tuesday by the Subcommittee for Intelligence and Secret Services and Defense Committee on the attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight revealed that 1,240 aircrew members from countries that do not have relations with Israel entered the country over the past year. They included Syrian and Lebanese citizens.
During the committee discussion, the National Security Council was asked to work with the Mossad and Shin Bet to draw up a list of countries considered high-security threats. Accordingly, lists of crew members from those countries would be submitted 48 hours before flights to Israel for review and approval by security agencies.
In addition, at the Transportation Ministry’s request, the Population and Immigration Authority would be required to provide the ministry’s Security Division with lists of passengers and aircrew members holding passports from countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Meanwhile, following a preliminary Transportation Ministry investigation, Transportation Minister Miri Regev sent an urgent request to National Security Council chief Samuel Benezra, calling for “immediate measures” to reduce the risk of and prevent a recurrence of similar serious incidents.
The measures should remain in place “until the investigation by the relevant agencies is completed and coordinated by the head of the National Security Council,” she wrote.
Regev said that “several proposed measures have been raised at the Transportation Ministry, but since the authority does not lie with the ministry, I am asking you to instruct the relevant ministries.”
Among the measures, Regev detailed: “Creating a one-time aviation visa procedure — or any alternative document acceptable to the Population and Immigration Authority — for all passengers and all aircrew members on every flight arriving in Israel from abroad, whether operated by foreign or Israeli airlines or as charter flights. The visa will be completed 48 hours before departure and approved by the Population and Immigration Authority. Implementation of the directive beginning Sunday will be the responsibility of the Interior Ministry and the Population and Immigration Authority.”
Another measure she recommended, which was also discussed by the committee, was: “Obtaining from the Mossad and Shin Bet a list of destinations posing a security threat. On flights from these destinations, airlines will provide the names of passengers and aircrew members 48 hours in advance to the Transportation Ministry’s Security Division, which will submit them to the Mossad or Shin Bet for approval before departure. Providing the list of destinations posing a high security threat by Thursday will be the responsibility of the Mossad and Shin Bet.
“The decision as to which agency the Transportation Ministry will submit the lists to for review — the Mossad or Shin Bet — will be the responsibility of the head of the National Security Council,” she wrote. “Issuing this directive Thursday to all airlines flying to Israel will be the responsibility of the Transportation Ministry’s Security Division. Implementation of the directive will begin Sunday. I ask the head of the National Security Council to instruct the Budget Division to immediately arrange the necessary funding and positions.”
Following the Cabinet meeting at the beginning of the week, the Transportation Ministry demanded that its Security Division and the Shin Bet issue security instructions to foreign and Israeli airlines in accordance with the new procedures and ensure that the directives are incorporated into the airlines’ operating procedures.
Some of these proposals had previously been raised by the Security Division during discussions of the aviation forum headed by the National Security Council but were rejected.
Regev also asked the National Security Council chief to convene an urgent discussion Thursday to “ensure that these directives are implemented and put into effect beginning Sunday and until the investigation you are coordinating, at the prime minister’s instruction, is completed.”
Meanwhile, Regev held a conversation Monday with the Emirati ambassador and a representative of the United Arab Emirates’ royal family regarding the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel — 10 flights a day — alongside an increase in the number of Etihad flights.
The minister was invited to visit the UAE next week to finalize the details and to “restore things to the way they were and honor the Abraham Accords.”
During the conversation, Regev demanded that, alongside the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, approval be granted for a security screening system for Israeli airlines in accordance with the requirements of the Shin Bet and other security agencies. She also demanded blanket approval for two regularly scheduled daily flights by each Israeli airline. Regev further demanded that the screening arrangements allow an X-ray machine to be brought in.
Regev’s planned visit to the UAE has not yet received final approval, but at this stage it appears that flydubai flights will be cleared to resume service to Israel as an Israeli security delegation heads to Dubai.
Shin Bet personnel arrived in the United Arab Emirates this week and are taking part in the interrogation of Omani terrorist pilot Hamam al-Hammami, a citizen of a country that has no relations with Israel. During questioning, he said he was motivated by a desire to take revenge on Israel for what it had done in the Gaza Strip.
Investigators also ruled out the involvement of the flight attendants in the attempt to hijack and crash the plane, as they were extremely frighted. However, passengers had suspected that they had collaborated with the pilot-terrorist.
The investigation also found that the pilot planned to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport. His backup plan was to crash it into a U.S. military base in Jordan if he was unable to carry out the attack in Israel.
The Omani terrorist pilot had planned to carry out the attack in July, but because of a personal connection to one of his crew members, he “took pity on him” and postponed the attack until another opportunity.
According to the investigation, al-Hammami had landed in Israel as early as June and prepared himself to become a “shahid,” or martyr.

France successfully conducted the first test launch of the new M51.3 intercontinental ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced this on his social media accounts.
The launch took place from aboard the nuclear submarine Le Vigilant, and the test was monitored from aboard the frigate Auvergne.
The Directorate General of Armaments, the Atomic Energy Commission, Ariane Group, Naval Group, and the French Navy participated in testing and developing the new missile.
À bord de la frégate multi-missions Auvergne, j’ai assisté au premier tir du nouveau missile balistique M51.3 depuis le sous-marin nucléaire lanceur d’engins Le Vigilant.
Très peu de nations disposent d’un tel savoir-faire.

Ce succès technique est une nouvelle démonstration de la crédibilité de notre dissuasion, dont la pérennité est assurée.
Pour être libre, il faut être craint. Et pour être craint, il faut être puissant.

“To be free, you must be feared. And to be feared, you must be powerful,” Emmanuel Macron said.
The test launch took place without a nuclear warhead off the coast of the French department of Finistère in an area with restricted navigation.
This followed extensive maintenance on the submarine Le Vigilant, which began in the fall of 2023 at the Île-Long base.
As part of the work on the submarine, maintenance was performed on the reactor, the weapons system, and other key onboard systems.
The M51.3 is a three-stage, solid-fuel, sea-based intercontinental ballistic missile developed as an evolution of the M51 family.
The new version retains the dimensions of its predecessors: about 12 meters long, 2.3 meters in diameter, and approximately 52 metric tons.
For previous versions of the M51, the range was estimated at 8,000–10,000 km with a maximum speed of up to Mach 25.
The M51.3 missiles will serve as the primary armament for France’s future SNLE 3G-class nuclear-powered submarines, which will replace the Le Triomphant-class submarines after 2035.

Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money | Chris Stokel-Walker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:30:17 UTC
00:30:17 KST

Tech bros’ messianic streaks can show up in subtle ways. But one of Sam Altman’s flaws is that he often lacks that subtlety. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” said the OpenAI chief executive in an interview with Politico last weekend.
That’s easy for Altman to say. But it’s pretty galling to hear for the rest of us. Lest we forget, we didn’t ask for OpenAI to unleash AI agents that went rogue and weaselled their way into government IT systems and private businesses around the world. Nobody voted for ChatGPT to be released, but the company put it out into the world as a test product that happened to catch the zeitgeist. That kickstarted an arms race among AI companies to push the frontier of the technology ever further and faster, resulting in the mess we now find ourselves in.
OpenAI’s competitors, including Anthropic, have started to step back from the brink – as has OpenAI itself, deciding not to release its latest model because it’s purportedly too dangerous. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has talked about needing to “pace the frontier”: tech-bro jargon for pumping the brakes to bring down the speed at which the runaway vehicle is skidding out of control.
Yet we’re expected to take these incidents – and the harm they cause – as the natural consequences of OpenAI’s continued march towards an IPO that would bring its investors millions. It’s hard to escape the idea that Altman wants to privatise his company’s gains while socialising the risks of untrammelled AI development.
Every useful technology – and AI is a useful technology, despite the holdouts and occasional users’ carping – carries risk. Cars can and do crash, while medicines that save us often have harmful side effects. Very rarely, aircraft fall from the sky. But we accept those risks because the benefits are substantial, and we build rules to limit the harm. We also make companies liable. And most importantly, we get some say in deciding what level of risk is and isn’t acceptable.
Altman seems to suggest that his company’s messes are our problem to sort out – or worse, that the consequences of his tech are ours to tolerate. But Altman would do well to think about this differently. OpenAI gets to decide how fast it develops its technology and when it releases it. Its investors benefit financially if those bets pay off. But it feels as if he’s suggesting that when the tech creates problems outside OpenAI’s own walls, the costs of cleaning up are ours to bear, not his company’s.
The idea that private companies profit while we’re left to deal with the consequences becomes even harder to defend as AI stops being something we opt into using as a chatbot, and becomes something that acts on and changes the world around us. If I ask ChatGPT something and it gives me a bad answer, I chose to expose myself to that risk, so should share that burden. But the same isn’t true for a government department that suddenly finds an OpenAI agent lurking in its files and rooting around. It didn’t opt in; it became an unwilling participant in someones experiment.
That’s why Altman’s argument sounds so disingenuous. OpenAI shouldn’t be able to decide for all of us what is and isn’t an acceptable level of failure, then ask everyone to live with the result. The burden ought to be on it to prove its technology can be trusted – and to pick up the bill if it can’t.
It’s no wonder that OpenAI wants to travel quickly. The company is seeking $30bn in new funding, and a valuation of $1.4tn ahead of a public listing likely next year. There’s money to be made – never mind at whose expense.
To his credit, Altman also acknowledged in the Politico interview that there will need to be a liability framework for companies offering models such as OpenAI’s, and that the company will have to take responsibility for at least some of what goes wrong during training. But that “some” is doing a lot of work.
If Altman believes some bad things are an acceptable price for AI’s progress, OpenAI can dig into its deep pockets to pay that price itself – for instance if its agents go rogue and do damage to government or private company systems, or compromise user data. It can’t, and shouldn’t, get the financial upside when everything goes right, then ask the rest of us to accept the consequences when things go wrong. That’s especially the case when we never agreed to the unregulated experiment in the first place.
- Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

Air Force: Drone interceptors will not be available in necessary quantities until at least end of November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

Air Force: Drone interceptors will not be available in necessary quantities until at least end of November
According to Ukrinform, Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko, deputy commander of the Ukrainian Air Force for air defense, announced this during a meeting of the Temporary Investigative Commission.
“The number of jet-powered drones has increased significantly since July. It now accounts for about 40% of all unmanned aerial vehicles deployed across Ukraine, and in certain areas, it makes up as much as 60% of attacks. And it continues to grow. We predict that jet-powered drones will account for about 80% of attacks,” he said.
According to Cherevashchenko, to counter attack drones, the Air Force is actively collaborating with manufacturers of jet-powered UAV interceptors. Currently, about 20 companies are in communication with the military, each at different stages of readiness for their products. The Air Force has established test zones where these drones are being deployed in combat conditions.
“Fourteen companies already have specific products and have begun test flights; of these, six companies have achieved certain results in destroying jet-powered drones, and three of them have results that can be considered promising solutions. We are currently actively collaborating to improve their performance,” said the deputy commander.
He noted that mass production of such drones is not currently on the table, as they are quite expensive and the companies do not always have their own funding. Production is currently in the tens of units.
“One of them has already been adopted into service and has shown the best results. Two have undergone codification, one of which is the ‘Predator,’” Cherevashchenko reported.
Some of these systems, he said, were originally designed for other tasks but were quickly adapted specifically for intercepting aerial targets. In response to a follow-up question about how they work, the deputy commander confirmed that an operator on the ground views the drone’s feed and controls it in real time.
“Their speed is about 460–500 kilometers per hour. Some manufacturers claim speeds of up to 700,” he noted.
Regarding scaling up production, Cherevashchenko noted that it would be best to check with the manufacturers for specific volumes.
“For our part, we are already training personnel: first, basic pilot training, then specialization specifically in interception,” explained the deputy commander.
According to him, the Air Force is considering two types of interceptor drones: classic rotorcraft and high-speed jet drones; deliveries of interceptors in the required quantities are not expected until at least the end of November.
As reported by Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, stated that air defense forces have already begun shooting down enemy UAVs using robotic turrets.
