Montenegro Moves to Seize Vast Real Estate Empire of Fugitive Crime Boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:52:00 UTC
23:52:00 KST

Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.
The Special State Prosecutor's Office asked Tuesday the High Court in Podgorica to permanently confiscate a sprawling portfolio of real estate and luxury vehicles it believes is in his or his wife’s possession. While the official statement only identified the targets by their initials, R.Z. and his wife, T.Z., the request appears to be detailing the hidden wealth of the reputed Kavač clan leader Radoje Zvicer and his wife Tamara Zvicer. Local media reports also name the two as the targets of this request.
The timing of this massive forfeiture request is no coincidence. It serves as one of the first major tests of Montenegro's sweeping new "Anti-Mafia Law," passed on September 4. The government hailed the legislation as a "historic step" that has already caused an "earthquake in criminal circles," specifically because it empowers the state to permanently confiscate assets in organized crime cases even before a final judicial verdict is reached.
Crucially, the law shifts the burden of proof, requiring accused cartel figures to prove their wealth was acquired legally. Following the law's passage, the government declared that crime will "never again be a business model" in the country.
The confiscation request was immediately welcomed by Deputy Prime Minister Aleksa Bečić. In an official statement reported by local media outlet Vijesti, Bečić noted that targeting illicit wealth and purging corrupt officials represent "the most deadly blows to the foundations of organized crime." Pledging that Montenegro will "never return to the dark ages of mafia occupation," he said the new legal framework allows the state to rapidly dismantle criminal infrastructure.
For Zvicer, the legal foundation for the seizure was triggered by his final 16-year prison sentence in Montenegro for drug trafficking and creating a criminal organization. However, his rap sheet stretches far beyond a single conviction.
In July 2026, he was handed a separate 40-year maximum first-instance sentence for orchestrating a drug smuggling and assassination syndicate alongside corrupt police officers. He also holds a final conviction in Serbia for identity forgery, while a raft of active indictments for murder and organized crime remain pending against him across Montenegro, Serbia, and Greece.
The 43-year-old, whose whereabouts have been unknown since 2021, remains the target of a sweeping Interpol red notice and is actively hunted across borders. Earlier this year, Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service offered a 20,000 euro ($22,540) reward for the armed and dangerous fugitive, seeking him for his role in organizing an 83-kilogram cocaine pipeline into Vienna.
According to Austrian authorities, the athletic, blue-eyed boss operates under at least 15 aliases and bears distinctive gunshot scars across the left side of his upper torso. The manhunt was so intense that in August, the Montenegrin Ministry of Internal Affairs escalated the stakes, offering a 500,000 euro ($562,834) bounty for information leading directly to his arrest.
Once a single Montenegrin syndicate smuggling South American cocaine into Europe, the Kavač and Škaljari clans violently fractured in 2014 over a botched drug deal in Spain. Their ensuing turf war for control of the billion-euro narcotics trade has claimed dozens of lives and deeply polarized the Balkan criminal underworld.
Prosecutors are now seeking to seize at least 54,567 square meters of property believed to have been purchased with criminal proceeds and carefully concealed behind a network of proxies, including front companies, legal counsel, and close family members.
The bulk of the targeted real estate is concentrated in the Kotor region on Montenegro's Adriatic coast, with heavy investments right in the clan's namesake stronghold of Kavač. Assets there include multi-story buildings, orchards, and more than 20,000 square meters of land and forest. Among the most prominent are a massive complex featuring a 355-square-meter duplex, as well as a separate residential space with an attic and garages—both formally registered to T.Z., according to prosecutors. Two other residential buildings and 10 garages are registered to multiple individuals, including her father, while a local company formally holds the rights to the majority of the forest, their documents say.
The seizures even reach into Škaljari, the ancestral territory of the Kavač clan’s deadly rivals, where the wife formally holds a half-share of a 188-square-meter courtyard.
Further along the Kotor coast, the dragnet caught a multi-story building in Dub containing five residential and ten non-residential spaces, alongside four commercial units. In Dobrota and Sutvara, prosecutors laid claim to a 140-square-meter apartment, a residential building with a private swimming pool, and tracts of meadows and forests formally registered to local businesses, associates, and a lawyer.
In the capital of Podgorica, authorities are targeting five apartments—including two duplexes—hidden behind a corporate entity. The remaining properties include 18,113 square meters of land in the Tivat village of Bogišići, and real estate registered to the fugitive’s mother in Herceg Novi.
Rounding out the seizure request are two heavily armored Mercedes G500 SUVs. While formally registered to an associate, prosecutors allege they belong to the crime boss’ illicitly acquired fleet. The prosecution noted its filing contains concrete evidence linking the entire portfolio directly to his criminal activities.

Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:51:56 UTC
23:51:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
Saudi Arabia's defence alliance with Turkey and Pakistan has moved from words to action for the first time, as escalating fighting in Yemen puts the two-month-old pact's collective defence commitments to the test.
The three members of the Mecca Alliance agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Sunday to begin the "practical implementation" of their collective defence commitments following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
They also agreed to make previously agreed military forces and capabilities available for rapid deployment to the kingdom.
But the move does not necessarily mean Turkish and Pakistani forces will join Saudi Arabia in directly fighting the Houthis.
Instead, experts told The New Arab that Pakistan could concentrate on territorial defence and military support inside Saudi Arabia, while Turkey provides capabilities including surveillance, air defence and drones.
For Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King's College London's School of Security Studies, the decision marks a significant evolution of the alliance.
"This is the first point at which I would describe the Mecca Pact as operational rather than primarily declaratory," Krieg told The New Arab.
"The critical development is not simply that the three governments have invoked collective defence. It is that Turkey and Pakistan are altering their military posture in response to attacks on Saudi Arabia and have committed to deploy previously agreed capabilities," Krieg said.
"That is the threshold the pact had to cross if it was going to have any deterrent credibility."
What will Pakistan and Turkey actually do?
The Mecca Alliance was established in August amid growing regional instability. Its collective defence principle means an attack against one member is treated as a threat to all three.
The arrangement has drawn comparisons with NATO's Article 5, but Krieg cautioned against taking the comparison too far.
"I would describe the pact as Article 5 language without Article 5 infrastructure," he said.
NATO has spent decades developing integrated military commands, common doctrine and joint planning. The Mecca Alliance has existed for only two months.
"This is meaningful activation, but it is the operationalisation of a flexible alliance rather than the creation of a unified war-fighting structure," Krieg said. "Yemen is now providing its first real operational laboratory."
The three countries have not publicly disclosed exactly which forces or military capabilities Turkey and Pakistan will deploy.
Krieg expects their roles to be substantially different.
Pakistan could provide territorial and air defence, training, advisers and manpower to protect strategic infrastructure, but is likely to be cautious about offensive operations against the Houthis partly because of its relationship with Iran.
Turkey could provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, radar and air defence, unmanned systems, electronic warfare and naval surveillance.
Saudi Arabia would remain the principal combatant.
"That allows all three states to say collective defence is functioning without requiring all three to fight the same war in the same way," Krieg said.
What does it change inside Yemen?
For Saudi Arabia, the most important effect may not be additional forces fighting inside Yemen but greater protection from attacks at home.
Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said the Houthis were likely among the threats Saudi Arabia had in mind when the agreement was designed.
Saudi Arabia is "the more vulnerable member state in this alliance, security-wise", she told The New Arab.
The Houthis have developed increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities with Iranian support, allowing the group to strike targets well beyond territory it controls in Yemen.
Shuja al-Deen said Saudi Arabia's size and extensive economic infrastructure make defending against such attacks particularly demanding.
"No, it will not change the military situation inside Yemen," she said of the immediate effect of Turkish and Pakistani support.
Rather, "it will make the Saudis less vulnerable" to Houthi attacks.
That could nevertheless affect the war.
Saudi Arabia remains the principal external supporter of the Yemeni government and other anti-Houthi forces. If Riyadh reduced that support, Shuja al-Deen said, those forces would be placed in "huge trouble".
Stronger Saudi defences against missiles and drones - and the possibility of renewed Houthi ground operations towards the Saudi border - could therefore allow Riyadh to sustain its support for anti-Houthi forces for longer.
"When they become stronger in that sense, they can continue to support these anti-Houthi camp forces," she said.
Shuja al-Deen also warned that the threat to Saudi Arabia may not remain confined to missiles and drones.
She believes Houthi preparations and rhetoric indicate the group could eventually attempt another ground incursion across the Saudi border, although she stressed that it was unclear when such an operation might take place.
"I think the Houthis... are going to invade or to expand through the Saudi territories at some point in this war," she said. "I'm not sure when, but it seems from their preparation and from their discourse and media that they are going to do something like that."
The assessment comes amid heightened military activity in the Houthi stronghold of Saada along the Saudi border, where weapons and equipment have been moved towards frontier areas in recent weeks.
That possibility further increases the importance of the territorial defence Pakistan can provide, while Turkish and Pakistani support against missiles and drones could make Saudi Arabia better able to withstand Houthi pressure.
Turkish drones and Pakistani military expertise could provide additional support, Shuja al-Deen added, but she did not expect large numbers of Turkish or Pakistani troops to enter Yemen.
"Yemenis have plenty of fighters on both sides," she said.
Are Turkey and Pakistan now part of the Yemen war?
Direct Turkish or Pakistani intervention against the Houthis could risk widening a conflict already entangled with the regional confrontation involving Iran.
Shuja al-Deen said she did not currently expect the Houthis to retaliate directly against either country. Turkey is geographically removed from Yemen, while Pakistan occupies a sensitive position in Iran's regional calculations and maintains an important relationship with Tehran.
"I don't think they are going to widen the conflict at this moment to that extent," she said.
Krieg similarly expects Pakistan to remain wary of offensive action against the Houthis because Islamabad has strong incentives to avoid confrontation with Iran.
Turkey, meanwhile, is attempting to strengthen Saudi Arabia's position without closing the door to diplomacy.
Krieg said Ankara's preferred outcome was not the military destruction of the Houthis but a stronger Saudi negotiating position that could eventually produce a settlement.
Is the alliance aimed at Iran?
When Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan established the pact, they sought to reassure Iran that it was not intended as an anti-Iranian military bloc.
Its first activation has now come amid a war involving the Houthis, an armed movement closely aligned with Tehran.
Shuja al-Deen said the members had been explicit from the beginning that Iran was not the target.
But "it seems now, very obviously, that the Yemen war is the first test for this agreement", she said.
Krieg also cautioned against viewing the alliance simply as an emerging Sunni bloc designed to confront Iran.
"Iran and the Houthis are the immediate catalyst, but they are not the fundamental explanation," he said.
Instead, he sees the alliance as part of a broader Saudi effort to reduce the risks of relying overwhelmingly on the United States for its security.
Riyadh continues to depend on Washington for advanced aircraft, intelligence, missile defence, logistics and other high-end military capabilities, and is not attempting to replace its US security relationship.
"In that sense, I think Mecca is best understood as a supplement to the US architecture rather than an alternative to it," Krieg said.
Saudi Arabia brings financial resources and political weight to the arrangement, while Turkey contributes technology and its growing defence industry and Pakistan offers manpower, established military institutions and strategic depth.
"The Houthis triggered its first activation, but the alliance is really about how Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan intend to operate in a regional order where American power remains important but American reliability can no longer be taken for granted," Krieg said.

Book weighing over 200kg illustrated by Dalí and Cocteau stolen in Auvergne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:51:50 UTC
23:51:50 KST

On the night of 4 to 5 October, the "Book of the Apocalypse", a 210‑kilo volume with works by Salvador Dalí, Jean Cocteau and Bernard Buffet, was stolen from an art centre in Issoire, Puy‑de‑Dôme.
Another theft in the art world: the "Book of the Apocalypse", described as one of the most expensive (and heaviest) books in the world, was stolen from a private museum in Issoire, in Auvergne, overnight from Sunday to Monday, the Clermont-Ferrand public prosecutor’s office has said.
The original and unique copy of this book, conceived by the Auvergne publisher Joseph Forêt, was designed as a total work of art inspired by the Apocalypse of Saint John.
Weighing 210 kilos in total, this work made up of 150 parchments was produced between 1958 and 1961 by seven leading writers and seven leading painters of the time, among them Ossip Zadkine, Léonard Foujita, Jean Cocteau and Jean Giono. Salvador Dalí, for his part, sculpted the cover using the lost-wax casting technique.
A work that has travelled the world
After being shown in nearly 150 exhibitions around the globe between 1961 and 1972, the book disappeared from view for several years. Stored in Switzerland, it was eventually sold to Japanese collectors.
As they were preparing to auction it off, piece by piece, it was bought in 2003 by Christian Karoutzos, CEO of an art restoration company in Issoire. He decided to display the cover and several parchments in his contemporary art centre in the town until the autumn.
"It is a cathedral-like work, a masterpiece, unique in the world", the new owner lamented to ICI Pays d’Auvergne after the theft, adding that"France was murdered last night, French heritage was murdered".
"This was a privately owned work kept in a small private contemporary art museum that also housed other, less valuable pieces", said Issoire’s mayor, Bertrand Barraud. He stressed that the loss was "incalculable" and that it was "the work of a lifetime".
An investigation has been opened by the Clermont-Ferrand gendarmerie’s research unit. The work is estimated to be worth several million euros.
This theft recalls the events at the Louvre on 19 October 2025, when thieves managed to steal jewels valued at 88 million euros_._

European Commission proposes suspending voting rights of prospective EU members failing to meet commitments
Ukraine

2026-10-06
17:49:44 EEST
23:49:44 KST

The European Commission is proposing to introduce a series of precautionary measures for future European Union member states in the event they fail to fulfill their commitments, including the suspension of their voting rights in the EU Council.
These proposals are outlined in a package of documents regarding the European Union's preparations for future enlargement, specifically concerning sectoral and institutional safeguard measures.
In particular, the commission said future accession treaties should include "stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitments undertaken during the accession negotiations."
"Today, the Commission is proposing a common framework for these safeguards. Future accession treaties would strengthen the existing sectoral safeguards and introduce a new institutional safeguard. In particular, the period during which safeguards can be activated in areas such as the economy, the internal market, and justice and home affairs, would be significantly extended after accession," the press release reads.
Specifically, "the period during which safeguards can be activated in areas such as the economy, the internal market, and justice and home affairs, would be significantly extended after accession. A dedicated institutional safeguard would address serious breaches of Article 2 TEU values and the principle of sincere cooperation. In the most serious cases, measures could include the suspension of Council voting rights. Transitional arrangements could also be used where needed, including for the free movement of workers and services, agriculture, sensitive products, funding and participation in common systems. For a limited period, a new Member State could also commit not to block future enlargements because of bilateral disputes." the commission said.

Trump approves execution by firing squad for Fort Hood terrorist Nidal Hasan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:49:18 UTC
23:49:18 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has formally approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who went on a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, killing 13 people. Hasan’s execution would be the first carried out by the U.S. military itself, rather than the civilian justice system, since 1961.
The Pentagon said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended the death sentence be carried out by firing squad and Trump approved the recommendation. The date and location of the execution will be determined later. “Hasan’s day of reckoning has finally arrived,” the statement said.
Hasan, a U.S.-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, carried out the attack on Nov. 5, 2009. He entered a clinic at the sprawling military base, which at the time served as a staging point for troops preparing for deployment to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan, then pulled out two handguns and several magazines he had prepared in advance and opened fire on soldiers waiting for medical examinations and vaccinations while shouting “Allahu Akbar.”
The massacre was the deadliest shooting at a U.S. military installation in the country’s history. Hasan killed 13 people, including 12 soldiers, and wounded another 32, almost all of them service members. A civilian police officer responding to the attack eventually shot and incapacitated him, leaving Hasan paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan, now 56, was born in the United States to Palestinian parents who had immigrated from the West Bank. His mother came from the town of al-Bireh. Years before the attack, Hasan himself visited the West Bank and remained in contact with relatives there. At the time, reports said his family owned several apartments in Ramallah and that one of his brothers had moved from the United States to the West Bank.
The investigation and trial that followed the attack found that Hasan had carried out the terrorist attack under the inspiration of the global jihadist group al-Qaida, after he said he had “switched sides” in what he called “America’s war against Islam.”
Hasan said he carried out the attack because he opposed the U.S. presence in Iraq and Afghanistan and wanted to prevent the military from sending troops there who would kill his Muslim brothers, including Taliban leaders.
Before the attack, he had been in contact with radical cleric and notorious terrorist Anwar al-Awlaki, a U.S. citizen affiliated with al-Qaida who was regarded as a “spiritual mentor” to prominent terrorists and was later killed in a U.S. drone strike in Yemen.
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013, after a trial in which he chose to represent himself and refused to call witnesses or deny the charges against him. Court-appointed defense attorneys said at the time they feared he was deliberately seeking his own execution.
Hasan is now expected to become only the second person since 2010 to be executed by firing squad. Three other inmates are being held on death row in the U.S. military justice system and could also face a similar fate.
Since 1608, at least 144 civilian prisoners have been executed by shooting in what is now the United States, almost all of them in Utah. However, only four such executions have been carried out since 1977, the year capital punishment resumed after a decade-long suspension.
The most recent civilian execution by firing squad took place last year, when South Carolina carried out the death sentence of Brad Sigmon, who murdered the parents of his former girlfriend with a baseball bat.
This year, the U.S. Justice Department announced that it would allow executions by firing squad in an effort to increase the pace of executions for death row inmates.
In many U.S. death penalty cases, executions are delayed for years and sometimes decades through appeals or legal challenges over the planned method of execution and its effectiveness.
Just last week, controversy erupted after an attempt to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike in Tennessee failed when two lethal injections did not kill her and apparently caused her severe suffering. Pike’s lawyers had warned in advance that the injections might fail and even proposed that she be hanged instead.
At the state, nonfederal level, only five U.S. states currently allow execution by firing squad, all of them reliably Republican: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

AI generated
BRUSSELS - The European Commission proposed measures on Oct 6 to prepare the EU to take in countries such as Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova in coming years while trying to reassure existing members about potential political and economic costs.
The proposals by the European Union’s executive body reflect a renewed interest among EU members in expanding the 27-nation bloc, driven largely by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Kyiv’s desire to join the bloc as part of a peace settlement.
The proposed reforms include a measure to allow other EU countries to suspend a new member’s voting rights during the first 15 years of membership if it stops adhering to the bloc’s values, and a plan to limit financial support to Ukraine’s large farming sector.
The Commission also proposed strengthening an existing policy of gradually integrating would-be members into EU programmes and economic sectors such as energy, transport, digital and defence. But countries would have to meet criteria for each scheme and align with the EU’s overall strategic direction.
The small Balkan state of Montenegro is likely to be the next country ready to join the bloc, possibly wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year, according to EU officials. Albania, Moldova and Ukraine are also seen as frontrunners but are probably at least still several years away from membership.
“As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a written statement.
“This means preparing our institutions, adapting our policies for new realities, and ensuring our budget reflects our shared ambitions.”
The Commission’s suggestions will require approval from the EU’s current 27 member states to become reality. Those countries are expected to begin discussions on the proposals in the coming days. REUTERS

Norway files FIFA ethics complaint over Infantino, governance concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:48:53 UTC
23:48:53 KST

Halis Sunnetci
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
By Halis Sunnetci
ISTANBUL (AA) - The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) filed two formal requests with FIFA bodies Tuesday over governance and ethics concerns involving President Gianni Infantino and three controversial cases, the federation said in a statement.
The NFF submitted an ethics complaint asking FIFA’s Ethics Committee to examine the conduct of Infantino and any other individuals identified during an investigation for potential breaches of the governing body’s Code of Ethics.
A separate referral to FIFA’s Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee (GACC) asks whether the organization’s governance, financial oversight, internal controls and decision-making processes functioned as intended.
Both filings concern three issues: the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project, the handling of US forward Folarin Balogun’s suspension during the 2026 World Cup and the creation and awarding of the FIFA Peace Prize.
“The purpose of these inquiries is simple: to establish the facts in the cases and ensure accountability within FIFA’s own regulations,” NFF President Lise Klaveness said.
Balogun case
The NFF is seeking an examination of possible political intervention in the disciplinary process involving Balogun during the World Cup.
Balogun received an automatic one-match suspension after being sent off in the US’ win over Bosnia and Herzegovina, but FIFA subsequently made implementation of the ban conditional, allowing him to play against Belgium.
The decision came after US President Donald Trump contacted Infantino and asked him to review the red card.
The Norwegian federation wants FIFA to examine communications surrounding the decision, whether outside contacts influenced the disciplinary process and whether requirements concerning the independence of FIFA’s disciplinary bodies were followed.
 
FIFA Forward Enterprise
The NFF is also seeking clarification over the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which involved plans to allow private investors to acquire minority stakes in a new FIFA-controlled commercial entity that would manage rights to major FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.
The proposal involved selling around a 20% stake in the entity to outside investors.
The filing asks how the project advanced to such a stage, whether FIFA’s internal controls worked properly, how the organization’s leadership communicated about the proposal and whether any financial interest or future role for Infantino was contemplated.
The project was withdrawn in July following opposition from football governing bodies.
 
FIFA Peace Prize
The third issue concerns the FIFA Peace Prize, which was created in 2025 and awarded to Trump later that year.
The NFF is asking for an examination of how the prize was created, who approved it, the FIFA Council’s involvement and whether its creation and awarding were consistent with FIFA’s requirements on political neutrality.
The Norwegian federation has previously raised concerns about the prize and FIFA’s relationship with political leaders.
Klaveness said the NFF wants the three matters thoroughly examined and relevant documentation and communications made available to FIFA’s member associations.

====================================================================================================

EU-China trade tensions: Five things to know as Brussels and Beijing face crunch talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:48:40 UTC
23:48:40 KST

The next ten days will be critical for EU-China relations. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will travel to Beijing later this week for high-level talks aimed at rebalancing the trade relationship and securing “tangible” results ahead of next week’s meeting of EU leaders.
After months of tensions, relations between Brussels and Beijing are entering a crucial phase, with the European Commission having set October as a deadline to secure "tangible” results with Beijing to rebalance their trade relationship.
The stakes are high for the EU, whose trade deficit with China has now reached a record €1 billion a day.
Key talks will take place in Beijing at the end of this week between EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. They will be followed next week by a meeting of EU leaders, with China set to top the agenda.
For European policymakers, the diagnosis is increasingly clear: the situation is unsustainable, with a new wave of Chinese competition putting pressure on the EU’s industrial base two decades after China’s rapid economic expansion began — and putting thousands of jobs at risk.
“A massive industrial shock is affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.],” reads a Franco-German document which was sent on Monday to capitals and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Ahead of these crucial ten days, Euronews takes a deep dive into the EU-China relationship. Here are five things to know.
1. Brussels seeks a breakthrough in Beijing
After several weeks of discussions held at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, Šefčovič will travel to Beijing on Thursday and Friday for high-level political discussions with Wentao.
Negotiations were launched last June, with the Europeans hoping to secure commitments from Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship. At the heart of the discussions is Chinese access to the EU market of 450 million consumers, with the Europeans seeking to protect EU industry from a wave of low-cost Chinese imports.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," EU Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné told Euronews in an exclusive interview three weeks ago, adding that the EU had already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year.
The Europeans also want to secure exports of rare earths from China, which are essential for EU industry, after Beijing blocked them amid a trade war with the US in 2025. Exports eventually resumed, but the truce runs only until 10 January 2027.
For the Commission, this week’s talks are essential, as EU leaders expect concrete results from the EU executive for their meeting next week.
2. The German shift
EU member states’ approach to China has evolved since Germany came to recognise that its economy — the bloc’s largest — was increasingly exposed to Chinese competition. In 2024, Berlin opposed EU tariffs on low-cost Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). But in recent weeks, Germany has moved closer to France, which has taken a tougher stance and advocated stronger measures towards China.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called on Monday, in a letter to Commission President von der Leyen, for “the full use” of the EU’s existing trade defence instruments and for a “comprehensive framework” with new legal instruments.
In a document accompanying the letter, they listed proposals, including a new tool that would be in the hands of the Commission to allow a “decisive and systemic reaction,” including measures that could lead to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.”
The Commission would activate the tool unless a qualified majority voted against it. By introducing a reversed qualified majority voting system, the two leaders hope to make EU action easier and faster.
However, among member states, Madrid remains one of the most cautious towards China, despite having sought Chinese investment for several years.
Spain’s domestic political situation, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling for new elections, could nevertheless limit Madrid’s opposition to the EU’s strategy towards China.
3. Industry is bracing for tougher measures
Across Europe, European businesses are calling for tough action despite the risk of retaliation.
They want the EU not only to protect European industry through trade policy, but also to reduce its dependence on China, given the bloc’s critical vulnerabilities. Beijing demonstrated the risks of these dependencies in 2025, when it restricted exports of rare earths and chips essential to the automotive industry amid a dispute involving Dutch-based Nexperia.
The Federation of German Industries, the BDI, published a report on 25 September, saying that “systemic competition with China’s economy is increasingly calling into question the resilience of the open social market economy.”
It added: “Even if de-risking entails costs — including in the form of countermeasures — inaction would be significantly more costly economically in the long term and irresponsible from a security policy perspective.”
On 29 September, the Commission launched a consultation with EU businesses to help shape new measures, including a diversification tool aimed at addressing situations where reliance on a single supplier country poses a risk to the EU’s security of supply.
4. Will China play ball in the negotiations?
Since they began last June, negotiations between the Commission and Beijing have made little progress.
Beijing wants to maintain access to the EU market, while the Commission is seeking to negotiate import quotas by product. However, China holds important leverage in the talks, as it has a global monopoly on the production and processing of rare earths, which are key to the EU’s green tech, defence and car industries.
China already pushed back against a Commission proposal for “voluntary export restrictions” on EVs. On 20 September, a Chinese spokesperson said that such measures were contrary to the “principle of fair competition.”
"China's position is consistent. Any solution between China and the EU must ensure a balance of interests, comply with WTO rules and their respective domestic laws, and fully accommodate the interests of industries on both sides," the spokesperson said.
5. Is a trade war on the horizon?
Tensions are mounting between the two sides, with both refraining from more aggressive moves.
Before negotiations started in June, the EU had already proposed the so-called Industrial Accelerator Act and the Cybersecurity Act, restricting access to the EU market for Chinese companies, with Beijing threatening of retaliation.
Since June, the Commission has continued to open probes into Chinese products over unfair trade practices, irritating Beijing, which over the summer forbade its companies from cooperating with Brussels on antitrust probes.
According to several people familiar with the matter, EU countries are also holding back the launch of an investigation into the chemicals sector that could lead to safeguards — tariffs and quotas.
Finally, last Saturday, China put pressure on the Europeans ahead of this week’s critical talks by launching an investigation into EU chemicals, suspecting dumping of EU p-nitrotoluene. The move follows an investigation by the EU, opened in September, into polyvinyl chloride imports from countries including China.

‘Not the act of a friend’: Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:47:39 UTC
23:47:39 KST

‘Not the act of a friend’: Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate nears
Former British consul Sir Vincent Fean says Israel is acting unlawfully in the wake of a new wave of sanctions.
London, United Kingdom – The deadline Israel imposed on the United Kingdom to close its East Jerusalem consulate is fast approaching.
Thursday marks 30 days since Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar’s order, a retaliatory move against the UK’s wave of sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements.
“It’s not the act of a friend or ally,” Sir Vincent Fean, former British consul general to Jerusalem, told Al Jazeera. “The British Consulate General has every right to be in Jerusalem, in East Jerusalem, part of the state of Palestine.”
From 2010 until 2014, Fean held the post as the de facto ambassador to occupied Palestinian territory. He is now a trustee of the Britain Palestine Project, advocating for equal rights for Palestinians and Israelis.
“In international law, for [the UK], and for the vast majority of the world, Israel does not have the right to interfere with the diplomatic relations between the state of Palestine and the state of the United Kingdom. It is doing so by closing our office, and that is unlawful,” he said, adding that he is “particularly concerned” for the consulate’s 50 or so Palestinian staff.
UK-Israel ties have reached a nadir. On Monday, reports claimed that the UK could expel 27 Israeli diplomats if the consulate closure goes ahead.
British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell has reportedly held talks with Israeli officials in a visit that was not disclosed by the UK government, but an agreement to keep the consulate open was not reached.
Israel’s response was furious following the UK’s import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, as well as an overall change of tone. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has, for instance, lamented Israel’s “ethnic cleansing” against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband expected Israel to retaliate, but said the UK had “weighed the costs and benefits of acting”.
In addition to the consulate closure order, Israel expelled the UK from the Washington-led coordination centre for post-war Gaza and barred 11 lawmakers from entering Israel, including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana.
“It is illegal and unlawful for Israel to act in this way,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “There’s been a reset in UK foreign policy since [Prime Minister Andy] Burnham and Miliband came in.”
Israel’s hostile actions towards the UK “will not be forgiven or forgotten anytime soon”, he added.
In a brief by the Britain Palestine Project that was endorsed by former UK Attorney General Dominic Grieve KC and shared with Al Jazeera, the threatened closure is described as “an unlawful assertion of sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory”.
“The Israeli announcement usurps the rights of the State of Palestine,” it reads.
Resolution 478 was adopted by the United Nations Security Council – of which the UK is a permanent member – in 1980, resolving that Israel’s attempts to alter the status of Jerusalem are “null and void”.
In 2016, Resolution 2334 reiterated this, “condemning all measures aimed at altering the demographic composition, character and status of the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem”.
The UK formally recognised the State of Palestine in September of 2025.
If the UK resists Israel’s orders, there are various logistical challenges Israel could feasibly impose on the consulate and the diplomats within it.
“The practicality is that the Consulate General depends on Israeli electricity [and] water. So there are means by which Israel could force the expulsion, the closure, of the Consulate General,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “I don’t know what’s going to happen, but this Israeli government has broken many laws,” he said when asked if Israel may use electricity or water cut-offs as a means to expel British diplomats.
While reiterating that the UK’s East Jerusalem consulate should remain open despite orders, Fean said that “if that proves to be made impossible by force of the Israeli government, then there are alternatives.”
Foreign embassies in Ramallah could be an alternate route to manage consulate affairs, he said.
The consulate acts as the channel of communications between the UK and the Palestinian government and manages consular affairs for British nationals in the region, including pilgrims to the West Bank.
“Yet again, Israel is taking it out on the Palestinians for something that somebody else has done,” said Fean. “The impunity of Israel needs to be challenged. The fact that this Israeli government seems to see itself as above the law needs to be challenged.”
Human rights advocates have urged the UK to resist Israel’s orders.
“Such a retaliatory step from Israel suggests that any further measures taken by the UK could trigger further responses,” said Zena Agha, deputy director of the British Palestinian Committee. “But that should not deter the UK from meeting its obligations under international law – nor pursuing measures towards accountability for Israel’s genocide and occupation.”
Shamiul Joarder, director of Friends of al-Aqsa, reiterated the illegality of Israel’s actions and told Al Jazeera, “If Britain accepts this order, it risks allowing Israel to dictate the terms of Britain’s diplomatic presence in occupied East Jerusalem. That would set a deeply concerning precedent.”
The Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on Israel’s orders to close the British Consulate, nor on the UK’s intended response.

Brussels eyes agricultural carve-outs from Ukraine's EU membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:46:32 UTC
23:46:32 KST

The European Commission proposed excluding Ukraine's agricultural products from the EU market and agricultural funding even when Kyiv joins the EU, in a move to smooth the country's accession process and address concerns from several member states.
The European Commission proposed to exclude certain agricultural products from accessing the European market and receiving EU funding even after Ukraine becomes a full member of the bloc.
The proposal comes as part of an enlargement strategy meant to prepare the Union to better absorb new countries, and is meant to address concerns from several member states that their agricultural sector could be undercut by the Ukrainian one.
“One area where we have to be very careful is agriculture. Why? Because the structure and the size of agriculture in Ukraine is really unique, therefore, we are proposing that we do special arrangements, which would limit the financial support, and market access for some of the Ukrainian agricultural products,” EU’s Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said.
Agricultural carveout
For the enlargement chief, Ukraine’s partial integration is possible, and the objective is to make Kyiv a full member state, but the Commission is proposing targeted amendments to exclude Ukrainian wheat and grain from the EU’s agricultural framework.
“What we propose now is about protecting European farmers,” Kos noted, adding that the Commission will propose to include the measure in the EU’s common position on agricultural policy when negotiating the accession of Ukraine.
According to the Commission, the idea is to help Ukraine regain access to its traditional markets, in particular in Northern Africa and the Middle East, which Russia’s war of attrition made it difficult to reach.
The EU executive argues that, if such regions were deprived of Ukrainian grain as it was diverted to the European market, it would substantially harm the food security of the importer countries and even trigger risks of mass famine.
Troubled accession
However, the measure is also meant to address concerns from EU countries like Poland that Ukraine’s agricultural exports might seriously challenge their national farmers and markets, Euronews understands.
Kyiv applied to become an EU member shortly after Russia’s war of aggression started in 2022, but its accession bid has stalled until earlier this year due to opposition from Viktor Orbán’s Hungary.
However, as Orbán was ousted from power earlier this year, the accession process started moving, with two more accession clusters expected to be opened as early as next week.
Thus, the Commission’s move seems meant to prevent these concerns from affecting Ukraine’s sensitive enlargement process from being delayed further.
“It doesn't mean that Ukraine will not become a member of the EU,” Kos continued. “We can afford that Ukraine will become a member of the EU, but we will set special conditions for agriculture.”
Tentative timeline
At the same time, Brussels is conscious that Ukraine, because of its size and ongoing war effort, poses a specific challenge to the EU’s enlargement process. Nevertheless, Kyiv has been included in a group of four “frontrunners” that will receive a dedicated roadmap later this month.
The roadmap will include an indicative timeline for joining the Union and a breakdown of the most important steps to get there. Still, for the other three frontrunners, Montenegro, Albania and Moldova, the timeline is relatively intuitive.
Montenegro’s declared ambition is to become the 28th member by 2028. Albania is poised to see its ambition to conclude the accession homework by the end of next year formally endorsed. Moldova is similarly targeting the first half of 2028.
For Ukraine, there is no obvious timeline, since the accession path might inevitably become linked with the eventual peace process with Russia.
“The country is at war. We will have to see. There are so many ifs [for Ukraine’s roadmap],” Kos said.

With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump.

Separatists win in French-speaking Quebec, eye Canada exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:46:00 UTC
23:46:00 KST

Quebec’s separatist Parti Québécois returned to power after winning Monday’s provincial election but failed to secure a majority, setting up a minority government as the party pushes for another referendum on independence from Canada.
The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decade but denies it the majority it sought, forcing the separatists to rely on opposition parties even as they try to revive Quebec’s independence debate.
The party was on track to win nearly 60 seats as the final votes were counted, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority in Quebec’s 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature. A minority government means PQ will need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes.
St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that voters had denied his party a majority. "Quebecers elected the Parti Québécois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message,” he said.
He has pledged to hold another referendum on independence, though he has said he would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump is no longer in office.
St-Pierre Plamondon framed independence as essential to preserving Quebec’s French-speaking identity, saying it was a "question of survival” for a French-speaking population that represents only a small fraction of North America. He said Quebec "just wants to exist on its own like other countries of the world” and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future.
"I continue to dream and visualize that country,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. "That dream will be realized one day.”
He also sought to reassure Canadians outside Quebec. "The project for independence is not about excluding you,” he said. "Quebec will never change its geographical position, so we have an interest in working together.”
Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the "difficult result.” The CAQ, which entered the election with 79 seats, was shut out of the legislature, and Fréchette lost her own seat in Trois-Rivières.
But the PQ's victory does not mean most Quebecers support leaving Canada.
"This was not an election about independence, which is not popular in Quebec right now, but about getting rid of the CAQ, the party in power since 2018,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Support for independence remains at about 30%, low by historical standards, he said. Béland said the minority result is likely welcome news for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government because it could make it harder for the PQ to prepare for and eventually call an independence referendum.
The PQ would face opposition from both the Liberals and Conservatives, whose leaders have said they would fight efforts to hold a sovereignty referendum. Québec solidaire, another pro-independence party, could hold the balance of power and potentially support the PQ on a referendum.
Carney congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and signaled that Ottawa would work with the incoming separatist government. "Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said. He said the two governments would work together to support businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, create jobs and build housing.
Still, Béland said a separatist government in Quebec poses a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching elsewhere in Canada.
The Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote Oct. 19 on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada.
"Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Béland said.
Quebec voters have twice rejected sovereignty, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.
Quebec, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant autonomy. The province of 9.1 million collects its own income tax, has immigration policies favoring French speakers and has laws giving the French language priority over English.
Even with the PQ victory, Trump’s tariffs and 51st-state rhetoric have complicated the separatist argument by stirring Canadian nationalism and giving some French-speaking Quebecers another reason to value remaining part of Canada.
Trump’s tariffs and repeated threats against Canada became a defining issue in the 2025 federal election, helping lift Carney’s Liberals to victory after the party had trailed badly before Trump returned to office.

Germany is shaken by an espionage and treason scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:45:00 UTC
23:45:00 KST

Germany shaken by espionage and treason allegations
October 6, 2026
If the allegations are confirmed, it would be an espionage case of historic proportions for Germany: August Hanning, former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), has been arrested, with the federal prosecutor accusing him of espionage, treason and attempted treason.
August Hanning, now 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. But even before then, he had enjoyed a meteoric rise within the security apparatus. After leaving the BND, he served as state secretary in the Federal Interior Ministry, then moved into the private sector and worked as a security consultant.
According to the federal prosecutor's office, his informant was his former chief-of-staff, named in the statement only as Manfred D.*, who went on to hold this position under Hanning's successors from March 2012 to March 2026. D. thus had access to a great deal of classified information.
Classified information from the chancellor's office
Manfred D. is alleged to have passed on nearly 2,000 BND documents — some of them highly sensitive — to Hanning over the course of several years in exchange for money. Hanning is then said to have used the information in his private consultancy business.
The most serious allegation is that Hanning is said to have maintained close contact with an employee of a foreign intelligence service for years and to have leaked classified information to him. It is not known which country was involved, but reports say it is not Russia.
Investigators also mention an analysis that Hanning is said to have prepared for an employee of another foreign intelligence service. However, it is not certain whether the analysis ever reached that person.
The classified information also concerned the routine meetings of the heads of German security agencies at the chancellery. Topics included, among other things, the Iranian nuclear program and analyses of the Russian armed forces.
Since intelligence from foreign partner agencies is also said to have been shared in this context, this could also undermine their trust in the German BND and lead to difficulties in future intelligence cooperation with Germany.
Hanning came under scrutiny in an entirely different context
"A good agent is one who doesn't draw attention to himself," Hanning was once quoted as saying. When he finally drew attention to himself, it was in an entirely different context.
In September 2025, the Hamburg state police searched Hanning's home and offices in connection with the famous case of the kidnapping involving Christina Block, heiress to the steakhouse restaurant chain Block House. State prosecutors in Hamburg accused her of having ordered the kidnapping of her two youngest children in late 2023 due to a custody dispute.
A little over a year before the operation to bring the children back, there is said to have already been a failed kidnapping attempt. At the time, there were suspicions that Hanning was involved, which he denies.
But during a search in 2025, investigators found an electronic storage device containing top-secret BND documents. The police handed the documents over to the federal prosecutor's office, which launched a covert investigation against Hanning and Manfred D. in May 2026. The most recent documents found so far are said to date from June 2022.
Greens demand consequences
Throughout its history, the BND has seen a number of espionage cases, some of them spectacular. In the 1960s, Heinz Felfe headed the "Counterintelligence: Soviet Union" division while simultaneously working for the Soviet secret service, the KGB.
In 2014, a BND employee was exposed as a spy for the US CIA. There is also an ongoing trial against a BND agent accused of betraying secrets to Russia's FSB in September and October 2022 — that is, after the start of the war in Ukraine. Yet never before has a former official of August Hanning's stature been at the center of suspicion of espionage.
"The BND launched extensive internal investigations early on and without delay, which corroborated the suspicions," said current BND President Martin Jäger. "For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security."
However, there was some fierce criticism from the political sphere. Günter Krings of the conservative governing party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told the Rheinische Post newspaper: "The mere suspicion that a former BND chief is selling secrets is damaging to trust in our security agencies."
Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party and deputy chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services said: "These are serious and grave allegations that have been leveled against August Hanning." Speaking on behalf of his party, he called for greater scrutiny of lobbying activities by former top officials and those with the highest security clearances. "These are clearly also a gateway for hostile intelligence services," von Notz said. The federal government must put an immediate stop to these "illegitimate practices."
Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the socialist Left Party group in the Bundestag, went even further: "The investigations against former BND chief Hanning show once again: The intelligence services themselves are a security risk."
This article was originally written in German.
*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

AfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time
- Published
A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.
Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".
Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties.
"The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.
This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment.
"We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.
The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community.
Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.
Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December.
His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events.
Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD.
Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD.
Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media.
Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature.
The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote.

Milan court rules against Google in right to be forgotten case

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:43:45 CEST
23:43:45 KST

The Court of Milan on Tuesday ruled
against Google in a landmark collective injunction lawsuit
organized by members of the non-profit digital rights
association Algopolio over the EU's right to be forgotten or
right to erasure rules.
                                    
The court ordered Google to fundamentally restructure its system
for processing "Right to be Forgotten" (de-indexing) requests.
                                    
Google must overhaul its internal procedures by November 15,
2026.
                                    
The court ruled against Google's reliance on overly
standardized, automated responses. If Google rejects an
individual's request to remove specific search links tied to
their name, the company must provide explicit, personalized
justification.
                                    
The updated process must allow users to attach supporting
documents to their de-indexing claims so they can thoroughly
substantiate their case.
                                    
The ruling focuses on proper compliance with Articles 17 (Right
to Erasure) and 21 (Right to Object) of the European Union's
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
                                    
A Google spokesman said:
"We disagree with the decision of the Court of Milan and will
appeal. We have invested significantly in dedicated teams that
meticulously review each case to fulfill our legal obligations
and balance individual privacy with the public's right to
information. Our review process is rigorous, compliant with
regulations, and fair. We will vigorously defend our actions in
the appropriate courts."

3 years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza: Women face death, loss, miscarriages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:43:19 UTC
23:43:19 KST

Three years into Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip, Palestinian and UN data show sweeping consequences for women and girls, from deaths, injuries and disappearances to rising miscarriage rates, unsafe births and malnutrition.
The collapse of Gaza’s health system has also deprived pregnant women of medical care, forcing some to give birth at home or in displacement shelters, while changes in family structures have left tens of thousands of women responsible for supporting their households.
Data released by the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics on July 18, 2026, showed that 12,400 women, excluding girls, had been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023.
The bureau also said women and children accounted for 4,700 of the 11,200 people reported missing, with the fate of many still unknown amid fears that some remain under the rubble of destroyed buildings.
 
Human toll
UN Women, in an April 2026 report titled The Cost of War on Women and Girls, estimated that more than 38,000 women and girls were killed between October 2023 and December 2025 -- an average of nearly 47 per day.
The report added, “there are close to 11,000 women and girls with lifelong injury.”
Survivors continue to face daily risks from bombardment, hunger, repeated displacement and restrictions on access to essential services, the report said.
According to the report, more than 71,200 Palestinians were killed during the period it covered, with women, children and older persons together representing more than half of all fatalities.
It cautioned that the figure was likely lower than the actual death toll “given the collapse of health information and reporting systems.”
The highest proportion of deaths among women and children was recorded during the first six months of the war, when they accounted for nearly two-thirds of documented fatalities.
The report said that despite a ceasefire agreement that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, women and girls continued to be killed and injured, while humanitarian and health conditions threatening their lives showed no significant improvement.
 
Reproductive health deteriorates
From the early months of the genocide, rights and health organizations documented a sharp deterioration in women’s reproductive health amid attacks on medical facilities, lack of access to health care, repeated displacement and malnutrition.
In July 2024, the International Planned Parenthood Federation said miscarriages in Gaza had risen by at least 300% during the first nine months of the war.
Physicians for Human Rights said in January 2026 that its report, Destroying Hope for the Future: Reproductive Violence in Gaza, documented 2,600 miscarriages during the first half of 2025.
The report also documented 220 pregnancy-related deaths and 1,460 premature births, while more than 2,500 newborns required intensive care.
Earlier data from Gaza’s Health Ministry showed that 57.1% of registered pregnant women in 2025 suffered from anemia.
 
Unsafe births
Rights reports said pregnant women in Gaza faced growing difficulty obtaining prenatal and delivery care as the health system deteriorated.
UN Women said Gaza was recording about 130 births per day as of March 2025, with more than a quarter delivered by cesarean section, placing additional strain on an already weakened health system.
The collapse of health services forced many women to give birth at home and in displacement sites, away from emergency medical care, the report said.
Even after the ceasefire, around 15 births per week continued to take place outside hospitals, often without skilled midwives and in unsafe conditions.
Hunger and malnutrition also heightened risks for pregnant women and newborns, including low birth weight, premature delivery, stillbirths and maternal deaths.
By July 2025, 40% of pregnant and breastfeeding women in Gaza were suffering from malnutrition, while around half a million women and girls faced the risk of famine, according to UN Women.
The report estimated that 37,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women, along with 50,000 girls, would require treatment for acute malnutrition during the year following the ceasefire.
In another report issued on June 19, 2026, UN Women said 1 million women and girls in Gaza lacked access to clean water, 690,000 were living in overcrowded shelters and 328,000 girls were out of school.
 
Miscarriage rate triples
The latest figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry show that risks facing pregnant women continue despite the ceasefire.
The ministry recorded around 3,958 miscarriages between January and June 2026.
An infographic published by the ministry on July 20 showed the miscarriage rate reached 208.5 per 1,000 live births during the first half of 2026, compared with 64 per 1,000 live births in the second half of 2025 -- about 3.3 times the previous rate.
April recorded the highest monthly miscarriage rate at 377.25 per 1,000 live births, while June recorded the highest number of miscarriages at 790.
The data show that 73.6% of miscarriages occurred during the first trimester, before the completion of 13 weeks of pregnancy, while 26.4% occurred during the second trimester, between 13 and 24 weeks.
 
More households headed by women
The war has also reshaped thousands of families in Gaza, forcing more women to assume responsibility for supporting their households following the deaths, injuries or disappearance of their husbands and the loss of income.
According to UN Women, the proportion of Palestinian households in Gaza headed by women rose from 9% before the war to 14%.
The report said 58,600 households were now headed by women as a result of the war.

What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:42:33 UTC
23:42:33 KST

What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure?
President Pezeshkian is spearheading a new coordinated effort to reduce the strain on Iranians.
The Iranian government seeking to reduce the severe financial pressure on its populace from the United States’s siege and sanctions on the country.
President Masoud Pezeshkian recently discussed measures with several cabinet members to ameliorate the economic effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran, including the depreciation of the Iranian lira and the cost-of-living crisis.
“The enemy’s plan in recent months has been to cut off the country’s vital arteries with the aim of pressuring the noble people of Iran,” Pezeshkian said on social media,
Though full details of the government response are not known, the scope of the meeting and Pezeshkian’s subsequent comments give some insights into these policies.
Here’s what we know.
How are Iranians faring as the war drags on?
Iran’s economic situation has deteriorated sharply since the war started on February 28, with US and Israeli strikes killing top Iranian political and military figures.
US-Israeli bombing since then has inflicted an estimated $270bn in damages on the country.
The situation worsened further after the US launched Operation Economic Outcast in late August, seeking to totally isolate the country from international trade.
Iran’s gross domestic product (GDP) has contracted by 10 percent with the collapse in energy exports due to the US naval blockade. The Iranian rial has in turn sunk to record lows.
Iran has made the lifting of the blockade a key demand in negotiations with the US about reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Maryam Ashrafi from the Bourse and Bazaar Foundation, a London-based think tank, told Al Jazeera that the economic situation has deteriorated for Iranian consumers, particularly in higher food prices.
In turn, Iranians are “increasingly turn[ing] to cheaper, inferior goods”. Shortages of raw materials used in the production of some staples, such as margarine, have also affected prices.
Imports of wheat and grains have also declined due to the US naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports.
“Large bulk carriers serving … [these] can carry upwards of 80,000 tonnes of agricultural commodities,” she told al Jazeera.
Some ships using the alternative route of the Caspian Sea ports, which are not under the embargo, have loads of only 7,200 tonnes, she said. Trucks using land routes are limited to about 20 tonnes per vehicle.
Increases in the price of packaging has also left businesses facing supply chain disruptions.
Insurance costs have also increased, even as war-related losses are generally not covered by insurers.
While medicines are not sanctioned, the raw materials used by Iran’s pharmaceutical industry are “increasingly difficult and expensive” to find, she said.
The disruptions to air travel caused by US sanctions on Iranian airlines have added to fears of medicine shortages in the country.
What does Iran plan to do?
At Saturday’s meeting, Iran’s Plan and Budget Organisation presented a seven-point package to deal with the crisis, but the details have not been revealed.
Iran’s semi-official news agency Tasnim reported that the proposal aimed to “help the country overcome the challenges ahead in a more orderly and less costly manner”.
Pezeshkian responded to the meeting the following day by ordering the formation of a committee to coordinate the new economic arrangement.
The committee includes the central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati, Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni and the conservative mayor of Tehran Alireza Zakani.
The goal of the committee is to help stabilise prices across the country, state broadcaster IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian told MPs on Monday that economic policy should be focused on helping the most vulnerable groups in the country, including female-led households. He said energy efficiency would be one of the main ways of tackling the country’s current woes.
“We are working to ensure that under no circumstances are electricity and energy supplies to producers and businesses cut off,” he said.
He called for the implementation of “car-free Tuesdays”, during which people would avoid using their vehicles to conserve energy.
Despite being a major oil and gas producer, Iran has suffered from shortages of petrol and experienced power cuts since the start of the war.
Pezeshkian also urged state employees to adopt the car-free days to encourage wider engagement.
Are these measures enough?
Saeed Laylaz, an economist who previously advised the Iranian government, said that Pezeshkian should have acted sooner.
When there were signs that war was imminent, the government should have prepared for a reduction in resources and disruptions to imports and exports, he said.
While Pezeshkian’s response was delayed, Laylaz believes that tackling the price of basic commodities – the target of the new measures – would be beneficial for the country.
“That said … we have enough basic commodities in stock, and even if the embargo continues, we will not face a problem in securing them, because we have suitable routes, sufficient resources, and trading partners who can help us,” he added.

In Gaza, we cannot even begin to recover from trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:42:22 UTC
23:42:22 KST

In Gaza, we cannot even begin to recover from trauma
The genocide has killed many and left the rest broken. For us, survivors, recovery is not on the horizon.
It has been three years of the genocidal horror in Gaza. Three years of death, destruction, despair and doom.
More than 74,000 people have been killed, including more than 1,400 since the so-called “ceasefire” took effect in October last year. Countless others have died preventable deaths due to lack of healthcare.
The rest of us survivors live in permanent trauma – a trauma we can’t begin to recover from because the genocide has not stopped.
The scale of the psychological devastation is difficult to put into words. There are some numbers that international organisations have started to use to call for urgent attention to the “mental health crisis”.
Analysis by the United Nations Population Fund has concluded that more than one million children in Gaza require psychosocial support, and 96 percent of them feel that death is imminent.
Among adolescents and young adults, approximately 61 percent suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), 38 percent from depression and 41 percent from anxiety.
One study estimated that some 88 percent of adults in Gaza have PTSD.
These are children and adults who had already been traumatised by repeated wars before. By 2020 – after three months-long wars – half of Gaza’s children displayed symptoms of PTSD. By 2022, 71 percent of adults had depression.
What these numbers do not say is what it is like to live with trauma when the chance of recovery is not even on the horizon.
We had known war before, but not total genocidal war.
Nothing prepared us for it. Not running from our homes when the Israeli army invaded in 2008. Not taking cover when Israeli bombardment levelled homes in 2012, 2014 and 2021.
Total, never-ending war is different. It overpowers; it crushes because it eliminates the hope of survival.
I had read about it in books. Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms comes to mind.
I remember the detailed descriptions of shelling and gunfire, of mangled limbs, dead bodies carried away on stretchers, doctors covered in blood like “butchers”.
Death in Gaza is nothing like that. It has a smell: of gunpowder, of burning rubble, of something rotten. It has a sound: a whoosh of a missile and the muffled screams from under the rubble. It has a bodily feeling of pure terror.
Nothing in the war prose I read prepared me for what I have seen and experienced.
In the first two months of the war, six houses in my immediate neighbourhood were bombed, and 60 of my neighbours were killed. One bomb fell so close that it burst a wall and windows of our house, injuring my younger sister, my mother and me.
The bombing was incessant – day and night. During the day, the smoke would fill up the air and hide the blue of the sky. At night, the dark and dust would be pierced by phone torches, as we would rush to dig our neighbours out of the rubble.
I saw a child’s body lodged in a shattered wall next to a man’s severed hand.
I lifted the corpse of a baby from under the ruins.
I watched a mother get out from under a collapsed home, blood streaming down her cheeks, while smoke-filled faces screamed and terror-stricken neighbours rummaged through pulverised concrete walls looking for their families.
And one horrific day, I found my own eight-year-old student Mohammed face down in the rubble. I rolled him onto his back to check for a pulse. No pulse, no breath. He had been coming to my house for English lessons with his sister. The bombing took his innocent life, but spared his sister. I pulled her out alive.
The classics are gentle. Gaza is not.
My trauma is stuck in my body like shrapnel. It tightens my chest when a drone passes overhead. It shakes my hands when I hear the crack of gunfire nearby.
I feel numb. I cannot concentrate. I almost never smile.
“The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially,” Hemingway wrote.
Indeed, it is not just the trauma that has overcome us, the broken people. It is also the survivor’s guilt. The very best and the most noble have been taken away from us. I have lost relatives, friends, students: the brightest, the most generous, the kindest.
I no longer read to learn and enrich myself. I read to forget. I read until my vision gets blurry and sleep overcomes me, as I try to keep images of death out of my head.
Fiction can no longer move me, shock me. I saw humanity die and the rest of the world watch on, indifferently. What could be more fictional than this?
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
