====================================================================================================

Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
The northern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv is now targeted by Russian drones as well as missiles, but the city lives on mayor Ihor Terehhov told ERR.
Being just 30 kilometers from the Russian border, Kharkiv has suffered a lot over the past four and a half years but is unbowed and is trying to rebuild what has been destroyed,
The mayor noted the coming winter will be very hard without any "energy truce", but the city survived the last winter and the previous ones too.
Mayor Terehhov was talkng to ERR at a time when Russia has been hitting Kharkiv in lethal strikes involving bombs, missiles and drones.
It is mid-autumn already and winter is approaching. How is Kharkiv preparing, and how did it survive the last winter?
If there is no so-called energy truce — Ukraine ending strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for Russia ending attacks on energy and other critical infrastructure in Ukraine, which is currently widely under discussion — then the coming winter will be very hard. We understand that perfectly.
I warned everyone last autumn that the winter would be tough, and so it has turned out to be. The enemy has been destroying energy infrastructure, targeting thermal power plants and water supply, leaving residents without basic utilities.
We all understand this all too well, yet we survived last winter, even though it, too, was hard. Due to the strikes on the power plants, we had not a single megawatt of electricity generation of our own. The heating system was damaged. There had been 50 attacks on electricity and heating networks. So it was a hard winter, but we held out. As for next winter, we are preparing for that too. We have been preparing since 2022.
Two years ago, in our previous interview, you spoke about the need to create energy "islands". What are these islands, and have they been created?
We wouldn't have survived last winter without those energy islands. I can't tell you everything, but if I were Estonia, I would be setting up energy islands too. It is effective. In essence an energy island is an autonomous energy source fed by small boiler houses. People get electricity, heat and water from it.
How many people currently live in Kharkiv? Initially people left, and then, as you said, they began to return. Two years ago you estimated the population at 900,000. Kharkiv has also become a destination for internally displaced people from the front line and occupied areas. What is the trend today?
During the war there have been times when the city's population fell to 350,000 and even to 320,000. But the trend has been positive, and currently around 1.4 million people live in Kharkiv, of whom 225,000 are internally displaced persons. This is a serious challenge for the city — these people have to be resettled and cared for.
Our hospitals cater to these people; their children attend our schools. They have lost everything, and it is our duty to care for them, but they also need help from the state. They have been left homeless, so the state should issue them housing certificates, but so far no state program has been implemented. So there are many challenges we face every day. But the fact that there are 1.4 million people living in Kharkiv today is actually good news.
How is responsibility for internally displaced people divided between the city, the oblast and the central government? Is the city obliged to provide them with housing?
In my view, providing housing for those who have lost everything — that is, internally displaced people — is the state's obligation. I mean a construction program for internally displaced people, so they have the opportunity to get living space where they want. The situation is not like this in Kharkiv alone. Yes, most of our people are displaced from Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. So such a program is needed.
As for Kharkiv residents, we currently have 160,000 people who have been left without shelter. No other major Ukrainian city has suffered destruction like Kharkiv has. As of today, we have 10,000 damaged, severely damaged or completely destroyed residential buildings, but during the war we have managed to repair and restore nearly 4,000 buildings. Of course, the city's budget deficit is very large, and according to government forecasts it will be even larger next year.
Where is the money coming from?
Financial assistance from international partners is required. It is no secret that we depend on funds allocated by our international partners. This is public information; both the president and the government have said so. We have to use state and city budget funds very carefully.
On September 28, Russian attack drones destroyed practically the entire stairwell of a multi-story block. Do you have reserve apartments to relocate residents somewhere?
We offered people accommodation in a dorm. Two families initially agreed, but then said they would go to live with relatives. Most of the residents of that building are internally displaced people who were renting apartments there. And now they are looking for other apartments.
For our part, we closed the building shell (a temporary measure where holes in walls and broken windows are covered with plywood — ed.), restored the electricity supply and restarted the heating and water systems. All of this is financed out of the city budget. The victims have been documented and are receiving payments. But the stairwell is still destroyed, from the third floor to the fifth, and with this I think the state should already allocate money for restoration. At first we were restoring everything ourselves at our own expense, but the city budget is already exhausted.
So what is the city's current budget deficit? How much money do you need?
That is a complicated question. You could say there is a deficit, but also say there isn't, depending on how you calculate it. Without reconstruction costs, we are on the edge, but still not in deficit. If we want to carry out the programs we consider necessary, then a deficit comes up. For us, the most important thing is to ensure reconstruction support and that payments are not delayed, as sometimes happens.
I saw three buildings in [residential district of Kharkiv] Saltivka that had been heavily damaged at the start of the war, then repaired, and now they are in order and people are starting to return (apartment repairs are not the city's responsibility but the residents' — ed.). But the Saltivka area is not the safest place in Kharkiv, to put it mildly. Is it worth spending money on rebuilding something that could be destroyed again the very next day?
I am convinced that rebuilding is essential. If we don't do it, people will stay in other countries and not return. People do not come back to places where there is nowhere to live, work or educate their children. We consider it important that Ukrainians, Kharkiv residents, come back from abroad, which means we have to rebuild in any case. Moreover, the current situation is such that a strike can hit practically any Ukrainian city. There is no city in the country so safe that you could say it definitely won't be attacked.
Have you been taking part in international conferences on Ukraine's reconstruction? In June a conference like that took place in Gdansk, Poland; next January one is going to be held in Tallinn.
I was at the Gdansk one. We held a special event and we managed to attract money from international partners, specifically for preparing for the heating season. That meeting was a productive one for Kharkiv.
I was in the Pyatykhatky neighborhood, and anti-drone nets are being installed over the road there. At the same time, some nearby streets are not covered with nets; I saw at least one car destroyed by a drone strike. On what criteria do you decide what to cover with nets and what not to?
The nets are not installed by the city but by the regional military administration, and they are installed where the military says so. Only the military decides where the anti-drone nets get placed. For our part, we are also installing protection against fibre-optic FPV drones. We do this in conjunction with the military, but at the city's expense. This protection is our know-how, developed in cooperation with the military and engineers.
Which places in Kharkiv are currently the most dangerous, and which are the safest?
In Kharkiv, as in the rest of the country, there is no safe place. I can't tell you that Pyatykhatky is dangerous but the city center — say Shevchenkivskyi or Kyivskyi districts — is more or less safe, because at any moment it could be hit by anything, from a missile to an FPV drone. As long as the war continues, nowhere in Ukraine can be a hundred percent safe.
Do you have any advice for your Estonian colleagues — mayors, municipal leaders — on preparing for crises?
Estonia is a sovereign state and we respect that. If you need our advice, there is no problem there. We will talk and show everything as openly as possible, though that information is not intended for the wider public consumption.

- Avoid traveling to destinations under a Level 4 travel warning: Jordan, Qatar, Somaliland and Egypt, including the Sinai Peninsula.
- In Level 3 destinations, minimize speaking Hebrew in crowded places.
- Stay away from demonstrations and large gatherings.
- Do not post on social media content that reflects your service in the security forces.
- In an emergency, contact local security forces first.
The NSC concluded its statement by publishing the number of its travel warning hotline, which handles terrorism-related inquiries only and operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week: +972-2-6667444.
Meanwhile, earlier Tuesday, ambassadors from European Union countries in Israel visited Kibbutz Nir Oz to mark three years since the massacre, holding a memorial tour at the community. The visit was led by EU Ambassador to Israel Michael Mann, who requested that the ambassadors’ annual memorial ceremony be held in Nir Oz this year. During the visit, the ambassadors toured the kibbutz, heard accounts of the events of October 7 and lit memorial candles in memory of those murdered and killed.
Among other places, they visited the home of the Siman Tov-Kedem family, where Yonatan “Johnny” Siman Tov, Tamar Kedem Siman Tov and their three children — 5.5-year-old twins Arbel and Shahar and 2.5-year-old Omer — were murdered. They also visited the Bibas family home, from which Yarden and Shiri Bibas and their children Ariel and Kfir were abducted. Yarden was released from captivity after 484 days. Shiri, Ariel and Kfir were murdered in captivity.
“What happened here was not a battle. It was not resistance. It was a massacre of civilians inside their homes, a heinous crime against humanity,” Mann said in his remarks.

Abdullah said the federal government was directing the campaign, while Jammu and Kashmir police were conducting verification and eviction drives.

The Rohingyas are a stateless Muslim minority from Myanmar who have faced decades of discrimination and displacement. More than 700,000 fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State following an outbreak of violence in August 2017, with most seeking refuge in Bangladesh.

Machine Gunner in the 12th &quot;Azov&quot; Brigade: Duties, Selection and Professional Training
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:25:00 EEST
23:25:00 KST

Machine Gunner in the 12th "Azov" Brigade: Duties, Selection and Professional Training
Kyiv • UNN
The 12th "Azov" Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine is looking for machine gunners and trains recruits from scratch. You can join through mobilization or under a contract.
Despite all the technological aspects of modern warfare, the position of machine gunner remains no less relevant. Wherever infantry operates, it is the machine gunner who provides the most substantial fire support, reports UNN.
The 12th Special Forces Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, "Azov," has opened recruitment for candidates for the position of machine gunner. A lack of military training or experience handling weapons is not an obstacle. If there is motivation and a desire to learn, the unit's instructors will provide everything necessary from the very beginning.
Selection criteria: who can become a machine gunner
To take up the position of machine gunner in "Azov," prior combat experience is not required. Motivation and a willingness to work are valued most. It is also important to have certain basic qualities:
-  A desire to master heavy weapons and work toward the unit's common goal; 
-  Working with a machine gun and ammunition requires strength, but it is developed during training; 
-  The ability to remain calm and focused during intense combat; 
-  An understanding of one's role, since the safety of the entire group depends on one's work; 
-  No critical contraindications to military service. 
What a machine gunner's duties include
The machine gunner position in "Azov," in addition to working with large-caliber weapons, requires precise calculation and coordination:
-  Providing fire cover for infantry during defensive and assault operations; 
-  Suppressing enemy firing points and personnel, and restricting their maneuverability; 
-  Controlling and holding designated areas of responsibility; 
-  Maintaining weapons, monitoring ammunition expenditure, and quickly clearing malfunctions; 
-  The ability to promptly change firing positions and work as part of a team with other soldiers. 
From basic skills to full control of the weapon
The "Azov" brigade has a clear training system in place. First, every recruit completes an intensive basic combat training course. During the BCT course, the recruit develops physical endurance, tactical medicine skills, teamwork, and movement in combat conditions.
After BCT, the soldier undergoes a specialized stage. "Azov" combat instructors teach recruits to operate both conventional weapons and modern Western machine guns. The recruit practices firing from any position. Training concludes with tactical coordination as part of a squad, where teamwork and position coverage are honed to automaticity.
How can one join?
To become a machine gunner in the 12th Special Forces Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, "Azov," you need to fill out an application on the azov.org.ua website or visit the nearest recruiting center. Recruiters will answer all questions, help with the Military Medical Commission, and guide applicants through every stage of the paperwork.
You can join the "Azov" brigade either through mobilization or under a contract. And if a candidate is already serving in the Defense Forces, recruiters will explain how to arrange a transfer from the Armed Forces of Ukraine to the National Guard of Ukraine, as well as from other structures.

Hungary plans to introduce wealth tax from 2027

22:24:52 CST
23:24:52 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced Tuesday that the government plans to introduce a wealth tax from Jan. 1, 2027.
The tax will be 1 percent on wealth exceeding 1 billion Hungarian forints (3.1 million U.S. dollars) and 1.5 percent on wealth exceeding 100 billion forints (310 million dollars), Magyar said in a Facebook video.
It will cover property, investments and company stakes, including assets held abroad or through asset-management structures, he added. Debts will be deductible from the tax base, while property and vehicle taxes can be credited against the liability.
The first annual self-assessed payment will be due by Aug. 31, 2027, based on assets held at the end of 2026, Magyar said.
The proposed measure will undergo broad public consultation before being adopted. ■

South Korea Faces Questions Over Russia Fuel Shipments

South Korea reportedly handled large fuel shipments to Russia through its ports between July and August.
An investigation by The Guardian, based on port records and ship-tracking data, found that more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, mostly diesel, were loaded at South Korean ports in July and August onto seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s Far East.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Three of the vessels were under UK or EU sanctions. One received its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters, a method that can make a shipment’s origin harder to trace.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Finland-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told The Guardian that the shipments “undermine” Western sanctions and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.
The shipments do not appear to violate South Korean law, the report says, as Seoul’s sanctions on Russia primarily focus on export controls covering goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
However, the shipments also cast doubt on Seoul’s stance on the war in Ukraine, particularly as Seoul has publicly supported Kyiv while stopping short of providing lethal weapons.
South Korea has supplied Ukraine with humanitarian aid and non-lethal military equipment and pledged $2.3 billion in support in 2023, largely through loans.
At the same time, Seoul has sought to preserve its economic ties with Moscow and has ruled out directly providing weapons to Ukraine.
Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
Fuel flows to Russia surge
The Guardian found that the sanctioned tanker Layla made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a combined 57,000 tons of diesel. On one voyage, it declared Vladivostok as its destination, while on another it listed Japan.
Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria, loaded nearly 11,000 tons of fuel at Ulsan before sailing to Vladivostok. The vessel is also under Australian sanctions.
The third sanctioned vessel, the Chongchon, did not enter a South Korean port. Instead, it received around 26,000 tons of fuel from the unsanctioned tanker Celeste I during a ship-to-ship transfer off Yeosu before heading toward Vladivostok.
The findings echoed a report from Reuters in early July, which said Russia sought jet fuel from Japan’s Chiba port to Russia via South Korea, though it’s unclear whether the operations relate to the latest findings presented by The Guardian.
In the rumored plans, the cargo was expected to arrive in Russia in the first half of July after a likely ship-to-ship transfer off Yeosu, South Korea. Its final destination remained unclear.
The reported route would mirror a similar shipment in 2022, when around 22,000 barrels of jet fuel were transported from Chiba to Russia’s Far Eastern port of Vladivostok via Yeosu.
South Korea declined to comment, while the Japanese and Russian ministries did not respond.
The owners and managers of the four tankers contacted by The Guardian did not respond to requests for comment.
Russia has faced growing fuel shortages after Ukrainian drone strikes disrupted its refinery network. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than two decades, while diesel production was down nearly 30% from a year earlier.
By July, Ukraine’s General Staff claimed to have knocked 43% of Russia’s refinery capacity offline.
According to The Guardian, Kpler data analyzed by CREA showed that Russia imported 368,000 tons of oil products by sea in August, more than seven times the previous month. However, the figure appears to be higher than the 172,000 tonnes listed by CREA in its August report.
The outlet also said South Korea accounted for 112,000 tons, or about 31% of Russia’s overall imports, second only to India, while CREA’s publication noted that Egypt, not South Korea, followed India in terms of volume.
Kyiv Post has reached out to CREA for clarification.
The increase began in July, around the time South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a NATO summit in Turkey.
Diplomatic rift between Kyiv and Seoul
The fuel shipments come as relations between Seoul and Kyiv face a separate diplomatic dispute over two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces.
The soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting alongside Moscow forces in Russia’s Kursk region and were reportedly transferred to South Korea in September 2026.
President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly disclosed the transfer during his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, but South Korea says the transfer had been agreed to remain confidential to protect the soldiers and their families in North Korea.
Seoul subsequently demanded an explanation and apology from Kyiv.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday that Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had apologized in messages exchanged over the incident, but that the apology did not meet Seoul’s expectations.
Cho added Seoul was considering several responses, including recalling its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Hee-chang.
Ukraine has described the dispute as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Zelensky’s office said Seoul had been informed of the president’s UN speech in advance and that the address did not disclose identifying information about the soldiers.
Cho said the soldiers’ safety, and that of their relatives in North Korea, had been the primary reason for the confidentiality agreement. He also suggested, while stressing that it was his personal interpretation, that Zelensky may have wanted to demonstrate at the UN that Ukraine had acted appropriately as a liberal democracy.

Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:23:52 UTC
23:23:52 KST

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions.
Lithuania has taken a step towards removing a constitutional ban on nuclear weapons from its territory, bringing the Baltic state closer to the legal position of its neighbours as European allies debate how to strengthen NATO’s deterrence in the face of Russia.
The Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted 106-18, with six abstentions, on Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment removing a provision that bars weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from Lithuanian territory.
The change still requires a second vote after a constitutionally mandated three-month waiting period. At least 94 of the Seimas’ 141 members must back it on both occasions. The final vote is expected on January 12.
“This constitutional amendment would enable Lithuania’s armed forces to participate fully in the planning and exercises of all of NATO’s deterrence measures,” said Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement parliamentary group.
Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and military bases of foreign states may not be located in Lithuania, which borders Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. This means that under current laws, allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons could not enter Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Added urgency in Lithuania's case
Supporters of the amendment argue that the constitutional provision has become a legal obstacle to Lithuania’s full participation in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and leaves the country at a disadvantage compared with other NATO allies.
“Our neighbouring countries, such as Latvia, Estonia and Poland, have no such restrictions either,” Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee, said during a parliamentary session in September. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries. We must send a signal that Lithuania is a full part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence.”
NATO describes nuclear deterrence as part of its collective defence, alongside conventional and missile-defence capabilities. The Alliance also says its nuclear policy remains consistent with its commitments to arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation.
For Lithuania, the issue has taken on added urgency. “NATO deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is part of collective defence,” Motuzas said, adding that Russia has rapidly modernised its nuclear arsenal in recent years and deployed nuclear weapons close to Lithuania — in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions, Reuters reported.
The warnings come as Russia has stepped up its nuclear rhetoric towards NATO. Moscow recently threatened nuclear retaliation in the event of what it described as attempts to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Lithuania and Poland.
Finland has already made the move
Lithuania is not acting in isolation.
Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 after decades of military non-alignment, removed its own statutory prohibition on nuclear weapons earlier this year, citing the need to ensure that Finnish law did not restrict the country’s ability to fulfil its obligations as a NATO ally.
In June, the Finnish parliament approved amendments to the Nuclear Energy Act repealing the country’s ban on nuclear explosives. The legislation entered into force on July 1.
“This historic reform strengthens the security of Finland and of NATO as a whole,” Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on X.
Helsinki has stressed, however, that the change does not mean Finland intends to acquire or host nuclear weapons, and that NATO has no plans to station them there.
Finland has since joined a French-led initiative aimed at strengthening European security through closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed what Paris calls “forward deterrence” — closer cooperation with European allies around France’s independent nuclear capabilities.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative.

Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says some suppliers cannot build weapons ordered, and drops contracts to free $346 million for front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:23:16 UTC
23:23:16 KST

Ukraine is canceling part of its planned military purchases and moving the money to other priorities. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has announced that it, together with the General Staff and the Logistics Forces Command, will free about $346 million by terminating some weapons contracts and dropping some planned purchases.
What the army planned to buy in 2024 and 2025 may no longer be suitable for the front, the ministry noted, because technology and tactics change quickly. The review comes four days after the Ukrainian government drew about $1.1 billion from the defense reserve to pay soldiers in October amid a looming economic crisis.
The ministry gives five reasons for the review: some weapons no longer match combat tasks, certain suppliers cannot build the planned volume, certain models have not been codified, partners already cover some needs, and cheaper means can perform specific jobs in larger numbers.
"For us, there is one criterion: does the item work for results in combat today. Every hryvnia released from irrelevant contracts must reach the troops as the weapons needed right now and in the right place," Col. Yurii Pohribnyi, commander of the Logistics Forces, says.
The procurement agency calls each producer
The General Staff set the final list of purchases for review, and the ministry forwarded the documents to the Defense Procurement Agency to implement the decision. For specific items, delivery volumes were adjusted rather than canceled, which the contracts allow when needs change.
Affected producers have been informed, and the agency is discussing each item with suppliers based on the status and payments of each contract. Artem Romaniuk, acting director of the agency, has explained that further steps on each contract will depend on the army's current needs and the contract terms. The list of weapons stays secret for security reasons.
Funds freed up by terminating contracts and canceling planned purchases will be redirected to the urgent needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.

France protests: What we know as schools brace for nationwide action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:22:36 UTC
23:22:36 KST

France protests: What we know as schools face nationwide action
Now in their third week, the protests have grown.
Protests have continued across France for a third week as tens of thousands of school pupils and trade unionists have taken to the streets across many cities.
Students initially began boycotting classes in deprived areas of Paris on September 21 over teacher shortages and poor conditions, but protests have quickly morphed into a nationwide movement, with some of the largest demonstrations taking place on Tuesday.
School blockades have turned violent, with protesters accused of hurling items at police and officers allegedly responding forcefully using batons, tear gas and rubber bullets. In one case, a teenager lost his hand in a grenade explosion.
The mass demonstrations, which also coincided with a public sector strike over government budget plans last week, have presented another challenge for President Emmanuel Macron’s cash-strapped government ahead of next year’s elections, amid an ongoing fiscal crisis as government debt has rocketed in recent years.
Here’s what we know:
What do protesters want?
Students have been protesting over what they say are poor conditions in France’s high schools – or lycees – especially in poorer areas. Protests have been held in Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Nantes, Marseille, Lyon and other towns and cities.
Students say absent teachers are not replaced, dilapidated school buildings are sometimes rodent-infested, there are inadequate tables and chairs, large class sizes and long classroom hours.
The intense heatwave which hit France in the summer exacerbated existing problems in neglected school buildings, which also suffer from a lack of air conditioning, school pupils say.
The protests have coincided with ongoing nationwide public sector strikes over a proposed 2027 cost-cutting budget that aims to achieve 54 billion euros ($61.3bn) in savings as Macron’s government races to bring a large public deficit under control.
Public sector staff and unions object in particular to a government plan to freeze salaries to save about two billion euros ($2.27bn).
Parents are also increasingly present at protests amid widespread anger about the police response to demonstrating minors.
But the protests are happening amid wider discontent over soaring fuel and commodity prices and reduced public spending under Macron.
Government officials have meanwhile accused political opposition groups and unionists of taking advantage of the student movement. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu accused political opponents last week of encouraging escalation.
What has happened so far?
At least 6,100 people had been arrested by early Tuesday, many of them under the age of 18, as police tactics come under intense scrutiny.
Serious injuries have also been reported.
A 15-year-old lost a hand in the northern city of Lens on Monday after he reportedly came into contact with a police stun grenade, which then exploded. Public prosecutors say investigations are ongoing into whether the youth actively picked up the grenade or if it landed on him.
Overall, at least 190 high school students have been injured, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Monday. On Sunday, he said 78 teaching staff had been injured, and 24 schools had been burned or ransacked.
Some 715 police officers have been injured, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Tuesday.
Officials said as many as 589 schools have been disrupted this week, down from 735 on Friday last week.
Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have criticised the use of force against minors amid media reports of students being hit with batons and rubber bullets, as well as sprayed with tear gas.
What happened on Tuesday?
Protesters again blockaded schools on Tuesday as thousands demonstrated over their demands.
Placard-waving crowds were reported in southern Marseille, eastern Strasbourg and other major cities.
In Paris’s 20th district, protesters outside the shut Helene Boucher lycee tipped over rubbish bins and bicycles and created a makeshift barricade, The Associated Press news agency reported. Parents, meanwhile, positioned themselves between the demonstrators and police to protect their children.
“They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children’s rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands,” said Emilia Sichili Suriam, one member of a parents’ association.
Interior Minister Nunez rejected criticism of the police on Tuesday, saying the response has been proportionate in “almost all cases”. He claimed that the protests were transforming into “riots”.
What does this mean for the French government?
These are only the latest in a series of high-profile protests that have marked Macron’s presidency and undermined his government’s reform efforts ahead of elections in April and May.
Macron will not run in next year’s elections, but his image and that of his government have no doubt been tainted by photos of police chasing students in the streets, France expert Jacob Ross, from the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), told Al Jazeera.
“He is not taken seriously any more because many think of him as already out of government,” Ross said of Macron. “But this is still very significant for his government because it has become clear that they don’t have the capacity to calm things down. There’s clearly little fiscal room to manoeuvre.”
Macron’s terms have long been beset by political and financial instability. Successive prime ministers have faced difficulties in pushing through policies in the highly polarised National Assembly where Macron’s centrist Renaissance party and allied blocs lack a majority.
Critics have taken aim at Macron’s deeply unpopular austerity measures, which have seen drastically reduced government spending taking a toll on pensions and healthcare. Officials, however, have defended these policies amid rising debt following COVID-19-era spending.
On Sunday, Lecornu said the government had kickstarted initiatives to address the protesters’ demands and that a report was expected by the end of the month. He, however, added that Paris would not “yield an inch” to violence.
Meanwhile, frontrunner and opposition leader Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally party submitted a shadow budget on Tuesday promising 140 billion euros ($157.6bn) in cost savings by 2032 if elected next year.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) now has a state parliament speaker, the first time a far-right party has captured such a position in the nation's post-World War II history, media reports said Tuesday.
The state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt elected 35-year-old Tobias Rausch to its highest office in the first round of voting. In the balloting in the eastern city of Magdeburg, he got 48 votes of state parliamentarians in favor, versus 29 against, and five abstentions.
The AfD won a plurality in the Sept. 6 state election with 43.8% of the vote, but fell short of an absolute majority. The left populist BSW, which is represented by five members in the state legislature, had agreed in advance to support Rausch’s election, citing the tradition that the party with the most seats should get the seat.
Together, the AfD and BSW caucuses have 44 members. However, the election was held by secret ballot.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, has classified the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as a confirmed far-right extremist group.
The election of an AfD state parliament speaker president drew criticism in advance, with the Social Democrats, the Greens, and The Left all announcing that they would vote against his taking the post.
The caucus leadership of Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) recommended that its members abstain from the vote. During the previous legislative term, various AfD candidates for the vice parliament speaker position repeatedly failed to win the vote, and the post stayed vacant.
 
Hundreds protest against AfD taking position
Even before the opening session of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt began, hundreds of people demonstrated in front of the parliament building in Magdeburg, chanting “Nazis out,” according to the German Press Agency (dpa).
Protesters held up banners saying "No cooperation with right-wing extremists” and “Never again fascism.”
The rally was primarily directed against the election of an AfD state parliament speaker.

Ukraine becomes one of world's main targets for cyberattacks – Microsoft report

Ukraine becomes one of world's main targets for cyberattacks – Microsoft report
Ukraine ranks first in Europe and third in the world in terms of the number of cyberattacks against countries, organisations and users – it accounts for 4.8% of all recorded attacks in the first half of 2026. Only the United States and Israel were attacked more often, according to the new Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Unsurprisingly, Ukraine remains one of the main targets of Russian state hackers, accounting for 14% of all recorded activity. They only carried out more attacks against the United States.
Looking at the overall situation, the public sector is most frequently targeted by cyberattacks – government institutions and services accounted for 27% of all activity, compared to 17% in 2025. The share of phishing attacks also increased significantly, from 7% in 2025 to 23% in the first half of 2026.
The report also noted the impact of artificial intelligence (AI), which significantly reduces response times. Thanks to AI, attackers can exploit an opportunity less than 24 hours after it is discovered. The number of publicly disclosed software vulnerabilities (CVEs) in 2026 is projected to reach a record 72,000.
In addition, attackers are staying undetected for longer. According to the report, the time between gaining access and detecting or stopping cybercriminals increased across several sectors in 2026. At the same time, once detected, organisations began to respond faster.

State of Corruption: Zelensky crosses tipping point in new poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

23:21:44 KST

State of Corruption: Zelensky crosses tipping point in new poll
Ukrainians are increasingly disappointed with serving officials and ashamed of their actions, a recent opinion poll indicates. A majority now insists that Vladimir Zelensky must not seek a second term as president, as he once pledged.
Mounting disillusionment with the government, which was highlighted on Monday by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology’s (KIIS) latest omnibus survey, comes on the back of multiple corruption scandals in Kiev involving people close to Zelensky.
Kiev relies heavily on Western financial and military support to pursue its conflict with Russia. Even its staunchest supporters acknowledge that the Zelensky government’s assurances that it is actively tackling corruption are not necessarily sincere.
No second term for Zelensky
The KIIS phone survey, conducted among over 1,000 adults in September, indicates a stark shortage of positive emotions among Ukrainians for public servants. The pollster offered respondents a list of 12 options to indicate their feelings, from which they could pick up to three. The most popular was “disappointment,” chosen by 44%, followed by “shame,” picked by 33%.
More respondents reported negative emotions towards the authorities compared to a similar poll conducted in December 2025, while the share of positive options remained stable. In both surveys, 23% said they were hopeful regarding the authorities and 16% said they sympathized with them.
Asked whether Zelensky should take part in the next presidential election, 53% told KIIS he should not, compared to 46% last year.
Zelensky pledged to be a single-term president during his election campaign in 2019, but has since suggested he may run again. His mandate expired in 2024, but he has retained power under martial law, which critics say violates the Ukrainian Constitution.
Other polls have consistently suggested that in a hypothetical presidential contest, Zelensky would lose in the second round to any of as many as three more popular possible candidates.
Zelensky sinking in graft bog
The Ukrainian leader’s domestic popularity has dropped amid a series of corruption scandals triggered by investigations conducted by Western-backed anti-graft agencies.
The latest major development came in September, when the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) exposed a suspected protection racket run by a senior officer in the Prosecutor General’s Office. The chief suspect was fired, while his boss, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, fled the country before being removed from his position by the Ukrainian parliament.
Previously, Zelensky fired a deputy head of his office after NABU accused her of laundering millions in cash to pay the bail for a former energy minister who is a suspect in a separate anti-graft investigation linked to the Ukrainian leader.
NABU’s reputation in Ukraine is so strong that some crooks are trying to profit off of it. This week, the agency reported helping the police arrest a swindler who had posed as one of its detectives to extort $280,000 from a local businessman, saying the money would allow him to sink a criminal case “commissioned” by competition.
KIIS previously reported that half of respondents in a survey named government corruption as their biggest concern – more than Russian long-range strikes – while 72% said Zelensky personally was responsible for the problem.
German minister admits Kiev has a graft problem
Political opponents of Zelensky, such as his former spokesperson turned vocal critic Yulia Mendel, claim he personally protects corruption networks entrenched in his government. NABU has stressed he is not a suspect in any of his cases, referring to immunity from prosecution that Zelensky retains as long as he claims presidential authority.
The Ukrainian government largely operates on donations and credit provided by foreign sponsors, primarily the European Union. Brussels recently reacted skeptically when asked by Kiev to cover a $27 billion hole in the Ukrainian military budget.
A joint statement by the European Commission and Ukraine last week said they had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026.” The vaguely worded press release was broadly interpreted as a refusal of Zelensky’s request to send “more money, much more.”
Corruption in Kiev is a major concern for foreign donors too, even if they rarely admitted this publicly.
“We want to be sure that this money is used precisely for that [weapons and infrastructure buildup] purpose,” German Economics Minister Katherina Reiche told Bild TV on Monday, when asked about aid sent by Berlin. She stressed that Kiev needs to prove it is actually tackling corruption.
There is an assurance that work will continue. However, we will also have to ensure that this does not remain just an assurance, but that we have measurable results.
EU officials who are not bound to demonstrate support for Kiev by their political allegiances have used more direct language.
“Ukraine is so corrupt. We have no idea how much money is really spent on the functioning of the state or on defense purposes. We don’t know how much is just disappearing,” MEP Fernand Kartheiser told RT’s Rick Sanchez in a recent interview.
Kartheiser, a conservative lawmaker from Luxembourg, said the leaked photo of a golden toilet allegedly owned by Zelensky’s long-time associate Timur Mindich was the turning point for many Europeans who no longer accept the pro-Kiev narrative pushed by their governments. NABU last year accused Mindich of running a $100 million extortion scheme at a state-owned energy company, just after he narrowly escaped pending arrest.

Japanese PM condemns alleged killing of woman by US Marine
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the alleged killing of a woman in Okinawa by a US Marine, calling it a “heinous crime” and demanding tougher discipline and measures to prevent a recurrence. The incident has also reignited public anger and protests over long-time American military presence.
The controversy erupted on Sunday after Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha and stealing her wallet and backpack. Security footage showed the man entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone with what appeared to be her belongings. Ballard has denied the accusations.
Addressing parliament on Monday, Takaichi called the case “extremely regrettable” and a “heinous crime,” urging Washington to fully cooperate with the investigation and prevent similar incidents in the future. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned US Ambassador George Glass, while Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi separately summoned US Forces Japan commander Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost to lodge protests.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja also called the case “absolutely unacceptable,” adding that “efforts to enforce discipline among US military personnel and provide human rights education are not working.”
The US embassy in Japan extended its “sincere condolences to the victim’s family,” adding that US officials are cooperating with Japanese authorities. The Third Marine Expeditionary Force stated that the “Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior.”
Neither President Donald Trump nor senior cabinet officials, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have publicly commented on the case.
The case also sparked backlash from Okinawa residents, with about 160 people rallying in Naha, the capital city of the prefecture, condemning the killing and renewing calls for US bases to be removed from the island.
The anger over US military presence on Okinawa – which has been there since 1945 – has been simmering for several decades. Despite accounting for only about 0.6% of Japan’s territory, Okinawa hosts roughly 70% of the country’s US-exclusive military facility area.
Crimes involving US personnel have repeatedly triggered major protests. In 1995, three US servicemen abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan girl, fueling mass demonstrations. In 2016, former Marine and US base worker Kenneth Franklin Gadson raped and murdered 20-year-old Rina Shimabukuro and was later sentenced to life imprisonment.

Historic drought in France has left tens of thousands of people without access to drinking water
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:20:31 EEST
23:20:31 KST

Historic drought in France has left tens of thousands of people without access to drinking water
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the drought, more than 83,000 people in France are receiving water by tanker truck or in bottles. Restrictions are in place in almost all departments.
Due to a prolonged lack of rainfall, restrictions on water use have been introduced in almost all departments across the country. In the worst-affected areas, more than 80,000 people have been forced to receive drinking water by tanker trucks or in bottles. Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to France’s Ministry of Ecology, as of September 23, drinking water supplies were considered insufficient for approximately 1 million people. According to a ministry representative, more than 83,000 people were affected by emergency measures, including around 47,000 who receive water by tanker truck and approximately 33,000 who receive bottled water.
The water shortage has affected communities across France, with the Alps and the southeast of the country, as well as the southern regions, among the hardest hit. Restrictions on water use are in effect in almost all of the country’s departments. According to the Ministry for Ecological Transition, no cases of adverse health effects have been recorded, and the authorities are prioritizing the prevention of disruptions to the operations of hospitals, medical clinics, and care homes.
The lack of rainfall began in March and intensified after a record-hot summer, the state meteorological service Météo-France reports. In September, rainfall was 70% below normal, while across almost the entire country, soil dryness reached levels observed once a decade, French meteorologists said.
The drought in France has already affected the country’s energy system, causing a record decline in nuclear power generation due to low river levels, which limited the ability to cool reactors, according to a BNEF analysis. The depletion of reservoirs and drying soil have reduced crop yields and threaten to extend the water shortage through 2027, analysts added.
The drought has spread across Western Europe. A prolonged lack of rainfall in September caused record-low water levels in the Rhine, leaving vessels stranded and driving up transport costs along this important waterway.

Freeze or Liberation? How Ukrainians Expect the War to End
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Four in 10 Ukrainians now consider a de facto freeze of the war with some territory remaining under Russian occupation the most realistic outcome, although a majority still envisage the liberation of at least part of the occupied land.
The findings were published by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on Tuesday, Oct. 6, following a nationwide survey conducted from Sept. 12-21.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
KIIS asked respondents to choose the scenario they considered most realistic – “not what you want, but what is possible in the current situation.”
Some 41% selected a scenario in which Ukraine preserves its statehood and independence but accepts forced territorial losses, compared with 33% surveyed in February 2025.
The institute stressed that the answer did not imply formal recognition of the occupied territories as Russian. Based on its previous surveys, KIIS said most respondents likely understood the option as freezing the conflict approximately along the current front line.
Majority still foresee some deoccupation
A combined 53% of respondents chose scenarios involving the liberation of at least some Ukrainian territory, down from 60% in February 2025.
The answers were divided as follows:
- 14% considered a return to the de facto borders before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 the most realistic scenario, compared with 16% previously.
- 4% expected Ukraine to liberate the entirety of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, down from 5%.
- 23% selected the restoration of Ukraine’s internationally recognized 1991 borders, including Crimea, compared with 25%.
- 12% envisaged Ukraine fully restoring its territorial integrity and transferring hostilities onto Russian territory, down from 14%.
Another 6% were unable to select a scenario.
The results point to a gradual shift toward more cautious expectations rather than showing what settlement Ukrainians would personally prefer or accept.
Earlier polling found that most Ukrainians placed sovereignty and territorial integrity above economic prosperity. Different poll results can vary significantly depending on whether respondents are asked about their desired outcome, the most realistic outcome, or a detailed ceasefire proposal containing security guarantees.
Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
Ceasefire support depends on conditions
The same survey found that 75% of Ukrainians would allow negotiations with Russia to take place to end the war, while 21% opposed holding talks, and 4% were undecided.
KIIS explicitly warned that willingness to conduct negotiations should not be interpreted as support for concessions to Moscow.
Some 69% said they would support an immediate and complete ceasefire along the current line of contact if Ukraine did not legally recognize the occupied territories as Russian, continued strengthening its military, and maintained its course toward NATO and EU membership.
Another 22% rejected that proposal, while 9% were undecided.
KIIS noted that support drops when a ceasefire proposal lacks specific security guarantees. In a previous survey, only 32% accepted withdrawing Ukrainian forces from Donbas in exchange for what the institute described as abstract US and European guarantees.
Most Ukrainians still believe in victory
Despite increasingly cautious expectations about territorial liberation, 79% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would ultimately win the war.
Of those, 47% were certain of victory and another 32% said Ukraine would probably win. Some 7% expected Russia to win, while 14% could not answer.
Overall belief in Ukraine’s victory fell from 85% in late July and early August. The share expressing complete confidence declined more sharply, from 60% to 47%.
A majority of respondents (62%) also said they were prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary.
Another 4% were prepared to endure it for about one year, while 23% selected a shorter period ranging from several months to six months.
How the poll was conducted
KIIS interviewed 1,002 Ukrainian adults by telephone from Sept. 12-21 using randomly generated mobile numbers and statistical weighting.
The poll covered residents of Ukrainian government-controlled territory, including internally displaced people from occupied regions.
It did not include residents currently living under Russian occupation or Ukrainians who left the country after Feb. 24, 2022.
Under normal conditions, the maximum statistical margin of error would be approximately 4.1 percentage points for results near 50%. KIIS cautioned that wartime conditions could create additional systematic distortions.

'Busification': Inside Ukraine’s controversial recruitment practices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:19:58 UTC
23:19:58 KST

'Busification': Inside Ukraine’s controversial recruitment practices
Recent reports and videos of alleged recruitment irregularities are fuelling tensions between mobilisation authorities and Ukrainian society, while raising questions about the oversight and implementation of military recruitment.
In a video posted on September 4, a man was forcibly taken into a police vehicle on Mykhaila Boichuka Street, in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district. His clothes were torn as he struggled to resist being put into the car. Several people filmed the incident. Police officers in black uniforms were present, alongside unidentified individuals who appeared to use physical force against the man.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"They tackled him like a dog"
We contacted several witnesses present at the scene. An employee of a pharmacy located at the nearby intersection told us:
 “They blocked the street with their cars here. They tackled him like a dog. They tore his clothes.”
A woman living in a building on Mykhaila Boichuka Street said :
 “My neighbours told me that they beat him up and took him away. He lived right here, near me.”
According to a lawyer specialising in military law that we consulted, the way in which the detention was carried out may have exceeded the police’s legal authority. He noted that the presence of unidentified individuals using force alongside police officers is particularly worrying; and that the grey civilian vehicle against which the man was pressed appears to be a type commonly used by recruitment personnel during mobilisation activities.
We also contacted the Pecherskyi District Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centre (TCK) in Kyiv to ask for information about the reasons for the intervention and what happened to the man afterwards. TCKs are government institutions responsible for military registration and conscription. They did not respond to our requests for comment.
The footage of this incident has circulated widely on Ukrainian social media and Telegram channels, alongside many other videos depicting alleged “busification” – a neologism that emerged during the war to describe the alleged practice of forcibly taking men into minibuses or vans for mobilisation.
While some footage has been identified as AI-generated or manipulated – including by Russian-linked accounts – lawyers and witnesses told us they had encountered numerous cases involving what they described as irregular or coercive mobilisation practices.
After more than four years of war with Russia, the Ukrainian armed forces face significant manpower shortages. In the first months following Russia’s full-scale invasion, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians volunteered to serve. As the war continued however, recruiting sufficient personnel became increasingly difficult. In April 2024, Ukraine lowered the minimum age for mobilisation from 27 to 25 and increased administrative penalties for violations of military-registration and mobilisation rules.
Mobilisation is regulated primarily by the Law of Ukraine No. 3543-XII – adopted in 1993 and subsequently amended, most recently on 31 July 2026 – as well as by Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine Resolution No. 560, of 16 May 2024.
Ukrainian law provides exemptions and deferrals from mobilisation for several categories of people, including persons with disabilities, certain parents, caregivers, students, educators and workers, subject to specific statutory eligibility requirements.
TCK officers are authorised to verify military-registration documents and issue summonses. They are not authorised to carry out administrative detention; this power lies with the National Police. During document checks, officers must identify themselves.
“By the end of 2025, we had received 6 127 complaints”
The Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights (ombudsman) Dmytro Lubinets, had warned several times about the increasing number of complaints addressed to his office concerning the conduct of certain representatives of TCK.
He stated in February 2026 :
 “While we received just 18 complaints at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, by the end of 2025 the figure had risen to 6,127.”
His office informed us that the ombudsman processed 5024 requests between 1 January 2026 and 3 September 2026.
 “Monitoring visits by employees of the ombudsman's office to the TCKs in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Bila Tserkva and other cities recorded critical violations: illegal restrictions of freedom [Editor’s note: detention of individuals who had valid deferments or in circumstances where the legally prescribed procedure had not been followed], physical beatings and other forms of coercion.”
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
“I could accept forced mobilisation if it were carried out properly”
Andrii Dombrovskyi, a 26-year-old young man, says he had been injured during his forced mobilisation, on July 26, 2026. Although he was in the age of mobilisation, he was not subject to an arrest warrant or otherwise sought by the authorities. According to his lawyer, the recruitment officers could only have issued him with a summons and had no legal grounds to take him away from the street.
 “I was riding my bike in one of the alleys in Zhytomyr. From the corner came the car. It seemed like a regular civil car. It was a Renault Duster, but I knew from some Telegram chats that they are often used by the workers of mobilisation units. They stopped right near me. Some men came out, started saying something to me. I kept riding past them but they hit my bike and I dropped to the ground. My leg started hurting. No one introduced themselves or said anything. They just took me and put me in the car.”
After being taken for a mobilisation-related medical examination and then to a military unit, he was hospitalised with a broken leg. He is currently on medical leave at home and has initiated legal proceedings challenging the lawfulness of his mobilisation.
He explains why he does not want to serve:
 “I don't really want to kill people or die. I can understand that we are at war, we need people. I could accept forced mobilisation if it were carried out properly and in accordance with the law. But what is happening now is something I cannot tolerate in any way.”
Before being detained, he was avoiding the TCK officers with the help of local Telegram channels, in which users share the position of recruitment officers. Administrators of such channels take serious risks. In April 2023, in Lutsk, in the Volyn region, one of them was sentenced to five years in prison for obstructing the lawful activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
“We have cases of men being forcibly mobilised, despite a formal deferral”
Serhiy Kosiichuk is Andrii’s lawyer. He is a managing partner of the Ukrainian law firm Primus Partners, which specialises in military mobilisation and military law. At the moment, his team has approximately 30 active court proceedings across Ukraine concerning challenges to mobilisation carried out in violation of the law. He also regularly posts content about mobilisation on his social media accounts, including his TikTok page.
 “We have cases of men being forcibly mobilised, despite a formal deferral. While travelling in Ukraine, they are stopped at a checkpoint for a document check and told that their records need to be clarified. On this pretext, they are taken to the local TCK. Their information in the electronic military registration system is altered: their deferral disappears from the system and they are registered for military service in the district where they were stopped, despite not residing there, which is unlawful.”
Applications for the granting or renewal of a mobilisation deferral are reviewed by commissions established at TCKs and the existing deferral generally remains valid while the application is being considered.
To display this content from TikTok, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
“Even during wartime, mobilisation must take place within a clear legal framework”
For his work, Serhiy Kosiichuk received threats and was also detained:
 “Two years ago, because of my active public position on these issues, and after receiving anonymous threats allegedly linked to law enforcement officials, there was an attempt to mobilise me. I was detained without proper grounds.”
Criminal investigations were opened in connection with the incident, but at the moment they are effectively stalled.
 “I fully understand that Ukraine is fighting a war and that mobilisation is necessary for the survival of the country. My position has never been against mobilisation itself. My position is that even during wartime, mobilisation must take place within a clear legal framework and with respect for fundamental rights. That is why I try not only to speak publicly about these problems, but also to participate in creating legislative solutions.”
Serhiy Kosiichuk participated in the elaboration of Draft Law No. 15076-1, submitted to the Ukrainian Parliament on March 30, 2026. The bill seeks to clarify the respective powers of TCKs and the police during mobilisation, with the aim to prevent arbitrary detention.
“He was not allowed to see either a lawyer or anyone else”
Polina Marchenko, managing partner of the Polina Marchenko Law Office, also deals with the protection of the rights of military-liable citizens of Ukraine.
She mentions the case of one of his clients :
 “He was not considered liable for military service because of his health. He had all the relevant documents with him. Nonetheless, last February he was stopped in Bila Tserkvahim and taken to a TCK. They kept him there for seven days and he was not allowed to see either a lawyer or anyone else.
He has been mobilised and is serving in one of the military units right now. We are legally challenging the mobilisation decision.”
During his time in the TCK, her client was able to record a video on his phone. In the video, which was later published on social media, he claimed that many other people in detention were ill and were not medically fit to serve in the military.
As Serhiy Kosiichuk, Polina Marchenko, runs a legal blog where she talks about what people should do in case of unlawful mobilisations. She says that she has received intimidations from a state agency that she does not want to mention.
In a written response, Ukraine’s Ground Forces Command said it could neither confirm nor deny an increase in complaints against TCKs. It said allegations of misconduct by TCK personnel are investigated and may lead to disciplinary action, but that it has no consolidated data on the number of sanctions imposed. Regarding the cases cited in this article, the Command said that reports of possible violations of the law, abuse of official powers or improper actions by TCK military personnel – once officially received, are subject to verification in accordance with the established procedure.
Mobilisation irregularities, amplified through social media, are deepening tensions around Ukraine’s mobilisation system and contributing to growing hostility towards TCKs, including confrontations and reported attacks on recruitment personnel.

Russia is fuelling resentment against mobilisation personnel by disseminating contents about forced mobilisations involving TCK agents.
Moreover, Russian accounts disseminate contents created by AI about Ukrainian soldiers being handcuffed to go to the frontline or crying after their mobilisation.

At the same time, Russia faces its own manpower shortages and is also implementing forced mobilisation against its own population, while using coercive and exploitative practices to recruit foreign nationals into its military forces.
After more than four years of full-scale war, both countries are struggling to meet their manpower needs, making mobilisation an increasingly prominent issue in the information war.

New EU members face 15-year probation period after joining the bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:18:28 UTC
23:18:28 KST

The European Commission is proposing a new procedure to cut funding and voting rights of EU newcomers that breach the rule of law, available for 15 years after accession. The proposal also includes new procedures for the gradual integration of candidate countries and governance measures.
The Commission put forth on Tuesday a comprehensive proposal that includes institutional "safeguards" that could strip new member states of voting rights up to 15 years after they joined the EU.
The proposed measure is meant to avoid that regime change in a new EU country disrupts the EU decision-making process, and is accompanied by new suggestions on how to bring candidate countries closer to the Union.
“I was criticised heavily when I first mentioned that I don’t want to see new Trojan horses in the European Union. This was still before the elections in Hungary. Today I can say no more Viktor Orbán,” said Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos.
Safeguards
In June, five EU founding members pushed for enhancing safeguards in EU accession treaties to more swiftly address cases of democratic backsliding and breaches, as part of the lessons learned from Viktor Orbán's Hungary.
The Commission is now formally following up on this suggestion, considering that Hungary’s recent experience shows that Article 7 — the treaty provision that allows the EU to strip a member state of certain rights for violating EU values — takes too long and does not always work.
The proposal therefore adds a new procedure to complement Article 7. It would cut EU funding and even voting rights for newcomers that start acting against the rule of law, the bloc’s values and the principle of sincere cooperation.
The Commission sees Hungary’s handling of Ukraine as the clearest example: Budapest agreed to give Ukraine candidate status, then blocked the process. “Once we agree on one goal, we all have to work for this goal,” Kos continued.
The procedure would be available for 15 years after accession and triggered by serious breaches that affect the EU’s functioning. Consequences would be proportionate, with suspension of voting rights reserved for the most serious offences.
The Commission or several member states could start the procedure for a Council decision. The proposal does not indicate which decision-making process should be used, leaving it up to the member states to decide.
Safeguards are not new. Past accession treaties included them, notably for serious shortcomings in implementing the EU’s internal market, justice and economic rules.
The Commission wants these traditional safeguards to last longer than the previous three years, but does not say how much longer.
Drawing again on Orbán’s record, the EU executive also wants future accession treaties to include a statement that the new member will refrain from using unanimity in the enlargement process over bilateral issues.
The most recent example is Bulgaria, which keeps blocking North Macedonia’s accession bid over unresolved bilateral issues, notably Sofia’s demand for constitutional amendments.
Several proposals in this package, particularly internal reforms, will need member states’ approval. But the Commission intends to build the safeguards into the EU’s draft position on Montenegro’s last negotiating chapter in early November.
Gradual integration
The Commission has also picked up the idea of gradual integration put forward by France and Germany, to show candidate countries the early benefits of full membership.
“It is not a substitute for the full membership. It is only enabling those countries who are delivering well that, in the areas where they are delivering, they could integrate earlier in the subsystems or policies of the European Union,” Kos said.
She said gradual integration would apply where member states and candidates both stand to gain, citing supply chain and energy security as examples.
Other examples include participation in EU programmes such as Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe, support from agencies such as Frontex, single market integration, connectivity projects and observer status in expert groups and bodies.
The plan also envisages an “enhanced” form for candidates that align with Brussels on strategic areas and meet the rule of law criteria. How that strategic alignment will be assessed remains to be defined.
Some forms of early integration already exist. The Commission says this approach is far more systematic and would allow tailor-made benefits to be developed in a structured dialogue with each candidate, backed by dedicated financing.
Governance
On governance, the Commission wants to extend its annual rule of law reports to more candidate countries and sharpen its recommendations on aligning with the EU’s democratic standards.
The aim is to strengthen independent rights-enforcement bodies and prepare candidates to take part in the European Public Prosecutor’s Office from the moment they join.
Appropriate measures could be taken in case of arising issues, including postponing the accession of the candidate countries to a later date in the most serious cases.
Brussels would also work with candidates to test their enforcement capacity before accession in priority areas such as border management, single market supervision, food safety standards, transport networks and cohesion funding.
Tailor-made transitional arrangements would be negotiated, particularly in areas such as agriculture and labour mobility.
Public procurement procedures, independent audits and anti-fraud capacity would also be tested before accession.

Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant
October 6, 2026
Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.
The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.
The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.
Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?
The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.
The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.
Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.
As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.
Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.
Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

EU countries to discuss suspected plague outbreak in Russia

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:17:49 UTC
23:17:49 KST

European health authorities are closely following the suspected plague outbreak in Siberia, Russia. The European Commission and member states are set to discuss the matter on Wednesday morning.
Representatives from the European Commission and member states plan to discuss the suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia, Russia, as national authorities scramble to get a clear picture of the situation.
A meeting of the Health Security Committee, which evaluates serious cross-border health threats, will take place on Wednesday morning in Brussels. The meeting was already scheduled, but the item has been added to the running order.
"I can confirm the incident in Russia will be on the agenda of the Health Security Committee," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
The case revolves around a female lab worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, in south-eastern Siberia, who died on 2 October in uncertain circumstances. Her death was attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology".
Russian authorities say they have found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and insist the situation is under control.
The hospital where the lab worker was treated was placed under quarantine. About 200 people who had been in touch with her went into strict medical observation.
Separately, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan introduced precautionary measures at their borders to prevent the possible spread of infectious diseases.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday that none of those people has shown symptoms so far and early testing has been negative, although it noted it was "unclear" which pathogens were tested.
The WHO noted the risk for the European region was "very low".
In a statement, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the suspicion of a plague outbreak was "not yet confirmed".
"There is little travel between Irkutsk and the EU, particularly at present due to Russia's war against Ukraine," the agency said.
"Based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases or sustained human-to-human transmission."
Brussels and Washington are closely monitoring the evolving situation and have urged Russia to provide accurate and transparent information.
Pneumonic plague occurs when plague, an infectious disease caused by bacteria, infects the lungs. It is the most serious form of the disease and can be spread from person to person. If left untreated, it has a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 100%.
