====================================================================================================

Don't Cancel Your Plans. Shrink Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:15:30 UTC
23:15:30 KST

When you said yes to dinner at that new sushi place last week, it sounded like a great idea. Now that the agreed-upon day has arrived, you’re exhausted, and the prospect of putting on real pants and traveling across town feels like the least appealing way to spend your evening. You want to see your friend, but you’d rather lounge on the couch.
Yet before you send a cancellation text, consider a smaller proposition: Could dinner become a 20-minute walk? Could your friend come over for takeout? Could you catch up in the clothes you’re already wearing, without making “getting ready” a production?
Jana Rundle, a clinical psychologist in Austin, regularly helps her clients make these adjustments. When people are overwhelmed, she says, they tend to think they either have to follow through on a planned elaborate outing or skip it altogether. Shrinking the plan gives them another option.
“Let’s identify what’s hard about this and solve that problem so we can still get the connection we need,” she says. “The goal is just to get together.”
Here’s how scaling back can help you reap the benefits of socialization—and how to make sure you have ample energy for your next plan.
Why shrinking your plans can help your friendships
Having time to see someone isn’t the same as having the energy. That distinction is central to a model of social relationships co-developed by Katherine Fiori, a professor and associate dean for foundational psychology and faculty involvement at Adelphi University in Garden City, N.Y. The model considers time and energy separate resources people invest in their connections.
You might have two free hours, for example, but feel depleted by everything involved in using them: getting ready, traveling, making conversation with people you barely know. Spending time with a close friend can require less effort, Fiori says, because there’s less pressure to present a polished version of yourself. The person who’s known you for years probably doesn’t need you to be dazzling over appetizers.
Making a plan less demanding can help you follow through on a night when you’d otherwise cancel. When you bail on something that feels overwhelming, the immediate relief can reinforce the habit, says Shannon Sauer-Zavala, a professor of psychology at the University of Kentucky. The next time you feel stretched thin, you’ll be more inclined to do it again.
Over time, you can start to believe you’re only capable of socializing when you feel your best. You’ll also miss opportunities to discover that seeing someone was more enjoyable—and probably less taxing—than you anticipated.
A manageable get-together gives you a chance to find out you’re up for more than you thought. And sometimes, Fiori says, the connection supplies some of the energy you thought you were missing: “You can actually get some of that energy back, in a way.”
Figure out what makes social plans feel overwhelming
Rundle suggests a quick thought experiment: Imagine the outing lasted 20 minutes, was easy to get to, and went smoothly. Would you want to go?
If that sounds lovely, the problem may be the logistics surrounding the visit. “Is it the commute to get there? Is it the cost? Is it the cleaning and cooking you would have to do if you were hosting?” she says. “Is it how long the event is?”
Once you know what’s making a plan feel overwhelming, you can suggest a change that takes some of the pressure off, like meeting halfway to cut down on the drive or ordering pizza so you don’t have to cook. If you’re dreading getting dressed up, propose something you can do in sweatpants. For Rundle’s clients, who are often dealing with new motherhood, a stroller walk can feel much more feasible than a fancy dinner.
There are also ways to fit time with friends into things you already need to do. Fiori likes the idea of “admin nights,” when people gather with their laptops to tackle the tasks they’ve been putting off. Normally, those chores eat into the time and energy available for socializing. “To be able to combine those is kind of brilliant,” she says. You can pay bills or unsubscribe from emails with someone beside you to talk and joke with, making an otherwise tedious evening more pleasant.
These smaller get-togethers can be especially useful for keeping up with friends you already know well, Rundle says. A quick coffee or a walk lets you stay in each other’s lives during weeks when a whole evening out feels impossible.
How to change plans without making friends feel rejected
Asking to change plans can feel awkward, especially if you’re worried your friend will interpret it as rejection. Rundle recommends starting by saying how much you want to spend time together, then explaining what would make that possible.
For example: “I really want to see you, but I’m running on fumes. Would you be up for takeout at my place instead?”
Or: “I’m excited to catch up. Could we make it a quick walk? I need an early night.”
Your friend might even be relieved, Rundle says: They may be struggling to muster the energy for the original plan, too. “These are your friends and they love you,” she says. “So they’ll meet you where you are, typically.”
Make getting together easier from the start
If everyone were to wait for a clean house and the energy to make a cheese board, they might never host again. Rundle suggests being the friend who makes it clear that neither is required. “Come as you are, come in sweatpants,” she says. You can order pizza and leave the mess where it is.
“Somebody’s gotta send out the text,” she says. Otherwise, everyone can end up staying home because hosting sounds like too much work.
Of course, sometimes canceling is the right call. If you’re sick or genuinely need rest, give yourself that time, Rundle says—and take the initiative to reconnect when you’re able. If even the easiest version of a visit fills you with dread, consider how you tend to feel around that person. Consistently leaving feeling judged or depleted warrants a closer look at the relationship.
But when you want the company and can’t face the production, try making the plan smaller. “It doesn’t have to be some version of perfect,” Rundle says. “It should just be staying in each other’s lives and connecting in those moments.”

Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:15:09 UTC
23:15:09 KST

Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable?
Gulf oil flows surge despite escalating ship attacks in the critical Strait of Hormuz energy corridor.
Oil exports from the Gulf have resumed significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say.
Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported.
However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs.
On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
So, how are ships getting through the strait, and how long can producers maintain the increased flow through one of the world’s most important energy corridors while attacks and harassment of ships continue?
What do we know about the recent attacks on ships?
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz has continued to deteriorate even as more oil moves out of the region.
At least seven incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to shipping intelligence service Marisks.
The Kuwaiti-flagged Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) MT Kazimah III caught fire after being struck on October 1 while travelling through the strait, causing a fire on board. Five staff were safely rescued following the incident.
On October 4, the Liberian-flagged Aframax tanker Lipsi was struck northeast of Oman’s Jazirat Umm al-Fayarin, damaging its engine room, with no casualties reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or the Gulf of Aden, where Iran-backed Houthis are targeting Saudi-linked shipping, since October 2.
Threats continued on Monday, when a tanker entering the Hormuz strait near Oman was hailed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and ordered to turn around or risk attack, according to UKMTO.
How much oil is getting through the Hormuz Strait?
Despite those attacks, oil exports from the region have risen dramatically.
According to provisional data from Kpler, the seven-day moving average for Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with an average of about 18 million bpd during the 12 months before the war.
Vortexa separately estimated that the 14-day moving average for Middle East crude and condensate exports had reached 18.6 million bpd.
However, not all of that oil is actually being shipped through Hormuz.
Kpler estimates that about 40 percent of oil exports now bypass the strait, while much of the crude that does cross is transferred between tankers offshore.
Partly as a result of the increased oil exports, oil prices continue to fall, with Brent crude – the global benchmark – dropping 0.75 percent to $99.57 a barrel on Tuesday. US West Texas Intermediate crude also fell 1.2 percent to $88.37 a barrel, according to data from Oilprice.com.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly taken credit for the apparent increase in oil flows, boasting that Washington controls the strait and that US forces were succeeding in protecting vessels passing through Hormuz.
Iran has disputed claims that oil flow through the key waterway has increased, saying the amount passing was “negligible” and that it still has effective control of the strait.
How are oil exports bypassing Hormuz?
The recovery of oil exports has been made possible largely by Saudi Arabia’s use of alternative export infrastructure and an increasingly complex system for moving crude around Hormuz.
“The increasing availability of crude oil from the Middle East is due to two factors: the effective use of the East-West pipeline by Saudi Arabia and ship-to-ship transfer around the Strait of Hormuz,” Tamas Varga, an analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told Al Jazeera.
Saudi’s East-West pipeline carries oil from fields in the east of the country to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the West.
Ship-to-ship transfers happen when smaller shuttle boats, which often turn off their transponders to make them hard to detect, physically transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz, before offloading their cargoes onto larger tankers waiting just beyond it.
Is this sustainable?
Varga said current flows could be maintained as long as those methods and routes remain secure.
Saudi’s East-West pipeline has already suffered temporary closures as a result of drone strikes, such as those launched by Iran-backed groups in Iraq in September.
“The flow will be sustainable unless attacks on ships and shipping lanes or on the pipeline resume, something that does not seem imminent at the moment but could happen at any time if geopolitical tensions flare up,” he said.
But maintaining those flows is also putting pressure on the shipping system.
“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
That demand has pushed freight costs higher and reduced tanker availability elsewhere, while Asian buyers are increasingly having to source crude from further afield, he added.
“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping,” Beauchamp said. “Ships don’t get built overnight.”
Varga said oil prices also remain comparatively high – currently hovering just less than $100 a barrel compared with around $72 before the war broke out – because of increased shipping and insurance costs.
Last week, members of the Group of Seven (G7) announced they would release up to 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves, including diesel, in a bid to control prices. Further releases of crude and diesel from strategic reserves could also ease prices, but with global inventories already thin, another deterioration in Middle East security could quickly push them higher again.
“Only a sustainable and credible peace deal between the US and Iran and the subsequent permanent and unconditional reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would re-establish the pre-conflict status quo,” Varga said.
On Monday, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser warned that the effects of the disruption could last well beyond the reopening of Hormuz, even if it does happen.
Speaking at the Energy Intelligence conference in London, Nasser said nearly three billion barrels of oil supply had been lost since the conflict began at the end of February and that rebuilding depleted inventories while meeting demand could take as long as two years.
“The system is already straining,” he added.

European Commission adopts documents on EU preparation for future enlargement
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:14:41 EEST
23:14:41 KST

The European Commission announced on Tuesday that it had adopted a package of documents regarding policy reviews in the context of future enlargement, having defined strategic guidelines and measures necessary to prepare the Union for the admission of new members.
According to the statement, the proposed measures aimed to prepare the Union's governance system, policies, and budget for enlargement while simultaneously strengthening the protection of the Union's values and the rule of law.
Commenting on the measures, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Europe's future depended on choices made that day, calling enlargement a geopolitical imperative. She noted that foundations were being laid to ensure a larger Union would also be stronger, more resilient, and effective, remaining firmly based on shared values and rules. She added that as aspiring countries advanced in their reforms, the Union had to be ready to welcome them by preparing institutions, adapting policies to new realities, and ensuring that the budget reflected shared ambitions.
The explanatory notes accompanying the package noted that it presented an in-depth analysis of EU policy in light of future enlargement, outlining how current legal frameworks and future accession treaties could be utilized to prepare the Union for an increased number of member states. The package also proposed safeguards for future accession treaties, including enhanced sectoral safeguards and a new institutional protection clause, to guarantee the stable implementation of commitments undertaken during and after accession negotiations.
Additionally, the package strengthened the gradual integration process by making it more coherent, structured, and predictable. The report detailed that such an improved process would help prepare candidate countries for membership through their participation in individual EU policy areas prior to accession, subject to fulfilling relevant requirements. This would build administrative capacity, increase readiness, and provide tangible benefits for citizens and businesses in both the EU and candidate countries before formal membership.
At the same time, the Commission emphasized that participation in the process would continue to be based on achievements, remain conditional and revocable, and depend on policy readiness and strategic coherence. The Commission noted that the document package would serve as the basis for strategic discussions among member states regarding enlargement and reforms at the October European Council meeting, as well as a guide for cooperation with the European Parliament and the Council concerning necessary institutional and operational changes.
Regarding policy adaptation for an enlarged Union, the press release stated that the reviews indicated the Union could admit new members within the framework of current Treaty provisions and accession treaties. The Commission explained that regardless of the policy area, the most critical requirements for both the EU and candidate countries were administrative capacity and the ability to ensure practical implementation. Until accession, professional skills, regulatory and supervisory capacities had to be strengthened, system compatibility ensured, and inter-agency cooperation established.
Regarding budgetary aspects, the policy reviews confirmed that the Union's budget was capable of financing new member states while continuing to support existing priorities. The press release detailed that under the proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034, candidate financing prior to accession would occur through Global Europe instrument, transforming after accession into funding within national and regional partnership plans, supplemented by resources for cohesion policy, agriculture, internal affairs, and the Interreg program.

At the time, many experts and the then-opposition – which won that election and is now in power – accused Orlen of cutting prices to help the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party’s re-election campaign.
Prosecutors say that the decisions made by the executives constituted “a gross violation of procedures” and caused “over 4.1 billion zloty” (€938 million) of financial damage to the company. If found guilty, the accused could face up to 25 years in prison.
Prokurator przedstawił pięciu menadżerom Orlen S.A. zarzuty wyrządzenia spółce szkody w wysokości ponad 4,1 mld zł w związku z nierynkowym kształtowaniem cen paliw w 2023 r. ⬇️https://t.co/yjiaX0ehHu
— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) October 6, 2026
At the end of August 2023, just over a month before the elections, Orlen, which controls around 60% of Poland’s fuel market, began sharply cutting its wholesale petrol prices as well as the prices at the large network of petrol stations it runs.
By early October, the wholesale price of unleaded petrol had fallen by nearly 12.7%, while average prices at petrol stations had dropped by about 10%.
The price cuts, however, puzzled experts because oil prices on international markets were rising and the zloty was weakening, both of which would normally push fuel prices higher.
The relatively low prices in Poland encouraged some motorists from neighbouring countries to travel to Poland to tank up, while some Polish drivers began stockpiling fuel. Just days after the election, held on 15 October, fuel prices began to rise.
State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections
Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 19, 2023
Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. Under the leadership of its then-CEO, Daniel Obajtek, the company had regularly carried out actions seen as beneficial for the ruling PiS party. Obajtek is now a PiS MEP.
In October 2023, Krzysztof Brejza, a lawmaker from the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then in opposition and is now Poland’s main ruling party – notified prosecutors of a potential crime. He claimed that strategic fuel reserves had been emptied as part of Orlen’s price-cutting move.
Now, after a lengthy investigation, prosecutors have announced that five current and former managers have been detained. One, named only as Michał R. under Polish privacy law, served as a member of Orlen’s board from 2018 to 2024.
The others are identified as an executive director, two office directors, and the head of a department responsible for pricing.
The National Prosecutor’s Office said that all five had been charged with causing large-scale economic damage, which carries a prison sentence of between five and 25 years.
“The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors.
They said that the main aim of that pricing policy was to keep the price of fuels below the psychological threshold of 6 zloty per litre, and that this was carried out “in a manner detached from market realities…in gross violation of numerous formal and informal procedures applicable to the managerial staff at Orlen”.
Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new @FT report on how state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million through a botched effort to buy Venezuelan oil under the former government https://t.co/LlGcgXOvGG
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026
Speaking anonymously to broadcaster TVN, one of the prosecutors involved in the case said that the executives’ actions had implications not only for Orlen’s finances, but also Poland’s national security, given that strategic reserves are meant to be saved for emergency situation.
“State security was jeopardised for the sake of politics,” they said. “These reserves are intended, at a time of war, to ensure there is fuel for tanks, to put it simply.”
Meanwhile, justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, wrote on social media that Orlen and Obajtek had, by “manually controlling prices”, “acted to the detriment of national assets in order to save the party’s [grip on] power”.
Na polecenie łódzkiego wydziału ds. Przestępczości Zorganizowanej Prokuratury Krajowej funkcjonariusze ABW zatrzymali wczoraj 5 byłych i obecnych menadżerów Orlen S.A., w tym byłego członka zarządu spółki z lat 2018-2024.

Obajtek today rejected the allegations and defended Orlen’s actions under his leadership. He accused the current government of acting to distract from its own failure to keep fuel prices under control.
“They couldn’t cope with rising fuel prices so – for show and without any substantive justification – they’re detaining experienced managers thanks to whom fuel cost less than 6 zloty [per litre] in the summer and autumn of 2023,” he wrote on social media.
“If I have to answer for the fact that Poles paid little for fuel, then I would be honoured,” he added.
However, speaking at a press conference, Żurek declared that, “in a state governed by law there are proper procedures for lowering prices”. Instead, under PiS, there was “a state of lawlessness, a state run like a private fiefdom”.

In a separate case, the European Parliament last year stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return.
Last month, the Financial Times reported on how, under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers.
Obajtek, however, argued that he managed to turn Orlen into one of Europe’s largest companies, including diversifying it away from its traditional focus on oil and towards other forms of energy, including gas, hydrogen and renewables.

Hungary government proposes wealth tax on ultra-rich

Hungary government proposes wealth tax on ultra-rich
BUDAPEST, Oct 6 - Hungary's government has proposed a wealth tax targeting individuals with assets exceeding 1 billion forints ($3.08 million), Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Tuesday, delivering on a campaign promise of his governing Tisza party.
The centre-right Tisza defeated veteran Prime Minister Viktor Orban's nationalist Fidesz party in an April election, ending his 16-year rule, and must now tackle a budget deficit projected at 7.5% of national output again this year.
• For those with wealth exceeding 1 billion forints, the government proposes an annual 1% wealth tax on the portion of their wealth above that threshold, starting in January 2027.
• Those with wealth above 100 billion forints ($308 million) would face a higher rate of 1.5% on the excess, Magyar said in a video posted on his Facebook page.
• The tax would include all forms of wealth, including real estate, investments, company holdings, and assets located outside Hungary, with loans deductible from the tax base.
• It remains unclear what impact the new tax will have on next year's budget. The government is set later this month to announce its 2027 budget and a roadmap towards adopting the euro.
• Hungary's wealthiest man in 2025 was Lorinc Meszaros, a childhood friend of Orban, who — along with his family — was worth 1.786 trillion forints ($5.50 billion) according to the 2026 list published by Forbes.
• Hungary's second richest man was Sandor Csanyi, chairman of OTP Bank, with wealth of 649.7 billion forints ($2 billion).
• Magyar said the tax proposals would shortly be published on the government website for public consultation. It is then expected to be approved by parliament, where Tisza has a large majority. REUTERS

Clashes erupt on ‘Day of Rage’ in France as tensions rise and arrests reach 6,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:14:01 UTC
23:14:01 KST

Protests continue to take place across France as students and unions demand that the cash-strapped government fix understaffed and dilapidated schools. Nationwide protests come after days of demonstrations which began in the deprived suburbs of Paris before spreading across the country, sometimes turning violent.
Clashes in the “student revolt” sweeping the country in recent days resumed Tuesday afternoon. Tens of thousands marched in several cities throughout the morning, in demonstrations that were largely peaceful, but by midday clashes were reported between protesters and police in Strasbourg, where demonstrators were filmed using trash cans to confront officers, as well as in Lyon and Caen. Police used tear gas in all three cities.
The scale of the clashes was not immediately clear, but tensions remained high across France throughout the day, which protest groups had declared a nationwide day of demonstrations.
The student protests in France erupted last week, when students at hundreds of schools, especially in poorer working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, began blocking entrances to their schools, obstructing roads, setting trash cans on fire and attacking police officers and passersby, ostensibly in protest over neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.
The demonstrations broke out as the French government is trying to pass the 2027 state budget, which is aimed at reducing the deficit.
Since the protests began last Monday, at least 24 schools have been set on fire or looted and 78 education staff members have been injured. At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers also have been wounded in clashes.
According to the latest official figures, 6,000 people have been arrested across France since the protests began, most of them teenagers. The Justice Ministry said Tuesday that 1,800 of them will be prosecuted, including 1,483 minors. Property damage caused by the violent unrest is estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Opponents of the protests have accused the France Unbowed party of radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel politician, of inciting violence and inflaming the unrest, while highlighting the role of immigrants and children of immigrants in the street violence.
Mélenchon, for his part, denied any active involvement in the protests. He and labor organizations supporting the students have instead accused police of using excessive force against them.
Police have defended their conduct, stressing that officers responded in a “proportionate” manner, against the backdrop of footage showing rioters attacking police officers, with at least one officer subjected to an attempted mob lynching.
“Be careful,” Mélenchon told young protesters at a large march in Paris on Tuesday afternoon. “What you are doing is extraordinary. This is the most powerful youth movement we have seen in 50 years, and no one can say that you are wrong, because you are right.”
Parents who support their children also joined Tuesday’s marches in cities across France, amid fears that they too could fall victim to violent police officers.
“Don’t touch my child!” read one sign held by a woman at a demonstration in Rennes.
At Hélène Boucher High School in Paris’ 20th arrondissement, which remained closed Tuesday and where protesters set fire to trash cans and bicycles to create a makeshift barricade at the entrance, parents also stood between demonstrators and police, acting as a kind of monitoring and buffer force.
According to student unions, 1,800 high schools across the country were closed Tuesday because of the protests, out of 3,700 in total. The Interior Ministry later said, however, that only 900 schools had been fully or partially disrupted.
In response to the widespread protests, President Emmanuel Macron’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed his ministers to find solutions to the students’ main demands.
Among other things, the students are demanding action to address the teacher shortage, a reassessment of the length of the school day, which in France is among the longest in Europe and runs from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., and consideration of longer lunch breaks.
The government also will examine renovation work needed at aging schools, and Lecornu said he had instructed ministers to submit their proposals by the end of October.
Finding funding for such measures, however, is expected to be difficult as the government is also trying to reduce the swelling deficit.
Concerns over the scale of French debt, weak economic growth and a lack of willingness to curb government spending have driven up yields on French government bonds in recent days. Last week, they briefly rose above 5%, their highest level in 24 years.
The current wave of unrest comes seven months before the presidential election, against an already tense social and political backdrop, with fuel prices rising and far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls.
For now, polls indicate that Le Pen would not win in the first round and would face radical-left leader Mélenchon in the decisive runoff, where she would defeat him.
Either way, such a showdown would mean France abandoning the political center and finding itself forced to choose between two parties regarded as extremist.
Against the backdrop of the protests, Le Pen on Tuesday presented her overall platform and promised even deeper cuts to public spending if elected, among other things in an effort to bolster her credibility with investors.

‘Cockroach stir stripped Modi’s carefully confected image’: Arundhati Roy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:13:55 UTC
23:13:55 KST

‘Cockroach stir stripped Modi’s carefully confected image’: Arundhati Roy
Acclaimed Indian author talks to Al Jazeera on a range of issues, including the Gen Z-led protests and allegations of vote theft by Modi’s government.
Award-winning Indian author Arundhati Roy says the ongoing protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government – mainly led by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – have stripped the right-wing Hindu nationalist leader of his “carefully confected image” propped up by India’s corporate-owned news channels and the governing Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) control over social media.
Speaking with Al Jazeera’s Imran Khan on a range of issues, including the Gen Z-led antigovernment protests and allegations of vote theft against Modi’s government, the 64-year-old Booker Prize-winning writer says she hopes the political climate in the world’s most populous democracy is about to change.
“I do feel that something is boiling just under the surface. Something is going to happen,” she said. “The emperor has been called out, and he has lost his power.”
Here’s the interview Roy gave to Al Jazeera TV, edited for brevity.
Arundhati Roy, thank you for talking to Al Jazeera. Your debut novel won the prestigious Booker Prize. Since then, you have written acclaimed novels, hard-hitting political pieces, and collections of essays. How would you describe yourself: novelist, writer or a political activist? Or you don’t really think about those boundaries?
Roy: Well, I actually refrain from describing myself. I will leave that to other people because, you know, why should we describe ourselves? And categorise ourselves? That’s for other people to do.
One of the things that links all of your different aspects is this idea of satire. You are not chiefly a satirist, but in The God of Small Things and in The Ministry of Utmost Happiness, you have used satire to devastating effects. But it always seems to be about politics. Is that a deliberate choice?
Roy: I don’t think so. I mean, in some ways it depends on how you define what politics is, right? To me, even a fairy tale is in some ways political, but not let-me-hit-you-on-the-head-with-a-hammer or let-me-display-my-manifesto type of politics. I am not. From my books and from the way I grew up, possibly the answer to your question is that there is no difference between the personal and the public space.
Let’s talk about India and its political climate. You wrote about the CJP movement. Now that’s a grassroots movement fuelled by young people who took an insult – of being called a cockroach – and owned it. And you started your essay with when hope seemed lost, in came these young roaches riding in the rain, “the progeny of the unholy union between a judge and a joke”, which is a brilliant line. What drew you to this particular movement?
Roy: Well, ironically, as we speak at this moment, there is a huge crisis brewing, and the cockroaches are back, saying they are going to be protesting all over the country in a few days because of the scandal exposed by a particular newspaper about the fact that India’s elections are completely compromised – which is something we have known and have written about for years. But now there is a sort of concrete proof. So what drew me to it was this young people’s movement, which was full of joy and unusual humour – this new way of messaging with their [Instagram] reels and so on. It stripped Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s very carefully confected image.
Is this a miscalculation on his part? Not understanding social media, not understanding young people’s use of technology? And is it going to have an effect on India?
Roy: No, I don’t think it’s a misunderstanding at all. He and the BJP were the first to wade into the field of social media, so they have been there before anybody else. But I just think there were too many things happening, one after another. And somehow this movement sort of broke. It was the straw that broke the camel’s back. It started out with the fact that in 2024 [election], Modi did not win a full majority… There’s scandals around elections. There’s scandals around the paper leak in exams. There’s massive unemployment. So it all sort of came together to create this sort of irreverent but serious explosion.
India publicly says we are an economic success story, a climate leader. But what is modern India to you?
Roy: Well, modern India is a very rich country full of very, very, very poor people. I mean, I don’t think there are many countries in the world where people live in such deep poverty, in such conditions of humiliation. And it’s a shame for people to boast about this being a super economic power, because, as I keep saying, it’s super poor. Surely, there are extremely rich people, extremely rich industrialists who control everything, but very little of that seeps down to the poor… So it’s a scandal to call India a superpower or an economic force, when the people are so disempowered.
But a lot of these problems are often blamed on British colonialism. Do you have any sympathy with that argument?
Roy: Not any more. There was a point at which it was true. But now we are watching a government just making everything much worse, including the idea of freedom. I was talking to some young people yesterday, and I said that what [Mahatma] Gandhi and [Bhimrao] Ambedkar and Maulana [Abul Kalam] Azad and [Jawaharlal] Nehru and all these people said and wrote during the British times, today, nobody can say those things because they would be put into prison. There are a lot of people, a lot of students, a lot of activists, lawyers in and out of prison constantly. We are threatened with the antiterrorism law. This Independence Day, from the ramparts of the Red Fort, Modi said the most dangerous people are “dimaghi Naxal”, which means intellectual Maoists, which includes all of us, of course. And that we must be isolated and so on. So I think that’s a tired horse to whip now.
I am glad you mentioned the Maoists. Earlier this year, India declared the six-decade-long Maoist insurgency effectively over. But all the problems that the Naxalites were fighting for still remain, don’t they?
Roy: Well, yes. I mean, who are the Naxalites? What were they fighting? And the fact is that they keep declaring the end of it, but then it resurfaces somewhere, somehow, because you can’t just hold so many people down and devastate their lives. Some people are going to take things into their own hands. So we are used to these declarations, you know.
During the Congress rule, I think it was around 2012 or 2013, the prime minister [Manmohan Singh] had signed over the homelands of indigenous people to big infrastructure companies. There were many MoUs signed. And then they declared something called Operation Green Hunt. They flooded the forest with security forces. Village after village was being burned down; women were being raped, villagers could not live in their houses for fear that they would be surrounded and burned down. And the media was calling all these poor people “terrorists”… What do you do when a thousand security personnel come and surround your house in the middle of the jungle? And they were brutally put down.
People who sort of crumbled and quivered under the Modi regime are suddenly finding a couple of vertebra, if not a spine, and it's creating little spaces.
You have always rejected the idea that writers should remain apolitical. Your stance on Kashmir, calling it not an integral part of India, comes to mind. I want to talk to you about the personal cost of being so forthright. How do you deal with that?
Roy: Well, after 2019, one cannot say that because it has been made an integral part of India. And that section of the Indian Constitution has been read down. But honestly, I am not a person who makes rules for writers and says they should be political or shouldn’t be or how they should be. I don’t have a prescription for that. I just know that if I didn’t write what I am really moved to write, then it would be like putting myself into prison before they put me into prison.
As I said in my memoir, it’s like a dance on a mined dance floor. One doesn’t know when the bombs will go off. But I do what I have to do, and I’m not the only person. There are so many people who stand up so bravely and who have paid huge prices. For what? For doing or saying what they believe in. So I don’t want to make a martyr of myself here.
But is there an intellectual movement in India that has a strong voice that is being listened to, or is it being drowned out by the shoutings of the politics?
Roy: Actually, that movement has always existed. It has been extremely strong, even though since 2014, it has been hammered down by these 24-hour television news channels owned by various corporations who try and shout everyone down. So, every time Modi wins an election, he comes out and tries to demonise us.
Is India still the world’s largest democracy – something to be celebrated? Or do you think it’s a democracy in sham?
Roy: This is exactly where the axe has fallen. The Modi government reconstituted the way in which the election commission is chosen. He appointed a chief election commissioner. The opposition [parties] and the chief justice normally had a voice in selecting the chief election commissioner, but they don’t any more. Now, there has been an absolute scandal about how the elections have been conducted. From the 2024 elections to the [regional] elections in Maharashtra, Haryana, West Bengal, Bihar, and Goa. You are finding a situation where thousands of electoral officers who are supposed to have the voter data with them have been locked out, and it’s all been controlled from New Delhi. And voters, especially minority voters or supposedly BJP-unfriendly voters, have been simply not allowed to vote. And I am talking about the numbers in the millions… We always say that elections are not proof of democracy. You need a constitution, you need other institutions, you need checks and balances. All of those were hollowed out. Now the election itself is impugned. And you will watch and see in the next few months, there is going to be big trouble in this country as we inch closer to the 2029 election.
So where are you landing right now? Is there hope for democracy, true democracy in the way that you see it in India?
Roy: Well, one of my collections of essays was dedicated to those who have learned to divorce hope from reason. I will always be hopeful that something will change here. And I do feel that something is boiling just under the surface. Something is going to happen. How that plays out, I can’t say because we are up against a pretty ruthless set of people.
What you’re seeing in India, after this “cockroach” uprising, is that everybody has been put on notice. So all the people who sort of crumbled and quivered under the Modi regime are suddenly finding a couple of vertebrae, if not a spine, and it’s creating little spaces. There’s a lot of protests in all kinds of places. As I said, one of the biggest things that’s happened is that the emperor has been called out, and he has lost his power. He is not even showing up publicly. His home minister is ducking and diving. Neither of them showed up even once for the entire [monsoon] session of Parliament last time when the cockroach movement was on. So there’s something changing. And I think they are running scared. Let’s see what happens. Certainly, I am more optimistic now than I was three months ago.
Before this interview, I was speaking to another writer friend of mine who is based in Israel. He said one of the questions you must ask Miss Roy is the fact that artificial intelligence (AI) and the weaponisation of social media is fuelling anti-democratic movements and government authoritarianism. Where do you land on that?
Roy: I think it’s the end. And I think it’s privatisation of human endeavour and civilisation. How it works in defence and in politics and in personal life, and the shiny gifts it offers with the darkness behind them, is something we need to think about. It’s something I am writing about.
Is there anything about modern India, about the world, that gives you hope?
Roy: Well, absolutely. As I have said, India is a country with such a deep culture of resistance, of intellectual thinking, of unusual thinking, of unusual kinds of dissent. So how can you not have hope? It’s a wonderful thing to see.

Escalation in Tigray raises risk of Ethopia-Eritrea war — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:13:27 UTC
23:13:27 KST

NAIROBI, October 6. /TASS/. The escalation of hostilities in Ethiopia’s Tigray region raises the risk of a direct armed conflict between Ethopia and Eritrea, Magnus Taylor, the Deputy Director of the Horn of Africa project at the International Crisis Group, was quoted as saying by the Africanews portal.
"The fact that Ethiopia and Eritrea are coming up against each other now suggests the regional picture is looking worse and you could see a kind of more broader escalation that goes beyond Tigray," Taylor said.
In his view, the escalation of the current standoff into a broader regional conflict would be "a worst-case scenario."
Taylor added that the retreat of the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) as a result of an offensive by Ethiopian federal forces may mean plans to shift from attempts to hold territory to insurgent warfare. In early October, Ethiopian troops established control over Tigray’s capital Mekelle.
Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea deteriorated in recent months as Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting TPLF jointly with Sudan and Egypt - a claim that the three countries strongly rejected. In early October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara, with Eritrea subsequently announcing that diplomatic ties with its neighbor have been severed.
The Ethiopian government’s remarks about the need to secure reliable access to the Red Sea coast remain an additional source of tension. Earlier, Eritrea’s authorities accused Ethiopia of plotting to put these plans into practice by seizing the port of Assab. Addis Ababa maintains that it plans to resolve the issue peacefully.
Ethiopia lost access to the sea in 1993 after Eritrea declared independence following a referendum. Eritrea was formerly an Italian colony and later a British protectorate. In 1952, it was incorporated into Ethiopia as an autonomous region, but in 1962 Emperor Haile Selassie dissolved the federation and annexed the territory.

Ukraine Will Receive Belgian F-16s Once the Transfer of French Onboard Electronic Warfare Systems Is Approved

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:12:44 UTC
23:12:44 KST

Belgium’s transfer of three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine will take place immediately after it signs an agreement with France to transfer the technology to a third party.
Belgian Defense Minister Theo Franken announced this in an interview with Ukrinform.
The need for additional approval arose because Belgium upgraded its F-16s with French radar warning systems. According to the defense minister, the approval process should not take long.
“We can do this fairly quickly. Our F-16s were modernized using French electronic warfare technology, so when we send them to Ukraine, we must have an agreement signed by France regarding transfer to a third party,” Theo Franken noted.
Immediately after receiving official permission from France, the Belgians will begin organizing logistics to ship the aircraft.
Belgian F-16 fighter jets are equipped with the French Carapace radar warning and threat detection system, developed by Dassault Electronique (now part of the Thales Group). The system is integrated into the aircraft’s fuselage and detects radiation from enemy radars, warns of missile launches, and automatically controls countermeasures, including the deployment of chaff and flares.
Belgium plans to transfer the first three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year.
On September 29, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the delivery timeline.
In June, Theo Franken said the country expects to deliver seven aircraft by the end of the year: four as a source of spare parts and three for combat missions.
The overall plan calls for transferring 53 Belgian F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
According to the schedule, five aircraft are planned for delivery in 2027, 14 in 2028, and another 27 are expected to arrive in 2029.

Lithuania’s decision on nuke weapons poses threat to all of Europe — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:10:37 UTC
23:10:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. Lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory could lead to anarchy and poses a threat to all of Europe, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
Earlier, the Seimas (parliament) of Lithuania voted to lift the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory. For the decision to take effect, a second vote is required in three months. During the plenary session, 106 deputies voted in favor of repealing the constitutional article prohibiting the deployment of nuclear weapons in the country, six abstained, and 18 voted against it.
"This leads to nuclear anarchy and opens the door to military nuclear technologies for countries that have no experience operating such complex systems, thereby creating additional threats for Europe as a whole. And if such decisions are adopted, as well as if plans to deploy nuclear weapons are implemented in practice, I believe that the Russian Federation will take all necessary steps to preemptively target such infrastructure facilities," Stepanov said.
The Seimas resolution provides for the removal of Article 137 from the constitution, which prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, on Lithuanian territory. The same article prohibits the presence of foreign military bases. Vilnius is currently seeking to have the United States establish such a base in the country. As Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas noted, the ban on the deployment of such weapons distinguished Lithuania from other EU and NATO countries.

Exhibition honours five Bulgarians who helped change America and the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:07:54 UTC
23:07:54 KST

News
Exhibition honours five Bulgarians who helped change America and the world
Tuesday 6 October 2026 15:33
Tuesday, 6 October 2026, 15:33
Petya Ilieva
PHOTO Desislava Shapkarova
Font size
The portraits of five people with Bulgarian roots who made their mark in the United States and achieved worldwide recognition can now be seen at bus stops in Sofia, Plovdiv, Veliko Tarnovo and Burgas. Alongside their faces are short accounts of their lives and achievements.
The exhibition is the latest project by Bulgarian painter Petya Ilieva, whose Art for Diplomacy initiative brings art and culture out of galleries and museums and onto the streets, where everyone can enjoy them. Bus stops were chosen deliberately: the idea is to give people walking through the city or waiting for public transport a chance to discover something new and perhaps take an interest in history, culture or science.
“All five have inspiring stories. As children, they had particular interests, and through hard work they managed to make their dreams come true,” Petya Ilieva told Radio Bulgaria in an interview.
“What they have in common is that they knew from an early age what they wanted to do. They received an excellent education in their chosen fields and pursued their work with great passion. For most of them, their parents played an important role, encouraging their curiosity with books and taking them to exhibitions across Europe.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
“We called the exhibition Bulgarian-American Angels. It was organised with financial support from the US Embassy in Bulgaria as part of the celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of American independence. We chose the name because these were Bulgarians who realised their full potential in America. They helped lay the foundations of engineering and space science, without which America would not be what it is today. None of the five ever lost touch with their homeland. Throughout their lives, whenever they had the chance, they made a point of mentioning their Bulgarian origins.”
Ilieva believes that the names of Assen Jordanoff, Peter Petroff, Viden Tabakoff, John Atanasoff and Viola Essen are probably unfamiliar to most Americans and many young Bulgarians. Yet in their respective fields, they remain pioneers whose work continues to inspire others.
Who are the five figures featured in the exhibition?
Assen “Jerry” Jordanoff (2 September 1896, Sofia – 19 October 1967, White Plains, USA)
From the skies over Sofia to the cockpits of American aircraft, Jordanoff was a Bulgarian aviation pioneer who helped shape modern flight.
An inventor, engineer and test pilot, he laid the foundations of aeronautical engineering in Bulgaria and wrote operating manuals for early American passenger aircraft. He is also credited with inventing the automotive airbag.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Viola Essen (stage name of Violeta Kolchagova)
A Bulgarian-American dancer who won over American audiences with her grace and freedom of movement, capturing the spirit of a new era in dance.
The daughter of Bulgarian immigrants, she became a dancer and choreographer with the renowned American Ballet Theatre and was among the pioneers of modern American ballet. She also had a romantic relationship with Marlon Brando.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Peter Petroff (21 October 1919, Brestovitsa – 27 February 2003, Huntsville, Alabama, USA)
Born in the Bulgarian village of Brestovitsa, Petroff went on to become an engineer whose ideas contributed to the early years of America's space programme.
He worked as an engineer at NASA and is credited with developing early satellite telemetry systems, the digital watch and wireless heart-monitoring technology.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Viden Tabakoff (14 December 1919, Stakevtsi – 6 June 2015, Cincinnati, USA)
From the small Bulgarian village of Stakevtsi to NASA's Apollo programme, Tabakoff devoted his career to engineering and scientific research.
An engineer, scientist, inventor and university lecturer, he helped advance jet propulsion technology, contributing to the developments that made space exploration possible.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
John Vincent Atanasoff (4 October 1903, Hamilton – 15 June 1995, Frederick, USA)
An American physicist and mathematician of Bulgarian descent, John Atanasoff is widely regarded as the “father of the computer”.
Between 1939 and 1942, he and his student Clifford Berry developed the world's first electronic digital computer at Iowa State University, laying important groundwork for modern computing.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Five different lives, five different stories, all connected by their Bulgarian heritage. Through Bulgarian-American Angels, Petya Ilieva hopes to encourage more people to discover who these figures were and how their work contributed to progress around the world.
The printed panels will also travel to other locations, giving more people a chance to learn about their achievements.
“I hope that one day we can take the exhibition to the United States as well, so that the wider public there can get to know these people too,” Ilieva said.
Author: Desislava Semkovska
Supervising editor: E. Karkalanova
This publication was created by: Elizabeth Radkova

Metsola to take action after MEP Rima Hassan removes Israeli flag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:07:15 UTC
23:07:15 KST

French pro-Palestinian MEP Rima Hassan removed Israeli and EU flags from an exhibition commemorating the victims of Hamas’s 7 October terrorist attack, sparking outrage among fellow lawmakers. She could face a suspension of her daily allowance.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she would take “all appropriate steps” against an MEP who sparked protests and criticism from fellow lawmakers in Strasbourg on Monday after throwing an Israeli flag to the floor.
Although Metsola did not name the MEP, the lawmaker was identified as Rima Hassan. Her office confirmed that she had removed an Israeli flag during an exhibition commemorating the victims of the 7 October 2023 terrorist attack in Israel.
According to parliamentary sources, she confronted Israeli artist Yaron Bob, who created the exhibition, accusing him of presenting a “one-sided account” of the attack.
"This house is a place where all of us must feel safe and secure and we reject in the strongest possible terms any action by any person that feels or makes anyone feel less protected," Metsola said in a statement in plenary session following the incident. "At a time of rising global antisemitism, we owe it to Europe's Jewish community to ensure that when they look at us, they see that this is their house too."
Metsola added that "all the appropriate steps" will be taken, "including the right of the person to be heard."
Born stateless in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, Hassan is one of France’s most prominent pro-Palestinian activists. She is currently on trial in France over alleged online remarks deemed to constitute an apology for terrorism, while Israeli authorities have accused her of being associated with Hamas.
Hassan could face a reprimand, a temporary suspension from Parliament’s activities, and/or a suspension of her daily allowance (€350 per day) for a period of up to sixty days.
An official in Metsola's office told Euronews that the Parliament’s presidency is now examining is now examining all available information to assess the incident and decide on the potential consequent penalty. The decision will not be taken during the current plenary session, the official added.
Hassan acknowledged in a statement from her office that she had removed the Israeli flag from its stand, but claimed the European Union flag, which was attached to the same base, fell as a result of the imbalance.
The statement said that “no flag was stepped on or damaged."
“Her gesture was directed exclusively at the holding, within the premises of the European Parliament, of an event organised in conjunction with the diplomatic representation of the State of Israel, during which objects presented as having been made from fragments of Israeli missiles were notably offered for sale,” the text said.
The gesture sparked reactions among MEPs and beyond the Parliament.
“Not even in the face of tragedy, her antisemitism can be put aside. Shame on her,” said Parliament’s vice-president Pina Picierno, from the Socialists and Democrats group.
Other lawmakers such as Renew Europe’s Nathalie Loiseau and European Conservatives and Reformists’ Nicola Procaccini also attacked her on social media and through statements in Parliament.
Israeli Foreign Affairs Minister Gideon Sa'ar described the incident as “shameful, outrageous, but sadly not surprising.”

EU Commission throws down the gauntlet to member states on reforming the bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:07:10 UTC
23:07:10 KST

The European Commission is proposing fewer commissioners and less unanimity to prepare the EU for 30 or more members. However, EU diplomats say capitals are unlikely to agree.
The European Commission has put forward far-reaching proposals, including cutting the number of commissioners and moving away from unanimity, testing member states' appetite for internal reforms that stop short of treaty change.
The proposals are part of a broader package to make the EU's structures and decision-making fit for a membership of 30 or more countries. They are bound to be controversial among European capitals.
"The main question has been: is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible. Our assessment shows that in most policy areas, the EU is already fit for enlargement," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters.
Unanimity
The Commission proposes identifying areas where so-called passerelle clauses could be activated, allowing the Council to move from unanimity to qualified majority. Activating those clauses, however, itself requires unanimity.
The idea of extending qualified majority voting is not new, particularly in foreign and security policy, where a veto can undermine the EU's ability to project geopolitical weight abroad.
Last month, 11 countries including France and Germany circulated a joint letter calling for the bloc to explore curbing obstructive foreign policy vetoes on the basis of sincere cooperation, notably through greater use of constructive abstention.
Asked whether member states back the move, Kos acknowledged that positions differ widely among EU countries. "It will not be easy, but it is worth trying," she said. A specific area she identified where less unanimity could be used is precisely during accession processes.
"Our proposal is to make our decision-making process more effective. We suggest using more QMV [qualified majority voting], which is nothing new. What is new is that we are suggesting that we will reduce the number of unanimity decisions in the accession process," Kos said.
Unanimity is required to grant a country candidate status and to close negotiations. In between, however, the current methodology gives any member state a veto over 150 steps.
The Commission also wants to make more use of enhanced cooperation, which lets at least nine member states pursue deeper integration on matters of crucial or strategic interest where blockages persist.
The most recent examples are the Ukraine Support Loan, from which Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out, and the European Public Prosecutor's Office.
Here too, Brussels may meet resistance from some capitals, notably the so-called "Friends of the Western Balkans", a group that includes Italy and Austria. They have pushed back against differentiated membership and regulatory asymmetry.
Institutional changes
The Commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which could prove problematic in a Union of 30 or more members.
Under the Lisbon Treaty, the Commission should have a number of members equal to two-thirds of the member states, chosen by "strictly equal rotation" that reflects the demographic and geographical range of all EU countries.
The system never took effect. In 2013, the European Council unanimously decided to keep one commissioner per member state, a concession to Ireland to secure a yes vote in its second referendum on the Lisbon Treaty.
Ireland was merely the most vocal opponent of losing a permanent presence in the Commission. Small member states widely fear their voice would be harder to hear in Brussels.
Rotation could also be hard to swallow for large countries such as France and Germany, which might find themselves left out of the College of Commissioners while the likes of Malta or Luxembourg are included.
"There are some candidates who say, no worries, this country can represent us. Other countries who say, yes, but not at the beginning. We would like to see how it [the Commission] works," Kos added.
The proposal for a leaner EU executive is well timed. The Commission is undergoing a so-called "large-scale review", and capitals are in intense talks on the bloc's next long-term budget, in which the EU administration is likely to face deep cuts.
Sceptical reception
Proposals that mainly affect candidate countries, such as safeguards against democratic backsliding and gradual integration, are likely to meet less resistance.
However, supporters of the reforms point out that, as candidates edge closer to joining the bloc, the question of how to keep an enlarged Union effective will be harder to dismiss.
Still, the suggestion is sure to raise eyebrows among European governments. Four EU diplomats who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity said these internal reforms are unlikely to fly.
The first test will come next week, when the enlargement reforms will land on the table of the EU leaders gathered for the European Council on 15-16 October.
"Some things are drafted to be killed," an EU diplomat said.

Everything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:06:40 UTC
23:06:40 KST

Everything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real
European Council President António Costa (L) speaks with journalists alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the EU summit, the meeting of the heads of state and government of the European Union, in Brussels on June 18, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Editor's note: this article was updated with comments made at a press conference given by the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission published a document on Oct. 6 about the future of EU enlargement, a first step toward making Ukraine's eventual accession feel real, but also laying bare some of the work the bloc needs to do to be ready.
"As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press release.
The Commission was also asked by EU countries to propose ideas on how enlargement should work in the future, primarily in order to prevent backsliding on the rule of law by future EU members.
The 25-page communication is a first attempt to address both of these questions and to make enlargement feel like a real prospect for which the current 27 EU member states need to prepare.
It will be accompanied in October by a set of progress reports on how Ukraine and other candidate countries are faring with the reforms required of them, as well as concrete roadmaps for the four most advanced countries.
Those roadmaps will lay out specific milestones, with dates, between today and the eventual completion of the work required for Albania, Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine to become EU members.
The Commission's decision to focus on four countries is also considered an important "political signal," four different EU officials have told the Kyiv Independent.
"These countries have shown significant progress in terms of readiness over the last years," said Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos at a press conference to launch the document.
For Ukraine, that message is especially important, as its pace of reform has slowed in recent months, and given that it is much larger than the other three, its entry into the EU raises more challenging questions.
That decision to include Ukraine has also been coupled with a forceful defense by Kos of the reform work done so far, on the one hand, and a similarly strong push for Kyiv to keep passing reforms on the other.
Ukraine could break the bank
Just the financial cost of the EU's relationship with Ukraine puts it in a different league than the other three countries being discussed.
"For Montenegro, the bill is one euro per person, per year, so it was extremely cheap," a senior EU official told journalists ahead of the document's publication.
"Most of the accession candidates are very small countries, so we expect this enlargement grant to be relatively affordable … Ukraine is a very different animal," they said.
In the next EU budget, which spans 2028-2034, funding for candidate countries is set to come from a pot of money called "Global Europe," which the original Commission proposal for the budget set at 200 billion euros ($225 billion).
That proposal mentioned 15 billion euros ($17 billion) to be available for all candidate countries — not just the four most advanced — and a 100 billion euro ($113 billion) reserve for Ukraine, intended to address reconstruction.
But the cost of Ukraine's reconstruction was already estimated at $588 billion by the World Bank in February 2026.
"If you look at what has happened with funding of Ukraine, it's been completely driven by the war," the senior EU official explained in answer to a question from the Kyiv Independent.
"There is a massive uncertainty, no one is pussyfooting about that," they said.
read also
And farms strike at the EU's foundations
The EU's farmers have jealously guarded their subsidy program, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since its introduction in 1962.
In exchange for complying with EU rules, EU funding enables the bloc's farmers to continue operating in a food landscape where they would otherwise be unable to compete on price.
But the sheer size of Ukraine's agricultural sector puts it in a different league, prompting the Commission document to argue that "targeted arrangements should significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products."
The farming sectors of Montenegro, Moldova, and Albania are "a small stone you put in a pond, it doesn't create a lot of shocks and waves," a second EU official explained.
They explained that forcing Ukraine to fully integrate with all EU rules in the sector would raise their costs to the point that it could price them out of world food markets.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a third EU official explained.
But equally, exempting Ukraine's agricultural sector from EU standards risks breaking the bloc's single market, which relies on all member countries' businesses operating on a level playing field.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," Kos said.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," she added.
The Commission's document does not lay out a specific plan for addressing this already, arguing that it needs to be properly negotiated between Ukraine and EU countries.
However, two senior EU officials told journalists that they could see the discussion becoming very detailed, distinguishing between agricultural products. One rule for chickens, another for sunflower seeds, another for plant proteins, another for wheat, and so on.
More clear for them is that the EU needs to open the fifth enlargement cluster with Ukraine, and soon, where these questions can be fully grappled with.
The document commits the Commission to helping prepare the draft agreement for cluster five, to "reflect the targeted arrangements for Ukraine in the area of agriculture … at an appropriate moment."
Ukraine already unlocked two of the EU's six enlargement clusters in June and July, to-do lists of reforms required by the bloc in order for Kyiv to become fully aligned.
Another two are set to open on Oct. 13, if Kyiv passes a law expanding protections for the country's Hungarian-speaking minority the day before.
But the remaining two clusters cover sectoral issues such as agriculture and the trucking industry, where Ukraine has a competitive advantage, which intimidates some EU countries.
For the Commission, opening those two remaining clusters is important to do soon.
With a sweep of elections due to take place in EU countries in 2027, "if we do not make a step now politically, the discussion is going to get pretty complex," one EU official warned.
read also
Two-tier EU membership ruled out
To help make the prospect of Ukraine joining the EU more palatable over time, the Commission also makes several proposals on "gradual integration" of candidate countries into the EU.
Essentially, the plan would be to reward alignment with the EU by already unlocking some of the benefits that come with membership.
The idea is not entirely new, with Ukraine already included in the bloc's mobile roaming area, and Ukrainians being able to participate in the Erasmus youth exchange program.
But now the Commission wants to map every EU policy area, institution, agency, and program, for what could be offered to candidate countries, and when.
What gradual integration is not, however, is an alternative to EU enlargement, the document notes.
Likewise, the Commission is not proposing that new EU countries have fewer veto rights than existing members, except for a small voluntary commitment for countries not to use bilateral issues to stop other countries from joining.
And the plan to introduce safeguards to curtail voting rights if a country backslides on rule of law "will only be in place if there are breaches," Kos said.
Some other ideas pitched to include candidate countries more in the EU, such as observer seats in the European Parliament and Commission, as proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, did not make it into the document.
"We don't want to open a new policy or political discussion," one senior EU official explained.
Instead, the plan is to show what is possible with the EU's existing framework, but if countries agree on other specific ideas, they can formally propose them.
One opportunity for EU countries to weigh such ideas will be when leaders are set to discuss the Commission's document as a whole on Oct. 15 in Brussels.
And it is expected that President Volodymyr Zelensky will be there with them.

Spain court lifts Puigdemont arrest warrant, clearing way for his return home ahead of November elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Catalan separatist Puigdemont cleared to return to Spain
October 6, 2026
Spain's Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted an arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, paving the way for him to return home ahead of a general election next month.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after leading a failed attempt for the wealthy northeastern Catalonia region to break away from Spain.
He had been wanted by authorities ever since, accused of embezzling public funds to hold an illegal independence referendum when he was head of Catalonia's regional government.
Judge Pablo Llarena lifted the arrest warrant shortly after Spain's Constitutional Court ruled that a 2024 amnesty for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement cases.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the decision, saying it would allow Catalonia to "look to the future."
"We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time," he told journalists in Madrid.
How did the amnesty come about?
While Puigdemont and other members of his government fled abroad after the 2017 independence bid, several Catalan ministers who remained in Spain were sentenced to lengthy prison terms.
In 2024, in the face of strong opposition from Spain's conservative and right-wing parties, the Sanchez government passed an amnesty law. It intended to cover all offenses related to the secession attempt and ease tensions in the Catalonia region.
It also allowed Sanchez to secure the backing of Catalan separatist parties and stay in power after a 2023 election produced no clear majority.
But Puigdemont's Junts party withdrew its support last year, accusing Sanchez of failing to fulfill promises such as providing amnesty for its leader.
Around 400 separatists have benefited from the amnesty, but Puigdemont had been excluded because Spain's Supreme Court initially ruled the law did not apply to those accused of embezzlement. That changed after the Constitutional Court on Tuesday sided with one of Puigdemont's allies who had appealed against the top court's ruling.
Last week, Junts voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez's government amid huge protests, prompting the prime minister on Monday to call a snap vote for November 29.

Two Spanish F-18s deployed in Romania under NATO command took off at dawn after two air targets were detected near the Ukrainian border. The objects did not ultimately enter Romanian airspace and were not intercepted.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed in Romania under NATO command took off in the early hours of Tuesday after radar detected two aerial objects near the border between Romania and Ukraine, Romania's Ministry of Defence reported.
The Spanish aircraft were scrambled from the Mihail Kogălniceanu air base, near the city of Constanta in the south-east of the country, after surveillance systems detected the two objects in Ukrainian airspace, close to the river border with Romania.
The objects did not enter Romanian airspace, so the Spanish jets did not have to intercept or shoot them down, according to the Romanian authorities.
Alert for residents near the border
The incident prompted the Romanian authorities to activate protection measures for people living in the northern and eastern areas of Tulcea county, a region on the border with Ukraine and very close to some of the areas repeatedly targeted since the start of the Russian invasion.
At 2:20 local time, the authorities sent a message to residents via the national RO-Alert system because of the risk of falling objects from the air. The alert ended at 3:14.
The two Spanish F-18s are part of the detachment deployed in Romania to take part in NATO's enhanced Air Policing mission, which is intended to step up surveillance and protection of the Alliance's eastern flank.
The incident comes against a backdrop of repeated drone-related episodes near the border between Ukraine and Romania since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022.

Russia on Tuesday proposed restoring cooperation with Afghanistan through the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) amid talks between the head of its Security Council and the Taliban administration's top diplomat
Russia’s Security Council head Sergey Shoygu told Afghan Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi during a meeting in Moscow that his country viewed Afghanistan’s integration into international relations, transport and energy projects, as a “key task in strengthening regional security and stability.”
“One step in this direction could be the resumption of engagement with Afghanistan within the framework of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, utilizing the previously established contact group,” Shoygu said at the meeting, according to Russian state news agency Tass.

Shoygu was further quoted as assessing Western statements about the possible return of US and NATO military infrastructure and facilities to Afghanistan as “absolutely unacceptable,” adding that Moscow hopes that other countries will follow Russia in recognizing Afghanistan’s Taliban-led government.
For his part, Muttaqi was quoted as thanking Russia's leadership for recognizing the current government in his country, stating that Kabul expects to strengthen cooperation with Moscow in areas such as the economy and security.
Muttaqi described the Moscow format of consultations on Afghanistan as an “important political initiative of the Russian Federation that has laid the groundwork for regular political consultations among the countries of the region.”
“We are convinced that this process must continue and be further developed,” he added.
Earlier Tuesday, Muttaqi held talks with Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk in Moscow, according to the Russian government's press service.
On Monday, Muttaqi took part in the eigth Moscow format consultations on Afghanistan held in Russia’s capital. That same day, he held bilateral talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in August 2021 after the withdrawal of US-led forces ended a two-decade war.
In July 2025, Russia recognized the Taliban administration as the official government of Afghanistan, making it the first country to do so.

Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
