MobilePay will change its name to Vipps in Denmark from January 12, 2027, the company behind the payment app announced Tuesday.
Some of the app’s nearly 4.7 million Danish users will begin seeing a redesigned logo during the transition.
The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.
MobilePay’s services in Denmark and Finland merged with Norwegian payment app Vipps in 2022, creating a shared Nordic platform.
Vipps MobilePay described the name change as one of the final steps toward operating under a common Nordic identity.
“We know that the new name will require a bit of getting used to,” said Jeanette Hertzum, the company’s Danish country manager.
The company wants users in Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Sweden and Finland to use the same name and logo.
The longer transition period is intended to give Danish users time to adjust before the new name takes effect.
The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.
Denmark’s parliament opens new year with royal visit and prime minister’s eighth address
The Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, opens its new parliamentary year Tuesday with a royal visit and a speech from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
The Constitution requires parliament to open on the first Tuesday of October.
The day begins with a 10 a.m. service at Christiansborg Palace Church for lawmakers, ministers and invited guests.
The parliamentary meeting starts at noon. Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates, the longest-serving lawmaker, will initially preside. He has served in parliament since 1994.
Lawmakers will elect a speaker and four deputy speakers before Frederiksen of the Social Democrats delivers her eighth opening address.
King Frederik, Queen Mary and Princess Benedikte will attend. Members of the Royal House have attended every opening since 1966.
The government will also publish its legislative program listing bills planned for the coming year.

Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.

Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

On Friday, at the Court in Svendborg, he was sentenced to three months of unconditional imprisonment for violence against another inmate in Nyborg State Prison in 2022.

In the case, two men of similar age have also been convicted. They have likewise received three months in prison, writes B.T.

The victim suffered a concussion and broke both his nose and a rib, according to the indictment.
The three men were charged under the severe violence section, but were only found guilty under the mild violence provision – section 244.
It is also under this section that the 31-year-old man is charged when he appears in court next week in the case from Islands Brygge.
In that case, he is charged with having struck a 32-year-old Swedish man with a powerful punch.
The Swede died three days later.
The violence took place at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June at around 20:45. A screening of the football World Cup was held here.
According to the case’s indictment, the 31-year-old man at one point stood up on a bench, from where he, with a powerful overhand throw, threw two beer cans in the direction of a group of people – including the 32-year-old Swede.

The blow hit the Swede on the left side of the head/neck, after which he fell to the ground.
Because of the blow, the Swede suffered, among other things, a rupture of the artery, which meant that the man later died.
In the case, charges have also been brought under section 247 of the penal code, which pertains to the 31-year-old man having previously been convicted of crimes against the person. Among other things, he has a conviction for attempted murder.

Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.
The German-owned supermarket chain said the redesign would improve the use of space, create a consistent appearance and make shopping easier.
Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.

The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.

Too Russian for the NHL? The tensions behind Ovechkin’s farewell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:37 UTC
23:00:37 KST

There will be no doubt as to where the tomb of Alexander the Great II will be, or where he will see out the twilight of his career. But has one of the greatest modern Russian hockey stars been forced from the heady heights of the National Hockey League too soon?
When Alexander Ovechkin appeared in an election promo video for the United Russia party, I questioned his reasoning. I wasn’t alone. An NHL beat reporter posted in a WhatsApp group chat “Ovi’s about to quit Caps.” Of the other 30+ North American sports reporters in there with me, all speculated as to his next move, while also worrying about the backlash. There wasn’t long to wait.
The Ukraine troll farms ignited the fire that burned all the way into US media and Russophobic elements, and reached Washington Capitals owner Ted Leonsis. Leonsis, who also owns the Washington Wizards NBA franchise, refused to buckle to pressure from the US sports press corps, backing his star man to the hilt.
The Greek-origin billionaire has always been protective of Ovechkin and his other Russian players. In 2018, he told a popular English-language sports radio show in Moscow, called Capital Sports, that “we need to judge athletes on their performance and behavior, not color, country and so on.” However, the same cannot be said of the Capitals’ head coach, Spencer Carbery, who appears to have used the furor for his own ends.
“Spence wants a rebuild and he can’t do it with [Ovechkin] on board. He can’t blow up the team while [Ovechkin] is still on the roster,” a Capitals’ source told me on Tuesday morning. In the pre-season, Carbery said that he would play Ovechkin less and was, privately, against extending his contract.
When I questioned whether the political party video played any role in his ‘retirement’, the source said “definitely, but not from the club’s side. But there was a fallout with the coach.”
Igor Nazarenko, of St. Petersburg-based sports outlet Sport Day by Day warned of Ovechkin’s displacement in June after Washington signed American Alex Tuch from the Buffalo Sabres on an eight-year, $86 million contract. The sharpshooting winger’s arrival heralded, Nazarenko predicted, the replacement of the Russian as the on-ice leader.
Additionally, Carbery has focused on youth development, and has spoken about giving talents like Russia’s Ivan Miroshnichenko (22), Belarus’ Ilya Protas (20), and the US’ Ryan Leonard (21) more game time.
Scott MacPherson, former General Manager of Kunlun (now Shanghai) Red Star of the Kontinental Hockey League (KHL) and personal friend of Alexander Ovechkin predicted this would happen last year.
In early-2025, he told Capital Sports that Ovechkin wouldn’t “linger” in the NHL and instead return to his roots in Russia. “Ovi’s got nothing to prove [in the NHL], but he wants to be back in the KHL.”
I asked why. He made his debut at the top of Russian hockey aged 16; now at 41, why bother?
“He’s Russian. He loves his country and he wants to give back to fans. One, two years more in the KHL and it will be memorable.”
Russian sports media is already speculating about who will land him. Dynamo Moscow, his original Russian club, are favorites, while the other two big Moscow clubs, Spartak and CSKA, are already ruled out. SKA St. Petersburg has been mooted as his retirement vehicle, though that has been ruled out by the local media.
A couple of years in the KHL, followed by a career in politics, or sports administration, or even coaching, lies ahead of Ovi. His exit from the NHL was not as simple as stepping aside to let youth have its fling. Neither was it only because he made a video that riled up the anti-Russian trolls, as hockey fans see past politics and want to watch the best perform for them.
Yet it cannot be ruled out that the offer made by his current NHL team, according to MacPherson, of $1.5 million for one-year extension until 2027-28, was beyond insulting. If Russian sports media is to be believed, for two last-hurrah seasons with Dynamo Moscow, he will earn ten times that per year, and put the KHL front and center on the global stage.
In any case, Alexander the Great II is coming home to where his heart is.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

The White House has sought to clarify US President Donald Trump's comments at a rally, explaining that he was not insinuating that he wanted Iran to attack American cities, but instead wanted to prevent Tehran from acquiring that capability.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said on social media on Tuesday that the president's comments at a Monday night rally have been misunderstood and misrepresented in a "media freakout" that is "not rooted in reality."
Trump was discussing the war on Iran and the resulting high gas prices during his remarks in Nebraska when he mentioned the possibility of an Iranian attack on US soil.
"It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said of the war and its economic fallout. "They can take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay."
The commentary, including Trump's casual mention of the two California cities, was delivered in the familiar meandering style that he uses at campaign rallies, when he speaks for extended periods — often an hour or more — and is only occasionally following prepared remarks on a teleprompter.
Critics, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, seized on his statements.
The governor, a Democrat who could run for president in 2028, called Trump "deranged and dangerous" for, in Newsom's framing, "saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego."
"The nuclear annihilation of an American city is no laughing matter," Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the US House of Representatives, said on X.
Cheung, in his response on Tuesday, said it was obvious that Trump was not calling for such an attack.
"The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality," he said. "He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President."
Cheung added that Iran "has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."
The White House's Rapid Response account on X took issue with a Los Angeles Times headline saying Trump had suggested "letting Iran 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego."
"No, he didn't, you buffoons. He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," it said.
Trump has often criticised US cities as he campaigns, especially the largest areas that lean heavily Democratic.
At a recent North Carolina rally, he described the state's cities as "blood-soaked killing fields." North Carolina's violent crime rate ranks in the middle third of states, according to FBI statistics.
Iran has said that it’s not pursuing nuclear weapons, but has enriched uranium to near-weapons-grade levels that have no civilian purpose.
US joined Israel in attacking Iran on February 28, with strikes quickly killing the longtime supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and much of the other top brass as well as hundreds of civilians.
But Iran quickly hit back by exerting control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passageway through which one-fifth of global oil once sailed, and it has rained missiles and drones on US-allied Gulf Arab monarchies, shattering the oil-rich countries' hard-earned reputation for stability.

People shift their political opinions to match the room in small group chats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:22 UTC
23:00:22 KST

When politics comes up in a small online group chat, people may adjust what they say to match the dominant viewpoint of the room, according to new research published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. In two experiments in which participants chatted with AI agents playing coworkers, people randomly placed in conservative-leaning chats expressed more conservative positions than those in liberal-leaning chats, even after accounting for their own politics. The findings suggest that what people say in everyday political conversations does not always mirror what they privately believe.
Much of what we know about online political expression comes from studies of large, public platforms like X or Facebook. In those open spaces, people often tailor what they post because they know a massive, invisible audience might see it. If a topic is too controversial, users can simply stay silent and keep scrolling without anyone noticing. But a lot of daily communication happens in smaller, socially bounded digital spaces, such as neighborhood forums, family group texts, and workplace messaging apps.
In these closed spaces, individuals talk with people they know and expect to interact with again in the future. Because of these ongoing relationships, staying completely silent during a heated discussion can draw unwanted attention. People frequently encounter differing viewpoints in these daily environments. For example, a 2006 study noted that conversations at work are one of the primary ways individuals are exposed to political perspectives that challenge their own.
To manage their relationships, people may feel a need to closely monitor what they say. A 2016 study demonstrated that individuals often act like “political chameleons” in conversations, adjusting the opinions they voice to match whoever they are talking to. A study of Reddit users covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that right-leaning users used more moralized partisan language among political allies than in mixed spaces, while left-leaning users’ language stayed consistently moralized regardless of audience.
The current research was driven by a desire to understand these less-examined digital spaces, building on prior work exploring how the internet warps our sense of consensus. “One starting point was work by Claire Robertson, Kareena Del Rosario, and Jay Van Bavel on how social media can distort perceptions of social norms, including by making more moderate voices less visible,” Cleone Mitsui, a doctoral candidate in the Graduate School of Sustainable System Sciences at Osaka Metropolitan University and the study’s lead author, told PsyPost.
“This made us wonder what happens in small group chats, where people may have ongoing relationships and staying silent can itself be noticeable,” Mitsui continued. “These settings have received less attention than large, publicly visible platforms.”
Studying how this social calibration happens in private group chats is difficult, as it is ethically and practically tricky for researchers to manipulate conversations between actual acquaintances. To get around this, Mitsui and co-author Yuta Kawamura, an associate professor at the university, turned to artificial intelligence. As noted in a 2023 paper, AI agents can be programmed to simulate believable human behaviors, including forming opinions and interacting with others.
In the first study, the researchers recruited 180 American participants and randomly assigned them to either a liberal-leaning or a conservative-leaning group chat. Participants were told to imagine they had just joined a new company and were invited into a casual messaging group with three coworkers. The coworkers were AI agents, which participants were told about in advance, programmed to consistently express either liberal or conservative views. Each chat focused on one topic drawn at random from five: gun ownership, immigration, abortion, vaccine mandates for children, and gender education in elementary schools.
The chat interface was designed to look like a familiar mobile messaging app, complete with typing indicators, delayed thinking pauses, and randomly assigned names and profile pictures. One of the virtual coworkers would share an opinion on a political topic and prompt the participant to weigh in. Participants then engaged in five rounds of open text messages.
Afterward, an AI language model (GPT-5.2) reviewed the entire conversation and rated each participant’s overall expressed political stance on a scale from -2 (very liberal) to +2 (very conservative). The researchers verified this automated scoring, finding that it closely matched human ratings by the first author and produced nearly identical scores when re-tested with a different model, Gemini.
The researchers found that participants shifted their expressed political stance toward the prevailing attitude of the group chat. Those in the conservative-leaning chats expressed positions that were more conservative on average (0.21) compared to those in the liberal-leaning chats (-0.56). Over the five rounds of conversation, neutral positions decreased, and the participants’ text replies became increasingly aligned with the political tone set by their simulated coworkers. Additionally, participants who expressed views against the chat’s political lean reported more irritation and anger, and fewer positive emotions, after the interaction.
To see if this effect held up when accounting for a person’s actual underlying beliefs, the researchers conducted a second study with another 180 American participants. The setup was nearly identical, but this time participants were asked to report their own political ideology on a five-point scale before entering the chat room. They also rated their personal support for all five discussion topics. The AI model that generated the coworkers’ messages was upgraded to a newer version for this second experiment, while the same GPT-5.2 model scored participants’ stances in both studies.
As expected, the participants’ baseline political ideology was a strong predictor of what they said in the chat. However, even after adjusting for these preexisting beliefs, the ideological tilt of the chat environment still predicted how participants expressed themselves. Those assigned to the conservative chat group expressed more conservative stances (an adjusted average of 0.12) than those in the liberal chat group (-0.38). Still, baseline ideology accounted for considerably more of the differences between participants (22% of the variation) compared to just 4% for the chat setting.
“This suggests that what people say in a group chat can reflect the immediate conversational environment as well as their existing political orientation,” the researchers noted. “One implication is that apparent agreement in a conversation may give an incomplete picture of the views people privately hold.”
The effect of the chat environment was smaller than in the first study. The researchers note that this is expected once baseline ideology is accounted for, and that asking participants about their views beforehand may also have prompted them to commit to their positions. Still, the setting continued to shape the direction of what participants said.
“In the second study, participants’ baseline ideology remained a substantial predictor of what they said, alongside the effect of the conversational setting,” Mitsui added. “These are average differences between groups in a brief experiment; they do not tell us how much any particular person’s private beliefs changed.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study measured what participants typed into a chat window, which does not necessarily mean their deeply held political convictions actually changed. The authors suggest that when people soften opposing views in conversation, a group can appear more unified than its members really are, although the study did not measure such perceptions.
“We measured the political positions people expressed during the conversation, so the results do not establish changes in their private beliefs or lasting attitudes,” Mitsui explained. “We also cannot separate the influence of group norms from the persuasive content of the messages, because both varied together.”
This matters because AI chatbots can be persuasive in their own right. Research covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that brief conversations with politically biased chatbots shifted people’s opinions and budget choices toward the chatbot’s bias.
There are also a few things to keep in mind regarding the simulated environment. Participants were informed ahead of time that they were interacting with artificial intelligence. Because they knew the coworkers were not real people, they may have had less reason to worry about long-term social consequences, like making things awkward at a real office. This lack of genuine interpersonal stakes might have made some participants more willing to go along with the group, or on the other hand, it might have made them feel freer to disagree.
“A simulated coworker chat cannot reproduce the history or real-life consequences of conversations with actual colleagues, friends or family,” the researchers cautioned. “Finally, we did not directly compare these chats with public social media, so we cannot conclude that the effect is stronger in small groups.”
In addition, the AI agents in the study expressed their political views quite directly to establish an obvious group norm. The authors note that this explicitness might have tipped some participants off about the study’s aim. In natural everyday group chats, people tend to be more subtle about their partisan views to keep the peace. Future research could explore how people respond to more subtle political cues, and test how these dynamics play out in other types of closed networks, such as family text groups or hobby forums.
The study, “People shift political expression to fit the room in small online group chats: Evidence from AI-simulated chat experiments,” was authored by Cleone Mitsui and Yuta Kawamura.

Rising electricity needs put Southeast Asia’s energy security at risk: report
The International Energy Agency report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity and diversify where they get their power
Risks to Southeast Asia’s energy supplies are multiplying faster than nations are coming up with solutions to meet rapidly rising demand for electricity, according to an International Energy Agency report released on Tuesday.
Southeast Asia has a seemingly insatiable appetite for energy, but the region is now in a pinch as energy costs rise, partly due to the Iran war. Fast-growing Southeast Asian economies also need more electricity to power data centres and keep homes and businesses cool.
To boost regional energy security, the report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity among each other and diversify where they get their power. But countries face multiple hurdles, from territorial conflicts between neighbours to differing types of national energy markets, according to analysts, who warn these barriers may keep the region vulnerable to energy shocks.
“Southeast Asia is one of the world’s most dynamic regions, but its rising needs for energy to power its economic growth face challenges in an increasingly uncertain global energy landscape,” Fatih Birol, the IEA executive director, said in a statement.

Who owns ‘brain rot’?: inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:16 UTC
23:00:16 KST

One of the most beloved characters in an absurdist genre of online video content has become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins.
Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan – a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. He sits under the umbrella of “Italian brain rot” internet videos.
Since his creation, Triple T has become a global sensation: YouTube and TikTok host dozens of videos with hundreds of millions of views starring the character. People dress like Triple T at cosplay conventions and lovingly create fan art and animations of the stick-like creature, and his likeness appears on plushies, perfume and stickers.
The character has generated a great deal of money and stands to create much more – he will soon be joining Fortnite as a skin. But who should benefit from this virality?
That question is at the heart of a lawsuit filed in the US district court’s northern district of California, where a games company is suing the French creative agency Mementum, which represents Noxa, over the right to use Triple T as a character in a popular Roblox game.
Eben Jeda, co-founder of Mementum Lab, said he started the agency with the goal of modernizing economic infrastructure around internet-native works, the creators of which are often completely cut out of any resulting profit.
“Brain rot is one of the first highly visible manifestations of a much larger transformation: internet native creativity can now become global almost instantly, while the people who originate it can remain economically invisible,” he said.
Opponents argue no one person should own a meme whose ultimate value has been amplified by the online collective. Fabian Mosele, a self-described “Italian brain rot expert” who has made several Tung Tung Tung Sahur videos, said they see brain rot as collectively owned.
“There are a ton of creators who made these characters come to life,” Mosele said. “Before, they were really just images. Having been part of making the virality of these characters, to gatekeep it to the original prompter of this character doesn’t seem right.”
What constitutes ‘human authorship’ in the age of generative AI?
Tung Tung Tung Sahur is one of many characters that have emerged as part of the Italian brain rot genre of meme – a universe of strange, AI-generated characters beloved by generation Alpha and younger members of gen Z. These include the likes of Ballerina Cappuccina (a ballet dancer with a coffee cup for a head), Tralalero Tralala (a shark wearing sneakers), and a variety of other intentionally bizarre creations.
Capitalizing on the virality of these mascot-esque characters, video game company Do Big Studios released a game populated by recognizable personae in May 2025 called “Steal a Brainrot”, which quickly became one of the most-played games within Roblox, where users can create minigames.
But in September 2025, Spyder Games LLC and Speedy Simulator Gaming LLC – the owners of Do Big – received a cease and desist letter from Mementum regarding the use of Tung Tung Tung Sahur in the game. Do Big initially pulled the character and attempted to negotiate a resolution with Mementum, but ultimately Spyder and Speedy sued the company instead, stating in a complaint: “Mementum’s claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify.”
Copyright law in the United States applies only to human-made creations – but AI is challenging the interpretation of that rule. A 2025 report from the United States Copyright Office declared that copyright protects “original expression” in work created “by a human author” even if the work also includes AI-generated material, but that it “does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements”.
The copyright office’s report does not offer a clear standard for ownership of creations that involve AI: “Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.”
Do Big argues that, in the case of Tung Tung Tung Sahur, the level of human intervention in the character’s creation is not sufficient to claim ownership. Court documents filed by Mementum in a separate trademark-related dispute in France show that Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created over the course of 15 minutes using seven prompts before he achieved his final form. The prompts included basic instructions like, “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”, then “human face”, and “no hands, legs like a human, and a human face”.
“We are not claiming in this case that AI-assisted work can never be owned by anybody,” said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer representing Do Big through the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp LLP. “In a case where somebody makes real creative choices, there is human authorship that is subject to protection. But it’s our position that sparse prompts – typing in a few words and picking [the image] you like – does not constitute human authorship.”
Italian brain rot, global consequences
The blurry nature of authorship in the age of AI is not the only complicating factor in the case – the global reach of online content also makes enforcement difficult. An Italian brain rot character that was created by a TikTok user in Indonesia and largely popularized in Latin America is being claimed by a French company in a California courthouse. Jeda said that as a French company, Mementum does not “view this question exclusively through an American legal lens”.
Case in point: Mementum issued a takedown request under the EU’s Digital Services Act, requesting the removal of Tung Tung Tung Sahur from Do Big’s Steal a Brainrot game, which was successful. Mementum then countersued in the United States for trademark infringement. The company does not yet hold a trademark for Triple T in the United States, but in some cases trademark infringement can be argued before registration.
“Our client is pursuing a global strategy on all of this,” said Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the US law firm representing Mementum Lab. “It is less about approaching it from a copyright law standpoint, and more about approaching it from the standpoint of – in this new wild west, where works are created with the involvement of AI, what can you do to make it so they are protectable under intellectual property law?”
How the lawsuit plays out will come down to a complicated, international web of legal dealings surrounding intellectual property laws – one that could have major implications moving forward, said James Grimmelmann, a professor at Cornell Tech and Cornell law school.
“This is the kind of case that could do one of two things: we could get a court decision that tells us, in a concrete setting, what is copyrightable and what isn’t when AI is involved,” he said. “It could also start establishing best practices and widespread norms on how people use AI.”
Such best practices could include better documenting creation processes, including what prompts are used to create characters. The prompt used to create Tung Tung Tung Sahur is at the center of this story – both in the legal case, where documentation of the process was revealed in pre-trial discovery – and online, where speculation over how Triple T was created has repeatedly gone viral.
Adam Aleksic, a content creator who has made multiple videos on the topic, said the frenzy over trying to back-solve the origin of the character reflects the mythological status and quasi-religiosity of brain rot characters.
“There’s this idea of origination when it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur – somehow out of the void, some memes are able to emerge into the cultural forefront, into our collective mainstream discourse,” he said.
The collective creation of such characters, which made brain rot popular in the first place, is exactly what makes it difficult to claim an origin for Tung Tung Tung Sahur, legally and culturally. When it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur, even speaking the name of the character has now come to inherently reference the absurdity central to brain rot, similar to how “skibidi toilet” became shorthand for “being really online”.
It is perhaps fitting, then, that of all of the Italian brain rot characters, the hero who has most come to represent virality itself has become a lightning rod for this kind of copyright battle.
“That’s the thing about archetypes – they are empty vehicles for you to project your expectations, desires, or narratives on to,” Aleksic said. “Triple T is a tool for you to tell your narrative, broadly, across the entire internet. That’s what memes do – they are a way for us to create our own stories in a time when it feels like our stories are meaningless.”

Chinese team creates ‘lifelike’ hydrogel that changes shape for smart devices
Light-activated hydrogel that can evolve with living tissue may ultimately help make more flexible brain-computer interfaces and robots
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Chinese researchers have developed a “lifelike” shape-changing hydrogel they say could provide a platform for next-generation developments, such as flexible tissue engineering scaffolds, brain-computer interfaces and humanlike robots.
Inspired by living organisms, the team created a light-triggered system called STERS, which uses liquid metal particles to generate slow, self-sustaining chemical reactions that allow a hydrogel to change its structure over time.
Capable of growing and changing alongside living tissues, this adaptive system could inspire next-generation biomedical materials and devices. It could also have broad implications in fields such as regenerative medicine and soft robotics, according to the researchers.
“This novel approach enables programmable, lifelike morphological evolution in hydrogels, spanning microscopic to macroscopic scales, minutes to weeks, and single to multiple transformation cycles,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Matter on September 4.

Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh held by ICE at Dulles, supporters say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:00:06 UTC
23:00:06 KST

US immigration authorities have detained Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh shortly after he landed at a Virgina airport, an advocacy campaign said.
"On September 24th, 2026, our friend and filmmaker, Arfat Sheikh was unlawfully detained by ICE coming off a plane at Dulles Airport (IAD)," the Support Arfat Sheikh's Release campaign said on Tuesday.
"Sheikh, along with award-winning, celebrated author and filmmaker Tara Dorabji, was en route to an Art as Resistance panel which was scheduled to take place at Busboys and Poets in Washington, DC. Sheikh was surrounded and arrested without a warrant by multiple ICE agents as he stepped off the plane at Dulles, even as he presented his immigration paperwork," the campaign added.
The 42-year-old artist, who resides in Alexandria, Virginia, arrived in the US on a student visa to pursue graduate studies in film at the Georgia State University.
He holds active work and residency authorisation under a pending immigration application.
Saffron Kingdom and Kashmir dispute
Sheikh is being held in the Caroline Detention Center in Bowling Green, Virginia, said his friend and author Azad Essa.
Sheikh is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge on Tuesday for a procedural hearing alongside a bond assessment.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security have not issued an official comment regarding the detention.
Sheikh gained international recognition for his debut feature film, Saffron Kingdom, which screened in more than 100 theaters and was streamed in 175 countries.
The film explores the Kashmir conflict through a family's journey from Srinagar in India-administered Kashmir in the 1990s to US state of Georgia in 2019.
The production received honours including Best Feature Film at the Anatolian International Film Awards, Chicago Filmmakers Award, and Los Angeles Film and Documentary Awards, as well as an Emerging Filmmaker distinction at the Teaneck International Film Festival.
Supporters of Sheikh have launched a GoFundMe Campaign to help cover his legal representation and support his immediate community needs.
Sheikh, who grew up in India-administered Kashmir during the 1990s, told TRT World in a 2024 interview that "the film was born from his desire to reclaim his people's narrative, who have often been negatively depicted by Indian cinema."
"This film is my way of breaking Bollywood's hegemony over our narrative. It's about debunking the lies they have been peddling for years," he told TRT World.
In the interview he recalled traumatic memories of being locked in a room with his family while the Indian military tortured his uncle.
His father, a renowned Kashmiri musician, was murdered while travelling to northern Indian state of Punjab. "His death was reported in newspapers, but each paper had its own version of events. We were not even given his body," he said.
Kashmir is split between India and Pakistan, both of which claim it in full but control only parts. The two countries have fought three wars over the territory since the partition of British India in 1947. China also holds a silver of Kashmir, making Kashmir world's only nuclear tri-junction.
A significant proportion of Muslim Kashmiris favour the right to self-determination as promised by several UN Security Council resolutions, seeking either full independence or accession to Pakistan.
In May 2025, India and Pakistan fought a brief war using missiles, fighter jets, drones and other weapons, which ultimately led to US involvement.
US President Donald Trump helped broker a ceasefire during the military confrontation, an intervention later publicly praised by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while India maintained that the truce was reached through direct bilateral military communications and that Trump had played no role in it.

Norwegian princess Märtha Louise and husband sue ex-friends for ‘betrayal of trust’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:59:17 UTC
22:59:17 KST

The Norwegian princess Märtha Louise and her husband, the American businessman Durek Verrett, are suing several former members of their inner circle for defamation over what they described as a “calculated betrayal of trust”.
Court documents filed in Los Angeles on 14 September claim the former friends and colleagues took “private access once afforded to them and weaponised it”. The accused include “former intimate partners, trusted business associates, a family member”.
The documents allege that information including “confidential communications, disputed accusations and claimed insider knowledge” was used against Märtha Louise, Verrett and his company, Ohana, in what the couple describe as a “coordinated series of devastating public attacks”.
The compensation claims total in excess of $80m, the newspaper VG reported.
The legal action comes during a particularly challenging period for the Norwegian royal family. King Harald died in August aged 89, to be succeeded by his son, Haakon, who is Märtha Louise’s brother. Harald’s sister, Princess Astrid, died aged 94, two days after attending his funeral in September.
At the same time, the royal family has been embroiled in several scandals including revelations about Queen Mette-Marit’s friendship with Jeffrey Epstein. Her son Marius Borg Høiby was found guilty of two counts of rape in June. The queen, who has pulmonary fibrosis, underwent a lung transplant in the same month.
Märtha Louise and Verrett have been the subject of multiple headlines in recent years.
In 2023, before marrying Verrett, who describes himself as a sixth-generation shaman, the princess renounced her royal duties to focus on the couple’s alternative medicine business. Last year they starred in a Netflix documentary about their lives, Rebel Royals: An Unlikely Love Story.
The papers, filed to Los Angeles county superior court, state that the case was prompted by a “calculated betrayal of trust” and mention the “recent loss” of the late king. The alleged “incessant misconduct” was said to have started years ago, but “continued and escalated” in 2025 and 2026.
“During that period, plaintiffs experienced significant medical and personal circumstances, including Verrett’s serious kidney failure, dialysis treatment, health deterioration and recent kidney transplant, as well as Princess Märtha Louise’s recent loss of her father,” the papers state.
“Although plaintiffs would ordinarily have preferred to devote this period to their health, family, grief, and recovery, the timing of this filing is governed by applicable legal deadlines. Plaintiffs must proceed at this unfortunate time to preserve their claims and protect their rights arising from defendants’ publications and conduct in 2025 and 2026.”
The lawsuit says the accused people, “far from being distant critics reporting from the outside”, were “at one time in the inner circle of Verrett and Princess Märtha Louise”. It adds: “They had been welcomed into Verrett’s private life, family relationships, communications, client-related affairs and business operations through relationships of intimacy, trust, confidence, and professional responsibility.”
The couple’s US lawyer Richard Roth told VG: “Our clients’ reputations have been judged by the public for years. Now the facts will be tested in a court of law.”
Court documents list two future hearings for the case in December.
The palace and representatives of the couple have been contacted by the Guardian for comment.

Memorial initiative brings October 7 survivors’ stories to stage and screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

22:59:09 KST

A staged reading of Love at the End of the Tunnel, a play about former hostages Aviva and Keith Siegel’s love story and captivity, will be performed at Habima Theatre on October 6 and 7.
It is the first production of the October 7 Global Memorial Project, an international initiative to preserve the memory of the Hamas massacre through theater, film, exhibitions, books, and other cultural projects.
Launched ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, the initiative seeks to bring the stories of survivors and hostages to audiences in Israel and abroad, while documenting the events for future generations.
Eytan Schwartz, a public diplomacy and international relations specialist, founded the project after spending 15 years leading international affairs for the Tel Aviv-Jaffa Municipality. Since the outbreak of the war, he has focused on documenting October 7.
The Siegel play, a collaboration between Schwartz and playwright Michal Aharoni, stars Sandra Sade and Moni Moshonov. Performances are planned for the US.
A second production, a one-person play based on former hostage Omer Wenkert’s story, is scheduled to premiere in 2027. Schwartz and Meron Sasson are writing it.
The initiative is also developing an English-language feature film in partnership with Kastina Communications.
Funding for the October 7 Global Memorial Project’s productions will come from philanthropists, foundations, and organizations committed to documenting October 7 and preserving its memory.
Memorial initiative based on two October 7 documentaries
The new venture builds on two documentaries produced in partnership with Kastina Communications and philanthropists Carol and Joey Low: Screams Before Silence and The Children of October 7.
Screams Before Silence, featuring interviews conducted by Sheryl Sandberg, examines the sexual violence committed by Hamas terrorists during the attacks.
According to the organizers, it has screened at the White House, the US Congress, and 20 parliaments worldwide, aired on 20 television networks, and been translated into 18 languages.
The Children of October 7 features activist and social media influencer Montana Tucker in conversations with children who survived the massacre.
The organizers said Paramount+ acquired the documentary for streaming in 20 countries.
Other activities include bringing international journalists and influencers to the attack sites in southern Israel and advising on From Here We Rise, a video-mapping installation by photographer Ziv Koren and writer Noam Horev. The installation, documenting the past three years, is currently displayed on the rooftop of the Azrieli Mall in Tel Aviv.
The project’s advisory board brings together survivors, bereaved relatives of those killed on Oct. 7 or in the subsequent war, and specialists in documentation, diplomacy, and communications.
October 7 survivors amongst project's board members
Members of the board include Israel Prize laureate Dr. Cochav Elkayam-Levy, founder of the Civil Commission on October 7 Crimes by Hamas against Women and Children; Anat and Shimon Elkabetz, founders of Sivan’s House in Kibbutz Kfar Aza; and Ella Shani, a survivor of the massacre at Kibbutz Be’eri.
Also serving are Dr. Tsuriel Rashi of Ariel University; Uwe Becker, the German state of Hesse’s commissioner for combating antisemitism; Eran Masas, a recipient of Israel’s Medal of Civilian Heroism; and Joanna Landau, a nation-branding and strategic communications specialist.
“Documenting the stories of October 7 is the mission of our generation,” Schwartz said in a statement. “On that terrible morning, we awoke not only to a catastrophe of biblical proportions, but also to a machinery of denial on a scale humanity had never before witnessed.
“This new initiative is one piece of a much larger mosaic of people and organizations around the world working to ensure that the memory of these events continues to live on for generations to come.”

The UK Green Party is facing a growing internal revolt over its adoption of a “Zionism is racism” policy, with senior members resigning or considering resignation and the European Greens distancing themselves from the party’s position.
As reported by The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, the UK Green Party voted in the controversial “Zionism is Racism” motion at its party conference in Brighton, UK, on Sunday, passing the motion 1,022 votes to 813.
In doing so, it became the first mainstream party in Europe to declare itself openly anti-Zionist.
Following the result, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar announced that Green Party leader Zack Polanski was barred from entering Israel.
Israel’s foreign ministry described the motion as a “clear antisemitic text” and beyond “the boundaries of legitimate political debate.”
UK politicians, Jewish groups condemn Green Party move
The passing of the motion has sparked condemnation from across the UK, including from politicians, Jewish groups and officials.
The Spectator revealed Monday that over a dozen Labour members of Parliament (MPs) – led by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp – reported the Green Party to Sussex Police and the Equality and Human Rights Commission over its “Zionism is racism” policy, and asked the commission to examine whether events at the Green conference may have crossed into criminally actionable racial or religious hatred against Jewish people.
However, some of the greatest losses have come from within the party itself.
Amnesty International UK chair Sandy Ruthven has left the Green Party following the party’s adoption of its “Zionism is racism” motion at its conference over the weekend.
Ruthven, who received 44% of the vote as Green candidate in the Bristol Mayor election in 2021, wrote on LinkedIn, “My heart has always been with the Green Party of England and Wales, and I have been a member for longer than I can remember. But this motion at conference marks the end of the line for me.”
“I have resigned my membership. In seeking to court the hard-left vote, we have failed to confront prejudice when it appears on our own side. In doing so, we have led ourselves into a political cul-de-sac. I sincerely hope the party finds a way back,” he said.
A man named Julian Mellor said he too was leaving the party, despite a long-standing membership.
“I first joined what was then the Ecology Party in 1981. Having spent a life supporting them, this motion seems to indicate that they’ve taken a direction different to my own. The fact that a motion that seems better suited to student politics made its way into the policies of what should be a serious national political party is a rather sad testament to the quality of leadership,” he said.
The chair of Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, told the BBC she will likely leave the party as a result of the motion.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today program, she said, “I haven’t decided yet… It is quite possible that I will leave the party… I’m giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues.”
Former party chief speaks out against vote
Former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas spoke against the motion during the debate.
Following the result, she posted a statement saying that even though she “views the Israeli government as racist, that its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and [supports] the BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) campaign,” she remains “firmly opposed to this motion.”
She went on to say that Zionism is “both racist AND a response to racism” and said there is “oversimplification at the heart of the motion [which leads] to many Jewish members feeling scared.”
Similar views were echoed by MPs such as Ellie Chowns and Carla Denyer.
The European Greens – the coalition of Green parties across Europe – announced it was distancing itself from the UK branch as a result of the motion.
In a statement, the EU Greens said it had contacted the UK Greens before the vote to express “deep concern” about the motion. The fact that the motion passed “goes against our agreed positions,” EU Greens said, adding that it therefore “unequivocally distances [itself] from it.”
“As EGP (European Green Party), we will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW (Green Party of England and Wales) to understand the official party policy, how they position themselves toward the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people.”
While the motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813, it is worth noting that this is only a tiny proportion of the Green Party’s overall membership. With 230,000 members, the vote represented less than 1% of the party.

First female Armored Corps combat company to begin IDF training in November
Unknown

22:58:52 KST

The IDF Ground Forces have completed preparations to receive the Armored Corps’s first company of female tank soldiers designated for maneuvering combat, with the new track set to begin when recruits enlist in November, Walla learned on Tuesday.
Following a series of staff studies, pilot programs, and examinations of a dedicated training track adapted for women, and amid a heated public debate and opposition from rabbis, the High Court of Justice ruled in April that the IDF must establish an all-female maneuvering tank company as an organic combat unit without further delays.
The tank crews in the first company will consist entirely of female soldiers, who will serve for the first time as an operational maneuvering force in a role similar to that of male combat soldiers.
The IDF Ground Forces have not yet decided which armored brigade will receive the company.
Female tank soldiers have previously served in border defense missions under the 80th "Edom" Division along the Egyptian border. They fought during the October 7 massacre, at both Gaza border communities and at military posts in the sector overseen by the Gaza Division’s Southern Brigade.
The soldiers killed terrorists and prevented further attacks and attempted infiltrations into Israeli communities. Despite their actions, the IDF's General Staff did not authorize them to participate in maneuvering operations deep inside the Gaza Strip during the war.
Training for female Armored Corps soldiers slated to take place at different base to male compatriots
According to IDF Ground Forces plans, the training track for the female combat soldiers will be similar to that of male soldiers, but will take place at a separate base.
The ground forces also decided that the facility would serve as the recruits’ basic training base for the duration of training. The base currently serves as a facility for repairing IDF equipment in southern Israel.
The IDF’s training apparatus has made adaptations at the base ahead of the arrival of the female combat soldiers.
The recruits are scheduled to enlist in the dedicated track in November 2026.
The IDF also decided to establish additional medical and logistical support for the training program because of the base’s distance from the Shizafon base, home to the Armored Corps’ 460th Training Brigade.
