Royad Mammadov had departed Ukraine carrying grain and was heading to the Italian port of Ravenna. The vessel had sailed from the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail in mid-September before entering the Black Sea on October 3.
The sinking came amid further Russian attacks on commercial shipping. On October 6, Odesa regional authorities reported that a Russian drone damaged a Marshall Islands-flagged vessel carrying rapeseed oil, killing one person and injuring seven.
The Royad Mammadov was not the first foreign-flagged merchant vessel to come under Russian attack in recent weeks.
On September 23, an overnight Russian strike hit a civilian cargo ship flying the flag of Antigua and Barbuda in the Black Sea, setting it ablaze and killing its captain, a Ukrainian citizen. The Ukrainian Navy evacuated the surviving crew members and extinguished the fire.

Iranian-German writer Shida Bazyar wins German Book Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:14:25 UTC
22:14:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Iranian-German author Shida Bazyar wins German Book Prize for 'The Gaps'
German author of Iranian origin Shida Bazyar has won the 2026 German Book Prize for her novel "The Gaps", which examines the mechanisms of collective silence surrounding political crimes.
The novel was selected from 205 German-language works in two stages: a longlist of 20 titles and a shortlist of six novels.
The award was announced at a ceremony held in Frankfurt on Monday, 5 October.
"The Gaps", published last month by Kiepenheuer & Witsch, revisits nearly a century of German history through the stories of residents in a fictional town that conceals its Nazi past.
The judging panel praised the novel for its combination of documentary and fictional elements, as well as its structure, which allows the story to transition between different periods, describing the work as "a novel that stands against indifference".
The judging panel also said the novel connects, across its two narrative periods, those who witnessed the disappearance of Jewish residents under Nazi rule with the experiences of migrants in Germany today, questioning their sense of belonging.
The novel is set in a fictional town in the Hunsrück region, where stories of Jewish families whose property was confiscated are intertwined with those of people who benefited from Nazism and later portrayed themselves as innocent post-war, as well as migrant families who arrived in Germany from Iran.
The story is narrated by a dead woman who had previously sought refuge in the town in the 1990s. As chapters move in a non-chronological order, links slowly emerge between the characters' fates and their family histories.
The setting serves as a narrative container for conflicting experiences, as the novel recounts what is said about the town and what is left out of public discourse, while depicting the contradiction between the safety it offers newcomers and their ignorance of its history.
In a newspaper interview with radio station Domradio, Bazyar explained that the idea for the novel began in 2019 after she read a study by Heinz Gantz Ullig about the Jews of Hermeskeil.
She spoke about her own ignorance regarding the history of the place where she grew up and her desire to address the responsibility of ordinary residents who chose to support Nazism.
Bazyar previously published "Night in Tehran Is Quiet" in 2016, followed by "Three Comrades" in 2021, which was longlisted for the prize.
Her works often explore racism and belonging.

What Would Europe Do in a Taiwan Crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:11:00 UTC
22:11:00 KST

Imagine that, one morning, Chinese coast guard vessels begin stopping commercial ships approaching Taiwan. Beijing offers the official explanation that the operation is necessary to enforce customs regulations and maritime safety and makes clear that it does not consider this a blockade, let alone an act of war. Taipei clearly sees things differently and calls it an attempt to blockade the island. Washington agrees with Taipei.
Europe, however, is less certain, with some governments demanding that China stop its actions while others start calling for restraint and dialogue. Officials begin debating whether the operation constitutes an armed attack, what international law permits, and whether sanctions against China would be justified. Meanwhile the effects on global trade start to be felt as insurers raise premiums, shipping companies start to reroute vessels, and financial markets react nervously.
At that point, Washington steps up and asks its European allies to impose economic costs on Beijing. The answer from Europe could very likely be an attempt to win more time to determine what is happening. That delay could incidentally be precisely what Beijing is aiming to achieve: deliberate ambiguity, namely the systematic creation of legal and political uncertainty designed to make an adversary hesitate over how to respond.
We have already seen elements of this approach tested on Taiwan. In June 2026, Chinese coast guard vessels conducted patrols east of Taiwan, described by Beijing as lawful maritime enforcement, while Taiwan accused China of asserting jurisdiction over commercial shipping. The United States, Britain, France, and Germany subsequently expressed concern about the operations but their protest remained at the level of rhetoric. Barely a week later, in July, Taiwan observed a sharp increase in Chinese coast guard and research vessel activities and publicly warned that such operations could be connected to preparations to disrupt maritime supply routes.
Even though such actions can be seen as acts of rehearsal, they cannot be interpreted as definitive proof that Beijing has undeniably decided to blockade Taiwan. They definitely show one thing, though: namely, how easily a future crisis could be presented in opposite ways by different sides, and how this difference could complicate a unified response between Washington and its allies.
This is one fallacy Washington should avoid: assuming that because Europe is an ally and it has enormous collective economic power, that power will automatically be available as a coherent instrument in a crisis, side by side with Washington. It may not be. The United States should therefore be encouraging and, where necessary, nudging, European governments to develop contingency plans before a crisis begins, precisely so that their institutional structure does not become an advantage for Beijing.
There is a structural reason why Europe could struggle to use its leverage quickly. The European project was built above all through economic integration – a common market, common rules and, for much of the European Union, a common currency. Foreign and security policy evolved differently and remains largely in the hands of national governments. The EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy generally requires unanimity, as do the sanctions decisions that would be among the most important instruments available in a Taiwan crisis.
This division matters because a blockade would sit precisely at the intersection of economic and foreign policy: European governments could agree that Taiwan’s security matters while disagreeing over whether Chinese actions constitute a sufficient trigger for collective economic measures. The European Parliament has already recognized the need for contingency planning, explicitly calling for preparations for scenarios including an economic blockade of Taiwan. But planning for a contingency is not the same thing as having a common response ready to deploy.
A blockade could therefore confront Washington with two crises at once: a crisis around Taiwan and a crisis within the coalition supporting Taiwan.
Beijing could exploit precisely those divisions by threatening restrictions against particular European countries or companies, using its monopoly on critical materials and rare earths as leverage, or offering selective economic incentives. The objective would be to make European governments reluctant to support measures that might trigger further retaliation.
And to this point, there is another complication that Washington should not overlook in its strategic planning. European governments are already reassessing their dependence on the United States as they assume a greater share of the burden for Ukraine and confront uncertainty over the future of the transatlantic relationship under President Donal Trump. At NATO’s 2026 summit, European allies and Canada acknowledged that they now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine, while Reuters has reported growing European efforts to diversify away from U.S. defense technology amid doubts about the reliability of American commitments.
European governments are not abandoning the alliance – many continue to emphasize its importance – but they are increasingly preparing for a world in which U.S. priorities may shift more abruptly than in the past. In such an environment, a Taiwan crisis could arrive at precisely the wrong moment: when Washington expects Europe to follow its lead, some European governments may opt instead for asking how far they should go in assuming the economic and political costs of confronting China and of following the United States, in spite of the obvious fact that a Taiwan crisis would have direct consequences for Europe’s own security, economy, and strategic interests.
Europe and the world should prepare for such contingencies. In less than two years Taiwan is scheduled to hold another presidential election on its regular four-year cycle, following the January 2024 election. This makes 2028 a useful planning horizon, since a new government in Taipei could produce renewed tensions with Beijing, depending on its policies and Beijing’s reaction. The point is not to predict that a crisis will occur in 2028, but to ensure that Washington and its European allies do not discover the limits of their respective contingency plans only after a new political configuration in Taiwan has already raised tensions.
Therefore, the United States and its European allies should privately work through concrete scenarios – prolonged inspections of commercial vessels, selective denial of port access, Chinese coast guard “escorts,” restrictions on shipping insurance, interference with critical infrastructure, and economic retaliation against individual European states. The objective would not be to predetermine every possible scenario or response, but to prevent the first days of a crisis from being consumed by arguments over terminology and definition.
More concretely than that, such preparation also needs to extend beyond the level of governments by including shipping companies, insurers, ports, banks, technology firms, and semiconductor manufacturers – actors who would would make decisions before diplomats reached an agreement. This would also have a plus side: European governments will be more willing to support collective measures if they know that the costs of Chinese retaliation will not fall disproportionately on one or two vulnerable countries.
None of this would require Europe to adopt Washington’s China policy or promise military intervention in a Taiwan conflict. The goal, instead, is agreement in advance about which forms of coercion would cross a line, what economic measures could be considered, and how their costs could be shared.
The United States has spent years strengthening military deterrence around Taiwan, yet the next Taiwan crisis may not begin with an invasion but with a disagreement over what to call what is happening. Washington’s task, therefore, is not to lament Europe’s fragmentation or demand that it simply follow the American lead, but to work with European governments now to overcome the structural obstacles that could turn hesitation into paralysis when a Taiwan crisis comes.

Ukraine's Defence Ministry reviews defence procurement and will "free up" US$347.8m
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry, together with the General Staff of the Armed Forces and the Logistics Forces Command, will free up UAH 15.6 billion (US$347.8 million) for the military's current needs by terminating some contracts with manufacturers and cancelling planned purchases.
Source: Ukraine's Defence Ministry
Quote: "Technologies, methods of warfare and the needs of units are changing rapidly. What was planned for procurement in 2024-2025 may no longer correspond to the situation on the front line today."
Details: The Defence Ministry, together with the General Staff and other bodies, analysed the military's current needs, existing contracts and planned procurements.
"As a result, UAH 15.6 billion will be freed up. These funds will be allocated to supplies that are currently a higher priority for the military," the ministry said.
The reasons for the review included some equipment no longer meeting the requirements of current combat missions and suppliers being unable to produce the planned quantities. In addition, some items have still not undergone codification.
Quote: "Some needs are being fully covered by partners, while some tasks can be carried out using cheaper equipment, allowing us to purchase it in larger quantities.
Some contracts will be terminated, while some planned procurements will not go ahead. All decisions regarding existing contracts will be implemented in accordance with the law."
Details: The ministry said that manufacturers affected by the changes "had been informed and had communicated with Defence Procurement Agency DOT regarding further action on the contracts, taking into account their implementation status and payments made".
The ministry is not publishing the list of weapons whose procurement has been reviewed, citing security considerations.
Background:
- It was previously reported that following talks with the EU, Ukraine is still seeking funding for most of its additional defence needs of US$27 billion using domestic resources, while funding for the remainder is still being sought.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the deficit in funding for Ukraine's defence "astronomical" and said the authorities are preparing proposals to address the problem.
- Ukraine's state finances are close to a critical situation, while delays in the necessary votes in the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) could cost Ukraine a significant portion of US$29.5 billion in international funding.

Kenya confirms first Ebola case after patient dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:09:01 UTC
22:09:01 KST

Kenya confirms first Ebola case after patient dies
Kenya has confirmed its first Ebola case after a citizen returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) died in a Nairobi hospital, extending a regional outbreak that has killed more than 4,000 people.
In a statement on Tuesday, Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient lived in DR Congo for seven years and received treatment at several hospitals after falling ill about a month ago. He traveled by road to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, before boarding a Jambojet flight to Nairobi on October 3.
He underwent routine screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport before a relative and a friend took him directly to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated, the minister said. Two laboratories confirmed the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, and he died on Monday night, according to the statement.
The authorities have identified 28 contacts, including relatives and healthcare workers, and are tracing another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight as the patient.
“I wish to reassure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” Duale said.
DR Congo declared the outbreak in May and recorded 8,442 confirmed infections and 4,080 deaths as of October 2, according to the Health Ministry. The World Health Organization (WHO) says insecurity, a humanitarian crisis, and extensive population movements have complicated containment.
There is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain, although trials are underway. Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, including those of deceased patients.
Uganda also recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths before the WHO declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Kenya had never recorded an Ebola case despite repeated outbreaks in other African countries. The 2014-2016 epidemic that devastated Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone killed more than 11,000 people, while DR Congo’s 2018-2020 outbreak infected 3,481 people and killed 2,299, according to the WHO.
Nairobi announced heightened surveillance and screening in May following the outbreaks in DR Congo and Uganda. It agreed to host a controversial US-backed quarantine facility at Laikipia Air Base for Americans exposed to the virus abroad, prompting protests and a legal challenge over fears of importing infections.
In June, Kenya’s health minister was found in contempt of court after construction continued despite a High Court order suspending the project. Duale apologized and said he ordered “the immediate and complete cessation of any intended construction, site preparation, or related activities” at the facility.
However, the Law Society of Kenya and constitutional watchdog Katiba Institute alleged in July that the facility was operating despite the court ban. US-based Christian relief organization Samaritan’s Purse confirmed that seven employees returning from DR Congo were quarantined in Kenya but did not disclose their location. Katiba Institute called reports that they had been transferred to Laikipia Air Base “deeply alarming” and a violation of the court’s orders.

Explainer-What do we know about plague institute lab worker's death in Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:09:01 UTC
22:09:01 KST

Explainer-What do we know about plague institute lab worker's death in Russia?
MOSCOW/LONDON, Oct 6 - A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media.
Here's what we know about the case, which officials have not linked to her work or plague, and about the disease she studied.
WHAT HAPPENED?
Russian media named the victim as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The authorities said she died of an unknown type of pneumonia but that as a precaution they quarantined everyone who had come into contact with her.
Unconfirmed reports of how she fell ill have circulated on social media.
One version said she had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria at work, a theory rejected by Russia's health watchdog. Another said she became sick after travelling to Thailand. A third said she fell ill after going to an area near the border with Mongolia.
There is no evidence in the public domain to support any of those theories.
DID SHE DIE OF PLAGUE?
There is no confirmation she died from plague although one regional governor said she "may" have died from plague.
Health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said she died of an unknown type of pneumonia and that no relevant pathogens had been found in anyone who came into contact with her.
Elena Sofina, a local official in Siberia, said 60% of those quarantined had since been released. Local media said about 200 were initially quarantined.
Sofina said "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.
WHAT IS PLAGUE AND CAN YOU TREAT IT?
Plague circulates mainly among small animals and fleas. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, it can also infect humans. Outbreaks include the "Black Death", which killed over 50 million people in Europe in the 1300s.
It is transmitted between animals and humans by the bite of infected fleas, inhalation of infected respiratory particles and — rarely — ingestion of infectious materials. The disease's mortality rate is 30%-100% if left untreated. If identified quickly, plague can be treated with antibiotics.
HOW COMMON IS PLAGUE?
Plague is endemic in many African countries, the former Soviet Union, the Americas and Asia, but most human cases in the last six years were reported from the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as Yersinia pestis is present there among small wild mammals and their fleas. It's rare for Russians to have plague.
WHAT ABOUT INTERNATIONAL REACTION?
US President Donald Trump said the laboratory worker's death was a "big problem for Russia" and offered to help Moscow deal with it. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russia should share more information about the death.
The WHO in Geneva said Russia had told it there were no plague cases in the city of Irkutsk. Reuters could not establish whether this meant plague could be ruled out in the lab worker's case.
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan said they were stepping up precautionary measures at their borders to guard against the possible spread of infectious diseases.
WHAT IS THE PLAGUE INSTITUTE IN SIBERIA?
The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was set up in 1934 to control plague outbreaks. Its founding scientist helped quell outbreaks in Siberia, Mongolia and China, its website says. It later worked with other dangerous diseases including cholera and anthrax.
WHAT ARE THE TYPES OF PLAGUE?
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, the most virulent and least common form, is an infection of the lungs which prompts patients to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
Bubonic plague is the most common form, occurring chiefly when an infected flea bites a person, and causes swollen lymph nodes or "buboes". Septicemic plague, which does not spread from person to person, occurs when plague bacteria multiply in the blood.
One form of plague can develop into another.
Infected persons usually start with flu-like symptoms after an incubation period of one to seven days. They experience fever, chills, head and body aches and weakness, vomiting and nausea.
WHY IS THIS DEATH IN THE SPOTLIGHT?
The COVID-19 pandemic heightened concerns about the risk of new deadly diseases emerging, and reports of clusters of unknown illness or laboratory accidents now cause panic online.
Most scientists believe the coronavirus that caused COVID-19 came from animals, but some have suggested a lab leak caused it.
Public health experts have urged caution about the incident in Siberia, saying only one case has been reported and that Russian authorities say there is no evidence the lab worker was infected with plague. REUTERS

Jailed Lego collector’s insurance scam highlights UK’s £1.3bn fraud problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:07:23 UTC
22:07:23 KST

An insurance fraudster who pocketed more than £14,000 for the supposed theft of Lego sets, fishing gear and gaming consoles was behind one of last year’s most high-profile bogus claims.
Investigators uncovered £1.34bn of fraud in 2025, a 14% increase on the year before, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI).
The Lego fraudster, Matthew Johnson, was sentenced to 28 months in prison last December after an investigation by the City of London police’s insurance fraud enforcement department.
Johnson, of Misterton in Nottinghamshire, submitted false claims to Axa Insurance between May 2021 and January 2022, relating to alleged burglaries at properties in Shetland and Goole, East Yorkshire.
He claimed that high-value items had been stolen, including MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and large quantities of collectible Lego sets. Johnson received more than £14,000 in insurance payouts across four claims. He was ordered by Nottingham crown court to repay the money.
Axa raised concerns after inconsistencies were identified in the documentation provided by Johnson, including repeated use of the same receipts across different claims and invoices that appeared to have been altered to match the policy address.
The ABI and police warned that insurance fraud pushed up the cost of premiums for all customers.
Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the association, said: “Anyone considering committing insurance fraud should be under no illusion – it’s a serious crime with serious consequences, including a criminal conviction and imprisonment.”
While the number of detected fraudulent claims fell by 2.7% to 93,900 cases last year, the value of scams rose sharply. The ABI said this was a sign of its growing scale and sophistication.
The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year – the second-highest figure on record, just below the peak of £14,600 in 2022.
Motor insurance was again the area with the most fraud, accounting for 55% of all cases. With 51,900 fraudulent motor claims worth £625m uncovered last year, the figures point to fewer but more costly cases. The average value rose to £12,000, the second-highest figure since 2015.
A fraudster who staged motor collisions using women he met online was sentenced for the “crash for cash” scheme designed to generate fraudulent insurance claims, the ABI said.
Aviva discovered bogus insurance claims worth £233m last year, it said in June. Scammers tried new tricks including using artificial intelligence to fake car accident scenes and documents.
Simon Klust, who heads the City of London police fraud team, said more than 250 bogus claims were detected each day but this was “likely to be just the tip of the iceberg”.
The travel sector had the sharpest rise in the number of bogus claims. Investigators uncovered a £300,000 insurance scam that used multiple fake identities, fabricated medical documents and bogus websites to support false medical emergency claims.
Exaggerated loss remains the most common type of fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately increases the cost of a claim beyond its true value.
Ursula Jallow of the Insurance Fraud Bureau, which is funded by insurers, said: “Insurance fraud is devastating. It costs honest consumers when times are already tough.”

Search investigations have begun into the burial sites of people who were killed or went missing during the Second World War in the territory of the village of Laskiv, Mircze gmina, Hrubieszów County, Lublin Voivodeship, Republic of Poland. This was reported by the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR), UNN writes.
The investigations are being conducted pursuant to the agreements reached following the work of the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on dignified burials. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance is ensuring that the search operations are carried out. The work will be conducted by "Dolya," a municipal enterprise of the Lviv Regional Council responsible for searching for the graves of participants in national liberation struggles and victims of wars, deportations, and political repressions
It is noted that the relevant permit to conduct the expedition was obtained from the Polish side on August 31, 2026.
The purpose of the search investigations is to identify the burial sites of Laskiv's civilian residents who died as a result of an attack by units of the Home Army and Peasant Battalions in March 1944.
These are already the second search operations conducted by the Ukrainian side in Poland after a lengthy hiatus. In the autumn of 2025, the first Ukrainian search-and-exhumation expedition was held on the basis of official authorization from the Polish authorities. The work took place in the village of Yurechkova
It is noted that, according to various historical sources, more than 300 people were killed during the mass murder of Ukrainians in Laskiv on March 10, 1944. Historical research conducted by historians and experts from Ukraine and Poland has established data on 327 Laskiv residents who died in 1944. At the same time, some historians cite a higher number of victims—about 350 people. The final number of victims may be clarified as a result of further historical and search investigations.

Spain approves new emergency housing measures
October 6, 2026
Spain's government approved two extraordinary decrees on Tuesday to deal with the country's housing crisis.
The decision comes after violence broke out in Barcelona when tens of thousands of people took to the streets.
Monday night's protests in Barcelona demanded measures to resolve a crisis triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in central Madrid.
In Barcelona, what began as a massive, peaceful march turned violent when groups of radical activists clashed with police, throwing rocks and setting fire to rubbish bins.
Housing decrees expand on failed laws
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's government approved measures similar to housing reforms rejected by parliament last Friday. That legislative loss led Sanchez on Monday to call for early elections on November 29.
The Socialist leader said the 21 measures in the decrees included "some very positive additions" to the unsuccessful proposed laws.
The government's housing measures will be sent for ratification to an interim legislative body known as the "standing commission," made up of 69 of parliament's 350 members.
Necessary housing reforms
Alejandro Quiroga, a political science professor at Madrid's Complutense University, told AP that calling on the interim legislature to approve government decisions was constitutional and an important political step on Sanchez's part.
"I don't think Sanchez had an alternative. If they're calling snap elections to keep the public focus on housing, they can't sit idly by and do nothing. That wouldn't have been smart," Quiroga said.
Among the measures are protection against evictions for vulnerable Spaniards until 2030, the regulation of room rentals and a new tax on seasonal leases ranging from 32 days to 11 months. In addition, speculative purchases of real estate will be banned, and tax exemptions will be granted to landlords, Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez said.
Rising costs and housing shortages are keeping many Spaniards out of the property market despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters are demanding more protections for tenants, measures to combat fraud, and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is not available.

Germany’s far-right AfD struggles to form first state government after landmark election win

Germany’s far-right AfD struggles to form first state government after landmark election win
- The far-right AfD won the Saxony-Anhalt state election but fell three seats short of an absolute majority, preventing it from forming the first state government.
- Mainstream parties maintain a "firewall" policy refusing cooperation with AfD, causing a stalemate despite AfD's symbolic gains like electing Tobias Rausch as state Parliament president.
- AfD seeks support from the BSW party for a minority government, yet challenges remain as AfD's leader Ulrich Siegmund may call new elections if no majority is secured.
AI generated
MAGDEBURG, Germany - The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) convened for the first sitting of the Saxony-Anhalt state Parliament on Oct 6. But a month after its landmark election win, the party still lacks a clear path to forming what would be its first state government.
Despite winning the vote in the Sept 6 election in the eastern German state, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority that candidate Ulrich Siegmund had aimed for.
Siegmund said before the Oct 6 sitting that he aimed to win parliamentary backing to become state premier in a first round of voting that he said would only take place in December, giving him more time to build support. He did not elaborate.
The party has so far failed to secure enough support from potential partners or publicly win over defectors from rivals, leading to a stalemate in its efforts to form a government.
'Firewall’ complications
The impasse underlines a challenge that has dogged the AfD for years: translating growing electoral support into executive power in a political system where mainstream parties have refused to cooperate with it under the “firewall” policy.
Founded in 2013 as a eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after around a million people fled to Germany in 2015.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with the mainstream parties, though many remain strongly opposed to cutting any deals with the AfD.
About 400 protesters gathered peacefully on Oct 6 outside the state Parliament in Magdeburg and read aloud Germany’s constitution ahead of the session, with dozens holding up a long red banner that read: “No cooperation with the extreme right.”
Symbolic victory
The Oct 6 inaugural sitting, which the state constitution requires to take place within 30 days of the election, nevertheless offered the AfD a symbolic victory.
Tobias Rausch, a 35-year-old real estate entrepreneur and Siegmund confidant, was elected president of the state Parliament with support from the left-wing populist BSW, becoming the first AfD member to hold one of the highest offices in a German state legislature.
Rausch used his inaugural speech to call on lawmakers to work together, adding that “the days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past”.
The AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and two other state elections in September has put Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s struggling government under pressure and raised questions within his conservatives about the effectiveness of the firewall.
The AfD has been working for weeks to win over lawmakers from Merz’s party, whose support halved from the last state election, but no defections have been announced so far.
Reliable partners with the BSW?
The Oct 6 vote was also closely watched for signs of whether the AfD can reliably count on the BSW, the only party that has not explicitly ruled out cooperation, though it has rejected the idea of joining the AfD in a coalition government.
The BSW, which like the AfD opposes mass immigration and wants to restore energy ties with Russia, has said it would abstain in any vote for Siegmund for state premier.
That could lead to the AfD forming a minority government with passive tolerance from the BSW, under a model seen in neighbouring Thuringia, though Siegmund has previously rejected such a setup as making him too reliant on the smaller party.
Siegmund has also floated the possibility of new elections if he does not secure the required majority the first time around.
In the Oct 6 secret ballot to become state Parliament leader, Rausch secured 48 votes, suggesting he attracted support not only from his own party and the BSW - totalling 44 votes - but also from at least four other lawmakers. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:03:47 UTC
22:03:47 KST

Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
Scientists have found a way to rejuvenate existing cartilage cells, regrow damaged knee cartilage, and potentially open a path toward treating arthritis without joint replacement.
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Stanford Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have found a surprising way to regrow damaged knee cartilage by blocking a protein that becomes more abundant with age. In old mice, the treatment restored naturally lost cartilage and also helped prevent osteoarthritis after ACL-like knee injuries, while human cartilage taken from knee replacement patients began producing new, functional joint cartilage after exposure to the same inhibitor.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a way to restore cartilage in aging knee joints, at least in mice, by blocking a protein whose levels rise with age. The approach not only reversed naturally occurring cartilage loss in older animals, but also protected mice from developing arthritis after knee injuries similar to ACL tears in people.
The findings also showed promise in human tissue. Cartilage samples collected during knee replacement surgeries responded to the treatment by beginning to produce new, functional cartilage.
Together, the results suggest that cartilage damaged by aging or arthritis may be more capable of repair than previously thought. If the strategy ultimately works in people, researchers believe it could potentially lead to an oral medicine or injection that regenerates cartilage and reduces the need for knee or hip replacement surgery.
Targeting the damage behind osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease in which cartilage gradually breaks down, leaving joints painful, swollen and increasingly difficult to move. It affects about one in five adults in the United States and is estimated to account for roughly $65 billion in direct health care costs each year.
Current treatments mainly focus on controlling pain and other symptoms. Once the disease becomes severe, replacing the damaged joint surgically may be the only remaining option. There is currently no drug that can reliably slow or reverse osteoarthritis itself.
The Stanford Medicine-led study instead focused on a protein called 15-PGDH. The researchers have described it as a gerozyme, a term for enzymes that become more abundant with age and contribute to the gradual loss of tissue function.
Previous work by the same group showed that 15-PGDH acts as an important regulator of aging in multiple tissues. Blocking the protein with a small molecule increased muscle mass and endurance in old mice. Doing the opposite, increasing 15-PGDH in young animals, caused their muscles to shrink and weaken. The protein has also been linked to the regeneration of bone, nerve and blood cells.
In many of those tissues, healing depends on tissue-specific stem cells multiplying and developing into specialized cells. Cartilage turned out to behave differently. Instead of relying on stem cells, existing cartilage cells called chondrocytes changed their patterns of gene activity and shifted toward a more youthful state.
"This is a new way of regenerating adult tissue, and it has significant clinical promise for treating arthritis due to aging or injury," said Helen Blau, PhD, professor of microbiology and immunology. "We were looking for stem cells, but they are clearly not involved. It's very exciting."
Blau, who directs the Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology and is the Donald E. and Delia B. Baxter Foundation Professor, and Nidhi Bhutani, PhD, associate professor of orthopaedic surgery, are the senior authors of the research, which was published in Science. Instructor of orthopedic surgery Mamta Singla, PhD, and former postdoctoral scholar Yu Xin (Will) Wang, PhD, are the lead authors of the study. Wang is now an assistant professor at the Sanford Burnham Institute in San Diego.
"Dramatic regeneration" of cartilage
"Millions of people suffer from joint pain and swelling as they age," Bhutani said. "It is a huge unmet medical need. Until now, there has been no drug that directly treats the cause of cartilage loss. But this gerozyme inhibitor causes a dramatic regeneration of cartilage beyond that reported in response to any other drug or intervention."
Cartilage is not all the same. The human body contains three major types, each designed for a different job.
Elastic cartilage is soft and flexible and helps form structures such as the outer ear. Fibrocartilage is tougher and better suited to absorbing force, including in areas between the vertebrae of the spine. Hyaline cartilage is smooth and slippery, allowing bones to move against one another with very little friction in joints such as the ankles, hips, shoulders and parts of the knee.
In joints, hyaline cartilage is also known as articular cartilage. It is the type most commonly damaged by osteoarthritis.
Osteoarthritis can develop as joints experience stress from aging, injury or obesity. Chondrocytes begin producing inflammatory molecules while also breaking down collagen, a structural protein that gives cartilage much of its strength.
As collagen disappears, cartilage becomes thinner and softer. Inflammation adds swelling and pain, creating the familiar symptoms of osteoarthritis.
The problem is that articular cartilage normally has very little ability to repair itself. Researchers have identified possible stem or progenitor cells capable of forming cartilage in bone, but efforts to find similar cell populations within articular cartilage itself have not been successful.
An aging protein becomes a target
Earlier research from Blau's laboratory found that a molecule called prostaglandin E2 is important for the function of muscle stem cells. The protein 15-PGDH breaks down prostaglandin E2.
Blocking 15-PGDH, or otherwise raising levels of prostaglandin E2, has been shown to support regeneration in damaged muscle, nerve, bone, colon, liver and blood cells in young mice.
That raised an important question for Blau, Bhutani and their colleagues: Could the same biological pathway contribute to the deterioration of cartilage as animals age or recover from injury?
The researchers compared 15-PGDH levels in knee cartilage from young and old mice. They found that the amount of the gerozyme roughly doubled with age.
They then gave older animals a small molecule drug designed to inhibit 15-PGDH. In one experiment, the drug was injected into the abdomen so it could have effects throughout the body. In another, it was delivered directly into the knee joint.
Both approaches produced striking results.
Cartilage in the knees of older animals had been noticeably thinner and less functional than cartilage in young mice. After treatment, however, it became thicker across the surface of the joint.
Importantly, the cells were making hyaline cartilage, the smooth articular cartilage needed for healthy joint movement, rather than the less suitable fibrocartilage.
"Cartilage regeneration to such an extent in aged mice took us by surprise," Bhutani said. "The effect was remarkable."
Protecting knees after ACL injuries
The researchers also tested whether the treatment could help after traumatic knee injuries.
ACL tears are particularly common in sports such as soccer, basketball and skiing, where athletes frequently pivot, stop abruptly or jump. Surgery can repair the torn ligament, but fixing the immediate injury does not necessarily prevent long-term joint damage.
About 50% of people who experience these injuries go on to develop osteoarthritis in the affected joint within approximately 15 years.
In the mouse experiments, researchers administered the gerozyme inhibitor twice a week for four weeks after injury. The treatment dramatically reduced the likelihood that the animals would develop osteoarthritis.
Mice that received a control drug had 15-PGDH levels twice those of animals whose knees had not been injured, and they developed osteoarthritis within four weeks.
The treated mice also moved more normally and placed more weight on the paw attached to the injured leg than untreated animals did.
"Interestingly, prostaglandin E2 has been implicated in inflammation and pain," Blau said. "But this research shows that, at normal biological levels, small increases in prostaglandin E2 can promote regeneration."
Making old cartilage cells act younger
To understand what was happening inside the joint, the researchers took a closer look at chondrocytes from young and old mice.
Older cartilage cells showed more activity in genes associated with inflammation and with the unwanted conversion of hyaline cartilage into bone. At the same time, genes involved in normal cartilage development were less active.
Treatment shifted that balance.
One population of old chondrocytes that produced 15-PGDH and expressed genes associated with cartilage degradation dropped from 8% of cells to 3%.
A second population, which did not produce 15-PGDH but expressed genes linked to fibrocartilage formation, fell from 16% to 8%.
Meanwhile, a third group moved sharply in the opposite direction. These cells did not produce 15-PGDH and expressed genes involved in forming hyaline cartilage and maintaining the extracellular matrix needed for healthy cartilage function. Their share increased from 22% to 42%.
The extracellular matrix is the network of proteins and other molecules that surrounds cells and gives tissues their structure. In cartilage, it is especially important because it helps the tissue withstand pressure while maintaining the smooth surface joints need for movement.
Overall, the treatment appeared to push cartilage toward a younger biological state without recruiting stem or progenitor cells.
Human cartilage also responded
The researchers then examined cartilage taken from people with osteoarthritis who were undergoing total knee replacement surgery.
After one week of treatment with the 15-PGDH inhibitor, the human tissue contained fewer chondrocytes expressing 15-PGDH. Activity in genes associated with cartilage degradation and fibrocartilage also declined compared with untreated tissue.
Most notably, the samples began regenerating articular cartilage.
"The mechanism is quite striking and really shifted our perspective about how tissue regeneration can occur," Bhutani said. "It's clear that a large pool of already existing cells in cartilage are changing their gene expression patterns. And by targeting these cells for regeneration, we may have an opportunity to have a bigger overall impact clinically."
The findings do not yet establish that the treatment can regrow cartilage or prevent osteoarthritis in people. The mouse results and experiments on human tissue represent important early evidence, but clinical trials specifically testing cartilage regeneration will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective for patients.
An oral 15-PGDH inhibitor has already reached clinical testing for a different age related problem: muscle weakness.
Blau added, "Phase 1 clinical trials of a 15-PGDH inhibitor for muscle weakness have shown that it is safe and active in healthy volunteers. Our hope is that a similar trial will be launched soon to test its effect in cartilage regeneration. We are very excited about this potential breakthrough. Imagine regrowing existing cartilage and avoiding joint replacement."
Researchers from the Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute contributed to the work.
The study was funded by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01AR070864, R01AR077530, R01AG069858 and R00NS120278), the Baxter Foundation for Stem Cell Biology, the Li Ka Shing Foundation, the Stanford Cardiovascular Institute, the Milky Way Research Foundation, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, a Stanford Translational Research and Applied Medicine Pilot grant, a GlaxoSmithKline Sir James Black Postdoctoral Fellowship, and a Stanford Dean's Postdoctoral Fellowship.
Blau, Bhutani and other coauthors are inventors on patent applications held by Stanford University involving 15-PGDH inhibition for cartilage and tissue rejuvenation. Those applications are licensed to Epirium Bio. Blau is a cofounder of Myoforte/Epirium and holds equity and stock options in the company.

Aircraft Leasing and International Agreements: The BEB’s New Interpretation Threatens the Industry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:03:29 EEST
22:03:29 KST

Aircraft Leasing and International Agreements: The BEB’s New Interpretation Threatens the Industry
Kyiv • UNN
International treaties take precedence in cross-border taxation. The BEB considers aircraft leasing to be royalties and has opened cases against at least five carriers.
When a Ukrainian company does business with a nonresident, it is not enough to consider only the Tax Code of Ukraine to determine the applicable tax rules. Cross-border transactions also require consideration of international treaties for the avoidance of double taxation concluded by Ukraine with other states. If an international treaty establishes rules different from those of Ukrainian legislation, the provisions of that treaty must apply. UNN, together with lawyers, examined how these rules work using the example of Ukrainian aviation, which currently operates abroad and mostly leases aircraft from nonresidents of Ukraine.
From a model convention to an international treaty
The system of international tax treaties is based on two model conventions — those of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the United Nations (UN). They are not international treaties in themselves, but serve as a basis for negotiations between states. During these negotiations, countries agree on specific tax rules, which are then enshrined in bilateral conventions.
In practice, states often use the OECD Model, the UN Model, or individual provisions of both documents. During negotiations, they agree, in particular, on rules concerning residency, permanent establishments, the taxation of dividends, interest, royalties, and business income, the elimination of double taxation, and the exchange of tax information
According to the lawyers, the OECD Model is more focused on taxation in the state of residence of the income recipient.
The key difference between the UN Model and the OECD Model is that the UN Model generally provides greater taxation rights to the state where the income is directly earned. For example, the UN Model establishes lower thresholds for the creation of a taxable presence through a permanent establishment. It also provides broader opportunities for taxing certain types of income in the source state
Therefore, for a specific transaction, what matters is not the OECD or UN Model, but the convention in force between Ukraine and the state of which the counterparty is a resident. According to the Ministry of Finance, 70 bilateral conventions and agreements on the avoidance of double taxation are in force between Ukraine and other states.
Why an international treaty cannot be ignored
Under the Constitution of Ukraine, current international treaties ratified by the Verkhovna Rada are part of national legislation. At the same time, the Law "On International Treaties of Ukraine" provides that if an international treaty establishes rules different from those set out in the relevant act of Ukrainian legislation, the rules of the international treaty apply.
The same principle is enshrined in the Tax Code of Ukraine.
If the relevant cross-border situation is regulated by an international agreement, its provisions must be taken into account together with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine
Do international rules work in Ukraine
In practice, it turned out that not all international conventions operate in Ukraine. The situation involving aircraft leasing became a striking example.
The overwhelming majority of commercial aircraft used by Ukrainian air carriers are leased from foreign owners — nonresidents of Ukraine. Therefore, payments under such agreements are cross-border transactions, and their taxation cannot be assessed exclusively in isolation from Ukraine's international treaties.
The problem arose after the Bureau of Economic Security, acting independently and without corresponding amendments to tax legislation or international conventions, began interpreting airlines' leasing payments to nonresidents as royalties. In other words, investigators began treating the rental of air transport as the use of equipment.
Based on this approach, the BEB opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Windrose," N3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline, "Urga," may also be involved in a similar case.
The investigations were launched despite the fact that almost all air carriers successfully pass tax audits, and the tax authorities' remarks concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legislative provisions and requires the development of a unified state approach. Moreover, treating aircraft leasing as royalties—something that does not occur in any other country in the world—makes Ukrainian carriers uncompetitive in the international market.
The current definition of royalties in the Tax Code of Ukraine is linked to remuneration for the use of, or the right to use, intellectual property rights, including patents, trademarks, designs, formulas, processes, and know-how. Leasing is not included in this list.
Some of Ukraine's bilateral conventions with other states provide for royalties for the use of industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. For example, such a provision is contained in the current Convention between Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates. However, aircraft are not defined as equipment and, in accordance with international practice, royalties are not charged on the leasing of aircraft and helicopters from nonresidents.
State authorities are bound by Ukraine's international obligations
The situation with aircraft leasing demonstrates a much broader problem than a dispute over one type of payment between a state authority and an airline. It concerns, more generally, the predictability of state tax policy in international relations.
If Ukraine has concluded an agreement with a foreign state, consented to be bound by it, and it has entered into force, state authorities, when addressing matters covered by that agreement, must act with due regard to its provisions.
They cannot create a different system of international taxation for businesses merely by interpreting a transaction themselves. The classification of a specific payment must be based on national legislation and international law, while businesses must have clear operating rules.
For airlines, this issue is particularly sensitive, since international leasing is the fundamental mechanism for building an aircraft fleet. If the tax rules for such transactions can be changed through a new interpretation by state authorities without amending legislation or international treaties, businesses cease to be competitive and risk losing international contracts.
For a country that is integrating into the European and global economic space and seeking to attract foreign investors, the predictability of operating rules is no less important than their substance. For state authorities, the starting point must be unambiguous: cross-border tax relations must be assessed exclusively with due regard to Ukrainian tax legislation and Ukraine's international treaties in force.

October 7, genocide and Yemen
TEHRAN – Since the Second World War, West Asia has emerged as a region in which the fate of the world is increasingly determined.
The region’s importance has only grown with the emergence of the Zionist regime and the strategic significance of oil. It has consequently witnessed a series of bloody regional and international confrontations.
Al-Aqsa Flood, carried out by Hamas’s armed wing with the participation of other Palestinian resistance groups, shook the world. It shattered the Zionist narrative surrounding the Palestinian people and their rights, exposed the hollowness of the capitalist discourse on democracy and human rights, and disrupted efforts to expand the Abraham Accords and bring the largest Arab oil-producing state into the fold.
 
Amid a U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza, it returned the Palestinian cause to the forefront of global affairs and reminded the Arab world once again that Palestine is not solely the cause of the Palestinian people. Nor is it an “Israeli-Palestinian” dispute. It is the cause of the entire Islamic and Arab world.
The Axis of Resistance: Hezbollah, Ansarallah, the Iraqi resistance movement, and Iran, soon entered the battle through a support front. Its impact would undoubtedly have been greater had the Hamas operation, whatever its calculations may have been, gone beyond the initial element of surprise and expanded to some form of communication within the resistance axis.
The reason is that the enemy camp, the American-Zionist alliance, had already laid the groundwork for setting the region ablaze in pursuit of a “Greater Middle East” project.
In light of all this, several points deserve emphasis:
Every confrontation with the U.S.-Zionist alliance is subjected to a process of preemptive demonization, with the culture of resistance itself blamed for the human and material costs of war. Yet Europe, for example, lost 50 million people in two wars fought on its own soil, while numerous European capitals, including London, were nearly destroyed in the process.
The same is true of the wars of liberation fought by Vietnam, China, Algeria, and others, in which millions of people were sacrificed.
The Israeli regime’s losses since October 7, and its illegal wars with Lebanon, Yemen, and Iran, exceeded all the losses it had suffered since it was founded in 1948.
For those who question the seriousness of these confrontations, it is worth recalling that most of the first- and second-tier leadership of Hezbollah and Hamas, as well as a number of Iranian leaders, were martyred in these battles.
Those who expect any given battle, war, or confrontation to produce immediate strategic breakthroughs and then judge it according to that expectation inevitably fall into despair, accusations, or even outright rejection of the struggle when those breakthroughs do not materialize. Such people overlook, or fail to understand, that the struggle against the Zionist regime and its imperialist and reactionary extensions is far broader, more complex, and more difficult than anything that has taken place so far.
Nor have any resistance forces demonstrated greater sacrifice, selflessness, courage, heroism, discipline, organization, and commitment to martyrdom than Hezbollah, Palestinian resistance forces, as well as Yemen and Iran.
There can be no doubt that not a single drop of blood shed by their leaders, fighters, or people will have been in vain. More importantly, these experiences constitute a solid foundation for continuing a long road that has yet to reach its destination.
One war gives birth to another: Yemen
Following American statements that Washington would not permit the loss of, or any transfer of control over, Bab al-Mandab, warnings have emerged of a new crisis resembling the one surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Amid these warnings, forces backed by Saudi Arabia, the U.S., and other regional and international actors have begun a military campaign to besiege the Sanaa government forces.
The prelude to this was a campaign of fabricated accusations alleging that Ansarallah had attacked Islam’s holiest site, Mecca.
Ansarallah responded with mass demonstrations numbering in the millions, demonstrating the Yemeni people’s support for the Sanaa government. It then launched a broad military campaign, seizing the equipment of entire military units.
Bab al-Mandab itself came within their missile range, and before long, the entire Red Sea had effectively become part of the battlefield. Ansarallah’s missiles also reached the land routes that the oil-rich Persian Gulf states had been relying on as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.
Ansarallah were fully aware of where this was heading and expected hundreds, even thousands, of American, Atlantic, and Saudi airstrikes in response to the defeats suffered by their forces on the ground.
According to preliminary estimates, the combined number of airstrikes and missiles launched against Yemen by the Americans and their allies since March 2015 rivals the scale of the Normandy campaign against Germany during the Second World War.
The air campaign can point to the scale of its bombardment and, once again, try to confuse the picture. But Ansarallah’s experience has demonstrated and reaffirmed a historical lesson repeatedly shown by Yemeni resistance: every invading power and every local force serving it has ultimately faced defeat.
Neither Portugal, the Ottoman Empire, nor Britain at the height of their power escaped defeat at the hands of the Yemenis. Nor could any of them break the Yemenis’ sense of dignity or pride in their history, including their resistance to Wahhabism and its extensions, which sought to dominate and control Yemen throughout the 20th century.
The same pattern is being repeated today, this time with the backing of the U.S. and its European and regional allies, alongside a group of Yemeni political figures who claim to represent Yemen’s legitimate government, even though their claim to legitimacy is based solely on the support they receive from Riyadh and Washington rather than from Yemen itself.

Gallery: Young Estonian artists' fall exhibition opens in Tallinn

Gallery: Young Estonian artists' fall exhibition opens in Tallinn
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition has opened at Tallinn's Art & Tonic gallery where visitors can see works by 88 young Estonian artists free of charge. The exhibition will conclude with an art auction on October 23.
Nearly 400 works by 203 artists were submitted for this year's fall exhibition, with the jury selecting works by 88 artists. According to Reigo Kuivjõgi, organizer of "Buy Young Art" and gallerist at Art & Tonic, this year's selection is characterized by the high quality and diversity of the works.
"I am pleased that this time the selection includes more completely new artists than usual who will make their debut at the fall auction. This also makes the exhibition particularly interesting, as young artists with very different styles and approaches have come together under one roof," Kuivjõgi said.
Now in its 11th year, the "Buy Young Art" exhibition and auction gives young artists an opportunity to introduce their work to a wider audience while also bringing young Estonian art closer to enthusiasts and buyers.
"This year's selection is truly diverse and offers an opportunity to explore different artistic media, as in addition to painting, it also features graphic art, drawing, collage, photography and sculpture. The prices of the works also vary widely and start at just €1. When it comes to young art, there is always something for everyone, whether an experienced collector or someone buying art for the first time," Kuivjõgi explained.
Entrepreneur and art enthusiast Kristjan-Thor Vähi, head of Invego and a member of the selection jury, said the high quality of the works made choosing among the candidates quite a difficult task.
"There are many different approaches and truly fresh ideas in the work of young Estonian artists and I really like the fact that they dare to experiment. The exhibition offers a good opportunity to become better acquainted with their work and see what our young artists are doing right now," he said.
According to Vähi, initiatives such as "Buy Young Art" are important for young artists because they help their work reach a broader audience beyond the art world.
"When an artist is at the beginning of their career and is still relatively unknown, an opportunity like this to show their work is very important. It is important for young Estonian art to be visible and accessible and the more young art reaches the public, the more confident people will become about buying it and thereby supporting local artists," he said.
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition is open at the Art & Tonic gallery through October 22. All works displayed at the exhibition will be offered at a public auction on October 23.

Advertisement
Five British men were arrested on Sunday, 27 September, on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act, after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase. From desalination to irrigation: How countries are adapting to water scarcity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

From desalination in the UAE to modernising irrigation systems in Uzbekistan, countries facing water pressure are finding ways to secure supplies and reduce losses.
Roughly half the world's population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year, according to the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a figure climate change, population growth and rising demand are expected to push higher.
The pressures vary by location. In the UAE, where rainfall is scarce and no permanent rivers exist, most drinking water comes via desalination of seawater. In Uzbekistan, agriculture depends on irrigation networks moving water across dry landscapes. Both countries are turning to technology and infrastructure to stretch limited supplies further.
Securing water in an arid climate
In the UAE, limited rainfall and the absence of permanent rivers have long shaped how communities obtain and use water.
Efforts to manage scarce resources predate modern desalination by centuries. Traditional falaj irrigation systems channelled water through settlements and agricultural areas allowing communities to sustain local economies.
Abdulla Balalaa, the UAE's Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said such systems were engineered over 1,000 years ago.
Today, much of the country's drinking water comes from desalination. Balalaa said the UAE has achieved universal access to water and is also applying newer technologies, including artificial intelligence, to the sector.
As populations and cities grow, limiting water use and reusing existing supplies are becoming increasingly important.
Few places demonstrate that principle as clearly as the International Space Station.
Emirati astronaut Dr Sultan Al Neyadi spent six months aboard the station, where water is needed for drinking, hygiene, food preparation and oxygen production.
“Every drop on board the International Space Station is accounted for,” Al Neyadi said. “We recycle about 95% of our water.”
Water passes through several stages of filtration before being used again, providing an example of how a limited resource can be repeatedly recovered rather than discarded when there are no other options.
The UAE is also seeking to push water higher on the international agenda. It will co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from 8 to 10 December. The event will bring together governments, international organisations, businesses and other stakeholders, with investment, technology and innovation among the areas under discussion.
Balalaa said solutions will vary by location. Technology and innovation can help bridge gaps, he said, alongside financing and cooperation needed to turn ideas into active projects.
In Uzbekistan, the pressures are different. Much of the country's agriculture relies on moving water over long distances, limiting losses along the way and ensuring it reaches farmland when it is needed.
Getting water to Uzbekistan's farms
Canals, reservoirs and pumping stations carry water across Uzbekistan's dry landscapes. In some areas, scarcity is therefore also a question of whether available water can reach agricultural land at the right time.
In the Fergana Valley, a World Bank-backed project launched in 2017 has modernised irrigation infrastructure.
At one site, water from local springs is collected and pumped around nine kilometres to areas where access has historically been difficult. The pumping station and pipeline are expected to improve irrigation for around 9,740 hectares of farmland.
More reliable irrigation has also allowed previously difficult-to-cultivate land to be farmed.
At one orchard in the valley, drip irrigation is used to deliver water to peach trees planted in 2024. The farm harvested around 200 tonnes of fruit the following year.
Moving water across the desert
Farther west, water from the Amu Darya is pumped across the desert through the Amu-Bukhara Machine Canal. The wider network irrigates more than 350,000 hectares across Bukhara and Navoi regions and supplies drinking water to Bukhara and Kogon.
The new Amu-Bukhara-1 pumping station replaced older infrastructure as part of a wider modernisation effort. Its digital control system tracks water and electricity use, and the new equipment has cut energy use by up to 15%.
Moving water over long distances is only one part of the process; preventing it from disappearing before reaching farms is another.
In parts of Bukhara, water losses through seepage previously reached around 37%, according to Sherzod Sharipov, a representative of the regional water delivery service. Canals are now being lined with concrete to reduce losses and provide steadier flows to farmers.
Farmer Hikmat Nazrullayev said large amounts of water once disappeared before reaching wheat and cotton fields. Since canals were lined, he said, irrigating crops has become easier.
Water beyond the fields
The irrigation network also connects agriculture with the wider environment.
Drainage and return flows from farmland feed Dengizkul, a wetland of international importance in Bukhara region and an important resting and wintering site for migratory birds.
Professor of Water Engineering Malika Ikramova said the lake receives water from precipitation and groundwater as well as drainage returning from irrigation systems. Its water is highly mineralised, but supports fisheries and provides habitat for migratory birds.
As populations grow and climate conditions change, Ikramova said reducing losses, improving water accounting and expanding water-saving irrigation will remain important.
“We are going to have to adapt,” she said.
From desalination in the Gulf to irrigation canals in Central Asia, the methods differ considerably. But the underlying task is similar: reducing losses and making limited water supplies go further.

Remaking scents: could fragrance tech help take pressure off endangered plants?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:15 UTC
22:00:15 KST

Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit.
The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree?
With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes.
Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.
“Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells.
Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory.
BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant.
The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year.
“The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.”
But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned.
“Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline.
Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant species,” she said.
There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work.
Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent.
“What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said.
Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents.
Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year.
Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows.
It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said.
“What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”

What to know about Mistral's ML4 as it bets on EU sovereignty in the US-China open-weight AI race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

Known as “Le Chonk,” the new frontier AI offering from French company Mistral says it will be the strongest open-weight AI outside China, as it bets that European "sovereignty" can win customers in a race increasingly framed as US versus China.
French artificial intelligence champion Mistral AI on Tuesday launched a public preview of a new frontier model that it says will be the most capable open-weight model developed outside China once its weights are released.
The launch comes as the race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge.
Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites.
Mistral is betting that its new open-weight model, called ML4, which has strong defence capabilities, will attract customers who want a European alternative built around "sovereignty."
Here is everything to know about the model.
ML4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," meaning the large chunky one, is "a new generation of models," Guillaume Lample, chief scientist and co-founder of Mistral, said in a press conference that Euronews attended.
The model focuses on cybersecurity and defence capabilities, which the company claims are stronger than those of its Chinese competitors.
“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks,” said Lample.
Mistral’s launch comes just a day after Reflection, a US startup, unveiled Beam as its first open-weight model and a Western counterweight to Chinese open models. Its weights are due later this month, and its performance claims have not been independently verified.
The rogue AI agents
Pierre Stock, Mistral's first employee and vice president of science, said that building a new AI model was "like building a spaceship".
He said every AI company is "moving at full speed". Though Mistral is only three years old, it is "definitely closing the gap" with its competitors, and in some aspects its new model is "basically stronger than China’s models from this summer," he said.
Last month, the company announced it raised €3 billion at a valuation of more than €21 billion, which it says is the largest equity round ever completed by a European technology company.
The model's release also comes as AI companies report AI agents acting on their own and hacking websites.
Stock argued that this has created a narrative for US companies to "market rogue events" as "only a few trusted players can take care of the technology."
He added that the "monopoly is controlled by the Americans but that open-weight models allow people to access models."
The company also said it leads open-weight models on manufacturing and finance tasks and on multimodal use, and that in coding it is closing the gap with other frontier models. Mistral also claimed the best results of any model — closed ones included — on grounding capabilities, and top-level performance on semiconductor benchmarks.
The French company said ML4 will get better, as training is not finished and reinforcement learning will conclude in the coming days.
Made in Europe
Mistral said ML4 was trained from scratch over two months on 4,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European data centres.
ML4 covers more than 160 languages, including every official EU language, and works across Latin and non-Latin scripts.
When will it be available?
The model is now available through Mistral's API on Mistral Studio. Mistral plans to release the weights on October 27.
Until then, developers, cybersecurity leaders and state authorities will be able to test the model in real-world settings.
