Female supporters of the Islamic Republic of Iran have begun training with Misagh, a shoulder-launched surface-to-air missile system designed to engage low-flying aircraft and drones, as part of training for the regime’s Jan Fada (self-sacrifice) campaign, according to images published by Iranian state media.
The images were published on Monday.
In addition to training with the missile system, the women were photographed holding firearms, learning to operate drones, and participating in what was described as “urban exercises” as part of the campaign’s first military training course.
Sasan Zare, spokesperson for the Jan Fada Movement, told the Iranian Student News Agency that the idea of self-sacrifice is part of the identity of the Iranian people.
“Recently, we have encountered a strange phenomenon; a large number of people from abroad are sending messages and saying that we are not Iranians, but we are ready to fight side by side with the Iranian people in the fight against America and the Zionist regime,” she said.
“This phenomenon was formed with the national identity of Iranians, and today it is multiplying in the number of free and free people in the world.”
The training course was reportedly held in multiple cities across Iran and included training in self-defense, first aid and rescue, crisis management, wilderness survival, urban warfare, rappelling, shooting, operating first-person view drones, and familiarization with various firearms.
Women’s military service remains limited under Iranian law
Though women are exempt from compulsory military service in the Islamic Republic, they can volunteer for service. Under Article 32 of Iran’s Army Law, women may be employed by the army only in medical and health-related positions, while their transfers should, where possible, take their husbands’ service conditions into account, according to the Austrian Centre for Country of Origin and Asylum Research and Documentation.
Even though women are denied career positions in the Islamic Republic, under Article 151 of the Constitution, the Basij Mostazafan unit is obliged to provide optional basic military training facilities for female citizens.
Iran reportedly recruits minors amid military personnel shortages
Despite the compulsory military service, the Islamic Republic has reportedly experienced severe personnel shortages in recent years, leading to the recruitment of minors in violation of international law. In March, Rahim Nadali, the cultural and artistic deputy of the IRGC’s Mohammad Rasoulollah Corps, told Iran’s Defa Press Agency that children aged 12 and up would be enlisted to help at checkpoints.
His comments came within days of the death of 11-year-old Alireza Jafari, who was killed at a military checkpoint while “on duty,” the Basij Teachers Organization said.
Zare claimed that more than 500,000 women registered within 100 minutes of registration opening for the “National Resistance” battalions, filling the first 1,000 units.

Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.
Another 4% of respondents said they were ready to endure the war for about a year, while 23% said they could continue for only several months or up to six months.
The remaining 11% were undecided.
"Despite the intensification of Russian terror against the civilian population — and the fact that our Western partners' response has not always been sufficiently decisive or backed by concrete actions — Ukrainians are prepared to continue bearing the burden of war until an acceptable peace is achieved," KIIS Executive Director Anton Grushetskyi said.
The survey was conducted from Sept. 12-21, when Russia had begun a new campaign of attacks involving jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure. KIIS noted that the survey was completed before subsequent attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River.
The findings also show that 79% of Ukrainians believe Ukraine will ultimately win the war, including 47% who are certain of victory and 32% who said they rather believe Ukraine will prevail. Only 7% believe Russia will win, while 14% were undecided.
However, confidence in an eventual Ukrainian victory has declined since late July. At that time, 85% said they believed Ukraine would win, including 60% who were certain of it.
By September, the share who were certain of victory had fallen to 47%.
At the same time, 69% said they would support an immediate ceasefire along the current front line if Ukraine did not legally recognize occupied territories as Russian, continued strengthening its military, and maintained its path toward the European Union and NATO.
The poll was conducted through computer-assisted telephone interviews with 1,002 adults across all regions of Ukraine controlled by the government.
Residents of Ukrainian territories not controlled by Kyiv and Ukrainian citizens who left the country after Feb. 24, 2022, were not included.

As Brazil heads to run-off, Israel’s Latin America ties are placed in spotlight - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:47:10 UTC
21:47:10 KST

Brazil’s presidential election is heading to a run-off on October 25. The development came after presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro won the first round of elections, defeating left-wing President Lula da Silva by several million votes. Bolsonaro is the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula has been a fixture of Brazilian politics for decades and is a well-known figure on the Left. He once led BRICS and has taken a softer stance toward Moscow in the Russia-Ukraine war.
Former president Bolsonaro was a supporter of Israel while he was in office, joining a trend of right-leaning leaders in Latin America who tend to be closer to Israel. This is part of a larger trend in Central and South America, where more right-leaning candidates are winning.
In a January interview with The Jerusalem Post, Flavio Bolsonaro said that, if elected, he would move Brazil’s embassy to Jerusalem within the first six months of his mandate.
In April, Argentinian President Javier Milei and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced the launch of the Isaac Accords. This illustrated the growing partnership between Israel and Argentina.
At the time, the Foreign Affairs Ministry noted: “The Isaac Accords constitute a new strategic framework aimed at strengthening cooperation between Argentina, Israel, and like-minded partners in the Western Hemisphere, the descendants of Isaac and nations of the Judeo-Christian tradition, in defense of freedom and democracy, and in the fight against terrorism, antisemitism, and drug trafficking. Participating countries will pursue concrete actions based on these principles.”
Netanyahu, Milei launching Isaac Accords sets foundation for Israel-LATAM relations
Last month, when Netanyahu met with Milei on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the Isaac Accords were once again in the spotlight. The two leaders discussed continued cooperation between their countries, which makes an expansion of the Isaac Accords, led by Milei, possible.
“This will deepen security and economic cooperation between Israel and the countries of Latin America,” the Prime Minister’s Office said.
In June, the Post noted that the Isaac Accords have been supported by, or could receive future support from, Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela, Ecuador, Colombia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, and Panama.
The “rightward shift” in Latin American politics is currently getting a lot of attention. Some commentators in the US believe it is due in part to the influence of the Trump administration and the end of USAID in the region. They argue that USAID funded left-leaning programs. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has made it clear that it supports certain leaders, such as Argentina’s president.
The US explicitly supported Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, who narrowly won the elections. The Guardian even claimed that the elections in Brazil are part of the US’s search for “control” of Latin America. Some call this the Donroe Doctrine – a new American version of the Monroe Doctrine. The arrest of Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 was part of this.
The New Arab sees the shifting political landscape as helpful to Israel. It noted that “Nicaragua, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, Bolivia, Cuba, and Belize all intervened in support of South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), while Colombia went one step further, placing a total ban on coal exports to Israel and terminating its bilateral free trade agreement.” Now, it argues that Bolivia and Honduras have shifted tack and become closer to Israel. Chile and Honduras have since returned their ambassadors to Israel.
In August, The New Arab noted: “The new president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, is ready to renew ties with Israel by ramping up security coordination, resuming coal exports, and withdrawing from the Hague Group. This week, the new right-wing government also recognized Israel’s claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967, becoming only the second country to do so after the Trump administration in 2019.”
Israel, Venezuela ties improving after Trump admin. ousts Maduro
The ties between Venezuela and Israel have also improved. In August, Reuters noted that “Venezuela’s government, now led by Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, said an Israeli humanitarian delegation visited the country after deadly earthquakes in June, and discussions took place among senior officials from both nations, leading to the deal to resume consular services.”
Colombia has likewise moved to improve ties with Jerusalem. In July, Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bola Escobar met with Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar. Sa’ar visited South America in August and went to both Ecuador and Colombia.
Many Middle Eastern countries are watching developments between Israel and Latin America. For instance, Turkey’s Anadolu news agency closely tracked which countries are moving their embassies to Jerusalem. In an April article, it noted that Argentina had joined Honduras, Guatemala, and Paraguay in the move.
The changing political map of Central and South America also has ramifications for Israeli defense ties. Latin America accounted for only 2% of Israel’s defense sales in 2025 and has never been a major market for Israel’s defense sector. Latin America generally prefers not to spend large sums on defense. Brazil, the region's largest spender, ranks 21st globally. This makes its spending less than that of Spain, Australia, Japan, Turkey, and Italy. In fact, Brazil’s defense spending is only 1% of its GDP.
Mexico, Colombia, Chile, and Argentina round out the top five defense spenders in Latin America. In terms of their GDP percentage, Colombia, Uruguay, Ecuador, Honduras, and Chile put 1.3 to 3.3% of their GDP into defense.
In August, Defense Minister Israel Katz “signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Honduras’s Defense Minister Enrique Rodríguez Burchard to deepen defense cooperation between the State of Israel and the Republic of Honduras,” the Defense Ministry said.
It added: “The MOU with Honduras joins a series of defense cooperation agreements advanced by the Defense Ministry over the past year with partners around the world, as part of the ministry’s strategy to expand Israel’s circle of defense partnerships, strengthen strategic ties with friendly nations, and deepen cooperation between Israel’s defense industries and international markets.”
This demonstrates that Israel wants more defense sales in the region. However, the big question is whether Latin America’s political shifts will lead to major changes on this front and others. Although Latin America has seen many changes, their implementation and scope have been narrow. The continent is broadly democratic, except for Nicaragua, Venezuela, and Cuba.
Many countries retain their old political parties, such as the Colorado Party in Uruguay and Paraguay. Argentina's Peronist party was founded in 1946. Over the next decade, it's plausible that the Left may return to power in some of these countries.
Brazil’s election is a veritable juggernaut. With some 110 million voters, it has more voters than all the other countries in South America combined. Central and South America are, in truth, divided almost equally between the Left and Right, and it remains to be seen what Brazil’s elections will bring.

FACTBOX: Russian President Vladimir Putin’s biography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:45:01 UTC
21:45:01 KST

MOSCOW, May 7. /TASS/. On October 7, 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin turns 74.
Background, education, academic degree
Vladimir Putin was born in Leningrad (since September 1991 St. Petersburg) on October 7, 1952.
In 1975, Putin graduated from the Department of Law (International Law Branch) of the Leningrad State University. He underwent a retraining course of KGB operatives in Leningrad (1976) and in Moscow (1979) at the Dzerzhinsky Higher School of the KGB of the USSR. In 1985, he graduated from the Andropov Institute of the KGB of the USSR (currently the Academy of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service, SVR).
Academic degree - Ph.D. in Economics. In 1997, Putin defended a thesis entitled Strategic Planning of the Mineral and Resources Base Reproduction in the Context of Emerging Free Market Economy Relations (St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region) at the St. Petersburg Mining Institute.
Career in the USSR’s state security services (1970s-1980s)
Upon graduation from the Leningrad State University, Putin was assigned to a position in the KGB of the USSR. His first job was in the secretariat and then in the counterintelligence unit of the KGB Office for Leningrad and the Leningrad Region. After a course of studies in Moscow, he was transferred to Department No. 1 (foreign intelligence) of the KGB Office for Leningrad and the Leningrad Region.
In 1985, he was given an assignment at the KGB office in the German Democratic Republic (united with the Federal Republic of Germany into a single state in 1990) and worked in Dresden up to 1990. He held positions of a senior operative, assistant and senior assistant to the chief of a section. Putin returned to the Soviet Union in January 1990.
Jobs at the St. Petersburg city administration (first half of the 1990s)
Starting from February 1990, he worked as a foreign affairs assistant to the Leningrad State University’s rector and then, as an adviser to Leningrad’s Mayor Anatoly Sobchak.
In June 1991, Putin was appointed to chair the foreign relations committee of St. Petersburg Mayor’s Office.
On August 19-21, 1991, an attempted coup d'etat took place in the USSR, organized by the State Committee on the State of Emergency (GKChP), which included members of the top Soviet leadership. Vladimir Putin, along with other officials from the Leningrad city administration, opposed the GKChP. On August 20, 1991, he submitted his resignation from the state security services.
In 1992, Putin took the position of St. Petersburg’s deputy mayor while retaining the post of the foreign relations committee chief. In March 1994, when Sobchak took over as the head of the city’s administration, Putin was appointed his first deputy. Later, when the posts of the head of the city administration and mayor were merged, Putin’s position was renamed to deputy mayor, chairman of the city’s foreign relations committee.
Positions in the Presidential Property Management Directorate and the Presidential Staff (second half of the 1990s)
After Sobchak's defeat in the St. Petersburg mayoral election in June 1996, Vladimir Putin left his post. In August of the same year Putin was transferred to a position at the Presidential Property Management Directorate in the capacity of its deputy chief. He supervised the directorate’s department of law and foreign property-related matters.
In March 1997, he started serving as deputy chief of the presidential staff and chief of the presidential Main Control Directorate. In May-July 1998, Putin served as first deputy chief of the presidential staff (it was headed by Anatoly Chubais in 1996-1997 and by Valentin Yumashev in 1997-1998).
Director of the FSB, head of government (1998-2000)
Between July 1998 and August 1999, Putin served as director of the Federal Security Service (FSB). Simultaneously, from March to August 1999, he was the Russian Security Council’s secretary.
On August 9, 1999, President Boris Yeltsin said in a televised address that he had made a decision to dismiss the government and asked the State Duma to endorse Vladimir Putin as the country’s new prime minister. Yeltsin said he saw Putin as his successor and hoped that he would manage to consolidate society. On the same day, Putin was appointed first deputy chairman of the Russian government and acting head of the cabinet of ministers.
On August 16, 1999, the State Duma approved Putin’s appointment as prime minister (233 out of 439 deputies voted for him, 84 against, and 17 abstained).
During his tenures as President of the Russian Federation (2000-2008)
Between December 31, 1999, and May 7, 2000, he was Russia’s acting president after President Boris Yeltsin had declared his resignation thus placing presidential duties in Putin’s hands.
On March 26, 2000, Russia saw an early presidential election. Putin, nominated by a group of voters, emerged the winner to have collected 52.94% of the votes in the first round. Communist candidate Gennady Zyuganov was second with 29.21%. The inauguration of the newly-elected president took place on May 7, 2000.
On March 14, 2004 Putin was elected for a second term, receiving 71.31% of the vote in the first round (Communist candidate Nikolay Kharitonov was the runner-up with 13.69%). His inauguration took place on May 7, 2004. Putin took office for another four-year term.
Russia’s prime minister, United Russia party’s leader (in 2008-2012)
Dmitry Medvedev, first deputy prime minister, was elected Russia’s president in 2008. On May 8, 2008, the State Duma approved Vladimir Putin as head of government (392 deputies out of 448 voted in favor, while 56 opposed the appointment). A presidential decree appointing him was signed that same day. Vladimir Putin succeeded Viktor Zubkov as prime minister and led the government until May 7, 2012.
In 2008-2012, he led the United Russia party (without being the party’s member).
Head of state (since 2012)
On September 24, 2011, at the proposal of Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, the 12th Congress of the United Russia party approved Vladimir Putin as the party's candidate for head of state in the 2012 election.
In the March 4, 2012 election Putin was elected president by a 63.6% majority vote in the first round. Communist candidate Gennady Zyuganov was second with 17.18%. Putin took office on May 7, 2012. Starting from 2012, the presidential term of office was extended to six years in accordance with an amendment to the Constitution.
On March 18, 2018 Putin was re-elected as Russia’s president by a 76.69% majority vote. He participated in the election as a candidate from the United Russia party. The runner-up, Pavel Grudinin of the Communist Party, received 11.77%. On May 7, 2018, Putin took office for a term of six years.
On March 17, 2024, Putin was re-elected president once again, garnering 87.28% of the vote, the highest figure in the history of Russia’s presidential elections. He ran in the election as an independent candidate. Communist contender Nikolay Kharitonov came second with 4.31%. On May 7, 2024, the inauguration ceremony took place for Vladimir Putin to assume the office of Russia’s president for a new six-year term.
As head of state, Putin is commander-in-chief of the Russian Armed Forces and chairman of the State Council and the Security Council. He also leads Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission (since September 10, 2014).
Chair of the presidential councils: On Interethnic Relations (since June 2012); On Countering Corruption and On Science and Education (both since July 2012); On the Development of Physical Culture and Sports and On the Development of Local Self-Government (both since August 2012); On Strategic Development and National Projects (since July 2018); and On Culture (since October 2025).
Serves as chair of the presidential commissions On the Development Strategy of the Fuel and Energy Complex and Environmental Safety, and On Military-Technical Cooperation between Russia and Foreign States (since June 2012).
Public activities
Vladimir Putin heads the All-Russia People's Front public movement, established in 2013 on his initiative as a coalition of socio-political forces.
He serves as chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Russian Geographical Society (since 2010), Lomonosov Moscow State University (since 2013), and the Russian Academy of Sciences (since May 2025), as well as Chairman of the Supervisory Board of the non-profit organization Russia - Land of Opportunity (since 2019).
Titles and Awards
Retired Colonel.
1st Class Active State Counsellor of the Russian Federation (1997).
Holder of the Order of the Badge of Honor (1988) and the Order of Honor (1996). He also holds foreign awards: Grand Cross (Grand-croix) of the Legion of Honour (France, 2006); the Order of Ho Chi Minh (Vietnam, 2001); the Order of the Golden Eagle/Altyn Qyran (Kazakhstan, 2004); the Order of Ismoili Somoni, 1st Class (Tajikistan, 2007); the Order of King Abdulaziz (Saudi Arabia, 2007); the Order of Zayed (UAE, 2007); the Order of Outstanding Merit/Buyuk Xizmatlari Uchun (Uzbekistan, 2008); the Order of the Precious Wand (Mongolia, 2009); the Order of the Liberator (Venezuela, 2010); the Order of Friendship of Peoples (Belarus, 2013); the Order of Saint Charles (Principality of Monaco, 2013); and the Order of Jose Marti (Cuba, 2014), the Order of the Republic of Serbia, 1st Class (2014), the Order of Manas, 1st Class (Kyrgyzstan, 2017), the Grand Cross of the National Order of Merit (Guinea, 2017), the Order of Friendship (China, 2018), the Order of Uatsamonga (South Ossetia, 2018), the Order of Agostinho Neto (Angola, 2019), the Order of the First President of the Republic of Kazakhstan - Leader of the Nation Nursultan Nazarbayev (Kazakhstan, 2019), the Order of Friendship, Highest Class (Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik, Uzbekistan, 2022), and the Order For Special Patriotic Care and Love for Republika Srpska (2023). In addition, Vladimir Putin’s awards include the Bronze Medal of Merit of the National People's Army of the GDR (1988) and the Gold Medal of the Parliament of Greece (2005).
He was awarded the A. M. Gorchakov Commemorative Medal (of the Russian Foreign Ministry, 2001).
Putin holds a number of ecclesiastical awards, including the Order of Saint Vladimir, Equal-to-the-Apostles and Grand Prince, 1st Class (Russian Orthodox Church, 2002); the Order of Glory and Honor (Russian Orthodox Church, 2007); the Order of Saint Sergius of Radonezh, 1st Class (Russian Orthodox Church); the Order of Saint Alexander Nevsky, Right-Believing Prince (Russian Orthodox Church, 2024); and the Order of Saint Savva, 1st Class (Serbian Orthodox Church, 2011).
He is an Honorary Citizen of Kazan (2005), St. Petersburg (2006), Astrakhan (2008), Sortavala (2010), and Sevastopol (2016), and the Chechen Republic (2024)
Recognition and language skills
Honorary doctor of a number of Russian and foreign academies and universities, including the Russian Military Medical Academy, St. Petersburg State University, Turkmen State University, Yerevan State University, Baku Slavic University (Azerbaijan), the University of Belgrade (Serbia), and Jawaharlal Nehru University (India). Honorary member of the Russian Academy of Arts.
Recipient of the Peter the Great National Public Award (2001), the award For Outstanding Activities in Strengthening the Unity of Orthodox Peoples (2002), the Order of St. Andrew the First-Called for Faith and Fidelity (2004), and the Confucius Peace Prize (China, 2011).
Named Person of the Year by the American magazine Time in 2007.
Topped the list of the world's most powerful people according to the American magazine Forbes in 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016.
In 2017, the US cable channel Showtime aired The Putin Interviews, a documentary by director Oliver Stone based on more than a dozen conversations with the Russian President held over the course of two years.
An avenue in Grozny, the Chechen Republic (2008), a peak in the Tian Shan mountain range in Kyrgyzstan (2011), and streets in Bethlehem (Palestine, 2012) and Tskhinval, the capital of South Ossetia (2019), have been named after Vladimir Putin.
Co-authored (with Vasily Shestakov and Alexey Levitsky) the book entitled Learning Judo with Vladimir Putin.
Speaks German and English.

Plague risk to UK 'very low', officials say after Russian woman's death

Former German intelligence head arrested on suspicion of espionage had traveled to Russia at least seven times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:44:55 UTC
21:44:55 KST

Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has reported the arrest of August Hanning, the former president of the country’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), on suspicion of espionage and treason. Along with Hanning, the agency detained Manfred D., the former head of his office.
Hanning headed the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. According to prosecutors, in 2010 Hanning made an arrangement with Manfred D. to receive information from the BND in exchange for payment.
Hanning intended to use the documents he received in his private consulting business. From 2010 to 2022, he obtained approximately 2,000 documents this way, many of them classified.
These materials were intended solely for the BND’s internal use and included, among other things, data from situational briefings. According to information from the German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR, the documents included materials from foreign partner agencies, documents on Iran’s nuclear program, and documents on the Russian military.
In at least one instance, Hanning is known to have prepared a security report for an unnamed foreign intelligence service (not a Russian one, according to media reports).
Meanwhile, after leaving the BND, Hanning made at least seven trips to Russia, The Insider found — all of them within the period from 2015 to 2019.
Often, Hanning would fly into Moscow in the evening and fly out the next day. In the summer of 2016 he flew from Munich to Moscow on the evening of July 6 and flew out to Berlin on the afternoon of July 7. A similar trip between Berlin and Moscow took place in May 2019.
The investigation into Hanning has continued for several months. He came to the attention of law enforcement last year in connection with his possible involvement in the abduction of the children of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block. As part of that case, Hanning’s home was searched in September 2025; some of the BND documents were found during those searches.

US trade deficit hits $105.6B in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:44:17 UTC
21:44:17 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The US international trade deficit reached $105.6 billion in August, marking a significant increase of 13.7% from the previous month due to a surge in imports, according to official figures released Tuesday.
The US Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced that the goods and services deficit stood at $105.6 billion in August, rising by $12.7 billion from July's revised figure of $92.8 billion.
August exports increased by 1.4% or $4.5 billion from the previous month to reach $315.2 billion.
The country imported goods and services worth $420.8 billion in the month, up 4.3% or $17.2 billion from July.
The wider gap in August reflected a $12.8 billion increase in the goods deficit to $136.6 billion, while the services surplus grew slightly to $31 billion.
For the first eight months of the year, the goods and services deficit fell by $138.2 billion, or 19.9%, compared to the same period in 2025.
Year-to-date exports jumped by $267.7 billion, or 11.8%, as imports grew by $129.5 billion, or 4.4%.
The US recorded the largest goods trade deficit with Mexico at $27.7 billion, followed by Vietnam with $24 billion and Taiwan with $18.3 billion.

Video: Should Finland ban homeschooling?
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:44:17 EEST
21:44:17 KST

The topic of homeschooling children has sharply divided public opinion in Finland over recent years, especially as the practice has grown in popularity.
According to figures from the Finnish National Agency for Education, there were 945 children being homeschooled in Finland last year — a figure that has tripled over the course of seven years.
While that share remains small (just 0.18 percent) compared to the overall number of schoolchildren, the growing numbers have raised concerns among education professionals and authorities about the welfare of homeschooled children.
The reasons that parents decide to homeschool their children vary widely — from keeping their child away from bullies to a belief that the child's neurodivergent needs are better catered for at home.
"I suppose every parent would want to protect their child from all possible pain and suffering, but we can't do that. Every day I was able to let my children grow and strengthen at home in peace, and that made them more prepared to face that world," one former homeschooling parent told Yle.
However, monitoring teachers interviewed by Yle noted that all too often the reasons behind the decision to homeschool a child are so-called "value-based", such as religious beliefs or extremist ideologies.
Jari Andersson, a school principal in the Pirkanmaa region who also works as a monitoring teacher for homeschooled children, told Yle that other concerns range from whether a child is getting a good education based on the national curriculum to the impact homeschooling can have on a kid's social skills and sense of belonging.
"In some cases, homeschooling is legalised neglect," Andersson stated, adding that he would want Finland to introduce an outright ban on the practice.
Unlike countries such as Sweden and Germany, Finland has no law on compulsory school attendance. This means that a simple note from a parent or guardian to the local municipality is enough to start homeschooling a child.
Although a child's progress is monitored by officials such as Jari Andersson, authorities have very limited powers when it comes to putting a stop to a child's homeschooling, even if they struggle to pass the basic tests.
Ombudsman for Children Elina Pekkarinen told Yle that she was not in favour of a complete ban on homeschooling, but she acknowledged that "homeschooling makes it possible to avoid authorities".
The high-profile disappearance of the Karf family from their home in Ostrobothnia last year has been linked to a dispute over homeschooling.
Juha Martelius, head of the Finnish Security and Intelligence Service (Supo), has also warned of the dangers of homeschooled children becoming marginalised or even radicalised.
In an interview with Yle, Education Minister Anders Adlercreutz (SPP) said authorities should have more powers to suspend homeschooling, especially in cases where a child's compulsory education requirements are not being met.

A Test for NATO and a “Small Victory” — Will Russia Start a New Conflict in the Baltics, and Is the Alliance Ready to Fight Back?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:44:09 EEST
21:44:09 KST

A Test for NATO and a “Small Victory” — Will Russia Start a New Conflict in the Baltics, and Is the Alliance Ready to Fight Back?
Kyiv • UNN
Russia may try to destabilize NATO through acts of sabotage, drones, and limited operations. The expert believes that the allies have enough strength to fight back.
Against the backdrop of Russia’s failures in its war against Ukraine and increasingly frequent statements by Western politicians about possible Kremlin provocations against NATO countries, the security of the Baltic region has once again come into focus. In a comment to UNN, Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, explained the methods Moscow could use to test the Alliance’s strength and whether the allies would have enough forces to repel an attack without guaranteed U.S. support.
As Zemlyanyi noted, the question of why Russia would attack the Baltic countries is quite complicated, since, from a military and political standpoint, the attack on Ukraine also did not seem entirely logical.
And, in fact, this is why many people in the West, as well as in Ukraine, did not believe that such a scenario could unfold. If we are talking about the Baltic countries in general and a potential conflict with NATO, then this is, first of all, an attempt... there could actually be several main objectives of such a military conflict. First and foremost, it is an attempt to destabilize NATO and the Baltic/Northern region and Eastern Europe, in order, above all, to disorganize these countries, undermine support—military support—for Ukraine, and thus divert attention from the war in Ukraine
He notes that a war with NATO could also be necessary for Russia to mobilize its domestic contingent and internal resources within Russian society, because a “small victorious war” always motivates a certain number of such passionate people who are ready to fight or seek some kind of victory for Russia.
This is precisely an example of a situation in which something is not working out for you on one front and things are going quite badly, although you demonstrate that you have made territorial gains. At the same time, a large part of Russian society that follows the war sees that things are not so simple and not so smooth, so one can launch some kind of, once again, small operation that would provide a positive impetus and demonstrate Russia’s strength. If, once again, we consider whether such an operation will take place, then first and foremost it would be an attempt, firstly, to test NATO and, in fact, disorganize it in such a way that resources and attention would be concentrated more on defending Europe itself than on supporting Ukraine
According to him, one should also not forget the constant attempts to carry out sabotage on the territory of European countries, as well as various information operations, which are conducted in order to undermine aid to Ukraine, disrupt supply routes, and complicate the situation for us.
This actually began in 2022. Here I would really single out three main vectors of Russian influence: the political one—an attempt to strengthen various political movements, including right-wing radical, left-wing radical, and anti-establishment movements. These include Germany’s “Alternative for Germany,” Italian right-wing forces, French right-wing forces such as Marine Le Pen, and so on. One of these vectors is military operations, sabotage operations, and hybrid operations on the territory of Europe. And, to a certain extent, information and cyberattacks carried out on the territory of and against the information space of European countries
Which Baltic countries remain vulnerable
According to the expert, all countries remain equally vulnerable, since this concerns a potential conflict, and it is not entirely clear how high the threshold for aggression could be.
So, if we are talking about some sub-threshold operations, sub-threshold actions aimed at examining in greater detail the response threshold of the Baltic countries and NATO itself, these could be operations involving drones. That is one possible option. And in this format, when we are talking about similar operations involving drones, some reconnaissance operations around the Baltic countries, absolutely all countries are under threat, from Poland to Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. But if we are talking about some purely military operation, some intervention into the territory of these countries, then first and foremost, it is probably Estonia that is meant here. And, in fact, it is probably no secret that the city of Narva, which is located on the border with Russia, is involved. This is the main area where it would be possible, so to speak, to "victoriously" seize some territory, bring it under control with fairly small forces and, in this way, achieve a primarily media victory in this operation
NATO and US response
The expert emphasizes that the question of US participation remains open in view of the latest developments, the latest changes in Donald Trump's policies and, in general, those of the administration in Washington.
He notes that it is obvious that the US is currently focused on Poland in Europe as its main foothold and principal ally in Europe through the combination and integration of the Polish and American military-industrial complexes.
Therefore, the issue remains open on the US side, but I am sure that NATO allies are still counting on support and assistance from the US. As for forces and resources, there are actually enough forces and resources to repel some limited military operations. Again, we are not saying that Russia would be able to deploy several combined-arms armies in order to launch a full-scale invasion of the Baltic countries. Most likely, these could be some sabotage operations, military operations, as was the case, for example, in Crimea, when some unidentified troops appeared and then effectively occupied the Ukrainian peninsula. The same could happen there. And the forces and resources available in the Baltic countries, as well as the units of allied countries — there should generally be enough of them to repel such aggression

Philippine inflation rises to 7.2 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:43:37 CST
21:43:37 KST

MANILA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- The Philippines' inflation climbed to 7.2 percent in September, up from 6.1 percent in August, driven by higher food, housing, and transport prices, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) said on Tuesday.
September inflation is significantly higher than the 1.7 percent recorded in the same month last year, according to the PSA.
In the first nine months of this year, the Philippines' average inflation reached 5.4 percent, surpassing the government target of 2.0 percent to 4.0 percent.
Food inflation rose to 6.7 percent in September from 4.6 percent in the previous month, contributing 2.6 percentage points.
Meanwhile, inflation in housing and utilities rose to 8.4 percent from 7.9 percent, with higher rent, electricity, and cooking gas prices, contributing 1.7 percentage points.
Transport prices also continued to increase in September, with inflation in the basket accelerating to 14.6 percent from 13.5 percent, contributing 1.3 percentage points. ■

Saxony-Anhalt elects first AfD state parliament president in Germany
China
Unknown Publisher

21:43:10 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- The state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday elected far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmaker Tobias Rausch as its president, making him the first AfD member in Germany to hold such a post.
The newly elected state parliament convened its first session in Magdeburg, the state capital. Rausch, 35, received 48 votes in favor in the first round, while 29 lawmakers voted against him and five abstained.
The AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote in the state election last month, becoming the largest parliamentary group but falling short of an absolute majority.
The president of the state parliament chairs parliamentary sessions and represents the legislature externally. Since 1990, all previous presidents of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament have come from either the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) or the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
According to German media reports, hundreds of protesters gathered outside the state parliament building on Tuesday to oppose Rausch taking office as president of the legislature. ■

UN chief urges developed nations to deliver finance, tech to build climate resilience ahead of COP31 in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:42:23 UTC
21:42:23 KST

Saadet Gokce
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres Tuesday urged developed nations to deliver finance and technology to build climate resilience ahead of COP31 in Türkiye.
"Leadership from vulnerable developing countries cannot substitute for responsibility from developed countries," Guterres said during a joint news conference with Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad. Guterres is visiting the country from Tuesday to Thursday.
The G20 represents 80% of global emissions, he said, emphasizing the need for "a drastic reduction in those emissions this decade."
"The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities must apply, but all countries must do their part," Guterres said, urging developed countries to respect their commitments, particularly "those established in COP29 in Baku and deliver the finance, technology and support developing countries need to build resilience and accelerate a just transition."
Developed countries agreed at the Baku climate summit to mobilize at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035 to support climate action.
Guterres also recalled his last visit to Pakistan in 2022, when he traveled to the country following devastating floods.
"Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions. It is also on the frontlines of the response," he said.
The UN's COP31 conference will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, from Nov. 9-20.

Kabul hosting 180-member Iranian private sector trade delegation
TEHRAN- Afghan media reported the arrival of a 180-member trade delegation from Iran’s private sector to participate in the Kabul International Exhibition and discuss expanding exchanges and investment between the two countries.
According to IRNA, a 180-member trade delegation from Iran’s private sector, headed by Mahmoud Siadat, head of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce, entered Kabul on Tuesday.
According to this report, members of this large economic delegation are scheduled to attend the “Imam Abu Hanifa” International Exhibition in Kabul and meet with Afghan economic actors to examine ways to expand trade exchanges and opportunities for joint investment between the two countries.
Afghan economic experts consider the meetings between the Tehran and Kabul delegations important for strengthening economic and commercial ties between the two countries, and say these meetings can pave the way for expanding trade cooperation, investment, and transit.
Abdul Nasir Rashtia, an Afghan economic expert, said in this regard that establishing strategic and favorable relations with neighboring countries is of vital importance for Afghanistan.
Referring to the lack of regular transportation and an equipped railway network, he added: The more we use the routes of neighboring countries for exports and imports, the more the costs of transporting goods will decrease.
The exchange of economic delegations between the two countries comes as Tehran and Kabul have set a target of raising the volume of bilateral trade to $10 billion per year.
According to reports, the fifth national and international Imam Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) Exhibition begins on October 7, and runs for one week.
According to reports, traders, investors, and companies from more than 20 countries, including the Islamic Republic of Iran, Russia, India, Turkey, Japan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan, are participating.

2 Months Under Drapaty: Ukraine’s Army Is Winning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:42:21 UTC
21:42:21 KST

Ten weeks into the job of commanding all of Ukraine’s armed forces, Lt. Gen. Mykhailo Drapaty has defeated Russian troops in sectors across the front, inflicting punishing casualties, forcing embarrassing retreats, and creating the uncomfortable reality for the Kremlin that Ukrainian soldiers are now liberating ground faster than Russian forces are capturing it.
Alongside deliberate, incremental, and slow-paced attacks that exploit Ukraine’s greatest tactical strengths, drones and skilled drone operators, while risking human soldiers only as a last resort, Drapaty, 43, has also been carrying out a deliberate house-cleaning of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) upper ranks. Legacy-era, older, or exhausted senior officers are being shifted to training roles, retirement, or rear-area assignments, while younger, combat-tested commanders with experience in 21st-century warfare are taking their place.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Drapaty’s command style, which emphasizes delegating authority, providing sufficient weaponry, and granting initiative to local commanders, has in some sectors effectively neutralized the Russian army’s numerical advantage over the AFU. The result has been a military buzz saw capable of shredding Russian assaults regardless of how many troops the Kremlin throws forward. Where the AFU has attacked successfully under Drapaty’s command, the formations leading those assaults have consistently been experienced combat units with excellent fighting records, commanded by officers with deep expertise in drone warfare and modern combat tactics.
Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
In the critical Donetsk-region sector Dobropillya, currently the focus of heavy Russian infantry attacks, Kremlin daily losses have reached some of their highest levels of the war in repeated failed attempts to break into positions held by the 1st Azov Corps, a National Guard formation commanded by Brig. Gen. Denys Prokopenko, a 35-year-old former English teacher. Azov Corps recruits nationwide and promotes itself as one of the AFUs most disciplined and hardest-fighting major combat formations.
Drapaty’s greatest offensive success has come in the northeastern Lyman sector, where a former historian and part-time politician, Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, 47, has at the head of the 3rd Corps “Troika” recovered some 176 square kilometers (105 square miles) of territory held by Russia since 2022, capturing hundreds of prisoners and inflicting a reported 5,000 Russian casualties, killed and wounded, in about three months of fighting.
Biletsky’s counteroffensive, Operation Vivaldi, is still in progress, and both 3rd Corps and AFU sources say more ground gains are coming. Thanks to its links to the capital and Kyiv’s urban, educated population, as well as Biletsky’s political connections, the 3rd Corps is one of the AFU’s most professionally skilled and best-resourced formations.
An offensive launched by Drapaty’s predecessor in January in the eastern Oleksandrivka sector has, since the summer, maintained its pace, with AFU forces scoring incremental ground gains day after day. Estimates of territory recovered from Russian control over the past nine months range from 600 to 750 square kilometers (232 to 290 square miles), with around 15,000 Russian casualties reported and 26 settlements liberated.
The commander of that counteroffensive, Maj. Gen. Oleh Apostol, 39, is a professional officer with combat experience stretching back to 2014 and Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine. A trained paratrooper and infantryman, he is the overall commander of the AFU’s elite Air Assault Forces, both corps of which, the 7th and 8th, currently form the backbone of offensive operations in that sector.
In all of those operations, the Drapaty-led AFU has rejected legacy-era massed tank assaults preceded by artillery bombardments and air strikes. Instead, both on the offensive and in defense, the first act of an AFU battle is relentless drone reconnaissance, strikes against Russian drone operators, interceptor missions targeting Russian drones in the air, and drone attacks on detected Russian positions and on the trucks, motorcycles, and foot soldiers carrying supplies to those positions. Only when Russian defenses are judged sufficiently weakened are human troops risked in an attack. When assaults do take place, AFU soldiers ride forward in armored vehicles escorted by more drones.
A Monday article by the major news magazine Ukrainska Pravda described Drapaty’s command style in blunt terms: “The first word with which brigade and corps commanders describe the application months of Drapaty’s work is ‘freedom.’”
As fighting operations have gone forward, Drapaty and his chief of staff, a combat-seasoned paratrooper named Ihor Skybiuk, 49, have carried out a slow-motion purge of senior officer billets across the AFU, while shifting command structures to give the most effective formations more authority and responsibility. A key change, ordered into effect in September, placed the junior brigadier generals Denys Prokopenko and Andriy Biletsky in effective command of defenses in the Donetsk region, Russia’s declared top territorial objective in Ukraine.
Young commanders who in the past had been shunted into reserve assignments or backwater jobs, sometimes for openly criticizing stand-and-die orders issued by previous AFU leadership, have found themselves rehabilitated by Drapaty and Skybiuk and placed at the head of major formations. One of the most prominent examples was the promotion of Col. Serhii Sobko to command the 11th Corps. As an air assault officer, Sobko resigned his brigade command in 2025 because Kyiv and the General Staff were unwilling to send it support or allow it to withdraw from exposed positions. Now, Sobko and the 11th Corps are responsible for the defense of the fortress city of Sloviansk, another priority Kremlin objective.
Military analyst Giorgi Revishvili, in a Monday analysis of Drapaty’s command priorities and plans for the future of the AFU, wrote that Drapaty’s outlook goes beyond the day-to-day task of engaging and defeating Russian Federation forces. According to Revishvili, his goal is to build a Ukrainian military capable of deterring Russia and supporting Europe’s security for decades to come. The key to that, he wrote, is leveraging Ukraine’s edges in tech development so that the AFU “learns faster than Russia” and “gives subordinate commanders greater authority and responsibility” in order to make operations faster and more effective.
According to Monday reports, Drapaty’s team is currently working on an as-yet-classified strategic vision paper that has already been submitted in draft form to Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council. The document reportedly sets out AFU priorities and development plans for the next three decades. Once approved, the plan would give Ukraine’s military, for the first time in its history, a long-term roadmap for its future.
Drapaty, in a Sept. 2 open-source paper, said his goal for Ukraine’s armed forces is to “achieve a long-term and just peace and create such Armed Forces of Ukraine that in the future no aggressor will have reason to consider an attack on Ukraine an acceptable way to achieve its goals.”

A Spanish judge on Tuesday lifted the arrest warrant for former Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, clearing the way for his return to Spain ahead of a snap general election on November 29.
Supreme Court judge Pablo Llarena lifted the warrant after the Constitutional Court backed extending Spain’s 2024 amnesty law to cover the crime of embezzlement.
The decision marks a major development in the long-running legal and political dispute over Catalonia’s failed 2017 independence bid, which triggered Spain’s deepest political crisis in decades.
Amnesty reshapes Puigdemont’s legal battle
Around 400 people involved in the independence movement have benefited from the amnesty, which was introduced by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Socialist government to ease tensions in Catalonia and secure the support of separatist parties.
Puigdemont, who led Catalonia’s regional government when it held a banned independence referendum and later declared an attempted secession, had remained excluded from the measure.
He was accused of using public funds to organise the referendum, with Spanish courts previously ruling that the conduct amounted to embezzlement.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 to avoid detention and remained under an arrest warrant for nearly a decade. Spain’s Supreme Court had initially ruled that the amnesty did not apply to people investigated for embezzlement, including Puigdemont.
Sanchez welcomed Tuesday’s decision, saying it would allow Catalonia to “look to the future.”
“We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time,” he said at a news conference in Madrid.
Coming out of exile
Puigdemont briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 after almost seven years in exile, appearing before thousands of supporters and renewing his call for Catalan independence.
He disappeared before a regional parliamentary vote that installed Socialist Salvador Illa as Catalonia’s leader, evading a police operation aimed at arresting him before returning to Belgium.
The amnesty law has remained deeply divisive in Spain. The conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox have argued that it undermines the rule of law and accused Sanchez of exchanging legal concessions for the parliamentary support of Catalan separatists.
Puigdemont’s Junts party later withdrew its backing for Sanchez’s minority government, accusing him of failing to honour commitments, including the amnesty for its leader.
Junts’ seven lawmakers voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez’s government last Friday, helping trigger their defeat.
Sanchez responded by calling a snap general election for November 29, bringing the vote forward from its scheduled date by several months.
Meanwhile, Junts has seen its support weaken as the Catalan independence movement loses momentum and the far-right separatist party Alianca Catalana emerges as a growing rival.

Odesa’s budget missed out on more than UAH 500 million in rent for municipal properties: three managers of municipal enterprises suspected
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:41:55 EEST
21:41:55 KST

Odesa’s budget missed out on more than UAH 500 million in rent for municipal properties: three managers of municipal enterprises suspected
Kyiv • UNN
Three municipal enterprise managers were notified of suspicion over the undocumented lease of sewage facilities. Odesa’s budget missed out on more than UAH 594 million\r\n.
In Odesa, three managers of a municipal enterprise were served with notices of suspicion over the improper formalization of leases for reconstructed wastewater infrastructure facilities. As a result, the city budget received more than UAH 594 million less in revenue. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
In Odesa, a private company used wastewater infrastructure facilities renovated with community funds for more than five years without a properly formalized lease. According to the investigation, as a result, the city budget received more than UAH 594 million less in revenue. Under the procedural guidance of the Odesa Regional Prosecutor’s Office, the incumbent director of the municipal enterprise and two of its former heads were notified of suspicion of official negligence
In particular, according to the available information, the facilities in question are two sewage pumping stations and two collectors. In 2013, due to their unsatisfactory technical condition, they were withdrawn from the lease and transferred to the municipal enterprise for reconstruction.
At the same time, more than 45 million US dollars in loan funds from an international bank were spent on restoring the facilities, while the loans were repaid from the Odesa budget.
After the reconstruction, the facilities once again began to be used by a private company that provides the city’s water supply and wastewater services. However, the leases for them were not properly formalized, so the city did not receive separate rental payments. According to the investigation, from January 2020 to October 2025, the three heads of the municipal enterprise failed to take the necessary measures to formalize the paid use of this property. Instead, the company operated it under a maintenance agreement. Following the reconstruction, the value of the facilities increased, and therefore the rent should have increased as well
According to the investigation, a forensic economic examination established that, due to the absence of properly formalized leases, the Odesa budget received more than UAH 594 million less in revenue.
The suspects’ actions were qualified under Part 2 of Article 367 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. Preventive measures have now been imposed on them.

The 'death' of back-office jobs: office work in the AI storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:41:50 UTC
21:41:50 KST

From insurance payouts to banking, AI is taking over tasks that once took hours or days of human work – which office jobs are first in line for automation?
Two years ago, processing a health insurance claim at one of Greece's largest insurance companies took on average 14 days. Medical opinions, test results, invoices and policy details all had to be checked and cross-referenced before payment was given the green light.
Today, the processing time has been cut to around one minute and the compensation is paid out the following day.
Driving this change is AI Flows, an artificial intelligence tool for document processing and workflow automation developed by the Greek company Archeiothiki. The system handles around 1,500 claims a day, "reads" the documents, extracts the necessary information and cross-checks it against the policy and the insurance company's rules.
Above all, though, it enables something that was previously practically impossible: checking 100% of cases rather than just a sample. This makes it possible to spot potential fraud that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.
The example of the Greek insurer offers a snapshot of a much broader transformation unfolding in offices across Europe.
From 16 hours to a few minutes
In banking, similar technology is used to assess the ESG (environmental, social governance) criteria of companies seeking finance.
The process involves around 300 questions. To verify the answers, staff must hunt for data in company reports running to hundreds of pages, ranging from the ratio of men to women to information on environmental performance and corporate policies.
This check used to require about 16 hours of human labour. Now, an AI system can search for the necessary information even in reports running to 400 or 500 pages, identify the relevant passages and process them in a fraction of the time.
The final assessment of ESG criteria influences the interest rate at which the company will be financed.
Jobs on the frontline
Archeiothiki currently applies AI Flows to around 100 different workflows for ten clients, mainly banks, insurance companies and businesses in the healthcare sector.
But what is happening in Greece is far from unique.
Office roles that have traditionally formed the back office of companies are among those most exposed to the new generation of artificial intelligence.
According to the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure", published in May 2025 by the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Polish research institute NASK, administrative and clerical occupations remain the category of jobs most exposed to generative AI.
Among the most exposed roles are data entry clerks, staff involved in accounting and bookkeeping, and administrative secretaries. In high-income economies, roughly one in three jobs shows some degree of exposure to generative AI.
Artificial intelligence has already entered European workplaces on a large scale. According to the study "Digital Monitoring, Algorithmic Management and the Platformisation of Work in Europe" by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission, published in October 2025, 30% of workers in the EU already use AI tools in their jobs. Use is particularly high in office work.
The transition also has a clear gender dimension. More recent ILO research shows that occupations where women are in the majority are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI as those where men predominate: 29% compared with 16%.
One key reason is the greater presence of women in administrative, clerical and support roles.
"I will not hide it. There are jobs that are lost too," was the response of Archeiothiki executives when asked about this by Euronews.
The picture they sketch, however, is more complex. In many cases, automation is not used simply to carry out the same volume of work with fewer people. It allows companies to take on tasks that were previously practically impossible to perform at this scale.
One client, for instance, had around 50 people working on a single process and still built up a year-long backlog. In other cases, where only a sample of cases could previously be checked, now the entire set can be examined.
This aligns broadly with the ILO's assessment. The organisation warns that the "exposure" of a job to artificial intelligence does not necessarily mean that role will disappear. Few occupations consist solely of tasks that can currently be fully automated. For this reason, the most likely outcome for now is the transformation of jobs rather than their complete replacement.
The next data reservoir: the public sector
In Greece, the next major field may lie in the millions of documents that have already been digitised in the public sector.
According to Archeiothiki's chief executive, Andreas Papadakis, the company has carried out around 15% of the relevant digitisation projects for the state.
The problem is that much of this new digital archive remains effectively "blind". Physical documents were turned into digital files and given basic metadata so they could be searched. Their content, however, was not necessarily converted into structured data that can be analysed and put to use.
The first stage of digitisation was to turn mountains of paper into digital files. The next stage is already under way.
AI systems are no longer confined to reading and recording documents, but can extract information, cross-check it and execute entire workflows.
This shifts automation away from repetitive data-entry tasks to a much larger portion of the traditional back office.

Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:41:48 UTC
21:41:48 KST

Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Florida Museum of Natural History
- Summary:
- Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.
- Share:
About a century ago, archaeologists excavating pottery fragments around Tampa Bay encountered something puzzling. Some of the pieces carried decorations that looked strikingly similar to pottery found hundreds of miles farther north. On appearance alone, the fragments seemed connected to the Mississippian culture, which emerged more than 1,000 years ago and reshaped social, economic and political life across much of southeastern North America.
For decades, however, maps of the Mississippian world generally left out peninsular Florida. The Tampa Bay pottery suggested that the region's relationship with that culture may have been more complicated.
"It's been this open debate for a century," said Neill Wallis, curator of Florida archaeology, bioarchaeology and the Ceramic Technology Laboratory at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "Tampa Bay sites had some Mississippian-like traits such as platform mound-village complexes and iconography, but lacked others, like maize agriculture and shell-tempered pottery. The Mississippian-looking pottery has always begged the question: How did this stuff wind up in Tampa Bay?"
Mississippian pottery could provide some of the strongest evidence linking Tampa Bay communities with the broader culture. But decorative similarities alone could not reveal where the vessels had actually been made. Lacking the necessary technology and expertise to answer that question, museum curators stored the mysterious fragments while competing explanations remained unresolved.
Researchers at the Florida Museum have now conducted a study aimed at determining where the pottery came from and who made it.
"We were curious to find out if these vessels were imported from the heartland by trade, if they were local imitations of Mississippian motifs, or, as we ultimately found, if they were made by migrants who had made their way into communities in Tampa Bay to take up shop and residency there," said Trevor Duke, who began conducting the research for his doctoral dissertation at the University of Florida. In the years since, Duke and his colleagues have expanded on the initial scope of his dissertation to compile more evidence from a larger collection of samples.
By examining details of pottery production that are almost invisible from the surface, the researchers traced the decorated vessels to a small community of skilled craftspeople who likely traveled hundreds of miles from the Mississippian heartland before settling in Tampa Bay. Compared with the plain molded pottery widely used in the area, the decorated vessels were made with different clay, tempering materials, and production methods. Those differences suggest the migrants possessed specialized expertise and access to resources unavailable to many local residents.
Mississippian Culture Spreads Across the Southeast
Around 1000 A.D., a new cultural system developed in the Mississippi River Valley and spread across large parts of what are now the Midwest and eastern United States. In its core regions, Indigenous communities became organized into political hierarchies, with powerful chiefdoms exerting influence over surrounding settlements. Large areas were planted with maize, while enormous quantities of earth were moved to construct mounds topped by temples and residences for leaders.
Tampa Bay lay far outside those major northern centers.
The regional culture that occupied Tampa Bay and nearby areas during this period is known as Safety Harbor. Like Mississippian societies, Safety Harbor communities formed smaller chiefdoms and constructed flat-topped mounds. The region's largest settlement was home to the Tocobaga, while smaller Mocoso, Pohoy, and Uzita chiefdoms were scattered nearby.
Yet important differences remained. None of these groups accumulated the same level of political power seen in the major Mississippian centers farther north. Tampa Bay communities also never adopted the extensive maize agriculture associated with Mississippian society, relying instead on fishing and other marine resources.
Because of this mixture of similarities and differences, archaeologists have long struggled to determine how closely Tampa Bay was connected to the Mississippian heartland. The discovery of pottery decorated in Mississippian styles only deepened the mystery.
To investigate, Duke and other Florida Museum archaeologists assembled 58 plain and decorated pottery fragments from Tampa Bay. Both kinds of vessels were likely used for preparing and serving food, although the decorated pieces may have been reserved for special events.
Mississippian potters of the period commonly mixed crushed freshwater shell or fragments of older pottery, known as grog, into their clay. They also built vessels by stacking coils of clay rather than molding them.
Those manufacturing details offered researchers a way to distinguish genuine Mississippian traditions from local copies. If the decorated Tampa Bay vessels had been imported or produced by potters trained in Mississippian methods, the fragments should preserve evidence of these techniques. If local potters had simply copied the decorative appearance, the underlying construction would instead reflect familiar Tampa Bay practices such as sand tempering.
Local Clay, Distant Pottery Traditions
The researchers first used neutron activation analysis to measure the chemical composition of the pottery. They compared those results with raw clay deposits from the Tampa Bay area.
The chemistry matched, showing that the vessels had been produced locally. That finding ruled out the possibility that finished pottery had been manufactured in the Mississippian heartland and transported south through trade. It did not, however, eliminate the possibility that Tampa Bay potters had copied northern designs.
The team then examined thin slices of the fragments under a microscope using a technique called petrography. Researchers polish a section of pottery until it is roughly half the width of a human hair, allowing light from a polarizing microscope to pass through it. Tiny grains, cracks and empty spaces can then reveal how the clay was prepared and what materials were mixed into it.
"Looking at the section under a microscope, you can identify the minerals in it based on their color and shape. From that, we can figure out what was added to it. It's a sort of fingerprint of the people who made it," Wallis said.
That microscopic examination produced some of the study's most revealing evidence.
Several decorated fragments contained grog, the crushed pottery temper associated with some Mississippian traditions. Adding grog improves the durability of a vessel and helps it tolerate the intense heat of firing and cooking.
"This grog tempering is not something that we saw previously or in the plain samples in Tampa Bay," Duke said. "But up in the Tallahassee Hills, where the nearest massive Mississippian mound center is located, it's common in all vessels. It's the plain-Jane tempering technique there."
The connection extended beyond manufacturing technique.
The Tallahassee Hills lie roughly 200 miles north of Tampa Bay. Inside the grog used in the decorated vessels, researchers found mica, a reflective silicate mineral that is common in the Florida Panhandle but unusual in peninsular Florida. Although the surrounding clay in the vessels came from Tampa Bay, some of the crushed material mixed into it appears to have originated farther north in the Mississippian heartland.
Grog appeared in 80% of the decorated pottery analyzed, but researchers did not find it in a single piece of plain pottery. Most of the plain vessels instead contained dry clay fragments or sand, materials that had been used in local pottery traditions for about 3,000 years.
Other differences reinforced the distinction. The decorated vessels were constructed using the Mississippian technique of coiling clay and followed more consistent clay recipes, suggesting a higher degree of specialized knowledge. Plain vessels, in contrast, were molded. That simpler technique became increasingly common as the region's population grew and could be learned quickly by people without advanced pottery experience.
Migrants May Have Carried Pieces of Home
Together, the evidence points toward potters who migrated from the Mississippian heartland and brought both their technical knowledge and materials with them.
As these craftspeople traveled south from northern Florida, they may have carried pieces of older pottery made from clay found in their homeland. Once they reached Tampa Bay, those vessels could have been crushed, ground into small fragments, and mixed into newly gathered local clay.
The practice may have carried cultural meaning as well as practical benefits.
The migrants appear to have specifically selected decorated pottery from their homeland for use as grog. Every grog tempered vessel examined by the researchers contained what is known as multigenerational grog, in which one fragment of grog contains an even older piece of grog inside it. In effect, pottery from one generation had been incorporated into the pottery of the next.
"It's sort of like Russian nesting dolls because you have grog within grog within grog. You can trace this back several generations of pots," Wallis said. "And they're not using vessels from just anywhere. They're crushing up the same decorated vessels that include pieces of decorated pottery from before."
These embedded fragments were tiny physical pieces of the migrants' homeland that continued to be incorporated into vessels made generations later in Tampa Bay.
Their pottery expertise and their connection to Mississippian traditions may also have helped the newcomers establish a valuable role in their adopted community. Skills that were ordinary in their homeland could have become highly specialized and desirable once they moved south.
"Migrant communities often had to figure out their own niche in a new place," said Andrea Torvinen, collections manager of the Ceramic Technology Lab and Florida Archaeology at the Florida Museum. "What would have made these migrants stand out? How would they have established a role in this new area? Bringing a specialized knowledge of pottery production seems to have been one way they could do so."
Evidence suggests those skills were highly valued. The advanced techniques appear almost entirely in decorated pottery, while everyday plain vessels continued to be made with simpler local methods. Decorated pots were also produced using higher quality clay, suggesting that the migrant potters were allowed access to scarce, superior materials for their work.
How Specialized Pottery Skills Stayed Exclusive
The divide between decorated and plain pottery continued for centuries, raising another question: Why did local residents not simply learn the migrants' more advanced techniques?
The researchers suggest that the knowledge remained concentrated within a small group of craftspeople who worked closely together. Whether intentionally guarded or simply transmitted within tight social networks, the techniques were not widely shared.
"The group of potters making the decorated vessels likely had some kind of special status that they maintained through this secretive practice, even if it wasn't a secret in the sense that no one knew about it," Wallis said. "In fact, for secrets like this, you do have to broadcast some of the details so that people know there is a secret."
High quality decorated vessels would likely have circulated widely and been prized throughout the community. But many of the features that made them distinctive, including grog tempering, coiled construction and carefully standardized clay preparation, were hidden inside the finished pottery and therefore difficult to copy.
Without direct access to the small circle of migrant potters who knew these methods, Tampa Bay residents would have had little opportunity to learn them.
"People with specialized skills have direct relationships with the people learning from them. That's how we see knowledge passed down. When it's the way your mentor has always done it, that's how you're going to do it," Torvinen said. "And in this case, there could have been a more meaningful reason behind it. By tying the homeland pottery into this enchainment, they're bringing those pots with them into the next generation."
The study was published in American Antiquity.
