AI Voice Detector: How to Identify Synthetic Speech Online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:18:35 UTC
21:18:35 KST

Excerpt AI-generated and cloned voices are becoming harder to recognize by ear alone. This guide explains how AI voice detection works, why audio quality and source context matter, and how tools such as DetectVoice AI can support a careful verification process without treating one result as absolute proof.
An AI Voice Detector is becoming an important verification tool in a digital environment where a familiar voice can no longer be accepted as proof of identity. Synthetic speech can now imitate tone, rhythm, accent, and emotional delivery well enough to make ordinary listeners hesitate. As voice cloning moves into fraud, misinformation, impersonation, and social engineering, the ability to examine suspicious audio has become part of basic digital literacy.
The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded more than 22,000 complaints involving AI-related information and more than $893 million in adjusted losses. It also notes that voice cloning can be used in business email compromise and distress scams. The Federal Trade Commission has separately warned that AI-enabled voice cloning creates risks for consumers and businesses.
What Is an AI Voice Detector?
An AI voice detector is a system designed to examine spoken audio for patterns associated with synthetic or AI-generated speech. Instead of asking whether a voice simply “sounds real,” a detector analyzes characteristics in the signal that may be difficult for a listener to notice consistently.
These systems can look at acoustic texture, frequency relationships, timing, continuity, and other signal-level features. A model then compares the recording with patterns learned from human and synthetic speech. The output is best understood as evidence about the audio signal, not as absolute proof of who spoke, what tool was used, or whether the statement in the recording is true.
A human speaker can sound unusual because of compression, noise, emotion, or editing, while an AI-generated voice can sound highly natural. Voice authenticity therefore requires more than a single impression.
Why Synthetic Speech Is Getting Harder to Recognize
Modern generative audio systems can create speech with natural pauses, realistic breathing patterns, expressive intonation, and convincing pronunciation. Voice cloning can also imitate the vocal identity of a specific person from available samples. This makes casual listening less reliable than it once was.
Synthetic speech itself is not inherently harmful. It can support accessibility, narration, translation, entertainment, and education. The risk appears when generated or cloned audio is presented deceptively to impersonate a trusted person, manipulate public discussion, or request money or sensitive information.
For that reason, the central question is not simply, “Was AI used?” A stronger verification process asks where the recording came from, whether the source can be trusted, whether the audio has been edited, and whether the claim can be independently confirmed.
How AI Voice Detection Works
AI voice detection generally starts with the audio signal itself. The recording may contain subtle patterns related to synthesis, spectral structure, timing, or continuity. Detection models evaluate combinations of these features rather than relying on one obvious clue.
Recording quality plays a major role. Compression, denoising, background music, overlapping speakers, re-recording through another device, and editing can remove or alter information that would otherwise help analysis. A short or heavily processed clip may therefore produce less reliable evidence than a clean original recording.
This is why responsible tools communicate uncertainty. A detector can flag synthetic-like characteristics, miss AI-generated audio, or incorrectly flag human speech. As the FTC has noted in its work on voice cloning, there is no single technical solution that eliminates the problem. Detection is one layer in a broader verification process.
A Practical Way to Review Suspicious Audio
When a recording creates doubt, the first step should be preserving the best available source. Avoid repeatedly converting, cleaning, or editing the file before analysis. If possible, keep the original version and note where it came from.
Next, listen carefully without treating any one artifact as proof. Unusual rhythm, changes in texture, unnatural transitions, or inconsistent background sound may justify closer examination, but authentic recordings can contain the same characteristics.
Then use an AI voice detector to add a signal-based assessment. The result should be considered alongside recording quality and source history. If the message involves money, identity, reputation, security, or a public claim, verify it through another trusted channel. If an urgent voice message appears to come from a relative or executive, contact that person using a known phone number rather than replying through the suspicious message.
Finally, document what is known and what remains uncertain.
Where DetectVoice AI Fits Into the Verification Process
DetectVoice AI is built around this evidence-first approach. The platform allows users to analyze a recording for patterns associated with AI-generated or synthetic speech while keeping interpretation connected to recording quality, source context, and uncertainty.
Rather than presenting a model score as a final verdict, DetectVoice encourages users to examine the signal, review the audio closely, and decide what requires independent confirmation. Its workflow includes local listening tools, waveform review, precise seeking, segment markers, and private result history. The service currently offers one successful free analysis for a verified email without requiring a payment card.
A detection result alone cannot establish identity or intent. A synthetic-speech indication does not prove who created the audio or whether the spoken claim is false. Human judgment and corroboration remain essential.
Who Can Benefit From AI Voice Detection?
Journalists and newsrooms may use voice detection as one part of source verification before publishing audio that could affect a person or public event. Researchers and fact-checkers can use it to investigate questionable recordings while documenting limitations. Businesses can add audio review to fraud-response procedures when executives, employees, or customers appear to make unusual requests.
Content creators may need to examine recordings attributed to them or collaborators. Individuals can use detection for suspicious voice notes, voicemail, or audio shared through social platforms. The goal should be informed review rather than automatic accusation.
The technology is especially relevant when trust is created through familiarity. A cloned voice can sound persuasive because listeners recognize the speaker. That psychological effect makes independent verification more important, not less.
What an AI Voice Detector Cannot Tell You
An AI voice detector cannot prove a speaker’s identity. It cannot determine a person’s intent, establish that a statement is true or false, or guarantee that every synthetic recording will be detected. It also cannot fully compensate for missing provenance or poor source material.
False positives and false negatives are possible because detection models operate on learned patterns. New synthesis methods may differ from training data, while authentic audio can contain processing artifacts that resemble synthetic characteristics.
The most reliable approach is therefore layered: preserve the original file, examine the signal, check the source, verify important claims independently, and treat uncertain results as a reason to gather more evidence.
Why Voice Authenticity Matters for Digital Trust
The rapid improvement of generative audio is changing a long-standing assumption: hearing a familiar voice is no longer sufficient proof that the person actually spoke those words. That affects personal communication, journalism, customer service, corporate security, and online media.
As synthetic content becomes more common, digital trust will depend increasingly on provenance and verification. Detection tools work best when combined with source checking and clear documentation.
Responsible AI detection should also avoid sensationalism. Not every synthetic voice is malicious, and not every unusual recording is artificial. The purpose of analysis is to improve the quality of a decision, not to replace it.
Frequently Asked Questions About AI Voice Detection
Can an AI voice detector identify a cloned voice?
It can identify patterns that may be associated with synthetic or cloned speech, but it cannot prove the identity of the person whose voice was copied. Identity verification requires separate evidence.
Can background noise affect detection?
Yes. Noise, music, overlapping speakers, compression, and re-recording can obscure or change useful signal information. The cleanest available original is generally the best material for analysis.
Does a synthetic result mean the message is fake?
No. Synthetic speech can be used for legitimate purposes, and the truth of a spoken claim is separate from how the voice was produced. The claim should be verified independently.
Can people detect AI-generated voices by listening alone?
Sometimes listeners notice anomalies, but natural-sounding synthetic speech can be difficult to recognize consistently. Listening is useful, but it should be combined with technical analysis and source verification.
A More Careful Standard for Audio Verification
AI-generated speech is becoming part of everyday digital media, while voice cloning has made audio impersonation easier to scale. The practical response is not to distrust every recording, but to adopt a stronger standard for verification.
Tools such as DetectVoice AI can provide an additional layer of evidence by examining whether speech shows patterns associated with synthetic generation. The strongest workflow combines that assessment with the original source, recording quality, independent confirmation, and human judgment.
In an environment where a convincing voice can be generated, edited, copied, and shared within minutes, the ability to question audio responsibly is becoming a core digital skill. An AI Voice Detector does not replace trust; used carefully, it helps people decide when trust needs to be verified.

Program prepared for 117 technological projects in oil, gas

Program prepared for 117 technological projects in oil, gas
TEHRAN- The proposed package of 117 technological projects for the oil and gas industry, prepared with the direct cooperation of 42 entities, was reviewed at a meeting of the Special Headquarters for Technology Development chaired by Mohammad Reza Aref, First Vice President.
According to IRNA, at the meeting of the Special Headquarters for Technology Development, held under the chairmanship of the First Vice President, various proposed packages for applying new technologies in the oil and gas industry were reviewed.
These proposed packages include 117 projects prepared with the direct cooperation of 42 entities, and they pursue enhancing the resilience of the oil and gas industry, inter-sectoral coordination, support and facilitation for the private sector, prioritizing projects emphasized by upstream documents, developing dual-use technologies, and penetrating and expanding the application of driving technologies.
Enhancing oil and gas production, completing the value chain of the refining industry and resolving the gasoline and diesel imbalance, regenerating and upgrading the petrochemical industry, and increasing energy productivity in the production, transmission, distribution, and consumption chain are among the priorities of the oil and gas industry’s technological projects.
By supplying a modern drilling fleet and services and equipment related to oil well exploitation, an increase in crude oil production by at least 250,000 barrels per day has been targeted.
Increasing the country’s foreign exchange revenues by $5 billion, increasing the efficiency of oil fields, and diversifying and applying new production technologies are among the other goals of these projects.
In the South Pars pressure-boosting project, various contracts have also been concluded to begin the design and development of various turbines and the construction, installation, and commissioning of various in-well and wellhead compressors, and their implementation has begun.
One of these projects, which is due to be inaugurated by the Fajr Decade, will use the latest technologies for deploying pressure-boosting turbines for offshore and onshore platforms—a technology that had previously been in the possession of only five countries.
According to the presented plan, with the implementation of these projects over 40 years, surplus gas production equivalent to $500 billion from the pressure-boosting plan will be secured, and the stability of daily production of more than 700 million cubic meters of gas from the South Pars field will be maintained.
Maintaining the capacity of the electricity generation network and gasoline produced from liquids, and preventing an increase in energy imbalance, are among the other goals of these projects.
Using new technologies to facilitate the implementation of onshore flare management projects, as well as implementing surface storage projects for natural gas, was another part of the programs presented at this meeting.
With the implementation of these two plans, annual gas supply will increase by 8 billion cubic meters, non-oil exports will be supported by $1 billion, and the stability of the gas distribution network in the cold season will also increase.
In this regard, for the first time in the country, flare gases have been pre-sold after refining through the conclusion of a contract.
Also, the project to convert flare gas into value-added products has begun with the cooperation of the petrochemical industry and knowledge-based companies.
In line with improving the quality of heavy refinery residues and producing petroleum products with higher added value, various projects with high physical progress are underway in the country’s refineries, the realization of which will lead to the desulfurization of fuel oil.
For the first time, Group III base oil has also been produced in the country, and with the expansion of its production, imports of this product will decrease. Also, by the end of the Seventh Development Plan, fuel oil production will decrease by 49 million liters, and the quality of this product will also improve.
With the implementation of energy productivity plans in the production, transmission, distribution, and consumption chain, it will be possible to generate 800 to 1,600 megawatts of electricity at natural gas pressure boosting stations.
These plans will also make possible annual savings of 1.5 billion cubic meters of natural gas at gas pressure boosting stations and 2 billion cubic meters of gas at South Pars refineries.
To achieve these goals, projects including heat and waste energy recovery in natural gas and steam pressure boosting and reduction stations, and heat recovery from South Pars gas refineries, have been placed on the agenda.
Also, the implementation of projects in some provinces, including Yazd, has begun as a pilot, the result of which has been a 31 percent reduction in gas consumption in the residential sector.
At the Special Headquarters for Technology Development, emphasis was also placed on regenerating and upgrading the petrochemical industry and purposefully completing the chain of this industry using emerging technologies.
Various projects have been approved in this field, the implementation of which will help rebuild the petrochemical industry units damaged in the Ramadan War, prevent the closure of downstream complementary industries, reduce imports of petrochemical products worth $500 million annually, supply 530,000 tons of raw materials needed by the country’s complementary industries annually, and increase foreign exchange revenues from exports.
At the meeting, the First Vice President, thanking those who prepared the plans for applying new technologies in the oil and gas industry, said: There is sufficient capacity in the country to use new technologies in various sectors, including the oil and gas industry.
Aref added: The oil and gas industry has always benefited from elite, committed, and educated personnel, and relying on this same human resource, the enemy failed to achieve its goals in the two recent wars.

Emphasizing the economic effects of technology development in the oil and gas industry, the First Vice President said: Increasing productivity in the oil and gas industry through the use of new technologies helps increase national wealth and destroy the poverty line, and causes the government to be freed from embarrassment before the people.

Brunello Cucinelli transforms a historic Tashkent madrasah into a runway

2026-10-06

The Fall-Winter 2026 collection was presented inside the Abulkasim Madrasah, with Uzbek carpets, music and traditional craftsmanship shaping the setting.
Handmade carpets covered the courtyard of one of Tashkent’s historic madrasahs as Italian fashion house Brunello Cucinelli presented its Fall-Winter 2026 collection in the Uzbek capital.
Models walked across the carpets laid inside the Abulkasim Madrasah, while local music and performances accompanied the show.
The setting was unusual for an international fashion presentation. A madrasah is a traditional Islamic educational institution, and the Abulkasim complex dates from the 19th century. Built on the site of an earlier architectural complex, it was expanded with a second floor in 1864.
Today, it is a protected historical monument, but it is not simply a preserved building. Former student rooms overlooking the courtyard are used by craftspeople working in ceramics, wood carving, engraving, miniature painting and other traditional arts.
Fashion inside a working craft centre
Organisers said the choice of venue was intended to connect the fashion house’s emphasis on handcraft with Uzbekistan’s own artisanal traditions.
Carolina Cucinelli, Vice President and Co-Creative Director of Brunello Cucinelli, said she had spent time looking at some of the crafts produced locally during her visit.
“Artisanality is one of the most important key points between Uzbekistan and Solomeo,” she said, referring to the Umbrian village where the company is based.
“We had the chance to see pottery, jewellery and the fabric. This is amazing. Everything is very colourful.”
The show included both the men’s and women’s Fall-Winter collections, with tailoring, knitwear and outerwear presented against the architecture of the madrasah and the carpets covering its courtyard.
The choice of a historic craft centre also has a parallel in Cucinelli’s activities in Italy.
In 2025, Brunello Cucinelli received an honorary doctorate partly recognising his work on the restoration of Solomeo, the Umbrian village where his company is based. A school established there also trains students in traditional skills including tailoring, pattern cutting, gardening and masonry.
Uzbek fashion looks beyond its home market
The show comes as Uzbekistan’s own design scene is also looking beyond the domestic market.
Some local designers have already begun testing demand abroad, combining contemporary fashion with materials and techniques rooted in Uzbek craft traditions.
The Tashkent event was organised by luxury retailer Glamour Avenue.
Dmitriy Maschenko, CEO of Podium and Glamour Avenue, said the concept was designed around the cultural setting of the show.
“The concept of the show was to bring Italian culture together with our great Uzbek culture”, he said.
Maschenko also said he expected more international fashion brands to enter the Uzbek market in the coming years.
Brunello Cucinelli already has a retail presence in Tashkent. The October show, however, moved the collection into a historic complex where traditional Uzbek crafts continue to be practised.

Mert Davut and Emir Yildirim
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Turkish defense firm Roketsan is participating in high-level talks with global space agencies and aerospace firms to secure partnerships in launch systems and orbital technologies and ensure Türkiye’s independent access to space at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC).
Roketsan CEO Murat Ikinci, speaking on the sidelines of the event held in the southwestern province of Antalya, told Anadolu that the firm is advancing its Simsek-1 system to launch 400-kilogram (881.8-pound) payloads into orbit, while its heavier Simsek-2 launch system is designed to carry 1.5-ton satellites.
“We’re holding important talks with global space agencies and firms about our subsystems and payloads,” he said. “We developed numerous subsystems, such as space engines, liquid-fueled propulsion systems, solid-fueled boosters, space-qualified navigation systems for orientation and control mechanisms, maneuvering technologies, gas-powered propulsion systems, and navigation and control systems at our facilities.”
Ikinci stated that domestic research was key to building Türkiye’s space infrastructure, as major spacefaring countries rarely share rocket and propulsion technologies.
He noted that while Roketsan works with universities and local defense suppliers, the firm is attending the congress to seek global partners to carry payloads on its future launch vehicles, which are expected to enable both Türkiye and its partners to advance orbital capabilities faster.
The IAC 2026 kicked off on Monday and will run until Friday. It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and the SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.

Commandos land from German submarine on Scottish coast
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:12:21 BST
21:12:21 KST

British commandos have come ashore at Cape Wrath from a German attack submarine and directed the guns of a Portuguese frigate onto targets inland, during the largest test of every part of the UK Commando Force in fifteen years, according to the Royal Navy.
The landing took place during Exercise Strike Warrior, which the service describes as the first occasion since the war in Afghanistan on which all the specialist elements of the formation have worked together. More than 2,000 personnel from six nations are taking part, drawn from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, and deployed across the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea.
Navy and Army commandos from 148 Battery Commando Forward Observation Battery, the unit trained to carry out reconnaissance and call down naval gunfire from behind enemy lines, left the submarine in inflatable raiding boats and established an observation post on the cliffs at the most north-westerly point of mainland Britain. From there they directed the guns of the Portuguese warship NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida onto positions ashore.
The battery’s operations officer, who cannot be named for operational reasons, said: “This level of complexity and coordination of live assets has not been achieved by 148 Battery for nearly 30 years.
“We wanted to demonstrate to our partners across the United Kingdom Commando Force, wider UK Defence and NATO Special Operations Force community the type of missions we are prepared to execute against future threats.
“Warfighting is our focus, and we are prepared to employ specialist assets to deliver Multi-Domain Fires and Targeting.”
Three navies were involved in the single sequence at Cape Wrath. The German submarine found the targets, the commandos put themselves ashore without being seen, and the Portuguese ship supplied the firepower. The Royal Navy has not identified the submarine.
Earlier in the exercise the same battery controlled the naval gunfire of ships from Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s standing task group in northern European waters. The Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s both worked with commandos in observation posts to bring their guns onto targets.
Eight warships and 19 aircraft are taking part in Strike Warrior, which began on 28 September and finishes on Friday. Alongside the gunnery serials, the exercise has covered amphibious landings, boarding operations, intelligence and surveillance missions, logistics and sustainment, maritime security and anti-submarine warfare. Commandos have flown drone missions including strikes and resupply to troops in contact, and have built underground medical facilities.
Cape Wrath matters to this kind of training because it is the only place in Britain, and one of very few in Europe, where warships can fire live rounds at a land target. The range takes in Garvie Island off the headland, and the combination of the cliffs behind and the open Atlantic in front is what allows observation parties to work close to live naval gunfire.
The participation of a German boat and a Portuguese frigate alongside Dutch and Canadian ships reflects how the Commando Force now expects to operate, which is as the land element of a NATO maritime group rather than as a national force working alone. Norway and the United States also have personnel committed, and the stated purpose of the exercise is rehearsing allied crisis response in the High North and the North Atlantic.

France came out top overall, with nearly 3,000 unusual property listings on Airbnb, including more than 1,000 castles.

And if you’re looking for unconventional options in Europe, you should be heading to France as it just topped a new ranking of the countries with the most unusual stays around the world.
Produced by Holafly, the ranking looked at Airbnb listings around the world across eight property types: Caves, castles, treehouses, houseboats, windmills, lighthouses, earth homes, and domes.

France leads the rankings in several stay categories, too, with more than 1,000 castles, 400 houseboats, and 30 windmills you can book.
Where else to go in Europe for an unusual stay
Third place in the overall ranking went to Italy, thanks to its Tuscan castles, the trulli (aka cone-roofed stone huts) of Puglia, and cave dwellings in Matera.
Next up in Europe is the UK, which has 696 listings and places sixth overall. Here, you’ll find nearly 250 castles, almost 150 domes and more than 100 houseboats, alongside 23 lighthouses and 12 windmills.
The last European destination to make the cut was Greece, in ninth overall. Unsurprisingly, the country won for the number of cave stays, with 279, and it was also in second place for windmill stays, with 27.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday urged the US and Iran to return to diplomacy and end the war, while hailing Pakistan’s “pivotal role” in creating conditions for dialogue between the two sides, including a framework agreement this June.
 
“Your efforts helped deliver the 17 June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, the subsequent ceasefire, and the framework for further negotiations,” he said, adding that “every Pakistani should be proud of that pivotal role.”
 
His remarks came during a joint news conference with Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad. Guterres is visiting the country through Thursday.
 
“And from Islamabad, I want to send a loud and clear message to all parties: End the conflict. Return to diplomacy. Fully restore navigational rights and freedoms in accordance with international law,” Guterres said.

'Many countries believe they can do whatever they want'
 
Asked about several UN Security Council resolutions remaining unimplemented and "what mechanism the UN Security Council has to implement the resolutions on Jammu and Kashmir," Guterres said the council does not represent today's world, emphasizing that while three European countries have permanent seats, there is no permanent African member.
 
"Which means that the Security Council has a problem of legitimacy and has a problem of effectiveness," he said.
 
"The fact that we are witnessing today a situation in which superpowers, permanent members of Security Council are the first to start conflicts and sometimes violating international law creates a situation in which many countries believe they can do whatever they want, because nothing will happen to them," Guterres said.
 
This situation can "only" be solved with reforms to the Security Council that make it "more legitimate," as well as countries with capacity uniting to ensure that the principles of law are fully implemented, he said.
 
After serving two terms, Guterres’ time as UN chief is set to conclude at the end of this year.
 
His successor has not yet been chosen.

Union wants state-run school teachers' salary advantage retained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

Union wants state-run school teachers' salary advantage retained
The Estonian Educational Personnel Union (EHL) and the Ministry of Education and Research will begin negotiations next week on a collective agreement for the country's state-run general education schools.
According to EHL Chair Reemo Voltri, the desire to reopen the agreement was prompted by the need to preserve the previously secured salary premium in light of the general pay increase.
"The current collective agreement for teachers at state-run general education schools sets out salary figures based on this year's minimum salary. The national minimum salary for teachers is €1,970, while the collective agreement for state schools sets the minimum €100 higher, at €2,070. Since the general minimum salary will rise by at least 3 percent from the new year, state school teachers believe that the minimum salary agreed in their collective agreement should also increase by at least the same amount, or more," Voltri explained.
Voltri said the timing of the notification was dictated by law. "Under the Collective Agreements Act, a fixed-term agreement must be terminated with at least three months' notice if you do not want it to continue; otherwise, it becomes indefinite. That's what we did and next week we will begin new negotiations with the aim of reaching an agreement on a collective agreement for next year," he said.
The union's ideal outcome would be a more stable solution. "Our goal was and remains to secure a multi-year agreement that sets out very clearly the steps we will take going forward. Ideally, we would discuss the salary concerns and proposals of all teachers so that we would not have to hold salary negotiations every year, but could reach an agreement covering several years and focus on other matters," Voltri said.
However, Raino Liblik, head of the Ministry of Education and Research's state schools department, stressed that the push for new terms comes primarily from the union and is not necessarily a joint initiative by all teachers at state schools.
"Perhaps it should be clarified that it is not teachers who want the agreement reviewed, but the Estonian Educational Personnel Union. I would argue that a great many teachers are not union members. This is more the union's wish, as it is seeking new terms," Liblik said.
According to Liblik, the substance of any potential changes to the agreement is a matter for negotiations and it is still too early to say how those talks will proceed.
"I believe the main question is how the increase in the minimum salary for teachers could be reflected in a possible future collective agreement," Liblik said.
Asked whether the state was prepared to raise state school teachers' salaries by the same amount as the general increase in the minimum salary, Liblik was cautious.
"I wouldn't speculate at this point because we need to look at what options we have and under what conditions. That's what the negotiations are for — they have been sent an invitation and we'll see how it goes. I think the operator of the state schools has made considerable efforts to ensure that teachers have good working conditions in schools. In that respect, we do not need to make any major adjustments," Liblik said.
Liblik also dismissed concerns that state school teachers could end up worse off than employees of schools run by other operators. "That's not going to happen. If we look at the current increase in the minimum salary, it is still very small," the ministry representative said.
Representatives of EHL and the ministry will meet next week at the Ministry of Education and Research's Tallinn office at Tõnismäe 11.

North Korea ready to use force if faced with South Korean military invasion — MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:10:24 UTC
21:10:24 KST

PYONGYANG, October 6. /TASS/. Pyongyang will take immediate retaliatory action, including the use of force, in case of a South Korean military invasion, the North Korean Foreign Ministry said in a statement released by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The statement points out that if the Southern Korean military invades North Korea "even one millimeter deep, North Korea’s border forces will take immediate and powerful retaliatory action."
The Foreign Ministry noted that North Korea "will under no circumstances discuss military sovereignty applied to its own territory with a hostile state," but "will defend its sovereign territory not through talks but through a decisive use of force." The ministry added that this was the official position of the North Korean government.
The statement was issued after Seoul announced the final results of an investigation into an explosion that occurred in the demilitarized zone on September 21. The South Korean military claims that North Korean service members had deliberately planted anti-personnel landmines south of the Military Demarcation Line. Pyongyang has rejected these conclusions.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry described Seoul’s allegations as "a serious violation of sovereignty," saying that work to reinforce the country’s southern border was part of its sovereign rights. The ministry also stressed that Pyongyang was not responsible for any similar incidents that could happen in South Korea in the future.
South Korea’s military reported on October 5 that a demining operation had been carried out at the site of the explosion. The army also announced plans to continue clearing the area of mines. South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on October 6 that Seoul was considering various diplomatic measures with regard to the incident.

Poland to "invest" $26 billion in civil defense amid intensifying Russian attacks on Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Poland will allocate $26 billion for shelters, warning systems, and crisis stockpiles. The program was strengthened because of the war in Ukraine.
Poland plans to invest 102.4 billion zlotys ($26 billion) over five years in a population protection and civil defense program. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this on Tuesday, UNN reports.
Details
In recent months, amid intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine — particularly on its western regions — the Polish authorities have begun issuing warnings to the public about the possible impact of these airstrikes on Polish territory.
The program is also intended to prepare the country and its citizens for natural disasters, such as floods.
"Priorities in the area of civil protection include protective structures, shelters of all types, rescue equipment and infrastructure, as well as the creation of resource reserves in case of crises and natural disasters," Tusk said on Tuesday.
"We will finance alert systems, IT systems and secure communication between institutions and services," he said before a government meeting.
Against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine, Poland’s military spending has reached nearly 5% of gross domestic product.

Forbion raises €2.3bn, now Europe’s top biotech investor

Naarden-based venture capital firm Forbion, which specialises in life sciences companies, has raised €2.3 billion for 2 new biotech funds, its largest fundraising to date.
The firm says it is one of the biggest life sciences venture capital fundraisings in the past 5 years. It takes Forbion’s assets to around €7.5 billion, which it says makes it Europe’s largest specialist life sciences investor, citing data from research firm Preqin.
The funds will finance around 30 companies, ranging from early-stage firms to those already testing drugs on patients.

The cabinet named life sciences and biotechnology as one of 4 sectors in which it wants to recruit highly skilled foreign workers, under a national talent strategy agreed in July.

France’s Le Pen unveils economic platform brimming with eye-watering cuts — but few new ideas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:09:23 UTC
21:09:23 KST

France’s Le Pen unveils economic platform brimming with eye-watering cuts — but few new ideas
The far-right leader is desperately trying to reassure French markets with her €140 billion savings plan and improve the country’s dire fiscal outlook.
Marine Le Pen speaks during a press conference to present the National Rally's counter-budget for 2027 in Paris, on Oct. 6, 2026. | Mehdi Fedouach/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen offered her usual recipe for pulling the French economy from the brink of a debt crisis when she presented her plan Tuesday: curbing immigration, cutting contributions to the European Union and slashing red tape.
“If the French do not choose a political about-face, France will head toward default,” Le Pen said at a lengthy press conference at her National Rally party’s headquarters.
Le Pen spent much of her opening speech attacking what she called President Emmanuel Macron’s “disastrous track record” on the economy. For her, the event was an opportunity to cast herself as a responsible steward of the economy as France’s public finances fall deeper into the red, and erase a tumultuous week that saw her protégé, Party President Jordan Bardella, accused of authoring antisemitic views in his youth.
Advertisement
But critics were quick to argue her plan lacked crucial detail on one of her most costly campaign pledges: the promise to bring back France’s legal retirement age to 62, which is currently set to increase to 64.
Bardella, who stood by her at the press conference, struggled to draw a line under the antisemitism allegations that have been leveled at him. Le Pen left him to face the rolling barrage of questions about his alleged antisemitic Facebook messages and his ability to continue the campaign.
On stage, the duo presented their counter-proposal for next year’s budget, about to be negotiated in Parliament, as well as Le Pen’s proposed five-year, cost-cutting package. The far-right leader hinted she was ready to be more lenient towards the government this time around and not topple it during upcoming budget negotiations.
“As imperfect as it is, the pressure [from financial markets] is such that we can’t afford to have blanket red lines … knowing that this budget will only apply until the election and that we can amend it afterwards,” she said in answer to a question.
She also promised €140 billion in net savings over the course of a five-year term, if she is elected president. “If investors only lend at exorbitant rates, our state and our social system will collapse,” she said.
Le Pen’s proposal to cut €19.5 billion from France’s EU contributions by 2031 is bound to set up a showdown with Brussels. The party’s counter-budget proposal for 2027 includes an €11.1 billion cut in France’s gross contribution to the bloc as early as next year.
Advertisement
Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a National Rally lawmaker widely seen as a contender for economy minister should Le Pen win next year’s presidential election, said that Le Pen and her party would ramp up pressure for a fundamental rethink of EU priorities, rather than just renegotiating the country’s annual contribution.
“We are not only asking for a rebate; we are asking for the cancellation of entire programs,” Tanguy said, citing EU foreign policy initiatives but also EU funds deployed within pre-accession programs.
During past presidential campaigns, Le Pen and the National Rally have been criticized for floating unrealistic and unfunded proposals that lack important details. They’ve also been accused of inflating savings in some proposals — meaning the numbers unveiled Tuesday will likely be heavily scrutinized.
“To make savings, you make up billions. But reality will always catch up with you. What you offer does not add up,” he wrote.
Devil is in the details
Le Pen said slashing immigrationwould save €15 billion in the first year of her presidency, and €14 billion in the second.
Advertisement
She also said reorganizing France’s social security system would bring in a staggering €36.7 billion over five years, which also needs to absorb the cost of her flagship pension promise.
In August, Le Pen doubled down on her past pledge to lower the age of retirement back to 62, which she says will come at a cost of €9 billion per year. But that number is largely seen as an underestimation, with fiscally conservative think tank Institut Montaigne putting it at €34.7 billion.
Le Pen said other, yet undefined changes to the pension system would save €15–20 billion, promising to lay out its plans in detail at a later stage.
Hadrian Camatte, a specialist with the French investment bank Natixis, said Le Pen was being “overly-optimistic” and that the National Rally’s plan to cut billions on state spending was “massive, huge.”
“It will be very complicated if even [the party] are very aggressive regarding state agencies or state bodies,” he said.
She said she would put a so-called fiscal “golden rule” to a referendum, which would bind lawmakers and the government in setting the budget, similar to the way the German debt brake works.
Advertisement
Le Pen’s version would instead require successive governments to reduce France’s public debt as a share of gross domestic product each year until it reaches 60% — nearly half its current level. In practical terms, France could still run budget deficits, provided they are small enough for the debt burden to keep falling relative to the size of the economy.
Le Pen also said that she planned to introduce a funded component into the pension system, under which a worker’s contributions are invested for their future retirement rather than paying for current retirees — a proposal that had been pushed by the National Rally’s more pro-business wing.
A pair under pressure
Sold as a winning ticket, the Bardella-Le Pen duo came under intense scrutiny during their second public appearance Tuesdaywhen the antisemitism allegations were leveled against the party president.
Le Pen, the front-runner in the race to replace Macron next year, did not rush to Bardella’s defense during the press conference, declining to respond to the allegations. Instead she launched into a defense of another National Rally official Jean-François Jalkh, who has faced accusations of Holocaust denial.
Bardella meanwhile went on the offensive: “I imagine you would have loved to see me bow down, but that’s because you don’t know me,” he said.
He accused Mediapart, which published the report, of trying to dig up dirt on him by asking his former classmates to send screenshots of private conversations when he was as young as 12.
“I won’t accuse you of perversity, others will judge, but it doesn’t look like your little operation is having an impact in the country,” he said.
Bardella also said his party was looking into taking legal action against Mediapart.

Iran warns US, Israel against new attack, says arms production capacity up 2.5-fold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

21:09:17 KST

Sahin Demir
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Iran warned Tuesday that any new attack by the US or Israel would face a stronger response, saying it has prepared potential targets for retaliation and significantly expanded its weapons production capacity.
Defense Ministry spokesman Reza Talaei-Nik said any renewed attack would be met with a “decisive response” and result in heavier losses for Iran’s adversaries, the semi-official Fars News Agency reported.
Asked how Iran would respond to a potential attack on Kuh-e Kolang (Pickaxe Mountain), Talaei-Nik said targets that could be struck by the Iranian armed forces in response to renewed aggression had already been prepared.
He said advanced weapons and technologies, including missile and drone capabilities, upgraded air defenses and other naval, ground and air systems, had been made available to the armed forces.
He said potential targets that could be struck by Iranian armed forces in response to another attack have already been identified and prepared.
Talaei-Nik said Iran has provided its armed forces with “more advanced missile and drone technologies,” as well as upgraded air defense, naval and ground systems.
The spokesman said Iran’s production capacity for weapons, defense equipment and ammunition has increased 2.5-fold compared with levels before the war that began on Feb. 28.
“Production of some types of weapons has risen more than threefold,” he said.
He said more than 1,000 systems, weapons, types of equipment and ammunition are currently within the production capacity of the Defense Ministry and its partner network.
Talaei-Nik also said Iran’s defense cooperation with Russia and China has neither stopped nor declined despite recent developments.
He said strategic cooperation with Moscow and Beijing remains active under existing agreements, with exchanges continuing in political and defense fields.
The spokesman added that defense diplomacy and consultations with the two countries have intensified in some areas, without elaborating.
The latest tensions follow the US-Israeli war against Iran that began on Feb. 28, during which strikes targeted Iranian military and nuclear facilities and senior military officials, while Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks against Israel and US military targets in the region.

Sufa 53: What is Israel's military project in southern Syria?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:08:00 UTC
21:08:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Sufa 53 explained: Israel's new military project in southern Syria
The Israeli military resumed construction on Sunday of a trench and road project known as "Sufa 53" along the border with Syria, with excavation work taking place inside occupied Syrian territory.
The renewed construction came amid an expansion of Israel's military presence in southern Syria, where Israeli forces have seized territory, carried out repeated incursions and opened fire on Syrian civilians despite UN calls for Israel to withdraw and respect the 1974 disengagement agreement.
Excavation machinery accompanied by Israeli tanks entered from the vicinity of Al-Asha village, south of Quneitra, before beginning to dig trenches and construct massive earth embankments, indicating that Israel had resumed work on the "Sufa 53" project, which began in 2022.
The project has taken on renewed significance since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, after which Israel seized additional Syrian territory beyond the occupied Golan Heights and moved into the UN-patrolled buffer zone established under the 1974 agreement.
Researchers who spoke to The New Arab said the project has evolved from an engineering undertaking into part of a wider Israeli effort to reshape the geography and security arrangements of southern Syria and establish new facts on the ground.
What is 'Sufa 53'?
The project extends from the outskirts of Hader in Quneitra towards the villages of Jubata al-Khashab and Hamidiyah in the province's northern countryside, reaching Qahtaniyah, Ruwayhiyah, Bir Ajam and Bariqah in the central countryside.
From there, it heads south towards Al-Asha village before eventually reaching the Syrian-Jordanian border near the occupied Golan Heights.
The project involves the construction of an eight-metre-wide military road, according to the Sijil Centre, which specialises in documenting Israeli violations in Syria.
The route is fortified with trenches, earth embankments reaching five metres in height, observation posts and military positions.
The construction has also taken a growing toll on Syrian communities along its route, particularly farmers and livestock owners whose land has been affected by the Israeli works.
Local authorities have estimated that around 12,000 dunams, or 1,200 hectares, of agricultural land in northern and central Quneitra have been affected by Israeli construction, according to Anadolu Agency.
In Jubata al-Khashab alone, local officials said around 7,000 dunams of land had been lost, while thousands more dunams belonging to Al-Hamidiyah and Al-Hurriyah have been affected.
Residents have also reported damage to grazing areas, trees and other vegetation, while the trenches and embankments have disrupted the natural flow of rainwater and contributed to soil erosion.
The construction has taken place alongside repeated Israeli raids, detentions, checkpoints and restrictions preventing residents from reaching agricultural land.
Syrian accounts also say Israeli forces have advanced between 300 and 1,000 metres into the area in some locations as work on the project has expanded.
Syria's Foreign Ministry condemned the renewed construction on Sunday, describing "Sufa 53" as a "flagrant breach" of the 1974 disengagement agreement and a violation of international resolutions.
Damascus said the continuing Israeli incursions threatened regional security and stability and called on the international community to uphold Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Khaled Khalil, a researcher specialising in Syrian-Israeli relations, told The New Arab that available information suggests the "Sufa 53" project was never accompanied by a clear official Israeli announcement.
He said the project predates 7 October 2023 but underwent a significant change in function following the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024.
The project initially had an engineering character and was linked to Israeli plans to expand illegal settlements in the occupied Syrian Golan, while also being used as part of efforts to clear mines dating back to the 1973 war.
Following the fall of the Assad regime, however, Khalil said the project was transformed into a military tool to impose new realities on the ground in southern Syria.
Khalil noted that Israel's actions form part of a broader shift in its security doctrine since 7 October 2023, based on "moving the battle to the territory of its adversary" and establishing what it calls "safe zones", rather than waiting for potential threats to reach territory under its control.
He added that "Sufa 53" was not an alternative to the "Bravo" line, which marks the Syrian side of the buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement.
Instead, the engineering project overlaps with the Bravo line in some areas, while extending west of it in some places and east of it in others.
This, Khalil said, reflects an Israeli attempt to impose a new reality on the ground rather than adhere to the boundaries established under existing agreements.
He added that Israel is seeking to secure negotiating gains ahead of any future regional settlement, while putting pressure on Damascus and exploiting Syria's transitional period to reshape security arrangements on the ground.
Researcher Rashid Hourani told TNA that Israel began work on "Sufa 53" in mid-2022 to establish an area where its forces could mobilise and assemble, allowing them to launch attacks and advance further into Syrian territory.
He said Israeli incursions during that period initially took the form of "tongues" extending into Syrian territory. These were later connected, with Israeli forces taking control of the land between them and constructing roads.
Hourani said "Sufa 53" is primarily a land route, although it is supported by technological surveillance and monitoring systems.
The project relies on extensive engineering works, including trenches around four metres deep and four metres wide, as well as earth embankments reaching five metres in height.
Shift in Israeli doctrine
Hourani also linked the project to a shift in Israeli military doctrine following the Hamas-led attack on Israel in October 2023, after which Israel increasingly adopted the principle of moving fighting into the territory of its adversaries while establishing buffer and demilitarised zones beyond territory under its control.
He argued that Israel is using "Sufa 53" to impose new facts on the ground that could later be used as bargaining chips in negotiations with Syria.
Such talks are expected to be sponsored by the United States and could become more serious if the US-Israeli war on Iran ends, he added.
Wael Alwan, a researcher at the Jusoor Centre for Studies, similarly placed Israel's incursions and military intervention in southern Syria within a broader effort to change realities on the ground.
Speaking to TNA, he said part of this activity was directly linked to the "Sufa 53" project.
Alwan said Israel is proceeding with the project regardless of developments in its relations with Syria or whether an agreement is eventually reached between the two sides.
He described "Sufa 53" as a military engineering line, parts of which extend outside the demilitarised zone, while other sections run through it and through territory already occupied by Israel.
The project's main objective, he said, is to prevent a large-scale attack on Israel from Syrian territory.
But Alwan stressed that Israel's approach is driven by its own security calculations rather than the restrictions imposed by international agreements, treaties or UN obligations.
The continued construction comes amid a wider Israeli entrenchment in southern Syria, where its forces have expanded beyond the occupied Golan and the lines established under the 1974 agreement, creating new military positions and physical barriers on Syrian land.

Three years of genocide: How has Britain’s policy shifted on Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:07:22 UTC
21:07:22 KST

Since October 2023, the trajectory of British foreign policy toward Israel and Palestine has undergone an extraordinary evolution.
What began under Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration as strong diplomatic and military support for Tel Aviv has transformed into what some experts call one of the most significant pivots in modern British diplomacy.
In the immediate wake of the Oct. 7 attacks, Downing Street pledged absolute support for Israel's right to defend itself. Royal Air Force surveillance aircraft were dispatched over the Eastern Mediterranean and demands for a ceasefire were repeatedly brushed aside in line with Washington’s geopolitical posture.
Yet, over the months that followed, as civilian death tolls mounted, humanitarian access collapsed and concerns over grave violations of international law grew, that consensus fractured.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.
This staggering human loss was accompanied by landmark international legal assessments from UN special committees, human rights organizations and international legal experts warning that Israel's military actions and siege tactics in Gaza breached the threshold of genocide.
The arrival of Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband this summer brought a sharper tone to Britain’s policy toward Israel, building on cautious changes introduced under Keir Starmer.
Burnham’s government has pledged to take significant action against illegal settlements while speaking more forcefully in support of Palestinian rights
Yet, while ministers present this reset as a moral imperative, some observers question how far it reflects a change in principle and how far it is a response to public pressure, political risk and legal exposure.
At Labour’s recent party conference, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband addressed those who had protested over the treatment of Palestinians: “We hear you, you were right.”
"Under Andy's leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions,” he said.
Miliband pledged to ban imports from illegal settlements and disrupt British financial, construction and service-sector support for them.
Under Starmer, Britain resumed funding to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, in July 2024, suspended around 30 arms export licenses that September and formally recognized Palestine in September 2025.
His government also dropped plans to challenge the International Criminal Court’s jurisdiction over Israeli officials.
But Burnham has acknowledged shortcomings in Labour’s earlier response, saying the party “didn’t get it right.”
"The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed in Gaza,” he said. “Before I became Prime Minister, I said our country's response had been too slow and simply not good enough."
For Iain Overton, executive director of Action on Armed Violence (AOAV), the sequence shows both the extent of the changes and how slowly they came.
"I think there has been a genuine shift in British policy, but it has been painfully slow and has followed events rather than forged them," he told Anadolu.
For veteran British journalist Peter Oborne, the significance of the change in direction cannot be downplayed.
"The Burnham government has made the most significant change in British policy towards Israel in 50 years," he told Anadolu.
He stressed that this transition was far from cosmetic and “has been backed up by strong language and is deeply resented by Israel."
However, observers noted that this transformation was not forged purely in the quiet halls of diplomatic idealism, but rather in the electoral battlefield.
The Labour Party suffered severe blows among traditional Muslim communities and left-liberal voters angered by initial parliamentary hesitation over Gaza.
Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, argued that the policy shift is tied directly to domestic political realities.
“Miliband’s announcement is the product of genuine outrage at the settler violence but does have the benefit too of responding to widespread disillusionment of both Muslim and many non-Muslim left-liberal voters with what they saw as the weak stance on Gaza adopted by Labour under Starmer.”
Bale also said acting alongside other countries had made the tougher position easier to defend.
The UK’s move to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements came in coordination with France and Canada and meant they joined several other Western nations that had already done the same.
The 2025 recognition of Palestinian statehood was also coordinated with Canada and Australia.
"The fact that the government's hardening of its position was coordinated with other governments has given it a certain amount of cover when it comes to critics,” Bale said.
For Overton, public pressure and the scale of the harm in Gaza were central to the change.
“After Oct. 7, the emphasis was overwhelmingly on Israel’s right to defend itself,” he said. “What followed was an extraordinary and terrible level of civilian harm in Gaza, mounting concerns over international humanitarian law and enormous political and public pressure not to enable Israel.”
He argued that these developments made Britain’s earlier position increasingly difficult to sustain.
“The suspension of some arms licences, recognition of Palestine and measures against illegal settlements are substantive changes and were forged by public outcry. But I would not describe this as a sudden moral awakening in Westminster,” he said.
For Overton, arms exports remain a test of whether Britain’s actions match its stated concerns.
Under the UK’s export licensing criteria, the state is legally prohibited from issuing export licenses if there is a "clear risk" that military technology could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law.
The initial September 2024 suspension was limited. It covered around 30 licenses out of approximately 350, rather than imposing a comprehensive arms embargo.
Affected equipment included drones, naval systems, parts for military aircraft and targeting gear.
The UK government has since expanded curbs, with Stephen Doughty, the UK Middle East minister, saying last month that around 50 more licenses were blocked under a “tighter system.”
However, British-made parts of the F-35 fighter jet supply chain continue to be exempt from the suspension, despite legal challenges.
For Overton, the question is whether the government’s subsequent policy changes are accompanied by further restrictions on military support.
"Policy changed because the political, legal and humanitarian costs of maintaining the previous position became increasingly difficult to defend. Story after story landed on the UK’s complicity,” he said.
He argued that diplomatic recognition and condemnation would have limited effect without changes to the practical relationship.
"Recognition of Palestine matters, but it does not protect civilians from air strikes. Condemnation of air strikes on civilians matters, but it rings hollow if Britain continues materially to enable conduct it says it opposes in the form of military intelligence and selective arms export licence approvals."
Overton said the government’s willingness to accept the consequences of further action would determine how far its policy had changed.
“Yes, the change is real. But the issue is whether the Government is prepared to follow the logic of its own position when doing so carries diplomatic, commercial or strategic costs,” he said. “It seems, at the moment, they want to have their cake and eat it too."

The fire-damaged "Royad Mammadov" ship in the Black Sea.

Rubio calls on Russia to be more transparent about plague lab worker's death in Siberia
Geneva — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia to be more "transparent" about the recent death of a plague research center scientist and any risks associated with the incident, which Russian authorities have offered conflicting information about this week.
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio said Tuesday after arriving in Iceland's capital Reykjavik for a visit. He called on Moscow to be "transparent" a day after Russia's primary national health agency denied earlier reports by local officials that the Siberian lab worker might have died of plague after a lab accident and that anti-plague measures were imposed at multiple health facilities in the wake of her death on Oct. 1 or 2.
The World Health Organization said Tuesday that the public health risk in Russia and Europe was considered low after the incident in Russia's far-eastern Siberia region.
"The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region," the United Nations health agency's spokesman Christian Lindmeier told reporters at the agency's Geneva headquarters.
Lindmeier said Russian authorities had identified all people who came into contact with the worker from the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, who has been identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, before she died and that none had symptoms associated with plague.
The center where Shipilova worked is situated in a part of Siberia where plague is found naturally in wild animal populations, the WHO spokesman confirmed.
Lindmeier said her "illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection," but that Russian authorities "are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death."
"WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed," he said, and is ready to help Russian authorities if they seek assistance.
Russia's national health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, played down reports Monday by some officials in the Siberian region — some of which were quickly removed from online platforms — indicating that Shipilova had died after contracting plague in a lab accident.
The agency said she was not diagnosed with plague, but died of "pneumonia of unknown etiology," suggesting doctors didn't know the exact germ that made her sick.
She died in an Irkutsk hospital two days after contracting the illness. The hospital where she was treated, and where her roughly 200 close recent contacts were evaluated, was then partially shut down under quarantine conditions, Russian authorities said. They rejected reports that several other health facilities in the region were also put under restrictions as a precaution.
Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that an analysis of samples from Shipilova revealed no microorganisms associated with her work, which involved handling dangerous pathogens at the lab.
The agency said Tuesday that many of her close contacts, having been brought in for screening, were allowed to go back home. It said some cold and flu infections, including several COVID-19 cases, were discovered, but nothing more sinister.
President Trump assured reporters on Monday that U.S. officials were watching the case closely and stood ready to help.
"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," he said. "They call it pneumonia, and pneumonia, you know, years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger disproportionately. But we'll help them."

Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:04:50 UTC
21:04:50 KST

Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
Scientists have watched speeding quarks create ripples in primordial matter, revealing just how liquid-like the early universe really was.
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.
- Share:
In the universe's earliest moments, temperatures reached trillions of degrees, creating an intensely hot mixture of quarks and gluons. These elementary particles raced around at nearly the speed of light in a state of matter known as quark-gluon plasma (QGP). This primordial material existed for only a few millionths of a second before cooling rapidly, allowing quarks and gluons to combine into protons, neutrons, and other particles found throughout the universe today.
At CERN's Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland, physicists are recreating quark-gluon plasma to investigate the ingredients that filled the young universe. By colliding heavy ions at nearly the speed of light, researchers can briefly separate quarks and gluons and produce tiny amounts of the same kind of matter that existed during the universe's first microseconds.
Quarks Leave Wakes in Primordial Plasma
A CERN team led by MIT physicists has now found clear evidence that quarks generate wakes as they travel through this plasma, much like a duck creating ripples as it moves across water. The observations provide the first direct evidence that quark-gluon plasma responds to fast-moving particles as a unified fluid, producing waves, splashes, and swirling motion instead of simply behaving as a collection of independently scattering particles.
"It has been a long debate in our field, on whether the plasma should respond to a quark," says Yen-Jie Lee, professor of physics at MIT. "Now we see the plasma is incredibly dense, such that it is able to slow down a quark, and produces splashes and swirls like a liquid. So quark-gluon plasma really is a primordial soup."
Lee and his colleagues developed a new method for detecting these quark wakes. They plan to use the technique on additional particle collision data to search for more examples and study them in greater detail.
By measuring how large the wakes become, how quickly they travel, how far they extend, and how long they take to fade, scientists may be able to determine important properties of quark-gluon plasma. Those measurements could also offer clues about how the plasma behaved during the first microseconds after the universe began.
"Studying how quark wakes bounce back and forth will give us new insights on the quark-gluon plasma's properties," Lee says. "With this experiment, we are taking a snapshot of this primordial quark soup."
The study's co-authors are members of the CMS Collaboration, a worldwide group of particle physicists who conduct and analyze experiments using the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS), one of the general-purpose particle detectors at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Researchers used the CMS experiment to identify signs of quark wakes in this study. The open-access findings appear in Physics Letters B.
The Universe's First Liquid
Quark-gluon plasma is thought to have been the first liquid in the universe. It was also the hottest liquid ever known, reaching temperatures of several trillion degrees Celsius during its brief existence.
Scientists have also described QGP as a near-"perfect" liquid. In this unusual state, individual quarks and gluons appear to move together as an exceptionally smooth fluid with almost no friction.
This understanding comes from numerous experiments and theoretical studies. One influential model was developed by Krishna Rajagopal, the William A. M. Burden Professor of Physics at MIT, and his collaborators. Known as the hybrid model, it predicts that quark-gluon plasma should react like a fluid when energetic particles travel through it.
According to the model, a fast-moving jet of quarks should disturb the surrounding plasma and leave a wake behind, causing the material to ripple and splash.
Physicists have spent years searching for evidence of these wakes at the Large Hadron Collider and other high-energy particle accelerators. In these experiments, heavy ions such as lead are accelerated to nearly the speed of light and smashed together. The collisions briefly create tiny droplets of primordial matter that usually survive for less than a quadrillionth of a second.
Researchers must effectively capture a snapshot of that fleeting moment and use the resulting particle patterns to reconstruct the properties of the quark-gluon plasma.
Why Quark Wakes Were Difficult to See
Previous searches for quark wakes often focused on pairs consisting of a quark and an "antiquark." Antiquarks are counterparts to quarks whose certain properties have the same magnitude but opposite signs.
When a quark moves rapidly through the plasma, an antiquark may be produced traveling at the same speed in the opposite direction. Scientists therefore searched for quark and antiquark pairs, expecting both particles to produce detectable wakes in the surrounding plasma.
That approach created a major problem.
"When you have two quarks produced, the problem is that, when the two quarks go in opposite directions, the one quark overshadows the wake of the second quark," Lee says.
Lee and his colleagues realized that the wake from a single quark would be much easier to identify if there were no second quark creating an overlapping disturbance.
"We have figured out a new technique that allows us to see the effects of a single quark in the QGP, through a different pair of particles," Lee says.
Using Z Bosons as a Wake Tag
Instead of searching for quark and antiquark pairs after lead ion collisions, the researchers looked for events in which one quark traveled through the plasma in nearly the opposite direction from a "Z boson."
A Z boson is a neutral elementary particle associated with the weak force. It interacts very little with the surrounding plasma, making it useful as a clean reference point. Z bosons also appear at a distinctive energy, which makes them relatively easy for physicists to identify.
"In this soup of quark-gluon plasma, there are numerous quarks and gluons passing by and colliding with each other," Lee explains. "Sometimes when we are lucky, one of these collisions creates a Z boson and a quark, with high momentum."
When such a collision occurs, the quark and Z boson should fly away from each other in opposite directions. The quark can disturb the plasma and produce a wake, while the Z boson should pass through without significantly affecting the material around it.
That means any ripples appearing in the plasma on the quark's side can be attributed to the quark itself.
Working with Professor Yi Chen's group at Vanderbilt University, the researchers realized they could use Z bosons as a "tag" for locating and measuring wakes created by individual quarks.
Wakes Found Among Billions of Collisions
The team analyzed data from heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Among 13 billion collisions, they identified roughly 2,000 events in which a Z boson was produced.
For each of those events, the researchers mapped how energy was distributed throughout the short-lived quark-gluon plasma. They repeatedly found fluid-like patterns of splashes and swirling motion in the direction opposite the Z boson.
Because the Z boson itself barely interacts with the plasma, the researchers could attribute these wake patterns directly to individual quarks traveling through the material.
The observed wakes also matched predictions from Rajagopal's hybrid model. The results indicate that quark-gluon plasma really does respond collectively like a liquid when energetic particles pass through it.
"This is something that many of us have argued must be there for a good many years, and that many experiments have looked for," says Rajagopal, who was not directly involved with the new study.
"We've gained the first direct evidence that the quark indeed drags more plasma with it as it travels," Lee adds. "This will enable us to study the properties and behavior of this exotic fluid in unprecedented detail."
This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Department of Energy.

Vietnamese trade delegation in Tehran; exclusive interview on expanding bilateral ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
