Vietnamese trade delegation in Tehran; exclusive interview on expanding bilateral ties
TEHRAN- A Vietnamese trade delegation arrived in Tehran on Tuesday, October 6, and is scheduled to stay until October 18. During their stay, the delegation has a packed schedule of business activities, including visits to various regions of Iran, assessments of cooperation opportunities, and trade meetings.
In this connection, Tehran Times conducted an exclusive interview with the Delegation Head, Mr. Nguyen Dang Dinh, who is visiting Iran for the third time.
The full text of the interview follows:
What motivated you to join this business mission to Iran, and what specific opportunities do you hope to explore during the visit?
We joined this mission to expand our commercial reach in the Middle East and engage directly with Iran’s sizable market. The Vietnamese business community aims to boost direct exports of agricultural products (coffee, cashews, pepper, rice) and consumer goods, while exploring imports of high-quality Iranian industrial inputs and raw materials to support our domestic manufacturing.
Given the current sanctions environment and banking restrictions, what are your main concerns about doing business with Iran, and what practical payment or financial mechanisms do you think could help overcome these barriers?
The primary operational concern is the absence of direct, streamlined cross-border banking linkages. To facilitate smooth trade in civilian and consumer goods, we encourage trade agencies and financial institutions to support flexible settlement frameworks, such as bilateral barter trade mechanisms or compliant local-currency clearing solutions that lower exchange costs and transaction friction.
Official Vietnam–Iran trade is around $170 million, but much of the real trade may pass through third countries. How do you assess the actual potential of bilateral trade, and what can be done to make these flows more direct and transparent?
The real economic potential between Vietnam and Iran is significantly higher than current figures suggest, as our economic structures are complementary rather than competitive. To make trade flows more direct and transparent, businesses on both sides need greater access to market intelligence, active participation in trade expos, and official business-matching platforms that reduce reliance on third-country intermediaries.
Which sectors do you believe offer the most realistic and immediate opportunities for Vietnam–Iran cooperation, and why? For example: agriculture, food processing, mining, logistics, technology, healthcare, or petrochemicals.
The most realistic sectors for immediate commercial cooperation include:
• Agriculture & Food Processing: Exporting Vietnamese coffee, seafood, and spices; importing Iranian dried fruits, saffron, and nuts.
• Industrial Raw Materials: Sourcing specialty chemicals, construction supplies, and polymers from Iran.
• Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals: Exploring trade in medical equipment, active ingredients, and biotechnology products.
From your experience, what are the biggest obstacles in logistics, transportation, quality standards, and verifying business partners between the two countries, and what solutions would you recommend?
Key supply chain bottlenecks involve long transit times, high freight costs, and differing quality compliance frameworks (such as Halal certification). Practical solutions include establishing direct links with regional logistics providers and fostering mutual recognition between regulatory bodies to standardize quality inspections and expedite customs clearance.
Vietnam has 17 free trade agreements and access to 60 economies. How can Iranian and Vietnamese companies work together—through joint ventures, Vietnam-based production, or other models—to manage sanctions risks and reach regional and global markets?
Vietnam’s extensive network of 17 FTAs offers preferential access to major global markets. Iranian enterprises can collaborate with Vietnamese companies through joint ventures or local processing facilities. By adding value to raw materials inside Vietnam, both sides can jointly access ASEAN and wider international consumer markets under compliant commercial arrangements.
What concrete outcomes would make this mission successful for you, and what follow-up steps should governments, chambers of commerce, and the private sector take to turn these discussions into long-term trade and investment partnerships?
For the business community, a successful mission means establishing vetted business leads, securing initial commercial contracts, and signing MOUs for non-sanctioned goods. Moving forward, chambers of commerce and trade promotion agencies should maintain direct communication lines and organize regular exchange delegations to turn these initial discussions into long-term trade partnerships.

Spain approves new housing decrees ahead of November elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:03:20 UTC
21:03:20 KST

Alyssa McMurtry
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Spain’s government approved two new housing decrees on Tuesday, reviving measures rejected by the parliament last week as housing protests grow ahead of early elections on Nov. 29.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the package retained the substance of the earlier proposals, with additions to expand affordable housing, support first-time buyers and protect tenants.
“The government will continue governing,” he told a news conference after the Cabinet meeting.
Sanchez announced early elections Monday following the defeat of the previous housing decrees Friday. He urged lawmakers to endorse the revised package, describing it as a matter of “common sense and humanity.”
He argued that speculation had distorted the housing market, preventing it from functioning according to the normal logic of supply and demand and making public intervention necessary.
The package contains 21 measures, including a €10 billion ($11.2 billion) financing program offering interest-free loans of up to €50,000 to help people buy their first home.
It also provides tax deductions for tenants and incentives for small landlords offering affordable rents.
To increase supply, Sanchez announced €280 million in guarantees to support housing construction and €400 million for social housing providers. Public housing company Casa 47 will acquire thousands of properties from Spain’s social security system for affordable housing.
Tenants current on rent payments would be able to seek lease extensions of up to two years. Other provisions include limits on rent increases, protections for vulnerable residents without alternative accommodation and rules governing when landlords can recover their properties.
The measures would also regulate temporary and room rentals, restrict purchases by investment funds and require tourist apartments to be taxed as businesses.
Sanchez acknowledged insufficient support for the “more ambitious” automatic lease-renewal policy in last week’s decrees, which would have required landlords to compensate tenants if they declined to renew contracts without the required justifications.
Although parliament has been dissolved, the government remains in office and can approve emergency decree-laws. These must be endorsed within 30 days by the lower house’s Permanent Deputation, which exercises certain parliamentary powers between legislatures.
Its composition offers a possible majority without the Catalan separatist party Junts, whose opposition helped defeat the previous measures.
The Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) could instead prove decisive. It is negotiating safeguards for small landlords and vulnerable residents but has not committed to supporting the new texts.
Separately, Spain’s two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, agreed Monday to call a 24-hour general strike this autumn over wages and housing affordability.
The agreement requires approval by their governing bodies, and a date remains to be set in consultation with tenants’ groups and other organizations.
Demonstrations have continued across Spain, alongside a protest camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square, following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home.
The dispute has placed housing at the center of the election campaign as Sanchez seeks a stronger parliamentary majority.

Deputy Commander of the Air Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Yuriy Cherevashenko, commenting in the Verkhovna Rada on recent instances of Russian drones entering Moldova's airspace, expressed the opinion that these are planned actions.
"These are planned actions; perhaps 2-3% might have been influenced by electronic warfare (EW), but in the Black Sea they can organize good repeater coverage, so these are planned actions," Cherevashenko said on Tuesday in the Verkhovna Rada at a meeting of the Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) investigating potential violations of Ukrainian legislation in the sphere of defense, anti-corruption legislation, and compliance with human rights and freedoms under martial law.
He also spoke regarding Belarus's role in Shahed drone strikes on the western regions. According to him, Belarus helps Russian drones reach the western regions of Ukraine. Without repeaters, such strikes would hardly be possible. "The problem [with the placement of repeaters on Belarusian territory] remains. Infrastructure that facilitates drone targeting is still operating on its territory." However, he noted that direct launches from Belarusian territory are not recorded. "We record the transit of Russian drones through Belarus, but there have been no direct launches from there," Cherevashenko said.
He also noted that the appearance of Russian drones on the border with Poland is largely connected to Belarus. "Theoretically, a drone can fly autonomously using its own positioning systems. But under the conditions of our EW operating densely, this is significantly more difficult. Therefore, repeaters are precisely what makes it possible to guide the drone more accurately to the target." Cherevashenko gave an affirmative answer to the question that Belarus is effectively creating additional opportunities for Russia to carry out such attacks.

Migri fines six employers for hiring undocumented workers in Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:02:09 EEST
21:02:09 KST

Finland’s Immigration Service has imposed financial penalties on six employers for employing third-country nationals who were staying in the country illegally. The largest penalty reached €30,000 after authorities found that a construction employer had continued the practice despite previous intervention.
The Finnish Immigration Service, known as Migri, issued the penalties during summer 2026. None of the decisions has yet gained legal force.
Finnish law allows Migri to impose a penalty on an employer that employs a third-country national who has no legal right to remain in Finland.
Penalties range from €1,250 to €37,530 under the Employment Contracts Act. In some cases, employers also face responsibility for costs linked to returning an employee who was staying in Finland illegally.
“The purpose of the penalty is to reduce the attractiveness of illegal immigration and undeclared work,” Tuuli Huhtilainen, process owner for employed person residence permits at Migri, said in the agency’s statement.
Huhtilainen said authorities consider factors including whether the employer acted intentionally, whether the conduct occurred repeatedly and how many people without legal residence status the employer employed.
Migri handled 10 reports involving suspected illegal employment. The agency decided to impose penalties in seven cases. Two involved the same employer, leaving six employers subject to penalties.
The reports originated from the police, the Finnish Supervisory Agency and Migri’s own permit processing operations. Employers have an opportunity to respond to allegations before the agency reaches a decision.
The largest penalty, €30,000, went to an employer in the building construction sector.
According to Migri, at least four people staying in Finland illegally had worked for the company over several years. The agency said the employer continued its conduct despite warnings from authorities and a fine issued by police.
Migri imposed a €10,000 penalty on a food manufacturing company that had employed two people without legal residence status for three years.
Both employees held valid residence permits when their employment began. Migri treated that fact as a factor supporting a lower penalty.
Three other employers received penalties of €5,000 each. Two operate in the food and beverage service sector. The third operates in the construction of ships and floating structures.
Migri did not identify the employers.

Hungary to make public communist-era informant files
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:26 UTC
21:00:26 KST

Hungary has made a historic decision to release tens of thousands of communist-era police documents, allowing citizens to access information about informants and individuals who collaborated with the security services of that time, reports Reuters.
The release of these documents is part of a pledge by Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar to grant access to information previously held in Budapest archives, in an effort to reckon with the country's totalitarian past. The documents will become available to the general public on the 70th anniversary of Hungary's 1956 anti-Soviet uprising.
Although the communist era in Hungary ended back in 1989, there has until now been insufficient political will to fully release the documents. Previously, access to the full records was restricted to researchers, and ordinary citizens could only request information concerning themselves or immediate family members; now, however, anyone will be able to search for information in online databases. During the Cold War, secret police forces in Eastern European countries (such as the Stasi in East Germany or Hungary's security services) relied on information from informants, who were often recruited through blackmail, threats, or the promise of payment. Between 1959 and 1989, approximately 55,000 informants were registered in Hungary. 
They monitored family, friends, neighbors, and colleagues for signs of dissent or Western influence,
 and their reports frequently led to arrests and interrogations. Clandestine apartments located in Budapest's Old Town served as meeting places for secret police officers and civilian informants.
In the 1980s, informants frequently attended Budapest's underground rock concerts—events that attracted young people and were viewed by the authorities as potentially dangerous to the regime. Péter Muller, still a prominent figure on the contemporary music scene, recalled how his band, Kontroll Csoport, performed the song "Informers and Provocateurs" in 1983; the lyrics explicitly addressed the issue of informants. The musician recounted how spotlights were subsequently turned on the audience, revealing a crowd of about 1,000 people looking around, trying to figure out who the informant might be.
Muller was nearly expelled from college for his music, some of his concerts were banned, and he was interrogated by the police. His first punk rock band was named URH—the same as the radio frequency used by the state police—and it frequently became a target of police attention.
Despite these memories, Muller has mixed feelings about the release of the documents after so much time. He told Reuters that the idea of offering the public catharsis and a chance for cleansing after such a long period makes him uncomfortable. 
He believes that people who have already died or are now living different lives should not be ostracized, humiliated, shamed, or punished.
The documents from the former state security services, containing the names of 50,000 to 60,000 informants, are managed by the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security (ABTL). The archive's director, Bendegúz Gergő Cseh, praised the decision to make the documents public, calling it a historic step that goes further than anywhere else in the former Eastern Bloc. Poland opened its archives quite some time ago, but the public does not have the kind of unrestricted access to them that will be available in Hungary.
The law adopted in Hungary in September states that understanding the past and ensuring the transparency of public institutions are essential prerequisites for the existence of a democratic state. The release of four different types of documents will take place in two stages, beginning on November 4. In some instances, the documents will be redacted to protect sensitive information, such as details regarding health status, addictions, and sexual orientation.
Cseh emphasized that, both as an archivist and a historian, he believes it is inappropriate to pass judgment based solely on the contents of the documents. However, he also believes that the documents will enable a better understanding of life stories and allow for a more thorough confrontation with the past—not only for individuals but for society as a whole.

Rightwing ‘great replacement’ fears mask tech's real great replacement | Jason Stanley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

Across the world, “great replacement” theory has been employed again and again as the political foundation for fascism. Some of its fundamental tenets, such as the view that “whites are a dying minority”, have been amplified by tech billionaires and their platforms.
According to the version of this theory most employed in Europe and the United States, white replacement theory, white populations are being “replaced” by non-white populations, a replacement engineered by a shadowy global elite. For example, the need for skilled labor is supposedly being used by global elites as an excuse to bring in non-white immigrants to replace white workers.
Great replacement theory – a phenomenon Ibram X Kendi extensively documents in his recent book, Chain of Ideas – is the governing ideology of Europe’s far-right parties. It also serves as a justification for the US’s remorseless and violent politics of mass deportation or “remigration”, the term introduced by the far-right Austrian nationalist Martin Sellner in a 2024 book of that title. While a powerful international far right promotes this theory, a real great replacement is happening: of humanity with artificial intelligence.
Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is Europe’s most prominent extreme far-right party, whose central platform is, essentially, remigration. Elon Musk is a vocal supporter of this party, having given a speech remotely at the AfD campaign launch in January 2025, stating: “You have to go all out to convince people to vote for AfD.” AfD’s party program for Saxony-Anhalt explicitly uses the concerns of the fake great replacement theory to justify implementing the real one. Point 28 of its agenda for “Immigration and Remigration” begins:
 An AfD-led state government will develop a strategy for Saxony-Anhalt focused on technological upgrading, digitalization, and AI. This strategy is intended to help alleviate bottlenecks in the local labor market. Furthermore, it aims to avoid the immigration of skilled workers from culturally dissimilar backgrounds.
AfD proposes “financial support for technological upgrading, digitalization, and the use of AI by small and medium sized enterprises through the establishment of a dedicated funding program” as well as other kinds of support for companies to adopt AI. Again, this is not listed as part of AfD’s economic program – that is another section. Replacement of human jobs by AI is rather part of its immigration program – that is, its program motivated specifically by its central ideology of great replacement theory.
Palantir’s multibillionaire CEO, Alex Karp, while rejecting AfD’s Russia-friendly politics, has argued that AI will make mass migration obsolete, by obviating the need for skilled immigration into western countries.
At the same time as the global far right is promoting fear about non-white populations replacing white populations, tech companies are engineering the mass replacement of humanity by AI.
The panic about the replacement of white populations by non-white populations distracts attention from this real great replacement.
The global elite are in fact in a conspiracy to replace people. But the global elites in this instance are not liberals or Jews or Marxists or Islamists – they are the heads of giant companies. And their productions threaten not the replacement of white people by non-white people – they threaten to replace all people with AI agents.
On 18 April, Palantir posted a 22-point summary of Alex Karp and Nicholas Zamiski’s book The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the West. Point 21 was:
 Some cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive. All cultures are now equal. Criticism and value judgments are forbidden. Yet this new dogma glosses over the fact that certain cultures and indeed subcultures … have produced wonders. Others have proven middling, and worse, regressive and harmful.
According to this ideology, what makes for a superior culture are the skills and crafts it nurtures, and the productions (the “wonders”) that are the result of these skills.
If the goals of its creators are met, AI will replace human skills, and with it, human skilled production – indeed, even human cognitive skill by the cognitive labor of AI agents. And if you are in the game of ranking cultures, and in the business of replacing human production with AI production, you are going to logically end up with the view that humanity itself should ultimately be discarded.
Transhumanism is the view, popular among the Silicon Valley tech elite, that humans can be technologically augmented to give rise to a superior species, the “transhuman” (Elon Musk’s company Neuralink is devoted to merging humanity with AI).
Transhumanism can be viewed as a contemporary version of eugenics, the project of using genetics and selective breeding to engineer supposedly “superior” humans, an endeavor central to Nazism.
But I believe almost as popular as transhumanism among the Silicon Valley elite is AI successionism – the view that humans should give way to AI agents. With that handover, the center of moral concern should also change, from human welfare to the welfare of AI agents. It is not hard to imagine the creators of this new species wanting to survive in remote bunkers or outer space, with the knowledge that they have, like gods, been the agents of such a succession.
The fear that white workers will be replaced by non-white workers is masking the reality that all workers are being replaced by non-human workers. Similarly, the fear of the replacement of European civilization by foreign civilization is masking the threat of the replacement of all human civilization with an artificially designed one.
The global promotion of the fascist great replacement theory, the replacement of white workers by non-white workers, and the supposed displacement of “white civilization” is nothing other than a distraction from the real threat of a genuine great replacement, of humans by AI agents.

How to maximise the umami in mushrooms | Kitchen aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

How do I cook mushrooms at home so they have the umami you get in restaurant dishes?
John, by email
For Chantelle Nicholson, chef-patron of Apricity in London, boosting the savoury side of ’shrooms comes down to three main things. First, they hold a lot of water, so “you need to cook that out of them, so heat is super-important, as are fat and salt”. Tomás Gormley, chef-owner of Cardinal in Edinburgh, adds that he can “almost guarantee” that John isn’t using enough of the latter: “As a rule, I use 1.5% of the weight of whatever I’m seasoning. With mushrooms, especially, season early, before they hit the pan, to draw out their moisture. That resulting mushroomy water then cooks the mushrooms while it’s reducing and concentrating the flavour.”
But there are so many varieties of mushrooms out there, and they all behave in different ways, so John needs to be using the right ones for the job. “If you’re making a soup, puree or paté, field, portobello or button mushrooms are fine,” Nicholson says. “But if you’re looking for a delicious sauteed mushroom, say, ideally you need something with less water content – chestnut, shiitake or blue/grey oyster mushrooms. Heat oil in a pan, then add the shredded or sliced mushrooms, and season with fine salt straight away.” Nicholson would be inclined to toss in a bay leaf and some thyme or sage, too, and maybe a smashed clove of garlic. “Cook over a high-ish heat until lightly golden, then add a bit of butter and keep cooking until golden. If you want to enhance the flavour even further, a splash of dry sherry works really well.”
That said, Buttons Mira, author of The Mushroomery, throws her ’shrooms into a dry frying pan: “That’s right, no oil or fat! I put a lid on top and let them sweat out that rich, umami flavour.” Alice Zaslavsky, author of Weeknights with Alice, deploys a similar tactic: “Cooking mushrooms the traditional way in fat can inhibit the intensification of umami and lock in too much moisture, which is why I’ve taken to wet-frying my mushrooms.” She first lets them bubble away in a little water “spliced with condiments: umami-rich soy sauce and/or Worcestershire sauce work well”, until all the liquid evaporates. “Only then do I add oil and/or butter to lift off the flavour in the base of the pan and encourage caramelisation for extra depth and sweetness.”
Heading out of the frying pan and into the oven, a properly roasted mushroom can also be meaty and deeply flavoured: “That makes them super-nutty and delicious,” says Mira, who then uses them in pastas and risottos. The best way to do this is, again, with high heat, salt and oil, Nicholson says: “I’d also suggest using chestnut mushrooms over button mushrooms, and quartering them – hard herbs, such as thyme, bay or rosemary, will help as well.”
Just like the rest of us, though, sometimes those mushrooms need a bit of a helping hand: “Up the umami potential by doubling down on the right kind of mushroom,” Zaslavsky says, which in her book includes sprinkling over dried shiitake or porcini in powdered form: “Both offer a deep, savoury aroma and flavour that helps enhance milder varieties.” Magic mushrooms, indeed.

Parents of transgender youth faced declining mental health after the 2025 inauguration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

A recent study found that parents of transgender youth experienced worsening mental health and well-being following the 2025 United States presidential inauguration compared to parents of cisgender youth. The research highlights the immediate emotional toll that shifting political climates and federal policy changes can take on the family members of marginalized groups. The study was published in Psychological Science.
Following the 2025 presidential inauguration, the new federal administration issued several executive orders aimed at transgender youth. These orders sought to ban gender-affirming medical care for minors, penalize schools that support transgender students, and restrict transgender girls from competing on gender-aligned sports teams.
Prior research has established that such macrolevel policies can act as institutional signals. These signals communicate how broader society views specific groups, which can influence the well-being of those targeted and their families. Policies limiting self-expression and resources contribute to minority stress, a framework explaining how marginalized groups experience worse well-being due to societal hostility.
Researchers wanted to understand how this specific political shift affected both transgender adolescents and their supportive parents. The research team was led by psychologist Rachel A. Leshin of Princeton University, along with Aditi Kodipady, Grey F. Raber, Natalie M. Gallagher, and Kristina R. Olson. They designed a study to compare the mental health trajectories of transgender youth and their parents against a similarly situated group of cisgender youth and their parents.
The researchers tracked 160 youth between the ages of 12 and 17, as well as 167 parents. Within this group, 73 of the youth identified as transgender or nonbinary, and 87 identified as cisgender. The participants were drawn from larger, ongoing longitudinal studies of gender development across the United States.
The families involved in the research were predominantly white, highly educated, and high-income. Because both groups of parents skewed politically liberal, the study offered a controlled comparison. It allowed researchers to differentiate between general frustration with the new administration and distress specifically tied to raising a transgender child in a hostile political environment.
In their primary analysis, the researchers compared mental health data collected annually between 2022 and 2024 to weekly data collected in the seven weeks following the January 2025 inauguration. Youth and parents completed separate self-report surveys measuring depression, anxiety, and positive emotional states. Participants rated how frequently they experienced specific symptoms, such as being unable to stop feeling sad or worrying at bedtime, over the previous seven days.
The researchers observed widening gaps in mental health between the two groups of parents. Before the election, parents of transgender youth and parents of cisgender youth reported similar levels of depression and positive emotions. After the inauguration, parents of transgender youth reported higher levels of depression and lower positive emotions than their counterparts.
Anxiety levels also diverged. While parents of transgender youth reported higher anxiety than parents of cisgender youth before the election, this gap more than doubled in size after the inauguration. To ensure these differences were not just reflecting voting behavior or a parent’s own gender identity, the researchers ran additional analyses. The patterns remained the same when excluding the small number of parents who voted for the current president or who identified as transgender or gender-diverse themselves.
The team also conducted a secondary analysis tracking participants continuously over an eight-week period surrounding the inauguration. They found that parents of transgender youth experienced steady linear increases in anxiety and depression throughout this window. In contrast, parents of cisgender youth showed no consistent changes in these measures.
To understand why parents experienced these outcomes, the researchers analyzed weekly measures of parental worry and perceived social support. Their exploratory analyses suggested that elevated worry for their children may help explain the differing mental health outcomes between the two parent groups, though the researchers noted the causal direction could not be definitively established. Perceived social support did not differ between the groups and did not explain the results. Both groups reported high levels of social support, indicating that community backing was not enough to offset the distress caused by the new political landscape.
The researchers also examined the mental health of the youth themselves. In the primary comparison between pre-election and post-inauguration periods, the differences in well-being between transgender and cisgender youth were subtle and not statistically significant in most models. Transgender youth showed a drop in positive emotions after the inauguration. However, the mental health trajectories of the two youth groups largely diverged only in anxiety. During the post-election period, cisgender youths’ anxiety lessened, while transgender youths’ anxiety remained stable.
To explore why the mental health declines were more prominent in parents than in the youth, the researchers analyzed open-ended survey responses. Two independent reviewers, blinded to the participants’ demographics, coded these responses. They found that parents of transgender youth were much more likely to explicitly mention transgender issues and express severe negative emotions than the transgender youth were. Some parents shared statements like, “I have cried almost every day this past week,” and “Every week is a new wave of fear, frustration, and utter disbelief.”
The authors suggest that parents often anticipate long-term threats more acutely than adolescents do. At the time of the surveys, the executive orders targeting transgender youth had largely been blocked by federal judges and had not yet altered daily life for most participants. The youth might not have felt the immediate impact, whereas their parents were already processing the institutional signals and preparing for potential future consequences.
The study focused on a specific demographic of liberal-leaning, supportive parents. Parents who hold different political beliefs or who do not support their child’s transgender identity might not experience the same mental health changes. Research involving more politically, racially, and socioeconomically diverse families is necessary to see if these patterns hold across the broader population.
The number of participants involved also limits how broadly the conclusions can be applied. The group differences observed among the youth were small and less consistent than those among the parents. Further research with larger groups of adolescents is required to track how federal policies affect the long-term mental health of transgender youth. Future studies could also track whether the deteriorating mental health of supportive parents eventually impacts the well-being of their children over time.
The study, “Reduced Mental Health and Well-Being in Parents of Transgender Youth Following the 2025 U.S. Presidential Inauguration,” was authored by Rachel A. Leshin, Aditi Kodipady, Grey F. Raber, Natalie M. Gallagher, and Kristina R. Olson.

Alyssa McMurtry
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Spain’s Supreme Court on Tuesday provisionally lifted an arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, clearing the way for his return nearly nine years after he left the country following a failed independence bid.
Judge Pablo Llarena ordered the immediate withdrawal of domestic arrest warrants against Puigdemont and former Catalan ministers Antoni Comin and Lluis Puig, according to a court statement.
The decision followed a Constitutional Court ruling upholding an appeal by former Catalan minister Dolors Bassa against the refusal to apply Spain’s amnesty law to her embezzlement conviction.
Although the full judgment has yet to be available, Llarena said similarities between the cases justified lifting the warrants while he examined its implications.
Keeping the warrants in force in the meantime could lead to a detention that later proved unjustified, the judge said.
Puigdemont, who led Catalonia’s regional government during its 2017 independence referendum and unilateral declaration of independence, left Spain for Belgium that October to avoid prosecution.
He has since lived abroad, although he briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 to address supporters before escaping again without being arrested.
The amnesty law, approved in 2024, emerged from a deal between Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Socialists and Puigdemont’s Junts party, whose parliamentary support helped Sanchez secure another term after the 2023 elections.
The Supreme Court, however, had refused to apply the law to Puigdemont’s embezzlement charge, keeping his arrest warrant active.
Tuesday’s decision comes amid renewed tensions between Junts and the government, just one day after Sanchez called an early general election for Nov. 29.
Junts joined opposition parties in rejecting the government’s housing decrees last Friday, delivering Sanchez a parliamentary defeat that helped push his decision to seek a broader mandate.
Sanchez welcomed the lifting of the arrest warrant, saying it would also help Catalan society “look forward and move forward.”
Puigdemont and the main opposition parties have yet to comment on the ruling.

How melting glaciers are redrawing Switzerland's maps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

How melting glaciers are redrawing Switzerland’s maps
Switzerland’s glaciers lost vast amounts of ice in this summer’s baking heat. The changes are increasingly visible on the country’s maps.
Thousands of aerial photographs are currently arriving at the Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo) in Wabern, near Bern. The images were captured by swisstopo’s aerial survey service, which this year focused on the Alps in cantons Valais and Vaud. Every year, the federal government flies over roughly a third of Switzerland to document changes in the landscape.
“I’m a child of the mountains,” says Tobias Providoli, who heads a team of 35 people at swisstopo. Yet he can barely bring himself to look at the latest images. “I try not to compare them with the old ones, because the decline is so dramatic. I don’t even open those images in the first place.”
More
A fifth of Swiss Alpine ice has vanished in five years
Since 1838, the institution that is now swisstopo has been documenting and mapping Switzerland. Among the most striking changes is the retreat of the country’s glaciers. “It is not just the glacier itself that is changing in size,” Providoli says. “The entire glacial foreland is changing too: the rocks, the loose material and moraine areas. It’s a highly dynamic landscape.”
The Federal Office of Topography has been taking aerial photographs of Switzerland since 1926 and has operated its own flight service ever since. Today, two aircraft are used to re-photograph around a third of the country each year. As a result, Switzerland is fully re-mapped every three years.
A high-resolution digital camera captures several images simultaneously, including standard colour photographs and infrared images.
Most flights take place in summer. In spring, aircraft typically survey the central Swiss Plateau region, when vegetation is still sparse and the terrain is clearly visible. The Alps, by contrast, are photographed in August and September, when most areas are free of snow.
Good weather and clear visibility are essential for all aerial photographs.
Morteratsch Glacier in 2022 and 2025
>>The Morteratsch Glacier near Pontresina, canton Graubünden, in 2022 and 2025 (right). During this period, the glacier tongue retreated by dozens of metres Use the slider to compare. (Images: swisstopo)
The aerial photographs provide the basis for Switzerland’s digital national map as well as traditional paper hiking maps. But maps are only two-dimensional and often fail to show the true extent of glacier retreat, Providoli explains.
When comparing current and historical images, most people notice how far the glacier tongue has retreated. “In our computer images, we can also see the loss of glacier volume,” he says. In that respect, the summer 2026 heatwave has left a clear mark.
More
The beneficial effect of avalanches on Alpine glaciers
The slow death of the glaciers
According to the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (Glamos), average glacier ice thickness fell by between 2.5 and 4 metres between 2025 and 2026. In some places, little ice will remain and so-called “dead ice” will form. Providoli is also observing this development first-hand.
“Dead ice refers to ice masses that have separated from the original glacier. They are slowly moving towards their demise, which is where the term comes from,” he explains.
If no ice is visible in the latest aerial photographs, a glacier is considered dead and its name is removed from the register. According to Glamos, at least two glaciers are likely to have disappeared permanently this summer: the Bella-Tola Glacier in canton Valais and the Griessfiren in canton Glarus.
Bella-Tola Glacier in 1976 and 2021
>>The Bella-Tola Glacier in canton Valais. The first map section dates from 1976, the second from 2021. By the summer of 2026, the glacier had effectively disappeared. Use the slider to compare. (Images: swisstopo)
It takes several months for changes in the natural environment to be reflected on maps. Although software helps to update the data, human expertise is still needed when it comes to glaciers, Providoli says.
“Mapping the glacier tongue is relatively straightforward. Along the sides of the glacier, however, it is much harder to distinguish between scree, rock and ice.” As a result, aerial photographs still have to be interpreted by experts, with changes manually recorded in the system.
And the work does not stop there. Even in the high mountains, on the snow-capped peaks, glacial retreat leaves its mark.
“If I have a snow-capped mountain and the glacier melts away, it loses height,” Providoli says. “That elevation then has to be adjusted as well.”
Over the coming months, Providoli and his team will calculate and record exactly how much height individual peaks have lost as a result of this year’s glacier melt. One thing is certain: Switzerland’s snow-capped summits have shrunk.

‘Ebola takes the people children depend on’: UNICEF

‘Ebola takes the people children depend on’: UNICEF
The Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is robbing children of their loved ones – with some succumbing to the deadly disease themselves, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) reported on Tuesday.
The update comes as regional neighbour Kenya confirmed its first case and death from the disease, believed to have come from DRC.
“Ebola takes the people children depend on and unravels their lives,” said Halimatou Amadou, UNICEF Chief of Communication in the DRC, speaking to journalists in Geneva.
“The parents fall ill, a child may be exposed, the parent is taken for treatment or dies. At the very moment a child most needs someone, fear and stigma can keep relatives and neighbours away.”
Nearly 2,000 children affected
More than 1,900 boys and girls have either lost one or both parents, or their caregivers, since the outbreak was declared in May, or have been separated from them.
Most of these children, 1,581, are in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis. A further 322 are in neighbouring North Kivu province.
“And these are the children we know about because these figures cover only the area where UNICEF works with social affairs teams in the affected provinces,” she said.
Fighters and survivors
Ms. Amadou put names behind the numbers, such as Lina*, a seven-month-old girl who she met at a UNICEF-supported nursery next to an Ebola treatment centre in Bunia, the Ituri capital.
Lina’s mother died and her father is missing. Her grandfather, who lives nearby, has visited twice and the hope is that they will soon be together.
Another child, Raphael*, just eight months old, survived Ebola but lost eight family members. He stayed at the nursery for more than three weeks until his older brother could take him home.
Young lives lost
“Children are not only losing their parents. They're also losing their own lives,” Ms. Amadou said.
As of 29 September, at least 2,017 children had been confirmed with Ebola in DRC. At least 1,062 have died.
She noted that children make up just over one in four confirmed cases, but around one in three deaths. However, the situation is worse among under-fives where the death rate is seven in 10, up from six in 10 just a few weeks ago.
“Many die before the virus is ever detected, before they ever reach treatment,” she said.
Care and access
While in Bunia Ms. Amadou “also saw what works” for young lives upended by Ebola.
UNICEF supports 12 nurseries in Ituri and North Kivyu that care for babies and young children who have been exposed to the virus, or whose parents are in treatment, or who are on their own.
“Children are fed, they are held, they're cared for, they are also watched closely so that if symptoms appear, they get paediatric care fast,” she said.
UNICEF is calling for nurseries at every Ebola treatment centre in the DRC, while underscoring the need to maintain health essential services. That way children receive early detection and quick referral to Ebola care, as well as protection from common childhood diseases.
First case in Kenya
Meanwhile, the World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring the situation in Kenya, which on Tuesday confirmed its first case and fatality, according to media reports.
Spokesman Christian Lindmeier the case was “likely imported from DRC” but more information was not available.
He said colleagues on the ground are working with the Kenyan authorities to get more details.
*Names have been changed to protect the children’s privacy and identity

When streets become pharmacies: Booming illicit markets in Central Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

When streets become pharmacies: Booming illicit markets in Central Africa
Antibiotics, malaria treatments, painkillers, opioids. More than 250 tonnes of medical products were seized over six years in Central Africa. Behind those numbers is an illicit market that thrives not simply despite the region’s fragile health systems, but in part because of them.
When medicines are scarce, unaffordable or simply too far away, illicit sellers have proved adept at filling the void.
That is the dynamic described in a new report released Tuesday by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). The illicit trade extends far beyond falsified drugs. It includes genuine medicines diverted from legitimate supply chains, unapproved products and drugs smuggled across borders.
251 tonnes seized
From 2020 through 2025, authorities seized 251 tonnes of medical products in Cameroon, Republic of Congo, Gabon, Central African Republic and Chad. Annual seizures rose from about five tonnes in 2020 to nearly 116 tonnes in 2024, before exceeding 97 tonnes in 2025.
The United Nations cautioned against interpreting the increase as a straightforward measure of the trade’s growth. Larger seizures can reflect both greater trafficking and more aggressive enforcement, and the available data vary considerably among countries and from year to year.
Still, the scale is striking. Cameroon accounted for nearly all of the seizures recorded in 2025, with 96 tonnes intercepted, compared with just 2.5 tonnes five years earlier. The products intercepted across the region range from antibiotics, antimalarial and anti-inflammatory drugs to painkillers and such psychoactive substances as tramadol and pregabalin.
“The report outlines a multimodal trafficking system that uses maritime, riverine, air and road routes and involves a broad range of actors,” said Sylvie Bertrand, UNODC’s regional representative for West and Central Africa.
High costs fuel illicit markets
But the report, produced with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), suggests that the roots of the trade are partly beyond the reach of law enforcement.
Malaria, tuberculosis and HIV remain widespread across the region, while public health systems often struggle to provide treatment. In 2023, the WHO’s universal health-coverage index placed all six countries in the Central African economic bloc among the world’s poorest performers. Chad scored just 26 out of 100, compared with a global average of 71.
Distance and cost compound the problem. In the Central African Republic and Chad, more than half the population lived at least two hours from a public hospital providing emergency care, according to data cited in the report. In Chad, a prefilled insulin syringe cost the equivalent of nearly 16 days’ wages for the lowest-paid government employee.
Competitive pricing
Under those circumstances, buying medicine on the street can become less an alternative to the formal health system than a necessity. Consumers in the Central African Republic told researchers that informal sellers allowed them to “buy one or two tablets for about 100 CFA francs” – roughly 20 cents – rather than “buy the medicines in a box of 12 [at a pharmacy]”.
The result is a marketplace where legitimate, falsified and substandard medicines can be difficult to distinguish.
From 2013 to 2025, WHO’s surveillance system recorded incidents involving 228 medical products in the Central African economic bloc. Of those, 71 per cent were classified as falsified and 11 per cent as substandard. Perhaps more troubling, a third of the incidents were detected in regulated supply chains, suggesting that buying medicine from an authorised outlet does not eliminate the risk.
In April 2025, the WHO reported falsified batches of amoxicillin in Cameroon and the Central African Republic that did not contain the active ingredient listed on their labels. In September 2026, Cameroonian authorities seized thousands of cartons in Yaoundé containing, among other things, counterfeit medicines, packaging materials used to repackage drugs and psychotropic substances.
From ports to armed groups
The trafficking routes largely follow the arteries of legitimate regional commerce. The ports of Apapa in Nigeria and Douala in Cameroon, along with river ports in Brazzaville and Bangui, were identified as major entry points. Authorities also seized 7.3 tonnes of medical products at airports across the region from 2020 through 2025.
The criminal networks behind the trade are equally varied. They include clandestine manufacturers, wholesalers, informal vendors, couriers, health care workers, corrupt public officials and online sellers.
Armed groups have also found ways to profit, according to the report, by looting health facilities, reselling medicines or collecting “taxes” from convoys crossing territory under their control.
Dire consequences for patients
For patients, the consequences can be dire. Medicines containing the wrong ingredients or incorrect doses can cause poisoning, treatment failure and death. They can also contribute to antimicrobial resistance, allowing bacteria and other pathogens to evolve in ways that make existing medicines less effective.
The illicit market is responding to a demand the formal health system has failed to meet
In 2023, 12 children in Cameroon died after taking a pediatric syrup containing contaminated ingredients, according to UNODC.
Yet, the same weaknesses that expose patients to illicit medicines also complicate efforts to stamp out the trade.
“No State can tackle this transnational challenge alone,” said Ms. Bertrand, the agency’s regional representative.
The report calls for countries to harmonise their laws, strengthen controls and improve cross-border cooperation. But, it also argues for expanding access to safe and affordable medicines, for the illicit market is responding to a demand the formal health system has failed to meet.
Cutting off illegal supplies without addressing the shortages, high prices and distances that drive patients toward them risks leaving the market for illicit medicines largely intact.

In Islamabad, Guterres calls for end to US-Iran conflict

Regional escalation
The crisis began in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
In response, Tehran launched counter attacks on targets in Gulf countries and Jordan, and blocked transit through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.
The maritime corridor is critical for global trade in crude oil, fertilisers and liquified natural gas. Hundreds of ships and their crews have been stuck at sea for months.

The Secretary-General also acknowledged the “immense suffering” Pakistan has endured due to deadly terrorist attacks.
Mr. Guterres concluded by addressing the climate crisis, recalling that his last visit to Pakistan came during the catastrophic floods in 2022.
Climate action leader
“Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions,” he said, but “it is also on the frontlines of the response.”
He pointed to the country’s leadership in establishing the Loss and Damage Fund, and the growing clean energy transition in the country.

Djibouti faces ‘overlapping emergencies’ as Yemen’s refugee exodus continues
Djibouti is facing “overlapping emergencies” as refugees fleeing the conflict in Yemen arrive on its shores while migrants continue to travel in the opposite direction, the UN migration agency (IOM) warned on Tuesday.
More than 3,700 refugees have reached the Horn of Africa nation in the past three weeks after a dangerous crossing of the Red Sea, said Alexandre Coissac, head of IOM’s mission in the country, briefing journalists in Geneva by video link.
At the same time, IOM has recorded more than 20,000 journeys made from Ethiopia since 10 September, as migrants on the east African route continue to head for Yemen, in the hopes of finding work in the Gulf.
Another 539 Ethiopian migrants have arrived from Yemen on their way home.
“Djibouti is therefore confronting movement in both directions: people fleeing Yemen are arriving as refugees, migrants continue travelling towards Yemen, and other migrants are returning,” Mr. Coissac said.
Stranded in the desert
Between 20 and 30 September, more than 3,000 stranded migrants were observed along migratory routes in Djibouti, facing dehydration, exhaustion and shortages of food and water.
Mr. Coissac said IOM had received reports of migrants dying in the desert near the border with Ethiopia.
The agency is providing food and water and helping those who request assisted voluntary return – but migrants are increasingly using secondary routes, making them harder to reach.
He said most migrants bound for Yemen were unaware of the grave situation as fighting between Government and Houthi forces intensifies, and that many aim to reach Saudi Arabia and other Gulf States.
The Djiboutian authorities have responded rapidly, he said, but the scale and complexity of needs are stretching resources. He called for more support for new arrivals, migrants in distress and the host communities in Obock.
“The country is now responding to people moving in different directions, for different reasons, but often facing the same immediate reality: they need safety, protection and basic assistance,” he said.
Conflict continues
Meanwhile, news outlets on Tuesday reported that Yemen’s Saudi-backed Government forces say they have re-taken control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea, after launching a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis who control much of Yemen, including the capital.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has condemned the continued Houthi cross-border attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressing his deep concern over the escalation in fighting.

Testing and monitoring underway in suspected Russia plague death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Testing and monitoring underway in suspected Russia plague death
The death of a lab worker in Russia’s Siberia region has sparked concerns over a possible plague case, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday, adding that it was following the situation closely.
“A woman who worked at the laboratory in Irkutsk oblast has died, and the authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death,” WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told reporters in Geneva.
He underscored that her workplace was “an institute that studies dangerous pathogens, including plague, in a part of Siberia where plague occurs naturally in wild animals.”
Highly contagious
Plague is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria infect the lungs. WHO notes that this form of plague infection is especially contagious and “can trigger severe epidemics through person-to-person transmission via respiratory particles”.
According to WHO, pneumonic plague “can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours of disease onset if left untreated, but common antibiotics for enterobacteria can effectively cure the disease if they are delivered early”.
No official cause of death
No cause of death has been officially confirmed to date and laboratory testing is reportedly underway, Mr. Lindmeier said.
Sharing with reporters a message received from the Russian health authorities moments earlier on Tuesday, the WHO spokesperson said that “according to the test results, no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”
The authorities’ message indicated that the illness “initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection”.
Explaining the timeline of events, Mr. Lindmeier said that on 2 October “the internal monitoring system picked up the media reports of a suspected death from pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk oblast and started monitoring the situation.”
The next day, WHO contacted the Russian health authorities to get more information under the International Health Regulations “to verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway and their results, the rationale for contact tracing and the health status of the contacts as well as any potential international public health implication”, Mr. Lindmeier said.
No sign of spread
All of the patients' contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored, he added, stressing that “none to date have shown symptoms of illness.”
Mr. Lindmeier stated that WHO’s initial risk assessment from the information available “estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region”.
He stressed that this assessment will be updated as more information comes in.
WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed and stands “ready to support the Russian authorities if they ask”.

From drought to deluge: ‘Super’ El Niño’s expanding reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

From drought to deluge: ‘Super’ El Niño’s expanding reach
Across Papua New Guinea, water sources are drying up, crops are failing and food prices are rising months before the worst agricultural impacts are expected. Behind those warning signs is an El Niño whose Pacific Ocean temperatures have already surpassed the equivalent measurements during the historic 1997 and 2015 events – part of an unfolding climate pattern being dubbed a “Super El Niño” by some climate watchers.
Fast facts
More than 347 million children in nearly 100 countries and territories are expected to experience unusually wet or dry conditions between October and December 2026 due to El Niño, increasing the risk of extreme floods and droughts with potentially devastating consequences, according to latest UNICEF data.
Here are highlights of the risks facing children:
- As extreme weather events become more widespread, youngsters could face increased risks of family separation, violence, exploitation and child marriage
- Colombia, Fiji, Papua New Guinea and the Philippines are among those expected to experience drier conditions that could likely to lead to drought and water scarcity, increasing displacement and worsening acute malnutrition
- In the Greater Horn of Africa, wetter-than-normal conditions could trigger flash flooding, spread water-borne diseases and disrupt schooling
- In crisis and conflict-affected countries such as Afghanistan and Chad, El Niño can be a direct threat to survival, worsening hunger and malnutrition among already vulnerable children
- Every $1 invested in disaster risk reduction and prevention can save up to $15 in recovery costs, yet less than one per cent of humanitarian funding currently goes to anticipatory action
The 2026-2027 El Niño is forecast to become one of the strongest on record, threatening to intensify drought, floods and other weather extremes across countries already grappling with food insecurity, displacement and economic pressures.
Children on the frontlines, again
El Niño can shift rainfall patterns thousands of kilometres from the tropical Pacific, leaving some regions facing drought and water shortages while others contend with heavier rains, flooding and heightened disease risks.
More than 347 million children in nearly 100 countries and territories could be exposed to unusually dry or wet conditions between October and December because of El Niño, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) warns in a new analysis.
“For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern. It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages and disease outbreaks,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “Children are also at risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship.”
Already, 1.1 billion children – nearly half of the world’s children – are already exposed to at least three overlapping climate-related hazards such as drought, extreme heat or floods.
In Papua New Guinea, impact is already here
Some of those consequences are already visible in Papua New Guinea, a mountainous Pacific island nation where remote terrain and difficult logistics have complicated responses to previous droughts. El Niño conditions have been present since mid-2026 and are forecast to peak between October and December.
In September, the Niño 3.4 index – a measure of sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific used to track El Niño – surpassed those recorded during every previous El Niño event, including 1997 and 2015.
The Government, which declared the event in June, has established a dedicated task force and approved a $112 million supplementary budget.
Yet, needs are mounting.
Some 1.2 million people are estimated to require direct food relief, with water shortages, crop losses, dwindling food reserves and higher prices already reported. Schools are being disrupted and concerns are growing over health, nutrition and bushfires.
The largest impacts on agriculture and food security are expected from November.
One ocean, very different extremes
What dries out one part of the world can bring deluges to another.
Across the Greater Horn of Africa, wetter-than-normal conditions could raise the risk of river and flash flooding, increase the spread of waterborne diseases and disrupt schooling.
In the wider region – including Yemen, Sudan and Afghanistan – children living amid conflict and displacement face particularly acute risks because El Niño can magnify existing hunger, malnutrition and difficulties accessing essential services.
A race to act early
For governments, the forecasts offer something disasters often do not: time.
Asia and the Pacific is expected to bear a particularly large share of the exposure, with some 190 million children – more than half of the global total identified by UNICEF – living in areas forecast to experience unusually wet or dry conditions between October and December.
The World Food Programme (WFP) is urging countries across the region to strengthen social protection systems that can rapidly expand when droughts, floods or economic shocks threaten household food security.
“A flood, drought, or sudden economic shock can wipe out a family’s progress in a matter of days,” said Samir Wanmali, WFP Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific. “Social protection systems that are inclusive, nutrition-sensitive and ready to expand during a crisis can prevent a temporary shock from becoming a lasting setback.”
Lessons from a not-so-distant past
The urgency is sharpened by lessons from earlier El Niño episodes.
In analysis published in May, the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) pointed to the 2015-16 event as a warning of how climate extremes can cascade through economies and societies.
More than 70 per cent of Southeast Asia’s land area experienced drought during that episode, exposing more than 200 million people to severe drought at its peak.
The pressures this time are unfolding against tighter government finances, elevated debt and persistent economic uncertainty and supply chain worries, potentially reducing the ability of governments and households to absorb another shock.
Warmer world raises the stakes
Meanwhile, climate change is raising the baseline risk. Higher temperatures accelerate the loss of moisture from soil and vegetation, potentially intensifying drought when rainfall falls short.
For governments, that means preparing for extremes in both directions – from failing rains, water shortages and crop losses to intense rainfall, flooding and landslides. The challenge is to turn forecasts into decisions before harvests fail, reservoirs run low or floods force families from their homes.
That will be the focus of a regional El Niño exchange beginning on next week in Bangkok, bringing governments, meteorological experts, UN agencies and frontline practitioners together to compare emerging impacts and lessons from previous crises.
For Papua New Guinea, however, the warning period is already giving way to impact.
Water shortages, damaged crops and rising prices offer an early glimpse of what an exceptional El Niño could mean far beyond the warming waters of the Pacific.

South Korea sent over 176,000 tonnes of fuel to russia on sanctioned tankers - The Guardian

South Korea sent over 176,000 tonnes of fuel to russia on sanctioned tankers - The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
In July-August, seven tankers delivered over 176,000 tonnes of fuel from South Korea to russia. Three vessels were under sanctions.
South Korea supplied Russia with significant volumes of fuel amid shortages caused by disruptions at Russian oil refineries. Some of the shipments were carried out by vessels under sanctions from the United Kingdom and the EU. The Guardian reported this, citing an analysis of port records and vessel-tracking data, UNN writes.
Details
In July and August, more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, were loaded at several South Korean ports onto seven tankers, which made 14 voyages to Russia’s Far East.
Three of these vessels were under sanctions. The largest of them, Layla, delivered diesel twice from the South Korean port of Ulsan to Vladivostok. In total, it transported 57,000 tonnes of fuel. During its second voyage, the vessel listed Niigata, Japan, as its destination, but ultimately headed to Russia.
Another sanctioned tanker, Astoria, flying the Russian flag and also subject to Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel in Ulsan on 1 August. It listed Japan as its destination, after which it headed to Vladivostok.
The third sanctioned tanker, Chongchon, did not enter the port. In early August, it carried out a ship-to-ship transfer of about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from the tanker Celeste I near the port of Yeosu, after which it headed to Vladivostok, listing Singapore as its destination.
Although sanctioned vessels took part in the shipments, this likely does not violate South Korean law. Seoul’s own sanctions against Russia mainly concern the export of industrial equipment, electronics and vehicles.
It was not possible to identify the owners or sellers of the fuel, as the relevant data is not available in South Korean port registers. The owners and operators of the other four tankers could not be reached.
According to the maritime analytics company Kpler, the fuel buyers included Rosneft — a Russian state-owned oil company under sanctions from the United Kingdom, the United States, the EU and Australia — and the Russian oil group NNK. Its owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and the company NNK-Oil are also under UK sanctions.
Russia’s oil-refining industry suffered serious disruptions due to Ukrainian drone strikes. According to the International Energy Agency, in June the throughput capacity of Russian oil refineries fell to its lowest level in more than 20 years, while diesel fuel production declined by nearly 30% year on year.
At the same time, throughout the Russian-Ukrainian war, South Korea has tried to balance supporting Ukraine with its desire to improve relations with Russia. Seoul ruled out direct arms supplies to Ukraine, adhering to a policy of not supplying lethal weapons to countries at war. At the same time, South Korea provided Ukraine with humanitarian aid and non-lethal military equipment, including helmets, body armor and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3 billion in support, primarily in the form of loans.
The volume of oil shipments from South Korean ports began to rise sharply in July, when the country’s President Lee Jae-myung promised at the NATO summit in Türkiye to allocate $100 million for Ukraine’s reconstruction.
In response to a request, South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not comment on the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, the ministry said that, as a "responsible member of the international community," the government supports and actively participates in international efforts to end the war in Ukraine and peacefully rebuild the country.

U.S. Navy, Australia pay $66M to upgrade Triton spy drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:59:35 UTC
20:59:35 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman a $66 million order to retrofit fielded MQ-4C Triton drones with 17 U.S. Navy and 16 Australian design changes.
- Australia is contributing about $12.4 million through its cooperative program with the U.S. Navy, and the work is due to finish by June 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Northrop Grumman a $66 million order to retrofit MQ-4C Triton surveillance drones already in service with the U.S. Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force, bringing both fleets up to a common configuration.
The firm-fixed-price delivery order covers engineering work, materials and spare parts to install 17 engineering change proposals on U.S. Navy aircraft and 16 on Royal Australian Air Force aircraft. Engineering change proposals are approved modifications to an aircraft’s design, and the U.S. Department of War said the work supports fleet standardization and mission readiness. The announcement did not describe what the individual changes involve.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, placed the order. Of the money obligated at award, about $53.6 million comes from fiscal 2026 U.S. Navy aircraft procurement funds and about $12.4 million from Australia under the two countries’ cooperative program. The order was not competed. Work is expected to be finished by June 2030.
Most of the work will take place in California, with 63 percent in Hayward and 31 percent in San Diego, where Northrop Grumman builds the Triton. Smaller shares are split among Red Oak and Waco in Texas, Tukwila in Washington, Elyria in Ohio, Irvine in California and other U.S. sites.
The MQ-4C Triton is a large, high-altitude drone derived from the U.S. Air Force’s RQ-4 Global Hawk and designed for long maritime patrol missions. It can stay aloft for more than 24 hours and uses radar and other sensors to track ships across wide stretches of ocean. The U.S. Navy flies it alongside its crewed P-8A Poseidon patrol aircraft.
Australia is the only foreign operator. It ordered four Tritons through a cooperative program with the U.S. Navy and Northrop Grumman. The first arrived at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the Northern Territory in June 2024, and the second and third followed in June 2025. The Australian Department of Defence has said the fourth and final aircraft is scheduled for delivery in 2028. The aircraft are flown by the Royal Australian Air Force’s No. 9 Squadron, which was re-formed to operate the Triton, and work alongside Australia’s P-8A fleet patrolling the country’s northern maritime approaches.

Maardu quits all Estonian football amid match-fixing probe
Football team Maardu Linnameeskond has withdrawn from Estonia's second-tier league after being placed under investigation over suspected match-fixing, the club announced Monday.
Since the club has played more than half the season, under Estonian FA (EJK) rules all results up to now stand, but the remaining matches in the season will be forfeited. The club is losing its license, meaning it has dropped out of all licensed leagues and not just the second-tier Esiliiga.
Estonian prosecutors launched criminal proceedings over suspected betting fraud in the Esiliiga fixture between FC Tallinn and Maardu Linnameeskond played on Thursday, September 10. The match was abandoned in the 78th minute after Maardu conceded three goals in the space of seven minutes, giving away a penalty during that time too.
That match's result has been recorded as a 4-0 win for Tallinn, and the points amassed in the first half of the season alone mean Maardu finishes last in the Esiliiga.
The EJK banned three people connected with the club from football activities for the duration of its disciplinary investigation. Maardu announced on September 22 that it was suspending its participation in the league and halting training.
The team was founded in 1997 and played one season, in 2019, in the top-flight Meistriliiga. The Estonian football season runs March to November.

The Digital Transformation Office is now testing several models for analytics on attacks on energy and their consequences, as well as on outages, "so that there is a fairer distribution," he said.
Asked about the consequences of Russian strikes on data centers, Shuhaliy said a hybrid system of measures is used to protect against such strikes, including multi-layer data backup and stress tests.

Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says

Ukraine's battlefield successes appear to be forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his theory of victory and shift focus toward long-range strikes to compel Ukraine to surrender, rather than advances on the battlefield, the Institute for the Study of War said on 4 October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia used more than 800 jet-powered drones during the week of 27 September to 4 October. Ukraine currently intercepts only 50–60% of jet-powered drones, leaving it vulnerable to the large number of new drones Russia is deploying.
The late-September start and the campaign's aim
ISW said Russian forces began their winter 2026–27 strike campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure in late September and that the campaign is aimed at making civilian life unbearable enough to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defense industry sites, and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry said on 4 October, according to Reuters. The announcement followed Zelenskyy's vow to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The ministry also claimed its recent strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions were a response to alleged Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. Among the grievances it named were Ukraine's strikes on Leningrad Oblast during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June and alleged strikes on electoral infrastructure in Moscow during the 18–20 September State Duma elections, according to ISW.
ISW called the Russian Defense Ministry's framing of the recent strikes as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian targets unfounded, saying many of its specific claims are "blatantly false." Russia has provided no evidence that Ukraine targeted electoral infrastructure, and Ukraine's 19–20 September strikes on Moscow targeted oil refineries and warehouses, the think tank said. The Russian strikes "are not an actual response to specific events," it concluded.
The 135 drones, the bridges struck seven times
Overnight on 3–4 October, Russia launched 135 Shahed-type and Gerbera-type drones, while also using decoy drones and Banderol or Dan-T loitering munitions. Ukrainian forces downed 123 drones and two loitering munitions, and strikes hit five locations, according to ISW, which cited the Ukrainian Air Force. Russian forces struck Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges seven times between 1 and 4 October in an effort to disrupt Ukraine's economy and daily civilian life, ISW said.
Ukraine builds new layers of defense against jet drones
More than 12 .50-caliber machine-gun turrets are already working in Kyiv against jet-powered drones, and eight more will be installed in Kyiv Oblast, Zelenskyy said, Suspilne reported. He added that F-16s help a lot against the drones, according to Ukrinform. Ukraine is set to receive 2,000 Bars interceptor drones through joint production with Germany, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Ballistic missiles may be Russia's next wave
Zelenskyy said Ukraine estimates Russia has up to 700 ballistic missiles in reserve and produces 130–140 a month. Switzerland's Partners Group set to wind up UK fund

Switzerland’s Partners Group set to wind up UK fund
Swiss asset manager Partners Group is set to wind up its private equity fund, Partners Group Private Equity (PGPE), which is listed on the London Stock Exchange.
A large majority of investors, representing 74.12% of the share capital, voted in favour of exiting this fund by converting their securities into so-called ‘realisation’ shares, according to a press release dated Monday. The threshold for approving this proposal was set at 40%.
In June, against a backdrop of fears of a private equity bubble, PGPE had given its shareholders the choice of continuing their involvement in the company’s long-term strategy following a restructuring, or opting for a tradable security that would guarantee liquidity.
This latter option will therefore be the only one put forward for shareholders’ approval at the extraordinary general meeting scheduled for Wednesday. Should it be adopted, the board of directors would proceed with a controlled liquidation of the entire investment portfolio.
Should it be rejected, the fund will continue to be managed “in accordance with its current investment objective and policy, and the directors will reassess the options available at that time”.
The reorganisation proposal has, meanwhile, been withdrawn.
This decision comes at a turbulent time for Partners Group, which has come under criticism for its exposure to private markets.
In June, the firm had restricted redemptions from its “evergreen” funds – those with no maturity date – which led to a fall in its share price.
Last week, the asset manager reorganised this perpetual fund. Global Value SICAV, with assets under management of €6.6 billion (CHF6.16 billion), has thus been incorporated into a fund with separate sub-funds, which will be divided into two sub-portfolios.
One of these aims to generate long-term capital gains, whilst the other is designed to facilitate easier exit.
