Breadcrumb
Top Israeli rabbi says Arab rule better for Jews than Zionism
One of Israel's most influential ultra-Orthodox rabbis said Jews could have lived well under Arab rule and blamed Zionism for creating hostility towards Jews, according to footage broadcast by Israeli television this week.
Rabbi Dov Lando, the 96-year-old head of the prestigious Slabodka Yeshiva and a leading authority within Israel's Lithuanian Haredi community, made the comments during a private discussion at his home in Bnei Brak.
The footage, broadcast by Israel's Channel 12 on Monday, was recorded around a year and a half ago. Some of Lando's remarks had previously been reported by Israeli media.
"I don't know what would have happened if at the beginning there had been no state and they had established UN rule here - it would have been an excellent situation," Lando said.
"It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state," he added. "It would have been quite good if the Arabs ruled here. It would have been the best situation."
Lando also said the Zionist movement worsened relations between Jews and Arabs, saying that while Arabs had "never been good", Zionism had caused them to hate Jews.
"They made the Arabs hate us," he said.
He accused Zionism, which emerged as a modern Jewish nationalist movement in Europe in the late 19th century, of bringing "physical disasters, not only spiritual ones" upon the Jewish people.
Lando is an important religious authority for Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian Haredi faction within the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) political alliance.
UTJ has played a major role in successive governments led by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with disputes over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men from military service repeatedly threatening the stability of Netanyahu's coalition.
Unlike Religious Zionism, which regards Jewish sovereignty in Israel as religiously significant, large sections of the Haredi community historically opposed Zionism.
The opposition was rooted partly in the rejection of the predominantly secular Zionist movement and the belief that Jewish religious life should not be subordinated to a nationalist state.
Many Haredi groups nevertheless gradually adopted a pragmatic relationship with Israel after its establishment in 1948, participating in elections and governments while maintaining separate religious institutions and resisting compulsory military service.
Lando also used the recorded conversation to launch a fierce attack on Religious Zionists, many of whom combine religious study with service in the Israeli military.
Asked about Haredi men who felt troubled by the deaths of Religious Zionist soldiers while ultra-Orthodox students remained in yeshivas, Lando rejected the comparison.
"They are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah," he said.
He argued that Torah study, rather than military power, ultimately protects Jews living in Israel.
Lando also accused some soldiers of fighting "for the honour of the state", adding: "They kill people for honour."
The remarks drew condemnation from several Israeli opposition politicians after the footage was broadcast.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett described Lando's comments as "shame and disgrace" and accused Netanyahu of politically empowering ultra-Orthodox leaders who reject Zionism and military service.
Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot also condemned the remarks, describing them as an expression of "anti-Zionism in its purest form".
Avigdor Liberman, leader of the secular nationalist Yisrael Beiteinu party and a longstanding advocate of compulsory military service for Haredi men, attacked UTJ over its relationship with the state.
"The money from the state they know how to take. To serve and defend it? No," he said.
The controversy comes weeks before Israel's 27 October election, with the question of ultra-Orthodox military exemptions again emerging as a major political dividing line.

Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
The prize was awarded for his work on subatomic particles at the South Pole.
What's next?
This is Nobel week, with prizes for chemistry and literature to be handed out over the coming days, with the peace prize announced on Friday, local time.
Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old scientist is affiliated with the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US.
"This year's prize is about ghostly messengers from space," Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference, on Tuesday morning, local time.
The Academy noted that Mr Halzen's "vision and scientific leadership" had been fundamental for the observatory, which it described as "a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors".
Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos — rare subatomic particles — "from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe".
"This Nobel Prize is about a giant ice cube positioned at the South Pole of our globe. The ice cube enables the detection of neutrinos," Professor Eva Olsson, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physics, told reporters.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, ($1.718 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation.
"It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn't expect it," Mr Halzen told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced.
"But it's a great pleasure to hear about this prize."
Last year, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in Physics for research on the strange behaviour of subatomic particles called quantum tunnelling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.

Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:07:00 UTC
20:07:00 KST

Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
October 6, 2026
Dozens of people were reportedly placed under observation after a laboratory worker at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and other infectious diseases died of severe pneumonia.
The case quickly became the subject of intense speculation on social media. Posts have ranged from expressions of fear and comparisons with the COVID-19 pandemic to claims about the laboratory incident that have not been substantiated.
DW Fact Check has examined several of the claims circulating online.
Alleged plague lab accident in Irkutsk remains unproven
Claim: "For those who don't get it: in Irkutsk, a lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus and became infected with the disease, dying a few days later," a user posted on X in Russian. "This happened on September 25, and by October 2, she was already dead. In the meantime, she had infected several hundred people." The post, which included a photo of the alleged laboratory worker, garnered over 320,000 views.
DW Fact check: Unproven
There is no independent evidence confirming that a leak of the plague pathogen occurred at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.
On the contrary, Russia's public health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, said that two commissions investigating biosafety procedures at the institute found "no evidence of an accident involving pathogenic microorganisms." The Russian news agency TASS, citing Rospotrebnadzor, also reported that tests on the deceased employee detected no microorganisms linked to her professional activity.
Some social media users have tried to debunk the claim about a broken test tube, pointing to safety standards in high-containment laboratories, where the use of glassware may be restricted or completely banned to reduce the risk of accidents.
The Irkutsk institute does work with highly pathogenic microorganisms, including strains classified in Russia's highest pathogenicity groups, such as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.
However, DW could not independently verify the formally designated biosafety level of the institute's laboratories. Biosafety level, or BSL, is an international classification describing the containment measures required when handling dangerous pathogens, with BSL-4 reserved for the most hazardous agents.
DW asked the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute to comment on the alleged incident and its laboratory safety procedures but had received no response by the time of publication.
WHO website update unrelated to the Russian case
Claim: "The WHO appears to have updated its fact sheet on plague the same day the Irkutsk lab worker presented at hospital, with (probably) the plague." This claim appeared in a number of posts on X, each reaching thousands of users.
DW Fact check: Misleading
The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its plague fact sheet on the same day the Russian laboratory worker was hospitalized, but no evidence links the two events.
According to media reports, the laboratory worker may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis around September 25. Four days later, on September 29, she was hospitalized in Shelekhov with severe respiratory symptoms.
The WHO updated its plague fact sheet on September 29, the same day it published a news release on global trends in cholera, meningitis and plague. The update was part of a broader WHO publication cycle on infectious disease.
The release reported global surveillance data covering 2019 to 2025 and said the findings were published in the latest edition of the Weekly Epidemiological Record, which was released on September 25.
The timing therefore appears coincidental. The previous version of the WHO's plague fact sheet, accessible as an archived page, was dated July 7, 2022.
The social media account sharing the claim also changed its name in October to one that suggests it is reporting live from Irkutsk. Its profile describes itself as providing "sourced updates on the Irkutsk lab leak" and "latest news as it breaks live." However, the account's profile indicates that it was created in May and is based in Australia.
Such accounts can emerge quickly during breaking news events, presenting themselves as local or specialist sources while sharing unverified information.
Old video falsely linked to current plague claims in Russia
Claim: As news of the plague spreads, some old videos are being repurposed, adding to the disinformation. In one such video posted on X, a user claimed that the plague has also spread to other parts of Russia. The caption in Russian reads, "The plague marches across Russia. God has heard our prayers!"
DW Fact check: Misleading
The video is old and unrelated to the current developments in Irkutsk. A reverse image search reveals that the video was initially posted on August 31 this year, claiming that it showed the Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, a tourist destination around 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miiles)from Irkutsk.
The old video has been viewed more than 1.7 million times on Instagram. The same video was also posted on Telegram. The Russian news agency TASS reported on August 31 that the plague pathogen had been detected in local squirrels and that the area had been closed to tourists.
In the video, a person can be heard saying, "It's at the turnoff from the paved road toward Serebryany Istochnik" in Russian. Serebryany Istochnik, or Silver Spring, is a spring located in the Dzhily-Su area in Kabardino-Balkaria.
The situation in the Irkutsk region is still being investigated, but there are no confirmed reports of a plague outbreak in Russia. Health authorities have introduced precautionary measures following the death of the laboratory worker, while tests are reportedly being carried out.

El Nino could signal extreme Amazon heat 7 months in advance: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:05:28 UTC
20:05:28 KST

Faisal Mahmud
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
El Nino and warming in the tropical Atlantic could provide warnings of extreme heat across parts of the Amazon as much as seven months in advance, according to new research.
The study, published in the journal Earth’s Future, examined how major patterns of natural climate variability influence temperature and rainfall extremes across the Amazon Basin.
Researchers found that extreme heat was more likely after unusually warm conditions associated with El Nino in the tropical Pacific and warming in parts of the tropical Atlantic, according to the Australian climate research center ARC Centre, which published the findings Tuesday.
The clearest long-range signal emerged for March-May, when extreme Amazon heat was associated with ocean conditions observed up to seven months earlier.
“It is quite surprising that heat extremes are linked to conditions in the Pacific and tropical Atlantic Oceans observed up to seven months in advance,” said UNSW Associate Professor Andrea Taschetto, a study co-author.
Researchers analyzed monthly climate data from 1950 to 2023 across six Amazon regions and also used machine learning to examine compound hot-dry events.
Those events can increase wildfire risks, damage ecosystems and threaten human health, food security and water supplies.
The researchers cautioned that the seven-month relationship applies to extreme heat, not reliable seven-month forecasts of combined heat and drought.
Predictability of compound events varied considerably by season and region, with useful signals generally limited to shorter periods.

New Ebola hotspots multiply in eastern Congo’s North Kivu: MSF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:04:27 UTC
20:04:27 KST

James Tasamba
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) on Tuesday voiced concern over the deteriorating health situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo’s North Kivu province, saying new Ebola disease hotspots are emerging every week amid insufficient treatment capacities.
Since the Ebola outbreak declaration in mid-May in Congo, the cumulative caseload stands at 8,554, including 4,114 deaths, the Health Ministry's latest situation update showed.
In a statement, the French medical charity said the Ebola disease outbreak in North Kivu province has intensified dramatically since early September, with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, up from 24% at the end of August.
It warned that the situation has placed current patients and entire communities at even greater risk.
“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator of the MSF Ebola treatment centre in Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations. As long as new hotspots continue to emerge while the virus spreads across northern North Kivu, containing the epidemic will remain extremely difficult.”
The latest epidemic has affected seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
MSF said North Kivu is bearing a growing share of the country's Ebola burden at a time when access to specialized care remains insufficient.
As of Sep. 28, 34% of confirmed Ebola patients were still being treated in non-specialized health facilities because of limited bed capacity in dedicated treatment centres and delays in diagnosis, according to the medical charity.

Court ruling clears key hurdle for separatist leader Puigdemont's return to Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:03:57 UTC
20:03:57 KST

Catalan separatist Puigdemont set to return home after court lifts arrest warrant
BARCELONA/MADRID, Oct 6 - Spain's two top courts cleared the way on Tuesday for self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont to return without being arrested, just as Spain is gearing up for an early national election on November 29.
The Constitutional Court ruled that an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applies to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont. Shortly afterwards, the Supreme Court responded by lifting a warrant for Puigdemont's arrest.
The likely homecoming of the former Catalan head of government could further unsettle an already volatile political landscape ahead of the election. Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an independence referendum for his region that Madrid had declared illegal.
In a televised address from his home in the Belgian town of Waterloo, Puigdemont hailed the court rulings as a victory that "obliges us to put an end to political repression", but gave no indication of when he plans to return.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had enacted the amnesty under a 2023 agreement between his Socialist Party and two Catalan parties, including Puigdemont's Junts, in exchange for their support for him to remain prime minister. The move triggered intense social and political opposition from the government's critics at the time.
The Supreme Court had initially ruled that the amnesty did not apply to the crime of embezzlement, which meant Puigdemont and others could still be arrested on charges of embezzling the funds spent on the referendum.
But the Constitutional Court, which has a progressive-leaning majority, ruled in an appeal that disallowing the amnesty for embezzlement unconnected with private enrichment would violate the purpose of the amnesty law.
A year ago, Junts withdrew its support for the minority central government. Unable to pass laws, Sanchez called the snap election on Monday. Sanchez told reporters on Tuesday he did not regret launching the amnesty, and welcomed the court ruling.
"I believe the important message is that of coexistence among Catalans," he said.
FRESH DRAMA
Although separatism has lost ground and Junts is trailing in opinion polls, Puigdemont's return could spark fresh political drama.
Spain's conservative People's Party is leading in opinion polls ahead of the election and may need to seek the support of Junts and other centre-right parties to govern.
Catalonia unilaterally declared independence from Spain in 2017 after the referendum. Although some 90% of voters backed independence, Catalans who wanted to remain part of Spain mostly boycotted the ballot and many polling stations were shut.
Puigdemont then fled the country, while several of his former ministers stayed and were jailed until later being pardoned by Sanchez. REUTERS

More than 60% of Ukrainians willing to endure war as long as necessary – survey

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:03:00 EEST
20:03:00 KST

More than 60% of Ukrainians willing to endure war as long as necessary – survey
A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) shows that 62% of Ukrainians, like the majority of Kyiv residents, are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, whereas 23% are ready for only a few months or half a year.
Source: a survey by KIIS
Quote: "The majority of Ukrainians – 62% – say they are ready to endure the war for as long as necessary. Another 4% say a relatively long period – 1 year.
To endure a shorter period – a few months or half a year – are ready 23%. The remaining 11% could not decide on their opinion."
Details: Results of the Omnibus survey, conducted September 12-21, remained virtually unchanged compared to the previous survey in late July – early August.
In particular, the figure did not decrease among surveyed Kyiv residents – 72% of respondents are ready to endure the war for as long as necessary (in late July – early August, this figure among Kyiv residents was 69%, a difference within the margin of statistical error). The KIIS noted that it should be taken into account that this survey was conducted after the onset of active terror by Russians involving reactive drones.
Quote: "That is, these data, at least as of September 12-21, did not lead to demoralisation of the population. At the same time, the survey was completed before the attacks on the bridges across the Dnipro began."
For reference: Questions regarding war and peace were added to the survey at the request of the Forum NGO.
Sociologists interviewed 1,002 citizens of Ukraine aged 18 and older via telephone interviews who, at the time of the study, resided in government-controlled Ukrainian territory.
The survey did not cover residents of occupied territories or citizens who went abroad after 24 February 2022. However, internally displaced persons from occupied territories were included among the respondents.
Under normal circumstances, the statistical margin of error for such a sample with a 95% probability and accounting for the design effect does not exceed 4.1% for indicators close to 50%, 3.5% for indicators close to 25%, 2.5% for indicators close to 10% and 1.8% for indicators close to 5%.
The KIIS notes that in wartime conditions, possible systematic deviations are added to the formal error. All percentages are rounded to whole numbers.
Background: Survey results also showed that 75% of Ukrainians are open to holding negotiations with Russia now to end the war.

Pro-Palestine Greens challenge Labour’s grip on Starmer’s former seat

Pro-Palestine Greens challenge Labour’s grip on Starmer’s former seat
Green Party leader Zack Polanski hopes to shake Labour, which has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.
London, United Kingdom– At a meeting organised by a Muslim group in London ahead of a closely watched by-election, candidates from the Green and Liberal Democrat parties made their cases to residents beside empty seats. Their Labour and Conservative peers did not turn up.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi Wali, a Somali-Muslim woman, told The Guardian she did not attend because she had a prior obligation and the invite had come too late. But the organiser, the Camden Muslim Network, pushed back, saying that she was invited earlier.
Fifteen candidates are in the race for former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s old seat, including Green Party leader, Zack Polanski, who hopes to become a member of parliament.
Since the seat was created in Holborn and St Pancras in 1983, the Labour Party has held it. Starmer was first elected in 2015 and held it until his resignation, which triggered the by-election due to take place on Thursday.
At the meeting, the conversation ranged from local issues such as housing to Israel and Palestine.
Lib Dem candidate Patrick Stillman said his party had long called for Palestinian statehood but would not support a full boycott.
But Polanski had a different opinion.
“I think the Labour government’s position is deeply cynical to apologise over Gaza, to recognise that mistakes have been made but to continue to sell arms to Israel, a country that’s committing a genocide,” he said to applause, adding that his party, which recently voted to describe Zionism as racism, supports a full boycott.
In leaflets sent to constituency residents, the Green Party focused on Abdi-Wali’s time as a Labour councillor and, more recently, as leader of Camden council – a role she secured in May.
One reads: “Bring change, Replace Labour, Vote Green”. On its reverse: “Every single Camden Labour councillor refused to sign the Palestine solidarity pledge or support pension fund divestment. Only Greens continue to stand firm on Palestine.”
Last month, Abdi-Wali spoke to the Camden New Journal, a local newspaper, about Gaza and the Green Party’s leaflets.
It was “obviously inaccurate” to say the Labour council did not feel strongly about the issue, she told the paper. “I want to focus on making sure that we’re able to put the message of what [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband is now doing with the government and on Palestine and Israel and Gaza and the West Bank.”
In January, Camden Friends of Palestine (CFOP), a local group that formed in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, presented a petition to the local council with 4,000 signatures calling for the council to divest its pension fund from companies involved in Israel’s actions in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Abdi-Wali, then a Labour councillor, did not support the motion. Rather than committing to divestment, most councillors voted to refer the question to the pension board for review.
“My impression of her and her politics is that she’s just really incredibly silent on everything, if there isn’t a career motive for her, and that’s kind of disappointing,” said 38-year-old Shadin, a resident and CFOP organiser, who plans to vote for Polanski.
“Watching a livestreamed genocide has made a lot of people that I know … disengage from mainstream politics or parliamentary politics”.
Like many London constituencies, a key issue is housing.
According to a “2026 state of the borough” report by Camden council, 8,380 households were on the waiting list for social housing at the end of March 2025, “an increase of 9.5 percent on the year before.”
On Friday, in the constituency’s more affluent area of Primrose Hill, one resident said they would vote for Labour in the upcoming election, while another believed that regardless of who wins, life will not change.
In Camden, another resident told Al Jazeera that while they live in the area, they were not aware of the election, as Labour canvassers buzzed to gain entry into a nearby estate in the background.
As both parties make their final efforts to secure victory, recent polls predict a close race.
In the 2024 general election, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate came second, with 19 percent. The British gambling firm Ladbrokes and Stats for Lefties, which examines polling, both predict Labour will win.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Tuesday that Hamas could attempt an attack ahead of Israel’s election in an effort to influence the vote, saying Israel was prepared to thwart such a move and would respond “with tremendous force.”
Speaking at the opening of a government meeting marking three years since the October 7 massacre, Netanyahu began by remembering those killed in the Hamas attack and the war that followed.
“On the eve of October 7, we remember with grief and pain our heroes who fell in the War of Revival and our brothers and sisters who fell in the terrible massacre in the Gaza border communities,” Netanyahu said. “Women, men, children, babies who were murdered and burned by the Hamas monsters.”
“Over the past three years, we have eliminated 4,000 of those 6,000 monsters,” he said, referring to those who crossed into Israel during the attack. “None of them has immunity. We will reach them all, and Hamas rule in Gaza will be eliminated.”
The figure mirrors an assessment presented to ministers at a Security Cabinet meeting this week, when Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder said roughly 4,000 of the approximately 6,000 Gazans who crossed the border on October 7 had been killed and about 2,000 remained. Binder told ministers that Israel would pursue those who remained.
Netanyahu, who was prime minister when the massacre occurred, has not accepted personal responsibility for the failures that preceded it. Yoav Gallant, who served as defense minister at the time, is no longer in office, as are the senior security officials who headed the defense establishment on October 7.
Netanyahu instead highlighted what he described as Israel’s achievements in the three years since the attack.
“We turned the tables,” he said. “The State of Israel is the strongest country in the Middle East, and our enemies are weaker than ever.”
He also pointed to the rebuilding of communities near Gaza, saying 90% of residents had returned home and that others had moved into the area.
“There is a tremendous wave of construction and rehabilitation in the Gaza border region, in the cities, kibbutzim and moshavim,” Netanyahu said. “Young couples are coming there to begin new lives. This is the victory of spirit over evil, the victory of Israel over its enemies. Exactly the same thing is happening in the north.”
Netanyahu then turned to the coming election, warning that Hamas could use its remaining capabilities to challenge Israel.
“Precisely because Hamas is so weak, it will try to challenge us with the remnants of its forces ahead of the elections in an attempt to influence them,” he said. “We are prepared for this. First of all, we will thwart such attempts, and in any case we will respond with tremendous force if they make that mistake.”
“I say to all our enemies: Look at what we did to you on seven fronts in the War of Revival. Don’t mess with us.”
The warning comes after Shin Bet chief David Zini told ministers that Hamas was preparing for the possibility of an attack or a localized kidnapping attempt close to the election or shortly afterward. Intelligence officials have also identified efforts by Hamas to recruit personnel and stockpile weapons as it prepares for possible renewed fighting, according to information presented to the Security Cabinet.
Netanyahu has used the term “War of Revival,” the name adopted by the government for the conflict, throughout his remarks and campaign messaging. The designation has not been embraced by all bereaved families and remains politically and socially contentious.

Misuse of AI is brands’ top reputational threat, new survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:00:35 UTC
20:00:35 KST

Misusing artificial intelligence (AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders.
Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands could precipitate existential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry.
The index’s publisher, the Global Risk Advisory Council, acknowledged that misuse of AI is not a particularly new concern in its area of focus, having been identified as a top worry repeatedly since the first edition of the survey in April 2025.
But the council said what was new was its attaching an advisory to its latest survey advising business leaders to “take immediate and decisive action to mitigate potential long-term brand damage” with respect to AI, as the technology has “become a clear and present danger to public confidence for many corporations”.
“As AI is rapidly deployed for productivity gains, we have also seen diminishing public trust in the technology, elevating the need for businesses to take measures to protect their brands,” council chair Isabel Casillas Guzman said in a statement. “In this environment, AI use or overuse can quickly damage a company’s standing with customers, investors, or other key stakeholders, making it essential for companies to deploy preventive tactics now.”
The creators of the council and the Reputation Risk Index – the Washington DC-based public affairs firm Global Situation Room – said such tactics include removing or reducing the use of AI content and relying on humans for customer service.
The Global Situation Room said that the Reputation Risk Index released on Tuesday surveyed former heads of state, government ministers and senior executives from more than 20 countries in five continents who were invited to participate after establishing their credentials in responding to crises.
Respondents to that survey collectively perceived the technology to have shown great promise in creating “organizational efficiency” – while simultaneously “accelerating safety and data concerns, hacks, fraud, straining privacy protections, upending the workforce, and dragging companies into court as lawsuits increasingly link AI products to real-world harm”.
Meanwhile, actions or accusations of putting children at risk of mental, emotional or physical harm also ranked highly behind misused AI – along with infringing individuals’ sensitive information, according to the index results published on Tuesday.
Unethical or illegal behavior used to gain a strategic advantage or profit and, separately, poor strategic or operational decisions resulting in reduced financial or public standing rounded out the top five, according to the index.
The index noted that its preceding edition released in July identified supply chain issues, divisive political stances and other factors associated with the war that the Trump’s administration started in Iran alongside Israel as the leading risk to companies’ reputations. But those surveyed indicated that those anxieties had eased as the conflict dragged out – and perhaps despite it remaining unresolved since it was launched in February.
“The geopolitical shock … hasn’t gone away, but its first, sharpest reputational blow has faded, and the conflict has slipped out of the top tier [of concerns] even as it grinds on,” Guzman said in a “message from the chair” included in the index.
Guzman put out her message two days after Donald Trump’s administration named a new AI czar: the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president said in a social media post that Clayton would oversee an entity coordinating “the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and” AI tech companies.
Clayton had previously told federal lawmakers that AI was a “gamechanger” but also posed “a threat”.

Kenya confirms first Ebola case as patient dies

20:00:12 KST

Kenya on Tuesday confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, one day after a man died in a Nairobi hospital, the country's health authorities said.(Xinhua/Xie Jianfei)
The patient was a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for the past seven years, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said in a statement.
He fell ill about a month ago and was treated at several hospitals while still in the DRC. He traveled by road from the DRC to Kampala, Uganda, then boarded Jambojet flight 8523 and arrived in Nairobi on Oct. 3.
A relative drove him directly from Jomo Kenyatta International Airport to Nairobi Hospital, where he was quickly placed in an isolation facility, the statement said.
He presented with fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at injection sites.
"Based on the above presentation and history of travel to DRC the doctor considered this a case of viral hemorrhagic fever and collected a sample for testing which turned positive for Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the KEMRI Lab," Duale said, referring to the Kenya Medical Research Institute.
The patient was treated but died on Monday night, Duale said, extending condolences to the family.
"Arrangements for safe and dignified burial of the deceased are ongoing, and the burial is planned for later today in line with the public health standards," he said.
Authorities have listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and health workers who attended to him, and are pursuing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight, Duale said. Quarantine arrangements for those at risk are underway.
He said Kenya has maintained a high level of alert for Ebola since the outbreak began in May 2026. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, began in the DRC's Ituri Province.
Duale urged the public not to panic, saying all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease. He advised frequent handwashing or the use of alcohol-based hand rubs, and avoiding close contact with sick people arriving from countries with active Ebola transmission.
The ministry has opened a toll-free line for public inquiries, saying that it will keep the country updated as more information becomes available. ■

20:00:08 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- El Nino and warming in the tropical Atlantic could help provide early warning of extreme heat in the Amazon, with some signals appearing as much as seven months earlier, new research has found.
Researchers from the Australian Research Council Center of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and Brazil's National Institute of Space Research studied how major patterns of natural climate variability influence temperature and rainfall extremes across the Amazon Basin, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Australian center.
The study found Amazon heat extremes were more likely to follow unusually warm conditions associated with El Nino in the tropical Pacific and warming in parts of the tropical Atlantic.
The clearest long-range signal occurred from March to May, when extreme heat across much of the Amazon was associated with climate conditions observed up to seven months earlier, according to the study published in the journal Earth's Future.
The research also found early-warning potential for compound hot-dry events, particularly in the northern and lower central Amazon, although predictability was considerably weaker elsewhere.
Researchers said machine learning allowed them to examine relationships with extreme compound events, which are harder to predict.
Compound hot-dry events can increase fire risk, damage ecosystems and threaten human health, food security and water supplies, while weakening the Amazon's ability to absorb carbon dioxide, they said, noting that hot-dry events have become more frequent and intense, with early warnings helping communities and governments prepare for dangerous heat and drought.
The study identifies regions and seasons where Pacific and Atlantic climate conditions could provide early warning, but further research is needed to translate these relationships into practical warning systems. ■

====================================================================================================

Meta Muse gives AMD a boost as AI momentum shifts to personal agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

The personal AI agent boom is giving Advanced Micro Devices and Intel new life after the companies spent years watching Nvidia and its GPUs dominate the artificial intelligence market.
The central processing unit, or CPU, was once the primary workhorse of a computer server before Nvidia's graphics processing units took center stage with the launch of ChatGPT and the start of the generative AI era. Now CPUs are back, lifting the fortunes of market leaders AMD and Intel, whose chips specialize in powering long-running agents that can work for hours on their own.
Last week OpenAI released its AI agent Dots, following the lead of Meta, which debuted Muse in early September. Muse caught on so quickly that it topped the Apple App Store in less than two weeks. Well before that, AMD and Intel were already huge winners in the stock market this year due largely to surging demand for CPUs, but they've picked up steam in the past month, jumping 32% and 21%, respectively, as of Monday's close beating all of tech's megacaps.
The rally continued on Tuesday, with AMD jumping almost 3% to a fresh high of $649.42. AMD's growing strength in both CPUs and GPUs has pushed the company into the trillion-dollar market cap club.
"As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65, which consults on AI hardware and costs.
Users learned about the power behind the new agents by asking them. Muse tells users that it runs on an AMD-powered computer, while Dots said it runs on a virtual computer powered by AMD's EPYC-branded CPU.
A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that the company designed its system to use whatever kind of CPU is available.
"We take a diverse approach to our hardware and are largely CPU-agnostic by design, which gives us the most flexibility in acquiring capacity," the Meta spokesperson said in a statement.
OpenAI similarly uses multiple CPU providers, meaning AMD isn't the only game in town.
Most servers at hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft — use CPUs made by Intel or AMD. But nearly every major cloud provider is also developing custom chips of their own, typically based on Arm technology. Arm announced its own CPU for agents in March, with Meta as the debut customer, and its stock price has more than doubled since.
Earlier this year, Nvidia released Vera — a fully redesigned central processor — along with an entire rack filled only with the CPUs. The chip giant says it built the new Vera CPUs specifically for agents and expects CPUs to be a $200 billion market by 2030.
But it's one part of the chip industry where Nvidia isn't currently the favorite, analysts say.
"It's just a new product and they're going to be competing against a lot of different players," Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview, adding that he believes AMD currently has the "best product."
CPUs are driving a healthy portion of AMD's growth. Revenue in the company's data center business more than doubled to $6.7 billion in the quarter ended in June, accounting for almost 60% of total sales.
"The conversation has changed quite a bit over the last eight to 10 months in terms of agentic usage," said Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI. McNamara added that CPU sales are going to "really ramp."
GPUs think, CPUs do
Muse, Dots and even coding software like OpenAI's Codex use AI models to plan tasks that can run autonomously. The agents need their own computer that can run for hours or even days in the background, explained Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman.
GPUs are still needed for inference, or processing an AI model, but an agent also needs a CPU.
"CPUs are actually performing the workflows while GPUs are doing the thinking," Newman said.
Meta and OpenAI use virtual machines, which partition a server into several lighter virtual computers, so one server can support scores of users.
Some AMD EPYC processors have up to 192 CPU cores. According to benchmarks and the agents themselves, Muse's virtual computer uses two cores and Dots uses nine.
CPUs are less expensive than GPUs.
Benchmarks and queries show Dots using an AMD EPYC 9V74 CPU, which is available from resellers for under $3,000. The EPYC 9D25 reportedly used by Meta for Muse costs even less on the secondary market. Nvidia GPUs can cost more than 10 times that for a single chip, and they're usually sold in clusters of hundreds or thousands of chips.
Investors are watching how Meta plans to serve Muse users, after downloads surpassed 5 million since last month's launch, according to Sensor Tower. Morgan Stanley estimates Muse's serving costs at $3 to $130 per month, with an average of $37 per user, depending on inference usage.
The firm says Meta's agent could account for 20% of AMD's 2026 chip sales.
There's a lot of money to be made in CPUs, and forecasts for the segment's growth are accelerating.
Futurum estimates $118 billion in total CPU sales in 2027, almost double the firm's previous forecast in May.
In July, AMD predicted the entire CPU market would hit $220 billion in sales in 2030, up from a previous 2025 forecast of $60 billion. AMD said in July that it expects to take more than half of the market.
AMD currently commands about 46% of the market for x86 CPU units, Mercury Research said in August. Intel is also seeing a surge in demand.
But AMD has a foothold with hyperscalers, which is where many of the virtual machines for agents will be deployed. It also has the benefit of using an x86 architecture for its chips, allowing agents to use older software without worrying about compatibility issues.
"AMD is probably getting the most of this because they have the largest market share and the cloud hyperscaler world for CPUs," Klein said, adding that he "wouldn't rule Nvidia out."
"If you are a company that can supply both types of chips, you're in the best position," Klein said.

Your voice is more than sound. It’s part of who you are
Meet Jules Rodriguez. He’s a dad, husband, former science teacher, podcaster and stand-up comedian — someone who has always had a lot to say.
But ALS has taken away his ability to speak. Now, Jules communicates by typing with his eyes, and an AI-generated voice clone speaks his words aloud.
What do we lose when we lose our voice?
In this episode of The Deep End, hear Jules’ story, as well as perspectives from scientists and clinicians on why a voice is so much more than a way to communicate. Human brains are poised to seek out voices, and all the various kinds of information they can hold.
Jules’ experience reveals just how much of our identity is created by the way we sound — and what it means when that sound disappears.

GamerCard Review: A Flawed Pocket-Size Retro Handheld
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Fantastic screen, especially for retro or arcade games. Miraculously small form factor. Solid battery life.
TIRED
Unresponsive, inconsistent controls. Gets warm with use. Slow to load. Lacks basic functions for a modern handheld. Emulation is unreliable.
I can’t remember the last time I felt as conflicted about a piece of gaming tech as I do about the GamerCard. It’s a brilliant idea, brimming with potential. But it’s immensely frustrating.
GamerCard should be an easy sell. A small, versatile portable gaming device that’s intended to be both an accessible handheld for impulse shoppers—designed to sit alongside gift cards at cash registers, integrated hook and all—and is advanced enough for power users to experiment with. Crucially, it’s also affordable at £99 (approximately $130), which feels like a minor miracle in 2026, when a stick of RAM alone is practically a mortgageable expense.
Yet at nearly every turn, that pick-up-and-play promise clashes with the reality of using it.
Slender Silicon
The device is an adapted Raspberry Pi Zero 2W, powered by a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 processor. The 4-inch IPS screen (720p, 1:1 aspect ratio display), control inputs, and speakers all live directly on the motherboard, along with a 1,600-mAh battery—expect approximately four hours of use between charges.
That’s all crammed into a 128 x 88 x 6.5-millimeter shell weighing a meager 100 grams. It’s almost impossibly slim yet still packs a comprehensive array of ports: one USB-C, two Micro-USB, a mini HDMI-out, and even a Qwiic connector along the right-hand edge, below two tiny Start and Select buttons, while the top houses a microSD card slot.
Photograph: Matt Kamen
Photograph: Matt Kamen
Although it’s comfortable to hold, the GamerCard gets notably warm during use, a result of its incredibly svelte design. You’re essentially holding a motherboard, and the casing is so wafer-thin—you can trace the circuitry with your fingers—that you soon notice the heat emanating. It’s never dangerously hot, but it’s an unusual sensation.
The GamerCard’s operating system is tailored to its square screen. Games and apps are displayed in a three-by-three grid, automatically sorted alphabetically. It comes with a handful of games installed—platformer Bloo Kid 2, arcade shoot-’em-up Astro Blaze, and the Saboteur trilogy of stealth action games—and an online store, albeit one still in beta. At the time of writing, there's a mix of indie, open source, and shareware games, plus a few apps such as a music player and a Linux terminal emulator. It’s all smart, clean, and refreshingly minimalist—no ads or distractions.
Out of Control
Unfortunately, playing anything on GamerCard feels more like battling the hardware. Controls are stiff and unresponsive. What look like trackpads on the front are actually silicone pads covering four discrete inputs on each side. That’s fine for the right hand, where the inputs map to the individual ABXY buttons on an Xbox controller, but the lack of a connected D-pad on the left makes moving around any game world a chore. There’s no flow between movements because you have to press each direction manually. There’s noticeable lag between press and response, too.
Having to slowly, deliberately input cardinal directions makes even slower 2D games annoying to play. For 3D games, like the shareware version of the classic Quake available through the store, I found it essentially impossible to move and line up shots. The underside has extra buttons on either side, akin to shoulder buttons, but not every game seemed to recognize them. Clunky controls also make basic tasks like entering your Wi-Fi password an absolute slog, and those silicone pads begin to show wear almost immediately, collecting fingerprints and retaining impressions of the buttons underneath.
Courtesy of Grant Sinclair
GamerCard doesn’t help itself with unmarked and inconsistent inputs. Sure, it makes for an elegant product design, but is it the right-hand “south” button to confirm selections or the “east” button? It changes from game to game, making it all too easy to select the wrong thing.
Worse still are the buttons that don’t exist at all—the hardware lacks a Home button to suspend a game and go back to the system menu. Holding Start and Select resets and exits a game, but it either doesn’t work for every game or the button combo isn’t always recognized. I occasionally had to turn the console off and on again to get back to the home screen. The boot cycle takes approximately 35 seconds. That doesn’t sound long until you’re repeatedly waiting 35 seconds for your quirky ultraportable gaming gadget to turn back on.
Also missing are physical volume controls, a bizarre omission. Audio controls are entirely software-based, which means that thanks to the absent home button, it’s entirely possible that you'll have to power cycle the device to get into the system menu to adjust the sound. “Use headphones,” you say? The GamerCard lacks a 3.5-mm jack but supports Bluetooth, although connectivity seems hit or miss. It would occasionally list my phone as a pairable device, but it never recognized any of my headphones while in pairing mode.
The Emulation Situation
While the GamerCard’s native games and in-progress store don’t yet impress, its greatest potential lies in its emulation capabilities. The Raspberry Pi community has a huge emu scene, and a version of RetroPie is already available for the GamerCard, supporting a huge assortment of retro and arcade platforms. As I’d already backed up a few SNES and Game Boy cartridges I own as ROMs when reviewing Epilogue’s SN Operator and GB Operator, I was ready to go.
Or I would have been if there were any easy way to load ROMs onto the device. First, there’s no push-to-eject mechanism for the microSD card, and the slot is so tight I had to use steel tweezers to pry out the included card. (The manufacturer says future production runs will adjust allowances to prevent this problem.) Then, I realized I couldn’t just drag and drop files onto the card, as Windows wanted to format the card’s unrecognized file system first. Instead, I had to use a file transfer protocol (FTP) client, FileZilla, to send the ROMs to the device over my home network.
Once loaded, games do look fantastic. Pixel art titles in particular really pop on GamerCard’s bright, colorful, 60-frames-per-second display—classic SNES RPG Secret of Mana and platformer Super Adventure Island looked especially lovely. The only hitch is that the GamerCard stretches games to fit its square screen, regardless of aspect ratio display settings in RetroPie. (Finding these is another chore—you can access an emulation menu by holding Select and the “north” face button, although this is never explained anywhere.) Hopefully this is corrected in the future, allowing players to enjoy games in their original dimensions.
The problem with emulation in general, on any platform, is that performance and compatibility can vary wildly. How well the core mimics original hardware, the ROM file, and the hardware it’s running on can all impact how well a game plays. RetroPie wouldn’t load any Game Boy ROMs I tried, and although it launched SNES games, creating saves was unreliable. It’s hard to pin that on hardware or software, but again, I hope the company irons it out. Playing the games that did load had all the same problems the GamerCard presented for its native titles—inconsistent control layouts, laggy inputs, and a general unresponsiveness that frustrates.
Who’s Holding the Cards?
The GamerCard has an identity crisis. Is a casual consumer who picks up a fun-looking gadget next to an Amazon gift card likely to want—or know how to—acquire ROMs and set up an FTP client to get them onto the device? Will they have the patience to figure out which unmarked button does what, and why that keeps changing? Or do they want some recognizable games they can play with ease?
Conversely, are more technically proficient users likely to want a Raspberry Pi with the compromises this brings in the name of portability rather than just building their own machine for retro gaming? Ultimately, I’m just not sure who this is for.
Its potential is clear. Like any Raspberry Pi, this is a full computer in and of itself. The company claims it’s “easily programmable” in MicroPython, C, C++, and Basic, and there’s even a version of the Pico-8 game dev engine available. There's enormous promise for educational and creative purposes. The sheer passion behind it is also evident—it’s the brainchild of Grant Sinclair, nephew of inventor Clive Sinclair, who built the Sinclair ZX Spectrum 8-bit home computer.
Anyone content to dig into the programming and kitbashing side of Raspberry Pi may find a great product here. For everyone else, a future GamerCard 2 with a more intuitive interface, games designed explicitly for the platform and, critically, much better controls could be fantastic. I hope that version exists someday. Right now, the GamerCard feels more prototype than retail-ready.
Matt Kamen is a freelance journalist specializing in media, video games, and technology coverage. Beyond WIRED, his work can be found in The Guardian, Empire, and elsewhere. ... Read More

France tests upgraded nuclear missile against backdrop of Russia tensions
Unknown

2026-10-06

France tests upgraded nuclear missile against backdrop of Russia tensions
- France tested its upgraded M51.3 submarine-launched ballistic missile without a nuclear warhead to certify its nuclear submarine's readiness amid rising tensions with Russia.
- President Macron highlighted the test as a strong message of France's defence capability and commitment to expanding its nuclear arsenal.
- France spends €5.6 billion annually maintaining its nuclear stockpile, ranking fourth globally, with the M51.3 missile offering extended range and modernised deterrent capability.
AI generated
PARIS - France’s defence ministry said on Oct 6 it had conducted the first test launch of its latest-generation M51.3 submarine-launched ballistic missile, underscoring its nuclear deterrent amid heightened tensions with Russia.
The M51.3 missile, which was not equipped with a nuclear warhead, was launched off the coast of Brittany as part of an operation to certify the nuclear-submarine Le Vigilant’s ability to deploy the weapon following a major maintenance overhaul, the ministry said in a statement.
It said the launch was conducted without a payload and in strict compliance with international obligations.
While the announcement made no mention of Russia, the test comes after President Vladimir Putin warned the West last week not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between EU members Poland and Lithuania and which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Macron hails clear message
NATO has said none of its “exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation”. Putin also said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
“Today we are stronger. The message has been sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received,” President Emmanuel Macron said in a video on X showing him watching the launch.
Macron said in March France would expand its nuclear arsenal and launched an initiative offering European partners joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Since then, the message of being prepared to bear the costs of defending France’s values and security has been a constant theme.
France spends roughly €5.6 billion (S$9.3 billion) a year to maintain its stockpile of 290 submarine- and air-launched weapons - the world’s fourth-largest arsenal.
Britain has 225 nuclear warheads. Russia and the United States have more than 5,000 each.
The M51.3 is the latest version of the missile that entered service in October 2025 as part of the modernisation of France’s nuclear deterrent.
Paris does not disclose the range of the M51.3. Publicly available estimates for the M51 family generally place its range at around 9,000km or more, while French officials have said the new version can travel further.
France maintains a nuclear arsenal based on air- and sea-launched weapons, with four ballistic missile submarines forming the backbone of its ocean deterrent. REUTERS

Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:58:30 UTC
19:58:30 KST

An Oct. 5 report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia is increasingly turning to cheaper, maneuverable “quasi-cruise” missiles to supplement its conventional strike capabilities, a tactic that is pressuring Ukraine’s already overstretched air defenses.
Building on the relative success of the jet-powered variants of the Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones, Russia has been introducing the so-called Banderol and Dan-T weapons and is believed to be developing other variants, increasing production and testing new launch platforms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mass attacks combining these new weapons with ballistic and conventional cruise missiles and jet-powered drones are exacerbating Ukrainian interceptor missile shortages.
While Ukraine is developing countermeasures including faster interceptors, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence-enhanced automatic gun towers, these will, as President Volodymyr Zelensky has admitted, take time to develop and bring into service. Meanwhile, Kyiv will struggle to protect itself from the onslaught these weapons will unleash.
The Banderol
Russia’s S8000 “Banderol” (meaning a small parcel in Russian) is a jet-powered medium-size cruise missile analog manufactured by the Kronshtadt Group.
It uses the Chinese Swiwin SW800Pro-A95 turbojet engine, giving it a range of up to 500 kilometers (312 miles) at speeds up to 650 kph (400 mph) and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The Ukrainian Air Force describes it as a “hybrid of a drone, an aerial bomb, and a missile.”
It first appeared during a strike on the Odesa region in early 2025 before taking part in 40 separate strikes between May and September this year, while Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported in July that Russia had completed testing and the weapon had entered mass production.
They have been used in attacks targeting ports, logistics hubs, terminals, food warehouses and infrastructure in Kharkiv, Odesa, Zhytomyr and Kyiv.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Kyiv’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said in July that Banderols had been used in 80% of Russian strikes on the Odesa City port.
The Dan-T
Russia unveiled its Dan-T at the El-Alamein airshow in Egypt in September. It is based on the 1990s Dan-M target aircraft, which was designed to simulate US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense training.
According to the ISW report, Russia’s state-owned arms conglomerate Rostec, which makes the missiles, converted Dan-M stockpiles into air-launched loitering munitions by adding 135-kilogram (300-pound) warheads. It has an all-up weight of 270 kilograms (600 pounds) and a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range.
ISW assesses that construction of Dan-Ts has not yet reached scale but is another indication of Moscow’s efforts to repurpose existing technology into strike weapons. As an example, Soviet-era RM-48U missiles – originally designed for S-400 air defense training – have been converted into ballistic missiles for ground attacks on Ukraine.
The extent of Dan-T use is unclear. While Rostec and some Russian milbloggers claim hundreds have been successfully used in strikes on Ukraine, it was not until Sept. 13 that Ukraine began to differentiate between Banderols and Dan-Ts.
Launch platforms
Banderols and Dan-T were initially designed to be air-launched from Orion drones, helicopters and tactical aircraft – which some estimates say would potentially double their range.
HUR has reported ground launches from occupied Crimea, with Ukrainian analysts suggesting Dan-T could eventually launch from ground and naval systems.
Cost versus performance
These “quasi-cruise” missiles have inferior performance to conventional missiles, but their cost allows more to be manufactured and used, while their capabilities are more than sufficient for Russia’s purposes.
Compared to the Kh-101 cruise missile’s 2,500-kilometer (1,560-mile) range, 1,000 kph (625 mph) speed, and 480-kilogram (1,050-pound) warhead, the Banderol has a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range, speed of up to 650 kph (400 mph), and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
The cost differential is even more stark. A Ukrainian aviation expert estimates that each Banderol costs less than 10% of the approximately $2million cost of a domestically produced Kh-101 cruise missile.
Banderols present especially difficult targets when used in attacks that combine them with Geran/Shahed drones and conventional missiles. They are maneuverable and have a smaller turning radius, which complicates tracking and interception.
Russian mass production
The report claims that Russia has prioritized production of jet-powered drones and quasi-cruise missiles in order to increase its strike capability at an affordable cost.
In September, Zelensky claimed that Russia would spend $12 billion on the weapons, with Ukrainian defense analyst Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov saying that Russia not only aims to increase the numbers of Banderol, Dan-T, Dan-M and jet-powered drones, but also aims to boost speeds to 750 kph (470 mph) while improving low-altitude flight and maneuverability.
HUR estimated in August that Russia was producing about 80 Banderols a month, with Beskrestnov setting the target at 120 and Ukrainian sources estimating Dan-T production at 14,000 in 2027.
Ukrainian countermeasures
Ukrainian developers recently unveiled upgraded interceptors, such as the LITAVR+ and Sting 2.0, capable of taking on jet-powered Geran/Shaheds flying at speeds over 400 kph (250 mph).
Beskrestnov said up to five such interceptors are in development and still require testing. Ukrainian developers have also reportedly deployed unspecified Banderol countermeasures and are scaling production.
Electronic warfare could reportedly play a role, as both Banderol and Dan-T reportedly rely on satellite and inertial navigation for guidance.

Ukraine Claims Record Barrage on Russia With 1,750 Drones, 17 Flamingo Missiles

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine launched a record-breaking number of drones and missiles at targets across Russia over the past 24 hours on Tuesday, according to Russia’s defense ministry.
Russian air defenses claimed to have intercepted and destroyed 1,750 fixed-wing drones and 17 Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles, as well as two guided aerial bombs and a US-made HIMARS rocket.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The reported drone total exceeds the previous record of 1,671 Ukrainian drones claimed by Russia on Aug. 18, when attacks were reported across 15 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The number of Flamingo missiles reported over the 24-hour period is also unprecedented. Russia had previously claimed to intercept no more than three to six Flamingos in a single day.
The figures have not been independently verified.
Moscow among the main targets
The record-breaking barrage included repeated attacks on Moscow and the surrounding region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were heading toward the capital early on Oct. 6, with 105 destroyed as they approached the city. He later reported another 68 drones intercepted by air defenses.
Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were destroyed across 16 municipalities.
According to Vorobyov, two people were killed and nine injured. Forty-seven private homes were damaged in several towns, while an apartment building in Lobanovo, near Domodedovo, was also hit.
Major oil facility targeted
Among the reported targets was the Volodarskaya Linear Production and Dispatch Station, a major Transneft facility and one of the Moscow region’s key fuel-storage and distribution hubs.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products annually, including gasoline, jet fuel and diesel supplied from the Moscow and Ryazan refineries. Some of the fuel is delivered to airports serving the Moscow aviation hub.
The extent of any damage to the facility was not immediately clear.
The scale of the attack also disrupted air travel across Moscow. More than 200 flights were reportedly delayed or canceled at the capital’s airports from midnight.
The Sheremetyevo airport saw the largest disruption, with around 47 departures and 106 arrivals affected. The Vnukovo airport reported disruptions to 28 departing and 23 arriving flights, while four flights were affected at the Domodedovo airport.

Singapore refers eight civil servants to police over property purchases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:55:46 UTC
19:55:46 KST

Singapore refers eight civil servants to police over property purchases
Minister announces referrals after think tank paper finds link between purchases and unannounced MRT stations.
Singapore has referred eight civil servants to the police following an inquiry into the suspected use of nonpublic information to buy properties near planned railway stations.
Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing announced the referrals on Tuesday after a working paper by a United States-based think tank found that civil servants were disproportionately likely to buy homes near future Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations.
In remarks to Parliament, Chan said the government had identified eight individuals who warranted further examination following a review of property transactions by 191 civil servants.
“Let me emphasise that a referral does not mean that wrongdoing has been established,” Chan said.
“The police will look into the facts independently and due process will be followed.”
Chan said the government took the misuse of government information seriously and would act “firmly” in any cases where wrongdoing was established.
“The fundamental principle is clear,” he said.
“Public officers must never use information obtained through their official duties to advance their own private interests or those of others.”
The announcement comes after the National Bureau of Economic Research last month published research suggesting that Singaporean civil servants were 60 percent more likely to buy homes in areas where planned MRT stations had yet to be announced.
The paper, written by economists at Stanford University, Columbia University and the University of Hong Kong, found that purchases were concentrated among mid-level officials linked to public transport planning and generated “meaningful” financial gains for those involved.
Singapore has long prided itself on being a leader in clean governance, proclaiming zero tolerance for corruption.
The city-state’s public sector was ranked third-cleanest in Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perceptions Index last year, trailing Denmark and Finland.
In 2024, a Singaporean court sentenced S Iswaran, a former transport minister, to 12 months in prison for obstructing justice and accepting gifts worth more than $300,000 while in office.
Iswaran’s conviction marked the first prosecution of a cabinet official in Singapore since 1975, when then-Environmental Minister Wee Toon Boon was found guilty of receiving kickbacks from a local businessman.
In 1986, Teh Cheang Wan, a minister for national development, was under investigation by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau. He died before charges were brought against him.

Unidentified aerial and surface drones attacked two merchant vessels within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
According to Maritime.bg, the incident occurred about 80 nautical miles east of the town of Byala, near Cape St. Atanas.
The vessel ALFA WATAN (IMO 7510884), flying the Togolese flag, was attacked while sailing from El Arish, Egypt, to Sulina, Romania.

According to Maritime.bg, this is the first known attack on merchant vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
In connection with the incident, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives from the Ministry of Defense, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Transport, security services, and other government agencies.

Dali artwork worth millions stolen in French museum heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:54:38 UTC
19:54:38 KST

Dali artwork worth millions stolen in French museum heist
A multimillion-euro artwork featuring a massive bronze cover designed by Salvador Dali has been stolen from a museum in central France. It is the latest in a string of high-profile thefts targeting the country’s cultural institutions.
Thieves took the artwork from the Centre of Contemporary Art in Issoire overnight to Monday. Prosecutors described it as an “exceptional and unique” work of “great value” and opened a criminal investigation.
The stolen work is Joseph Foret’s ‘Livre de l’Apocalypse’ (The Book of the Apocalypse), a monumental 210kg volume produced between 1958 and 1961 with contributions from prominent figures in 20th-century art and literature, including Dali, Jean Cocteau, Bernard Buffet, and Jean Giono.
Its roughly 150kg bronze casing, designed by Dali, is decorated with gold, precious stones, and seashells. The one-of-a-kind book has been described as among the world’s heaviest and most expensive, with its value estimated at several million euros.
The Issoire theft is the latest in a string of high-profile robberies to hit French museums. In September, thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in southeastern France and grabbed four paintings from the walls. Two were abandoned in the museum garden as the thieves fled, while two remain missing. The four were initially valued at €9 million ($10.1 million), with the missing pair later valued at €4.2 million.
In July, three masked thieves raided the Lalique Museum in northeastern France, escaping with 27 valuable pieces worth €4.5 million in just 11 minutes. Despite the museum receiving “special attention” after the Louvre robbery, its security company reportedly failed to alert gendarmes when the alarms went off, leaving a cleaner to call police.
The wave of robberies follows a spectacular Louvre heist in October 2025, when thieves stole eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels worth around €88 million in broad daylight. Hours later, nearly 2,000 prized coins were reportedly stolen from the Denis Diderot House of Enlightenment in northeastern France. A month earlier, thieves had broken into the National Museum of Natural History in Paris and made off with 6 kg of rare gold nuggets, with the loss later estimated at around €1.5 million.
The string of thefts triggered a national scandal over museum security. A parliamentary inquiry released in May found widespread shortcomings, pointing to aging infrastructure, staff shortages and inadequate surveillance. Only 23% of French museums had an emergency and risk-prevention plan in 2024, while just 54% had video surveillance, according to the report.
Following the Louvre robbery, the Lalique Museum was designated a “sensitive site” and placed under “special attention.” Yet a source close to the investigation said the additional protection was “not sufficient.” The government unveiled a new 33-point museum-security plan in July, but did not specify how the measures would be funded.
France has also cut heritage spending while ramping up military expenditures. The country’s 2026 heritage budget was reduced by €106 million, or 8%, while the Louvre lost €5 million in funding. By contrast, the defense budget rose by €6.7 billion to €68.4 billion as the government accelerates what it calls France’s “rearmament.”

Vsevolod Chentsov, Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration of Ukraine, urged lawmakers to pass Bill No. 15412 "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language" at the first reading only after consultations with the European Commission and other stakeholders.
Specifically, during a committee meeting on Tuesday morning, discussing the bill on the educational rights of national minorities (No. 16119), which aims to unblock the opening of two negotiation clusters on Ukraine's EU accession by lifting Hungary's veto, Natalia Pipa (Holos faction), a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation, proposed that before the parliamentary vote on that bill, the Rada should pass Bill No. 15412 ("On amendments to сertain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language") at the first reading.
In turn, Roman Hryschuk (Servant of the People faction) also supported this idea: "This is the right moment—not just for the opposition, but for society as a whole—to explain why the Rada passed the bill on national minority languages and significantly expanded the use of language in the educational process. Bill No. 15412 would balance the situation. My position is that we should ultimately pass both."
"We must approach the adoption of this bill (No. 15412) in a highly responsible and measured manner. You are absolutely right that strengthening and protecting the Ukrainian language is our sovereign right. However, we are currently engaged in a negotiation process. And this is not just about the Hungarian community. We have an action plan regarding national minorities, approved by the European Commission, the Council of Europe, and the High Commissioner on National Minorities, and we need to present a comprehensive picture to our partners. This law will become part of a broader body of legislation regulating the use of both the state language and the languages of national minorities. This bill has already raised questions from the European Commission," Chentsov said at a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation on Tuesday.
The Deputy Prime Minister added that he understood the logic behind the MPs' proposals to pass Bill No. 15412 at the first reading, with consultations and further refinement to follow.
"If we hadn't found ourselves in the current situation regarding the adoption of the education bill (No. 16119) and the opening of accession clusters, we might have been able to do this. But the risk is very high. There could be a negative reaction from the European Commission and national minority groups, which is quite possible, and we have many opponents, primarily the Russian Federation, who are watching our every move very closely," he emphasized.
In light of this, he urged the MPs to first work through Bill No. 15412 "calmly" with the European Commission and other stakeholders, and only submit it to Parliament for a first reading after this review process.
"We could manage these risks. That is my proposal. I have already discussed this with Mr. Poturaev [Mykyta Poturaev, Head of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy] and with other MPs. If we want to achieve our goal, we need to be extremely cautious right now. Because we risk both failing to pass the education bill and falling short on the state language protection law," the Deputy Prime Minister stated.
Earlier, a number of civic initiatives and organizations called upon the Rada, as well as parliamentary factions and groups, to vote for Bill No. 16119 only on the condition that Bill No. 15412 is first adopted at the first reading.
"We urge you to submit both of these bills to the upcoming plenary session and demonstrate a balanced, responsible approach to protecting and supporting both the Ukrainian state language and the languages of national minorities," the open appeal states.
As previously reported, in August, the Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt Bill No. 15412 "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the status of Ukrainian as the state language" at the first reading.
In September, the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation also recommended that parliament adopt Bill No. 15412 at the first reading.
Specifically, the bill proposes expanding the list of individuals required to be proficient in the state language and to use it while performing their official duties. This requirement applies, among others, to Members of Parliament, heads of state scientific and cultural institutions, private enforcement officers, insolvency administrators, auditors, and other individuals.
Furthermore, the bill proposes strengthening the protection of the right to use the Ukrainian language in the workplace by guaranteeing this right at the hiring stage, rather than only after an employment relationship has been established. The document also outlines requirements for ensuring official documents comply with state language standards and aims to improve state oversight mechanisms and specific complaint-handling procedures.
