Ecologist: The year's first autumn storm could hit this Friday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:31:00 UTC
18:31:00 KST

Ecologist: The year's first autumn storm could hit this Friday
Estonia's first fall storm is forecast to hit this weekend, said Hannes Tõnisson, senior researcher in geoecology at Tallinn University. Temperatures are expected to turn sharply colder around October 18–21.
Ordinary people often use the word storm to describe any stronger gust of wind. For scientists, however, a storm means winds of at least 15 meters per second. Tõnisson said winds must average that speed for at least 10 minutes and isolated stronger gusts do not constitute a storm in scientific terms.
"The first somewhat bigger storm looks set to arrive this weekend. It will probably make a detour into western Estonia on Friday afternoon or perhaps head into Latvia — we don't know exactly yet," Tõnisson said on ETV morning show "Terevisioon," describing the approaching fall weather.
Forecasts predict gusts of more than 30 meters per second in coastal areas this weekend, although the cyclone's exact path will only become clear in the final days before it arrives. The storm will likely pass over the islands, with winds reaching their highest speeds on the Sõrve Peninsula and in western Saaremaa. Based on initial estimates, the wind direction should not disrupt ferry traffic.
Weather models are constantly changing in the run-up to the storm. Tõnisson noted that a 50-kilometer shift in its path would change the situation. In one scenario, Estonia's islands would take a battering; in another, the brunt of the storm would shift to Latvia.
The second half of October will bring a sharp change in the weather. "There could be a sudden change in the weather sometime between October 18 and 21," Tõnisson said. A colder air mass will bring sleet and push temperatures down toward freezing — according to the ecologist, more cautious drivers could start switching to winter tires from then on.
People should not expect lasting snow cover before November. Tõnisson said it is too early to make any firm predictions about longer-term winter weather. "At the same time, we can certainly expect surprise sleet or snowfall, as well as morning frosts and black ice," he said.
El Niño might bring more precipitation to Estonia
At the global level, this year's weather is being shaped by the most powerful El Niño on record. In South America's Andes, the phenomenon caused record snowfall as a large amount of moisture encountered cold air. In previous El Niño years, southern Europe has tended to see more moisture than usual. In Estonia, the phenomenon likewise means the potential for greater precipitation.
El Niño's effects extend directly to Estonia's sporting life. Out of personal interest, Hannes Tõnisson examined the relationship between the Tartu Marathon and El Niño events over the past 15 years. "Only once has the Tartu Marathon been canceled during an El Niño year," he said. According to the ecologist, the statistic gives winter sports enthusiasts reason to hope for good snow conditions.
However, those who develop weather models face uncertainties in real time. The main problem this year is the exceptional nature of the El Niño event, which leaves scientists with little to go on. "There is a great deal of uncertainty [...] an event like this has never happened before," Tõnisson said. There is no historical data, meaning computers cannot calculate its precise local effects.
Using the torrential rains that hit Spain as an example, Tõnisson said scientists can anticipate extreme rainfall events two to three weeks in advance. "A week beforehand, we already have a fairly good idea of what the amounts could be in different places and two or three days beforehand where exactly that amount will fall," Tõnisson said. The lengthy advance warning gives society time to prepare for hazardous conditions.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Airika Harrik
Source: "Terevisioon"

Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs Assures NATO Secretary-General of Latvia’s Readiness to Defend NATO’s External Border

On Wednesday, 17 June, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs met with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at NATO headquarters in Brussels (Belgium), to discuss the Alliance’s security and defence priorities, the strengthening of NATO’s Eastern Flank, support for Ukraine and Latvia’s contribution to collective defence.
During the meeting, the Prime Minister reaffirmed that security remains a priority for the new government and that Latvia will continue to contribute to strengthening defence capabilities.
“Latvia is a responsible and reliable Ally. Military forces from 14 NATO countries are present in Latvia. This sends a clear message that Latvia is not to be taken lightly. This year, the national defence budget amounts to 5% of GDP, and we plan to continue allocating this level of funding to core defence expenditure in the coming years. Given the rising number of incidents, we must build a drone defence wall. Strengthening air defence is a national security priority,” emphasised Andris Kulbergs.
The Prime Minister expressed his gratitude for the support of NATO Allies, highlighting the operational response of the French Air Force in shooting down the drone that had entered Latvia’s airspace.
“This is clear evidence of the Allies’ unity in action and their determination to defend one another. At the same time, we are constantly adapting to actual threats, investing in the development of counter-drone defence capabilities. The drone industry in Latvia is developing rapidly, offering more affordable and effective solutions. Latvia is ready to host additional Allied air defence capabilities to protect NATO’s external border,” said the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister also thanked the US, Canada and other Allies for their military presence in Latvia.
Support for Ukraine was also discussed during the meeting. The Prime Minister informed the NATO Secretary-General of the recently concluded agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on cooperation in the field of drones, which will enable Latvia to draw on Ukraine’s battlefield experience to enhance its defence capabilities. He also informed the NATO Secretary General of the Latvian Government’s decision on 16 June to contribute EUR 7 million this year to the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, thereby continuing Latvia’s military support for Ukraine.
At the conclusion of the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their shared commitment to strengthening NATO’s capabilities, increasing defence investment and continuing long-term support for Ukraine.

On 18–19 June, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs attended the European Council meeting in Brussels (Belgium), representing Latvia’s national interests and emphasising the need to accelerate the implementation of European Union (EU) defence projects aimed at strengthening the Eastern Flank.
It is vital for Latvia that the EU-level defence projects (EDPCI) to strengthen the eastern border – Eastern Flank Watch and the Drone and Counter-drone Capabilities Project (DECODER) – be implemented as soon as possible. “Our country’s external border is also the European Union’s external border. Therefore, the defence capabilities of both Latvia and Europe as a whole must be strengthened. Latvia already allocates 5% of its GDP to defence, but European security is a shared responsibility, and all Member States should allocate a similar level of funding to defence,” emphasised Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs.
During a discussion with EU leaders, also attended by the President of Ukraine, Andris Kulbergs emphasised that long-term support for Ukraine remains a consistent priority for Latvia and that the EU must continue to provide all forms of support, including military assistance. Latvia’s position also includes strong support for strengthening the resilience of Ukraine’s economy and society and its national defence capabilities, including by increasing pressure on Russia, further isolating it internationally, including in sport and culture, and imposing economic restrictions.
Latvia also supports Ukraine’s integration into the European Union, calling for the launch of full-fledged accession negotiations and the opening of all clusters, starting with the ‘Fundamentals’ cluster.
Discussions at the European Council also covered the EU’s multiannual budget for 2028–2034 and the updated negotiating framework document (NegoBox)prepared by the Cypriot Presidency. Latvia’s main priority is a mechanism for strengthening the eastern border.
“Russia’s war in Ukraine has had a significant impact not only on the security situation in Europe, but also on national economies, the energy sector and the business environment. Our security begins with a strong and resilient economy. Special support instruments must be established for all countries along the eastern border that face security risks posed by an aggressor state and adversely affect investment attraction, tourism and the well-being of the population,” emphasised Andris Kulbergs.
The need to address inequalities in direct payments to Latvian farmers and to increase the level of these payments was also emphasised.
Discussions on the Middle East focused on the Iran–US peace talks, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon. As regards global security challenges, Latvia emphasised that stability in the Middle East is an essential prerequisite for international security and that Iran must not be allowed to continue deliberately threatening civilians and civilian and industrial infrastructure or restricting international trade routes.
In view of the need to reduce the EU’s economic dependencies and address the growing trade deficit with China, discussions on strengthening the EU’s global competitiveness also continued at the European Council. Leaders also addressed internal aspects of the Single Market, as well as the impact of the crisis in the Persian Gulf region on energy prices and disruptions to supply chains for critical raw materials. Alongside the pursuit of the EU’s global competitiveness objectives, work must also continue on improving the Single Market and ensuring a level playing field both internally and globally.
Ahead of the European Council meeting, the Prime Minister met in Brussels with the President of the European Council, António Costa, and the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. During his meeting with President Costa, which focused on the European Council’s agenda, Andris Kulbergs emphasised Europe’s role in strengthening the security of Latvia’s and the EU’s entire eastern border. He also briefed President Costa on the situation in Latgale, where residents and businesses require state support. The Prime Minister’s discussion with the President of the European Commission also covered the strengthening of European security and defence, the EU budget and progress on the Rail Baltica project. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine was also discussed.
The Prime Minister also took part in the Friends of Cohesion meeting organised by Italy and Romania, where leaders from 15 countries discussed cohesion policy and compared their national positions ahead of negotiations on the multiannual budget. Meanwhile, a meeting of the NB6 countries (Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Sweden, Finland and Denmark) with the leaders of Ireland and Poland focused on regional security challenges, cooperation with Ukraine and a common approach to strengthening Europe’s eastern border.

Philosopher Among New AI2050 Senior Fellows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

David Danks, professor of philosophy, artificial intelligence, and data science at the University of Virginia, has been awarded a $1 million three-year senior fellowship for a project on “human-AI value coevolution.”
The fellowship is from Schmidt Sciences, a science-supporting philanthropic organization founded by Eric Schmidt (former Google CEO) and his wife, Wendy.
The Senior Fellowships are part of the Schmidt Sciences “AI2050” initiative, which funds research to “address the most important long-term problems in AI which need to be solved for AI to be truly beneficial to society by 2050.”
Professor Danks’ AI2050 project is described as follows:
Beneficial AI supports our values, but current systems focus only on our present goals and needs. Previous technologies have changed our values; we should expect that AI will similarly impact us. AI systems are also increasingly learning from and adapting to us. Our and AI values will thus likely coevolve over time, each changing the other. Effective design of AI that is beneficial both today and into the future requires understanding these dynamics, both possible and actual. Danks’ research project will develop the required multidisciplinary understanding of human-AI value coevolution, including practical guidance for AI design, development, and governance.
Danks is the only philosopher among the six newly selected Senior Fellows. There are no philosophers among the 22 Early Career Fellows.

====================================================================================================

Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) Review: Noise-Canceling Champ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Bose’s sequel to the QuietComfort Headphones is incredibly comfortable and has excellent noise-canceling, but those traits are no longer enough to beat the competition.
Excellent ANC. Very comfortable. Detailed sound. Comes with hardshell case, wired cable for lossless audio and charging.
TIRED
So-so battery life. Voice quality is pretty bad during calls. No wireless high-res audio support.
The Bose QuietComfort has been the business traveler's headphones. For many frequent fliers, Bose has been the go-to for noise-canceling headphones and has dominated the market. I’ve spotted close to a dozen of them at every airport and on every flight I’ve been on. That’s staying power for the company that pioneered noise-canceling technology in consumer headphones and has released many versions of the QC since 2000.
But with the new QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), I just don’t know if they’re still the travel headphones to get. They improve on the first-generation version where it matters—they are more comfortable and have even better active noise-canceling (ANC). The sound quality is also among the best you can get. But noise cancellation has become one of the most competitive segments in the premium over-ear headphone market, and the QuietComfort Headphones 2 take a few missteps, namely battery life and price point, that make them hard to recommend over the competitors.
True to Its Name
At 230 grams, the QuietComfort Headphones 2 are very lightweight—far lighter than nearly every other pair of premium over-ear headphones. This means greater comfort, less tension on my head, and less clamping force to keep the headphones stable. Another comfort win is the spacious fit—I don’t feel any mesh or material brushing against my (rather large) ears. I once wore them for an entire eight-hour workday, and they didn’t feel overly clampy, warm, or heavy.
When it comes to ANC, these headphones cancel most noise effectively, and live up to Bose’s reputation for great noise-canceling. I wore them in a cafeteria full of about 60 people chatting and eating, and I could barely hear anything outside my music. They aren’t quite as powerful as $400-plus headphones like the Bose flagship QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), Sony WH-1000XM6, and Apple AirPods Max, but they’re close.
I take sound quality in premium headphones for granted—they’re generally excellent—but it’s worth highlighting here. Bose knows how to produce a clear, detailed, entertaining sound. There is great detail across bass, lows, mids, and highs. The headphones have your typical V-shaped curve emphasizing bass and treble, but the mids aren’t lost at all—I actually found them more distinct and defined than on similar headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM4C. (Though Bose’s simple but limited three-band EQ might disappoint tinkerers.)
The design hasn’t changed drastically from the last-generation QuietComfort (2023). Both earcups have physical buttons for easy control, but the headband adjuster is new. It’s made with smooth-sliding plastic instead of the previous version's notched metal. This is more aligned with the competition—most over-ear headphones I’m testing these days have smooth, not notched, adjustments, which give you a better fit than being “in between” sizes, so to speak. This version also ditches the wired 3.5-mm port but comes with a USB-C-to-3.5-mm cable for wired, high-resolution audio; it doesn't support lossless over wireless.
Software-wise, these headphones support Bose’ Immersive Audio and Cinema spatial modes, which launched with the Ultra 2 and QuietComfort Ultra 2 Earbuds. I still don’t find either very appealing for most use cases, but the optional head-tracking does an admirable job placing sounds directionally.
Missed Expectations
These headphones get the big things right. It’s when you dig a little deeper that things start to feel a little underwhelming.
Battery life is not great: 24 hours with ANC enabled is simply not long enough. I had to charge these midweek, every week. Yes, charging is quick, but compared to headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM4C (27 hours with ANC), Nothing Headphone (1) (35 hours with ANC), and Sonos Ace Ultra (also 35 hours with ANC), I noticed how fast the Bose ran out of juice.
I am baffled that these headphones don’t have wear detection. It sounds like a little thing; you can just hit pause before you take off your headphones, after all. But after testing so many headphones with wear detection, many of which are cheaper than these Bose, I was honestly shocked at the omission and thought I needed to change something with my settings, until I remembered: This is by design.
Call quality may be the most overtly bad thing about these headphones. My colleagues have called out that I sounded oddly quiet and processed on Zoom calls, which typically shouldn’t happen with premium, $300-plus headphones. If I have to take these off and switch to the $170 Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro earbuds to take calls in a quiet room, it’s an issue that Bose needs to address.
The $370 MSRP might be my biggest issue with these headphones, since that’s pretty close to the $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen)—which happened to be on sale for $400 on Amazon at the time of writing this review. That’s a $30 price difference for a much better pair of headphones.
Passing the Crown
Bose's QuietComfort-series headphones are iconic for a reason. This midrange option is comfortable, sounds great, and blocks out the world. But so do a lot of headphones in 2026. The $300 Sony WH-1000XM4C’s ANC isn’t as strong, but it has wear detection, better battery life, and a lower price. The $300 Nothing Headphone (1) is a bit less comfortable but has similarly great button controls and a vastly superior 35 hours of battery with ANC. Bose’s own QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) outclasses its sibling in most ways and doesn’t cost much more.
In the past, Bose could command such prices, but the competitive landscape has changed. By no means are these bad: The Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) are indeed quiet and comfortable and have great audio quality, more so than most headphones. For a lot of people, especially Bose loyalists or those who value music over phone calls, that might be enough. But at this price and with all the gripes, there are really good alternatives. I would wait for these headphones to go on sale (like they are right now, as of publication), or even consider the first-generation version if the price is right (under $200).
Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Some children bring their own salt to school as cafeterias cut sodium

While older students ask for salt or bring their own, many younger pupils have given up sauces. As a result, many plates at Raatuse School today held only rice or buckwheat with vegetables.
Hugo, a student at Raatuse School, chose corn and rice today because he doesn't like sauces very much.

The remarks, published by the Sunday Times, followed South Africa’s third formal diplomatic protest against Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III since he took up his post in February. Lamola said the envoy’s public interventions amount to interference in South Africa’s domestic affairs.

“You can’t have a diplomat who says the time for talking is over… It’s our job to talk. So if you can’t talk as a diplomat and you cannot dialogue, get out of the kitchen,” Lamola told the Sunday Times.

The confrontation is the latest sign of deteriorating relations between Pretoria and Washington since US President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Sign a Defence Cooperation Agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:29:47 UTC
18:29:47 KST

On Tuesday, 9 June, at the Baltic and Nordic (NB8) Summit in Tallinn, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed an agreement on comprehensive defence cooperation between the two countries, providing for Latvia to draw on Ukraine’s experience in defending its airspace against drone attacks.
Under the agreement, Ukraine has undertaken to help transfer expertise, particularly in unmanned systems and air defence, by sharing its unique military and civilian experience. Ukraine has also pledged to support the export of products to expand the capabilities of Latvia’s National Armed Forces. Where support is provided to Ukrainian industry, the parties will explore opportunities for co-production, localisation and technology transfer. The agreement sets out a commitment to develop bilateral cooperation between Latvia and Ukraine. Latvia will support Ukraine’s path towards NATO and the European Union at the political level. The agreement also envisages donations of products from Latvia’s defence industry and equipment from the National Armed Forces, training for Ukrainian soldiers, and contributions to international initiatives, including the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). In addition, it provides for a new dimension of cooperation: procurement from Ukraine’s defence industry, strengthening the defence industry partnership between the two countries.
"Ukraine currently knows better than anyone else in the world how to counter drones. This agreement will enable us to strengthen Latvia’s anti-drone defence capabilities. When signing the cooperation agreement, we agreed that the defence forces of both countries would work closely together to implement it. Sharing knowledge, experience and resources makes us much more effective in strengthening our national defence,” says Andris Kulbergs.
The main areas of military support under the agreement include Latvia’s continued cooperation with Ukraine in the research and development of new military technologies and support for Ukraine over the next 10 years, with its specific form and scope to be decided separately each year. The agreement also covers intelligence sharing, facilitating export licences for procurement to meet the needs of the National Armed Forces, and post-war cooperation. The latter includes sharing experience and helping to rebuild Ukraine, particularly defence-related infrastructure such as communications networks, logistics infrastructure and defence industry facilities. Any budgetary commitments on the part of Latvia will be made only with the explicit approval of the Government and, where necessary, the Saeima.
Andris Kulbergs’ government has committed to focusing on tasks that can be accomplished during the term of the 14th Saeima, with the coalition partners having agreed on a specific list of priorities. National security is one of the key priorities, including support for the defence and internal affairs services in strengthening the border, improving air defence and reinforcing Latvia’s internal and external security.
One of the tasks the government plans to carry out is to promote the use of modern technologies by the defence and internal affairs services, by providing them with additional unmanned systems and organising joint training in the use of modern technologies and unmanned systems. The government also plans to establish an effective unmanned aerial vehicle detection system and to improve air defence and electronic warfare systems, with particular attention to municipalities in border areas.
The government plans to allocate 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) to defence while developing Latvia’s defence industry and technologies in cooperation with its closest allies. The Cabinet of Ministers will continue working to expand the presence of NATO allies in Latvia and will consider allocating additional European Union funding to defence. The government also remains committed to providing comprehensive support to Ukraine.
Agreement on Cooperation in the Field of Defence between the Republic of Latvia and Ukraine (ENG)
The Government Declaration is available on the Cabinet of Ministers’ website, along with the Cooperation Agreement of the coalition parties.

====================================================================================================

France’s political, financial challenges threaten eurozone with new debt crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:29:20 UTC
18:29:20 KST

Political developments and financial issues in the eurozone’s second-largest economy, France, threaten to bring a new debt crisis to the bloc.
France is experiencing a historic period of deepening fiscal indiscipline, political turmoil and protests all at the same time.
The country’s public finances deteriorated and pushed its borrowing costs to their highest levels in recent years, while the euro depreciated against the US dollar, falling to 1.116, marking its lowest level in about a year and a half.
Economists are uncertain whether this trend, starting in Paris and rapidly spreading, will engulf the rest of the eurozone in a new debt crisis.
France’s public deficit reached 5.8% of its gross domestic product, above the EU’s 3% threshold, while the country aims to reduce this deficit to 5% by next year, according to the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies.
France has not posted a budget surplus since 1974, and public spending has risen despite slow growth in tax revenues.
More than half of the €1.3 trillion ($1.5 trillion) added to the debt since 2017 stemmed from COVID-19 and energy-related spending, while the rest was due to tax cuts for households and businesses.
The country’s total public debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to reach 121.7% by 2027 as a result of these chronic budget deficits.
France’s nominal debt stock hit its highest level since 1945 at €3.6 trillion ($4 trillion), equivalent to 119% of GDP.
Analysts say France fell into a structural debt trap in which nominal growth rates remain below borrowing interest rates, while the country’s public debt-to-GDP ratio twice exceeded the 60% Maastricht criterion.
The current situation of the French economy fuels concerns about contagion risk due to budget deficits in the European bond market, while the selling pressure facing Paris has already begun to spread to other eurozone countries like Italy, Belgium and Greece, experts note.
Paris is prompted to borrow from the markets every year due to the structural gap between France’s public revenues and spending, which affects borrowing costs, driving them up to around 4.5% from near 0% in 2020, as investors lose confidence amid broader global monetary tightening to combat inflation.
France’s annual interest payments are expected to reach around 7% of the budget, or as high as €65 billion ($73 billion). The interest burden is growing to become the single largest spending item in the country’s budget for the first time in history, exceeding even spending on elementary and secondary school education.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s minority government prepared a radical €54 billion ($60.6 billion) package to gradually reduce the budget deficit to 5% by next year, but this program faced massive public resistance in street protests.
Firefighters and public sector workers protested the budget cuts, while high school and university students took to the streets in protest.
For days, protesters have been demanding an end to the long-standing shortage of teachers, inadequate education conditions and a lack of physical infrastructure.
High school students barricaded their schools while demanding more funding for education.
The police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against protesting students, sparking a backlash from the opposition.
Some 170 students, 65 education staff members and over 600 law enforcement officers have been injured in the protests, while legal proceedings have been launched against more than 5,000 people.
Some 400 high schools suspended in-person classes, accounting for around 10% of all high schools in the country.
Meanwhile, France’s inflation continues to erode purchasing power, as its EU-compliant annual inflation rate surged from 2.6% to 3.4% in September due to rising oil and natural gas prices amid the Middle East conflict.
Energy prices in France rose 2.1% on an annual basis in September, driving the broader rise in inflation.
The yellow vest movement, organizing due to price hikes, demands not only an increase in the education budget but also a freeze on energy prices and additional taxes on large corporations.
With President Emmanuel Macron’s term nearing its end, opposition parties are resisting unpopular budget cuts in parliament.
Paris’ efforts to pass the budget without a parliamentary majority continue to drag the country deeper into a political crisis.
The crisis is affecting the euro, as the region’s currency started the week with a sharp decline, testing below the psychological threshold of $1.12.
Growing concerns over Paris’ public finances, the widening interest rate difference between the US and Europe and surging oil prices contributed to the decline.
Thu Lan Nguyen, head of foreign exchange and commodity research at Commerzbank, stated that while the euro remained largely unaffected by the bond market’s volatility in recent months, these concerns are no longer limited to France and are taking center stage among investors.
The unease in the bond market affects the risk premiums of other countries, as the yield spread between French and German 10-year bonds widened by 32 basis points to 141 last week, while nearing 150 basis points on Monday, the largest weekly widening since 1990.
James Smith, developed markets economist at ING, recently said that France is facing a major impasse in reducing its budget deficit below the 6% threshold amid a fragmented political structure.
The minority government’s new budget plan would not bring lasting relief to the bond markets, according to a joint analysis by ING.
Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid said the real question hinges on whether these developments mark the beginning of a new euro debt crisis or whether the markets are simply overreacting to the turmoil.

====================================================================================================

One year on, Trump's Gaza plan has not stopped Israeli fire or disarmed Hamas - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:28:48 UTC
18:28:48 KST

US President Donald Trump’s year-old plan to end the Gaza war has stalled, and Israel and Hamas have been battling in the Gaza Strip for almost three years.
The initial phase resulted in a ceasefire on October 10, 2025, and secured the release of the last remaining hostages seized in Hamas’s 2023 attacks on Israel, in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees held by Israel.
But other goals, including disarming Hamas, securing Israeli withdrawal - as the IDF currently controls about two-thirds of the strip - and rebuilding Gaza, appear far from reach.
The first phase of Trump’s 20-point plan included a suspension of all military operations, Israeli withdrawal from part of the strip, hostage and prisoner releases and a surge in aid.
Later phases called for Hamas to disarm and for a Palestinian body to assume governance, overseen by the Trump-led Board of Peace. Israel would gradually withdraw, handing territory to a temporary International Stabilization Force (ISF).
“Gaza will be redeveloped for the benefit of the people of Gaza, who have suffered more than enough,” the plan said.
Israeli strikes continue despite Gaza ceasefire
There has been no return to full-scale military operations, but Israeli strikes have continued. Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry claims at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the October ceasefire, many of them women and children, although it does not disclose terrorist casualties.
Israel says its strikes have targeted Hamas, accusing the group of trying to carry out attacks and rearm.
Five Israeli soldiers have been killed by Palestinian terrorists, including both terror attacks and in combat, since the ceasefire, according to the IDF.
The initial phase of Trump’s plan foresaw Israel withdrawing to a Yellow Line that left Israeli troops in control of 53% of Gaza. Since then, the military has expanded its effective control to around two-thirds of the territory.
Israeli-backed Palestinian militias opposing Hamas use the Israeli-held zone to launch attacks into Hamas-controlled areas.
Gaza aid increases but falls short of humanitarian needs
Global hunger watchdog Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) says more than 1.2 million people still face acute hunger in Gaza despite a major scale-up of aid operations after the ceasefire.
In an August report, it cited data showing that an average of 227 trucks a day carried humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza from the ceasefire to the end of May - less than half the minimum 600 trucks stipulated in the Gaza plan.
The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), which controls access to Gaza, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the figure cited in the IPC report.
Israel says around 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid and commercial goods enter each day, that Gaza is getting enough goods to meet its needs, and that it is meeting its obligations.
Aid agencies say Israel is blocking essential items, including metal tent poles, engine oil and spare parts, from entering Gaza, on the grounds that Hamas could use them for military purposes.
Disarmament remains key obstacle in Trump Gaza plan
Trump said Hamas and other terror organizations had accepted a 15-point roadmap drawn up by the Board of Peace to give up their arms. Israeli forces would withdraw as Hamas disarmed. The ISF, working with a new Palestinian security force, would secure Gaza. Trump called it historic.
Hamas said it had agreed to hand over its weapons to be stored under the control of the US-backed Palestinian technocratic government. Though Hamas rejected the word ‘disarmament’, this marked a once-unimaginable position for the Iran-backed group.
But Israel, skeptical that Hamas will give up its arms, called the plan unacceptable and said it would not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is fully disarmed.
Plans have taken shape, but it has yet to be assembled. There is a commander - US Major-General Jasper Jeffers - and Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo, and Uganda have committed personnel.
Jeffers has said the long-term plan is for the ISF to use 20,000 troops and train 12,000 Palestinian police.
The technocratic Palestinian governing body, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, was appointed in January, led by Ali Shaath, who formerly served as a deputy minister in the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority. It has yet to enter Gaza.
Gaza reconstruction remains far short of estimated needs
A year on, Palestinians are still scavenging in the rubble of wrecked buildings for materials to prop up tents and other shelters.
The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion plan in September to begin rebuilding Gaza.
That is a fraction of what is needed. The Board of Peace cited an EU and UN assessment released in April that estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4 billion over the next decade.
Gaza’s future becomes campaign issue ahead of Israeli election
While the Trump plan promises to encourage people to stay in Gaza, Israeli right-wing politicians have stepped up calls for the mass removal of Palestinians through “voluntary emigration”.
Defense Minister Israel Katz said last month there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration."
The defense ministry in 2025 established an office tasked with overseeing “voluntary emigration” from Gaza, after comments by Trump suggesting Gazans could be permanently displaced.
Trump later backed away from the idea, which faced strong resistance from Arab states and was widely rejected internationally. Israeli officials have said there are no plans to move Gaza's population out by force.
Israel will hold a general election on October 27, the country's first since the October 7 massacre. Some leading opposition figures have supported Trump's plan.

Lionel Messi to play final match for Argentina in Buenos Aires farewell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

18:28:29 KST

More than two decades after making his senior national team debut, Lionel Messi will play his final match for Argentina on Tuesday night.
The 39-year-old star will bid farewell to the Albiceleste in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires, in an evening expected to serve as a tribute to the man who led Argentina back to the top of world soccer.
More than 85,000 fans are expected to fill the stadium, with many of Messi's teammates from Argentina's 2022 World Cup-winning squad also expected to attend. Rodrigo De Paul, Nicolas Otamendi and Giovani Lo Celso are among those returning for the occasion, while nearly the entire squad that lifted the World Cup in Qatar is expected to be at the Monumental to say goodbye to the captain. They will be joined by several young players expected to lead Argentina in the post-Messi era.
Messi enters his final national team match with 207 appearances and 125 goals, both national records. His international career has included the 2022 World Cup, two Copa America titles, the Finalissima and an Olympic gold medal. When the final whistle sounds against Benin, an international career spanning more than 20 years will officially come to an end, with his 208th appearance also set to be his last.
"I gave everything I had; I have nothing more to give, and besides, there are excellent young players coming through, and they deserve to get their opportunity," Messi wrote when he announced his retirement from the national team in August.
Coach Lionel Scaloni acknowledged that the void Messi will leave will be impossible to fill. "Messi leaves behind something that has no equal. We have to keep playing, but the feeling of having him on the field is unique. I have never seen anyone who transmits what he transmits on a soccer field, and that is what we will miss."
Messi begins emotional farewell to Argentina
Messi has already begun saying goodbye. Overnight, he posted a series of photos of himself in Argentina colors on Instagram and wrote: "Special moments that I know I will miss." Just hours before his final national team appearance, the brief message offered another glimpse into his mood as a chapter lasting more than two decades comes to an end.
Scaloni, however, is confident Argentina will remain among the world's top teams after the retirement of its legendary No. 10. "The Argentina national team will continue. We will remain at a high level, I have no doubt about that," said the coach, who is also in advanced talks over a contract extension.
Argentina has already offered a glimpse of what the future could look like without Messi. In the last two matches he did not play, the team beat Bolivia 4 to 0 and Burkina Faso 7 to 0, giving opportunities to players including Nico Paz, Franco Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni.
For tonight, however, the future can wait. In Argentina, attention is focused almost entirely on saying goodbye to the greatest player in the national team's history. Ahead of the match, Ole published an unusual tribute looking back at the "boy who was born in Rosario" and who went on to become one of the defining figures in world soccer, despite never behaving like the kind of superstar the system expected him to be.
"There are not many times when something like what will happen on Tuesday night takes place. The world stops," Ole wrote, describing the farewell as an event that goes far beyond a soccer match. "Today the world stops for Leo's farewell to the shirt he loves most. We know that nothing will ever be the same, but we also know how wonderful it was."
Argentina prepares to celebrate the captain it once questioned
The column also reflected on Argentina's complicated relationship with Messi over the years, from criticism, constant comparisons with Diego Maradona, and defeats in major finals, to the moment everything changed when the captain led the national team to Copa America and World Cup titles. Ole noted that the fans celebrating Messi tonight are the same supporters who spent years demanding he prove he could lead Argentina to a major trophy.
Toward the end, the writer returned to the boy from Rosario who used to arrive at the Grandoli club with his grandmother Celia and wanted little more than to keep playing with the ball. The idea was simple: Even after becoming one of the most famous people in the world, Messi never lost the child who chased the ball around a neighborhood field. The final line read almost like the ending of a movie: Evening fell; it was time to go home, and tomorrow there was school.
The Argentine Football Association is also preparing a full evening of events around the match. The stadium will open several hours before kickoff, musical performances will take place throughout the evening, and a drone show, fireworks, and other surprises are planned for after the game.
For the more than 85,000 people in the stands and millions more watching around the world, however, it will all serve as the backdrop to one moment: the final time Lionel Messi takes the field as an Argentina national team player.

Vulnerability was discovered in Meta’s Muse AI agent before launch and hastily fixed - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:28:25 EEST
18:28:25 KST

Vulnerability was discovered in Meta’s Muse AI agent before launch and hastily fixed - media
Kyiv • UNN
Meta engineers found vulnerabilities in Muse that could have allowed escape from the virtual machine and access to internal databases. Security teams urgently fixed the issues before launch.
Several weeks before the launch of Meta’s personal AI agent Muse, Meta engineers discovered several vulnerabilities in the security system of the company’s viral product. At least one of them could have allowed attackers to escape the environment designated for Muse and gain access to confidential Meta databases and services. 404 Media learned of this, reports UNN.
The problems were reportedly so serious that they reached Mark Zuckerberg, and employees worked overtime to fix them.
Details
These specific vulnerabilities were discovered before the product’s launch, but required a "frantic race" by several teams to address a "sudden surge in reports of KVM escapes," according to an internal message from Meta team leaders to the core infrastructure team, seen by 404 Media.
To use Muse, a user gives the AI agent access to various important services and accounts they own. On Meta’s side, each individual Muse instance runs on a kernel-based virtual machine that connects to Meta’s own critical infrastructure but is supposed to be isolated from it. A "KVM escape" is when a Muse instance, using a vulnerability in the security system, can break out of the virtual machine and interact with the system on which it is running or with other users’ virtual machines.
According to a Meta source, as well as internal security documentation and internal messages reviewed by 404 Media, at least one of the vulnerabilities could have allowed an outside attacker—that is, an ordinary Muse user—to gain access to data in confidential internal Meta databases. At least one of the vulnerabilities was related to an exploit discovered in the code of the Linux kernel-based virtual machine in July.
Some of the vulnerabilities were discovered in the underlying Linux virtualization software that Meta uses for Muse. The security issue was deemed serious enough to be brought to Mark Zuckerberg’s attention, and several different groups of security specialists worked nights and weekends ahead of the launch to fix the problems. Such heightened security measures before the launch of a major product are not unusual, but are notable given that outside researchers discovered several other security issues after Muse launched, as well as in the broader context of large-scale hacker attacks by AI agents from OpenAI and other companies, the publication notes.
A source at Meta said that, in their view, security specialists were required to release fixes for these bugs as quickly as possible without delaying Muse’s launch, which resulted in what they described as "a hastily released, insufficiently thought-out solution to ensure the launch. Many leading engineers believe that a major data breach at Hatch is inevitable." Within the company and in Meta’s codebase, Muse is called "Hatch."
A Muse virtual machine escape is potentially a very serious security issue and is classified as such in Meta’s bug bounty program. The company says it is prepared to pay $300,000 to any security researcher who discovers a bug that allows an escape from the virtual machine—the maximum payout listed on the bug bounty program’s website, the publication reports.

Spain extends border controls on travelers from Italy until Oct. 22

Beyza Binnur Donmez
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Spain has extended temporary border controls on travelers arriving from Italy by air and sea for another 15 days, until Oct. 22, according to an order published in the Official Gazette on Tuesday.
The Interior Ministry order said the extension will take effect at midnight on Oct. 8 and remain in force until midnight on Oct. 22.
The ministry said the reasons for "urgency and serious threat to public order and internal security" that prompted the controls continue to exist, making their extension necessary under the Schengen Borders Code.
Spain initially introduced the controls for 30 days from Aug. 8 to Sept. 7, before extending them twice -- first until Sept. 22 and then until Oct. 7. Tuesday's order marks the third extension.
The controls apply to Spain's internal air and maritime borders for passengers arriving from Italy. The original order limits them to passenger flights and maritime connections whose last airport or port of departure is in Italian territory.
The latest order says the measure will be continuously assessed and may be lifted before Oct. 22 if the threats disappear or can be addressed through less restrictive measures.
Any further extension would require a new decision based on an updated assessment of its necessity and proportionality, according to the gazette.
The controls were initially introduced after Italy imposed border checks on travelers from Spain following the mass arrival of around 72,000 migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 and 31.
More than 3,000 migrants, including several hundred minors, are still living on the streets of the Spanish enclave in North Africa, according to the latest estimates.
Spain responded by introducing controls on travelers arriving from Italy on Aug. 8, formally citing migration pressure on the Central Mediterranean route and unauthorized onward movements from Italy to other Schengen countries, including Spain.

‘Hitting the right nail’: Refugee rescue group defiant as Greece targets it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:25:14 UTC
18:25:14 KST

‘Hitting the right nail’: Refugee rescue group defiant as Greece targets it
Aegean Boat Report founder Tommy Olsen insists he is defending the rule of law, as Greece opens trial against him.
Athens, Greece – To Greek authorities, he is the nefarious Norwegian mastermind of an international criminal organisation “operationally structured to commit repeated crimes”, which he secretly controls from his hometown of Tromso, north of the Arctic Circle.
To thousands of distressed asylum seekers on the Aegean, he is a hero who may have saved their lives by publicly alerting search and rescue authorities who might rather not have known of their whereabouts.
A Greek court will open trial proceedings on Tuesday against Tommy Olsen to decide who is right.
Olsen is the creator of Aegean Boat Report, an independent monitor of distressed vessels in the Aegean. When contacted, he alerts the Greek or Turkish asylum service and coastguard, depending on whose jurisdiction the refugees find themselves in.
The public prosecutor on the island of Kos, in the east Aegean, has accused Olsen of conspiring to smuggle refugees into Greece and to conceal them from authorities.
Olsen won’t be at the Kos court because Norwegian authorities thought the evidence against him too flimsy to grant extradition.
“They looked at what the Greek authorities described I had done, and they said, ‘There’s nothing illegal here. It’s actually protected activities,’” Olsen told Al Jazeera.
“When I inform Greek authorities of asylum seekers in their territory, on land, and give them their location, their names, and everything, that, supposedly, should be a good thing… But this the Greek authorities see as facilitating,” Olsen said.
‘Judicial harassment’
The case is important far beyond the fate of Olsen, 54, who could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.
Human rights organisations see it as Greece’s latest attempt to silence independent monitors of human rights abuses, for which the country has previously been convicted at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR).
“The ECHR asked us to confirm certain testimonies that featured in cases before it, and since then, those decisions have condemned Greece for pushbacks,” said Maria Gavouneli, head of the Greek National Committee for Human Rights, the country’s top independent human rights authority.
Pushbacks are illegal turnarounds of potential asylum seekers. Under the Geneva Convention of 1951, signatories, including Greece, are obliged to provide an asylum hearing to anyone who requests one.
Aegean Boat Report is one of a group of organisations which provide verified evidence for ECHR cases.
“We’ve asked NGOs in the field … to provide information about pushbacks. This is not hearsay. This is a signed witness statement that can stand up in court. We record these and we can help the witness go to the prosecutor,” Gavouneli told Al Jazeera.
Evidence provided by Aegean Boat Report has also helped shed light on at least two dozen instances of improper practices employed by the Hellenic Coastguard.
Last month, the Council of Europe, Europe’s principal human rights body, said retraining of Greek law enforcement officers and other measures “do not yet appear adequate to comprehensively address the ‘systematic practice of “pushbacks”‘ identified by the [ECHR], while serious concerns continue to be raised in this regard by a large number of different sources”.
Ultimately, Greece can face the suspension of European Union funding if it fails to provide “genuine and effective access to international protection procedures”.
That, said Olsen’s lawyer, is why Aegean Boat Report’s work is undesirable from the perspective of Greek authorities.
“The whole logic here is judicial harassment. They harass the organisations and humanitarians to get them away from the border so there can’t be any record of irregular or illegal coastguard practices,” Zacharias Kesses, the managing partner of Athens Legal Firm, told Al Jazeera.
Smuggling or humanitarian assistance?
Greek governments have long tried to prove that certain aid groups help to smuggle people into Greece.
In the last eight years, prosecutors have shut down two organisations by arresting their members and charging them with trafficking and espionage.
But in January, all 30 members of Emergency Response Centre International, a Greek search and rescue group, were acquitted of charges similar to Olsen’s. Sarah Mardini, a Syrian Olympic swimmer, was one of their members.
Smuggling charges against Mare Liberum, a German search and rescue group, were also shelved for lack of evidence in 2024.
Still, both organisations were shut down.
“They force you to stop doing what you’re doing and spend money to clear your name. It took Sarah Mardini eight years to be acquitted, with all the help she was receiving,” said Kesses, who has represented all three groups.
Despite the fact that there has never been a smuggling conviction, the suspicion persists in the minds of Greek officials.
Last February, the government passed a law that cuts off public funding to an entire aid group if any one of its members is merely accused of a felony.
Defending the bill in parliament, Minister of Migration Thanos Plevris said aid groups that receive funding cannot justify the use of volunteers.
“If you receive money, you cannot have volunteers. Your people get paid legally from government money and European Union money. They’re not volunteers,” Plevris said. “If they’re not getting paid, they’re using their access to rejected asylum seekers in camps. I don’t want them to say, ‘Don’t worry, meet me here at night and I’ll help you get to Athens.’”
‘My family is collateral damage’
Even though Greece doesn’t control any of Olsen’s funding, it has cut it off. Fearing reputational damage, his sponsors have ended support for Aegean Boat Report.
“The bills for one year for the lawyers is perhaps 10 annual budgets for Aegean Boat Report,” he said. Two weeks ago, he sold his car.
“I’m sitting with the invoices for 19,000 euros ($21,000), without any ability to pay them.”
Then there is personal cost. Olsen, a former kindergarten teacher who left his job to become a full-time aid coordinator on the island of Lesvos during the 2015-16 refugee crisis, hasn’t been on holiday with his family for years because he devoted all his time to refugees. Four of his five children have grown up and left home during that time.
“I feel really guilty for putting them through this, because I have done this with open eyes,” he said. “I would take responsibility for this, but I also have to take responsibility … for the collateral damage around me. And my family has been this collateral damage.”
Kesses believed this case would be dismissed or end in acquittal, like the others before it. Unlike them, it may not succeed in silencing Olsen. Aegean Boat Report still bears witness to the distress of asylum seekers on the high seas.
“The attacks from the Greek authorities give me a sense that I’m doing the right thing,” he said. “I’m hitting a nail that hurts… The more they act up, the more they try to get me, the more I understand that I’m hitting the right nail.”
In 1923, when the refugees coming from Turkiye were Greeks fleeing the burning of Smyrna, another Norwegian, Fridtjof Nansen, engineered the world’s first population exchange between the two countries, probably saving hundreds of thousands of lives.
Although he does not draw a parallel with Nansen, Olsen also sees his life as devoted to a greater cause.
“I’m defending the rule of law,” he said, “and defending human rights. It doesn’t concern a small group of people coming into Greek islands. It concerns all of us. It’s something that we pass on to our children.”

Turkish defense emerges as Europe’s defense partner as global footprint grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:24:12 UTC
18:24:12 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Türkiye’s booming defense sector continues to play an increasingly important role in its economy while elevating the country’s standing as a complementary manufacturing powerhouse, helping Europe address critical military supply shortages, according to a recent report by BBVA Research.
Heightening geopolitical tensions and surging military spending around the world prompted defense demand to “enter a more structural phase,” as governments are prompted to “rebuild capabilities and invest in new technologies,” according to the report titled Türkiye – Defense Industry Potential on Sept. 25.
The report noted that the European defense industry is facing bottlenecks in production scale, speed and stockpile replenishment despite strong infrastructure, with the most pronounced capacity gaps coming to the fore in integrated air and missile defense, unmanned aerial vehicles and counter-unmanned aircraft systems, loitering munitions, long-range firepower and ammunition stocks.
The report’s authors designated unmanned aerial vehicles and ammunition manufacturing as the two areas of highest potential alignment with Europe’s needs, while noting that the mere complementarity of the Turkish defense industry does not by itself guarantee access to the European market, as the requirements for local content and design rights under the SAFE framework restrict non-EU suppliers.
Türkiye’s deeper integration into European defense could be achieved via joint production, local assembly, joint ventures, supply chain integration and technology sharing, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the weight of the defense and defense-related sectors in the Turkish economy increased, with defense exports projected to reach $10 billion by 2025 and the domestic production rate in missiles and rockets exceeding 90%.
Türkiye’s defense-related sectors employ 176,700 workers, and the Turkish defense industry boasts opportunities not only in Europe but also in export markets in Africa, Asia and the Gulf.
The report identified cost-effective and rapidly deployable systems as a priority in Africa, while joint production and technology transfer opportunities lie in Asia, and joint venture and technology partnership potential exists in the Gulf countries.
Türkiye’s competitive edge in the coming period will depend on boosting the production of existing platforms and making progress in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, cybersecurity, space and other advanced technologies, according to BBVA Research.
While Europe needs scale, speed and operationally deployable capabilities, Türkiye provides flexible production capacity and experience in modern warfare, which position the country as a complementary partner for the bloc.
The report added that Türkiye-EU defense cooperation could be one of the most important industrial and geopolitical opportunities in the coming decade.

Palestine weekly: Olive harvest opens under assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:22:09 UTC
18:22:09 KST

Palestine weekly: Olive harvest opens under assault
Israeli settlers and forces beat Palestinians, set property on fire and steal crops across the occupied West Bank.
While olive picking season is yet to officially begin, Palestinians began early efforts to reach their groves this week – and so did the Israeli settlers.
Across the occupied West Bank, harvesters were beaten, trees were burned, crops and tools were stolen, and Israeli soldiers closed land to its owners.
Meanwhile, in Gaza, Israeli strikes continued to ignore a year-old “ceasefire” as the territory’s humanitarian and medical systems slid further towards collapse, with winter around the corner.
A harvest under siege
The week’s violence suggests a bloody olive harvest to come in the occupied West Bank. On October 3 in Jabal Qamas, between the towns of Osarin and Beita south of Nablus, settlers from the illegal Mevaser Shalom outpost attacked a family of harvesters. The pogrom left one man, Hussam Adily, in critical condition, and injured his brother and mother, according to Israeli activist Jonathan Pollack and Arabic-language media reports.
The settlers then entered Osarin, ransacking a home and smashing cars. Although the Israeli military opened an investigation, it said the attackers had fled before soldiers arrived, The Times of Israel reported.
Similar pogroms on Palestinian olive pickers occurred across the north and centre of the West Bank, including in the villages of Rantis, Sebastia, Beit Imrin, Deir Sharaf, Aqraba, az-Zawiya, Ramin and Arrabuna. Farmers were pepper-sprayed, run over, or struck with sticks and fists, with several requiring hospital treatment, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa and local field reports.
In Beita’s Jabal al-Arma, Israeli settlers opened fire on pickers and forces lobbed tear gas directly at them.
With attacks also came theft: Settlers made off with harvested olives, ladders and tarps in Sinjil – where thefts have been a near-daily occurrence for more than a week, according to Sinjil resident Ayed Jafry – as well as in Rafat, Kafr Ra’i, Faqqua and elsewhere, according to Wafa.
Trees were targeted, too. Near Abu Dis, settlers torched roughly 55 olive trees, along with a family’s freshly picked harvest, according to Wafa. Elsewhere, settlers drove their flocks through Palestinian-owned groves, ruining crops in villages including Burqa, al-Mughayyir and Beit Duqqu, according to local field reports.
Where settlers were not blocking the harvest, soldiers often were. Israeli forces turned farmers away from their own land in Deir Istiya, Farkha, Haris, az-Zawiya and Silwan, confiscating identification cards and, in some cases, tools, according to Wafa.
In Beita, the Israeli army halted a harvest after settlers showed up. The incident was the fourth such shutdown that weekend, Haaretz reported, in an area beyond the army’s jurisdiction. Soldiers forced out international volunteers accompanying Palestinians at gunpoint and assaulted journalists covering the attack.
Beyond the olive groves, two Palestinians were shot dead in separate incidents involving settlers and Israeli forces within a day of each other. Mashhour Yassin, 51, was shot dead on October 1 as settlers stormed homes in Yasouf, east of Salfit. The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said that soldiers seized the keys to the ambulance carrying him and threw them away, delaying his evacuation.
Bahaa al-Natsheh, 19, was shot dead the next day near an illegal outpost outside Kobar, according to Wafa and other media reports. Israeli authorities are still withholding his body from his family.
Meanwhile, at a checkpoint east of Tulkarem, a 45-year-old Palestinian man died of cardiac arrest while being detained, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.
Israeli courts push back
After weeks of increasingly bellicose campaign rhetoric, Israeli institutions this week moved to check some of the governing coalition’s ambitions ahead of the October 27 election.
The Supreme Court unanimously reinstated the Arab-majority political lists – the United Arab List and the Joint List – to the ballot after an election commission voted to ban them. The court also voted 7-2 to reinstate far-left lawmaker Ofer Cassif. However, Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of Balad, a component party of the Joint List, withdrew his candidacy under pressure from the justices.
Separately, the election commission chairman fined National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for using his access to a Hamas prisoner for a campaign video, Israeli media reported.
Israel President Isaac Herzog said this week that Israeli politicians “have not done everything” they could to rein in settler pogroms – remarks that followed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s dismissal of a mass settler attack on Jalud as the work of a “small number” of rioters, The Times of Israel reported.
Haaretz reported that the administration of US President Donald Trump is weighing sanctions against Israeli military units and a blacklist of officers over the pogroms, though any such measures are reportedly being held back until after both Israel’s election in October and the US midterms in November.
The United Kingdom, meanwhile, confirmed that it suspended or rejected more than 80 arms export licences to Israel since 2024, while continuing to supply components that feed into the international F-35 programme, a global defence partnership led by Lockheed Martin. Israel said the UK must close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem by October 8.
Gaza: Killings persist under ‘ceasefire’
In Gaza, daily Israeli strikes continued to defy the year-old “ceasefire”. The Gaza Health Ministry’s toll since the so-called truce rose from 1,422 killed on September 29 to 1,460 by October 5. This brings the cumulative death toll since October 2023 to 74,243, after 181 previously unverified deaths were added this week.
Five people, including a mother and daughter from Gaza’s small Christian community, were killed when an Israeli strike hit the al-Asala building in Gaza City on October 3, an attack Israeli media said was targeting a Hamas official.
Six people were killed when a drone hit a passenger van in Tal al-Hawa on September 30, among them Ammar al-Sharafi, the brother of Al Jazeera correspondent Momin Alshrafi. A man was killed when his tent in al-Mawasi was struck on October 1.
On October 4, a six-year-old girl died after reportedly being shot by Israeli troops in Deir el-Balah, according to Wafa. A Palestinian journalist, Muhammad al-Najjar, was killed on September 30, becoming the 263rd reporter killed since Israel’s genocidal war began, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
Israel also continued to demolish damaged buildings in eastern Gaza City. Satellite analysis put the number of damaged structures across Gaza at roughly 200,000.
Meanwhile, hundreds of Palestinians attended a mass funeral for 105 people recovered from the rubble of several buildings flattened in October 2023.

Russia plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over the next three years on its system for filtering and blocking internet resources, according to an appendix to the draft budget reviewed by the business magazine Forbes Russia.
The funding will go to the Chief Radio Frequency Center (GRChTs), an entity under Roskomnadzor, Russia’s federal media regulator, which operates the automated system that secures the Russian segment of the internet (ASBI).
Two years ago, the plan called for allocating 32 billion rubles for ASBI’s operation over the same period. It remains unclear why the costs have doubled. The press services of the Finance Ministry and the Digital Development Ministry did not respond to Forbes Russia’s request for comment. A source close to the Digital Development Ministry suggested that explanations “haven’t been written into the bill yet — they should be expected by the end of the year.”
Experts say the costs are rising along with equipment prices. Traffic volumes keep growing, requiring more powerful processors, RAM, and storage drives for filtering, and the prices of those components keep climbing. At the same time, sanctions are making it harder for Russia to obtain imported components.
ASBI’s reach is also expanding geographically. Under the “sovereign Runet” law, telecom operators must install Russia’s internet traffic filtering system (TSPU) on their networks. This equipment lets Roskomnadzor filter, slow, and block internet traffic. It has yet to be installed on operator networks in the occupied territories of Ukraine, according to Alexey Amelkin, president of the Association of Telecom Operators Makatel:
And new equipment for the TSPU will cost more because of sanctions and the global rise in prices for certain components like RAM. If the TSPU keep getting “smarter,” that is, start using AI, that will also require funding

Al-Aqsa Mosque is the world's third-holiest site for Muslims. Jews call the area Temple Mount, claiming it was the site of two Jewish temples in ancient times.
The ministry also documented an increase in Talmudic rituals inside the Al-Aqsa compound, including public prayers and what it described as “epic prostration.”

Latvia, Estonia and Finland test new recycling models under €2.64 million SustainaCycle project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:20:27 UTC
18:20:27 KST

Five mobile waste collection points in Latvia, three self-service circular economy hubs in Estonia and a digitally guided textile sorting station in Finland form part of a joint initiative to make recycling more accessible and keep more materials in use.
Partners in Latvia, Estonia and Finland are testing different approaches to collecting and sorting textile, plastic and electronic waste through SustainaCycle, a €2.64 million cross-border project supported by the Interreg Central Baltic Programme.
The pilots are tailored to local needs: reaching smaller communities in Latvia’s Vidzeme region, combining waste collection and reusable-item donations in Estonia’s Viimsi municipality, and helping consumers sort end-of-life textiles correctly in the Finnish city of Imatra.
Once the three countries’ pilots are operating, the project aims to collect at least 40 tonnes of waste annually in total and direct at least 60% of the collected material to reuse or recycling.
Latvia: mobile collection points to serve smaller communities
In Vidzeme, waste management company ZAAO plans to introduce five mobile collection points that will travel between communities on a set schedule. The approach is intended to improve access to textile, plastic and electrical and electronic waste collection in places where establishing a permanent collection site would not be economically justified.
Before operations begin, the partners will define the collection schedule, accepted materials and practical information for residents. The pilot will assess how a mobile service works in settlements of different sizes.
“Residents’ willingness to sort waste often depends on how convenient and straightforward the service is to use. Mobile collection points will bring the service closer to people, including in less populated areas,” said Māris Ozols, a project expert at the Valmiera Development Agency.
He added that the project would assess both collection volumes and opportunities to return materials to circulation through reuse or recycling.
Estonia: three self-service hubs planned in Viimsi
Viimsi municipality plans to establish three self-service circular economy points, called Ringpunkt, by spring 2027. They will be located in Püünsi, Randvere and Viimsi, making the service accessible across different parts of the municipality.
Each point will consist of two modular units measuring 3 × 6 metres. One side will contain containers for separately collected textile, plastic and electronic waste, while the other will provide shelves for reusable items such as wearable clothing, working electronic devices, plastic toys and household goods.
A partner organisation will collect the reusable items and direct them towards resale, people in need or other reuse opportunities. Visitors will not be able to take items directly from the points.
The service will be free for registered Viimsi residents and people with a waste collection contract in the municipality. Electronic identification will control access, while video surveillance will support site security.
“By bringing separate waste collection and reuse together in a place that residents can reach easily, we can improve recycling options and extend the life of items that are still usable,” said Aet Põld, a specialist in Viimsi Municipality’s Environmental Department.
The modular design will also allow the points to be adapted or relocated as needs change.
Finland: touch-screen guidance for textile sorting
In Imatra, LAB University of Applied Sciences is piloting a digitally guided sorting station at the entrance hall of the Prisma hypermarket. The trial runs from 15 September 2026 to 30 April 2027, and the service is free to use.
Residents bringing clean end-of-life textiles answer questions about their condition on a touch screen. Based on those answers, the system automatically opens either the compartment for material recycling or the residual waste compartment. A light indicator helps users identify the correct opening.
Users can also rate the service and leave feedback after depositing their textiles.
LAB is working with SaimaanVirta ry, a non-profit organisation promoting employment and the circular economy, which empties the collection containers. Fill-level sensors notify staff when a container is approaching capacity, allowing collections to be scheduled according to actual need.
The pilot will assess whether digital guidance improves sorting accuracy, alongside the user experience and the efficiency of the collection process.
Shared research into material recovery
Beyond the collection points, SustainaCycle partners will map material flows and work with businesses, waste management companies and other organisations to identify reuse and recycling opportunities for the materials collected.
The project also includes circular economy seminars, public information activities and educational materials for younger audiences, alongside an assessment of residents’ responses and changes in behaviour.
SustainaCycle runs from 1 May 2025 to 30 April 2028, with a total budget of €2,644,194.50. Its partners are Valmiera Municipality and ZAAO in Latvia; Viimsi Municipality and the Estonian Circular Economy Industries Association in Estonia; LAB University of Applied Sciences in Finland; and Sustainability InnoCenter in Sweden.

I Want to Live Project: In 2026, Ukraine captures average of 107 more Russian soldiers per month than Russia captures Ukrainians
Ukraine

2026-10-06
12:20:15 EEST
18:20:15 KST

In 2026, Ukraine has been capturing an average of 107 more Russian soldiers per month than Russia has captured Ukrainians, according to data from the I Want to Live project.
"In the first eight months of the year, 858 more Russian servicemen were taken prisoner by Ukraine than Ukrainian servicemen were taken by Russia—an average of 107 people per month," the project stated on its Telegram channel on Tuesday.
It is noted that back in 2023, Russian propaganda spread false claims about there being "more than 20,000 Ukrainian soldiers" in Russian captivity. "In January 2024, Putin claimed that the ratio of Russian to Ukrainian prisoners was supposedly 'one to ten.' In reality, since mid-2023, Ukraine has begun capturing more Russian soldiers than Russia has captured Ukrainians. In 2024 and 2025, Ukraine's pool of prisoners available for exchange grew faster than Russia's. In 2026, this gap widened further," the message reads.
Ukraine achieves this primarily thanks to its soldiers, who risk their lives to capture the enemy alive. Systematic information outreach also plays a role: Russian troops are shown that surrendering offers a chance to save their lives and that, once in captivity, they will live in normal conditions. Since September 2022, the I Want to Live project has been explaining to Russian military personnel how to surrender safely and what awaits them afterward. During this time, the project's website has received over 50 million visits, primarily from within the Russian Federation. Interviews with prisoners and information regarding their detention conditions are widely circulated among Russian audiences. Ukraine also incentivizes its troops to capture enemy soldiers alive, offering financial rewards for doing so.
"An entire system is at work here: Ukrainian troops gain additional motivation to take Russians prisoner, Russian POWs are held in decent conditions, and information about this reaches Russian military personnel. Every Russian held in Ukrainian captivity represents an opportunity to bring home another Ukrainian defender or civilian hostage," the I Want to Live project stated.

Wikipedia detects ‘rogue’ OpenAI agent activity, calls on developers to prevent risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:17:00 UTC
18:17:00 KST

Yasin Gungor
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Wikipedia detected unauthorized activity by automated artificial intelligence agents operated by US developer OpenAI across its digital platforms, warning that aggressive bot traffic threatens community infrastructure and volunteer resources.
“We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these ‘rogue’ OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms,” the Wikimedia Foundation said Monday.
The foundation said the incidents involved unauthorized bot operations, including test edits in “sandbox” staging areas, configuration changes to a citation utility to probe remote data fetching and unsuccessful attempts to access its public Etherpad note-taking tool.
It said there was no evidence that its systems or data had been compromised or that the agents had managed to coordinate among themselves on the platform.
Mounting infrastructure strain
Automated systems linked to the developer also conducted aggressive web scraping.
“Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made millions of automated requests to our public APIs to access the knowledge on Wikimedia projects, crawled millions of pages … and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS),” the foundation said.
It noted that the heavy traffic may have contributed to a partial outage of the query service in May. The disruption added to longer-term strain, following reports in 2025 that bandwidth usage had jumped 50% due to an influx of bot traffic since 2024, with automated systems generating 65% of the most resource-intensive activity on its servers.
Wikimedia emphasized that while its policies allow bots to make edits once reviewed and approved by the community, no such approvals had been sought for these actions.
Demands for corporate accountability
Warning that volunteer editors bear the burden of cleaning up disruptions caused by autonomous tools, the foundation said technology companies must take responsibility for securing their systems.
“AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause,” it said.
The foundation added that AI companies “must also acknowledge their responsibility to monitor and prevent these risks,” and should, “at a minimum,” operate in a way that website owners “can easily identify, and choose how they interact with our services.”

Kenya reports 1st Ebola case as patient dies after arriving from DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
