18:15:40 KST

Andrew Wasike
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died following his arrival in Nairobi, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said Tuesday.
“The Ministry of Health wishes to inform members of the public that it has confirmed the first imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease,” Duale said.
The man had lived in Congo for the past seven years and became ill about a month before returning to Kenya, according to the Health Ministry. He received treatment at several health facilities in Congo before traveling by road to neighboring Uganda.
He later flew from Uganda to Kenya aboard a Jambojet flight carrying 23 passengers and landed at Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport at about 1.10 pm local time (1010GMT) on Saturday, Oct. 3.
The patient underwent routine public health screening at the airport before proceeding through immigration, according to the ministry.
Relatives and friends then drove him directly from the airport to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately placed in isolation.
The patient subsequently tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola and died.
 
28 contacts identified
Health authorities have identified 28 people who had contact with the deceased, including family members and health workers, as officials move to prevent further transmission.
The patient’s journey through Congo and Uganda, his commercial flight to Nairobi and subsequent contact with relatives and medical personnel are now part of the government’s contact-tracing operation.
Kenya had already strengthened disease surveillance at airports and land border crossings in response to the Ebola outbreak in Congo, including measures to improve screening, laboratory capacity and preparedness at health facilities.
Ebola is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or through contaminated materials.
Health authorities are monitoring the identified contacts for symptoms as surveillance continues following confirmation of the country’s first imported case.

The tanks that fuel Moscow’s airliners are reported burning after Ukraine’s latest drone raid on the capital region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:14:13 UTC
18:14:13 KST

Drones attacked Moscow and Moscow Oblast overnight on 6 October, and a fire broke out at the Volodarskaya pipeline station, the region's largest oil depot, monitoring Telegram channels reported. The station supplies jet fuel to Moscow's main airports. Local authorities did not mention the fire, while claiming to have downed hundreds of drones.
Ukraine's long-range drones have spent years working through Russia's oil industry, and Kyiv says its strikes have now disabled more than half of Russia's refining capacity. The storage and pipeline hubs that move the remaining fuel are what keep the army, the capital, and the export flows supplied.
Fire at the Moscow region's largest fuel depot
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ wrote that the Volodarskaya station was burning after the attack, and Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported the strike on the depot. Exilenova+ then posted the site's coordinates near the village of Konstantinovo. Supernova+ said a storage tank was on fire, and Exilenova+, citing locals, later wrote that two tanks were burning.
Russian news Telegram channel Astra geolocated a Supernova+ video to Konstantinovo in Ramensky district. The station had not been reported attacked before, Astra said.
The station lies 40 km from central Moscow, Militarnyi reported. Drone alerts in the area began at 23:43 on 5 October. From 03:24, reports came in of Ukrainian Peklo drones flying through Oryol Oblast toward Moscow Oblast, the outlet said. Ukraine's military has not commented on the strike.
Early in the night, Exilenova+ claimed a strike on the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya. It later said the footage circulating from there was most likely archival.
Jet fuel for Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo
The station has 27 tanks with a combined capacity of about 250,000 m³, according to Militarnyi. It connects to the ring pipeline for petroleum products around Moscow, which carries aviation fuel to Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo airports. Russia's state pipeline operator Transneft has said the station can move up to 3 million tonnes of jet fuel, 2.8 million tonnes of diesel, and 1.6 million tonnes of gasoline a year.
Astra gave a lower figure: about 3 million tonnes of petroleum products a year in total, arriving from the Moscow and Ryazan refineries. Supernova+ described Volodarskaya as a branch of Transneft–Upper Volga, as did Militarnyi, while Astra named Transnefteprodukt.
Russia has warned its cities about every strike for years. During the heaviest raid yet, on election day, it left the sirens silent
Russia claims hundreds of drones downed
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that 650 drones flew toward the Moscow region from the evening of 5 October to the morning of 6 October. Most were downed far from the city, and 105 near Moscow, he claimed, without mentioning any damage. Adding up his later posts, Astra counted at least 718 drones aimed at Moscow. Moscow Oblast Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed that 185 drones were downed over 16 municipalities. He later called it one of the largest drone attacks and put the toll at two killed and nine injured, with 47 detached houses damaged in seven municipalities.
Fifth drone-related NORSI shutdown in under five months leaves all major Lukoil refineries offline
Not the first Transneft site or Moscow fuel target
Ukraine has targeted Russia's pipeline network before. On 2 October, drones set Transneft's Samara station on fire. During Russia's Duma elections on 20 September, a strike reached Moscow's fuel supply. The Moscow refinery fully stopped processing oil after that attack. Days later, Kyiv offered to halt refinery strikes if Russia stopped hitting Ukraine's power grid. Russia has not taken the deal.

Jordan and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) on Tuesday condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting two airports in the country’s south.
Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke by phone with his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan and expressed Jordan’s “absolute solidarity” with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks, the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Safadi said Amman supports all measures taken by Riyadh to protect its security, stability, sovereignty and citizens.
He reiterated Jordan’s condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including attempts to target the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina and continued attacks on civilian and economic facilities.
Safadi also reaffirmed Jordan’s support for Yemen’s internationally recognized government and efforts to resolve the conflict “in a way that restores security and stability and preserves the country’s unity and sovereignty,” the ministry said.
The two ministers also discussed regional developments and efforts to end the ongoing escalation in the region.
Separately, GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi strongly condemned the attacks targeting King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia.
Albudaiwi said attacks on Houthi airports and civilian facilities represented a “dangerous escalation” and posed a “direct threat” to civilians and air navigation.
He expressed the GCC states’ full support for Saudi Arabia and measures taken by the kingdom to protect its security, stability and territory.
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said Tuesday that the two airports were attacked Monday evening, leaving three people with minor injuries and causing material damage.
Yemen’s Houthis confirmed that they had carried out missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia, including against what they described as sensitive sites in Jazan and Najran.

8 public officers in Singapore referred to police after property review
The review identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to unannounced MRT stations
Eight public service officers have been referred to Singapore police after a review of 191 officers’ property transactions, Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing has told parliament.
The review followed a working paper by the US-based National Bureau of Economic Research, which identified 2007 to 2011 as the period of concern.
The Public Service Division (PSD) extended the scope to 2014 as a matter of prudence, Chan said on Tuesday, because many new MRT station locations continued to be announced after 2011.
Based on administrative records, PSD identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to locations later announced as MRT stations, he said.

Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday rejected a motion to remove a member of the country’s election commission over her past legal consultations for the Nemunas Dawn political party and an alleged attempt to conceal the relationship.
In a secret ballot, 45 lawmakers voted to remove Laura Matjošaitytė from the Central Electoral Commission (VRK), while 61 voted against and seven ballots were invalidated. At least 71 votes were required for her dismissal.
Those who initiated the removal procedure said Matjošaitytė had lost their confidence because she deliberately concealed her links to Nemunas Dawn.
Lithuanian news portal Delfi reported that Matjošaitytė, who was working as a lawyer at the time, advised Nemunas Dawn before the 2024 parliamentary election and sought from the outset to keep the cooperation secret.
Further reading
According to Delfi, in September 2024, just over a month before the election, Matjošaitytė emailed Nemunas Dawn vice chairman Robert Puchovič a draft response she had prepared for the election commission regarding the party’s sources of financing.
In the same email, she asked Puchovič to transfer her response into a new Word document he had created “so that my metadata would be gone”.
Neither the party nor Matjošaitytė, who is now a member of the election commission, disclosed their previous cooperation.
In a written response to the parliament, Matjošaitytė said she had provided the consultations while still working as a lawyer and had not violated any laws. Some lawmakers, however, said her explanation did not meet the required standards of transparency.
Matjošaitytė declined to attend Tuesday’s parliamentary session.
She previously served as chairwoman of the Central Electoral Commission from 2017 to 2021. She returned to the commission in May 2025 after her candidacy was put forward by then-Justice Minister Rimantas Mockus, who had been delegated to the government by Nemunas Dawn.
The newly formed commission last year considered alleged violations of Nemunas Dawn’s political campaign financing rules. Matjošaitytė voted in favour of findings that the party had committed violations in some cases and abstained in others.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Coast Guard seized about 815 kg of illegal drugs worth an estimated NT$1.62 billion (US$50.9 million) in New Taipei’s Ruifang District, marking its largest marijuana seizure in nearly a decade.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) and Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) attended a press conference Monday to announce the case. They praised investigators for disrupting a major drug-trafficking operation before the drugs could reach the wider public, per a Coast Guard press release.
The seizure included 766.09 kg of marijuana, 43.25 kg of amphetamine, and 5.34 kg of ketamine and mixed drugs, according to the Coast Guard.
Investigators said the syndicate used a truck as a mobile warehouse, leaving its keys in an accessible location so buyers could retrieve drugs without meeting the driver. The truck was moved frequently between Keelung and the North Coast, while the alleged ringleader, a 45-year-old man surnamed Li (李), reportedly drove around the area to monitor transactions.
The investigation led authorities to a parking lot in Ruifang on June 3, where three suspects were arrested while transferring drugs from the truck to two cars. The suspects included a man surnamed Wang (王), his girlfriend surnamed Hsieh (謝), and a man surnamed Fang (方).
Authorities later traced the operation to Li and identified the truck’s owner as a man surnamed Ho (何). The Coast Guard said the investigation involved cooperation among its units, prosecutors, and police.
Investigators suspect the syndicate smuggled the drugs by sea before transferring them ashore by boat and loading them onto rented vehicles. The group had allegedly been operating around the Keelung and Ruifang coastal areas.
The Keelung District Prosecutors Office indicted four suspects in August in connection with the case. At Monday’s press conference, officials commended the task force for preventing the drugs from entering schools and communities.

Environmental groups seek halt to LNG terminal breakwater construction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:12:47 UTC
18:12:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Environmental groups announced Tuesday that they would seek to halt breakwater construction at the Guantang LNG terminal in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District.
The Supreme Administrative Court ruled on Aug. 20 that the Ministry of the Interior had failed to conduct a review verifying whether state-owned CPC Corp.’s Guantang LNG terminal development project satisfied all the requirements under the Coastal Zone Management Act for the issuance of a project permit, per UDN.
The court said the ministry’s coastal zone management review committee had examined only whether CPC’s land use was minimal, failing to investigate the company’s measures to compensate for or restore environmental damage.
The ministry expressed surprise at the ruling and said it would hold internal deliberations to decide its next step. CPC, meanwhile, stressed that the case did not affect construction of the breakwater or the project’s core area, adding that LNG flows would not be impeded.
Algal reef referendum leader Pan Chung-cheng (潘忠政) said at the time that because the terminal was already operational and the reef had already been damaged, the ruling would do little to make up for the loss. Taoyuan Coastal Zone Ecological Conservation Association Honorary Chair Yeh Ssu-kuei (葉斯桂) called on the government to designate the area as a conservation zone to protect the algal reefs from further damage, per EDN.
Wild at Heart Legal Defense Association lawyer Tsai Ya-ying (蔡雅瀅), who is handling the lawsuit seeking a halt to construction, said Tuesday that because the terminal had already reached its maximum output in June, suspending construction would have little impact on the public interest, per CNA.
Fellow association lawyer Chen Hsien-cheng (陳憲政) said the 2026 ruling was the first case in which an Interior Ministry coastal development permit had been revoked.
Chen stressed that allowing construction to continue after the court’s ruling would render remedies through the administrative courts moot. He called on CPC to respect the ruling by halting construction and undergoing another review.
A major point of contention between CPC and environmental groups has been whether construction damaged the algal reefs in the area, per Our Island. Environmental groups have claimed that CPC’s construction harmed the local ecology by causing excessive sedimentation, killing algae, and directly damaging the reefs.
CPC, however, commissioned teams from National Chung Hsing University and National Taiwan Ocean University that rejected the claim that the sediment came from CPC’s construction or that construction directly damaged the reefs. A report published by National Taiwan Ocean University suggested that the reefs were thriving in the site’s G1 and G2 areas.
At a meeting between CPC and environmental groups in February, the two sides continued to debate the reefs’ ability to recover and the general causes of their poor health, per Our Island. Data provided by National Taiwan Ocean University indicated that the algal reef was in decline, though the two sides could not agree on the cause.
National Taiwan Ocean University argued that the change was caused by climate and sedimentation, while environmental groups believed the decline resulted from CPC’s construction. Regarding the extremely fine sediment, environmental groups rejected a possible connection with the construction, while CPC argued that it might have come from other sources.
The breakwater construction is currently under legal scrutiny over possible project cost inflation. CPC has also said that another lawsuit filed by environmental groups could cause construction of the breakwater to cease, per UDN.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taoyuan prosecutors on Tuesday indicted a retired Air Force captain and his son for allegedly collecting personal information about Taiwanese intelligence personnel for China.
CNA reported that the retired officer, surnamed Fei (費), left the Air Force in 1976 and served as head of a township in China’s Hebei Province in 2021. Prosecutors said he later began gathering information on Taiwanese intelligence personnel for a Chinese contact.
In January 2024, Fei allegedly received instructions from a man who identified himself as Gao Jin-li (高金力). In exchange for an unspecified payment, Fei gathered details about an intelligence officer’s job, vehicle, home address, and workplace.
He also hired a private investigator to track the officer’s movements and workplace. Prosecutors said the investigator did not know the surveillance was allegedly linked to an intelligence-gathering operation.
Fei then asked his son, a real estate agent, to use his company’s system to obtain property records belonging to the officer. He later passed the information to Gao, according to prosecutors.
In July 2024, Gao allegedly asked Fei to gather similar information on a second intelligence officer. This included details about the officer’s movements, workplace, and vehicle, per FTV News.
Investigators later gathered evidence in the case and searched Fei’s home before detaining him on Aug. 17. A court subsequently approved his detention and barred outside contact, while prosecutors questioned his son and other witnesses.
Fei was charged under the National Intelligence Work Act, National Security Act, and Personal Data Protection Act. His son was charged under the Personal Data Protection Act. Prosecutors filed the case for trial under the Citizen Judges Act, per UDN.

China Focus: Lights, camera, tourists! Short dramas rewrite the script for "China's Hollywood"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:11:39 CST
18:11:39 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Wang, a retired teacher from Shanghai, has just wrapped up her turn as an emperor's mother, filming a scene inside a replica palace at Hengdian World Studios, known as "China's Hollywood."
"I never imagined I'd get to act. I finally got my drama fix," Wang said, smiling as she adjusted her headdress. "I rehearsed the lines three times to memorize them, and the director even said I had a real air of authority."
Wang is part of a holiday phenomenon. During the National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, tourists paying to star in short dramas have become a common sight in Hengdian, east China's Zhejiang Province. As destinations across China explore new ways to attract visitors, Hengdian has flipped the script, transforming tourists from spectators into actors.
Hengdian drew over 9 million visitors in the first half of this year, up 21.2 percent year on year. At peak times, more than 100 people would sign up for the short-drama experience a day. During the holiday, it rolled out upgraded short-drama shoots and film-themed activities designed for different types of visitors.
An admission ticket is all it takes to join more than 10 short-drama crews. Directors hand out scripts and coach performers on the spot, and visitors can complete a scene in 10 to 45 minutes.
For a more professional experience, full production resources are available, including costumes, makeup, lighting and set design, along with chances to perform alongside veteran actors.
"Our team of over 30 people has been working around the clock," said Ma Qianyi, a staff member at Hengdian Micro Film. "We film more than a dozen shoots a day, and we often bring in external costume, makeup and camera crews."
From costume selection and script reading to filming and post-production, a finished video is ready within two days, Ma added.
"The best way to turn film from something you watch into something you feel is to let tourists become the actors," said director Zhang Jinquan.
Imperial palace dramas, "dragon king" fantasy and time-travel stories are the most popular genres, Zhang noted, with a dedicated screenwriter updating scripts to keep pace with audience tastes. Visitors can choose from more than 40 scripts. A solo short drama starts at 218 yuan (about 32.37 U.S. dollars) and a full package with professional makeup and styling costs 388 yuan.
With overnight stays, role-playing continues well into the night, extending immersion beyond the sound stage.
At the Rossyli Hotel in Hengdian, check-in marks the start of production and check-out the wrap. Guests can even trade the "film fees" they earn for perks like a personalized wake-up call.
Hengdian is not alone in this shift. Across China, scenic spots are turning landscapes into interactive stages. Zhusha Ancient Town in southwestern Guizhou Province offers period-drama shoots against nostalgic backdrops, while "the Longest Day in Chang'an," a themed immersive cultural block in northwestern Shaanxi Province, lets visitors travel back in time to live a day in the Tang Dynasty (618-907).
For industry observers, the phenomenon signals a broader shift: tourists are paying for emotional resonance and immersive experience. As a report by market analytics firm Meadin Research Institute put it, tourists are no longer satisfied with a tour that is just about moving from one place to another. They want a trip that connects them with a culture, lets them express who they are, or offers something new.
That is what Hengdian is betting on. Using its filmmaking know-how, it has broken production into replicable modules, so tourists can star in their own short dramas. Staff are on hand to help solo visitors get into character, ensuring no one feels awkward on set.
"The model is lightweight, fast to produce, and boosted by free social media promotion, as visitors share their clips online," said Chen Shaofeng, a professor at Peking University's Institute for Cultural Innovation.
To keep visitors coming back, experts suggest giving them more say, such as choosing scenes, adjusting camera angles, even tweaking dialogue, so each shoot feels unique.
Hengdian is already planning ahead. Serialized short-drama experiences are in development to draw visitors back, and the studio aims to combine AI short dramas with cultural tourism, alongside public training programs and merchandise.
"We came specifically to act," said Huang Yanfang, who drove from Suzhou, in neighboring Jiangsu Province, after seeing videos of the experience online. "I want to know what it feels like to be the lead, even for just a few minutes." ■

Flu vaccine deliveries to Estonia delayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

Flu vaccine deliveries to Estonia delayed
This year, flu vaccines will reach Estonia later than usual, with the final delivery arriving only in January.
The reason is that, on the recommendation of the World Health Organization (WHO), all influenza virus strains included in the vaccine were updated at once for the upcoming flu season — a change that delayed production and delivery schedules across Europe, the Estonian Agency of Medicines say.
The first shipment of flu vaccines will arrive in Estonia at the end of October, the second in mid‑November, and the third in January.
The deliveries will make up 40 percent, 20 percent, and 40 percent of Estonia's total flu vaccine volume, respectively. These figures are manufacturer forecasts and may change.
A total of 233,000 doses of flu vaccine will arrive in Estonia this season — slightly more than last season, when 210,000 doses were delivered.
Vaccination of risk‑group patients will begin first, at the end of this month and the beginning of November. 93,000 doses are expected for this group.
The Health Insurance Fund will announce when the vaccines have arrived and are available in vaccination clinics; after that, appointments can be booked via the health portal.
The Fluenz nasal spray used for children and adolescents, and the Efluelda vaccine used for older adults, are available in Estonia.
Based on current data, the Health Board assesses flu circulation in Estonia as low, and European surveillance data also do not indicate an imminent flu wave. It is difficult to predict when this season's flu activity will intensify.

Over 15% of kids in Finland take neurological medication
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:09:12 EEST
18:09:12 KST

An increasing number of Finnish children are taking ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) and antidepressant medicines, according to a study by Kela and the University of Tampere.
The share of children using medicines that affect the nervous system rose from 10.7 percent to 15.5 percent between 2017 and 2025. The category includes ADHD and antidepressant medicines as well as painkillers.
This news follows Kela's figures on Monday showing that more than five percent of all six- to eight-year-old boys in Finland were taking ADHD medication last year.
The number of children using methylphenidate, a common ADHD medicine, more than tripled, while use of lisdexamfetamine increased more than eightfold.
Finland once prescribed ADHD medicines to children relatively sparingly compared with other Nordic countries. It is now among the countries with the highest rates of childhood ADHD medicine use in the comparison.
Researchers say the increase reflects changes in the recognition of ADHD, the threshold for treatment and access to services.
Antibiotic use, meanwhile, has fallen: the proportion of children using antibiotics dropped from 29.8 percent to 23.7 percent between 2017 and 2025.
Heini Kari, Kela's research manager, says the overall situation with antibiotics in Finland is good and moving in the right direction, but the use of broad spectrum antibiotics should still be reduced. Avoiding such medicines helps curb the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
The study covers every child under 18 in Finland between 2017 and 2025 and all prescription medicines nationwide. It is the first study of its kind in Finland.
Yle News' All Points North podcast has explored the surge in ADHD diagnoses among children in Finland.

Kenya has registered its first confirmed case of Ebola. It is a Kenyan citizen who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and arrived in Nairobi on Saturday, Health Minister Aden Duale said. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
The patient has since died, and 28 contacts have so far been identified, including family members and healthcare workers, Duale said at a press conference.
The Congo is battling its largest Ebola outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, but may have begun months earlier and is still resisting containment efforts, with more than 8,000 cases and over 4,000 deaths recorded in the Central African country.
The outbreak previously spread to Uganda, where 20 cases and two deaths were recorded, but the World Health Organization declared Uganda free of the disease in August.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. It can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

Fatal miscalculation: Three years on, Netanyahu faces October 7 reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:06:34 UTC
18:06:34 KST

The warning was clear and hard to miss.
“Convey a message to them that I am preparing the mother of all surprises. A terrifying operation. Something extraordinary.”
The words, attributed to Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, were passed to a Palestinian intermediary in the weeks before October 7, 2023. According to a recent Haaretz investigation, they would eventually travel through Abu Dhabi and reach the highest levels of the Israeli government.
Sinwar, assassinated by Israel later, reportedly used the word zilzal, Arabic for earthquake, to describe what awaited them.
Weeks later, Hamas fighters broke through the Gaza boundary and launched an attack that stunned Israel and reverberated across the Middle East.
For much of what followed, October 7 was portrayed as a catastrophic failure of Israeli intelligence and security.
But three years later, a series of revelations in the Israeli media is raising a more troubling question: How much did Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu know before the attack?
Reports by Haaretz and Yediot Ahronot suggest Netanyahu and his aides had received warning about a looming Hamas blitz.
The revelations emerged in September, just weeks before Israel's October 27 general election, bringing renewed scrutiny of Netanyahu's handling of the warnings as he seeks another term in office.
Those accounts point not to a single warning, but to messages that travelled through Palestinian intermediaries, the Emirati leadership and, according to other reports, Egyptian intelligence.
After different rounds of consultations with his advisers, the UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, decided to inform Netanyahu about Sinwar’s designs in mid-September.
While Netanyahu quickly organised a security meeting, which discussed warnings, at the end Israeli leadership did not make any serious decisions and preparations on Hamas’ potential attack planning.
“Everyone on the face of this planet informed them (Israelis),” Dania Koleilat Khatib, an expert on Arab-American relations with extensive experience with Gulf leaderships, tells TRT World.
According to Khatib and Israeli sources, the Palestinian intermediary “Coal Eyes” was Sufyan Abu Zaida, a former Minister of Prisoners and Former Prisoners' Affairs in the Palestinian Authority, with whom the analyst met in the past in Prague.
Khatib also says that Zaida’s close friend in Abu Dhabi is Mohammed Dahlan, a former top Fatah official and an adviser to Mohammed Bin Zayed.
“It is not a conspiracy anymore. There is more and more indication that Netanyahu knew about it. Egyptians told him, Coal Eyes (Zaida) told him, and the Emirati leadership told him,” says Khatib.
Both Haaretz and the Wall Street Journal reported that in early October 2023 Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also personally warned Netanyahu about an impending Hamas attack to no avail.
Netanyahu denied reports of warnings from Egypt and the UAE, claiming that neither the UAE leadership nor Egyptian intelligence informed him. He called the UAE warning report “an absolute lie” and said that “no Israeli intelligence source conveyed an Egyptian warning to the Prime Minister”.
But according to the WSJ, citing Arab officials, Kamel personally called Netanyahu to convey the imminent threat in a third warning after his previous two warnings went to deaf ears.
Despite Netanyahu’s denials, neither the UAE nor Egypt issued any statement about their warnings to the Israeli leadership.
Netanyahu’s calculations
Before the October 7 attack, Israel and Hamas had been engaged in serious negotiations, with Sinwar seeking to lift Israel’s blockade of Gaza.
“Sinwar wanted to lift the blockade on Gaza and promised if they don't, there will be an earthquake,” Khatib says.
Sinwar, who learned Hebrew during his imprisonment in Israeli jails, was also aware of Israel’s deepening political divisions.
Netanyahu was facing corruption charges and widespread protests over his proposed judicial overhaul, which critics described as a “judicial coup”.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, was struggling with mounting political problems, as former mainstream allies distanced themselves from him over questions about his credibility.
Khatib believes Netanyahu saw a possible Hamas attack as an opportunity to strengthen his political standing.
“Netanyahu was facing corruption charges. People were protesting against his attempt to change the judicial system to escape accountability. The society was highly divided. And October 7 was a good excuse to shove everything under the rug,” Khatib tells TRT World.
But according to the analyst, Netanyahu’s calculations went beyond his immediate political survival.
While the first purpose was “to evade the ongoing scrutiny, the second was to launch a war on several fronts and achieve the dream of Greater Israel,” Khatib says.
“Actually, the two are linked together. If he achieved a victory and enlarged Israel, then the Israeli people would forgive him. This is why it is difficult for him to stop.”
Haaretz also reported that Hamas was initially prepared to release civilian hostages without conditions after October 7, but Netanyahu rejected the proposal, with the report attributing to him the position that “he only wants war and the elimination of Hamas”.
For Khatib, the account lends weight to her interpretation of Netanyahu’s broader political objectives.
Other analysts also argue that Netanyahu sought to use the October 7 attack to advance a wider agenda, including territorial expansion and the forced displacement of Palestinians.
Despite decades of Israeli policies and efforts since the state's establishment in 1948, Israel has been unable to secure an overwhelming Jewish majority across historic Palestine, says Sami al Arian, a Palestinian professor and director of the Center for Islam and Global Affairs at Istanbul Sabahattin Zaim University..
“They found an opportunity in these attacks to embark on ethnic cleansing and genocide to force Palestinians out of their land to resolve Israel’s population problem,” Arian tells TRT World.
War of narratives
The latest revelations about Israel-Hamas negotiations and warnings reportedly received by Netanyahu before October 7 also highlight how different sides of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict have sought to shape international perceptions of the attack and the subsequent war in Gaza.
Netanyahu and his allies have portrayed October 7 as a brutal Hamas attack on Israeli civilians, while recent Israeli media investigations suggest the country's leadership had received warnings about the scale of the operation being planned.
The revelations raise further questions about Netanyahu's handling of those warnings, particularly as Israeli officials used the attack to justify a devastating military offensive in Gaza.
The Biden administration, which was also reportedly informed by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed about a possible Hamas attack, backed Israel's military response as an act of “self-defence”, even as the offensive killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.
Palestinian analysts, however, say the debate over who knew what before October 7 risks overlooking Hamas’s own agency and the warnings it had issued.
Ramzy Baroud, a Palestinian political analyst and writer, argues that focusing primarily on warnings passed through regional governments can obscure that part of the story.
“The media’s hyper-focus on third-party state warnings ignores a glaring reality—Palestinians themselves issued explicit, direct warnings,” Baroud tells TRT World.
Sinwar’s impending "earthquake" and "roaring flood" warnings were “open and documented,” he adds.
For Baroud, overlooking these warnings reflects a broader tendency to deny Palestinians agency in shaping events.
“This reflects a historical refusal to recognise Palestinian agency. Israel has long viewed Palestinian resistance through a paternalistic lens, convincing itself that native uprisings are merely top-down manipulations to be managed through periodic military campaigns like ‘mowing the lawn’.”
His argument introduces another dimension to the debate over Netanyahu's foreknowledge. Even if the Israeli leadership received warnings and failed to act, Sinwar had his own strategic objectives and political calculations.
“Framing October 7 strictly as an ‘Israeli intelligence failure’ or a breakdown in Arab diplomatic communications perpetuates this same racist myth—that nothing occurs in Palestine unless Israel permits it or fails to prevent it. It reduces a structural conflict to a mere lapse in Israeli border management,” says Baroud.
“The attack did not occur in a vacuum; it is part of an ongoing war for survival against a multi-year siege and ongoing military violence. Palestinian actions do not hinge on Israeli permission, and any analysis that ignores native agency misses the core reality of the ongoing confrontation.”
Sami al Arian, meanwhile, offers another explanation for Netanyahu's response to the warnings, pointing to what he describes as the Israeli prime minister's growing arrogance and confidence in his own political calculations.
According to Arian, Netanyahu had become increasingly convinced of his own “ideological bubble”, leaving little room for warnings that contradicted his assumptions.
“He thinks of himself as the smartest person on the earth. Whatever warnings he was getting did not align with his perceived strategy and his own understanding of things on the ground.”
Warnings about a possible Hamas attack sounded like “noises” to Netanyahu, Arian argues, because he believed Israel could pursue normalisation with Saudi Arabia and other regional powers while expanding its influence across the Middle East, despite continuing Palestinian resistance.
“And October 7 came and disrupted all these things.”

Israeli army investigations have found that three people its forces shot in two separate incidents in southern Syria Monday were unarmed, according to Israeli media reports.
In the first incident, the Israeli army announced early Monday that it had killed a "suspect" who allegedly attempted to infiltrate a military post inside the security zone occupied by Israel in southern Syria.
According to the Israeli army’s account, the young man continued attempting to enter the site despite being fired upon. A soldier then fired at him again, killing him. The army later confirmed that the young man was unarmed.
The second incident occurred Monday afternoon, when Israeli forces spotted two people on a motorcycle heading toward a military post in the area the army refers to as the "buffer zone."
The army said its forces carried out what it described as an "arrest procedure for a suspect," which involved firing live ammunition at the motorcycle and resulted in one of the two people being wounded.
The army arrested both men and transferred them to Israel for interrogation, while the wounded man was taken to an Israeli hospital for treatment. The army confirmed later that neither man was armed. No Israeli soldiers were injured in either incident.
The Israeli account of the incidents has been framed in terms of what it claims are "security concerns," with calls "to strengthen security in the Golan and allocate the necessary resources, including maintaining a presence in the buffer zone and the Mount Hermon area."
The two incidents came amid continued Israeli military aggression against Syria. On Oct. 2, Israeli patrols entered the villages of Hamidiyah and Bir Ajam in the Quneitra countryside, searched a number of homes and abducted a young man.
The Sijil Center documented 280 Israeli violations in Syria in September, including ground incursions, with Quneitra governorate recording the highest number.
Since the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel has continued to violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement through repeated incursions by its forces beyond the buffer zone adjacent to the Golan Heights, extending as far as Mount Hermon, which separates Lebanon from Syria. Israel has also announced its intention to establish a so-called "demilitarized zone" in southern Syria.
Syria, meanwhile, is demanding Israel’s withdrawal from its territory, stressing that all measures taken by Tel Aviv are null and void and have no legal effect under international law.

- Category

‘Pre-War State’ Is Poland’s New Security Concept, With Warsaw Drafting Legislation to Counter Hybrid Threats
Poland is preparing a bill on a so-called "pre-war state" to establish operational rules for circumstances where the nation is not formally at war, but the security threat level is substantially higher than in peacetime, as reported by Polskie Radio.
Should this status be enacted, the military would be granted greater operational latitude to address emerging risks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"To define this state of 'war – not war' that we are dealing with and which does not exist anywhere in legal acts. Previously, Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz always used the concept of 'hybrid war,' and now speaks of a 'pre-war state.' And whatever we call it, we definitely need to define what we mean by this state and what limitations will be lifted in connection with this so that the military can act effectively," stated General Roman Polko.
The drafted law aims to bolster defense capabilities, streamline cooperation between the armed forces and internal security services, and adjust current regulations to contemporary risks—principally hybrid operations, cyber security challenges, and foreign disinformation.
Under the proposed provisions, Poland could accelerate troop re-deployments, align its national Defense Response Plan with the NATO Response System, and better prepare infrastructure for military needs, according to Polskie Radio.
Additionally, authorities intend to increase the number of units assigned to constant defense duty while restructuring training programs, exercises, and professional courses to fit the new operational reality. The draft rules may reach the desk of the Polish president within a few weeks.
Previously, Polish authorities expanded military formations across the Lublin Voivodeship , near the border with Ukraine, which included the initial deployment of a Patriot air defense battery to the region.
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed plans focused on reinforcing the 18th Mechanized Division, the Air Force Academy in Dęblin, and the airbase in Świdnik. Key operational measures introduced a new 18th Motorized Brigade headquartered in the Opole Lubelskie and Poniatowa districts, alongside specialized air defense units and a battalion based in Biłgoraj.
Additionally, a dedicated drone systems brigade was positioned in Łuków, while infrastructure investments expanded facilities near Kraśnik for Abrams tanks, transferred land in Sobieszyn for the aviation academy, and prepared the Świdnik airfield for its upcoming role as a helicopter base ahead of scheduled AH-64E Apache deliveries in 2028.

The official document does not disclose the identity of the potential buyer, and the transactions will proceed without requiring additional approvals from Russian authorities, according to Korrespondent on October 5.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The approved framework allows UniCredit to split off a new corporate entity from its Russian bank, with shares transferring directly to UniCredit as the sole owner.
UniCredit plans to keep this spun-off unit under its control to manage international euro and US dollar payments for non-sanctioned corporate clients. The remaining portion of the Russian banking operation is set to be transferred to the buyer.

UniCredit expects to finalize the transaction during the first half of 2027 and estimates the negative financial impact of the sale to be between €3 billion ($3.3 billion) and €3.3 billion ($3.6 billion).
Under Russian regulation established in 2022, UniCredit Bank Russia was designated among 45 financial institutions prohibited from completing share transactions without special authorization.
The bank remains one of the last major European financial institutions operating in Russia since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Capital flight is being further accelerated by compounding volatility across domestic financial markets. Falling oil revenues and domestic energy deficits have previously triggered a 10.8% fall in the ruble’s exchange rate, prompting Russian entities and households to systematically acquire foreign currency assets to hedge against inflation.

Russia’s Oil Revenues Drop 17% Despite a 13-Year High for Urals Crude
Russian energy tax revenues from oil and natural gas production dropped by 17% to $64.43 billion during the first nine months of the year, despite global crude prices climbing to their highest levels in over a decade, according to data released by the Russian Ministry of Finance, as reported by Reuters on October 5.
These tax receipts account for roughly 20% of total federal budget revenue in Russia, where the budget deficit is currently projected to reach 3% of gross domestic product in 2026—nearly double the originally planned target.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
By late September, prices for Russia's flagship Urals crude topped $92 per barrel, according to market data from London Stock Exchange Group. This figure is double the level seen prior to the war with Iran and well above the Western-imposed price cap of $44.10 per barrel.
Before the outbreak of that conflict on February 28, Baltic-bound Urals crude loaded at the port of Primorsk on Free on Board terms traded around $45 per barrel.
Driven by spot market surges amid Middle East supply disruptions, Urals reached a peak of $113.89 per barrel on April 8, marking its highest price point since 2013, Reuters reported.
Reduced shipments out of the Black Sea hub of Novorossiysk also helped sustain Urals prices last month.
Market traders report that the port continues to operate below full capacity due to heightened security risks following a series of Ukrainian attacks, alongside an ongoing shortage of available tankers. Beyond maritime logistical disruptions, Moscow has also escalated economic retaliation against Western enterprise.
On September 17, Russia placed the local operations of Swiss food giant Nestlé and French supermarket chain Auchan under temporary administration, connecting the decision directly to European military aid for Ukraine.
According to registry data reported by Bloomberg, Vladimir Putin issued a decree transferring stakes in both firms to AO L.E.V. Menedzhment, a Moscow-registered entity created in 2024 with a charter capital of approximately $177 and just a single employee.
In response to the takeover, Nestlé announced it was weighing its options and pledged to take all necessary measures to safeguard its legal rights and support its workforce, while Auchan Retail Russia requested official clarification on the order.

Work has commenced on a renovation of the Royal College of Art's iconic modernist campus in west London, overseen by British studios Witherford Watson Mann and Clementine Blakemore Architects.
Now underway, the revamp will reinvigorate the Grade II-listed Darwin Building – the heart of the London university's Kensington campus, built in 1962.
Few details have been released, but the project will focus on striking a "careful balance of conservation and transformation", according to the Royal College of Art (RCA).
Stirling Prize-winner Witherford Watson Mann and Stirling Prize-nominee Clementine Blakemore Architects will honour the original design by Cadbury Brown while improving its environmental performance, accessibility and teaching facilities.
Renovation will enable "wider range of conversations to be hosted"
"Physically, the works are largely about stripping back to the structure," said Witherford Watson Mann.
"Later finishes on the concrete frame and brick walls will be removed, and the steel skeleton of the 1980s linear gallery exposed, revealing the values embodied in the building, economy of means, rawness and openness."
"Of course, the physical is always the outward face of the social. These works are also about reinforcing the collective culture, establishing space for collaborative working, celebrating the work produced at the college, enabling a wider range of conversations to be hosted," the studio continued.
The Royal College of Art (RCA) was founded in 1837 and is one of the world's leading art and design universities, with alumni including artist Tracey Emin and designer James Dyson. It also has campuses in Battersea and White City.
Witherford Watson Mann and Clementine Blakemore Architects have developed their plans with input from the RCA community, Westminster City Council and Historic England.
Studios adopting "a lean and low-carbon approach"
Works commenced in 2025 and are scheduled to be completed in 2032. The renovation will be carried out in stages, allowing teaching to continue throughout.
Reflecting on the project, Clementine Blakemore Architects said the studios are drawing on the original architect Brown's ambition for the building to serve as a backdrop to art.
"Drawing both on my own experience studying there over a decade ago, and insights from the current community, our proposals focus on flexible spaces which enable the testing and sharing of creative ideas," said Clementine Blakemore Architects.
"Noting Cadbury Brown's original concept for the building to 'act as the background to art and not to assert itself as an art thing', we have taken a lean and low-carbon approach to the fit-out, exposing original finishes and complementing these with natural and raw materials that can successfully wear over time," added the studio.
Other RCA news recently featured on Dezeen include the One Tool One Stool exhibition, in which design students created stools with single tools.
Recent graduate Oliver Stiff shared a collectable "fashion furniture" collection made using deadstock from Vivienne Westwood.
The visual is by Witherford Watson Mann.

Spain's Official Gazette publishes decree calling for early general election on Nov. 29
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:00:20 UTC
18:00:20 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Spain's Official Gazette on Tuesday published a royal decree dissolving parliament and formally calling for an early general election to be held on Nov. 29.
The decree, issued by King Felipe VI at the proposal of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez following a Cabinet meeting on Monday, dissolved the Congress of Deputies and Senate elected in July 2023 and called for elections for both chambers.
The vote will take place nearly eight months earlier than previously scheduled, beginning a 54-day electoral process under Spain's electoral law.
The official campaign will run for 15 days, beginning at midnight on Nov. 13 and ending at midnight on Nov. 27, two days before the election, according to the gazette.
Voters will elect 350 members of the Congress of Deputies across 52 constituencies, comprising Spain's 50 provinces and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla.
Madrid will elect the largest delegation with 38 deputies, followed by Barcelona with 32 and Valencia with 16.
A total of 209 senators will also be directly elected. Each provincial constituency will elect four senators, while Gran Canaria, Mallorca and Tenerife will elect three each. Ibiza, Formentera, Menorca, Fuerteventura, La Gomera, El Hierro, Lanzarote, and La Palma will elect one each, while Ceuta and Melilla will elect two each.
The newly elected chambers are scheduled to hold their constitutive sessions on Dec. 23.

Loss of green space could be issue that decides Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:00:08 UTC
18:00:08 KST

When HS2 construction began around London’s Euston station in 2017 and people living nearby watched parks and playgrounds give way to diggers and rubble, they were promised that the lost green space would be replaced. “They have to give it all back,” said Dorothea Hackman. “But they are destroying it – so there’s nothing to give back.”
As the dust from the political party conference season begins to settle, disappearing green spaces and housing developments have become central issues in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. On Thursday, Labour and the Green party will contest the seismic seat vacated by the former prime minster Keir Starmer.
Planning documents show that the high-speed railway project and surrounding developments will permanently swallow 14,404 sq metres of green space and playgrounds from the constituency, with more closed off as work takes place.
The work forms part of the Euston section of HS2. The government estimates that the full high-speed railway between London and Birmingham will open between May 2040 and December 2043.
The biggest park under threat is St James’s Gardens, an 18th-century burial ground designated as a site of importance for nature conservation. While HS2 Ltd originally committed to replacing the gardens by building a new park on a concrete deck above the railway tracks north of the station, government cost-cutting redesigns have dropped that replacement park from the scheme entirely.
Responsibility for the surrounding site now sits between public planners and private developers. While HS2 was approved directly by parliament, the private developer Lendlease is drawing up plans for commercial space and homes across the site. Camden council is assessing Lendlease’s plan, with a decision expected next year.
Alice Brown, a cofounder of Climate Emergency Camden, said it was vital that green space was retained for people to take a break from the bustle of the station. “Otherwise it’s just going to be the site of the massive office building.”
For people living around Euston, the development of their neighbourhood encompasses more than just the parks. The issue is about housing, frustrations with the council and a broader question of who London is for.
“They say this is all in order to be able to provide some affordable housing, but it’s a very small amount of affordable housing for the loss that’s being suffered,” Brown said of the construction sites. “By affordable, they mean 80% of current cost – they don’t mean social housing.”
Lendlease has said the scheme will provide up to 1,500 homes, but neither the final number or the amount that will be affordable has been determined.
Hackman is a governor at Netley primary school, a stone’s throw from Euston. She is worried about what the new buildings will mean for the area’s falling pupil numbers. “Camden’s policy of failing to provide family-size housing means that all our families with children are driven out of the borough,” she said.
“It’s very difficult to see how the social-cleansing consequences of what they’re doing can be of any benefit to our community.”
For some, the byelection will be a chance to shock Labour’s grip on the council and the constituency. The party has dominated control of the council since the 1960s and represented Holborn and St Pancras since the constituency was created in 1983.
Frustrations with the council could spill into a vote against Labour. “So much that Camden Labour are doing is seen to be not in the best interests of people who live here,” said Brown. “It’s either performative or it’s money generating. Every development, every bit that they sell off is to the detriment of the local residents.”
At Labour’s conference, the party’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, said she thought it was “unlikely” that Zack Polanski, the Green party leader standing in the constituency, would win the seat. Brown is not so sure. “I think he’d really roll his sleeves up and get involved in what’s happening here,” she said. “And that would include trying to get the council to perform better.”
A Camden council spokesperson said: “The Euston area plan sets out the council’s vision for future development at Euston until 2051.” They said the plan is being submitted to the Planning Inspectorate for public examination after a consultation this year.
A spokesperson for Lendlease said: “Working with our partners, we’re developing proposals that could deliver up to 1,500 new homes, including affordable ones, as well as public spaces, improved connections and places for businesses and communities to thrive.”

I witnessed the Pinochet regime’s fall. It offers hope – and a warning – for the US | Ariel Dorfman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:00:07 UTC
18:00:07 KST

A malignant, monomaniacal president, deeply unpopular, faces an election that could restrict his power and end his domination of his country.
It is true that, to influence the outcome, he counts on a supine supreme court and his ability to legislate through executive decrees, as well as an onslaught of fake news accusing his opponents of being unpatriotic communists, true that he has colossal financial support from an entrenched oligarchy that has thrived thanks to his rightwing neoliberal policies, true that he has gone out of his way to limit the freedom of those who vote and true that he has absolute command of the armed forces.
None of this seems sufficient to deter an electorate that is tired of his reign and determined, despite widespread intimidation, to make itself heard. Even as the polls indicate a rout, the delusional strongman, emboldened by sycophants and fawning courtiers too afraid to inform him of the facts, refuses to accept that the upcoming referendum will go against his divinely inspired will.
Donald Trump in 2026?
In fact, I was also describing the dictator of Chile, the Gen Augusto Pinochet, in October of 1988, when he insisted that he would win a plebiscite which would decide whether he remained as head of state for another eight years (and probably well beyond) or whether a transition to democracy should begin. On 5 October of that year, the military autocrat, who had misgoverned Chile since ousting the democratically elected president Salvador Allende in a 1973 coup, resoundingly lost, with 55.9% of his compatriots telling him to retire.
He did not go easily.
I was there, that night, as the results poured in verifying that the regime was being repudiated, I was there when the vote count was suspended and an informational blockade was established at 10pm; I was there, in front of the presidential palace in Santiago, when, at around 1am of 6 October, the air force general Fernando Matthei, a member of the junta, recognized publicly that the “no” vote had clearly won, thwarting an auto-coup that Pinochet was contemplating at that very moment.
These events have a significant bearing on the United States as the 3 November midterms approach and with them, a dire uncertainty: can the majority of Americans, by winning both chambers of Congress, constrain the ravings and corruption of a wannabe autocrat who is as unhinged today, and contemptuous of the law, as Pinochet was back then?
That Chilean October should serve, at this existential moment, as a way to encourage and inspire those who won’t let their voices be silenced. No matter how much supremacy, no matter how many resources deployed by a deranged chief executive, no matter the fear and funds and lies at a powerful ruler’s disposal, he can be beaten if courageous people are resolute and smart enough.
And Chile, in effect, subsequently transitioned to democracy, electing a center-left president in 1990 and, since then, an uninterrupted series of presidents of different ideological strains and policies.
But that October 1988 milestone in Chile also entails warnings for those who believe it is possible to limit Donald Trump’s authoritarian tendencies.
Just as Pinochet intended to disavow the results that were ousting him, the current occupant of the White House could try to do something similar – maneuvers that would far outdistance his violent and illicit attempts to annul his loss in the 2020 elections.
Only heightened civilian and institutional vigilance, the daily epic of everyday people resisting – and patriotic armed forces unwilling to obey illegal dictatorial orders – can guarantee, as in Chile, that such a potential assault on democracy will fail.
That will not be enough. Ridding Chile of its strongman saved it for democracy, but did not undo the vast damage he did to the country. He kept mutilating it grievously during the year and a half left in his mandate and then for another eight years as a threatening commander-in-chief of the army.
But more insidious was how he permanently changed Chilean society. Not just the dismantlement of the welfare state created by decades of struggle, replaced by a savage capitalism that did not care how much pain it inflicted or who was left defenceless. Worse perhaps was how the spreading of fear and mistrust affected the psyche of the country, sickened its soul.
Indeed, despite major advances in reversing Pinochet’s long legacy, his shadow still looms over Chile.
Despite the dictator’s appalling record of disappearances, torture, exile and persecutions, José Antonio Kast, an admirer of Pinochet who would like to pardon the agents of the dictatorship imprisoned for gross violation of human rights, is now Chile’s president.
His victory in December of 2025 can be partly explained by an economically distressed populace falling for his rabidly anti-immigrant platform and vows to deal with a narco crime wave that has shaken the country. Nonetheless, the fact that a whopping 56% of voters were willing to turn a blind eye to Kast’s denial of past atrocities is a cause for long-term concern and, in my case, of mourning.
It is disturbing to witness the erosion, perhaps the funeral, of the dream that once was Chile, a land of solidarity and thirst for justice and dignity that enthralled me when I arrived there as a lad of 12 in the winter of 1954. So strong was that enthrallment that I never doubted, during the eternal night of the dictatorship, that it would resurrect and, in effect, on 5 October 1988, thanks to so many Chileans who suffered and fought for it, that fearless, hopeful country proved it was alive, an indispensable stepping stone towards an indefinite future.
Something went wrong.
Maybe that is why I force myself to wonder, in this other promising and foreboding October, if we are aware in this other country, the United States, that is also mine, how much long-lasting harm have the Trump years wrought?
I ask this because back in October 1988, the democratic militants of Chile, carried away by the glorious illusion that the dawn of a new era was upon us, did not then fully deal with the vexing question of how such a monster could have arisen in our midst.
It was a public and private task, both intellectual and emotional, that enough Chilean men and women, given the triumphant return of a Pinochet fanatic to lead their country, have still not sufficiently grappled with collectively: what mistakes did we originally make to facilitate the existence of such a despicable and enduring regime and, most crucially, what could we have done better, what must we do better in the coming years?
My adopted US homeland should be wary of making the same mistakes.
Though the electorate at this moment is sensibly focused on achieving a victory that will grant some reprieve and solace, such an urgency should not postpone the need for an overdue reckoning with the dark imperfections in our history and national character that generated the conditions for the republic to be in such dire peril.
Those conditions, enabled by those who enabled Trump and ignored his danger, his nastiness, his serial mendacity, will probably endure well beyond the day (if it comes) when he leaves the White House. We will be left to contend with the worst traits of the US’s past that he exalted and exacerbated: the imperial arrogance, the nativism and misogyny, the ecological degradation, the assault on minority and workers’ rights, the myth of exceptionalism.
That is the somber lesson that Chile yesterday and today whispers to us from afar. Only a profound and painful self-examination of our identity, what the splendid guardians of this experiment that started 250 years ago are demanding, can help to stave off the ominous possibility that years from now the country will be facing a repetition of the current terrifying crisis.
By then, it may be too late.
- Ariel Dorfman is the Chilean American author of Death and the Maiden and the novels The Suicide Museum and Allegro, and the forthcoming collection of stories, What She Saw

A classified CIA assessment has warned that deepening political, economic and social divisions could put Israel at risk of civil war or state collapse, according to a report published Monday.
The assessment, titled "Fracture From Within," was prepared in August by the CIA’s Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging prevailing intelligence assumptions, Drop Site News reported, citing two U.S. sources familiar with its contents.
The CIA did not respond to the outlet’s request for comment.
The assessment points to a volatile mix of pressures ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election, including economic strain, rising military spending, anger over exemptions from compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews and escalating violence by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank.
It also identifies Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s fight to remain in power as a source of further political and constitutional tension.
Years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran have deepened existing divisions, according to the report, as soldiers return from prolonged combat, many suffering serious psychological trauma.
The military draft dispute has emerged as one of Israel’s sharpest internal fault lines, with resentment growing over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men following repeated reserve mobilizations.
The assessment also points to Israel’s growing international isolation, including eroding support in the U.S., as another factor that could deepen internal instability.

Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:59:16 UTC
17:59:16 KST

A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, in what prosecutors suspect could be the most egregious national security breach since the cold war.
August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005.
He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers.
Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation.
He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added.
Over several years, Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Hanning and his legal team denied the allegations following his arrest. There was no immediate response from Manfred D. or his legal representatives.
Several properties connected to both men were searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin.
Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday.
The allegations prompted shock in German political and intelligence circles, where memories resurfaced of historic espionage scandals. Hanning is thought to be the most prominent person to be accused of treason in Germany since Günter Guillaume, one of Willy Brandt’s personal aides, was exposed as a long-term Stasi agent in 1974. The “Guillaume affair” brought an abrupt end to Nobel peace prize-winning Brandt’s career, as he swiftly resigned as chancellor of West Germany.
Marc Henrichmann, chair of the Bundestag’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to AFP: “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.” If proven to be true, Hanning’s alleged behaviour would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”, he added.
Konstantin von Notz of the Greens, a prominent member of the same committee, urged the federal government to establish as soon as possible the “potential intelligence-related damage” that might have been done by Hanning’s alleged betrayal of Germany’s official secrets.
“This is a truly outrageous and deeply disturbing story,” he told Der Spiegel.
Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city.
Investigators were led to Hanning over allegations, which he denies, that he helped Christina Block, the heiress of a steak restaurant dynasty, to organise the violent cross-border seizure in Denmark of her children from her estranged husband who has custody of two of their children. Block denies the charges.
After he left the BND, Hanning worked as a global consultant in the fields of security and business, based on his credentials as former intelligence chief. He is considered to have been well connected with government and business sectors in Russia and China, and also had contacts with top-ranking intelligence authorities in Israel.
Hanning was an officer stationed at the embassy-equivalent organisation for West Germany in communist East Berlin. After his role as president of the BND ended in 2005, he became the highest-ranking official in Germany’s security sector as the head of all security agencies under the federal interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble.

South Korea considers steps to force North Korea apology for DMZ mine blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

South Korea considers steps to force North Korea apology for DMZ mine blast
Seoul has urged the North to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line.
South Korea is weighing measures to force an apology from North Korea over a recent landmine blast that wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries, a Defence Ministry spokesperson has said.
A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded on Monday that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.
“We are not ruling out any options or prejudging anything when it comes to additional measures,” Defence Ministry spokeswoman Chung Bin-na told reporters on Tuesday when asked if steps were being planned to force an apology from Pyongyang.
Chung did not offer specifics about what actions might be employed.
Seoul has also called on nuclear-armed North Korea to remove any other mines planted on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ, the heavily fortified frontier that has divided the Korean Peninsula since the 1953 Armistice Agreement.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the September 21 blast, with Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, slamming the call for an apology as “despicable”.
Chung said Seoul is calling on Pyongyang to come to the table to discuss a misalignment of the MDL. Differing views of the border line are one factor contributing to tension in the area, she said.
The comments come a day after South Korea’s military carried out a mine-clearing operation south of the MDL. It pledged to continue with clearing operations in the area if Pyongyang fails to remove the remaining explosives. The United States-led UN Command (UNC) confirmed the mine placement violated the 1953 agreement.
Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul told the Yonhap news agency on Tuesday that the military’s “decisive” response was “unprecedented in history”.
“All responsibility lies with North Korea,” Kang told reporters, adding that armed forces would “respond decisively” to any actions threatening national security.
The escalation comes as Pyongyang rejected diplomatic overtures from Seoul. Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed on October 2 that both sides jointly resurvey the MDL, noting that only about 200 of 1,292 original boundary markers remain intact and that Seoul and the UNC differ on roughly 60 percent of border coordinates.
Kim Yo Jong rejected the proposal as a “wild dream”, declaring Pyongyang would define its sovereign boundary “by the use of force, not by means of negotiation”.
