Estonian project to help attract more investment to northern Moldova
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:39:44 UTC
17:39:44 KST

The “IMPACT North” programme, launched in northern Moldova, draws on Estonia’s extensive experience in regional development, local government management and preparing projects for EU funding. The programme aims to help Moldova reduce regional development disparities and strengthen the capacity of local governments to attract investment and implement initiatives needed for community development.
According to Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, supporting Moldova is part of Estonia’s broader goal of strengthening the European values-based community and contributing to the development of the EU’s neighbouring countries.
“European Union enlargement makes Europe as a whole stronger and enhances our security. By supporting the accession of countries that share the EU’s values, the single market grows, opportunities for economic cooperation expand and the EU becomes an even stronger geopolitical force. Supporting Moldova’s path towards the EU is an investment in a stronger and more secure Europe, and Estonia is ready to share its reform experience and knowledge of the EU accession process with Moldova and provide practical support along its path towards membership,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
The project focuses on developing the practical skills of local governments and regional development agencies. More than 150 local experts and leaders from local governments, business centres, civil society organisations and universities will take part in the programme. As a result of the project, at least 15 project concepts meeting the requirements of international funding programmes will be developed.
According to ESTDEV CEO Andrea Kivi, Estonia knows from its own experience how important strong local-level capacity is for making use of the opportunities offered by the European Union.
“Moldova’s European integration will not happen only at national level, but also in local governments and communities, where projects are developed that improve people’s everyday lives. ‘IMPACT North’ will help create the knowledge, skills and partnerships needed for this,” Kivi said.
Kristiina Tammets, CEO of the Tartumaa Development Association, stressed that the programme focuses on practical cooperation and applying Estonia’s experience to address local needs.
“‘IMPACT North’ has been designed to benefit as many organisations involved in the regional development of northern Moldova as possible. We are bringing together experts from both Estonia and Moldova and focusing on preparing real development projects that will help improve the quality of life of local people,” Tammets said.
“IMPACT North” follows the “IMPACT Gagauzia” programme implemented last year, which was completed by more than 100 officials and community leaders involved in local development. Based on the positive feedback and interest from Moldovan partners, ESTDEV is now bringing the programme to northern Moldova.
An important part of the programme is also the exchange of experience within Moldova. Participants in “IMPACT North” will visit Gagauzia to learn about projects developed there, partnership models and practical lessons. In this way, in addition to sharing Estonia’s experience, Estonia is also supporting the exchange of knowledge between different regions of Moldova.
The Northern Moldova Development Region comprises the city of Bălți and 11 local governments, with a population of nearly 700,000. Through the programme, Estonia aims to help communities in the region become better prepared to attract investment, develop public services and make use of opportunities offered by the European Union.
As part of his visit to Moldova, Foreign Minister Tsahkna met the President and Foreign Minister of Moldova in Chișinău yesterday and opened the Estonian Embassy in Moldova.

Patients fear shortage of medicinal cannabis when rules change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:39:10 UTC
17:39:10 KST

Patients fear shortage of medicinal cannabis when rules change
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Patients who rely on medicinal cannabis are worried about supplies running out when the government ends its contract with the only Dutch licensed grower next year.
The health ministry is not renewing the contract between the Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC) and Bedrocan from 2027 as part of a plan to liberalise the supply chain by letting suppliers sell directly to pharmacies.
But the rule changes have been delayed, meaning that Bedrocan, based in Emmeloord, will be unable to sell its products at all from next year.
The government says it will import medicinal cannabis from abroad to ensure patients are not denied treatment. The BMC has ordered in extra stocks for the start of next year, but these medicines will go out of date in mid-2027.
Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed cannabis for conditions such as MS and epilepsy, or as a form of palliative care.
The MS Vereniging, which represents people with multiple sclerosis, warned that using a different variant of the medicine would be less effective for some patients.
Specific variety
In a letter to health minister Sophie Hermans, the MS association said some patients who had been prescribed cannabis long-term were dependent on a “specific variety” of the drug and switching to an alternative version would affect the quality of their treatment.
The ministry disputed this in its reply, saying there was “no scientific evidence that different varieties have different therapeutic effects”.
But Renger Witkamp, professor of pharmacology at Wageningen University, said different varieties of cannabis were known to work differently. “Cannabis is different from synthetic medicines,” he told the Volkskrant. “The plant contains dozens of chemicals that collectively determine the effect.
“The relationship between those chemicals is determined by the plant variety, but also by the conditions in which it is grown, such as light, soil and fertiliser.”

Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after man dies in Nairobi
Unknown

2026-10-06

17:38:57 KST

Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after man dies in Nairobi
- Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case on Oct 6 after a man who travelled from Congo died in Nairobi, making Kenya the third country linked to the eastern Congo Ebola outbreak.
- The patient was isolated in Nairobi Hospital, and 28 contacts plus flight passengers were being traced to prevent spread.
- Kenya has trained nearly 5,000 health workers and maintains high alert; the WHO expects the country to manage it effectively.
AI generated
NAIROBI – Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case on Oct 6 after a Kenyan citizen who travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo died in Nairobi.
Kenya is the third country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in eastern Congo, the second largest on record with more than 8,000 cases. Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in 2026 but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The patient, who lived in Congo for seven years, had been ill for about a month before travelling by road from Congo to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on Oct 3, Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale told reporters.
After arriving at Nairobi’s international airport, he passed through health screening and was later taken by a relative to Nairobi Hospital. He was admitted with fever, chills and bleeding beneath the skin and was quickly placed in isolation, Duale said.
He died late on Oct 5.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a statement that it was immediately sending a high-level team to Kenya to provide support, adding that the case “underscores the importance of sustained preparedness across the region”.
World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X that the WHO was supporting the Kenyan and Ugandan governments and recommended against any travel restrictions on countries affected by the outbreak.
The patient was due to be buried later on Oct 6 under protocols designed to prevent further spread of the virus, Duale said.
The health authorities have identified 28 people he came into contact with in Kenya, including relatives and healthcare workers. They are trying to trace another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on his Jambojet flight, Duale said.
Jambojet, a subsidiary of Kenya Airways, said it was working closely with the authorities.
Duale said Kenya was well-prepared to respond to Ebola cases, having trained nearly 5,000 health workers across the country on prevention and management.
“We have continued to maintain, as a country, a high level of alert for Ebola since the outbreak began in May,” he said.
“With a solid health response, which is what my colleagues expect from the Kenyan government, this will be managed,” Julien Harneis, the United Nations’ senior Ebola coordinator, said.
Nevertheless, the incident raised questions about measures meant to prevent the spread of the virus across borders.
Kenya’s health ministry director general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication masked his symptoms.
It was also not clear how he crossed from Congo into Uganda, given that the border has been closed since May. Africa CDC said he spent a night in Uganda before boarding the flight to Kenya.
Asked about this, Ugandan government spokesman Alan Kasujja said he had no idea what the man’s condition was while in Uganda.
“Leave Uganda out of this conversation,” he said in a text message. “We don’t have Ebola here.”
After the outbreak was declared in Congo, the United States built a 50-bed Ebola quarantine camp for Americans on an air force base in central Kenya.
The facility is currently empty and has only housed seven people. Kenyan officials have said it could receive Kenyans and other nationalities, but the US government has not confirmed that.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The outbreak in Congo was declared in mid-May but may have started months earlier. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, it has been blamed for more than 4,000 deaths. REUTERS

Latvian filmmaker wins €400,000 Grand Prix at Kazakhstan's AI film festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:37:39 UTC
17:37:39 KST

The first Astana AI Film Festival has concluded in Kazakhstan, with Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak taking the Grand Prix. The festival had a total fund of €1.8 million, with half allocated to prize money and the other half to investment in promising AI teams and film production in Kazakhstan.
Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak has won the $450,000 (€401,000) Grand Prix at the first Astana AI Film Festival in Kazakhstan for his film The First Honest Day, created using artificial intelligence.
The First Honest Day explores how people's actions shape who they become, with bad deeds making its characters physically uglier and good deeds changing them for the better.
Shestak, who started directing around four years ago and began making films with AI two years ago, said he did not expect to win.
"Honestly, I didn't expect to win. There were so many incredible works and different genres here that I'm curious myself why the jury chose my film," he said.
He plans to invest the prize money in making new films and developing his projects.
Second place in the main competition went to Indian filmmaker Abhik Banerjee for SITARA, earning him $200,000 (€178,000), while Spain's Ernest Desumbila received $100,000 (€89,000) for Looking For Perseida in third place.
Another $250,000 (€223,000) was distributed across five categories in the open competition, with each winner receiving $50,000 (€44,000).
Kazakh filmmaker Myrzakhan Zhumakhan won Best Character for his comedy It Was Just a Joke. China's 2xLabs won Best Story for The Last Span, while Italian filmmaker Jacopo Zanetti received Best Visual for What's the Job?. Another Italian filmmaker, Jacopo Reale, won Best Direction for The Fracture, and US filmmaker Zachary London took Best Concept for Pomegranate.
The films were judged not only on how AI tools were used but also on their artistic vision, storytelling and overall coherence, as well as how organically the technology was integrated into the creative concept.
The international jury included Audrey Azoulay, former Director-General of UNESCO and former French Culture Minister, Ping Ma of China Film Group, Wang Hao of Beijing Film Academy, entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan, and BytePlus executive Long Li.
This year's competition attracted more than 8,000 submissions from 125 countries, with 25 films selected for the final programme. The projects span 19 genres and were created using more than 80 generative AI models.
A festival drawing thousands of AI filmmakers
The festival had a total fund of $2 million (€1.8mn). Half of it, provided by the Freedom Shapagat Corporate Foundation under Freedom Holding Corp., was allocated to prize money.
Another half was set aside as investment capital for promising AI teams and the development of production in Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who opened the festival, highlighted how artificial intelligence is changing the industry.
"Filmmakers and production crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors. The barrier to entry has become significantly lower," he said.
At the same time, Tokayev said AI would not replace the creative role of filmmakers, but could become "an indispensable tool for everyone who has devoted their life to creativity."
He also said the festival was timely for Kazakhstan, pointing to the country's young population.
"Kazakhstan is a country of young people. The average age of our population is 33. I consider Kazakh youth educated, open to new ideas, intelligent and thoughtful," Tokayev said.
For AAIFF co-founder and creative director Aizat Kussainov, the rapid pace of development in artificial intelligence was one of the main reasons to launch the festival.
"The driving force of this festival was FOMO. We had a fear of missing the opportunity because the technology is moving very fast," Kussainov said.
"But no one had actually created a festival like this, and we wanted to be the first in the world — and we did it. We had the biggest AI film festival in the world."
Kussainov said the ambition goes beyond staging the festival itself and is also about bringing international creators to Kazakhstan.
"The main goal actually was not the festival. It was bringing the whole creative community here to Astana and making them see how our country is developing. We want them to move here and start creating their new movies from here," he said.
The competition films were also screened for the public in cinemas in Astana, allowing audiences to see the films selected for the festival and how artificial intelligence is being used in filmmaking.

Teenagers vs cops: France braces for day of school blockades and street protests

The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.
Prime minister promises a response
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government would also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
But finding spare cash will be difficult.
The protests have piled pressure on a government trying to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.
Thousands of arrests
France's Justice Ministry said 5,060 people have been arrested since the protests began, with 87% of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying the crimes. It said 790 cases had been dismissed.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and the far-right National Rally, led by presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. The LFI denies the accusation.
Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, a poor Paris suburb, said he opposed violence but stood beside the protesting students.
"I stand by being on the side of my residents, and high school students are my residents," he said.

Spain approves housing decrees that triggered snap election

Spain approves housing decrees that triggered snap election
MADRID, Oct 6 - Spain's government on Tuesday approved two housing decrees whose rejection by parliament last week prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election.
The measures, which include rent caps, a temporary ban on evictions and limits on corporate purchases of residential property, were "based on plain common sense", Sanchez said in a press conference, arguing that opinion surveys showed the public was broadly in favour of intervention in the property market.
"They protect the most vulnerable and, in some way, begin to bring order to what is currently a deeply dysfunctional market that does not operate according to the logic of supply and demand because of rampant speculation," he said.
Sanchez said on Monday he was bringing forward an election previously scheduled for 2027 because failing to garner enough support for his proposals to address a housing crisis made him realise he needed more seats in parliament.
Calling the election, on November 29, has allowed Sanchez to bring in the new rules with the support of a smaller caretaker body.
The measures will come into effect temporarily when the decree is published in the official state gazette but must then be sent for approval by the caretaker lawmakers who remain in place after parliament was dissolved, Sanchez said.
The standing body of 69 members, when including lower house speaker Francina Armengol from Sanchez's Socialist Party, has a slim majority in favour of the measures, according to state broadcaster TVE.
A second decree proposing the automatic renewal of rental contracts would only come into effect if approved by the reduced legislature since the government did not have a majority to validate it, Sanchez said.
The interventionist measures will only serve to drive away the investment needed to increase supply, said Carolina Roca, president of the Association of Property Developers of Madrid.
"The legal uncertainty inherent in both decrees will result in a sharp slowdown in the limited investment secured to date in the construction of affordable housing," she said.
The attempted eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid triggered nationwide protests including calls for a general strike before the election, which Sanchez said his government would respect. REUTERS

The evening’s events focus on the attack on Kibbutz Nir Oz, soldiers fighting in Gaza, and Israeli society’s responses to the trauma.
At 6:30 p.m., it will screen episode six of Yaron Zilberman’s documentary series "Nir Oz – Heaven/Hell".
The episode follows members of the Maor-Danzig family as they recount defending their home while their daughters sheltered in the safe room. Elsewhere in the kibbutz, Rachel Elgart-Danzig held a safe-room door shut for seven hours to protect her two granddaughters.

'First Among Equals': British bestselling novelist Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:30:52 UTC
17:30:52 KST

Bestselling British author Jeffrey Archer, whose political career was derailed by a perjury conviction, has died at 86.
Archer died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home on Monday, a day before the global release of his final novel, “Adam and Eve”, publisher HarperCollins said.
His writing career spanned five decades, beginning with his 1976 debut, “Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less”. He went on to sell 300 million books worldwide, including “First Among Equals”, and spend 14 years and five months on Britain's Sunday Times bestseller lists, according to his publisher.
Archer’s political career and conviction
Archer also rose through the ranks of the Conservative Party under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and was appointed to the House of Lords in 1992.
His political career collapsed after he was convicted of perjury in 2001 for fabricating an alibi in a libel case. He was sentenced to four years in prison and released early in 2003 after serving more than two years.
He later returned to the House of Lords as a non-affiliated member and retired in 2024.
Archer chronicled his prison experience in his three-volume “A Prison Diary” series. His political legacy also included campaigning for equal succession rights for royal daughters, efforts that helped inspire the Succession to the Crown Act 2013.
His final novel, “Adam and Eve”, explores class and war through two characters born on the same day to different social classes.

Short trade truce can’t paper over realities of US-China relationship
As long as the US’ transactional strategy towards China remains unchanged, the rhythm of crisis and managed de-escalation will continue
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
The recent US-China summit yielded a narrow, caution-filled outcome for bilateral trade: a two-month extension of the Kuala Lumpur trade truce, which now expires on January 10 next year. This reprieve eases fears of immediate tariff escalation and shows that head-of-state diplomacy can still curb spiralling confrontation. Yet the short timeline exposes the wide gulf separating the two sides’ priorities.
China’s position has been unambiguous: removal of all punitive tariffs and restrictive measures imposed since 2018. Beijing has repeatedly stressed that no one wins in a trade war. Even so, it responded to the extension with goodwill. The Ministry of Commerce said the pause gave both sides time to take stock of implemented consensus and deliver stable, predictable policy conditions for businesses.
Washington offered a different narrative. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent portrayed the two months as a compliance review, accusing China of failing to fully meet its commitments. He and other US officials did not celebrate the pause, instead speaking of obstacles remaining before any longer truce could be agreed.

Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:29:17 CEST
17:29:17 KST

The resilience of the Italian economy
should make it possible for wages here to recover over the next
two years, with soaring inflation linked to the Iran war
currently eating into households' purchasing power, European
Central Bank Chief Economist said in an interview with ANSA on
Tuesday.
                                    
"In our September projections, we see that wages in Italy will
grow faster than inflation in 2027 and 2028," Lane told ANSA.
                                    
"We believe that the strong performance of the Italian economy
should allow for an improvement in real wages and living
standards next year and the year after". Lane emphasized the
"fundamental solidity" of the Italian economy.
                                    
"Collectively, these very high energy prices represent a loss
for the European economy," he added.
                                    
"And, unfortunately, it is impossible to say that all workers
should be fully protected from this loss at all times".
                                    
When asked about criticism, including by politicians in Italy,
of the ECB's rate hikes, Lane countered that: "inflation is very
harmful and people really suffer if inflation gets too high.
                                    
"If the inflation rate had remained at 3% or 4% following the
Russian-Ukrainian energy shock, with the ECB remaining inactive,
that would have been very harmful to Italian workers and Italian
households," Lane continued.
                                    
"If the ECB did not raise rates when necessary, inflation would
be too high, and if people expected inflation to be too high,
long-term rates would rise".
                                    
Lane also commented on the Italian government's request for
greater flexibility in the application of the EU's budget rules
for measures to help with the effects of high inflation.
                                    
"It is important that low-income individuals receive special
protection through targeted measures," he said.
                                    
"A very broad, widespread fiscal expansion will not help.
                                    
"Income support within the (2027) budget law should be as
well-targeted as possible, because a 'broad-brush' fiscal
stimulus essentially boosts aggregate demand, and that will not
help inflation return to 2% quickly".

Yemen war: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:27:51 UTC
17:27:51 KST

Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest?
The internationally recognised government retakes territories from the Houthis as fighting rages on the western coast.
Yemeni government forces say they have seized several strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from the Iran-aligned Houthis, as fighting intensifies along the country’s western coast.
In response, the Houthis, an armed group also known by its Arabic name Ansar Allah, or Supporters of God, have claimed attacks on airports, oil infrastructure and military sites in Saudi Arabia.
The latest offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government army follows major Houthi gains in September, when the group swept over the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, has said the government’s new operation – Dawn of Yemen – announced on Sunday, aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.
So, where does the fighting stand, and what could happen next?
What is the latest?
Southwestern Yemen has witnessed the heaviest fighting, particularly along the Red Sea coast and around Taiz.
Yemen’s government forces backed by Saudi Arabia said they, together with the Popular Resistance Forces, had taken control of the al-Manzara, al-Ashari and Dhiban mountains in Haifan, south of Taiz.
Earlier, Yemeni government forces claimed they had captured Mocha and Dhubab, both in Taiz governorate, as well as positions around Bab al-Mandeb, in a rapid Saudi-backed counteroffensive.
Government forces, supported by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha on Monday as Houthi fighters retreated towards the highlands, four government sources told the Reuters news agency.
Yemen’s Defence Ministry later said the city had fallen.
Without revealing any specifics, a Houthi military spokesman on Tuesday said the group remained in control of its battlefield gains and described reports from its opponents as “fabricated heroics”.
Al Jazeera has not independently verified the full extent of the government’s territorial gains.
Fernando Carvajal, a former United Nations Security Council adviser on Yemen, said the battle for Mocha will be key to the next phase of fighting.
“This will be a vital sign for us if the Yemeni government forces, led by the Southern Giants and other southern forces, can hold this city. Because, at the moment, when you look at the battle plan, Mocha is surrounded by Houthis from all three sides, and you have the Red Sea,” he told Al Jazeera.
“So, we need to wait just a little bit more to see if indeed the government forces can hold this city and then use it as a staging point to take on the Houthis on other fronts.”
The fighting has also extended northwards along the Red Sea coast to Hodeidah, which has been under Houthi control since October 2014. The Houthis had captured Sanaa weeks before that.
The Saudi-led coalition’s spokesman, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said its naval forces struck Houthi “military targets” in the Hodeidah governorate, including weapons depots and facilities used to store explosive-laden boats and naval mines.
Al-Maliki said the operation “thwarted a planned attack” on waterways in the southern Red Sea. The coalition also said its naval forces had carried out a military operation in Hodeidah.
Meanwhile, the Houthis said their forces carried out dozens of strikes on Tuesday targeting “enemy” reinforcements east of al-Jawf governorate, resulting in an unspecified number of casualties.
The Houthis have simultaneously stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Houthi-affiliated media. They targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait military base with missiles and drones, as well as sites in the southern Saudi cities of Najran and Jazan.
Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on all those specific claims.
However, on Tuesday, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the King Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz international airport in Jazan and the Najran international airport were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, causing three minor injuries.
Later in the day, the Houthis claimed another attack on a Saudi airport, this time targeting Abha International Airport in Asir Province, with a ballistic missile.
Riyadh has yet to confirm the alleged attack.
What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?
The escalation is worsening what was already one of the world’s gravest humanitarian crises.
The International Organization for Migration said on Monday that more than 184,000 people have been displaced since the war resumed.
According to the World Health Organization, the latest fighting has killed at least 959 people and wounded more than 4,200.
The fighting has also disrupted healthcare in the war-devastated country.
“Yemen’s latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point,” warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO’s emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.
What is the international reaction?
The escalation has drawn a response from Saudi Arabia’s regional allies, with Turkiye and Pakistan agreeing to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
Signed in August, the pact is designed to strengthen collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against Saudi Arabia, Pakistan or Turkiye will be regarded as an attack on all three.
The United States, one of Saudi Arabia’s closest allies, is providing intelligence support to Riyadh, according to media reports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government had “a right to defend themselves”.
“And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from,” he told reporters.

She also said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to form a government, as senior party figures attacked their rightwing rivals with a ferocity that appeared to make the chances of any pact more remote.
In her own conference speech on Wednesday, Badenoch is expected to announce plans to cut – but not abolish – inheritance tax, which is levied at 40% on all estates with property worth more than £500,000.
The Tories have promised to cut employers’ national insurance from 15% to 7.5% for people aged 21-24 in an attempt to drive down the youth unemployment rate. Badenoch is expected to say she will fund the £2.3bn scheme through welfare cuts.
However, she admitted it could be “difficult” to reverse Labour’s planned changes to the pensions triple lock once they had been brought in, as it emerged her party could head into the next election without a social care plan.
In several interviews, the Tory leader was forced to clarify her party’s “iron dome” defence policy, as she tried to distance herself from using the term. She told Times Radio it was a “semantic argument” and that the new system would protect Britain from increasing threats.
She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the description had come from newspapers – though the Conservative party press release described the system as “in essence a British Iron Dome”.
In a piece by Badenoch in the Sun, which illustrated its front page with an image of Israel’s Iron Dome, she wrote: “Modelled on Israel’s ‘Iron Dome’, Britannia Shield will invest £10bn over 10 years in the radar, missiles and technology needed to detect these threats and stop them before they reach British soil.”
But Badenoch told Today that was not the aim. “We are not building the Iron Dome. We are doing what other European countries are doing: Greece, Benelux countries – Belgium and the Netherlands – and Germany. We are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here.”
The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, likened the phrase “iron dome” to the vacuum cleaner brand name Hoover when asked why Badenoch had denied the Conservatives were proposing an Iron Dome-style system.
Asked on Times Radio if the aim was to be able to intercept any attack over the entire country, Badenoch said: “It should, but it needs to protect critical national infrastructure … Critical national infrastructure protects the entire country. If we lose even one thing, the entire country is in a real problem, and that’s what we mean.”
On Today, asked whether she was ready for an election, Badenoch said she believed polls would improve but admitted the party was still unpopular because of the previous government’s record, even though her personal popularity had improved.
“I think people still associate the Conservative party with the things they didn’t like about the previous government,” she said. “I need to work hard to change that … these things take time. I am the leader and I need to show that this party is different from the party that the people said no to two years ago.
“I am confident that when that election is called, people will see that the Conservative party has the best offer. We have a strong team, we have a plan and we’re all about common sense.”
A Labour source said: “It’s no surprise Kemi Badenoch wants to forget how the Tories hollowed out our armed forces. But hoping her half-baked defence promise based on fantasy numbers will be forgotten just hours after it was made shows how unserious she is about our country’s security. The Tories can never be given responsibility for keeping Britain safe again.”

Russia Tests Balloon Barriers to Snare Ukrainian Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:27:33 UTC
17:27:33 KST

Russia has begun testing a novel defense against Ukrainian drones: balloons suspended above the ground and linked by cables designed to snag incoming aircraft.
The system, shown this week on Russia’s state-run Rossiya 1 television channel, uses balloons to hold cables in the air. Kevlar strands hang from the cables, creating a barrier intended to entangle a drone’s propeller and send it crashing down.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian developers claim the technology is ready for mass production. But protecting a single large facility would require at least 10 balloons, according to the report.
The system appears designed not necessarily to stop every drone, but to force them to change course or fly higher to avoid the cables. That could make them easier for Russian radars to detect and air defense systems to engage.
The concept is far from new. Balloon barriers, known as barrage balloons, were widely used during World War II to protect cities, ports and other strategic sites from enemy aircraft. By forcing bombers to fly higher, they also reduced the accuracy of bombing.
Russia has increasingly experimented with unconventional ways to protect critical infrastructure from Ukraine’s growing drone campaign.
Earlier, a Russian chemical industry company launched a tender for balloons to protect its facilities from Ukrainian drone attacks.
Balloons take on new roles
Balloons are also being adapted for other military purposes.
Why Russia Wants Western Embassies Out of Kyiv – and Why They’re Staying
Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec has developed a balloon equipped with a radio module to extend communications. Raising the equipment above the ground can reduce the impact of terrain on signal quality compared with mobile ground-based stations.
Ukraine is also exploring military uses for balloons. Ukrainian developers have proposed using them as platforms to launch drones and missiles.
Stratospheric balloons could potentially launch missiles from altitudes of between 12 and 18 kilometers (7-11 miles), according to Ukrainian developers.

Italian economy's solidity will help wages recover in 2027-28 - ECB's Lane tells ANSA

17:26:45 KST

The resilience of the Italian economy
should make it possible for wages here to recover over the next
two years, with soaring inflation linked to the Iran war
currently eating into households' purchasing power, European
Central Bank Chief Economist said in an interview with ANSA on
Tuesday.
                                    
"In our September projections, we see that wages in Italy will
grow faster than inflation in 2027 and 2028," Lane told ANSA.
                                    
"We believe that the strong performance of the Italian economy
should allow for an improvement in real wages and living
standards next year and the year after". Lane emphasized the
"fundamental solidity" of the Italian economy.
                                    
"Collectively, these very high energy prices represent a loss
for the European economy," he added.
                                    
"And, unfortunately, it is impossible to say that all workers
should be fully protected from this loss at all times".
                                    
When asked about criticism, including by politicians in Italy,
of the ECB's rate hikes, Lane countered that: "inflation is very
harmful and people really suffer if inflation gets too high.
                                    
"If the inflation rate had remained at 3% or 4% following the
Russian-Ukrainian energy shock, with the ECB remaining inactive,
that would have been very harmful to Italian workers and Italian
households," Lane continued.
                                    
"If the ECB did not raise rates when necessary, inflation would
be too high, and if people expected inflation to be too high,
long-term rates would rise".
                                    
Lane also commented on the Italian government's request for
greater flexibility in the application of the EU's budget rules
for measures to help with the effects of high inflation.
                                    
"It is important that low-income individuals receive special
protection through targeted measures," he said.
                                    
"A very broad, widespread fiscal expansion will not help.
                                    
"Income support within the (2027) budget law should be as
well-targeted as possible, because a 'broad-brush' fiscal
stimulus essentially boosts aggregate demand, and that will not
help inflation return to 2% quickly".

Honcharenko's expulsion from parliamentary group elicites mixed reactions from politicians and experts, ranging from accusations to predictions about formation of new party
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:26:37 EEST
17:26:37 KST

As of Tuesday morning, a significant number of MPs from the European Solidarity parliamentary group reposted the party's statement regarding the expulsion of MP Oleksiy Honcharenko, prompted by his recent remarks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, yet almost no one commented on the decision itself.
Before reposting the statement, European Solidarity MP Volodymyr Ariev explained that the delay in reaching this decision was due to the need for a measured response. "Everyone had been waiting a long time for a decision from European Solidarity. But decisions are not made without internal dialogue or democratic discussion within a party—this isn't the CPSU. And when decisions are made, they are made in a measured way, not hysterically," he wrote on Facebook.
Of all the European Solidarity MPs, only Volodymyr Viatrovych, a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy, published a personal post after reposting the statement about Honcharenko; he emphasized that the narrative "finally, someone has said what the majority is thinking" is being used to promote capitulatory initiatives within Ukrainian society.
"Its goal is to create an illusion of mass support. That is precisely why bots on social media are so actively spreading this narrative. At the same time, this tactic attempts to cast the actual proponents of such initiatives as courageous truth-seekers and defenders of the interests of the majority of Ukrainians. This is how unity is destroyed and divisions deepened, by pitting the 'party of peace' (portrayed as rational and responsible) against the 'party of war'—that is, those allegedly profiting from the continuation of the conflict," Viatrovych wrote on Facebook.
According to him, to counter this tactic, one must not remain silent but publicly declare that "capitulation disguised as peace is unacceptable." "And you will see how many like-minded people are around you. And what wonderful people they are," Viatrovych added.
Arsen Zhumadilov, former director of the defense procurement agency State Logistics Operator (2025–2026) and former head of the Biliayivka District State Administration in Odesa region (2015–2017), expressed the view that Honcharenko, "through his opposition activities (more likely) or due to treasonous motives (less likely), has lost touch with the pro-state efforts the country has been engaged in since the start of the full-scale war."
"I realized that the person is following a specific agenda. I hope, at least, it is his own—even though it increasingly echoes the Russian one," Zhumadilov wrote on Facebook.
Viktor Ukolov, a former MP of the Verkhovna Rada (6th convocation, 2007–2012) and a veteran of the Russia-Ukraine war, noted that Honcharenko and the European Solidarity faction had "diverged significantly in their statements and actions." However, he expressed regret over the expulsion, remarking that "losing such a prominent MP as Honcharenko is a loss."
Businessman and blogger Karl Volokh suggested that for Honcharenko, "everything is going according to plan, including his expulsion from the faction." "As a result, in the public eye, he is not only the only politician openly advocating for negotiations and an end to the war, but he has also become a martyr for the cause. Since the war will inevitably end at the negotiating table one way or another, a segment of the electorate will inevitably form the impression that he was the only one who possessed the 'foresight and courage' [to take this stance]," he explained on Facebook.
Volokh doubts that Honcharenko will "burst into the top tier of presidential rankings anytime soon," but suggests he might launch a new party of his own—one that could soon begin appearing in opinion polls.
Honcharenko himself has not yet commented on the faction's decision; however, on Monday, hours before the announcement, he posted a lengthy list of 50 achievements dating back to 2014 on social media to refute allegations of pro-Russian activity. Specifically, he highlighted his opposition to the occupation of Crimea, the sanctions imposed on him by Russia (including his designation as an "extremist"), the creation of volunteer hubs within his Honcharenko Centers, fundraising for equipment for the Defense Forces, participation in security forums, his own legislative initiatives (particularly those supporting the military), his work at PACE, and his efforts to prevent the undermining of the independence of the NABU and SAPO.
As earlier reported, the European Solidarity party issued a statement on Monday evening announcing Honcharenko’s expulsion from its parliamentary faction following his recent remarks. "Oleksiy Honcharenko’s public stances regarding the end of the war and Ukraine’s future security architecture diverge from the position of European Solidarity and its ideological principles. For this reason, the European Solidarity faction has decided that we can no longer continue our shared political journey due to ideological differences. This decision does not negate years of working together. However, party unity cannot be a mere formality masking fundamentally different answers to questions about the state's future," the statement reads.
The political group emphasized that their team "is not just a parliamentary faction but also tens of thousands of party members; the most respected among them are our colleagues currently serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, whose opinions and stance regarding the defense of the country are of fundamental importance to us."
Earlier, on October 2, Honcharenko published a series of posts on Telegram calling for the start of negotiations with the Russian Federation to reach agreements on halting strikes against ports, industrial facilities, schools, hospitals, residential buildings, and bridges. He suggested that, following this, discussions could move on to more complex issues, specifically the status of Donbas and Ukraine's neutral status.
Honcharenko is not a member of the European Solidarity party itself, though he is part of the parliamentary faction of the same name. He serves at the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget Issues and the permanent delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, and participates in numerous inter-parliamentary friendship groups. He also chairs the Verkhovna Rada’s temporary inquiry commission investigating potential violations of Ukrainian defense and anti-corruption laws and the observance of human rights and freedoms during martial law, and serves at other such commissions.
During the previous (8th) convocation of the Verkhovna Rada (2014–2019), he was a member of the Petro Poroshenko Bloc faction and party; however, he did not join the party after its reorganization into the revamped European Solidarity party (led by Petro Poroshenko). In the last parliamentary elections, he ran as an independent, non-partisan candidate in electoral district No. 137 (Odesa region).

The risk of the international spread of plague, including to Latvia, is considered very low even if the suspected case in Russia is laboratory-confirmed, according to Latvia’s Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (SPKC).
The SPKC issued the information following media reports of a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia’s Irkutsk region. The Moscow Times and Meduza reported that nearly 200 people had been hospitalised for observation after coming into contact with a patient who had allegedly died from pneumonic plague.
The SPKC stresses that reports of a death potentially linked to pneumonic plague and the introduction of large-scale quarantine measures have not yet been officially confirmed by the World Health Organization (WHO) or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
The centre explains that today, timely diagnosis, patient isolation, monitoring of contacts and effective antibiotic treatment make it possible to successfully contain the spread of plague and prevent larger outbreaks.

Breadcrumb
Obama to appear with Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit for US senate campaign
Former US President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, lending his support to the progressive nominee after a bruising Democratic primary exposed divisions within the party.
Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an 24 October rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party's nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press.
The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year.
Obama taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate that will be released in the coming days and weeks, in addition to more campaign stops soon to be announced.
He appeared earlier this year in a campaign ad with Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and campaigned in Texas with Senate candidate James Talarico and the candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa. This week, he will headline a Washington fundraiser supporting Democratic Senate candidates.
Shore up support in a key area 
El-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than a percentage point in a primary that became a national test of the Democratic Party’s ideological direction. El-Sayed drew support from leading progressives, including Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens was backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.
Some ads that supported Stevens showed Obama praising her, and she outperformed El-Sayed in Wayne County, winning about 51% of the Democratic primary vote compared with 45% for El-Sayed. The county includes Detroit, where more than three-quarters of residents are Black.
Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian person to serve as vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month.
Now the 24 October rally with Obama, the first Black president, could give El-Sayed a boost on the first day of Michigan’s required early in-person voting period. Obama spoke with El-Sayed by phone following his primary victory.
It will also be a boost for the other candidates in what is one of the most consequential elections in recent Michigan history. There are open races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general, in addition to control of the state legislature being at play.
Benson, who will also appear with Obama, is facing Republican Rep. John James in the race for governor.
Benson and James are set to debate for the first time on Tuesday, and El-Sayed and Rogers are scheduled to debate for the first time on 8 October.
Obama returns to campaign trail  
Obama has been selective in his involvement in the midterms so far, but his planned ramp-up in the final weeks follows a pattern from recent elections. He campaigned in Detroit on 22 October during the 2024 presidential election and was in the city 29 October during the 2022 midterms.
His campaign appearances can draw large crowds and prominent guests. Rapper Eminem introduced Obama at his Detroit rally in 2024.
This week, he will headline an event with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee that will include a conversation with Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester. That follows a September event with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Bennett unveils ‘Deri Law’: draft dodgers would be barred from Israel’s security cabinet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:24:50 UTC
17:24:50 KST

“Anyone who evaded IDF service will not be able to sit in the security cabinet. Anyone who evaded service, or encourages draft evasion, will not be able to sit in the cabinet. This is one of our core conditions for the next government,” former prime minister and Beyachad chairman Naftali Bennett said Tuesday.
Bennett said he was calling the proposed legislation the “Deri Law,” a reference to Shas chairman Aryeh Deri. Deri, who served for three months in the IDF, has not been an official member of the security cabinet since the current government was formed in January 2023.
Speaking at the Reichman Conference, Bennett framed the proposal as part of a broader campaign to expand military conscription. “For us to truly prevail, our soldiers need reinforcements,” Bennett said. “As long as Deri, Netanyahu and Smotrich continue encouraging and funding mass draft evasion, who will fight? Who will prevail?”
Bennett described draft evasion as “a strategic danger to Israel’s security” and said officers and combat soldiers he has spoken with report that the IDF is immediately short of 20,000 troops.
According to Bennett, that shortage is costing soldiers’ lives and limiting the military’s ability to achieve its objectives. “Soldiers are wounded and killed by drones because there are not enough observation posts and snipers to protect them,” he said. “Fighters are forced to leave positions they captured because there is no one to hold them. Then they have to return and capture them again, at the cost of blood.”
He said prolonged deployments were also wearing down troops. “The long rotations erode the soldiers. Alertness declines, and the price is human lives,” Bennett said.
Bennett pledged that a government including his party would impose a universal military-service requirement and cut state funding to those who refuse to serve.
“In the next government, we will apply the obligation to enlist to everyone, without compromise, and we will completely stop the money going to draft dodgers,” he said. “Anyone who does not enlist will not receive a single shekel from the state.”
Bennett then presented the proposed cabinet restriction as one of his party’s conditions for entering the next coalition. “I am revealing here and now one of our core conditions for the next government,” he said. “We will pass the ‘Deri Law,’ which states that anyone who evaded IDF service, or encourages draft evasion, will not be able to sit in the cabinet.”
“We will no longer accept a distorted situation in which someone who boasts that he does not send his grandchildren into battle is the one sending our sons and daughters into battle,” Bennett added. “Anyone who does not know what it is like to lie awake at night fearing a knock on the door cannot sit in a war cabinet.”

Swiss canton shot 17 wolves in September

Swiss canton shot 17 wolves in September
Authorised hunters and gamekeepers shot a total of 17 wolves in September in the southeastern Swiss canton of Graubünden.
According to Arno Puorger, head of the Large Carnivores Division at the Cantonal Office for Hunting and Fisheries, a total of 61 wolves are currently authorised for culling.
The wolf cull began on September 1 and will continue until the end of January at the latest. Authorised hunters can take part in the wolf cull during the main and special hunting seasons.
More
How many wolves are good for Switzerland?
Around 3,070 chamois were aslo shot by hunters in the canton – 200 fewer than during the hunting season last year. In addition, around 2,400 roe deer and 2,900 red deer were shot. In both cases, the numbers were lower than last year.
However, the main hunting season in Graubünden was also overshadowed by a tragic incident. On September 8, a 66-year-old man lost his life in a fall whilst in rough terrain in Val Lumnezia.
There was also an unusual incident in Avers, Graubünden, when, on September 6, a hunter shot a horse in a meadow because he mistook it for a stag. The hunter’s hunting licence was revoked on the spot.

Von der Leyen warns against EU budget cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:22:46 UTC
17:22:46 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addresses members of the European Parliament during a plenary session in Strasbourg, France on Oct. 6, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen cautioned against cuts to the EU’s next seven-year budget in a rebuke to Germany's calls to dramatically slash spending.
During a speech in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, von der Leyen said that reducing the size of the EU’s common cash pot would undermine critical EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness and energy autonomy.
“I would like to caution against large cuts. It would risk cutting deep into critical priorities that we all together have agreed on,” von der Leyen told MEPs.
Advertisement
The warning comes days before the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the budget talks, is expected to put forward a budget negotiating document with new figures.
Von der Leyen had previously hailed the Commission's budget proposal for 2028-2034 as “the most ambitious ever proposed.” But Tuesday, as negotiations among governments enter crunch time, she struck a more cautious note.
In a message to Berlin, von der Leyen recalled that the Commission’s budget proposal represents 1.26% of the European Union’s gross national income — a relatively small increase from the current seven-year cash pot.
She also underscored the need to approve “a significant package of new own resources,” which are EU-wide taxes to finance the budget and reduce national contributions to Brussels.
The bloc’s governments are racing to reach an agreement by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations.
Despite the looming deadline, EU leaders are still far apart over the size of the new budget.
Advertisement
Germany and its allies in Northern Europe have pressured Dublin to make cuts worth hundreds of billions of euros across the board.
But 17 EU countries from Southern and Eastern Europe — led by Italy and Romania — are pushing in the opposite direction. They asked to preserve farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, in a joint letter last week.
During a separate speech to the European Parliament on Tuesday, Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said that “there is no European competitiveness without cohesion, and no European cohesion without competitiveness.”
In a rebuke to the frugals, Montenegro said that Portugal’s contribution to the EU budget as a share of its gross domestic product is higher than that of Germany and other wealthier countries.
“Giving 10 out of 100 is much more than giving 50 out of 1,000," he told MEPs.
But Germany insists that its budget contributions are too high. In a thinly veiled threat on Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that “having no new financial framework is by far the most financially advantageous solution for Germany.”
Advertisement
However, he added that such a scenario would restrict the EU’s ability to act and renewed calls to end the negotiations by the end of the year.
Several European officials believe that Dublin will propose budget cuts exceeding €100 billion. The proposal is expected to be put forward Saturday and be discussed by EU ambassadors Sunday.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — AMD plans to increase its investment in Taiwan beyond US$10 billion (NT$317.6 billion) as strong artificial intelligence demand drives the need for more production capacity, CNA reported Tuesday.
AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su (蘇姿丰) visited several major Taiwanese technology companies during a brief trip. She met executives from Foxconn, Quanta, Asus, and Acer before traveling to Hsinchu to meet with TSMC.
Su said Taiwan is home to many of AMD’s customers, partners, and suppliers. She said close cooperation with them is becoming more important as demand for computing power continues to grow.
AMD has expanded capacity this year as demand rises for processors used in AI systems and data centers. Su said demand still exceeds supply, prompting the company to work with TSMC, chip-packaging firms, and other suppliers to increase capacity.
AMD announced in May that it would invest more than US$10 billion in Taiwan’s technology supply chain. Su said the investment is progressing as planned, but the company now expects to spend more as demand continues to rise.
The chipmaker has benefited from strong demand for AI and data-center processors this year. Its market value recently surpassed US$1 trillion.

South Korea considers Ukraine&apos;s apology over the disclosure of information about North Korean prisoners of war insufficient
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:18:23 EEST
17:18:23 KST

South Korea considers Ukraine's apology over the disclosure of information about North Korean prisoners of war insufficient
Kyiv • UNN
South Korea received an apology from Ukraine for disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war, but considers it insufficient. Seoul is considering decisive measures.
South Korea received a message of apology from Ukraine regarding the disclosure of information about the transfer to Seoul of two North Korean prisoners of war, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday. At the same time, he added that the apology did not meet Seoul’s expectations. Yonhap reports, UNN writes.
Details
Seoul demanded an official explanation and apology after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed information about the transfer last month. The Office of the President of Ukraine later stated that there had been no agreement to keep this information secret.
"I have maintained constant contact with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on this issue, and he expressed how difficult this situation is," Cho said during a parliamentary audit of his ministry’s activities, responding to lawmakers’ questions about whether Ukraine had apologized.
"The messages I received (from Sybiha — Ed.) contained an apology. But they do not meet the level we expect, so we intend to take decisive measures," he said.
The minister added that the government was considering various options, including the possibility of recalling South Korea’s ambassador to Ukraine, Park Hee-chan, as proposed by one of the lawmakers.
What preceded this
The two North Korean servicemen were captured in January 2025 during fighting on Russia’s side in the Kursk region. They arrived in South Korea in mid-September.
On September 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
Responding to a question about why Zelenskyy disclosed information about the transfer, Cho suggested — emphasizing that this was only his personal interpretation — that the Ukrainian president may have wanted to demonstrate to the United Nations that Ukraine had acted appropriately as a liberal democracy.
Cho said that an agreement to keep the matter secret had existed from the outset in order to protect the servicemen and their families who remain in North Korea. According to him, it was the Ukrainian side that first asked for the information not to be made public.
After Seoul demanded an official explanation and apology, Sybiha called the situation a "diplomatic misunderstanding" and expressed hope that it would be resolved soon.

Power outage schedules are returning in Ukraine — where and when
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

Power outage schedules are returning in Ukraine — where and when
Kyiv • UNN
Starting at 3:00 p.m., hourly outages and restrictions for businesses will be in effect in some regions. This is happening against the backdrop of rising consumption and attacks by the Russian Federation.
Power outages are returning to Ukraine. Starting at 3 p.m. on October 6, schedules are planned to be introduced in some regions. This was reported by the Ministry of Energy, UNN writes.
When to expect power outage schedules
From 3:00 p.m. until the end of the day, some regions plan to apply capacity restriction schedules for industry and business, as well as hourly outage schedules for all categories of consumers, covering up to one queue
"If the situation worsens in individual regions, emergency outages may be introduced," the ministry emphasized.
Current schedules and information about changes in electricity supply are posted on the official resources of regional distribution system operators.
"When electricity is supplied according to the schedule, please do not switch on several powerful electrical appliances at the same time. This helps reduce the load on the power system and shorten the duration of forced restrictions," the Ministry of Energy urged.
Where outages are occurring due to attacks by the Russian Federation
According to the Ministry of Energy, as a result of hostilities and Russian shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions are temporarily without electricity.
Where the security situation allows, energy workers are working to restore service. Energy workers are doing everything possible to return electricity to the homes of Ukrainians as quickly as possible. Restoration work is continuing around the clock, the ministry stated.
Consumption has increased
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has increased. Today, October 6, as of 09:30, it was 2.9% higher than at the same time the previous day — Monday. The reason for the change is cloudy weather in a significant part of Ukraine's regions. This is leading to low operating efficiency of household solar power plants and a corresponding increase in the amount of energy consumption from the general grid. Yesterday, October 5, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 1.7% higher than the peak of the previous working day — Friday, October 2.
"Using powerful electrical appliances today should be postponed until the period when industrial solar power plants operate most efficiently — from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.," the company noted.
"Due to Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, the situation in the power system may change," Ukrenergo emphasized.

Inflation data bolsters expectations for October rate cut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:17:31 UTC
17:17:31 KST

Türkiye’s cooler-than-anticipated September inflation has bolstered analysts’ confidence that the Central Bank will lower interest rates by 100 basis points at its Oct. 22 meeting.
Annual consumer inflation slowed to 29.7 percent in September, falling below 30 percent for the first time since November 2021, while monthly inflation came in at 1.84 percent, undershooting market expectations.
İş Yatırım said food prices were the main driver behind the downside surprise in September inflation, with vegetable and fruit prices falling sharply during the month. The brokerage said the inflation reading strengthened expectations for a 100-basis-point rate cut at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct. 22. It expects annual inflation to ease to around 30 percent by the end of the year and sees the policy rate ending 2026 at approximately 35 percent.
According to Gedik Yatırım, the weaker-than-expected inflation reading strengthened expectations for a 100-basis-point rate cut at the Oct. 22 meeting. It forecasts year-end inflation at 30 percent and the policy rate at around 35 percent.
Akbank Economic Research said the improvement in inflation dynamics, despite ongoing cost pressures, had created some room for monetary easing. The bank expects a 100-basis-point rate cut as its base scenario for October, but said a 150-basis-point reduction could also be possible depending on market and pricing developments in the coming weeks. Akbank maintained its year-end inflation forecast at 30 percent and its policy rate forecast at 36 percent.
The bank nevertheless cautioned that additional fuel-price adjustments, cost pressures not yet fully reflected in consumer prices and higher global interest rates argue for a cautious approach regarding the pace and continuity of rate cuts.
ÜNLÜ & Co said the widening gap between the policy rate and inflation provided the Central Bank with room for around 200 basis points of easing, and it expects a 100-basis-point rate cut in October, provided there is no significant change in domestic or global conditions before the meeting.
The brokerage maintained its year-end inflation forecast in a range of 28 percent to 30 percent.
Şeker Yatırım said an October rate cut now appeared almost certain, although the size of the move would depend on developments in energy markets and the trajectory of October inflation reflected in leading indicators. The brokerage also said it believed supply-side shocks had been largely offset by the slowdown in demand
The reports broadly agreed that the latest inflation data strengthened the case for monetary easing, while differing in their assessments of how much room the Central Bank has for rate reductions in the coming months.

UK events firm that hosts arms fairs and comic shows sold to rival for £2bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:16:48 UTC
17:16:48 KST

A British events business that hosts arms fairs and conventions for comic book fans has been snapped up by a FTSE 100 rival for more than £2bn.
Informa has struck a £2.24bn deal to buy the London-based events organiser Clarion from the private equity group Blackstone
The takeover will add more than 100 events to Informa’s portfolio – from the defence and security exhibit DSEI held at London’s ExCel, to the comic book and pop culture themed Awesome Con in Washington.
DSEI, which is held every two years in London as well as in Germany and Japan, has also attracted protests.
Last year, hundreds demonstrated outside the four-day fair in London in protest against Israel’s three biggest arms companies present at the event. Elbit Systems, Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries have supplied the Israel Defense Forces; the latter two are state-owned.
Clarion’s portfolio also spans travel shows, classic car meet-ups and events for the technology, gaming, design and technology industries. Its Classic Motor Show event in Birmingham next month is billed as the “world’s largest vehicle club gathering”.
Stephen Carter, the Informa chief executive, said the company was “accelerating the focus” on its core live events business, as it also laid out plans to spin off its academic publishing arm, Taylor & Francis.
Informa, which is headquartered in London and employs 14,000 people, hosts big industry events around the world, including London Tech Week and the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity.
However the FTSE 100 group’s shares have been flat so far this year as it was forced to reschedule several events in the Middle East because of the conflict in the region.
Last year Carter, who has led the group since 2013, moved his residency from the UK to the UAE and retired from the House of Lords. Informa makes more than a third of its revenue in India, the Middle East and Asia.
The academic publishing business made about $1bn (£760m) last year. Informa said that it had launched a formal process to separate Taylor & Francis, and that it would “review all options”. The outcome of the review will be reported alongside its full-year results in March next year.
Taylor & Francis, which was founded in London in 1852, joined Informa in 2004. It publishes journals and books about science, medicine, technology and engineering.
Informa told investors on Tuesday that in order to fund the Clarion deal, it will raise £940m through a share placing, which will include an offer for armchair investors through the broker RetailBook.
The takeover is expected to accelerate Informa’s growth and bolster its earnings per share from 2027, the company said. Shares in the business, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, rose by 1.4% in early trading on Tuesday.

British PM weighs delay to roadmap for higher defence spending, Times reports
LONDON – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering delaying an announcement on how and when Britain will raise defence spending to 3% of GDP, The Times reported on Oct 6, pushing back a key milestone on the path to meeting NATO’s target of 3.5% by 2035.
Britain is under pressure to spell out how it will meet the NATO commitment and respond to a heightened security threat.
Burnham has pledged to meet the 2035 target, but his government has yet to set out the steps required to get there.
Finance minister John Healey said earlier in 2026 he would outline an initial path to 3% of GDP at the next spending review, which was expected in spring 2027.
The Times cited a source as saying the “working assumption” was that the review would take place in October 2027.
A spokesperson for the finance ministry said it was wrong talk of a delay.
“The date of the Spending Review has not been set. This is pure rumour and speculation,” the spokesperson said in an email.
Highlighting the security challenges facing Britain, the US on Oct 4 removed bombers from an airbase in England after it was targeted in a suspected Iranian plot.
Ministers have repeatedly delayed decisions on additional defence funding over the past two years.
Healey, finance minister since July, resigned as defence minister in the previous government after failing to secure funding to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, a move that helped bring down then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
According to the Office for Budget Responsibility, reaching that interim goal would cost the government an additional £17.3 billion (S$29.3 billion). To meet the needs of the existing Defence Investment Plan, Healey needs to fill a £4.7 billion funding gap.
Healey is due to deliver his first budget on Oct 28. REUTERS

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended the execution and US President Donald Trump approved it. The Secretary of the Army will determine the date and location of the execution.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist and major, opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32.
A military jury convicted Hasan of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and sentenced him to death.
During the trial, Army prosecutor Colonel Steve Henricks said Hasan had created his own “personal kill zone” at the base.
The first firing squad execution since WW2
The planned execution would mark a rare moment in US military justice. The last US soldier executed by firing squad was Army Private Eddie Slovik, who was executed in 1945 for desertion during World War II.
The US Army's most recent execution was that of Private John Bennett, who was hanged to death in 1961.
Parnell said the recommendation had been made because “the day of reckoning has finally come” for Hasan.

The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois has won the general election in the Canadian province of Quebec, securing a return to power without capturing an outright legislative majority.
"Being elected Premier of Quebec is an immense privilege and a huge responsibility -- one I accept with great humility," party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Monday on US social media platform X, declaring that his administration will "reach out to others" to serve all residents regardless of political background.
The party advocates national sovereignty to establish Quebec as an independent state from Canada.
With 99.98% of polling stations reporting, the Parti Quebecois garnered 28.02% of the popular vote and led in 59 districts, according to Elections Quebec data. The tally leaves the party five seats short of the 64-seat threshold needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly of Quebec, prompting CBC News to project a minority government.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney congratulated Premier-designate Plamondon, emphasizing federal cooperation on regional priorities.
"Building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," Carney said, adding that Ottawa seeks to collaborate with the incoming provincial government to support local enterprises affected by trade tariffs, generate employment, and expand housing construction across the province.
Carney also thanked Frechette for her service to Quebec and Canada.
