Outgoing president: My chances to serve Estonia will be even better as ex-head of state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:03:00 UTC
17:03:00 KST

Outgoing president: My chances to serve Estonia will be even better as ex-head of state
President Alar Karis tells ERR in an interview that while he plans to take some time to reflect after leaving office, his calendar is already beginning to fill up and he intends to continue working on issues related to AI and technology.
One more week and you'll be at your country home by the Piusa River where Sirje Karis is already waiting for you and you'll start working your way through all the books you left unfinished or didn't get around to reading at all over the past five years. What can the president still accomplish in these final seven days?
The final days are a time to thank the people you've worked and traveled alongside. I've also recently completed my farewell visits to neighboring countries, the last of which was to see the king of Sweden. That's part of leaving office. A portrait has also been completed and I'll be shown it during my final week. It will be hung in Kadriorg.
So this is a big week of giving thanks for you?
In many ways, yes. You should thank people all the time, not just during your final week, but it's part of being an outgoing president — looking back a little and remembering the people you worked with.
From the outside, it seems that you grew increasingly comfortable in the presidency and that you grew into the role organically. Your most recent Independence Day speech this year was certainly one of your most memorable and could even be read as something of a testament. Are you a little sorry to leave, especially considering it was your own idea that a president could serve a single seven-year term? Perhaps the best years would only be starting now.
It's hard to say whether they would have been the best years because routine sets in whether the term is five years or seven. A lot of things repeat themselves. But yes, you look back a little and also think about what you could have done differently. The time isn't really ripe for that yet, though.
I've often held positions that I've left voluntarily rather than because I was forced to, so this isn't particularly painful. It's simply one chapter coming to an end and time will tell what the next one brings.
The arrival and departure of presidents always attracts a lot of interest. When did you actually know that you wouldn't seek another term? You said when you took office that it would be a one-time thing. Did you never reconsider, with your Victory Day speech simply making the decision official?
I left the door open a little. I said that a small miracle would have to happen for me to agree to run again. In the spring, political parties also started coming to see me and suggesting that I continue. So I gave it one more thought.
You have to announce that you're not running at the right time: You can't say it too early, but you can't say it too late either because the new president needs enough time to prepare for the job. Announcing it too early can also cause problems. I think Tony Blair said about a year in advance that he would no longer be party leader and after that nobody talked to him anymore. Everyone started looking around him to see where the new jobs would be.
So the miracle didn't happen?
I wouldn't want to make too much of that miracle; it was more of a metaphor. But I really did reconsider one more time before announcing my final decision in an understated way at the parade.
There's an old saying: lose an illusion, gain an experience. What illusions have been shattered for you over these five years and what have you personally learned from the experience?
I'll pick up on the word "experience." The biggest thing — I wouldn't call it a disappointment — was discovering that experience isn't really needed much in this job. You can share it with people who aren't directly involved in politics or who don't affect your day-to-day life as president. But generally, everyone has their own ideas and perhaps someday it will be possible to talk about how much that experience was put to use and how much it wasn't.
Why, then, is nobody interested in what a person has been through in life and the experience they have accumulated? Is everyone playing their own tune?
Everyone is in their own bubble with their own ideas and everyone wants to put those ideas forward. In my view, the biggest problem today is that no one has time to think and, unfortunately, no time to listen either. Put those two things together and no one knows what to do with experience.
Who's taking that time away from us? Weren't you able to set aside Mondays or Tuesdays when the president could read in his office without being disturbed?
I was, but then someone walks through the door and says, "I see you've got a gap in your calendar today." Everyone makes the case that their issue is important and in fact it is important — the president doesn't really deal with trivial matters. But there are so many of them and I have to say that I wasn't always able to create those gaps for myself.
I stole a few days here and there, for example in the summer when everything is quiet. But as for the president having a week or two of vacation, the Estonian president doesn't get that, although our neighbors do.
It seems to me that this came as a surprise to you: It's a job where you get into the carriage and it just keeps hurtling along with no other option. A university rector, at least, has somewhere he can reflect on things, gaze at the stars and listen to his heart.
A rector is still the master of his own time. He makes his own decisions, takes responsibility for them and knows what he's going to say and where. A president doesn't have that freedom. He serves the country in the most literal sense and has to do what the president of Estonia does. That's inherent in the office. Whether getting into a carriage is the right metaphor is another question, but you certainly have to keep moving all the time.
Despite having no time and everyone waiting at your door, Toomas Mattson undertook the task of compiling your writings from quite a long period into a major volume for the "History of Estonian Thought" series. It's a very substantial book, perhaps the largest ever published in the series.
Among Estonia's presidents, only Lennart Meri has previously been represented in the series, with several volumes of his speeches and his political testament. Now you're in it as well. When you looked through the series during your spare moments at Kadriorg, did you ever wonder why it doesn't include the statesmen and politicians who have been given a mandate by the people to exercise public authority?
I did. I have a bookshelf in the Blue Room. It doesn't contain every volume, but there's a very long row of them. I look them over from time to time and there are historical figures from the Estonian state represented there. I wasn't particularly keen on doing this myself because it's a very serious series and the thickness of a book alone isn't enough to warrant inclusion. Since people thought I should be included, I agreed, but I said I wouldn't interfere: Go ahead and do it and make the selections yourselves. Even in 1,000 pages, it doesn't contain everything I've ever written or said. It's a selection.
More volumes can always be added. Historically speaking, the series does indeed include a lot of people, but I'm thinking about the present day — the people who are active now and determining the country's future. We don't see them publishing books or thinking about these issues on a somewhat higher intellectual level.
Siim Kallas just had a book published in the same series, so perhaps we'll start seeing more now. Maybe I wasn't self-critical enough — although I'm relatively self-critical — to say that I don't belong in this series yet. Let someone compile a volume after I've passed into eternity. But this is how it turned out. The book has been done a little differently. We live in the age of artificial intelligence, so AI-generated summaries have also been included. It's simply a sign of the times. Since Toomas Mattson wanted to do it this way, I gave him free rein.
Your colleague Alexander Stubb in Finland published a very substantial book-length essay at the beginning of the year. Its title could perhaps be translated into Estonian as "The Triangle of Power" or "The New World Balance." What I have in mind is that an active politician is also participating in intellectual debate and contributing new ideas. What would we need to reach that level here as well?
That brings us back to the fact that before Stubb became president, he had time. He made the time to write and put his thoughts down on paper, producing material that could be published as books. He gave me an autographed copy of his book, with a rather large inscription and I leafed through it. It contains many interesting ideas that, as an active politician and president, he might not express quite so openly and boldly. In that sense, it's an interesting book to read.
Was this cleared with Hando Runnel — publishing AI-generated material in the "History of Estonian Thought" series? There's actually quite a substantial amount of AI-generated text in it. What did the poet say?
The poet didn't say anything to me, but I assume he gave his approval. You can always debate whether an AI-generated summary needed to be included after every article; perhaps one at the end would have been enough. But as I said, I gave the editor free rein, so I assume he obtained the necessary approvals.
Have you ever derived any profound literary or intellectual pleasure from an AI-generated text — thinking, "Now that was a good piece of writing"?
In a negative sense, yes. You look at it and see just how ridiculous a text can be. I used AI myself a couple of years ago for a speech marking the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' anniversary: I had AI write the first part and watched to see how the audience reacted. During speeches, people usually just sit and listen, but then I told them that part had been written by AI and that now my own text would begin. Everyone is experimenting with it, including with music. This is a period of experimentation when everyone is trying to figure out what the downsides are and how it can be put to positive use.
What's your overall sense of it? Have your five years in office also been characterized, in some sense, by the explosive emergence of AI? It's everywhere now. You've always been optimistic about progress — new opportunities in science and technology, grabbing the bull by the horns and forging ahead. Are you still an optimist?
I am. We know from history that the Luddites, the machine breakers, didn't get very far. I've had a similar experience in my own fields of developmental biology and molecular genetics. In the 1970s and 1980s, the fear was so great that scientists even gathered in California and asked: What are we doing? We're capable of playing God — where will all this lead? Scientists and politicians then came together, regulations and laws were introduced and ethical issues were examined because technology makes far more possible than what is actually put into practice. Technologies generally have limits; they don't develop endlessly.
What's frightening today is that everyone has this new technology in their pocket. It's precisely the speed of it that creates a certain amount of anxiety.
In your 2025 Independence Day speech, you called for a major leap forward in education: bringing AI into schools and having all students and teachers experiment with it. That has nevertheless drawn considerable criticism. It hasn't all gone smoothly and there are many questions surrounding it. Does AI actually help anyone learn or become more knowledgeable or does it end up doing the work itself and put an end to learning?
I believe there are many different sides to it when it comes to teaching children and training teachers as well. But what can we do? We can ignore it, we can switch it off or we can try to find as many positive uses for the technology as possible because it isn't going anywhere. There may be a stock market crash in the business world, but the technology itself will remain. We have to determine what it can do and — most importantly — where it doesn't need to be used. AI doesn't have to be used in schools either.
Is there anywhere it shouldn't be used? Is there anything you would consider off-limits? There's been discussion here that AI thinks better, solves math problems better and will build our houses for us — and in the end, it'll be a better lawyer too.
In some ways, perhaps the fine arts. But we know from history that electronic music has been made before as well. We're seeing the strongest backlash from people in creative fields because they see soulless music, soulless poetry and soulless works of art being produced. Today, even speeches are being written using AI.
But a presidential speech is still the real thing?
It's still the real thing. AI hasn't been used in them. Even if you do use it, you still have to go over the result using your own brain. It's very difficult to say because everything is developing so quickly. A year earlier, I had already said in a presidential speech: Look at what's in your pocket and learn how to use it. There wasn't much reaction at the time, so I had to get more hands-on myself and get something started.
You were recently in New York and gave a speech at the U.N. I understand that you also briefly crossed paths there with Jaan Tallinn who has prominently warned us about the risks and dangers, including fears that the world could soon come to an end. Did you ask Mr. Tallinn what he's afraid of?
Everyone has fears, Jaan Tallinn especially, because he has been involved in this himself and knows how it works. But as with genetic engineering, those fears may not come to pass. I spoke about AI at several events and this particular one brought together some of the more pessimistic voices. I tried to bring some positive light into the room. That's how it is: There are views on both sides and eventually we'll find a middle ground where AI is used sensibly. And as I said, it doesn't always have to be used.
I could talk at length about my past laboratory work where expensive machines were purchased and people tried to run scientific hypotheses through a particular machine. A great deal depends on the teacher, just as it did before AI and just as it does in the age of AI. That's why we started with teachers: to give them an understanding of what AI is today.
We all value our teachers and the work they do is extremely important. As president, your primary tool is your voice; the president's office doesn't have a large budget. But teachers have faced serious financial difficulties and they've made those concerns very clear over the past five years.
Looking at it from the outside, it's difficult to understand how, on the one hand, there isn't a cent to spare, while on the other, tens of millions go somewhere and nobody quite understands where the money went. How do those proportions look from Kadriorg? There's never enough money for teachers, cultural workers and others, while somewhere else the amount of money being spent just keeps growing.
With large sums of money, there are often strings attached: The money can only be used for the purpose for which it was allocated. What often happens is that the goal becomes spending the money no matter what and the result is that it isn't spent very wisely.
When it comes to teachers, I may be somewhat biased because my daughter is a teacher and I hear about their concerns. Salary is understandably important, but I see the real problems as lying elsewhere. The workload is enormous, especially for a young teacher and it isn't just about preparing lessons. There are also parents whose expectations for their children are extremely high and all of that gets channeled through the teacher. I think workload is the primary issue and should be addressed first and then salaries need to be reviewed. In reality, salaries are never quite enough because our desires and aspirations grow even when our salaries aren't particularly low.
Thinking about teachers and your idea of a "wise nation," which you've championed from the very beginning, you've said that you know only one path forward in life and that's the path of education. On the other hand, in your last major speech you said that, from the outside, Estonians may appear energetic and capable and the country may seem to be functioning well, but our souls are cold and there is a great deal of hidden loneliness and isolation. People don't feel included in society. Leaving the numbers aside, where does this profound sense of loneliness come from?
There is a sense of being left behind in Estonia, but not only in Estonia; it's the same in other countries. Perhaps it comes from the fact that somewhere we have people making decisions about the country who march to their own beat and forget that our people are out there and that our people aren't all alike. It's biodiversity — people are very different. If you move forward only with those who are at the forefront, who think ahead and love technology, then they'll do well in life. But there are people who aren't doing well, not because they can't be bothered to do anything, but because they've been caught in life's gears. We see this regionally as well. There's always someone who will pick them up and start influencing them, including through social media.
Focusing on just one segment of society isn't always the best approach, although I see politicians saying that of course they're engaging with everyone, going here, there and everywhere. Unfortunately, this indicator has continued to decline.
Perhaps this is the president's role: When it comes to foreign policy and standing up for Estonia, we aren't alone. We have many friendly countries and their presidents who do a great deal for us. But domestic issues in Estonia are something only the Estonian president deals with and I've tried to hold the pieces together as much as possible so that it doesn't all fall apart.
What gives us inner strength and restores us? Do you have your own prescription for coping with the sadness that can sometimes overcome us, especially now, with fall approaching?
November is probably the bleakest month when it's dark and there isn't any snow yet. But I think people actually tend to have these problems in the spring when everything is beautiful but they may not feel like doing anything. Everyone should find something to do. Sometimes our relationship with time seems paradoxical: A person feels lonely, yet has no time. The worst thing is to feel lonely among other people. But being on your own, taking that time and thinking — I find that restorative. Or reading a book and putting on some music. That certainly lifts my spirits.
Although I do let things affect me and take them to heart. I don't show it, but sometimes even the smallest thing can bring a tear to my eye.
Here's another trend from these five years: Thousands of children who might otherwise have been born haven't been, the numbers keep falling and people are sounding the alarm. The trend remains negative and we know this is a broader phenomenon. But looking specifically at Estonia, what do you think is the best explanation for why this is happening?
People have tried to explain it in all sorts of ways, but I don't have a particularly good answer either. Estonians might take some comfort from the fact that things are even worse in Latvia, but the problem is actually serious: The population keeps shrinking. It's easy for me to talk — I have three children and six grandchildren — but you can't force anyone to have children. The desire has to come from within and the broader environment should encourage that inner desire. One thing I definitely don't want to do is blame everything on the war in Ukraine. It's a combination of many things: anxiety about the future and perhaps the future of AI affects some people as well. These kinds of troubling factors always tend to coincide.
Another reason is that we want to live well at last. We want a life free of worries where we don't have to worry about what will happen to our child or whether they'll get into the right school or kindergarten. Perhaps it's easier to get a cat and a dog and then life is a little less stressful. This is a feature of an affluent society and it's a general problem in the Western world: We want to live better and better and we don't want to worry anymore. We're even talking now about how students shouldn't have to work all that hard at school. But learning requires effort and you have to make that effort because at some point you encounter real life and the rules there are entirely different. You have to be prepared for that.
You're a grandfather several times over yourself and your youngest grandchild was born just this spring. It's important for parents to have a support network — someone they can call and someone who will come and look after the baby. As grandparents, have you and your wife had a chance to bounce the little one on your knee? Have you had time to babysit so the parents can go to a concert or spend a little time reading?
There will probably be more time for that now because both my children and my grandchildren have largely grown up relatively independently. In one sense, that's good for children: They enter the world early and have to learn to manage on their own. Their mother and father have always had a lot of work. But this spring, my daughter — the same one who's a teacher — had a baby who turned seven months old yesterday. We've been to see them and perhaps now we'll have more time to worry as well.
As you get older, you start worrying more about your children and grandchildren. Life experience teaches you everything that can go wrong: When you're watching a small child, you notice a sharp corner over there, something else over here. It wears you out and you don't quite know how to play with them in the same way. I had my children when I was young and back then there wasn't time to think about those kinds of fears.
Let me return to the subject of books. I don't know whether you even managed to visit the National Library of Estonia as president. I think its doors had only been open for a matter of months when you took office and they've been closed (for renovation — ed.) ever since. I mean as a user. Aren't you the first president since Estonia regained independence who hasn't been able to set foot in it?
I've been there several times. The building isn't completely finished yet, but events are being held there. I've been given several tours and the archives are there as well. It's an impressive building. When I used to go there in the past, it somehow felt depressing and dark; even the ceiling was dark. Now everything is white and bright and the atmosphere is completely different.
It was supposed to reopen several years ago, so we should all be using it by now. I remember asking you five years ago whether we would celebrate the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra's centenary in a new concert hall. The Tallinn-Tartu rail project is dragging on just as it was five years ago. When you put all of that together, doesn't it seem to you that things have ground to a halt? Everything gets started and then it drags on and gets bogged down, the doors stay closed and people have to go somewhere else.
The comforting thing is that it's like this everywhere. Look at the Sydney Opera House: That project dragged on, too, ended up costing several times more than planned and the architect, who actually designed a magnificent building, even fell out of favor. Now we look at it as a great wonder. That's how these things go. As for the railway, I said back in 2016 that it wouldn't be completed on schedule, that it would end up costing several times more and that we should think about where the money would come from. Now 10 years have passed. I'm not trying to play oracle; you only have to look around to see that things aren't moving. We tend to argue over many things, we can't agree on anything and eventually people get tired and projects are put on hold. That's especially true of the concert hall, the opera house and the library as well.
I believe the library will eventually open and all the books will be brought together there nicely. I'm the kind of person who buys a book if I want it. I'm not much of a library person. I have sometimes used online libraries for specialist literature, but if I really want to read something, I want to have it on my shelf at home.
That's a privilege you have; not everyone can afford that. Books, incidentally, are becoming increasingly expensive. Even the book I have here now is from the library because its retail price is fairly steep. That's not to say it isn't worth paying for.
I certainly don't want to come across as being against libraries — quite the opposite. I've visited many small communities that have small libraries. They're wonderful places and people don't just read books there; they discuss books and do all sorts of other things. They're extremely important institutions.
Speaking about the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra five years ago, you said something along the lines of, "I'll try to make the case for that hall as well." Nothing has come of it and apparently nothing will for some time yet. More broadly, over these five years we've moved toward a world of power politics; it's been a time of war. It feels as though noble ideals and faith in the power of words get pushed aside when the strongmen arrive and start carving up the world. What's your own sense of it? How much can words actually accomplish in today's world when, generally speaking, power seems to be what counts?
I believe power has always mattered. Perhaps it simply wasn't as visible before as it is today. It's inevitable that the big countries lead the world, even though most of the world's countries are smaller states. The question is how that power is exercised. This isn't the best of times. It's more of a confused period in which the old world order no longer really applies and a new one hasn't yet been devised. That means countries the size of Estonia have to be extremely vigilant. But that doesn't mean you always have to speak loudly and forcefully everywhere. Diplomacy can also be conducted differently and sometimes more effectively than going on CNN every other week and repeating the same message. We have to combine all the options available to us.
As I understand it, you've even turned down some CNN interviews recently, believing or proceeding on the assumption that your words wouldn't carry much weight anyway?
No, I didn't say that my words don't carry weight. It probably comes from my scientific background: I want to say something new each time rather than repeat what's already been said. Although I know that in politics, constant repetition is itself a source of power.
But I'm not alone. In foreign policy, the balance of responsibility actually lies with the prime minister. The prime minister attends NATO meetings and European Council meetings, especially now, since the war in Ukraine began. So I've tried to find another kind of policy, another way of making Estonia bigger.
That alternative policy remained somewhat mysterious to the public. It was never entirely clear what it was supposed to mean. Is there something about your presidency that still weighs on you — that you tried, as president, to establish yourself and find your place on the foreign policy stage, but that effort ultimately failed?
I don't believe anything failed. This is where education comes into play again: You can say the same thing in very different words. The music is the same, the melody is the same, only the lyrics are different. I never got the sense that this was understood. But I wouldn't call it a failure. What I did — taking people from the cultural sector out into the wider world together with businesspeople, for example — created an entirely new way of thinking. They met abroad and wondered why they hadn't met more often back in Estonia because bringing them together generates so many good ideas.
This kind of soft diplomacy has somehow been pushed into the background, even though, to be fair, its impact can sometimes be considerably greater.
So during those visits, you were able to make connections behind the scenes and advance Estonia's interests in ways the public perhaps never fully saw?
The public does see it, but the public isn't particularly interested. When the president travels to other countries with people from the cultural and business sectors, opens doors for them or helps open those doors — something they're all grateful for afterward — it doesn't make headlines. Journalists aren't interested because there's no conflict and you have to accept that. It wouldn't be difficult to go abroad and start squabbling in public — with our prime minister and foreign minister, for example — but then you have to ask what that would mean for Estonia. There are plenty of countries where the prime minister and president don't get along in public.
Instead, we should look at countries whose systems are structured similarly to ours, such as Germany and many others. Nobody would say that Steinmeier, who has served twice as foreign minister, knows nothing about foreign policy, yet he conducts himself in a way relatively similar to the president of Estonia.
These five years also saw the unveiling of a monument to Konstantin Päts behind the Estonia Theater where you also gave a speech. The 150th anniversary of Päts' birth also fell during this period, but you didn't attend the Bank of Estonia's major event commemorating Päts. Peep Jahilo, then head of the Office of the President, attended to represent you.
I won't go into what kind of figure Päts was, but how much have you thought about Päts and Tõnisson and all those other names who were here in Estonia on the eve of World War II? When the war in Ukraine began — and it did come as a major shock — how much did you think about what could actually happen and have you ever felt fear in your heart during this period?
Not fear as such, but understandably, as head of state, you find yourself thinking about these things and looking at the parallels with the past and with the war in Ukraine today. We cannot afford a war like the one in Ukraine. I've often said: Take a pair of scissors, cut out the areas that are currently under Russian control and place them over a map of Estonia. Then you'll see that we cannot fight a war like that because Estonia would simply cease to exist. So we have to be a little more clever and think about how to prevent such a war.
As for Päts' era, my mother was born during Päts' time and there was plenty of talk about Päts at home, including idealized stories. But every president belongs to his own time and Päts belonged to his, with his own flaws and virtues. He was the president of our country. You can't simply ignore him, but nor can you accuse him of selling Estonia to Soviet Russia. These things aren't that simple.
Estonia's presidents have maintained a certain distance from Päts. I'm thinking again of that major ceremonial event at the Bank of Estonia: Was it preferable to send the head of the president's office rather than attend yourself?
I wouldn't say that's how it was. I only just read in the newspaper that I had avoided attending the opening of a factory. These things aren't that simple. It's easy to write a headline, but there are other obligations that require you to be somewhere else and do other things. I haven't avoided anything. I'm not afraid of uncomfortable meetings or events and an event at the central bank isn't an uncomfortable event.
That brings us briefly back to foreign policy. In foreign affairs, we like engaging with like-minded countries. It's pleasant company; we all think alike. But in my view, we need to pay more attention to those with whom we have some disagreements as well. Things may look different from their perspective, but we need to listen and then explain how we see the world.
In the spring, you said we'd heated the sauna too hot. Now that you're about to hand over the presidency, how would you assess the situation? Has the temperature in the sauna come down or are all our backs still red?
It's more like a smoke sauna: You keep heating it for quite a while and it stays warm for a long time too. But I think things will heat up again when we have the Riigikogu election in spring 2027. I've called for civility, although I know civility isn't much of a match for aggressive politics. But if you're taught at home to be polite, that should stay with you.
What comes next for you? Looking at Estonia's recent presidents, they've all sought, in one way or another, some kind of international role, without much success. Will you head to the Piusa River, reflect on your experiences by the Härma sandstone outcrop and write your memoirs? Or might there still be someone interested in all the experience you've now accumulated?
I think there will be. I also need time to sit and think and that's precisely what I've been missing in this job. I'll certainly make use of that time, but my calendar is already filling up. This summer, I joined the U.N.'s "AI for Good" commission, which brings together all the giants who are concerned about the future right now, whether Microsoft, OpenAI, Google and so on. I'll try to bring to it the experience we're gaining here from our AI Leap initiative and, in turn, bring international experience back here. Technology and innovation in general continue to interest me, as does their intersection with politics.
I'm fairly convinced that as a former president, I may actually have better opportunities to serve Estonia than I do now as president.
Your painted portrait will also be unveiled at the presidential palace this week. This isn't the first time you've had this kind of official portrait painted; you've long had one at the University of Tartu from your time as rector. You won't be staying to look at this portrait — the people who come after you will. In what situations might they look at it and what advice might your portrait offer them?
I haven't seen the portrait myself yet. Just as I didn't interfere with the book, I didn't interfere with the portrait either. I don't like interfering with the work of professionals: They do their job and ultimately it's their name on it. This is the third painting of me and they're probably all very different. I expect this one will be different as well. Since all of this is, so to speak, for after I'm gone and I'll probably visit Kadriorg very rarely in the future, I imagine some tour groups will look at it. The portraits of the presidents at Kadriorg are also very different from one another.
We're coming to the end of our conversation and you'll soon be able to get on with your week, but we still have Alar Karis' cultural recommendation to hear.
That's always the hardest question: what book to recommend or what work to suggest listening to. I've always said that you should try to seek out variety, especially in today's world where so much of what we read and listen to is presented to us. Don't assume that because you've finished one book, you should pick up another one just like it. Find opportunities to read very different things. The same applies to music. It will be better for us and for our peace of mind and we'll gain a better sense of the world around us.
We should listen to young people who are only just beginning their cultural journeys as artists, composers or performers. We've seen the caliber of artists Estonia has produced; some have already become internationally renowned.
--

Top OpenAI boss on hack apology tour 'can't explain' Australian AI distrust
Unknown

2026-10-06

OpenAI executive flew to Australia to apologise over Medicare hack. Here are the key takeaways
A top OpenAI executive who flew to Australia to mop up after the company's Medicare statistics hack said he could not explain why Australians are among the world's most distrustful of AI.
Chief strategy officer Jason Kwon made the comments to the ABC as he left a parliamentary inquiry into AI, in his first public appearance since the prime minister revealed the hack late last month.
Mr Kwon pledged to rebuild trust after the hack, while the company's handling of its disclosure drew criticism from the federal government.
After touting Australia's adoption rate of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Mr Kwon did not have an answer for why some polls show that a majority of the nation does not trust the technology, a higher proportion than in most other countries.
"I can't explain the current sentiment; all we can do is continue to get better," he said.
OpenAI says it made changes to prevent future hacks
Mr Kwon said OpenAI now alerts staff when its models use the internet in ways they should not during training.
But he acknowledged OpenAI should have told the Australian government about the Medicare hack sooner, rather than waiting to establish more facts.
He said the company identified the NSW Parks and Wildlife breach last week and reported it to the state government much sooner.
Mr Kwon also added that chief executive Sam Altman had not known about it when he met Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles on September 1, despite company staff having first found out about the hack several weeks prior.
While in Australia, Mr Kwon will interview several people for OpenAI's promised "taskforce" to help guide its own response to the hack, a spokesperson told the ABC this afternoon.
Anthropic would have told Australia if it had done the hack
Representatives of rival AI company Anthropic told the committee that it would have made a similar disclosure if it had discovered its technology had hacked another company.
The company also backed a proposal floated by the federal government's Office of AI that would require AI developers to report serious safety incidents, saying its current reporting commitments were largely voluntary.
Anthropic representatives also said it was finalising a deal to let Australia's AI Safety Institute independently test its models.
Its international envoy, former US ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich, told the committee that the company wants to train its AI in Australia.
But he said Australia's current copyright regime was an obstacle that needed to change, regardless of any licensing deals it might sign.
"You can't license the entire internet,"
he said.
Anthropic has not publicly disclosed signing any licensing deals in Australia.
Creatives and rights holders reject claims status quo isn't working
Groups representing musicians, writers and voice actors rejected calls to loosen copyright laws to attract AI investment, accusing the companies of taking their work without permission.
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd warned that such a deal would threaten Australia's music industry.
"Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," she told the committee.
The groups argued that AI companies could already seek permission and pay to use creative work under existing copyright law.
They also said members were not just after payment but also control over whether AI companies would train on their work.
"The idea that payment is the only thing we're haggling about is a step in the wrong direction," Australian Writers' Guild executive director Claire Pullen said.
Big tech's old guard warns against drastic regulation
Later in the day, both Google and Microsoft appeared before the committee urging a less catastrophic approach to regulating the technology.
Microsoft said Australia should build on its existing laws, including privacy and anti-discrimination protections, updating them where needed and adopting AI standards that work across borders.
Google also called for common industry standards and rules that work across borders, warning against duplication while saying AI was too important not to regulate.
The committee is set to have another hearing in Sydney tomorrow.

How to catch up with the school curriculum amid "gaps" caused by air-raid alerts - Ministry of Education released a guide
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Education and Science presented a guide to help overcome students’ learning losses caused by lessons interrupted by air-raid alerts. It contains steps for assessment and support.
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine has released a guide on addressing learning losses among students, which arise, in particular, due to interruptions to lessons during air raids, UNN reports.
Details
"Air raids interrupt lessons, forcing changes to the schedule and learning formats. Under such conditions, students may experience various learning difficulties, so it is important for teachers to identify them promptly and determine exactly what assistance is needed," the ministry said in a post.
The Ministry of Education and Science presented on cards the key steps for addressing learning losses: from diagnosing learning needs to planning support, selecting assignments, and monitoring progress. This is expected to "help identify priorities and work with specific gaps."
Reminder
Schools in Kyiv operate according to individual adaptive algorithms that take into account various scenarios for the development of the security situation. In particular, during remote learning, an air raid does not mean the automatic end of a lesson—the class is paused for the time students and the teacher need to move to a safer location, after which it can be continued.

Türkiye sets record for solar, wind power generation in August
Unknown

2026-10-06

17:01:00 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye’s combined electricity generation from solar and wind power reached a record 9.9 billion kilowatt-hours in August, the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry said on Oct. 6.
Solar power generation totaled 5.16 billion kilowatt-hours in August, accounting for 14.1 percent of total electricity generation, while wind power generation stood at 4.74 billion kilowatt-hours, with a 12.9 percent share.
Combined electricity generation from solar and wind marked an all-time monthly high.
Total electricity generation in August stood at 36.71 billion kilowatt-hours, with hydropower maintaining its position as the largest source of generation.
Hydropower accounted for 24.7 percent of total generation, producing 9.08 billion kilowatt-hours during the month.
According to the data, renewable energy sources accounted for 56.4 percent of total electricity generation, with 20.7 billion kilowatt-hours in August.
Domestic energy sources accounted for 69.7 percent, corresponding to 25.58 billion kilowatt-hours.
In the January-August period, hydropower generation reached 75.2 billion kilowatt-hours, wind power generation totaled 30.4 billion kilowatt-hours and solar power generation stood at 29.8 billion kilowatt-hours.
All three sources recorded their highest generation levels for the January-August period since 2000.
Electricity generation from domestic sources reached 181.8 billion kilowatt-hours, accounting for 73.2 percent of total generation, while renewable sources produced 149.8 billion kilowatt-hours, representing 60.3 percent of total generation.
“Both figures were the highest levels recorded in terms of volume and share for the same period since 2000,” the ministry said.

Israel was prepared to shoot down flydubai jet during hijacking attempt - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:00:56 UTC
17:00:56 KST

Israel was prepared to shoot down flydubai flight FZ 1073 during last Wednesday's suspected hijacking attempt, despite 166 Israeli passengers being aboard the aircraft, two Israeli sources with direct knowledge of the incident told CBS News on Monday.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot attacked the captain in the cockpit and attempted to crash the aircraft.
After the aircraft plunged 14,000 feet, the Israel Air Force attempted to contact the cockpit but received no response, CBS News reported. Israeli authorities activated a long-established procedure for dealing with a potentially hostile civilian aircraft, convening a predetermined committee and establishing a command center.
Israel scrambled fighter jets and closed its airspace; jets were later recalled after authorities determined that the aircraft, while about 400 miles from Israel, had turned toward Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia then scrambled its own fighter jets.
The captain managed to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door, allowing Israeli passengers and flydubai staff to overpower the alleged attacker. Two off-duty pilots traveling aboard the flight then took control of the aircraft and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Passengers were later brought back to Israel on a flydubai rescue flight that landed at Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday evening.
Israel's protocol for a suspected hijacking
Had flight 1073 continued toward Israel and reached a predetermined distance, Israeli fighter jets would have entered Jordanian airspace to investigate the aircraft, the two sources told CBS News.
The fighter pilots would have flown as close as possible to the passenger plane, attempting to visually inspect the cockpit and establish contact with the pilot. They would then examine the cabin from the air for signs of panic or other indications that control of the aircraft had been seized.
Their assessment would have been relayed to the Air Force and the committee overseeing the incident, the sources said.
If authorities concluded that the aircraft had been hijacked, while those controlling it continued to maintain radio silence and made no demands, the defense minister and prime minister would have been brought into the decision-making process to make the final call.
Notably, during a meeting of the Intelligence Subcommittee of the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, it was revealed that since the beginning of the year, more than 1,200 aviation crew members from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel have entered the country, including Syria, Lebanon, and Oman.
Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant

Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant
Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry.
Located in the city's Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building.
Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners' Catalan roots through their restaurant design.
"Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language," studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen.
In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood.
The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster.
"We drew inspiration from the energy of rural churches, dark woods and the movement of traditional fans," explained Romano and Cazenave de la Roche.
"We did not want these references to be literal, but rather to emerge through materials, textures and forms."
Classic, bentwood chairs feature alongside uniform timber tables. In one corner, a red-clad banquette subtly nods to traditional Parisian bistros.
All of the space's joinery was conceived bespoke for the restaurant by a Marseille-based carpenter and frequent collaborator of Bétyle Studio.
"We worked with different species of wood and experimented with various techniques to stain, ebonise and patinate the timber," said Romano and Cazenave de la Roche.
"The idea was to give depth to the surfaces and create elements that feel as though they could have belonged to the space for a long time."
Local studio Côme Clérino designed a selection of chunky plaster sconces specifically for the restaurant that loosely resemble elongated seashells.
Founded in January 2025, Bétyle Studio works across interior architecture and furniture design. Last year, the studio transformed an old farm building in Marseille into a compact, wood-lined home.
Elsewhere in Paris, architect Cyrus Ardalan recently renovated a corner apartment with a timber-heavy interior, complete with porthole-style openings designed to feel nautical.
The photography is by Axel Aurejac.

‘A return to prison is always looming’: Iran’s Nobel laureate recounts torture in jail and hopes for the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:00:06 UTC
17:00:06 KST

The human rights activist Narges Mohammadi has described being beaten so severely by Iranian security agents that she required two brain scans, before being held in solitary confinement for two months despite her grave injuries.
In an interview with the Guardian, the 54-year-old Nobel peace prize laureate said that during her arrest in December, security agents “inflicted extremely severe blows to my head and body.
“They grabbed and forcibly pulled me by my hair, kicking and punching me repeatedly with such force that massive, painful bruises covered my entire body,” she said.
Mohammadi suffered dizziness, nausea and vomiting in the days that followed, but said authorities refused to allow a forensic examination of her injuries. “Despite the severe physical injuries and trauma I sustained, I was immediately transferred to a solitary confinement cell,” she said.
“During the first few days in solitary confinement I was completely dazed and confused, had severe dizziness, was nauseous and was vomiting. They sent me from the detention centre twice for a brain CT scan in a hospital,” she said. “Despite this, they were not willing to allow the forensic medical examiner to come and prepare a report on my injuries.”
Mohammadi was temporarily released from prison for medical treatment in May, after being found unconscious in her cell after a cardiac arrest. She said she feared that another imprisonment could endanger her life.
“A return to prison is always looming,” she said. “Truthfully, it is a dangerous prospect. Imprisonment left me with severe physical damage to my heart, lungs and nervous system – injuries that have demanded ongoing medical treatment, medication, physical therapy and rehabilitation since I was transferred from Zanjan to Tehran.
“My medical treatment is far from over, and being sent back to prison under these conditions poses a grave threat to my life,” she said.
Mohammadi, who was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 2023 for her “campaign against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight for human rights and freedom for all”, was arrested on 12 December 2025 while attending a memorial gathering for the human rights lawyer Khosrow Alikordi in the north-eastern city of Mashhad.
In February, a court sentenced her to a further seven and a half years in prison and two years of internal exile to the town of Khosf. She was subsequently transferred to Zanjan prison.
Over the years, Mohammadi has endured 14 arrests, 10 trials and five periods of solitary confinement. She said her health had deteriorated further after multiple operations over the past decade, after which she was repeatedly returned from hospital to prison.
Her experiences of imprisonment and resistance also form the basis of her latest memoir, A Woman Never Stops Fighting, published last month. Written in secret during her incarceration, with fragments of the manuscript smuggled out of Iran with the help of fellow prisoners and trusted contacts, the book offers an intimate account of her struggle for human rights and the sacrifices that have accompanied it, including her prolonged separation from her children.
Beyond the physical injuries, Mohammadi described the psychological toll of prolonged isolation, which she characterised as “white torture”.
In a cell with nobody to speak to, nothing to embrace and no connection to the world beyond its walls, she said, even a prisoner’s sense of identity could begin to erode.
“When you are cut off from your family and surrounding environment … a person’s perceptions undergo a kind of distortion,” she said.
However, Mohammadi said her most painful doubts concerned not her political beliefs but the price her activism had exacted on her children during her incarceration. Alone in her cell, she says she repeatedly thought about her twins, Ali and Kiana, and whether her responsibilities as a mother should have taken precedence over the struggle for human rights.
“Was my duty to take care of Ali and Kiana, not leave them alone and ensure they had a mother?” she recalled asking herself. “Or was it human rights activism … the goals we hold in our hearts, like freedom, justice, democracy, human rights and lasting peace?”
Her children had seen her being arrested three times – when they were just three, five and eight years old – and she witnessed their distress each time. “In these harsh conditions, to be honest, I rarely doubted my ideals, my convictions, or whether or not I should have carried out these activities,” she said.
“But the truth is, when I thought about Ali and Kiana and what they suffered in my absence as a mother, what happened to them during the moments of my arrests … I thought about what happens to the minds and psychological wellbeing of such very young children when they drag me away before their eyes, and whether my children deserved to experience such escalating violence.”
Her account comes as Iran continues to grapple with the aftermath of the deadly crackdown on nationwide protests in January, alongside war and worsening economic hardship.
Mohammadi, who was imprisoned during the January violence, said she had since learned of the scale of the repression and was particularly alarmed by the treatment of detained protesters.
“What terrifies me most is the speed and intensity of the executions – carried out after trials stripped of due process, legal representation and fundamental fairness – inflicting relentless wounds on our society,” she said.
She warned that ordinary Iranians were facing mounting pressure from domestic repression, external conflict and deteriorating living conditions.
“The people’s economic situation is severely fractured; yet when they protest that they cannot survive under such dire conditions and political oppression, they are met with further violence,” she said.
Mohammadi is continuing to receive medical treatment after her transfer from Zanjan to Tehran. Despite the potential prospect of further imprisonment, she insisted she would remain in Iran and continue campaigning for human rights: “I have always chosen to stay in Iran, and I choose to stay even now.”
She said she continued to draw hope from younger Iranians, particularly women and young people. “They do not back down; they know their rights, understand them, strive to reach them and never relent,” she said.
“I have immense hope in younger generations, in the youth, and in women. I am certain that no power can erase hope from our hearts, and no power can sustain tyranny permanently.”

Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow region, injure nine more, governor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:53:49 UTC
16:53:49 KST

Ukrainian drones kill two, hit fuel hub in one of biggest attacks on Moscow region, Russian war bloggers say
Oct 6 - Ukrainian drones killed two people and hit a major fuel depot overnight in one of the biggest attacks of the war on Moscow and the surrounding region, Russian military bloggers said.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Ukraine had launched more than 650 drones towards the capital, most of which were shot down.
Andrei Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region which surrounds the capital, said that 185 Ukrainian drones had been destroyed or brought down over his region. He said seven people had been injured and that 47 houses, 4 apartments and 3 cars had been damaged.
Prominent war blogger Yuri Podolyaka said an oil storage tank was hit at the Volodarskaya oil storage and distribution facility, the biggest in the Moscow region. The facility stores diesel, gasoline and jet fuel. There was no official confirmation that it had been hit.
Volodarskaya is one of the major hubs in the distribution system of state pipeline monopoly Transneft and is linked to Moscow's main oil refinery. It supplies fuel to all three of the capital's large airports.
A Ukrainian war blog, Supernova+, published video purporting to show a huge blaze at the site. Reuters could not immediately verify it.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted oil refineries, depots and export terminals in an effort to deprive Moscow of the revenues it needs to finance the war that Russia began in February 2022.
Podolyaka and other Russian bloggers said, without citing evidence, that Ukraine's overnight attack was also intended to hit the Moscow oil refinery in the southeast of the capital, but that Russian air defences had prevented this.
The refinery, just inside the city ring road, has been hit several times, most recently on September 20, the main day of voting in Russia's parliamentary election.
Russia has recently intensified attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, sending waves of missiles and drones by night and day. Its latest targets have included bridges across the Dnipro river.
Vorobyov, the head of the Moscow region, said the body of a 71-year-old man had been pulled from under the rubble of a house and that a 20-year-old man had been killed in a nearby village.
The head of the town of Domodedovo, south of Moscow and home to the country's third-largest airport, said work was under way to restore electricity to villages that had been hit by drones. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Scientists finally see how nature moves energy so efficiently
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:49:51 UTC
16:49:51 KST

Scientists finally see how nature moves energy so efficiently
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
- Summary:
- Researchers have captured key steps in a chemical reaction that helps nature transfer energy with remarkable efficiency. Ultrafast X-rays revealed how changes involving electrons and protons are closely linked to the rearrangement of surrounding water molecules. Because similar reactions drive photosynthesis and other energy-conversion processes, the technique could help scientists develop better catalysts, fuel cells, and flow batteries.
- Share:
Some of the most important reactions in nature depend on positively and negatively charged particles moving in a coordinated way. These reactions are essential to processes such as photosynthesis, catalysis and biological energy conversion, but they happen so quickly that they are extremely difficult to observe.
A team led by the Department of Energy's Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, working with researchers at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and several universities, has now captured snapshots of these events after they are triggered by light striking a molecule.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, could deepen scientists' understanding of these reactions and eventually contribute to improved flow batteries, fuel cells and catalysts.
At the center of the study is the coordinated motion of positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. This type of energy transfer is among the most efficient known in nature. Plants use related processes to capture energy from sunlight and convert it into stored chemical energy.
When electrons and protons move in a coordinated way, molecules can avoid intermediate steps that would otherwise require more energy. That can make a reaction both faster and much more efficient. The researchers investigated how changes in a molecule's electronic structure, the arrival of a proton and shifts in the surrounding water environment are connected during this process.
Capturing a Reaction at the Molecular Level
Scientists have studied this interaction for decades, but no previous experiment had captured the process in a single study with both local and structural sensitivity. Advanced X-ray techniques at the Linac Coherent Light Source at SLAC, combined with state-of-the-art quantum chemistry calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, provided an unusually detailed view.
PNNL experimental chemical physicist Elisa Biasin, former PNNL scientist Abdullah Kahraman and PNNL theorists Niranjan (Niri) Govind and Amity Andersen worked with collaborators to study a light-driven proton-coupled electron transfer reaction, or PCET.
The team combined ultrafast X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray scattering and advanced simulations to capture important stages of the reaction. For the first time with structural sensitivity, the researchers were able to show how a molecule's electronic structure changes at specific locations as it gains a proton, while the surrounding water environment reorganizes at the same time.
"We have captured for the first time how electronic changes associated with proton transfer are coupled to reorganization of the surrounding solvent," said Biasin. "This gives us a new way to understand how molecules and their environments evolve together during fundamental chemical transformations."
Why Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer Matters
PCET plays an important role throughout nature. Plants rely on it during photosynthesis to harvest light, while animals use related processes to efficiently convert food into energy. It is also involved in many other forms of biological and chemical energy conversion.
For the particular experimental system examined in this study, researchers already understand the basic mechanism. But many questions remain about other PCET reactions, especially the precise timing and order in which electrons and protons move.
"Are they happening together or not? At which molecular site? And how is the water network facilitating the proton hop?" Biasin asked. "These are some of the possible open questions. To answer them, you need ultra-fast time resolution, chemical and structural sensitivity, and alignment with theory. We have made a step forward to shed light on these questions."
The new method gives researchers a way to investigate those questions more directly. The results show that local changes in electronic structure occur alongside a broader rearrangement of the surrounding water network as the molecule gains a proton.
Being able to examine these connected changes could eventually help researchers design more efficient catalysts, fuel cells, flow batteries and other technologies for converting and storing energy.
Following Electrons, Protons and Water
One major challenge is speed. Electrons move on extremely short timescales, and protons move nearly as fast. At the same time, water molecules surrounding the reacting molecules constantly shift and reorganize in ways that are notoriously difficult to observe directly.
Previous experiments could capture individual parts of this process, but they could not provide a combined picture of both the electronic changes inside the molecule and the reorganization occurring around it.
To create a system that would be easier to interpret, Biasin and her colleagues selected a well-studied ruthenium-based molecule. The molecule absorbs light and, in acidic conditions, captures a proton from its surroundings.
"We identified the metal complex used in this study because it does not undergo additional electronic and structural rearrangements that complicate interpretation of X-ray signals, allowing us to isolate signals associated with the electron, proton and solvent motion," said Christopher Larsen, a co-investigator and senior lecturer at the University of Aukland, New Zealand.
The researchers next used time-resolved characterization methods at the University of Geneva to identify the best experimental conditions and timescales for the X-ray measurements.
Combining X-Ray Techniques With Simulations
To track what happened during the reaction, the team combined two complementary X-ray methods.
Element-specific X-ray absorption spectroscopy using the chemRIXS instrument showed how electrons moved between different molecular sites. Meanwhile, time-resolved X-ray scattering from the X-ray Correlation Spectroscopy (XCS) instrument tracked how atoms rearranged, including the motion of solvent molecules around the reaction.
The team also relied heavily on theoretical modeling. Govind and Andersen contributed time-dependent density functional theory and molecular dynamics simulations, respectively. Those calculations were critical for interpreting the complex X-ray signals and uncovering the underlying behavior of the electrons and protons.
First author Abdullah Kahraman said the combination of methods was essential.
"Understanding the photochemistry of this complex required us to push the limits of our data analysis. By combining X-ray absorption spectroscopy with precise theoretical modeling, we gained an unprecedented look into the real-time electronic changes driving these reactions," said Kahraman, who worked on the project at SLAC while he was a PNNL postdoctoral associate.
Govind highlighted the theoretical aspect of the research.
"While this was an experiment-driven discovery, our theoretical work provided the molecular-level interpretation needed to translate the X-ray measurements into a detailed picture of the underlying coordination between proton, electron and solvent motion."
One Important Limitation
Biasin noted that the experiment could not directly observe the proton itself.
"X-ray scattering mostly sees atoms that are rich with electrons, and so the proton is not seen directly," she said. "But we observe the local reorganization of the electronic structure, together with the global reorganization of the water networks, and we can draw conclusions based on the agreement between data and calculations."
Even with that limitation, the combined X-ray approach provides a framework that researchers can now apply to PCET reactions in more complicated chemical systems.
"Many of the most important chemical reactions involve electrons, protons, and their surrounding environment moving together on ultrafast timescales," said Roberto Alonso Mori, senior scientist at SLAC and a coauthor on the study. "By combining complementary X-ray techniques at LCLS, this work provides a uniquely complete view of these coupled processes, opening new opportunities to understand and ultimately control the chemistry that underpins energy conversion and catalysis."
Coauthor and SLAC staff scientist David Hoffman added, "This is an important first step in combining X-ray scattering and spectroscopy to study these complicated processes in a model system. With the better signal-to-noise offered by the LCLS-II upgrade, we can use these methods to solve real problems in catalysis and energy harvesting."
Support for the Research
The research was supported by the DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, Chemical Sciences, Geosciences, and Biosciences Division, through the Condensed Phase and Interfacial Molecular Science (CPIMS) program and the Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Sciences (AMOS) program at PNNL.
Use of the Linac Coherent Light Source at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory is supported by the DOE Office of Science. Part of the research was also conducted at the Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory, a DOE Office of Science user facility located at PNNL.

Materials provided by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Original written by Karyn Hede. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Land tax could double in three Estonian municipalities in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:49:00 UTC
16:49:00 KST

Land tax could double in three Estonian municipalities in 2027
Land tax could rise by up to 100 percent in Kohtla-Järve, Ruhnu and Tori next year, Postimees reported, citing rates published by Estonia's Tax and Customs Board, Postimees reports.
The three municipalities have selected the maximum annual increase allowed under current law.
Kohila has set a 60 percent increase limit, while Tartu, Sillamäe, Saku, Raasiku, Narva-Jõesuu and Loksa have opted for 50 percent.
Municipalities set their own land-tax rates and annual increase limits, which range from 10 to 100 percent.
However, individual bills also depend on homeowner tax relief, which municipalities can set at up to €1,000.
Homeowners whose relief exceeds their tax bill will have nothing to pay.
Homes located on commercial land do not qualify for homeowner relief and can face rates of up to 2 percent of the land's taxable value.
Some municipalities also offer pensioner relief, including €250 in Paide, €100 in Lüganuse and €1,000 in Tartu.
Annual tax rates range from 0.1 to 1 percent for residential land and farmyards, 0.1 to 0.5 percent for agricultural land and 0.1 to 2 percent for other land.
Tallinn has selected residential and commercial rates halfway below the respective ceilings, while Tartu applies the maximum in all categories.

U.S. Army moves Anduril battle network from test to field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:48:30 UTC
16:48:30 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Anduril a contract worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to field its NGC2 command network, beginning with I Corps.
- The initial base period is valued at $162.8 million, following a year of prototype testing with the 4th Infantry Division.
The U.S. Army has awarded Anduril Industries a contract worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to roll out its Next Generation Command and Control network, known as NGC2, starting with I Corps, the Army headquarters responsible for much of its force in the Pacific.
The initial base period of the contract is valued at $162.8 million, Anduril said on Oct. 6. Options could bring the total to $1.8 billion over five years. The award moves NGC2 from prototype testing with a single division to operational fielding at corps level.
NGC2 is the U.S. Army’s effort to replace its patchwork of separate command, intelligence and fire-control systems with one shared data network. Instead of each system running on its own hardware and software, sensors, weapons, vehicles and applications from different companies plug into a common data layer, so information moves between them without soldiers re-entering it by hand. Anduril’s Lattice software provides that layer.
I Corps, headquartered at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, commands four Army divisions. Anduril said the Pacific mission is a much harder problem than its earlier testing, since units there can be thousands of miles apart, must coordinate with joint and allied forces, and have to keep operating when parts of the network go down.
The company did not say which I Corps units will receive the system first, how many devices or vehicles will be equipped, or when fielding begins.
The contract follows about a year of field testing with the 4th Infantry Division at Fort Carson, Colorado. The Army awarded an Anduril-led team that included Palantir and Microsoft a $99.6 million prototype agreement in July 2025, and Anduril engineers began working with soldiers weeks later through a series of exercises called Ivy Sting.
In the first of those, in September 2025, 4th Infantry Division soldiers fired M777 howitzers using artillery fire-control software running on Lattice. By Ivy Mass in May 2026, the whole division was operating on NGC2, with more than 2,500 end-user devices and a range of applications on the same data network, according to Anduril. The company says NGC2 cut artillery fire timelines by 90 percent compared with legacy systems and sped up airspace coordination. It also says later exercises showed U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Navy systems sharing data directly, and that the network kept supporting units after they lost connection to higher headquarters.
The U.S. Army ran a second NGC2 prototype in parallel. The 25th Infantry Division in Hawaii has tested a version led by Lockheed Martin through its Lightning Surge exercises, including during Exercise Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines. In June 2026, after both divisions’ exercises, the Army set a common data baseline for NGC2 and picked Anduril to lead it, working with Palantir and Raft.
Anduril says the architecture is designed so that no single company controls the Army’s whole command-and-control system. Under the common data layer, the Army can add new sensors, applications or weapons from other vendors without rebuilding the underlying network for each one.

Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
Two civilians have been killed and nine injured after Ukraine launched 650 drones toward Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, local officials have said.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in the early hours of Tuesday that most of the UAVs were destroyed at “distant lines,” while 134 were intercepted on the approaches to Moscow itself.
In Moscow Region, air defenses neutralized 185 drones, Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported. A 20-year-old man was killed in the settlement of Radumlya, northwest of Moscow, while rescuers found a 71-year-old man dead beneath the rubble of a destroyed private home in Barybino, south of the capital, with a woman in the same building receiving injuries.
A man in Pokrovskoye, west of Moscow, was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds, while two residents of the Istra area, also west of the capital, were taken to hospital. Three people in Lyakhovo, south of Moscow, received medical care but declined hospitalization, Vorobyov added.
Vorobyov said a total of 47 private homes were damaged across the region. In Lobanovo, south of the capital, windows and balcony glazing were blown out in four apartments, while a nearby boiler house was also damaged. Three cars were hit, and a small fire at a warehouse in Litvinovo, northwest of Moscow, was extinguished, according to the governor.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, a total of 868 Ukrainian drones were intercepted across the country overnight.
On Tuesday, Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking alleged Ukrainian war crimes, told TASS that 29 civilians, including two children, were killed and 206 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russian regions over the past week alone. He added that 98% were victims of drone strikes.
Ukraine has ramped up attacks deep into Russia in recent weeks, targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. After Vladimir Zelensky pledged to escalate the strikes even further, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that it had “taken note” of the statement, vowing to intensify attacks on Ukrainian military and defense industrial facilities as well as related infrastructure. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians.

Bab al-Mandab battle: government forces claim gains, Houthis warn Saudi skies ‘not safe’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:46:03 UTC
16:46:03 KST

Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Tuesday denied claims that Saudi-backed government forces had driven them from strategic territory overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, as rival sides offered sharply conflicting accounts of a rapidly shifting battle for one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group remained in control of its battlefield gains and dismissed reports of a government breakthrough as “fabricated victories.” 
He claimed more than 200 fighters aligned with the Saudi-backed government had been hit in dozens of Houthi attacks in recent hours, saying government losses in personnel and equipment were unprecedented. The claims could not be independently verified.
Forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government launched a major ground offensive dubbed “Dawn of Yemen” on Sunday, seeking to recapture territory seized by the Houthis during their rapid advance in September. That offensive gave the Houthis control over key areas near Bab al-Mandab, including territory around Dhubab and Mocha, tightening their grip on the maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Government forces said Monday that they had retaken Dhubab and other nearby areas and advanced as far north as the outskirts of Mocha under heavy Saudi air cover. International reporting has partially verified footage showing Saudi-backed forces at an airstrip south of Dhubab, but the full extent of the government advance remains unclear. The Houthis insist they have not suffered the retreat described by their opponents.
Saudi Arabia has thrown substantial air power behind the offensive. The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part in the opening phase of the operation and that 324 “high-value targets” had been destroyed. It also said naval forces carried out an operation near Hodeidah targeting Houthi weapons facilities, booby-trapped boats and naval mines.
The battle is particularly significant because Bab al-Mandab is a critical artery for trade between Europe and Asia through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Its importance has grown further amid the disruption of shipping elsewhere in the region, making control of the surrounding coastline a major strategic objective for both sides.
The Houthis, meanwhile, say they are continuing missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. Saree claimed strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh and the airport in Abha, and warned international airlines against using most Saudi airspace. Saudi authorities have not confirmed those claims.
Even as government forces reported gains on the Red Sea coast, the Houthis appeared to be advancing around Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and an important government stronghold. Government military sources said Houthi forces had cut or threatened key routes linking Taiz with Aden, leaving the city effectively surrounded, although another government source disputed that the road had been completely severed.
The expanding fighting has also drawn in Riyadh’s regional partners. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed at an emergency meeting Monday to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to the kingdom under their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August. The pact states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be treated as an attack against all. It remains unclear whether Turkish or Pakistani forces will take part directly in combat operations in Yemen.
The renewed war threatens to deepen Yemen’s already severe humanitarian crisis. Fighting has intensified across several fronts since the collapse of the fragile truce that had largely contained the civil war since 2022, with civilians again being displaced in large numbers as Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis battle for control of the country’s southwest.
