How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?
Angelique Chrisafis
Paris correspondent
School students say the education system is riven with inequality, that many buildings are in disrepair, class sizes are too big, and there are not enough teachers or funding.
The French prime minister has promised to address what he called “legitimate” complaints, including on class sizes, long hours, dilapidated buildings and teacher provisions.
So how bad are French high schools and what are the main problems?
Is the French education system blighted by social inequality?
Yes. A child born and schooled in a deprived neighbourhood in France has less chance of escaping their socioeconomic background than in most other developed nations, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Éric Charbonnier, a French education analyst at the OECD, said there was a marked gap between the performance of the most advantaged and disadvantaged school students in France. “And often disadvantaged students are in disadvantaged schools,” he said. This has raised issues of the quality of learning being delivered and higher absenteeism of teachers.
Teachers’ unions and sociologists have said children in France are often segregated by their background, postcode and income, with a direct impact on education outcomes.
Are French high school buildings dilapidated and rat-infested with collapsing ceilings?
Some are, namely in certain cities and low-income suburbs. Videos filmed by students and teachers have shown leaks, scurrying rats, holes in walls and ceilings, broken toilets and not enough chairs or tables, meaning teachers have to carry them from classroom to classroom. Some children said they had to learn in class while leaks were pouring into buckets, or move desks to avoid getting wet. Many school classrooms experienced temperatures over 35C (95F) in the heatwaves of last May and June.
Estimates in recent years have pointed to thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, in need of repair. These include many 1960s school buildings. French regions are responsible for upkeep of high school buildings, but have asked for higher budgets from the government. A senate report has advised that billions need to be spent in the coming years to renovate and repair schools, as well as to address the impact of the climate crisis.
Are class sizes bigger than other comparable countries?
Yes, and often in urban areas. Charbonnier said: “There are an average of 29 students in French language lessons, compared with 26 across the OECD. However, this average masks substantial differences – particularly between large cities and rural areas.”
Teachers and school students in Paris and its suburbs this week described many high school classes of 36 pupils or more, but in some rural areas it can be fewer. Figures from the French education ministry show class sizes have increased in recent years.
Does France spend less money on secondary education than its European neighbours?
No, France actually spends more than many other countries on high schools for children aged 15 and 18, but analysts question how the French government is spending its money and for what outcomes. For example, teachers’ middle and end-career salaries are comparatively low.
Macron summons top ministers for talks over high school protests
French president Emmanuel Macron is expected to hold political meetings with key several ministers, including education minister Édouard Geffray and interior minister Laurent Nuñez, this evening in response to today’s large-scale protests by high school students, BFMTV and Le Parisien reported.
'Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard,' as thousands protest in Paris
Thousands of people are taking part in the main demonstration in Paris.
“Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard,” 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen.
But there are also reports of some clashes with the police on the margins of the main march.

Ursa Major lands $91M to power a mini missile for F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:45:28 UTC
16:45:28 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Ursa Major $137 million for solid rocket motors for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile and the Naval Modular Missile.
- The $91 million CAAM contract covers a 7-inch motor, and the $46 million NMM contract covers a 10-inch quad-pack motor.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Ursa Major two contracts worth a combined $137 million to develop and qualify solid rocket motors for two new missiles: a small air-to-air missile for fighter jets and a ship-launched interceptor meant to eventually replace the Standard Missile family.
The Colorado company announced the awards on Oct. 5. The larger contract, worth $91 million, covers the motor for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile, or CAAM. The second, worth $46 million, covers the motor for the medium-range version of the Naval Modular Missile, or NMM. Funding comes through the Office of the Under Secretary of War.
CAAM is a short-range missile the U.S. Navy is developing for close-in air combat, sized to be carried inside the weapons bays of stealth fighters and future carrier-based drones. The Navy first showed the concept publicly in August, and service officials described it as an “inner boundary” weapon meant to increase how many missiles an aircraft can carry internally.
For CAAM, Ursa Major is designing a 7-inch (178 mm) motor. That is the same diameter as the AIM-120 AMRAAM and wider than the 5-inch AIM-9X Sidewinder, the Navy’s current short-range air-to-air missile. The company says the motor uses Highly Loaded Grain, a propellant design that packs more fuel into the motor case, giving a small missile more energy in the same volume. Ursa Major said it is building the development motor with the same methods it plans to use in full production, so it can move to high-rate manufacturing once the design is qualified.
The second contract covers a 10-inch (254 mm) motor for the medium-range NMM. The company described it as a quad-pack motor, meaning four missiles are sized to fit in a single shipboard launch cell, as the U.S. Navy already does with the Evolved Sea Sparrow Missile. Ursa Major said the motor is designed for high annual production volumes and compatibility with existing Navy shipboard launch systems. The U.S. Navy wants NMM to reach full capability by fiscal 2032 as a replacement for the Standard Missile family.
“By investing in CAAM and NMM, the Navy and OUSW are building solid rocket motor capacity now and getting new tactical air and naval capabilities into development sooner,” said Jason Meredith, president of Solid Missile Systems at Ursa Major. “Our Lynx manufacturing approach and growing energetics capacity enable us to design, build, test, qualify and field these motors faster to support the warfighter. Production is the bottleneck in missile programs right now, and that’s the part we’ve been building for.”
Lynx is Ursa Major’s name for its manufacturing process, which uses additive manufacturing, or industrial 3D printing, to produce most motor parts. Solid rocket motor production in the United States has for years been concentrated in two suppliers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris, which owns Aerojet Rocketdyne. The Pentagon has been funding new entrants to expand capacity as demand for interceptors and long-range missiles has grown.
The new awards follow earlier work with the U.S. Navy. In July, the Navy gave Ursa Major $10 million to take its version of the MK 104 motor through critical design review and static fire testing. The MK 104 is the dual-thrust motor that powers Standard Missile-2 and Standard Missile-6 interceptors on Aegis destroyers and cruisers. In February, the company completed a $25 million cost-share program with the Navy and the Office of Strategic Capital, in which it designed, built and static-fired a 10-inch Highly Loaded Grain motor and developed a proprietary propellant for it. That work was carried out with the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division at China Lake, California, and the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland.
Ursa Major is headquartered in Berthoud, Colorado, and runs additive manufacturing operations in Youngstown, Ohio. The company said its next steps on both programs are design, testing and qualification of the motors.

GENEVA, October 6. /TASS/. Fighting in Yemen has resulted in the displacement of more than 184,000 people since the beginning of August, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), part of the UN system, said.
"More than 184,000 people were forced to flee their homes due to heavy fighting in Yemen between August 1 and October 4, with most of the displacement occurring since early September," the IOM said. Nearly 21,800 people were displaced between September 27 and October 3, an increase of 26% from the previous week. About 4,500 people fled their homes on October 4 alone. All of them "need food, shelter and other basic humanitarian assistance."

The IOM warned that "as the situation remains unstable, further displacement may occur in the coming days."
Armed hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces have continued in Yemen since August 2014. In July, the rebels announced a naval blockade against the kingdom and subsequently struck several Saudi-owned oil tankers.
In early August, the Ansar Allah movement launched an offensive in southwestern Yemen, and on September 10-11 took control of the port city of Mocha and areas with access to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. On October 4, Yemen’s government forces announced the launch of a large-scale military operation to retake territory controlled by the rebels.

Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli‘alemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt apologized for a Nazi salute and the words "Heil Hitler" in a 2007 video. He stated that he rejects Nazism, antisemitism, and racism.
Samoa’s Prime Minister La'auli'alemali'etoa Leuatea Schmidt apologized after a 2007 video surfaced showing him giving a Nazi salute and saying "Heil Hitler." The BBC reports, UNN relays.
Details
In the seven-second video, filmed in July 2007, La'auli'alemali'etoa Leuatea Schmidt can be seen leading about a dozen people in a salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, and then thanks the group for responding".
Schmidt acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and could have offended and caused pain." He also added that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "was not intended for the public."
I reject Nazism, anti-Semitism, racism, and all forms of political extremism
According to the publication, at the time the video was filmed, Schmidt was the deputy speaker of Parliament. A member of his family said that the politician was hosting the event.
Samoa is an island state with a population of about 221,000, located between New Zealand and Hawaii. At the beginning of the 20th century, the country was under German control, but this ended after the outbreak of World War I.
Schmidt, who is of Samoan and German descent, took office as the country’s eighth prime minister in September 2025. During the swearing-in ceremony, he wore a Jewish prayer shawl and clearly stated his support for Israel at the beginning of his premiership, saying that Samoa "supports Israel.
If people around the world do not like this, that is their business, but Samoa stands on the side of the land of God... There is only one God in whom our country believes—the God of Israel

Heinen struggling to hit deadline for capital gains tax reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:40:37 UTC
16:40:37 KST

Heinen struggling to hit deadline for capital gains tax reform
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Finance minister Eelco Heinen is in a race against time to introduce a new capital gains tax system by his promised deadline of 2028, financial institutions have warned.
Heinen is under pressure from right-wing opposition parties JA21 and SGP to replace the current income tax regime as quickly as possible as part of the deal to pass next year’s budget.
The minister also needs to plug a €7 billion hole in the finances after left-wing parties Pro and Volt forced the government to drop its planned cuts to social security as the price for their support. The minority government needs the votes of at least two opposition parties in parliament to pass legislation.
Heinen said 2028 could be achieved with “the maximum stretch from everyone”. But banks and the Council of State, which advises the cabinet on the legal implications of its bills, cast doubt on his timetable when asked by NOS.
The Council of State said it was “impossible” to have its analysis ready by next Monday, October 12, so that parliament can debate the bill next week. A spokesman said October 19 was the earliest realistic date.
The Dutch banking association NVB said its members need time to adapt their IT systems so they can pass the relevant details of their customers’ income to the tax office.
Risk of fraud
If customers have to provide the information themselves it increases the risk of delays, inaccuracies and fraud, the banks have warned.
The tax office is also under pressure to update its systems to deal with other reforms, such as the introduction of compulsory work incapacity insurance for people who are self-employed.
Changing the income tax method at the same time would be likely to delay the insurance plan by a year, civil servants told NOS.
Every year that the cabinet delays the overhaul of the income tax system is costing the government an estimated €3.5 billion in lost revenue.
Assumed gains
Heinen’s latest draft does not explain how he plans to compensate for the income lost during the transition to capital gains tax, which will only raise tax on assets and investments when they are sold.
The current “box 3” method charges taxpayers on their assumed gains from their assets every year, but the Supreme Court struck out this system in 2021 because it was unfair on savers whose wealth was held in low-interest accounts.
Heinen included a proposal to lower the thresholds for the “box 3” wealth tax as a stopgap measure in his submission to the Council of State, but parliament has already indicated it does not support this reform.

Ukrainian recon drone maker Buntar raises $16 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:40:29 UTC
16:40:29 KST

- Ukrainian drone maker Buntar Aerospace raised $16 million in a round led by Freedom Fund VC, bringing its total funding to $30 million.
- The company plans to expand production of its Buntar-3 reconnaissance drone, develop its Copilot AI software and enter foreign markets with dual-use products.
Buntar Aerospace, a Ukrainian maker of reconnaissance drones and battlefield AI software, has raised $16 million to expand production and enter foreign markets, bringing its total funding to $30 million.
The round was led by Freedom Fund VC and an international private equity fund that the company did not name. Gardar Venture Capital, Iron Wolf Capital and Autonomy Capital also took part, Buntar said in an announcement on Oct. 5.
The Kyiv-based company was founded in August 2023 by Ivan Kaunov, Kateryna Bezsudna and Bohdan Sas. It builds two main products: the Buntar-3 reconnaissance drone and Buntar Copilot, an AI assistant that helps drone operators plan missions and make decisions in combat. Buntar says both are in use with frontline units across Ukraine and generate steady, fast-growing revenue.
Buntar-3 is an electric drone that takes off and lands vertically, so it does not need a runway or catapult. According to the company, it can stay airborne for up to four hours and navigate without satellite signals, which matters on a front where Russian electronic warfare routinely jams GPS and radio links. The company introduced the system publicly in 2025, describing it as a full reconnaissance system run through its own software platform.
The drone has been used to direct long-range strikes. In March 2026, operators from the 414th Separate Unmanned Strike Aircraft Brigade, known as Madyar’s Birds, used a Buntar-3 to provide reconnaissance and fire correction for a Ukrainian strike with SCALP cruise missiles and ATACMS ballistic missiles on a Russian Shahed drone base at Donetsk Airport. In July, the company added a feature that lets operators fly Buntar-3 over the internet from hundreds of kilometers away, with a small forward team launching the aircraft and then leaving the area.
Buntar plans to spend the new money on research and development, further work on Copilot, more production capacity and hiring experienced engineers and managers. The company said demand from the Armed Forces of Ukraine keeps growing. It also plans to expand abroad with dual-use products, including civilian applications.
Buntar says it is moving from a single product to a wider lineup covering reconnaissance, counter-drone systems and support for precision strikes.
“Our systems can fly, see and make decisions on their own, so that people can focus on what matters most. This is what Ukraine needs today, and what Europe must be ready for tomorrow,” said Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Buntar Aerospace.
Earlier this year, Buntar raised $10.4 million in a round led by U.S. company Axon Enterprise, best known as the maker of the Taser.

France braces for day of school blockades and street protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:38:58 UTC
16:38:58 KST

Students and teachers march in France on biggest day of high school protests
PARIS, Oct 6 - Students, teachers and parents marched in cites across France on Tuesday and protesters blockaded hundreds of schools, in the biggest day of action in a wave of demonstrations demanding the government tackle understaffed and dilapidated classrooms.
In Marseille, Nantes and Lyon, the street protests began peacefully mid-morning, with the largest demonstration expected in Paris in the afternoon.
Youngsters held aloft smoke flares and placards reading "Under our school books, anger" and "Where are the politicians? Do they even know we exist?"
Tuesday's demonstrations come after a fortnight of protests which began in Paris's deprived suburbs before spreading across the country. The government responded with riot police, saying the movement had now morphed into urban violence.
A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact circumstances, saying some 200 to 250 protesters had been hurling objects at police.
The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.
The High School Students Union said 1,800 high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online. The education ministry did not immediately make numbers available.
“When the answer is violence, it means democracy is no longer working," said Hugo Vetzel, a high school leaver in Strasbourg now taking classes for the entrance exams to France's top-tier universities. "There is such a gap between the elites and us.”
PRIME MINISTER PROMISES A RESPONSE
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government would also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
But finding spare cash will be difficult.
The protests have piled pressure on a government trying to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-skeptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.
THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS
France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. The LFI denies the accusation.
Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, a poor Paris suburb, said he opposed violence but stood beside the protesting students.
"I stand by being on the side of my residents, and high school students are my residents," he said. REUTERS

Up to 16 hours without electricity: should Kyiv residents expect prolonged outages in October, and what does this depend on
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:38:11 EEST
16:38:11 KST

Up to 16 hours without electricity: should Kyiv residents expect prolonged outages in October, and what does this depend on
Kyiv • UNN
An expert warned of prolonged outages in Kyiv due to new Russian strikes on the energy infrastructure. At temperatures as low as +5°C, they may last 14–16 hours.
This month, Kyiv may experience prolonged power outages if russia continues its strikes on energy facilities. Under certain conditions, there may be no electricity for 14–16 hours a day. Oleg Popenko, head of the Union of Utility Consumers, said this in a comment to UNN.
russia continues to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
According to the expert, Ukraine already had a similar experience last winter.
We have already been through this last winter, when we were without electricity for 20 or even 22 hours, and in the Kyiv region there was no electricity at all for five to seven days. Therefore, this is a real possibility. But there are certain factors that affect this. The main factors that could influence the continuation of the restrictions are attacks by the Russian Federation and damage to our energy facilities. Given that last week there were strikes on practically all components involved in supplying electricity to consumers, including the main generation facilities—namely the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant, and Thermal Power Plant No. 5. These facilities were hit
According to Oleg Popenko, further attacks could cause new damage to energy infrastructure, in which case restoring individual facilities could take a long time.
If the shelling continues, the destruction of energy facilities that russia has already struck in the past may await us. And all this will simply lead to a halt in electricity supplies, and we could simply be left without power for a long time
Oleg Popenko also explained that it is impossible to fully protect generating facilities from strikes.
"All facilities have different owners, but in most cases it is simply physically impossible to systematically prepare protection. We cannot fully protect generating facilities," Oleg Popenko emphasizes.
According to the expert, if the attacks continue, prolonged restrictions could begin as early as October. In addition, weather conditions will also affect their duration.
A drop in temperature is a decisive factor
If in February, amid low temperatures, we were without electricity for 20–22 hours, the situation in October could be different because the month is not yet as cold. But it is unknown what the weather will be after October 15. If the temperature falls to at least +5 °C, outages could last 14–16 hours
It is impossible to determine in advance exactly which districts of the capital may be affected most. This will depend on which facilities are damaged.
"There is no specific priority—it depends on where they strike. We have facilities supplied with electricity through Thermal Power Plant No. 5, others through the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, and others through the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant. In other words, depending on where the strikes occur, that is where there will be problems with electricity supplies. It also depends on the quality of our energy infrastructure—I mean DTEK in the city—which is capable of transmitting a particular amount of electricity to a particular district. This will also have an impact," Oleg Popenko concluded.
Thus, possible prolonged outages in the capital will depend primarily on further Russian strikes, the condition of energy facilities, and weather conditions.

Russia, Ukraine trade accusations over overnight drone strikes, killing 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:37:21 UTC
16:37:21 KST

Burc Eruygur
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
- Kyiv authorities say rescuers extinguished fire that broke out on roof of an educational institution in Obolonskyi district of Ukraine’s capital
 
Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes, which have killed at least two people in the region surrounding Moscow, according to local authorities.
 
In a statement on Telegram, Andrey Vorobyov, governor of the Moscow region, claimed that 185 drones were downed across 16 municipalities in the region as it was subjected to a drone attack overnight.
 
“Preliminary reports indicate six injuries. … Tragically, there was a fatality. A 20-year-old man died in the settlement of Radumlya (Solnechnogorsky District) as a result of the attack,” Vorobyov said.
 
He later updated the death toll in the region to two and the number of those injured to nine, noting that “one of the largest drone attacks” also damaged 47 private houses across seven municipalities.
 
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that 650 drones flew toward the Moscow region between 8.30 pm (1730GMT) Monday and 5 am (0200GMT) Tuesday, with 105 of them destroyed as they approached the capital.
 
He later reported that 29 more drones were shot down as they were heading toward Moscow.
 
Local authorities also reported that one person was injured in the Smolensk region, while two others were injured in the Russian border region of Bryansk due to overnight strikes.
 
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed in a statement that air defense systems shot down 868 Ukrainian drones overnight across 11 regions, as well as over the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
 
It further claimed that Russian overnight strikes in Ukraine hit a warehouse in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, as well as a dry cargo vessel in the port of Chornomorsk and berthing infrastructure in the port of Izmail.
 
In Ukraine, Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, said that at least five people were injured due to an overnight strike on a residential building in the regional capital.
 
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said 11 others were rescued from the apartment building in Zaporizhzhia, noting that search and rescue operations have been completed.
 
The service said that search and rescue personnel extinguished a fire that broke out on the roof of an educational institution in the Obolonskyi district of Ukraine’s capital Kyiv following a morning Russian strike, but that no one was injured.
 
Separately, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said a building belonging to a private enterprise was damaged in the regional capital during an overnight Russian attack, indicating that a fire broke out but was promptly extinguished by emergency responders.
 
“There were no casualties. Cleanup operations are currently underway at the site,” Kiper added.
 
Elsewhere, Dnipropetrovsk Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that four people were injured in the city of Kryvyi Rih following a morning strike.
 
Ukraine's Air Force claimed in a statement that its air defenses downed 114 out of 137 drones launched by Russia overnight.
 
Moscow and Kyiv have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports and energy infrastructure.
 
They deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Fake “I’m not a robot” verification — hackers are infecting Ukrainians’ PCs with a dangerous virus
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
10:34:35 EEST
16:34:35 KST

Fake “I’m not a robot” verification — hackers are infecting Ukrainians’ PCs with a dangerous virus
Kyiv • UNN
Hackers have replaced Cloudflare CAPTCHA on more than 100 websites and are tricking Windows users into running dangerous PowerShell commands. The virus steals passwords and provides remote access to PCs.
Hackers are massively targeting Ukrainians, disguising malware as an “I’m not a robot” check. Attackers replace Cloudflare CAPTCHA on compromised websites and force users to execute dangerous commands, after which the LUNEXSTEALER virus is installed on the computer. The State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection reports this, UNN writes.
Details
CERT-UA reports a new large-scale infection campaign: in September, attackers hacked more than 100 websites and replaced the Cloudflare check on them with a fake page. Windows users who visited such pages from Google or other search engines were instructed to copy text and execute a command in PowerShell. Following the instructions led to the LUNEXSTEALER virus being installed on the computer.
It is noted that the malware disguises itself as legitimate files, exploits vulnerable drivers, and covertly embeds a fake “Microsoft Office Word Editor” extension in the browser. The consequences include the theft of passwords and browsing history, and even full remote control over the PC.
The State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection warned that no genuine CAPTCHA or Cloudflare will ask users to open Win+R or PowerShell or paste commands.

The 30-day deadline for Britain to close the consulate ends on Oct 8, which will impact around 30 British diplomats who work there, along with their family members, the sources said.
If the consulate is closed, Britain is likely to respond by expelling a similar number of Israeli diplomats from Israel’s embassy to the United Kingdom, the sources said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
The sources did not say how quickly Britain would act if the consulate closes. After Britain announced the sanctions, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused London of interfering in Israel’s October general election.

The British sanctions announcement, and Israel’s response, marked a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticised Israel over its actions in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians. France and Canada joined in announcing sanctions. Israel has not taken action against Paris or Ottawa.

Taiwan has faced domestic and international challenges in recent years, Hsiao said. She added that people who support vulnerable communities and preserve traditional culture continue to strengthen the goodwill and resilience that help the country move forward.

Tiberius lands $500M deal for its ramjet artillery shell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:30:14 UTC
16:30:14 KST

- Tiberius Aerospace said it signed a $500 million contract with unnamed U.K. technology partners to manufacture, license and distribute its Sceptre ramjet artillery shell.
- The company has not disclosed who is paying, how many rounds are covered, or when production starts, and no government has announced a Sceptre order.
Tiberius Aerospace, the California-based developer of a ramjet-powered 155 mm artillery shell, said it has signed a $500 million contract to manufacture, license and distribute the round, called Sceptre, with a group of British technology partners.
The company announced the deal on Oct. 1. It did not name the U.K. partners or disclose the number of rounds covered, the end customers or the production timeline.
The cooperation runs under a Technical Assistance Agreement, the U.S. State Department authorization required under International Traffic in Arms Regulations before an American defense company can share controlled technical data with foreign partners. The agreement allows Tiberius and the British consortium to work together on engineering, technology development and manufacturing.
Sceptre is designed to give standard artillery much longer reach. Most extended-range shells use a short rocket burn after leaving the barrel. Sceptre instead carries liquid fuel for a ramjet, an air-breathing engine with no moving parts that keeps pushing the shell for much of its flight. According to Tiberius, the round can strike targets up to 150 km (93 miles) away at speeds of about Mach 3.5, flies above 19,800 meters (65,000 feet), and fires from existing NATO-standard 155 mm howitzers without modification.
In April 2026, Tiberius fired Sceptre from a NATO-standard 155 mm howitzer in New Mexico and achieved ramjet ignition in flight, which the company said was the first time a liquid-fueled ramjet projectile had been launched this way. Tiberius said the next phase of the program would move to larger ranges for further testing, validation and certification.
The company first unveiled Sceptre in May 2025 at the Future Artillery conference in London, after operating in stealth since its founding in 2022. Development has since included work under contract with the U.K. Ministry of Defence, support from the U.S. Defense Innovation Unit and a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center.
Tiberius describes the contract as the first scaled deployment of its Defense-as-a-Service model. Under that approach, the company develops, tests and validates a weapon, then licenses the technology to qualified manufacturers and partner nations so they can produce it locally. An AI-based platform the company calls GRAIL links requirements, engineering, suppliers, export compliance and manufacturing across those partners.
“The West’s greatest strategic advantage is the freedom to invent, compete and build,” said Chad Steelberg, founder and CEO of Tiberius Aerospace, who previously co-founded the artificial intelligence company Veritone. “Our ambition is to turn that advantage into our greatest weapon: the collective innovative power of the free market. GRAIL connects that ingenuity, while Defense-as-a-Service provides the commercial model to bring it into service. Sceptre is the first scaled manifestation of that vision.”
“Deterrence depends not only on having the right capability, but on maintaining a strong industrial and technological base that can respond rapidly to emerging threats. The collaboration on SCEPTRE demonstrates the value of bringing together UK and US technological expertise to explore advanced artillery technologies and strengthen transatlantic defence cooperation. Initiatives such as this help mature future concepts and reinforce the industrial relationships that underpin alliance advantage,” said Gen. Sir Roly Walker, Chief of the General Staff of the British Army.
“Modern conflict has reinforced a fundamental lesson: munitions capacity is essential to sustaining combat power. The United States is stronger when our allies and partners have the industrial capacity to produce interoperable systems at speed and scale, expand production when demand increases, and adapt as battlefield requirements change. Building greater depth, resilience, and responsiveness across the allied industrial base strengthens readiness and deterrence and gives the joint and coalition force the capacity to sustain combat operations and win,” said retired U.S. Navy Adm. Gary Roughead, the 29th Chief of Naval Operations.
Other manufacturers are also developing 155 mm ramjet rounds, including Norway’s Nammo, which has presented its own ramjet shell with a stated range of up to 150 km, and India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, which has shown a ramjet projectile for its ATAGS towed howitzer.

Drawing a New City: Brasilia, Fordlandia, and Ciudad Guayana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

A different social order is easier to imagine when it sits far from the one that already exists. In Latin America, that distance has often been territorial. Parts of the region have repeatedly been treated as places where another world could begin. These places were never empty.
For architects, this idea has a familiar starting point: the plan. Seen from above, a territory can look like a clean sheet, ready for an axis or a grid. At eye level, the same ground is already full of people and the paths they use.
Long before modern planning, El Dorado had already turned part of South America into an imagined territory. The story grew from Muisca rituals at Lake Guatavita, in present-day Colombia, where offerings were made to the water. Spanish chroniclers transformed these practices into stories of a gilded ruler and extraordinary wealth. Over time, El Dorado stopped referring to a person and became the name of a place, a city of gold imagined somewhere beyond the known map.
Related Article
Brasília: A Social Architecture
A specific place had become defined by what outsiders expected to find there. In the twentieth century, similar ideas began to take physical form through architecture and planning.
Importing an American Model to the Amazon
Fordlândia was planned thousands of miles from where it was built. In the late 1920s, Henry Ford set out to produce his own rubber on the Tapajós River, in the Brazilian Amazon, and to build a town around the plantation. From Michigan, he imagined a small American town rebuilt in the rainforest and run the Michigan way, down to square dances and a ban on alcohol.
The town took that image literally. Workers' bungalows lined up near the river dock, much like a mill town in the United States, and a steel water tower rose above them, its whistle marking the hours of work. The houses were designed in Michigan and shipped to Brazil, with metal roofs chosen over local thatch that trapped heat under the equatorial sun.
Daily routines followed the same model. Workers punched time clocks and ate American food in a company dining hall. Historian Greg Grandin, in his book Fordlandia, describes the project as an attempt to export an entire way of life.
The model did not hold. Rubber trees planted in dense rows were devastated by blight, and in December 1930 a protest over the dining hall turned into a riot that sent managers fleeing to boats on the river. Ford had imagined a small town that could be rebuilt anywhere. The Amazon and the people working there proved otherwise.
Building a New Capital in Brazil's Interior
Brasília was conceived as a new capital for Brazil, built inland as part of President Juscelino Kubitschek's national modernization project. The move was meant to mark a break with the coastal capitals that had governed the country since colonial times. Lúcio Costa won the 1957 competition for its urban plan, and by 1960 the city stood on the central plateau.
Costa's plan began with a single gesture. In his competition report, he described the Plano Piloto as born from the act of someone marking a place or claiming it as their own, which he drew as "two axes crossing at right angles, that is, the very sign of the cross." He tied that gesture directly to the colonial tradition. Four centuries after El Dorado, the founding of a modern capital still borrowed the logic of claiming land.
Those two axes organized almost the entire city. The curved Residential Axis contained the superquadras, housing blocks raised on pilotis and surrounded by shared green space. The Monumental Axis concentrated government and civic buildings, including some of Oscar Niemeyer's best-known projects. The result was a city of wide distances and open ground, laid out as if the plateau had been empty.
Constructing the new capital required tens of thousands of workers, known as candangos, many of whom came from Brazil's Northeast. They lived in construction camps and in the Cidade Livre, a settlement intended to disappear once the capital was completed.
Few of them found a place in the city they had built. While the superquadras became the model of housing for the new capital, many workers were moved to satellite towns such as Taguatinga, created for residents removed from an informal settlement, and later Ceilândia, founded in 1971 for the same purpose. Today, the protected Plano Piloto sits at the center of a much larger metropolitan territory and houses less than a tenth of the Federal District's population.
Planning a New Industrial City in Venezuela
Ciudad Guayana was created in southeastern Venezuela in the early 1960s to turn the region's iron deposits and hydroelectric power into a new industrial center, where the Orinoco and Caroní rivers meet. The Corporación Venezolana de Guayana worked with the Joint Center for Urban Studies of MIT and Harvard to plan the new city. For the planners, it offered something rare: the chance to design an entire city at once.
The plan drew Ciudad Guayana as a linear city. Avenida Guayana was intended to work as its spine, connecting industrial areas to commercial centers and housing. Researchers have since described the project as an urban laboratory, where planning ideas could be tested at the scale of a whole city.
The site, however, was already inhabited. On the west bank of the Caroní stood Puerto Ordaz, a company town for an American iron mining firm, designed by Josep Lluís Sert, one of the leading figures of CIAM. On the east bank was San Félix, originally a fishing village, where most newcomers settled. By 1962, around 20,000 people were living in self-built settlements in a city that was still being drawn.
The plan placed new housing near the industries in the west, yet most people continued to settle around San Félix. And while the planners hoped for socially mixed neighborhoods, Puerto Ordaz filled with middle- and upper-income residents.
That difference also appeared in the way people understood the city. Donald Appleyard, an urban designer with the Joint Center, asked residents to draw maps of Ciudad Guayana and compared them with the planners' drawings. The official plan organized the city as a complete system, while residents mapped the routes and places they actually used. Their maps revealed parts of urban life that were difficult to see in the masterplan itself.
What Happens Beyond the Plan
Fordlândia, Brasília, and Ciudad Guayana came from different moments and political projects. Each began with the same hope: that moving elsewhere would make it possible to organize society from the start. The plan made that hope feel achievable. Seen from above, a large and complicated place could be drawn and reorganized as if nothing were already there.
What happened afterwards was less controlled. Fordlândia confronted a climate and a way of life very different from the model it imported. Brasília grew far beyond the boundaries of the Plano Piloto. Ciudad Guayana developed through neighborhoods and daily routes that the planners' version of the city did not capture.
The appeal of beginning again elsewhere depends on how a territory is read before construction starts. That reading is rarely shared by the people who already live there. Who gets to decide what a place is, and what remains outside that decision?

Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Russia has finalized preparations to provide a $1 billion loan to Iran, with the funds ready for transfer once Tehran provides bank account details, Iranian media reported Tuesday.
Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency said the payment process had been finalized but disagreements among Iranian government bodies over how the money should be spent have delayed the transfer.
The loan was first reported in June and was described as the first installment of a planned $20 billion Russian loan to Iran, according to Fars.
According to the outlet, Iran’s Planning and Budget Organization wants the funds used for vehicle imports, while the Oil Ministry is seeking to purchase oil industry equipment and the Agriculture Ministry wants the money allocated to imports of essential goods.
No final decision has yet been made on how the funds will be used, and the government has therefore not provided the account details required for the transfer, Fars said.
Iran and Russia have moved to deepen their economic and financial ties, including efforts to expand the use of their national currencies in bilateral trade and reduce reliance on Western-controlled financial systems.
In June, Iran announced plans to establish a ruble trading board as part of efforts to strengthen banking and monetary cooperation with Russia. At the time, an Iranian lawmaker said Moscow was expected to provide Tehran with a $20 billion ruble-denominated loan at an annual interest rate of 6%.
The developments come as Iran remains under extensive US sanctions targeting, among other areas, its oil exports, banking sector and access to the international financial system.
Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran in recent months, including through secondary sanctions targeting foreign entities accused of facilitating Iranian transactions.
In September, the US Treasury sanctioned Russia’s VTB Bank over what it said were correspondent banking relationships with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions. Washington has also targeted financial networks it accuses of helping Tehran move funds and evade sanctions.

Saudi-led coalition forces recaptured several areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said Monday, as the Houthis claimed retaliatory strikes on Saudi oil facilities, airports and military bases.

They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.
The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under air cover by a Saudi military coalition.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, claimed in a prerecorded statement that the rebels used ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and an oil refinery in the Red Sea city of Rabigh.
Also attacked were Abha airport, military facilities in Khamis Mushait and other "critical sites" in the cities of Najran and Jizan, he claimed.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory.
Asked if the coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Rubio said that Saudi Arabia and the U.S. have a defense agreement but wouldn’t offer more details.
Since the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by the Houthis and the Saudis have come under attack, "they have a right to defend themselves," Rubio said.
The U.S. has provided support to Saudi Arabia in its ongoing campaign against the Houthis, according to a regional official and a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to reporters. The support included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the offensive, said the officials.

The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year cease-fire.
Houthis seized the town of Turbah Sunday. Turbah sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for government forces defending Taiz.
Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts, paving the way for the rebels to encircle Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September. They captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, through which 12% of global trade transits.
The Saudi-backed government said Sunday it was mobilizing troops across government-held areas.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government.
Hours after al-Alimi’s declaration, the Saudi military spokesperson al-Malki vowed "full operational support" to Yemeni government forces until the Houthis are "eliminated."
Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation – dubbed "Yemen Dawn" – had started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen’s rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup."
Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on Sanaa. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes on their territories, including Sanaa.
The rebels' taking of Turbah will likely constrain government forces’ ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis descended from their northern stronghold, capturing Sanaa and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. The war created one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters and killed more than 150,000 people.
The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the World Health Organization. The flare-up forced about 174,097 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported.
Last week, Yemen’s Health Ministry – part of the internationally recognized government – warned about the conflict’s impact on health facilities and medical staff across Taiz province.

The Museum of Contemporary Art in Antwerp, the M HKA welcomed a strikingly higher number of visitors in the first few months following Culture Minister Caroline Gennez’s Museum Plan. Exactly one year ago, that plan drawn up by the Flemish socialist politician sent shockwaves through the Flemish cultural landscape. The M HKA initially faced the threat of closure but was able to retain its status as a museum following talks with the minister.
Contemporary art museum M HKA in Antwerp increases visitor numbers following threat of closure
“Our visitors have remained loyal to the museum,” says Dieter Vankeirsbilck, acting director of the M HKA. Following Bart De Baere’s resignation, he has temporarily taken the helm of the museum.
De Baere tendered his resignation following the uproar over the new Museum Plan put forward by Caroline Gennez. On 6 October 2025, it seemed the M HKA was set to disappear, and its collection would have to move to the S.M.A.K., the contemporary art museum in Ghent, but that changed at the start of this year. The M HKA will remain a museum and must reinvent itself.
The initial news of the museum’s closure led to a significant increase in visitor numbers in the months that followed. In October 2025, the M HKA welcomed 15,426 visitors, making it the museum’s best October since 2018. The entire final quarter, from 1 October to 31 December, was the best since 2019, with 28,682 visitors.
Received a great deal of support
“We received a great deal of support from organisations and artists at the time,” Vankeirsbilck continues. “That had a major impact on those figures.” In the months that followed, visitor numbers fell back to the expected level.
Many people, including schools that have been coming on guided tours for years, still think the M HKA is closing. “There has really been a miscommunication about that,” says Vankeirsbilck. “Because of the changes we have to implement, people still think we’re going to close. Yet we’ve always remained open.”
Transition plan
On 1 October, the museum submitted a transition plan for 2026–2028 to the minister. “Over the past few months, we have undertaken an extensive process in which artists, arts organisations and other stakeholders from the sector were consulted about the museum’s future,” says the director. “That formed the basis for our transition plan.”
In that plan, the museum’s focus is on the collection and on collaboration with artists and organisations. “Collaboration with other institutions, like the KMSKA fine arts museum or the Fotomuseum, both in Antwerp, is also important in this regard. By January 2028, the M HKA must submit a new strategic plan for the period 2029–2033.”

Unhealthy food outlets dominate Dutch cities, say researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:23:10 UTC
16:23:10 KST

Unhealthy food outlets dominate Dutch cities, say researchers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The food in 10 major Dutch cities has become less healthy over the past decade, according to new research by Amsterdam UMC.
Health executives from the 10 cities have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to speed up a promised food law that would let councils limit unhealthy outlets, Het Parool reported on Tuesday.
The researchers scored 31 types of food outlet, from greengrocers to fast-food chains. The scores combined expert ratings with checks of more than 83,000 products against the “Wheel of Five” (Schijf van Vijf), the official Dutch healthy eating guidelines.
Each neighbourhood was then given a score from -500 (extremely unhealthy) to +500 (extremely healthy), based on the type, number and proximity of nearby outlets.
All 10 cities scored negative in both 2014 and 2024, ranging from -252 in Groningen to -327 in Leiden. Amsterdam fell from -287 to -301. Across the cities, 77% of neighbourhoods scored lower in 2024 than 10 years earlier.
In Amsterdam, 96% of food outlets fall into categories the researchers rate as unhealthy. Some 87 of the city’s 90 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in what the report calls a “very unhealthy” food environment.
The councils say they currently lack a clear legal basis to refuse outlets selling unhealthy food.
“That more than nine in 10 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in an unhealthy food environment means young people are surrounded every day by an offer that makes choosing healthily harder,” Amsterdam health executive Alexander Scholtes told Het Parool. “I am not willing to resign myself to that.”

Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:23:00 UTC
16:23:00 KST

Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan
Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 at Fort Hood, to face execution under rare military order.
United States President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad in the execution of a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, the Pentagon spokesman has said.
Nidal Hasan, a US citizen of Palestinian descent, would be the first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.
Hasan will be killed by a firing squad under the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the approval of the president, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement on X on Monday.
The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, he said.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.
Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for shooting a handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.
The attack killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.
Police arrested him at the scene, where he was shot and left partially paralysed.
The shooting took place weeks before Hasan was set to be deployed to Afghanistan.
He said during his court-martial that the shooting was an effort to stop the soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims, and made almost no effort to defend himself.
The Trump administration added death by firing squad as an appropriate method of execution in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.
Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. If the order is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out “by musketry” in November 1945, the center reported.

U.S. Army bomb plant will arm Eric Schmidt’s drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:22:23 UTC
16:22:23 KST

- The U.S. Army's McAlester Army Ammunition Plant will manufacture and load explosive payloads for drones built by Perennial Autonomy, a company backed by Eric Schmidt.
- The U.S. Army did not disclose which drones are involved, the production quantity, the value of the arrangement, or when deliveries start.
The U.S. Army’s McAlester Army Ammunition Plant in Oklahoma, one of the country’s main bomb-making sites, will manufacture and load explosive payloads for drones built by Perennial Autonomy, the drone company backed by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
The plant held a ribbon-cutting ceremony to open the partnership, the U.S. Army said. Under the arrangement, McAlester will build, load and deliver combat-ready payloads for Perennial Autonomy’s unmanned aircraft, while the company supplies the drones and their guidance systems.
The U.S. Army did not say which Perennial Autonomy drones will carry the McAlester payloads, how many will be produced, what the arrangement is worth, or when deliveries begin.
Perennial Autonomy is best known for drones that have fought in Ukraine. Schmidt started the effort in 2023, and it operated as Project Eagle before taking the Perennial Autonomy name. Will Roper, the former U.S. Air Force acquisition chief, joined the company along with engineers from Apple, SpaceX and Google. Its Merops interceptor, built around the AS-3 Surveyor drone, was developed to bring down Russian Shahed attack drones and costs roughly $15,000 per interceptor. The company says Merops has made more than 4,000 interceptions in Ukraine.
The company also makes the Bumblebee quadcopter family and the Hornet, a fixed-wing strike drone that has hit Russian logistics convoys in Ukraine at ranges beyond 100 km (62 miles).
Last month, Perennial Autonomy won the deep-strike category of Gauntlet II, the second evaluation round of the U.S. Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, scoring 80.1 points and receiving an order for 8,000 drones. The Pentagon has not published the value of that order.
In May, the Pentagon’s counter-drone task force, JIATF-401, awarded the company a three-year contract with a $500 million ceiling covering Merops, Bumblebee and Hornet. U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll had earlier told lawmakers the service bought 13,000 Merops interceptors in the early days of the war with Iran. Lithuania has also bought 48 Merops interceptors, joining the United States and Poland.
The plant, which falls under the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, produces, stores, ships, renovates and destroys conventional ammunition, and its workforce includes chemists, load-assemble-pack specialists and quality inspectors. Drone payloads give that workforce a new line of steady work alongside its bomb production.
The U.S. Army framed the deal as part of Army Materiel Command’s push to modernize the organic industrial base, the network of government-owned arsenals, depots and ammunition plants that supply the service.
“Integrating Perennial Autonomy’s advanced guidance systems with MCAAP’s proven ordnance manufacturing directly answers the call to modernize the OIB,” said Brian Lott, the plant’s civilian deputy. “This collaboration acts as a critical force multiplier, ensuring that next-generation drone fleets are armed with the precise, lethal and dependable capabilities required to dominate modern, high-threat environments.”
Partnerships with private companies also help the plant cover sustainment costs and pay for infrastructure upgrades, according to the U.S. Army.
“This partnership with Perennial Autonomy is a testament to the agility and generational skill of the workforce at McAlester,” said Col. Curtis Perkins, the plant’s commander. “Our employees are second to none. By applying their deep technical expertise to next-generation drone munitions, we are proving that our historic facilities and our people can rapidly pivot to support the warfighter.”

North Korea’s DMZ landmines sabotage the South’s peace push

North Korea’s DMZ landmines sabotage the South’s peace push
Seoul is seeking an apology for last month’s border blast even as Pyongyang fortifies a line it now treats as a permanent frontier
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Park Chan-kyongin Seoul
North Korea’s laying of landmines along its heavily fortified border with the South has laid bare how misaligned the two nations have become over their de facto land boundary, after three South Korean soldiers were wounded in an explosion last month.
Seoul blames Pyongyang for the blast near the military demarcation line (MDL) on September 21, in which one soldier lost a foot. On Tuesday, its Foreign Ministry said in a statement it was preparing a response to force an apology for the blast, without going into specifics, further urging the North to hold talks on the poorly signposted MDL.
Military personnel from both sides are technically forbidden from crossing the MDL under their 1953 armistice agreement. As the precise centre line of the 4km (2.5-mile) wide demilitarised zone (DMZ) that bisects the Korean peninsula, it serves as the effective land border between North and South Korea.
But the 250km (155-mile) long line is sparsely marked, with few of the more than 1,200 original markers that were installed over seven decades ago still in place.
A joint investigation by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that at least four mines at the site of last month’s blast, 10 metres (32 feet) south of the MDL, were deliberately planted by the North.

Drones hit two ships off coast of Bulgaria, sinking one, as government calls emergency meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:22:16 UTC
16:22:16 KST

Drones hit two ships off Bulgaria's coast and one of them sank, with the crew missing, the day after another drone attack sank a ship near Romania's shore in the Black Sea, in two consecutive drone attacks on NATO's Eastern flank countries.
A massive search is under way in the Black Sea for the crew of a cargo ship that sank after drones struck two commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast early Tuesday, the day after another drone attack sank a Turkish grain ship off the coast of Romania, killing 2 crew members.
Sea and aerial drones hit the ships at about 3am local time (2am CET), around 70 nautical miles east of the town of Byala in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria, which was in the area, saw an explosion on the first ship and rushed to the scene, Radev confirmed. They found an overturned lifeboat and life jackets but no one from the crew.
Officials have not said how many people were on board, nor the origin of the drones.
A second ship was attacked and caught fire, with all 18 of its crew rescued by the Dioscuria. Eleven are Turkish and seven Indian, according to the televised address from Radev.
Two of them were hospitalised, one with burns and one with a head injury. The other 16 were being brought ashore on a Border Police patrol boat.
Radev said two helicopters were sent to Varna to pick up rescue teams and a Su-25 aircraft was deployed to carry out aerial reconnaissance over the area. The operation is being run by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.
Both vessels sent distress signals during the night and one disappeared from Border Police radar at about 9am local time (8am CET), public broadcaster BNR reported.
Bulgarian shipping news site Maritime.bg named the sunken ship as the Alfa Watan and the second as the Palau-flagged Able. It said the strikes were the first attack on shipping in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Both vessels are Turkish-owned, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.
Ship tracking website vesselfinder.com shows the Alfa Watan was sailing under the flag of Togo and was headed for the Romanian port of Sulina.
The second ship was carrying wheat and sailing south, Radev said. The cargo of the sunken Alfa Watan is not yet known.
Radev, who called the attack "absolutely unacceptable", did not say who launched the drones, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the developments "concerning".
Three attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea within two days
Tuesday's attack occurred the day after a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine to Italy was attacked off Romania's coast in the Black Sea by at least one drone and sank after catching fire, killing two crew members.
Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry said the ship's captain, Azerbaijani national Rustam Ismayil oglu Hasanov, died and his body was being repatriated. A second Azerbaijani crew member, Mahammad Hamza oglu Suleymanzade, is still missing and the search and rescue operation is ongoing. Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry said their families were informed and they were receiving logistical and financial support.
11 other crew members were rescued by the Romanian authorities. Three Azerbaijani sailors and one Indian crew member among them are receiving emergency medical care in Romania.
Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry explicitly reiterated its urgent warning to Azerbaijani citizens to refrain from travelling to active conflict zones, working in high-risk areas, or taking employment on transport vessels operating along contested maritime corridors.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for yesterday's sinking of the cargo ship and called it "a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel" in neutral waters.
India condemned Tuesday's attack as part of the crew members were Indian nationals. The Indian Foreign Ministry released a statement saying that "India views these attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers with grave concern," adding that "the targeting of traffic in international waterways is severely undermining global commerce and welfare of people across the world."

Muhammed Yasin Gungor
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The ceasefire in Gaza has failed to provide stability or adequate humanitarian relief, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Tuesday, urging all parties to fully implement their obligations to achieve lasting peace.
“Last year’s ceasefire brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace,” Guterres said in a statement marking three years since the escalation began.
The UN chief called on all sides to advance to subsequent stages of the truce based on the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, stressing: “It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law.”

Guterres stressed that the ensuing military operations had caused “untold suffering” for Palestinians in Gaza through widespread deaths, displacement and catastrophic destruction.
Calling for an immediate end to civilian suffering in Gaza, Guterres reiterated that the international community must establish a credible political path ensuring Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side with equal rights and dignity.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, while destroying about 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.

Germany’s AfD poised to preside over state assembly for first time
- The far-right AfD won nearly 44% in Saxony-Anhalt and is set to preside over the state assembly for the first time, with Tobias Rausch likely to be elected Speaker.
- AfD needs support from the left-wing BSW party, which shares similar views on Russia and immigration, to govern but has alarmed other parties.
- The AfD’s rise adds pressure on Chancellor Merz, as his CDU struggles and AfD leads in national polls amid political disagreements.
AI generated
BERLIN – The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is poised on Oct 6 to preside over a state assembly for the first time following its landslide election victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD took nearly 44% of the vote in September in the state, located in the former communist East Germany, easily beating the centre-right CDU of unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
On Oct 6, newly elected state lawmakers will gather for the first time in the parliament building in the state capital Magdeburg to elect a Speaker, with the AfD’s candidate Tobias Rausch expected to win.
It would be the first time a far-right party has held such a position in post-war German history.
Several activist groups have called for protests outside the building on Oct 6 to urge other parties not to cooperate with the AfD, which in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as a “confirmed extremist” organisation by domestic intelligence.
Inside, the assembly is expected to start its session at 11am local time (5pm, Singapore time).
The anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly AfD narrowly missed out on an absolute majority, winning 39 out of 83 seats.
That means it will need to seek support from other parties, in the first instance from the five lawmakers from the small BSW, a left-wing party that nonetheless echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration.
The BSW has already said it will support a Speaker from the AfD.
Other parties have expressed alarm at the prospect.
The leader of the far-left Die Linke in the state, Eva von Angern, has drawn parallels with Hermann Goering’s time as Speaker of the Reichstag in the 1930s and his role in enabling Adolf Hitler’s takeover of power.
Merz under pressure
The AfD’s leader in Saxony Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, has said he hopes to be elected as state premier in December, which would be another first for the party.
The BSW has so far not committed to backing Siegmund for the post, although according to local media the two parties have already agreed to cooperate on other issues such as a commission of inquiry into government policies during the coronavirus pandemic.
The AfD is also courting support from the 15 CDU lawmakers.
But Sven Schulze, the CDU’s regional leader and current state premier, on Oct 5 insisted there would be no defectors from his party.
The AfD also placed first in a state election in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, although a coalition of left-wing parties is expected to continue governing.
In the city-state of Berlin, Die Linke notched a victory as both Merz’s CDU and the chancellor’s junior coalition partners, the centre-left Social Democrats, slumped.
The results of all three regional elections have added to the pressure on Merz, who took office in 2025 promising to sap the AfD’s appeal by kickstarting Germany’s spluttering economy and taking a tougher line on immigration.
But his coalition has instead been beset by disagreements over reforms while the AfD has surged to a clear lead in national opinion polls. AFP

Ukrainian Pilots Will Soon Begin Rafale Training in France, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale fighter jets in France, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared on October 5 following talks with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Zelenskyy announced the plans on his official Telegram channel after discussing Ukraine’s air defense needs and new French military assistance with Macron.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian pilots will begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the near future,” Zelenskyy wrote. “This is a strong step for Ukrainian combat aviation.”
France is also preparing a new defense package for Ukraine, which Kyiv expects to receive soon. Zelenskyy noted that the two leaders discussed the package’s contents but provided no details about the weapons or equipment involved.
Ukrainian and French teams are additionally working to localize the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine. Zelenskyy added that preparations for the FREYJA system are advancing and that the sides discussed ways to accelerate the work.
The Dassault Rafale is a French twin-engine multirole fighter designed for air superiority, air defense, precision ground strikes, reconnaissance, and long-range missions, with a maximum speed of Mach 1.8 and a capacity for up to 9.5 tons of external weapons and fuel.
In Ukrainian service, the aircraft could strengthen both air defense and strike aviation, using weapons including MICA and long-range METEOR air-to-air missiles, AASM precision bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
The agreement also provides for accompanying air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons, while Zelenskyy confirmed on October 5 that Ukrainian pilots would begin training on the Rafale in France in the near future.
Preparations for the Rafale program have been underway for months, and instruction for Ukrainian pilots and technicians was expected to begin in France as early as July, before the end of the year.
The early stages of the pipeline rely on GROB G 120TP trainers and Dornier Alpha Jet aircraft, which allow pilots to master navigation, flight controls, and combat maneuvers before moving on to frontline fighters. Kyiv and Paris have agreed on an initial batch of 16 Rafales, with the first four slated for transfer once training is complete.
The first aircraft are expected in Ukraine in 2028–2029, while plans reported in November 2025 envisioned as many as 100 Rafales over the longer term.
France's push to equip Ukraine with the Rafale builds on earlier fighter support for the Ukrainian Air Force. In February 2026, Ukraine was reportedly set to receive two Mirage 2000 jets from France by the end of the first quarter, along with additional training for pilots and maintenance crews. Over the long term, Ukraine was expected to field at least six French Mirage 2000 fighters.

Sahin Demir and Mohammed Sameai
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Tuesday that 100 Houthi fighters were killed and five drones were downed in the southwestern province of Taiz during ongoing military operations in the country.
The army’s Taiz Military Axis said in a statement that government forces carried out attacks on several fronts as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.
It said five operations were conducted Monday on the Al-Arbaeen front north of Taiz city, Al-Aqroudh to the south, Al-Anin and Jabal Habashi to the west, as well as Al-Bireen on the outskirts of the Al-Kadha front.
According to the army, around 100 Houthi fighters were killed and 150 others wounded, while five drones were shot down and six military vehicles and a tank were destroyed or damaged.
The army also said that its forces had retaken Jabal al-Manzara, al-Asharif and Dhiban in southern Taiz from the Houthis.
On Monday, Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced the launch of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, saying it aims to restore state institutions, retake the capital Sanaa and end Houthi control.
Government forces also announced Monday that they had retaken the Red Sea coastal city of Mokha and the strategic Bab el-Mandeb area from the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, meanwhile, disputed government accounts of battlefield advances and said the group maintained control of its positions.
He also claimed that Houthi forces had carried out dozens of strikes against what he described as Saudi forces in the provinces of Al-Jawf and Marib, as well as in Ras al-Ara and Al-Suqiya.
Saree claimed that more than 200 opposing fighters were killed or wounded in the attacks. Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-led coalition did not immediately comment on the claims.
Clashes resumed between government forces and the Houthis in July, marking the most intense fighting since a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that began in April 2022.
Fighting intensified in September, when the Houthis seized key areas in Al-Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including the strategic city of Mokha and Mayyun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
