Keeping up with the Bolsonaros: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win heralds rise of a political dynasty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:00:05 UTC
16:00:05 KST

The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.
As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.
Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.
Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.
Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.
His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)
The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.
Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.
Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.
During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.
The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections.
Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.
“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”
The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.
When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.
Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.
Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.
Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.
“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.
“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

Nine hours' work for CHF70: Uber drivers in Switzerland demand better conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Nine hours’ work for CHF70: Uber drivers in Switzerland demand better conditions
Uber drivers in Switzerland complain of falling pay, growing competition and a lack of transparency over the algorithms determining fares and rides. They want authorities to grant greater rights and protection.
Thirty-year-old Cem Kurun has been driving for Uber in canton Zurich since 2019. Over the years, he says, working conditions have deteriorated significantly, with lower fares and fierce competition among private transport providers and taxi drivers. The Covid pandemic and the arrival of Uber’s Estonian rival Bolt on the Zurich market in 2024 have made the situation worse, he says.
Kurun says he once managed to earn CHF1,200 ($1,437) working around 30 hours a week. Now, he makes just over CHF300. On the day he spoke to Swissinfo, he had made CHF70 after nine hours of work.
“How would I support a family? Would I have to turn to social services just to avoid starving?” he says. According to Kurun, many drivers are forced to rely on social assistance. “We drivers are the ones paying the price for this race to the bottom,” he says.
Beyond falling fares, Kurun complains that he has little real control over his work, despite operating as an independent driver. He suspects Uber’s app of algorithmic manipulation, including by penalising drivers who reject too many rides and displaying areas on the map that promise higher earnings, only for those to disappear once drivers arrive. He also casts doubt on whether drivers really have the freedom to set their own fares.
In theory, the Uber app allows drivers to set their own price. “But as soon as I set the price even 10 cents higher than Uber’s price per kilometre, I stop getting rides,” Kurun says.
Uber argues that drivers can accept or reject trips without penalty and that acceptance and cancellation rates are not used to determine how drivers are matched with passengers or to personalise fares.
Largest Swiss trade union: ‘Uber operates illegally’
The status of Uber drivers has been the subject of legal disputes in Switzerland for years.
According to the country’s largest trade union, Unia, the degree of control Uber exercises over its drivers is incompatible with actual self-employment. Drivers have no real freedom of choice and must comply with the working conditions imposed on them, says Philipp Zimmermann, a spokesperson for the union.
As a result, Zimmermann says, drivers are deprived of wages, expense reimbursements and social security contributions to which they are entitled as employees.
Several rulingsExternal link at the cantonal and federal level have found that drivers using Uber’s services should be considered employees. As early as 2018, Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) indicated that Uber drivers should be classified as such.
“What Uber is doing in Switzerland is completely illegal. Drivers continue to work under conditions of ‘false self-employment’. The authorities have a duty to put an end to this illegal model,” Zimmermann says.
Uber disputes this interpretation. The company points out that it has changed its operating model and the terms and conditions applying to drivers several times, and argues that previous court rulings, which concerned earlier contractual models, cannot automatically be applied to the current situation.
Uber also says the majority of drivers value the independence and flexibility offered by its app and that it provides independent partner drivers in Switzerland with free insurance coverage against certain risks.
The Geneva exception
After a years-long legal battle, Uber changed its operating model in the canton of GenevaExternal link. Today, most drivers using the platform are employed through a third-party company. Uber also reached an agreement with the cantonExternal link to regularise the preceding period and pay outstanding social security contributions.
For drivers, however, enforcing their rights does not always appear straightforward. Former Uber driver Guillaume Lemoine, who worked in Geneva, told Swissinfo that he had no choice but to take legal action against Uber to recover what he says are unpaid wages and work-related expenses from his time working for the company. The dispute is still ongoing.
Like Kurun, Lemoine describes falling fares since the Covid pandemic, “false autonomy” over pricing and penalties for behaviour such as rejecting rides. When he tried to contact Uber to report problems or technical issues, Lemoine says, “it felt like talking to robots”.
>> From Switzerland to Europe: how drivers’ fight against Uber began in Geneva:
More
‘I’ll be AI’s worst nightmare’: Uber drivers’ fight runs through Switzerland
A battle beyond Switzerland
Kurun believes authorities in Zurich should also do more to protect people working through platforms like Uber. In 2021, Zurich’s Social Insurance Court ruled that drivers using several Uber services should be considered employees. The Swiss Federal Court confirmedExternal link the ruling in 2023. Despite this, Kurun says nothing has changed and his working conditions have deteriorated.
Uber drivers are calling for more rights and protections in several other European countries as well. In early September, hundreds of thousands of drivers launched a collective action against Uber in the Netherlands, where the technology company has its European headquarters. Among other things, they are challenging its use of automated systems to determine pay and allocate rides.
At the same time, a group of French drivers, supported by Geneva-based organisation PersonalData.IO, specialising in personal data rights, is preparing a second collective action. According to Paul-Olivier Dehaye, the association’s founder, the compensation being sought could amount to €40,000 per driver.

‘I’ll be AI’s worst nightmare’: Uber drivers’ fight runs through Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

‘I’ll be AI’s worst nightmare’: Uber drivers’ fight runs through Switzerland
Uber drivers across Europe are challenging the opaque algorithms that determine their pay and assign rides. Their battle has roots in Geneva.
Early in his time with Uber, Brahim Ben Ali, a former driver in his forties from the outskirts of Lille, began to feel something was amiss with the platform. “I saw people making more money than me, even though I was out on the road for eight or ten hours. I couldn’t understand why,” he says. Ben Ali, who drove for Uber from 2015 to 2019, sometimes spent 60 to 70 hours per week behind the wheel, making less than €6 (CHF5.65) an hour – well below France’s minimum wage.
Ben Ali says the app encouraged drivers to go to certain areas, attracted by higher prices and greater demand, which then disappeared by the time they arrived. Drivers who rejected too many rides, he claims, would receive fewer offers or be disconnected from the platform.
“They played with us as if we were Pokémon,” Ben Ali says.
Growing suspicious, Ben Ali asked the platform to hand over all the data it held about him, hoping to better understand how the app worked. Each time, he says, his requests were either denied or only partially met.
That marked the beginning of his fight against the US tech giant’s algorithms and practices. Together with his union, Ben Ali organised large protests across France in 2019. He was subsequently disconnected from the platform without an explanation – “the equivalent of being fired”, he says.
Ben Ali believed that the decision to disconnect him had not been made by a human resources team but by an algorithm. To prove it, he first turned to France’s data protection authority. Then, through a mutual acquaintance, he met Paul-Olivier Dehaye, a mathematician and founder of PersonalData.IO, a Geneva-based association that helps platform workers – including drivers and delivery workers – exercise their rights over their personal data.
The French union and the Swiss association banded together to get to the bottom of Uber’s practices.
>> Uber drivers in Switzerland talk about their working conditions:
More
Nine hours’ work for CHF70: Uber drivers in Switzerland demand better conditions
Reconstructing the ‘Uber system’ from Geneva
“Everyone has the right to obtain the data that documents their working conditions,” Dehaye says. This right was strengthened in 2018, when the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) became applicable across the European Union. Drawing on GDPR, Dehaye began helping drivers across Europe get their data.
It wasn’t easy. Dehaye says that even finding out where to send a formal request was a challenge. And when Uber did respond, he says, their information was often incomplete. “There was always something missing,” he says. Dehaye persisted, pressing Uber for months. “I went all the way to the [European] headquarters in Amsterdam to force Uber to listen to us.”
Once they finally gained access to the data, Dehaye and the drivers began piecing together elements of the Uber system. They found that the platform collected large amounts of information, including how long a driver had been available, how long they had waited for a ride, where they were before accepting it, how many rides they rejected, when they began travelling towards a passenger and how long they transported them.
What emerges, says Dehaye, is a system of extensive algorithmic control of drivers’ work. Uber’s algorithms, he argues, do much more than simply connect drivers and passengers: they use AI and machine learning models to determine fares and play a role in deciding how rides are allocated, and automated systems can also be involved in decisions to disconnect drivers.
Algorithmic manipulation
In Zurich, Uber driver Cem Kurun told Swissinfo that on one occasion he compared what he had earned from a ride with what the passenger said they had paid and found a difference of almost 50%. He also recounts the case of a colleague who allegedly received just over CHF30 for a ride for which the passenger said they had paid CHF80.
Like Ben Ali, Kurun suspects that drivers’ behaviour may affect the allocation of rides and that drivers who reject many offers may be penalised.
“Often when I’m waiting in the same place as other drivers, I notice that they keep getting rides while I’m left there waiting,” he says. On the day Swissinfo spoke to him, Kurun said he had been working for around nine hours, since 8am, and had earned just CHF70.
Uber categorically rejects these allegations. The company describes as “completely false” claims that it adjusts the prices or rides offered to drivers based on individual behaviour, such as previous decisions to reject a ride.
Uber hit with million-euro fines
In 2023, Uber was fined €10 million for a series of breaches of its transparency obligations and of drivers’ rights regarding their data. The following year, it received a €290 million fine for transferring European drivers’ personal data to the US.
And this summer, the Dutch Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of almost €825 million on Uber for temporarily suspending or permanently deactivating drivers’ accounts through fully automated decision-making processes, in violation of GDPR rules.
These results are spurring further action across Europe.
With early help from Dehaye and his Geneva-based organisation, British former driver James Farrar became involved in the fight to gain access to drivers’ data. Worker Info Exchange International, the organisation Farrar leads, recently launched a new collective action in the Netherlands, where Uber has its European headquarters, on behalf of around 240,000 drivers across Europe.
Ben Ali believes the losses suffered by drivers go much further after years of what he calls poor working conditions. Together with Dehaye and around 19,000 drivers, he is now working on a separate collective action. According to his calculations, claims could amount to around €40,000 per driver.
“Why should Uber be the one getting rich off our backs thanks to our data?” Ben Ali asks. “We need to take back control of our data.”
“I’ll be AI’s worst nightmare,” he says. He promises to keep fighting.

Indonesia steps up border health surveillance after suspected plague-linked death in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:59:31 UTC
15:59:31 KST

Faisal Mahmud
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Indonesia has stepped up health surveillance at international entry points following reports that a laboratory worker in Russia died from pneumonia suspected of being linked to plague, according to the state-run Antara news agency.
Aji Muhawarman, head of the Health Ministry’s Bureau of Communication and Public Information, said authorities were closely monitoring developments while strengthening preparedness at airports and seaports.
He said that so far, there had been no notification through the International Health Regulations National Focal Point or the World Health Organization’s Event Information Site requiring specific vigilance.
Despite the absence of an international alert, authorities have intensified checks, including at international airports and seaports in Bali, Antara reported.
Measures include health declarations through the SATUSEHAT Health Pass system, monitoring travelers for symptoms, risk-based assessments of incoming vessels and surveillance of rodents and fleas.
Travelers showing symptoms such as fever, coughing or shortness of breath may be referred to designated infectious disease hospitals for isolation and treatment.
The measures follow the death of a 28-year-old employee of Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia.
Russian authorities have said she died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that testing found no microorganisms linked to her professional activities.
Nearly 200 contacts have reportedly been placed under medical observation as investigations continue.

Russia testing aerostats to defend against Ukrainian UAVs – media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:58:19 EEST
15:58:19 KST

Russia has begun testing aerostat-based barriers designed to counter Ukrainian drones; the tests were featured on the Rossiya 1 TV channel, and according to the designers, the technology is already ready for mass production, Militarny ezine reports.
"The system consists of aerostats connected by a cable with Kevlar lines hanging down from it. The concept is that a drone flying into such a net would get the lines tangled in its propellers and lose control. According to the designers, the technology is already ready for mass production. However, protecting a single large facility would require deploying at least 10 such aerostats," the report states.
Similar technology was used during World War I and World War II to counter enemy aircraft. It forced enemy bombers to fly at higher altitudes, thereby reducing the accuracy of their strikes. The expectation is that the situation will be similar with UAVs, making them easier to detect and forcing them to fly at higher altitudes.

Victory in the Quebec provincial election has given the pro-sovereignty Parti Québécois (PQ) the chance to take the reins of power for the first time since 2014, potentially posing a serious challenge for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the BBC reports.
Issues highlighted by the party include immigration and the monarchy, and the PQ has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence. A similar vote is planned for October in the province of Alberta. Quebec—where French is the first language for the majority of the population—has previously held referendums on secession (in 1980 and 1995), though polls indicate that only about 30% of Quebecers support the idea. Newly elected provincial Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon stated that the vote could take place after US President Donald Trump leaves office.
Depending on the outcome of the Alberta referendum, Carney could find himself trying to manage crises in different parts of Canada. Trump has two more years left in office, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his promise, a third Quebec independence referendum could take place in 2029 or 2030.
Beyond the issue of sovereignty, Plamondon has also made it clear that he will clash with Ottawa if he believes the federal government is infringing upon the province's interests. During the election campaign, Plamondon indicated he would pressure the capital on immigration matters, vowing to oppose any increase in migrant numbers that a Carney government might implement.

Rafael-linked firm gets first orders for drone laser pod

Microcon Vision, an Israeli maker of small camera systems for drones, has unveiled a 1.9 kg (4.2-pound) sensor payload that lets small unmanned aircraft mark targets with a laser for laser-guided weapons. The company said on Oct. 5 that the MICRO-D has already received initial orders, with first deliveries expected by the end of 2026.
Microcon Vision did not name the customers, the number of systems ordered, or the value of the orders. Its CEO said demand has been strongest in the United States, where the company works through its affiliate CONTROP USA.
Laser target designation has usually been done by ground troops with handheld designators or by larger aircraft, including medium-altitude drones and attack helicopters. A designator fires coded laser pulses at a target, and a laser-guided bomb or missile set to the same code homes in on the reflected energy. Putting that function on a drone small enough to carry a payload under 2 kg would let a small unit find a target and guide a strike onto it without bringing in a larger aircraft or putting a soldier within line of sight.
The MICRO-D’s designator has an output of 30 millijoules and complies with STANAG 3733, the NATO standard for laser designator coding used with laser-guided munitions. Microcon Vision has not published the designator’s effective range.
The company said the system is built for platforms flying at lower altitudes, including below cloud cover, where they can detect and track targets and designate them for compatible precision-guided weapons. Low cloud can block the view of aircraft flying higher up and has long complicated laser designation from the air.
The payload packs seven sensors and functional channels into a single two-axis gyro-stabilized gimbal, the company said. These include a daylight camera, a thermal imager, target tracking and the laser designator. The system also provides several simultaneous video outputs, line-of-sight stabilization, an airborne tracker and inertial navigation. Optional AI-based software adds video motion detection and automatic target recognition.
For integration, the MICRO-D connects over Ethernet and comes with a software development kit. It can optionally use MAVLink, a messaging protocol widely used by commercial and military drones to talk to ground control stations.
“The growing use of smaller tactical platforms is creating a need for capabilities that until now have largely been available on larger systems,” said Chen Almog, CEO and co-founder of Microcon Vision. “MICRO-D was developed to address this gap, allowing smaller platforms to take a more active role in the sensor-to-shooter chain. The initial orders we have received reflect the operational demand we are seeing for this type of capability, particularly in the U.S., where our cooperation with our affiliate CONTROP USA provides U.S. customers with local business presence, effective program execution, local technical and field support, significantly enhancing our ability to serve our customers and partners.”
The company is marketing the MICRO-D as free of International Traffic in Arms Regulations controls, which can make export approvals simpler than for U.S.-origin military hardware. It also says the system meets National Defense Authorization Act sourcing rules, which bar certain Chinese-made components from U.S. military drones, and contains no germanium. Germanium is commonly used in thermal camera lenses, and China, the dominant supplier, placed export restrictions on the metal in 2023.
Microcon Vision is part of CONTROP Precision Technologies, an Israeli electro-optics company, and the company describes itself as also part of Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. Its existing products include the MICRO300 and MICRO600 surveillance payloads and the STING seeker for small drones and loitering munitions. The MICRO-D is the company’s first laser designation payload.

The European Solidarity faction in the Verkhovna Rada has expelled non-party lawmaker Oleksiy Honcharenko following his recent remarks, the party said in a statement published on its official website on Monday evening.
"Oleksiy Honcharenko's public positions on ending the war and Ukraine's future security architecture have diverged from the position of European Solidarity and its ideological principles. That is why the European Solidarity faction has decided that we can no longer continue a shared political path because of ideological differences. This decision does not erase years of joint work. But party unity cannot be a formality behind which fundamentally different answers to the question of the state's future are hidden," the party said.
The party said the public debate triggered by Honcharenko's proposals showed that "the authorities must finally begin an honest conversation with society about how they see a realistic path to a ceasefire and a just peace," and said it is ready for such a discussion.
"But our starting position is unchanged: peace cannot be paid for by renouncing that for the sake of which and thanks to which Ukraine has survived in this war. Compromises can be part of the path to ending the war. But Ukraine's independence, its European future, questions of national identity and the right to determine its own security system are not subject to compromise. For us, the unity of a team based on shared values and principles is important. The ES team is not just a faction, but tens of thousands of party members, the most authoritative of whom are our colleagues now serving in the Armed Forces, whose opinion and position on defending the country are fundamental for us," it said.
Honcharenko posted a series of messages on Telegram on Oct 2 calling for negotiations with Russia to begin with agreements to stop strikes on ports, enterprises, schools, hospitals, residential buildings and bridges. After that, he said, more difficult issues could be discussed, including Donbas and Ukraine's neutral status.
Honcharenko is not a member of the European Solidarity party but belongs to its parliamentary faction. He is a member of the Verkhovna Rada budget committee, the permanent delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe and numerous groups on interparliamentary relations with other countries. He chairs the Verkhovna Rada temporary investigative commission on possible violations of Ukrainian law in defense, anti-corruption legislation and the observance of human rights and freedoms under martial law, and is a member of other such commissions.
In the previous, eighth, convocation of the Verkhovna Rada (2014-19), he was a member of the Petro Poroshenko Bloc faction and party. He did not join the renewed European Solidarity party, led by Poroshenko, after the bloc was reformatted, and ran in the last parliamentary elections as a non-party self-nominated candidate in constituency No. 137 (Odesa region).

Veteran-led drone company moves into North Texas airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:52:19 UTC
15:52:19 KST

- XMX Defense broke ground Oct. 3 at Mineral Wells Regional Airport in Texas, where it is converting leased facilities for drone assembly, maintenance and flights.
- The company has not disclosed its investment, hiring plans, customers or a production timeline for the site, which sits near the former U.S. Army Fort Wolters.
XMX Defense, a Texas-based developer of military drones, has begun converting hangars and buildings at Mineral Wells Regional Airport, about 80 km (50 miles) west of Fort Worth, into a site for assembling, maintaining and flying unmanned aircraft.
The company held a groundbreaking ceremony at the airport on Oct. 3. It has leased several existing facilities there and started preparing them for aircraft assembly, systems integration, engineering, maintenance, training and flight operations, XMX said in an announcement.
XMX has not said how much it is investing in the site, how many people it plans to hire, or when the first aircraft will be built or flown there. The company also did not name any military customers or contracts tied to the Mineral Wells operation.
XMX describes itself as an American defense technology company building unmanned aircraft for defense, government and special-mission users. Its lineup runs from smaller tactical drones to the ROGUE 450, a hybrid-electric aircraft that takes off and lands vertically and is designed for longer missions.
Hybrid-electric designs pair batteries and electric motors with a fuel-burning engine or generator. The setup lets a vertical takeoff drone launch without a runway while carrying enough energy to stay in the air longer than a battery-only aircraft of similar size. XMX has not published range, endurance or payload figures for the ROGUE 450.
“Most of us in the company are veterans of some kind,” said Clay Kroschel, co-founder and CEO of XMX Defense.
Kroschel said the company has “built XMX around a mission to provide the technology and capabilities that help bring our men and women home safe.”
“We’re honored to do that work in a community like Mineral Wells, with such a strong defense aviation history,” Kroschel said.
Just outside the city sits the former Fort Wolters, which served as the U.S. Army’s primary helicopter training center during the Vietnam War era, when large numbers of Army aviators learned to fly there before moving on to advanced training and deployment. The post closed in 1973, but the Texas Army National Guard still uses part of the former installation as a training area for air-supported exercises.
“There’s a real through-line in Mineral Wells’ aviation history,” said Mayor Pro Tem Beth Watson. “This community helped train a generation of helicopter pilots when vertical flight was changing the way the Army operated. Decades later, the next generation of vertical flight technology is coming to our airport through unmanned aircraft. We’re proud to welcome XMX and excited to see these facilities put back to work.”
The ceremony drew state and local officials along with county and civic leaders from Palo Pinto and Parker counties, where economic development officials hope the project will pull more aerospace and defense work westward from the Fort Worth area.
“Mineral Wells sits in a unique position,” said Chris Strayer, executive director of the Parker County Economic Development Council. “It’s connected to the aerospace and defense strength of North Texas, but it also has the space and infrastructure to grow something of its own. We’ve seen in other parts of the country how one unmanned-aircraft company can become the nucleus for a broader cluster of suppliers, manufacturers, engineers, and technology companies.”
XMX also plans to use the site to set up what it calls the Texas Unmanned Systems Defense Center of Excellence. The company says the effort would bring defense and unmanned-systems firms together to share infrastructure and operations at the airport.

Thousands mass in France for high school protests
- Tens of thousands of students and trade union members are protesting in Paris against school conditions, causing clashes with police and injuries on both sides.
- Protests highlight issues like missing teachers, poor school facilities, and government plans to make vandals pay for damages.
- Authorities face criticism for police brutality, with Amnesty International calling for an end to excessive force and internal investigations underway.
AI generated
PARIS - Thousands of demonstrators were massing under heavy police surveillance on Oct 6 in Paris and cities across France, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better conditions in protests punctuated by violent clashes.
Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools attended by those aged 15 to 17 since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
In the Paris suburb of Creteil, where the protests started in September, students have piled barriers outside the Saint-Exupery high school.
“We are here to make our voice heard, all too often forgotten,” student Abderrahmane Abdelkader said on the microphone.
In the western city of Rennes, teacher Romain Dubourgn said he and other teachers were present to show support.
“With about thirty colleagues, we talked about the police brutality we’ve witnessed and decided to be there for our students if they need us,” he told AFP.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have lit dustbin fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police, who have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement, with a 15-year-old losing a hand on Oct 5 after, according to a police union source, he picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers.
Television images on Oct 6 showed anti-riot police with shields pushing back crowds who had formed a human chain and blocked a road by a school in eastern Paris.
There were protests taking place in Marseille in the south, Nantes in the west and Lyon in the south-east, AFP correspondents said.
‘Protect high-school students’
The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron after his maximum two terms in office.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
The authorities are expecting some 20,000 to 40,000 demonstrators in Paris.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office has called for “peaceful” gatherings, calling for a return to “a structured, legal and democratic form of opposition”.
The head of the CGT labour union Sophie Binet has said its members would be there to “protect high-school students”.
Greens party leader Marine Tondelier has urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations”.
‘Disproportionate police repression’
Several unions and rights groups have accused the police of using disproportionate force against the protesters.
Amnesty International said late on Oct 5 that the French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests”.
“The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and policing techniques by the police,” Amnesty’s Anne Savinel-Barras said.
The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late on Oct 5.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.
More than 5,000 people, 87% of them minors, have been arrested.
Lecornu’s office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.
The prime minister has sought to address the issue of missing teachers and renovating buildings that are dilapidated.
The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of using public funds. AFP

By DANIELLA MATAR - AP Sports Writer
France left it late to beat Belgium 4-1 in the Nations League as Zinedine Zidane got his first home win as the national coach on Monday.
Substitutes Désiré Doué, Rayan Cherki and Michael Olise (two) netted four goals in 14 minutes to completely turn the match around for France, which trailed until the 77th minute.
"Tonight, this is soccer, this is what we love," Zidane said. "We faced some difficulties in the first half but that's part of the game; it's the kind of match you get from time to time. It's good to set things right - which is what we did - and we managed to play an extraordinary second half."
The win reinforced France's control of Group A1, three points above Italy, which beat Turkey 3-1.
Third-placed Belgium slipped four points below France. Turkey has no points.
Zidane started his time in charge of Les Bleus with wins over Turkey and Belgium before being held to a draw by Italy on his home debut on Friday.
"It's a collective effort, too," Olise said. "He (Zidane) brings in ideas, we follow them - we've done that well over the last four matches, we're going to continue like this."
France was still to book a spot in the quarterfinals. It would have been assured of one of the top two places in the group if it beat Belgium and Italy failed to beat Turkey.
France's star-studded bench to the rescue
At the Stade de France, Belgium took the lead in the 35th minute. Dodi Lukébakio sprung the offside trap to run onto a magnificent, long pass from Roméo Lavia, raced through one-on-one with debutant Guillaume Restes and powered it over the France goalkeeper and into the back of the net.
But Zidane's star-studded bench turned things around. Doué levelled in the 77th with a low shot into the bottom right corner, and Les Bleus took the lead in somewhat strange fashion four minutes later.
Maarten Vandevoordt appeared set to save Cherki's strike but the ball hit the Belgium goalie's foot and rebounded in off his left arm. Olise set that up and added two goals in three minutes himself to seal the match.
"We knew the substitutes could change the game because they are high-quality players," Zidane said. "But, once again, it was a complete team performance; while the substitutes might have made the difference when they came on, everyone has been good over these past two weeks - everyone played their part, and that's what stands out to me.
"We talk about Olise because he scored, and Désiré came on and scored - every player who came on scored - which means it was the right call."

Germany's far-right AfD bids to take helm of state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:45:56 UTC
15:45:56 KST

The AfD's Tobias Rausch was elected speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament on Tuesday, marking the first time the far-right party has held such a post in Germany.
A candidate for Germany's AfD was elected parliament speaker in the state of Saxony Anhalt Tuesday, the first time a far-right party has held such a post in the country since 1945.
Lawmakers gathered for the first time since the AfD's landslide election victory in the eastern region last month, with 48 MPs voting for the party's Tobias Rausch as speaker and 29 against.
The AfD won the state election on 6 September with 43.8 percent and now holds 39 of the 83 seats. As the largest parliamentary group, it has the right to nominate the president. For the election itself, however, a simple majority of valid votes cast is sufficient.
This means Rausch is reliant on votes from other parties. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), with five deputies, has announced it will back him. The conservative CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), the Greens and the Left Party intend to vote against the AfD candidate. If the BSW deputies vote for Rausch, he will have the votes he needs.
Why is this election so significant?
The AfD's state branch in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by the state office for the protection of the constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, which is a department within the CDU-led Interior Ministry. Observers therefore see Rausch's possible election as a political watershed.
The office of president of the state parliament is not merely ceremonial: the president chairs the plenary sessions and the council of elders and heads the parliamentary administration. Political scientist Nicolas Spohn told the magazine Focus that the president's power lies "above all in procedural issues and powers relating to the rules of the house".
Spohn stressed that it remains open how an AfD politician would actually exercise the office. Rausch has offered his own description of his political style. "I am not a hardliner, I am pragmatic," he said, according to the German Press Agency. He wants "to take the interests of everyone into account as far as possible".
The culture of debate in parliament, he said, should be "tough on substance but fair to individuals".
The election of the speaker of the state parliament does not decide who will lead the future state government. Nevertheless, it is likely to be closely watched.
AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund is aiming to be elected minister-president, the head of the state government, in December and needs at least 42 votes to do so.

Fuel in Italy, tax cuts expire: diesel prices rise as hauliers threaten strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:45:20 UTC
15:45:20 KST

With tax breaks expiring and the decree on flexible excise duties delayed, diesel prices are rising again. The haulage sector warns of a strike as the government summons oil companies that have introduced initial capped prices.
Diesel will once again cost €0.61 more per litre from Tuesday, after the expiry at midnight of the latest tax discount on fuel. In the absence of the ministerial decree due to be published in the Official Gazette, the much-heralded mechanism of "accise mobili" remains on hold.
Filling up at the pump is officially more expensive, marking the complete end of fuel tax cuts for the first time since last March, when the first decree was adopted in the wake of the outbreak of the conflict between the United States and Iran.
Despite assurances in recent days about the activation of the mobile excise duty, the joint decree from the Ministry for the Environment and Energy Security and the Ministry of Economy and Finance did not arrive in time.
The mobile excise duty is designed to reuse the extra VAT revenue generated by the previous month’s crude oil price increases. Unlike discounts financed directly from the public purse, this system does not add to the deficit, but it only allows for smaller reductions in prices.
The excise rate on diesel therefore returns to its standard level. This is the final step in a phase-out that began on 26 September, when the original discount of €0.122 per litre had already been halved.
On the government’s table, the issue of targeted measures for low-income households and haulage operators also remains unresolved, with no political agreement reached so far.
Palazzo Chigi had announced its intention to scrap across-the-board fuel cuts, which mainly benefit wealthier people who consume more, in favour of targeted aid for those categories most exposed to rising prices.
Hauliers sound the alarm
The end of the subsidies has prompted a backlash from the logistics sector. Assotir has issued a "cry for help", highlighting the dramatic situation facing companies.
"Road haulage is going through a dramatic time and if it does not come to a halt in protest, it will grind to a halt because of the price of diesel," said Assotir president Anna Vita Manigrasso.
The association’s secretary-general, Claudio Donati, has not ruled out a sector-wide strike.
"It is a last-resort weapon because it means bringing the country to a standstill. We would like to avoid it, but in the absence of answers the government will have to reckon with us," he said.
The response from government and business
In a bid to curb the impact of the international situation, Business and Made in Italy Minister Adolfo Urso and Environment and Energy Security Minister Gilberto Pichetto have summoned the main refining operators, including Eni, IP, Q8, Saras and Isab, to Palazzo Piacentini on Thursday to consider boosting domestic production.
At the same time, private companies have begun to move. Since 28 September Eni has introduced a price cap of €2.19 per litre for diesel and €1.99 for petrol, for 30 days across the Enilive network.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has welcomed the response from the oil groups and thanked "all those who are making an effort at a difficult time".
The overall outlook remains uncertain, clouded by warnings from Brussels of a "difficult winter" due to energy costs, which are pushing the European Union to consider postponing until 2028 the rules to curb methane leakage from energy imports.

Hedge funds can help financial markets become more liquid and efficient, but tend to amplify crises, according to new analysis by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Publishing a chapter of its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report ahead of its annual meeting next week, the IMF said hedge funds had become “increasingly important participants in financial markets,” with their gross assets trebling over the past decade to $13trn.
It warned that, “the growing market footprint of hedge funds can support market liquidity and efficiency in normal times but may amplify price dislocations and liquidity strains during periods of stress.”
In particular, it highlighted high levels of leverage, fragile investor funding, and “crowded trades,” with many funds making the same bet, causing big swings in markets if they are rapidly unwound.
The IMF calls for closer supervision of hedge funds by regulators, including “risk based leverage limits” to prevent them becoming too overstretched.

IMF urges governments to offer targeted support for poorest households hit by energy price shock
Heather Stewart
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged governments to respond to the latest energy price shock with targeted support for the poorest households, instead of by subsidising bills.
In a new blogpost, published ahead of the IMF’s annual meetings next week, the Washington-based lender says energy price spikes can have long-lasting effects, and hit low-income households hardest.
By analysing the impact of the last energy crisis, in 2022-24, the IMF shows that, “for every euro spent suppressing electricity, natural gas, and gasoline prices, less than 20 cents reached the poorest fifth of households”.
It also points out that by making energy cheaper for everyone, across-the-board subsidies, “weaken incentives to conserve scarce resources”.

Shares in the online fashion retailer Asos are down 13.3% now, after users of its mobile app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the company’s data. The company is investigating whether there has been a hack.
Marty Bauer, ecommerce expert at the software company Omnisend, said:
Asos’s website never went down, but the commercial damage can start the moment customers lose trust in the messages coming through its own channels. People let a brand onto their phone because they trust it. Once that channel has been used to threaten them, they may start questioning genuine messages too.
Push notifications are one of the hardest-working channels retailers have. Across brands using Omnisend, push automations had a 22.9% conversion rate last year. If customers now switch notifications off or stop engaging with them, that could have a direct impact on repeat sales.
The first practical step is to pause any automated promotional sends. A discount arriving before an explanation of that notification risks making customers feel their concerns are being ignored.
With Black Friday approaching, Asos will want existing customers to feel comfortable buying again. If shoppers disengage from push notifications and email now, that is revenue the brand may find difficult to win back.
Tatyana Shishkova, lead security researcher at the anti-virus provider Kaspersky, said:
The ability of hackers to directly contact potential victims through push notifications in the Asos app highlights how disruptive cyber incidents can be when threat actors gain access to trusted communication channels. Beyond the immediate technical impact, incidents like this can quickly undermine customer trust, particularly when alarming messages appear to come from a legitimate organisation.
While attackers have reportedly claimed to have compromised a Snowflake environment, organisations should avoid drawing conclusions based solely on statements made by cybercriminals. Establishing what systems were accessed, what data may have been exposed, and how attackers gained entry requires a thorough forensic investigation.
Regardless of the attack path, the incident reinforces the importance of strong identity and access management across cloud environments. Recent investigations by Kaspersky have shown that cybercriminals increasingly rely on misconfigurations, exposed services and legitimate tools already present within an organisation’s environment rather than sophisticated malware. In some cases, attackers have even abused trusted business systems, including corporate printers, to deliver ransom demands directly to employees and amplify the psychological impact of an attack.
She added that customers whose data may have been compromised should remain alert to follow-on phishing and social engineering attempts. Cybercriminals often exploit the confusion surrounding high-profile incidents, using convincing messages that appear to come from trusted organisations.
Here’s our full story on Asos, and a bit of a potted history below.
Snowflake, which stores data for many major companies including Asos, has reportedly been the target of a number of data breaches in recent years, including an attack on Ticketmaster which saw customer details stolen.
London-headquartered Asos, which owns brands including Topshop and Miss Selfridge, has 17 million customers around the world, in more than 150 countries. It employs 2,800 people.
The UK is its group’s largest market, accounting for nearly half (49%) of revenues in its first half results.
However, more recently Asos has struggled against competition from Boohoo, Shein and others, and is in the middle of a major turnaround programme as it tries to reverse a drop in sales and return to profit.
Late last year, the company said it was testing “Styled for You”, which uses AI trained on its database of 100,000 curated outfits to suggest items that could go together with those a shopper has already bought or has searched.
Marie Wilcox, vice president of market strategy at the automated cyber investigation platform Binalyze, said:
This notification was psychological warfare, designed to whip up panic. Attackers know that any panic piles on the pressure on Asos to think about paying up rather than taking time to develop a rational response.
This is a clear shift in how we see breaches: from learning after the fact, to thousands of users seeing the news pushed onto their phone home screens in real time.
The next few hours are crucial. Asos cannot let panicked pressure dictate its response. The priority must be investigation, and closing the gap that allowed this mass notification to go out. Activity like this will surely have huge noise around it that leaves a clear trail, so there should be plenty of evidence of what happened and how to fix it.
This is also further evidence of the pressure security teams are under. They are overloaded: 15% of security alerts have to be flat-out ignored, 37% of vulnerabilities go undiscovered, and the focus is so totally on alerts and response that teams cannot proactively hunt threats before they strike. In this environment something will inevitably break through.
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, part of the cybersecurity software company Nord Security, said:
This is an unusually brazen and threatening message. The attackers aren’t simply claiming to have breached Asos - they’re publicly telling the company to engage with them or they will leak what they say they have obtained.
What makes it even more concerning is how that threat appears to have been delivered. A message apparently written for ASOS’s data protection and IT teams has instead been pushed directly to customers through the company’s own app notification system. That suggests someone has gained unauthorised access to at least part of Asos’s systems, although we don’t yet know how extensive that access is.
The attackers claim they have ‘fully compromised’ Asos Snowflake instance. Snowflake is a cloud data platform businesses use to store and analyse large quantities of information. If that claim proves genuine, the critical question will be what information was held there and whether any of it was accessed or downloaded. At this stage, however, customers shouldn’t assume their personal or payment information has been stolen - that hasn’t been established.
What customers should be particularly alert to now is what happens next, Briedis said.
High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.
Don’t click links in unexpected messages, even if they look convincing. Go directly to the Asos app or website instead. Customers should also make sure their Asos password is unique and, if they’ve used the same password elsewhere, change it on those accounts too.
Until Asos completes its investigation, we won’t know exactly what has been accessed or how the attackers got in. But this incident shows how powerful access to a trusted communications channel can be. When an attacker can potentially speak to customers through a company’s own systems, it makes the threat considerably more convincing and potentially much more damaging.

Advanced Navigation opens U.S. factory in Huntsville
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:43:48 UTC
15:43:48 KST

- Advanced Navigation is opening a U.S. headquarters and factory in Huntsville, Alabama, to build GPS-independent navigation systems for defense customers, with production starting in 2027.
- The expansion is backed by a $110 million Series C round, and the plant will initially produce about a quarter of its Australian output.
Advanced Navigation, an Australian maker of navigation systems that keep working when GPS is jammed or spoofed, is setting up a U.S. headquarters and factory in Huntsville, Alabama, to build the gear closer to American defense customers.
The company’s U.S. arm, Advanced Navigation America, said the site will be a Positioning, Navigation and Timing Center of Excellence that researches, develops and manufactures navigation technology for military platforms. Product production is scheduled to start in 2027. Mike Cohen, president of Advanced Navigation America, told Axios Huntsville the facility should be running around March or April.
The plant will go into a former Line-X facility near Huntsville’s airport, Axios reported. At first, it will produce about 25% to 30% of what the company’s Australian operation turns out, Cohen said, with the goal of eventually matching it. The company has not said how much it is spending on the site or how many people it will hire.
The expansion is funded from a $110 million Series C round the Sydney-based company closed in March, led by Airtree Ventures with backing from investors including KKR and In-Q-Tel, the CIA’s venture arm. Cohen told Axios the money is also being spread across the company’s operations in Australia and the United Kingdom.
Advanced Navigation’s core products are inertial navigation systems, which work out where a vehicle is by measuring its own motion from a known starting point, without relying on satellite signals. The company’s high-end systems use fiber-optic gyroscopes, sensors precise enough to detect the Earth’s rotation. It also builds laser velocity sensors. Advanced Navigation says it is one of the few companies able to make strategic-grade fiber-optic gyroscopes at scale, a claim it has not backed with production figures.
“With technology this precise, you can’t separate engineering from manufacturing,” said Chuck Matheny, vice president of U.S. operations at Advanced Navigation America.
The company said the Huntsville site will also work on other ways to navigate without GPS, including MEMS sensors, vision-based systems, AI and quantum sensing, and will be used for U.S. acquisitions of companies with related technology. It said the facility will support classified U.S. Department of War programs.
Advanced Navigation said its customers include Anduril, Kongsberg, Rheinmetall, BAE Systems, Leonardo and Lockheed Martin. It works with the U.S. Navy and U.S. Army on future navigation requirements through programs including the All-Domain Persistent Experiment. The company said it has more than 100,000 systems in use worldwide, and in March reported that more than 80% of its revenue comes from the United States and Europe.
“We’re putting the people who build and missionize this technology within minutes of our defense customers, changing how quickly we understand a requirement, solve it and deploy it into the field,” said Mike Cohen, president of Advanced Navigation America.
Huntsville is home to Redstone Arsenal, the Missile Defense Agency, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center and the headquarters of U.S. Space Command, and hosts offices of most major U.S. defense contractors.
The company pitched the move against the Pentagon’s push into autonomous systems, for which the fiscal 2027 budget request includes $53.6 billion. Drones, robotic vehicles and guided weapons all depend on knowing where they are, and GPS jamming and spoofing have become routine in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Swiss media house Tamedia cutting further 34 jobs
Swiss media group Tamedia is making further job cuts across its various newspapers. The Zurich-based group said it would cut 34 full-time posts, affecting 41 people.
Of the 41 staff members affected, 28 work in the German-speaking editorial teams and nine in French-speaking Switzerland, where Tamedia publishes, amongst others, 24 Heures, La Tribune de Genève, Bilan and Le Matin dimanche. Four people from the print desk are also affected.
Employees who will lose their jobs will be informed by the end of October, subject to the outcome of the consultation process in French-speaking Switzerland. Tamedia adds that a “redundancy plan accompanied by support measures, such as opportunities for retraining or early retirement” will be offered.
Tamedia justifies these cuts by citing changing reader expectations, shifts in media consumption patterns and a sharply declining advertising market. With this new restructuring, “tasks will be consolidated, administration streamlined, and processes simplified and automated”, the publisher states.
It adds that it needs resources that can be “deployed in a more targeted manner where they create the most value for our subscribers”.
Jessica Peppel-Schulz, director of Tamedia, says she regrets these job cuts, which are, however, “imposed by the new market reality.” The company must restructure “so that it is economically viable and so that we can continue to invest in the future in quality journalism, strong brands and relevant products.”
Restructuring measures
The last major restructuring at Tamedia took place in 2024. At that time, the group announced, amongst other things, the closure of the printing centres in Bussigny and Zurich, as well as the loss of around 50 jobs across its newspapers.
The publisher subsequently guaranteed a freeze on redundancies, at least until September 2026. However, in early 2026, it announced a further 25 to 30 job cuts, mainly in its commercial division.
Tamedia is not the only media organisation to have undergone a series of restructuring measures over the past several years. Just last month, the Ringier Group (Blick, L’Illustré, PME) announced the loss of 14 jobs in French-speaking Switzerland, whilst GHI (Genève Home Informations) and Lausanne Cités indicated that they would cease publication in December (36 jobs at risk).
This summer, St-Paul Médias (La Liberté, La Gruyère, La Broye Hebdo) also announced the redundancy of 15 employees.

Artificial intelligence helping turn yeast into a better cell factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:41:00 UTC
15:41:00 KST

Artificial intelligence helping turn yeast into a better cell factory
Researchers at TalTech used AI to predict which genes could make oleaginous yeast more efficient at producing lipids and pigments. A newly developed metabolic model could help create raw materials for new foods, cosmetics and biofuels hundreds of times faster.
Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has helped humans turn sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide for thousands of years. In next-generation biotechnology, however, biologists are interested in oleaginous yeasts, among which Yarrowia lipolytica stands out for its ability to store large amounts of oil-like substances in its cells. An international research team led by Estonian bioengineers sought to determine how the yeast could be engineered to produce not only lipids but also valuable pigments known as carotenoids.
In its natural form, lipids make up between one-fifth and one-half of the yeast's dry mass. By making targeted genetic modifications, researchers can increase the proportion of oil-like substances to nearly 80 percent and induce the cells to produce carotenoids they would not normally make in nature. Scientists face a challenge, however, because thousands of metabolic processes operate as a single network, meaning that changing even one gene immediately alters the entire system.
When scientists screen for the best gene variants, they rely on genome-scale metabolic models run on computers. These models describe biological reactions taking place inside cells and help biologists narrow laboratory experiments down to only the most promising variants. Each reaction in a cell is controlled by specialized proteins called enzymes and the instructions for making them are encoded directly in the yeast's genes.
Earlier models had significant gaps in the data describing enzyme properties. Biologists addressed the problem using DLKcat, an artificial intelligence-based algorithm. Drawing on existing information, the computer program can predict how nearly all Yarrowia lipolytica enzymes will behave under different conditions.
Juliano Sabedotti de Biaggi, a researcher at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and lead author of the study, said AI sped up enzyme analysis by several hundred times.
"With previous mechanistic models, calculating the properties of a single enzyme took us several days, while DLKcat was able to provide answers for hundreds of enzymes in less than an hour," Sabedotti de Biaggi said.
This allowed researchers to study and compare enzymes on a much larger scale and conduct analyses that had previously been computationally impractical.
In laboratory experiments, the researchers also collected large amounts of proteomics data and fed them directly into the new computer model. The data accurately reflects which proteins the yeast begins producing and in what quantities at different stages of its life cycle. This led the biologists to develop ecYali5-GEM, a new and, to date, the most detailed metabolic model of the yeast.
A yeast cell's needs change drastically over its life cycle. A gene that boosts lipid production during the early growth phase may have no effect later on. The new model helps scientists identify precisely when the activity of a particular gene inside the cell should be increased or decreased.
When the researchers compared the computer model's results with laboratory experiments, they found that the new approach was accurate. The algorithm not only confirmed previous experimental results but also identified entirely new target genes. Scientists can therefore use the computer model to clearly identify which gene to target first.
Carotenoids and lipids are produced in yeast through similar internal pathways. When researchers direct a cell's resources into one pathway, fewer resources are inevitably available for the other. The detailed computer model can identify the optimal balance at which the yeast is able to produce both valuable substances at the same time.
AI and mathematics, however, do not solve all of the biologists' problems. The researchers found that modifying some of the genes recommended by the algorithm did not produce the expected results in laboratory experiments. The actual metabolism of a yeast cell remains too complex for current computer models to fully capture.
"This shows that yeast cell metabolism is more complex than current models are able to describe. But even unsuccessful predictions can help improve future models," Sabedotti de Biaggi added.
The researchers see broad potential for the new method across industrial biotechnology. Advanced computer models can help biologists engineer cells capable of consuming industrial waste and converting it into pure compounds. The authors wrote in the research paper that researchers studying other microorganisms could apply similar computational methods in the future.
Efficient cell factories could help humanity reduce its dependence on petroleum and intensive agriculture. AI can help biologists put yeasts to work profitably, allowing sustainable biofuels, novel cosmetics and dietary supplements to move from laboratories to factories sooner. The combined power of biology and mathematics brings us one step closer to changing everyday patterns of consumption.
The article was published in the journal Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology.

Editor: Sandra Saar, Marcus Turovski

Trump approved the first military execution in 65 years — by firing squad
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:39:45 EEST
15:39:45 KST

Trump approved the first military execution in 65 years — by firing squad
Kyiv • UNN
Donald Trump approved the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad for the 2009 attack at Fort Hood. This could become the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the use of the recently added execution method—firing squad—for a former U.S. Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood military base in Texas during a 2009 shooting. The U.S. Department of Defense reported this on October 5, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
Details
The execution of former U.S. Army major and Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad was approved by Trump on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar"—"God is great" in Arabic—during the attack, in which 12 unarmed service members and one retired service member were killed, and 32 people were wounded. The shooter later called it revenge for U.S. wars in the Muslim world.
The secretary of the Army will determine the time and place of the execution, Parnell said, adding: "Judgment Day for Hasan has finally arrived."
Death by firing squad was one of several execution methods that the Trump administration recently added to the permissible forms of execution for the most serious federal crimes, alongside execution by electric chair and gas asphyxiation.
The expansion of execution options at the federal level was partly linked to growing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which can also sometimes be difficult to carry out for other reasons.
Tennessee's plans to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years fell through last week when prison staff unsuccessfully attempted to administer a lethal injection, leaving death-row inmate Krista Pike alive but unconscious; she was hospitalized and placed on life support.
In August 2013, a military jury sentenced Hasan to death after finding him guilty on 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for shooting a pistol equipped with a laser sight at a medical facility on a large military base in central Texas.
The shooting took place several weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. As a result of gunfire from police during his arrest, he was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair.
Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence imposed by a court-martial cannot be carried out "until approved by the president."
If Hasan is executed, it will be the first military execution since 1961, the organization Death Penalty Action said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The last known execution conducted by a U.S. military firing squad was carried out by "musket fire" in November 1945, the organization said.
According to the organization, firing squads exist in at least five states. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Leonardo DRS to build counter-drone radars in Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:38:42 UTC
15:38:42 KST

- Leonardo DRS set up a UK subsidiary, DRS UK, and opened a factory to fully produce its tactical radars for counter-drone and air defense.
- The company did not disclose the site's location, cost, staffing or first customers.
Leonardo DRS has set up a British subsidiary and opened a purpose-built factory in the United Kingdom to build the tactical radars it sells for spotting drones, rockets and mortar rounds.
The Arlington, Virginia-based company announced the new unit, called DRS UK, on Oct. 5. It said the site will handle full local production of its tactical radars and serve as the hub for that business across the UK and Europe. The company did not say where the factory is, how much it cost, how many people it will employ or when the first UK-built radars will be delivered.
The radars are designed to detect, track and classify threats in the air and on the ground, including drones and incoming rockets, artillery and mortars. They are used for counter-drone defense, short-range air defense, base protection and active protection systems, which shoot down missiles and rockets fired at armored vehicles.
Leonardo DRS said more than 10,000 radar panels are now in service with the U.S. military, NATO allies and other customers.
“Establishing DRS UK and launching a full local tactical radar capability, strengthens our ability to support customers and partners with the proximity, responsiveness and manufacturing capacity needed to meet evolving operational requirements,” said John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS.
The radar line came to Leonardo DRS through its merger with Israel’s RADA Electronic Industries, agreed in 2022. RADA built a family of compact, software-defined radars, led by the Multi-mission Hemispheric Radar. A single unit covers a 120-degree arc, and four together give full overhead coverage. The radar can work on the move and is small enough to mount on tactical vehicles.
The U.S. Army uses the Multi-mission Hemispheric Radar on its Stryker-based short-range air defense vehicles, built to protect armored formations from drones and aircraft. The radars also have a history in Britain: in 2018, RADA radars were integrated into Rafael’s anti-drone system for the British Army’s counter-drone capability.
Leonardo DRS is the U.S. arm of Italy’s Leonardo, which already has a large British business building helicopters, electronics and sensors.
The company framed the UK factory as a way to work more closely with British prime contractors and system integrators, which build the vehicles and air defense systems that carry its radars. It also said the site will support future exports.
“By establishing this local capacity, we are creating high-value engineering and manufacturing opportunities while positioning DRS UK to support future export growth and deliver greater value to customers across the UK and Europe,” said Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager overseeing the company’s tactical radar portfolio.

Protests over housing rights ended in serious unrest in central Barcelona, with barricades and burning bins. Catalan police arrested 13 people, and 30 officers suffered minor injuries.
The demonstration for the right to housing held in Barcelona on Monday ended in disturbances in the city centre, with 13 people arrested, including a minor, and 30 Catalan police officers (Mossos) slightly injured, according to the latest police figures released early on Tuesday.
The mobilisation brought together around 20,000 people, according to the Guàrdia Urbana, and 120,000, according to the organisers. The protest, called by the Sindicat de Llogateres tenants' union together with other organisations defending the right to housing, had been postponed due to a red weather alert and the heavy rains that hit Catalonia over the weekend.
The march set off at around 7.30 pm from Plaça Urquinaona and passed through several points in the centre of Barcelona. The planned route had to be altered, and the mobilisation ended at the junction of Passeig de Gràcia and Gran Via. Along the way, those taking part denounced soaring rents and property speculation, calling for measures to guarantee access to housing.
One of the protest's main demands was the call for a general strike over housing. protest's main demands was a general strike over housing. Before the march, Sindicat de Llogateres spokesperson Carme Arcarazo said the aim was to trigger a mobilisation capable of "paralysing the country", in coordination with other sectors. The protest also coincided with the announcement of a general election on 29 November and came just a few days after the government's housing decrees were voted down in Congress.
Unrest after the end of the demonstration
The march passed without any serious incidents until it was called off at around 9.30 pm. Police then used loudspeakers to ask people to leave the area around Passeig de Gràcia and Gran Via, but some who remained there refused to leave. Objects were later thrown at the regional police deployment.
The incidents intensified when groups of hooded individuals began throwing stones, paving slabs, glass bottles and other objects at officers. Barricades were also erected using bins, barriers, bicycles, and materials from nearby construction work.
At around 10.15 pm, Mossos officers charged to disperse the groups confronting the police. The unrest then shifted towards the area around Plaça Catalunya and La Rambla, where objects were thrown, and bins and other materials set on fire. Police also used launchers firing 'foam' projectiles during the clashes.
The disturbances continued until around midnight. The Mossos reported 28 barricades and 22 fires during the unrest. Barcelona firefighters had to intervene to put them out, accompanied by police protection.
For the moment, it is not clear how many demonstrators were injured.
Street furniture and vehicles were also damaged during the unrest. In Carrer Casp, burning bins damaged a parked car, while in other areas, bicycles and building materials were used to build barricades.

IMF warns debt-financed tax cuts increase global interest rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:35:04 UTC
15:35:04 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that corporate income tax policies generate cross-border spillovers through profit shifting, investment reallocation and knowledge transfers.
The IMF released a chapter titled “Intangible Yet Real: Spillovers from Corporate Income Taxation” for its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, stating that tax competition remained a defining feature of the global economy while its nature changed over time.
Authors noted that the globalization of production, the rise of multinational corporations and the growing importance of intangible assets transformed the landscape of corporate income taxation.
The institution highlighted that multinational corporations accounted for more than 20 percent of global gross domestic product and approximately 15 percent of global corporate profits.
The study showed that differences in corporate income taxation generated cross-border spillovers as multinational corporations relocated profits and investments across countries to minimize tax liabilities.
The report warned that debt-financed tax cuts increased global interest rates and crowded out investment abroad.
Researchers emphasized that stronger anti-avoidance frameworks supported economic output while protecting tax revenues.
The organization added that a one percentage point increase in a country’s corporate income tax rate relative to rates elsewhere caused a cumulative decline in foreign direct investment inflows of about 0.5 percent of gross domestic product over three years.

Font size
Bulgarian students achieved remarkable success at the 19th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics (IOAA), held in Hanoi, Vietnam. The country’s five representatives won two gold medals, two silver medals, and one bronze medal, competing against around 320 students from dozens of countries around the world, the Ministry of Education said.
The gold medals went to Miroslav Draganov from the Academician Nikola Obreshkov High School of Mathematics and Natural Sciences in Burgas and Svetoslav Arabov from the High School of Mathematics-Varna. Martin Nedev from the Natural Sciences and Mathematics High School in Haskovo and Krasimir Stankov from the High School of Mathematics-Ruse won silver medals, while Anton Stoyanov from the High School of Mathematics-Varna won a bronze medal.
The Bulgarian national team was led by Nikola Karavasilev of the Union of Astronomers in Bulgaria and Miroslav Radomirov of the Faculty of Physics at Sofia University.
