Crystallized salt draws photographers to Türkiye’s Tuz Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:56:32 UTC
14:56:32 KST

(AA Photo)
Decreasing water levels driven by seasonal temperatures have formed unique crystallized salt structures across Tuz Lake in the central province of Aksaray, drawing photographers eager to capture the snow-like geological formations.
After surface water fully evaporated in the Eskil region of the lake, distinct solid formation, including mushroom-like structures, were exposed. Depending on the sun’s angle throughout the day, visitors walking across the dry bed experience shifting visual effects.
Photographer Nazmi Meral told state-run Anadolu Agency he monitored the area for about a month to capture the continuously changing landscape created by the interaction of nature, water and salt.
“We encounter completely different views every time we visit and plan to come again. Walking on the salt layer provides a different experience, it feels exactly like walking on snow,” he said.
Local resident Mustafa Güdendede said residents are accustomed to seeing a flat, watery surface rather than these textured features. The newly formed mushroom-shaped salt masses present unmissable, postcard-like scenery for photography enthusiasts visiting the region, he said.
Another resident, Mehmet Meral, compared the pristine white salt formations to the famous travertines of Pamukkale, inviting all visitors to see the natural area he described as a hidden paradise.
Tuz Lake is the second largest lake in Türkiye and one of the largest hypersaline lakes in the world. The shallow basin provides a significant portion of the country’s salt needs. It also serves as a crucial natural breeding ground for flamingos and migratory birds during the spring months before the waters naturally pull back to expose the crust.

Türkiye weighs new rules for foreign booking platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:56:14 UTC
14:56:14 KST

A parliamentary committee is set to debate rules for foreign booking platforms on Oct. 6 under a bill that could allow Booking.com to resume domestic hotel reservations in Türkiye.
The proposal, before the Public Works, Zoning, Transport and Tourism Committee, would require foreign platforms to obtain a Culture and Tourism Ministry permit and appoint a representative in Türkiye.
Platforms would have to verify accommodation providers’ license details and display them in listings.
Total fees and commissions would be capped at 17 percent of the sale price, excluding value-added tax.
Booking.com stopped accepting domestic hotel reservations from users inside Türkiye following a 2017 court ruling in a case brought by the Association of Turkish Travel Agencies (TÜRSAB).
Bookings for Turkish properties made from abroad remain available.
Some industry representatives say the commission cap could initially lower hotel prices but warn that foreign platforms could gain excessive market power over time.
The bill would also allow platforms to sell flight tickets directly
Combined sales of transport and accommodation under its provisions would not be classified as package tours.
Disputes arising from licensed activities would be governed by Turkish law, with Turkish courts having exclusive jurisdiction.
Mehmet Gem, head of the Consumers Confederation’s (TÜKONFED) tourism commission, said appointing a local representative alone might not ensure effective redress for cancellations, room disputes or unfair deductions.
He warned that platforms could seek to avoid responsibility by describing themselves solely as intermediaries.
TÜRSAB President Firuz Bağlıkaya also opposed the proposal, saying it would allow foreign platforms to operate without establishing a company in Türkiye or meeting the same obligations as domestic travel agencies.
Speaking at a press meeting on Oct. 5, Bağlıkaya said the resulting competition would put local agencies at a disadvantage.
He rejected suggestions that the bill would attract more tourists, saying foreign platforms already accept bookings for Turkish hotels from abroad and the principal change would concern access to the domestic market.
Bağlıkaya warned that greater dependence on foreign platforms could increase commission payments flowing abroad and force domestic agencies to close.

'Targeted killing': Gaza intel chief at center of Oct. 7 failures says IDF singles him out for blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:55:48 UTC
14:55:48 KST

Newly released court documents reveal how Lt. Col. Aryeh Amidror, the Gaza Division intelligence officer on October 7, fought to remain in the IDF after military leaders moved to end his service, arguing that he had been discriminated against and unfairly singled out over the failures surrounding the Hamas massacre.
The documents were made public after Israel’s Supreme Court permitted publication of Amidror’s identity at ynet’s request. They include the administrative petition he filed, relevant appendices, requests for interim relief and a publication ban, the state’s response and the transcript of a June 22 hearing. The opinion written by Deputy Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Tamir Yadai was not released.
Amidror argued that senior military officials had failed to treat him fairly and described the decision to terminate his permanent service as “arbitrary, discriminatory and selective.” His petition said he was “the only commander in the IDF who is paying a real price, in the form of lost rights, for the failures of the military and the state.”
A central part of his complaint concerned the loss of pension and other employment benefits. His representatives argued that other commanders held responsible for October 7 had retained their full social and pension benefits, while officers in positions comparable to his had either been promoted or continued serving.
‘I was the one who ordered the exercise to be analyzed’
Amidror also challenged the way the military portrayed his exchanges with a female noncommissioned intelligence officer identified only as V., who this week received a certificate of appreciation from the IDF chief of staff for what he described as “intellectual courage and professionalism.”
According to Amidror, when he became Gaza Division intelligence chief he discovered that the division had for some time neglected intelligence collection aimed at examining Hamas’ ability to carry out its operational plans. He said he therefore instructed a unit within the IDF’s Unit 8200 signals intelligence branch to analyze Hamas training exercises in order to assess the group’s tactical capabilities.
“Following the instruction given by the petitioner, and on the orders of her commanders, NCO V. carried out the analysis of the exercise and put the findings in writing,” his petition said.
Amidror argued that an email exchange later cited against him took place before the full analysis had been distributed and represented only an initial discussion. At first glance, he said, the exercise appeared to contain elements that were widely considered unrealistic at the time by Military Intelligence and the IDF more broadly.
He said that after V.’s findings were circulated, he sought to distinguish between capabilities Hamas could realistically execute and training designed primarily to create an impression or motivate its fighters.
Amidror also claimed that additional exchanges omitted from the deputy chief of staff’s assessment showed he was encouraging deeper examination rather than dismissing the warning. In one message, he said he wrote that “there seems to be quite a lot of gold here to mine.”
In another, he wrote: “For the avoidance of doubt, the purpose of my email was not to lower but to elevate,” adding that as more material was circulated, the area of agreement would grow. He also said he ordered additional Hamas exercises to be analyzed and sought to challenge assumptions held by the Gaza Division and Military Intelligence about possible Hamas courses of action.
‘A sense of a targeted killing’
The petition also disputed investigations into Amidror's conduct on the night of October 6-7. His lawyers challenged the significance of material gathered against him and complained that they had not been given access to all the investigations and documents underlying the decision to remove him.
The IDF announced on November 23, 2025 that Amidror would be removed from his post, and the process to terminate his permanent service formally began on February 14, 2026.
At the June 22 hearing, one of Amidror's lawyers sought a postponement, arguing that the defense still lacked access to material used by the deputy chief of staff.
“We are racing after materials that form the basis of the deputy chief of staff’s opinion,” the lawyer said. “We know for certain that there are additional materials on which he relied, and they have not been presented to us.”
The lawyer said some of those materials concerned the period before October 7, including emails involving V., who had warned Amidror about Hamas preparations and readiness for a scenario that ultimately unfolded during the massacre.
“Our feeling is that there is some kind of targeted killing here, and it seems no one is interested in transferring the material to us,” the lawyer said, adding that none of four investigations reached a specific conclusion personally against Amidror.
The state rejected those arguments, saying the process had begun months earlier and that Amidror’s representatives had been shown the investigations forming the evidentiary basis for the administrative proceeding. Prosecutors stressed that it was an administrative, not criminal, process and said the petitioners could not expect access to every IDF investigation into October 7.
The state said the deputy chief of staff’s assessment contained “very concrete claims concerning a series of professional errors and failures in the officer’s conduct,” rather than a general allegation that his performance had been flawed.
Amidror also challenged the authority of the deputy chief of staff to prepare the professional assessment, arguing that the head of Military Intelligence, as his professional commander, should have done so instead.
“The deputy chief of staff is not his commander,” his representatives argued. “He does not know the petitioner and is not familiar with intelligence matters.”
Amidror further alleged that he had been personally targeted, saying that other officers described as bearing command responsibility for October 7 had not faced termination of their service contracts. The state responded that the allegations against him were reviewed at several levels, including by the head of the IDF Personnel Directorate and ultimately the chief of staff, and noted that Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder had himself received a command reprimand following another review.
State cites ‘significant professional and ethical error’
In its response, the state summarized the deputy chief of staff’s assessment as finding “a series of professional errors and failures in the officer’s conduct,” both during the night of October 6-7 and in the months preceding the attack.
According to the state, the recommendation to continue the process of dismissing Amidror was based in part on a “significant professional and ethical error” in his assessment of a document concerning Hamas’ elite Nukhba force training routine and an email exchange titled “Death in the kibbutz at any cost.”
The state said Amidror’s conduct fell “significantly short of what is expected of those engaged in intelligence work,” particularly the obligation to question assumptions, actively seek opposing views and give them a central place in intelligence analysis.
It also cited a series of professional errors on the night of the attack and Amidror’s command responsibility for the Gaza Division intelligence branch’s failure to issue a warning ahead of the Hamas assault.
The state rejected Amidror’s demand that the process be transferred to an independent senior reserve officer, saying such a demand had no basis in military regulations and would undermine the established chain of authority.
The court ultimately rejected Amidror’s petition and allowed the IDF process aimed at ending his permanent service to continue.

Aselsan has signed contracts worth 2.46 billion euros with Türkiye’s Defense Industries Secretariat (SSB) to supply hybrid air defense systems, the company announced on Oct. 5.
The agreements, disclosed to the Public Disclosure Platform (KAP), mark the company’s largest contract announcement to date. No delivery schedule was released.
The latest package brings the combined value of four SSB air defense contract announcements this year to about 5.72 billion euros.
A separate 1.23 billion euro agreement with Roketsan for air defense components takes the total to nearly 7 billion euros.
Aselsan chief executive Ahmet Akyol said continued mass production was strengthening Türkiye’s Steel Dome air defense network.
Steel Dome is designed to integrate systems including Korkut, Hisar and Siper with radars and command-and-control units to counter threats at different altitudes and ranges.
Aselsan supplies the Hakim command-and-control system, designed to coordinate these elements.
The company also unveiled its Gökbağı communications satellite project at the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya on Oct. 5.
Known internationally as Astralink, the planned low Earth orbit network is intended to provide communications services for military, government and civilian users.
Akyol told Anadolu Agency that Aselsan had designed the project “from the chip level up” and planned to begin launching the first satellites within the next few years.
He said the company had also developed ground receivers that track satellites electronically without mechanically moving their antennas, drawing on its experience with active electronically scanned array technology.
Aselsan is also exhibiting the synthetic aperture radar payload for the Göktürk-3 satellite, designed to capture high-resolution images of Earth’s surface through cloud cover.
Akyol said the company was investing in facilities for its space activities at its Oğulbey campus.

Largest oil depot in the Moscow region caught fire following drone attack - OSINT analysis
Kyiv • UNN
Following a massive UAV attack, a fire was reported at the territory of the Volodarskaya Linear Production Dispatch Station. The station stores and transports 3 million tonnes of fuel annually.
The largest oil depot in Russia's Moscow Region is burning after a drone attack in the early hours of October 6. This is evidenced by an OSINT analysis by ASTRA, reports UNN.
Details
In the early hours of October 6, the Moscow Region was reportedly under a massive UAV attack for several hours.
"Between 8:30 p.m. on October 5 and 5 a.m. on October 6, 650 UAVs flew toward the Moscow region. Most of them were destroyed by air defense forces at long-range positions. 105 drones were destroyed on approach to Moscow," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on his Telegram channel, without reporting any damage.
Based on a video posted by the Supernova+ channel, ASTRA OSINT analyst determined that the fire occurred in the village of Konstantinovo in the Ramenskoye urban district of the Moscow Region. The source of the fire was reportedly located on the territory of the Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station (LPDS). No previous attacks on the Volodarskaya LPDS had reportedly been reported.
The Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) is the largest oil depot in the Moscow region and is part of JSC "AK Transnefteprodukt." It can separately store and transport motor gasoline, aviation fuel, and diesel fuel through pipelines. Its annual turnover amounts to 3 million tonnes of petroleum products. The raw materials come from the Moscow and Ryazan oil refineries, while an extensive network of product pipelines directly connects the station with the key airports of the Moscow hub (Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo).

Meanwhile, rain, thunderstorms, and gusty winds are forecast to cover up to 50 percent of the plain region and 60 percent of the plateau region.
"Based on this weather forecast, citizens are urged to remain highly vigilant against sudden downpours, lightning, and strong winds, especially those traveling by land or water," the ministry warned.
The ministry added that it will continue to monitor the weather patterns closely and provide timely updates if conditions change. ■

He described Riyadh’s approach to resolving the dispute as constructive.
The committee also appointed retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.
Fidan said discussions covered the secretariat’s structure and the appointment.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed on Aug. 7, treats an armed attack on any member as an attack on all three.

In the same period, the FCAI said that sales of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrids more than doubled.

China became the leading source of new vehicles in Australia for the first time in February after Japan had been the country's leading supplier of new vehicles every month for almost 30 years.
As of the end of September, China's BYD had sold 76,614 new vehicles in Australia in 2026, up 102 percent from 37,923 at the same point in 2025. ■

Feature: Ancient characters, guqin music bring Chinese culture to life in New York
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
13:44:52 CST
14:44:52 KST

Chinese artist and guqin performer Nie Hui introduces artworks inspired by oracle-bone inscriptions during a cultural activity in New York, the United States, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
by Vivien Liu
NEW YORK, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- An ancient pictograph evolving into a Chinese character; a child's mouth forming the sounds of a word; a brush sweeping across paper; and the centuries-old notes of a guqin filling the air...
For students and visitors in New York, these became different entry points into Chinese culture -- ways to encounter it not just through books, but through sight, sound and direct experience.
A series of cultural activities, recently held at the State University of New York at Old Westbury and the Long Island School of Chinese, featured exhibitions of Chinese poetry, calligraphy, painting and seal carving, guqin performances and a lecture on the origins and evolution of Chinese characters.
At the center of the programs were Chinese artist and guqin performer Nie Hui and her husband, cultural researcher Xie Feidong, who have worked together for years to study and share traditional Chinese culture and arts.
In one session, children were invited to say the Chinese word for "laugh" and observe what happened to their faces. As they pronounced it, the corners of their mouths lifted into a smile.
The exercise connected language with something the children could immediately see and feel. The lesson then moved to the visual origins of Chinese writing.
Nie drew early pictographic forms of the sun and moon, showing how ancient characters resembled the objects they represented.
"Chinese characters were originally pictographic characters. They were a picture," Xie said.
A discussion of oracle-bone inscriptions offered another glimpse into the early development of Chinese writing and the ways ancient people drew upon images of the natural world to express meaning.
For Christian D'Ambrosi, an American student pursuing a master's degree in education at SUNY Old Westbury, the presentation further sparked an interest in China that had taken root years earlier.
"I was here to learn more about Chinese culture, because I've always loved Chinese history," he said. "I hope to teach about Chinese history in the future."
The activities also explored connections across cultures, including a discussion linking the ancient Chinese story of Dayu controlling the floods to the biblical story of Noah's Ark.
"Art and culture have no borders," Xie said.
Catherine Fan, a high school junior and volunteer at the Long Island School of Chinese who plays the guzheng, particularly enjoyed hearing Nie perform Liu Shui (Flowing Water) on the guqin.
The ancient melody has traveled far beyond the classroom. A recording of Liu Shui was included on the Golden Record carried aboard NASA's Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977 with sounds and music selected to represent life and culture on Earth.
For Edmund Yan, a Chinese American attendee, the Chinese paintings were particularly striking.
"I think it's very impressive how detailed it is and how much personality you can put into it," Yan said. "Being able to show off the personality of the artwork with just black and white is very beautiful and very impressive."
Olivia Chen, a sixth-grade student who has attended the Long Island School of Chinese since second grade, said the program helped explain what lies behind the characters she learns in class.
"We actually learn the history of words and stuff like that here," she said. "In Chinese class, we learn how to read, write and memorize words."
"I hope that the children today can remember a particular character that touched them," Xie said.
Nie captured their approach in a single line: "Let art have the depth of culture, and let culture have the beauty of art." ■

Monogatari Corp., which operates the Yakiniku King barbecue restaurant chain, said Monday that more than 10 million pieces of customer information, covering almost its entire registered user base, were leaked following unauthorized access to a system supporting its smartphone app for restaurant reservations and rewards.

Meanwhile, Daiwa Securities Group Inc. said Monday that data on around 110,000 customers of its securities brokerage unit, along with other nonpersonal information, may have been compromised following unauthorized access to a server operated by one of its contractors.
The company said that even if the information had been leaked, it could not be used to conduct transactions, including online transactions.

====================================================================================================

Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:44:39 UTC
14:44:39 KST

Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
A young mother has lost two husbands and two children during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Gaza City, Gaza — For three years, Nisreen Touman has gone to bed every night in tears, remembering all she has lost since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.
By the time Nisreen was 34, she had been widowed twice. First, she lost her husband and her two children in June 2024. Then in July 2025, eight months after she remarried, Nisreen lost her second husband while she was pregnant.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Nisreen lived a happy and stable life in her home in Nuseirat, central Gaza, with her husband, Sami, 35, and their two children, Mahmoud and Laith, who were aged five and two at the time of their deaths.
“I had a home and a complete family. I got along with my husband, and we were friends,” she says, fighting back her tears.
Everything changes
On June 8, 2024, Nisreen was returning home with her husband and children after visiting extended family, who had been displaced to al-Mawasi in Khan Younis.
“We arrived and the children were playing in the street. Everything was normal. I was upstairs with my husband when suddenly we started hearing heavy, very close, bombing and gunfire.”
Her husband rushed outside to bring their children and his brother’s and sister’s children inside, where 25 members of her family were staying.
He then went outside again to see what was happening, as aircraft flew overhead.
“That was the last time I saw him. I later learned that he had been killed by a gunshot to the head from a quadcopter that was flying over the area that day,” she said.
Minutes later, while trying to calm the children as the bombing and gunfire continued, the house was targeted by an Israeli aircraft.
“I lost consciousness for a few moments, then woke up to thick dust that completely blocked my view,” she said.
“As the dust began to clear, I started to understand our place was bombed. I heard the family screaming and saw blood and body parts. I started shouting, ‘My children, my children.’”
Nisreen breaks down as she recalls seeing her two children lying on the ground. One had suffered severe head injuries, while the other appeared to be sleeping.
“I knew from that moment that I had lost them. It was clear that they were dead,” she says, recalling how she was unable to move from the shock.
Her husband’s brother came and placed the children in her arms.
“I could not speak. I was completely unable to speak, just tears running silently,” she said. “Everyone around me was screaming and crying.”
For two hours, Nisreen held her children in her arms as the family, including those who were injured, remained trapped in the damaged home as gunfire and bombing continued.
After repeated requests to the International Committee of the Red Cross for help, the family were eventually evacuated to a hospital.
The killing of Nisreen’s family came on one of the bloodiest days of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. On June 8, 2024, Israeli forces launched a military operation in the Nuseirat refugee camp, central Gaza, to rescue four Israeli captives who had been held following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
The United Nations said 89 inhabited houses and residential buildings were targeted in nearly four hours of bombing. Gaza’s Health Ministry said that 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 wounded on that day alone.
Eighteen members of Nisreen’s husband’s family were killed, including her husband and children, her sister Sabreen, 36, her mother-in-law, two of her husband’s brothers and their children, as well as members of the extended family.
A difficult decision
Nisreen returned alone to her family’s tent in al-Mawasi south of Gaza, where she struggled with the trauma and grief of losing her family. Four and a half months later, Nisreen found herself facing a difficult decision when her late sister’s husband, who was also her first husband’s brother, proposed to her.
He wanted to marry Nisreen and have her help take care of their four children, who had lost their mother.
“I strongly opposed it at first. I did not want to start a family or get married,” Nisreen said. She eventually agreed because she wanted to care for her departed sister’s children, especially the youngest, who was only one year old.
Nisreen does not hide the fact that there were no romantic feelings behind her second marriage. “I had lost my husband, and he had lost his wife. I had lost my children, and the four children had lost their mother,” she said.
The marriage allowed two people to fill the roles of the ones they lost. Nisreen found in her sister’s children a small comfort for the absence of her own.
But her new life came with significant challenges, especially during the first months. She was still grieving her first husband and her children, as she and her new husband attempted to adjust to each other.
Their different personalities and the new situation presented challenges, but gradually their lives became more stable. Nisreen even considered having another child.
“I used to see my children who had died, in my dreams every day. I would drift into thoughts about them, and they never left my mind,” she said. “So, with encouragement from my mother, I decided to become pregnant and experience motherhood again.”
The second loss
But eight months later, on July 8, 2025, Nisreen faced something she had never imagined: the loss of her second husband.
“Mohammed woke up, had breakfast with the children and said he was going to see a friend. A few moments later, we heard a huge explosion,” she said.
Shortly after, Nisreen was told by a neighbour that Mohammed had been killed in a strike on a group of people near al-Awda Hospital in Nuseirat.
For Nisreen, this second loss was even harder to bear than the first. After believing she had finally settled into a new sense of stability, her life was once again turned upside down.
“I felt like I was back at zero again,” she said. “I thought about the baby who had not yet been born, the children of my sister who had now lost both their mother and father, and the new loss I was living through.”
The remaining months of her pregnancy were heavy for Nisreen. Four months after Mohammed’s death, she gave birth to their daughter, Sidra.
Born into grief
Sidra’s birth brought back to Nisreen the pain of everything she had lost – her two children, her first husband and Mohammed.
While her daughter, who turns one in October, has brought Nisreen a “little compensation” for three years of sadness, it pains her that she will grow up without a father.
“Becoming a mother again brought me joy, but that feeling was deeply incomplete. She was a little compensation,” she said
Caring for Sidra has become Nisreen’s main priority.
“I have become more isolated. I prefer to stay quiet for hours and focus on my daughter,” Nisreen says. “I am afraid of making any new choices or trying to start another life after everything that happened to me.”
Nisreen now lives with Sidra at her family’s home in Gaza, while her late sister’s four children are being cared for by their grandfather. She visits them from time to time.
No matter how much time passes, she says she is unable to overcome the series of tragedies that have shaped her life.
“I never imagined I would go through all of this in my life. Sometimes it feels like I’m in an Indian film because of everything that has happened,” she said. “But under the war, unfortunately, anything is possible.”

Child left behind on Tallinn tram raises questions over driver care
An incident at the weekend involving a family on a Tallinn tram prompted similar stories online accusing drivers of a lack of due care and attention.
Tallinn Transport (TLT) says it reviews mistakes and trains drivers on safety accordingly, including by replaying video footage.
Over last weekend, a child got left alone at a tram stop in Tallinn after their father was unable to get off the tram with a stroller before the doors closed. Pressing the door button and speaking to the tram driver did not help things, and the father had to dash to the next stop on foot to retrieve the child safely.
The story has spread on social media and has brought to light other similar incidents in which small children have ended up on one side of tram or bus doors, their adult carer on the other. In some cases, families got reunited at the same stop, while in others, as in the one outlined above, the vehicle continued on its way.
Kaido Padar, TLT board member, rejected the idea that the issue is a systemic one. He said the company gets about 270 complaints a month, but most of these concern schedule time-keeping rather than safety issues.
"Something like this has happened between one and four times during my four years here," Padar said, though noted the weekend's incident was the second this year.
According to the TLT executive, 750 of the company's 1,500 drivers undergo practical, video-based customer service training each year.
"This morning we already agreed that we would also look at the driver's perspective and videos, showing how to act in one situation or another," Padar added.
Regina Peegel, a board member of the transport section of the rail workers' union (Eesti Raudteelaste Ametiühing), said tram drivers can see what is happening around the tram doors either through cameras or mirrors. Drivers close the doors only once there is no longer any movement around them, she noted.
"One thing is certain: the driver did not do it deliberately. In fact, that is what the job is about — letting everyone off and then letting everyone on properly," Peegel said.
"You see, quite often passengers are on their phones and only at the last moment realize it is time for them to get off, then they run to the door and start pressing the buttons. But the driver can't see who is running where. From a driver's perspective, if no one is getting off anymore, they close the doors and start driving. That means you really need to be ready when it is time to get off," Peegel continued.
However, Padar conceded the recent incident also clearly illustrated a trend of tram drivers being unnecessarily distracted while driving, or in this case, not grasping fully what had happened.
"The tram driver said this morning that they didn't really understand what the person wanted, because people ask all sorts of things and some people do stupid things to drivers through the glass, something which has happened to us many times. It is even more common for people to try to provoke the driver. So these kinds of incidents do happen and, unfortunately, yes, people also get caught in the doors," Padar added.
Other recent reported incidents involving TLT trams include one from March this year, when a dog got left outside a tram with its leash stuck in the closed doors. A quick-thinking passenger pulled the emergency brake lever, thereby avoiding the worst. However, the driver then assaulted the passenger who had pulled the lever, both verbally and physically. TLT said the driver has been fired and that the passenger had acted "100% correctly".
In March 2025, reported this summer, a man on the tram lines on Peterburi tee was killed when a tram struck him. Surveillance footage from inside the tram showed the driver had been viewing a video on a dashboard-mounted smartphone at the time of the incident. The driver received a two-year suspended sentence.
The tram incidents come amid a wider pattern of serious public transport accidents in the capital. In August 2025, a 26-year-old Ukrainian woman died after being hit by a bus at Narva mnt; police found she had crossed against a red light while wearing headphones. Last month, a 65-year-old woman died after a bus struck her at a pedestrian crossing in Haabersti — she had crossed on a green light, but the driver did not spot her. The circumstances of that case are still under investigation.

European Li-ion BESS manufacturer sets its sights further – on eight European markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:38:56 UTC
14:38:56 KST

GAZ ENERGY currently has battery projects with a total capacity of over 2 GWh in various stages of implementation, of which more than 1 GWh is accounted for by projects implemented in the Czech Republic. The European manufacturer of large-capacity Li-ion BESS is now building on its experience in the domestic market by expanding into Poland, Germany, Ukraine, the Baltic States, Italy, Spain, Romania, and Croatia. According to the company, growing European demand for energy storage creates opportunities for further growth, with GAZ ENERGY building on European manufacturing, safety, and long-term technical support.
The European energy sector is rapidly increasing the share of renewable energy sources, and with that, the need for flexibility and energy storage is growing. At the same time, issues that go beyond battery capacity itself are coming to the forefront—cybersecurity, the origin of the technology, control over software and data, and the long-term availability of technical support.
This is precisely what GAZ ENERGY’s offer is based on. It manufactures Li-ion BESS in the Czech Republic, uses European software, and provides engineering, integration, and technical support from Europe. It designs systems with due regard for the European regulatory framework, cybersecurity and data security requirements, and the specific requirements of individual energy markets. In doing so, it takes into account, among other things, the requirements arising from NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA), the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), and the Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), as well as the requirements of transmission and distribution system operators.
“When it comes to large-scale battery storage systems, customers today don’t base their decisions solely on price and the number of megawatt-hours. What matters is who they entrust their technology, data, and part of their critical energy infrastructure to—and who will be able to provide them with support even ten or fifteen years from now. We see this as a major opportunity for GAZ ENERGY,” says Tomáš Lev, Sales Director Li-Ion BESS at GAZ Energy.
GAZ ENERGY is already demonstrating its European ambitions through concrete projects. Its current project portfolio exceeds 2 GWh across various stages of implementation. A significant portion of this portfolio is in the Czech market, where GAZ ENERGY is involved in two of the country’s largest battery storage projects, with a total output of 487 MW and a capacity of 980 MWh. The portfolio also includes projects in other European countries: in Finland with a total output of 82.5 MW and capacity of 162 MWh; in Romania with an output of 72 MW and capacity of 150 MWh, in Poland with an output of 30 MW and capacity of 60 MWh, and in Germany with an output of 17.5 MW and capacity of 50 MWh.
“This year, we delivered and installed 900 MWh in the Czech Republic. This is a significant achievement for us and confirms our ability to reliably execute large-scale projects from start to finish. We are applying this experience to other European markets,” says David Vodička, a member of the GAZ Energy Board of Directors.

“Mere subjectivity, [Hegel] argued, insisting on the purity of its own principle, becomes entangled…”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:34:08 UTC
14:34:08 KST

“Mere subjectivity, [Hegel] argued, insisting on the purity of its own principle, becomes entangled in antinomies. It is brought down by its own mischief, by hypocrisy and evil, in so far as it is not objectified in society and state. Morality, autonomy founded on pure self-certainty, together with conscience, is mere illusion. […] This dialectical motif, operating on all levels of the system, is at once true and untrue. True because it unmasks the particular as a necessary illusion, the false consciousness of isolated things as being themselves alone and not moments of the whole; and this false consciousness it breaks down with the power of the whole. Untrue because the motif of objectification, ‘alienation’, becoming a pretext for bourgeois self-assertion of the subject, is degraded to a mere rationalization, as long as objectivity, contrasted by thought to bad subjectivity, is unfree and does not measure up to the subject’s criticism.”
– Theodor W. Adorno, Minima Moralia, 152

TIME100 Art Honorees Toast to Imagination, Inspiration, and Influence Across Generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:31:00 UTC
14:31:00 KST

Honorees at TIME’s first TIME100 Art Impact Dinner gathered in New York City on October 5, bringing together artists, collectors, curators, museum executives, dealers, advisors, and cultural stewards.
Guests attended the dinner to celebrate the launch of the first ever TIME100 Art list.
Seven different honorees offered toasts throughout the evening, each of them occupying a different space in the art world: businessman and art collector Ronald Lauder, art crime prosecutor Matthew Bogdanos, painter Amy Sherald, interdisciplinary artist Marie Watt, Citadel founder and collector Ken Griffin, and innovators Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz.
Here’s what each of them toasted to.
Ronald Lauder
Lauder, who was honored on the list for his collecting, philanthropy, and founding of Neue Galerie New York, began his toast by chronicling the beginning of his love of art at the Museum of Modern Art (MOMA) when he was just 12 years old.
“On one of my trips, I encountered Picasso’s Guernica…although I didn’t understand it at first, I went home and learned about the Spanish Civil War,” Lauder said. “I began to understand that art could do more than inspire—it could preserve history and expand the way we see the world.”
Lauder said he would sometimes spend an entire museum visit in one singular room, looking at each painting from every angle. It was this devotion that launched his love of art.
Years later, he explained in the toast, MOMA is still an inspiration to him as an art collector, after he spent 10 years as chairman of the museum.
“Today, it is especially meaningful to me that my daughter and grandsons are members of the museum’s International Council,” Lauder continued. “From one generation to the next is what legacy means to me.”
Lauder also discussed the importance of the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Met), another iconic New York City museum, to his journey as an art lover. At 14, his parents took him to a dinner there honoring a gift from art collector Florence Gould.
“At my table, I was surrounded by great collectors, and I began imagining what a life would be in collecting art, and what it might look like,” he said. “In many ways, Florence Gould gave me permission to follow my curiosity wherever it led.”
The final museum he toasted was the one he owns, the Neue Galerie New York, which showcases early 20th-century German and Austrian art on the Upper East Side of Manhattan.
“The Neue Galerie opened just months after September 11 [2001], when New York was still reeling,” he recalled. “And yet people came. They stood in lines around the block. It reminded me that art offers something we need in difficult moments: connection, continuity, and renewal.”
He finished his toast by describing himself and other collectors as “custodians” of the art that they live with.
“I’d like to raise a glass to the artists, and the institutions that preserve their work,” he said, “and the generations who carry that legacy forward.”
Matthew Bogdanos
Matthew Bogdanos, a retired Marine and chief of the Antiquities Trafficking Unit at the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office, has spent more than two decades hunting down lost and stolen art works and repatriating this art to almost 40 other countries.
In his speech, Bogdanos toasted to the fellow art-crime fighters in the world, claiming that whatever he has accomplished in his career has been only because of the “courage, passion, and dedication” of people across the world working with him.
“You should share the passion and action of his time, Oliver Wendell Holmes once said, ‘at peril of being judged not to have lived.’” I can tell you from having worked with these people for decades now, Justice Holmes would be proud of them, and so am I, and I hope now so are you,” Bogdanos said.
He then toasted to the cultural artifacts he works to find and repatriate, each of which he says is a “living breathing testimony to our shared cultural heritage.”
“I have seen them work their cathartic spell across cultures, across ethnicities, across religion,” he said.
This shared heritage that we are reminded of in these artifacts provides healing in a divisive world, Bogdanos added.
“Respecting the cultural heritage from the very dawn of civilization offers perhaps the best hope we have in overcoming the reductive dualism that is tearing apart our world today by reminding us of our common aspirations, of our common humanity, of our common attempts to make sense of the world we inhabit the cosmos surrounding,” he said.
He finished his toast by pledging to continue his work until he felt that he deserved the honor of being on the TIME 100 list.
Amy Sherald
American painter Amy Sherald, perhaps known best for her portrait of former first lady Michelle Obama, is now one of the most influential painters of her generation.
In her toast, Sherald began by saying that the room felt like a “family reunion,” shouting out other artists in the room that inspire her. She mused on the meaning of the word “influence,” and how it differs in the art world than any monetary or numeric goal.
“You can measure sales. You can count exhibitions, books, and audiences. You can count followers. You can count the number of people who walk through the doors of a museum,” she said. “ But I’m not sure any of those things tell us very much about influence, because influence is often much quieter than that.”
She explained how influence for many artists and art-enthusiasts comes in smaller moments—whether it’s an artist seeing another artist’s work, a teacher sharing advice that a pupil remembers for decades to come, or a curator “putting two things next to each other and changing the way we understand both of them.”
In this room alone, Sherald explains, are many people who have built institutions, supported artists, and changed the way the world saw art.
“And those things move outward. One person influences another person, who influences somebody else. An image enters the world and becomes part of somebody’s imagination,” she continued. “And eventually, you can’t even trace where it began. That’s powerful to me.”
She went on to quote her friend, Elizabeth Alexander, another TIME100 Art Honoree and president of the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, who says that imagination is a superpower. Imagination and influence are tied together, Sherald explained.
“People who were excluded from the promise of this country had to imagine themselves into that promise long before the country was willing to recognize them,” she said. “Someone had to imagine a life they had never seen. Someone had to make an image that didn’t exist. Someone had to open a door that had always been closed.”
It is that imagination that allows other people to walk through those doors, and that is what influence means to her, Sherald said: leaving something behind for others to use.
She finished by explaining that maybe influence is not about what anyone has accumulated, but about what has “moved through us and what we’ve helped move forward.”
“Because eventually the exhibitions come down. The lists change. The rooms change. And somebody else’s face is on the cover,” she finished. “But what we put into the world keeps traveling.”
Marie Watt
Marie Watt, a sculptor, textile artist, storyteller, and member of Turtle Clan of the Seneca Nation of Indians, used her toast to explain how Indigenous communities view art.
“In most Indigenous languages, there is no word for art,” she said. “But we know the act of making things—objects, stories, and songs—that activate our senses and engage our communities has been a way of life forever.”
For everyone in the room who creates art, Watts said, it’s not for “glory,” fun, or money—though those things can be a byproduct of the work—but rather to understand “what connects” humans, animals, the environment, and the planet.
“This is what painters and carvers and weavers and dancers and singers and potters, photographers and poets and drummers and storytellers have always done and will always do, whether we have a name for it or not,” she said. “To connect. To seek. To make. To understand.”
She finished her toast by raising a glass and calling on the larger community of curators, collectors, and art stewards.
“I ask you to remember our brothers and sisters and siblings throughout the world who have made—and every day are making—this choice to connect,” she said. “Our teachers, our peers, our students. Our ancestors. Our children.”
Ken Griffin
Ken Griffin, CEO of the hedge fund Citadel and one of the world’s most deep-pocketed and active art buyers, began his toast by recognizing the varied artists and art-lovers in the room.
“Your creativity, your exhibitions, your teaching, and your generosity have already inspired me a dozen times over, just this evening,” he said. “As a lover of art, nothing brings me more joy than to share works of cultural and historical meaning with children and young adults, and to partner with museums on ways to make art and learning feel exciting and open to everyone.”
He spoke of a recent project his team collaborated with the Pérez Museum Miami on—an exhibition of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s greatest paintings. He recently saw a photograph of a child leaving the museum with a book about Basquiat—an example of the kind of influence he hopes his work is able to have on young people.
“Imagine what that visit might spark in a young person—the creativity, the dinner-table conversations with family about what they saw, the happy arguments with friends about whose favorite painting was truly the best,” he said. “This is our community at its finest.”
He went on to say that he is inspired by the museums he works with, especially those that champion initiatives to make art more accessible, including his work in helping the MCA Chicago and the Whitney do everyday admission for children 18 and under.
“These initiatives have been nothing short of transformative,” he said. “What unites all of us is a shared belief in equal access to art and culture—and in the lifelong gifts it brings: sharper thinking, bolder expression, and a deeper love for the very best of what people can make.”
Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz
Grammy-winning music duo and couple Alicia Keys and Kaseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean do not just create award-winning albums, but they also lead The Dean Collection, one of the most significant private collections of contemporary art by Black artists.
Their collection contains nearly a hundred pieces by around 40 artists from the Black diaspora, including fellow honoree Sherald.
Keys spoke first, highlighting the energy and “magic” of a room full of artists.
“We get to architect the life that we want to imagine. We get to architect the art that we live and breathe,” Keys said. “And as an artist, I think one of the most incredible things—and that’s what I feel the most in this room—is a sense of real, true connection and a sense of desire to find your best self and to represent a diverse understanding of life.”
Keys said she hoped the honorees and guests, when they leave the room, would leave with that core mission in their hearts and with “openness.”
Dean highlighted the work of their traveling exhibition, Giants: Art from the Dean Collection, which has now travelled to seven museums so far.
“It’s not a transactional thing for us when artists enter the Dean Collection. It’s a welcome to the family,” he said. “We only can be custodians of the art. We can only put on display the art for you to see, but the Deans can never own any of these great artists’ work.”
He also highlighted the collection’s Deans’ Choice resale royalty program, which allows art sellers and consignors to voluntarily direct a percentage of secondary-market sale proceeds back to the living artist who created the work.
“Deans’ Choice is basically making collectors responsible to collect, protect, and respect the artists, because that’s our job,” Dean said.
Their joint remarks finished with a toast from Keys:
“Can we raise our glasses to the kindest love and power in our hearts, to the endless possibility that we all have within us, to celebrating that together we’re stronger than any singular component, and to promising that our intention of uplifting each other will never end, never stop, and never be dissipated.”
TIME100 Impact Dinner: Leaders Shaping the Future of Art was presented by Lawh Wa Qalam: M. F. Husain Museum, established by Qatar Foundation; Bank of America; and UOVO.

Irish budget to tackle childcare and energy costs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:30:06 BST
14:30:06 KST

Irish budget tackles childcare and energy costs
- Published
The Irish government has used its budget to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs.
Taxes on heating oil and gas will be cut and then frozen for the lifetime of the government.
Temporary tax cuts on petrol and diesel, which were introduced earlier this year, will be extended.
Childcare subsidies will be increased which will be worth up €2,220 (£1,882) per child per year.
Finance Minister Simon Harris and Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers announced a budget package worth a total of €8.65bn (£7.33bn), €7bn (£5.93bn) on spending and €1.65bn (£1.40bn) in tax changes.
Harris raised the threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax from €44,000 to €46,500 (£37,307 to £39,418.05).
He said that, alongside other changes, a single person earning €50,000 (£42,395) a year will pay €700 (£593.25) less in personal taxes.
Harris added that the government had heard "loud and clear" the importance of an income tax package for middle earners.
"People are working hard and doing their best. They need the government to work with them and we get that."
Ireland collects more taxes than it spends on services
Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services.
Harris said the government expects to run a surplus of €6.7bn (£5.7bn) this year and a surplus of €9.5bn (£8.1bn) in 2027.
Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments.
A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has previously criticised the government for not saving more.
Harris said an extra €1bn (£847m) of the surplus would be invested in 2027 on top of the already planned transfer of €4.8bn (£4.1bn).
€11m to support cross community projects in NI
Other new measures announced on Tuesday include a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK's stock and shares ISA.
It will allow people to invest up to €50,000 (£42,395) tax free, with sums above that taxed at a flat rate of 1% a year.
There will be a new €15m (£12.7m) fund to help keep rural pubs open, with the details of grants and eligibility to be developed in coming weeks.
Chambers restated the government's commitment to fund a range of cross-Irish border projects through the Shared Island Scheme.
These include the Narrow Water Bridge and a teaching block at Ulster University in Londonderry.
He said there would also be €11m (£9.3m) for the Reconciliation Fund, which supports cross community projects in Northern Ireland and additional money for next year's Belfast Fleadh.

Obra Blanca 2026: Materials as a Starting Point for Discussing Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Obra Blanca, the exhibition of finishes and design products for architecture, will celebrate its seventh edition from October 13 to 15, 2026, at Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City. Conceived for the architecture and interior design community, this initiative combines an innovation showcase with an international lecture program to shape the Obra Blanca Experience: three days of connection, knowledge, and immersion in the architectural finishes and design products sector.
The Activities Agenda for the seventh edition of Obra Blanca holds particular significance for the architecture and interior design community. Its strength lies in collaboration: a program co-designed with 32 strategic partners—including professional associations, business chambers, specialized media, and industry leaders—bringing diverse voices and perspectives to offer a broad and pluralistic view of the architecture and interior design landscape in Mexico.
Held in the Grand Auditorium of Obra Blanca, in partnership with Arquine, this year's international lecture program will gather prominent figures in contemporary architecture. On Tuesday, October 13, the program will feature Carme Pinós, founder of Estudio Carme Pinós, renowned for an architecture that integrates public space, context, and social dimension in projects such as the Escola Massana and the Art and Design Center in Barcelona. On Wednesday, October 14, the focus turns to Colombian architect Daniel Bonilla of Taller de Arquitectura de Bogotá (TAB >|), whose work is distinguished by exploring the relationship between architecture, landscape, and the city, seen in projects like the El Tintal Public Library in Bogotá. Finally, on Thursday, October 15, the schedule will close with 2012 Pritzker Prize laureate Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu, founders of Amateur Architecture Studio and curators of the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale, whose work focuses on reclaiming traditional Chinese construction techniques and materials, as exemplified by the Ningbo History Museum.
This international lecture panel is integrated into an Activities Agenda organized around three Content Tracks:
- Habitable Space Track, Tuesday, October 13: This includes the Fourth National Housing Forum, titled "City and Housing: Heritage and Rights," in partnership with the Federation of Architects' Associations of the Mexican Republic (FCARM), CANADEVI Valle de México, and the Mejor Ciudad Association, with the support of the Mexican Chamber of the Construction Industry (CMIC) Mexico City Delegation; the Third Corporate Interior Design Forum, "Design, Strategy, and Innovation for the Workspace," in partnership with the Mexican Association of Corporate Interior Design (AMIC); the lecture "Beyond Spaces: The Power of Design in Daily Life," in partnership with Glocal Design Magazine; and Architecture Insiders, featuring the lecture "THE AI ERA, Architecture in the Age of Artificial Intelligence," in partnership with the Nuevo León Association of Architects (CANL).
- Sustainability and Innovation Track, Wednesday, October 14: This day features the Third Sustainability Forum, "Materials, Nature, and Technology for the Next Generation of Buildings," in partnership with ECOStudio XV; the lecture "The Construction Industry in Mexico 2026: Current Landscape, Trends, and Outlook," in partnership with BIMSA Reports; and the lecture "Architecture Shaped by Place: Espacio Común on Practice, People, and Context," presented by ArchDaily's Editor-in-Chief, Christele Harrouk.
- Lighting Track, Thursday, October 15: This track presents the Fourth Lighting Forum, titled "Thinking Light: A Dialogue Between Lighting, Architecture, and Interior Design," in partnership with Iluminet and the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) Mexico—a space dedicated to exploring lighting through its relationship with design, architecture, and the spatial experience.
The lecture "Architecture Shaped by Place: Espacio Común on Practice, People, and Context," by ArchDaily Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk, will take place on Wednesday, October 14 at 3:30 p.m. in the main auditorium. The session will feature Paula Villa Pastor, co-founder of Espacio Común, a Peruvian practice she co-directs with Daniel Canchán.
Starting with the Main Floating Stage for Muyunafest 2025 designed by Espacio Común—winner of ArchDaily's 2026 Building of the Year—this conversation explores how architecture can emerge from the conditions, knowledge, and ways of life of a specific place. Designed in response to the fluctuating waters and local building traditions of the Peruvian Amazon, the project serves as the starting point for a broader discussion on architectural practice: how architects read a context before intervening, how local knowledge and collaboration influence design decisions, and how ingenuity and adaptation can become architectural tools. Moving from this project to the broader portfolio of Espacio Común, the discussion will examine what it means to practice architecture from and within a particular context, among other themes. The conversation will also reflect on what happens when a local project reaches a global audience, and what its selection by ArchDaily readers as Building of the Year reveals about the kind of architecture that resonates with people today.
Throughout the three-day event, visitors will be able to experience the Obra Blanca Space, designed for this edition by architect Augusto Quijano Axle. His proposal conceives the exhibition as a living journey, presented as a tribute to continuity, movement, and fluidity. This space will host interviews, panel discussions, and the display of the Obra Blanca 2027 CMF Dynamic: *La tendencia es emocionar* (The Trend is to Evoke Emotion), an exercise developed in partnership with La Jabonera Centro de Diseño. In this showcase, a new Creative Team comprising 12 architecture and interior design firms from Guanajuato, Querétaro, and San Luis Potosí reviews the trends of the Obra Blanca 2027 CMF Forecast: *Fractured Beauty*, *Living Matter*, and *Multisensory Sanctuary*.
 "From its inception, the vision of Obra Blanca has been to create a space for shared growth. Today, this vision materializes in an exhibition that elevates the quality of its offering year after year, and in an Activities Agenda that spans from major international figures to key discussion forums. Design Museum Gent Reopens with New Wing by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

In November 2019, London-based Carmody Groarke and Ghent firm TRANS architectuur | stedenbouw, now known as ATAMA, won the Baumeister international competition to design an extension for Design Museum Gent, Belgium's largest design museum, located in Ghent's historic center. At the time, the museum comprised three buildings: the eighteenth-century Hotel de Coninck, the Leten House, with a sixteenth-century core, and a 1992 wing. After four years of renovation and expansion, the museum reopened on October 3, 2026, within the UNESCO World Heritage city center. The project combines the restoration of these historic buildings with a new wing designed by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, alongside the restoration work led by RE-ST architectenvennootschap. The museum's collection spans design objects from the fourteenth century to the present, and the renewed building adds spaces for lectures, workshops, exhibitions and events, framing design as something visitors can use and engage with directly rather than only view.
The museum's transformation was guided by a question posed at the outset of the design process: "Is this a museum for me?" In 2025, a citizens' panel called DE40, composed of forty Ghent residents, was formed to help answer it, examining how Design Museum Gent could become accessible and relevant to a broad audience regardless of background or prior design knowledge. Their input shaped the project's conception as a "third space" within the public realm: an open environment for meeting, learning, creating and discovering, rather than a conventional display-only museum. The guiding premise, as stated by the museum, is that a design museum should not only display design, but use, test and embody it. This also frames the institution as a publicly accessible space meant to serve local communities and neighborhoods.
The museum's historic core includes the Hotel de Coninck, an eighteenth-century rococo mansion at Jan Breydelstraat 5-7, long organized around an inner courtyard. Before the renovation, this courtyard was flanked by a neglected southern passage and an unused plot at the center of the site. The new wing allows the courtyard to function fully as a garden, now serving as the museum's heart and a central point of orientation for visitors. The broader masterplan balances conservation with new construction: historic interiors have been restored, while later additions to the building have been adapted to provide more space and improved climate control. Materials were reused where possible, and sustainable solutions were applied throughout the renovation.
The new wing links the museum's existing buildings into a single visitor route, organized into six zones structured around three principles: welcoming, open and adaptable. At basement level, an art-handling area gives visitors a view into the museum's behind-the-scenes operations. From there, the route continues through the Stadskamer (reception and shop), the Forum (lecture space), the Atelier (workshop space) and the Vitrine (temporary exhibitions), before reaching the Loft on the fourth floor, an event space with views over Ghent. The new wing's brick dimensions match those of the historic Hotel de Coninck, and its light tone relates to the houses along Drabstraat, with the composition drawing on the scale of Ghent's traditional guild houses and merchant homes. The facade is built from Gent Waste Brick, a lime-cured brick made from locally sourced municipal waste rather than fired in a kiln, reducing its environmental footprint. More than 82,000 of these bricks were produced locally at Het Arsenaal in Ghent, a process the public could follow live.
Other recent news about heritage protection and restoration includes the launch of a citizen campaign in Lima, led by Red Lima Milenaria, seeking UNESCO recognition for pre-colonial sites in the Peruvian capital. The campaign seeks to improve conservation conditions and public awareness of the sites that resisted European colonization by promoting the nomination of a selection of structures for inscription on UNESCO's World Heritage List. On September 16, 2026, Google announced the redevelopment of Chicago's Thompson Center, a postmodern architectural landmark designed by Helmut Jahn and completed in 1985, as a space for work, culture and community. London-based art, architecture, and design collective Assemble recently announced a new workspace project in the English capital, involving the transformation of a Grade II*-listed historic building into a new creative and light industrial workspace.

Trump signed an executive order to lower diesel prices
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:29:55 EEST
14:29:55 KST

Trump signed an executive order to lower diesel prices
Kyiv • UNN
In the United States, the use of red diesel fuel on highways has been temporarily authorized, and the federal excise tax has been deferred until the end of the year. Prices have reached $6.53 per gallon.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on October 5 aimed at lowering the nearly record-high prices of diesel fuel in the country by lifting restrictions on cheaper, red-dyed diesel fuel. UNN reports this, citing CNN.
Details
Speaking at a campaign event in Nebraska, a state that has been severely affected by the sharp rise in diesel fuel prices, Trump said that the executive order "will allow any person to purchase red-dyed diesel fuel without paying taxes for any reason."
"This executive order will also lower the cost of all goods, including food," Trump said after signing the document.
Red-dyed diesel fuel is the same as regular diesel fuel. It is simply not taxed and is dyed red to distinguish it from regular diesel, and is intended only for off-road use, for example, in tractors or for industrial purposes.
Allowing widespread use of tax-exempt diesel fuel could be especially beneficial for truck drivers facing a historic surge in diesel fuel prices, which, the publication writes, were "caused by the war with Iran, intensified attacks on Russian oil refineries, and export restrictions in China."
Allowing the use of diesel fuel could help farmers who depend on trucks to deliver their produce to market, as well as to obtain fertilizer and other materials.
According to a fact sheet published by the White House, the executive order "will temporarily allow the use of dyed diesel fuel for off-road equipment on highways and defer payment of the applicable federal excise tax, reducing costs for Americans."
The fact sheet states that the executive order directs the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to defer payment for the use of dyed diesel fuel on roads until the end of the year without interest or penalties and to "explore ways to waive the obligation to pay the deferred taxes."
The White House added that the executive order directs administration officials to encourage similar measures in other states and to ensure that farmers have access to dyed diesel fuel in areas with high demand.
According to AAA, diesel fuel prices in the United States rose sharply from $3.76 per gallon (approximately $0.99 per liter) before the war with Iran to a record $6.53 per gallon (approximately $1.73 per liter) on September 22. The national average price of diesel fuel on Monday, October 5, was $6.32 per gallon (approximately $1.67 per liter).
Diesel fuel for road use is usually subject to a federal tax of 24.4 cents per gallon (approximately 6.45 cents per liter). In addition, diesel fuel is subject to state-level taxes, which, according to federal data, average 35.5 cents per gallon (approximately 9.38 cents per liter).
It is unclear how long the executive order on the diesel fuel tax will remain in effect.

Ukraine Targets Major Russian Oil Hub During Massive Drone Attack on Moscow Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:22:47 UTC
14:22:47 KST

Ukraine launched a massive overnight drone attack on Moscow and the surrounding region, with one of the apparent targets being a major oil depot that supplies fuel to three of the Russian capital’s airports.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 650 drones were launched toward Moscow between the evening of Oct. 5 and the morning of Oct. 6. Russian air defenses claimed to have destroyed most of them before they reached the city, including 105 drones on approaches to Moscow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow Oblast Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were intercepted overnight. More than 10 private homes were damaged in Istra, the village of Lobanovo and the settlement of Radumlya, he said.
“Six people were injured. Unfortunately, there is one fatality,” Vorobyov said.
One of the apparent targets was the Volodarskaya Line Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS), described by the Russian investigative outlet Astra as the largest oil depot in the Moscow region.
The facility is operated by Transnefteprodukt, part of Russia’s state-owned Transneft oil pipeline company. It can handle up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, including gasoline, aviation fuel and diesel.
Fuel from the facility is supplied to Moscow’s three major airports – Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Sheremetyevo.
The reported strike came just days after Ukraine attacked another major Transneft facility in Russia.
Russian Drone Debris Falls Across Kyiv, Setting Cars Ablaze
On Oct. 2, Ukrainian forces struck the Samara LPDS in Samara Oblast, Russia’s largest oil hub, according to Russian media reports. A fire broke out at the facility following the attack.
The Samara facility has 71 storage tanks with a combined capacity of more than 1.6 million cubic meters and serves as a junction for four major oil pipelines.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak also said that Ukrainian forces attacked four Russian oil refineries overnight on Oct. 2, although he did not identify the facilities.
Novak said Russian authorities and oil companies had strengthened security around refineries and were considering additional support measures for the oil-processing sector, including extending deadlines for planned modernization projects.
The attacks come as Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russia’s oil infrastructure, a key source of revenue for Moscow and a critical part of the country’s fuel supply system.
On Monday, Oct. 5, US President Donald Trump again blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for elevated gasoline prices, arguing that disruptions linked to the war with Iran were no longer the main factor.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, claiming record volumes of oil were now moving through the waterway. Instead, he pointed to Russian refineries “being blown up by Ukraine” as a driver of higher prices.
Trump also blamed refinery closures in Democratic-led states. His comments come ahead of next month’s US midterm elections, with Republicans fighting to retain control of Congress.

Iranian Ships Test Sri Lanka’s Sovereignty Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:18:00 UTC
14:18:00 KST

On Sept. 30, 2026, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that U.S. officials threatened Sri Lanka with sanctions if it continued supplying around 20 Iranian tankers stranded off its coast. According to WSJ, the tankers are running short of food, fuel, and fresh water.
Sources in Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry told The Diplomat that the U.S. embassy in Colombo and visiting American civilian and military officials have repeatedly warned Sri Lanka against providing the Iranian vessels with essential supplies, despite the potential humanitarian crisis. Sri Lanka’s national security establishment reportedly objected to these demands and called on the government to convey its displeasure to Washington, as they are opposed to leaving the Iranian crew stranded and suffering.
With the WSJ report, the matter has now become public, restricting the maneuvering space of the Sri Lankan government.
The incident reveals the limits of sovereignty of small states like Sri Lanka that depend on exports to the Global North. Washington has considerable means to punish any resistance from Sri Lanka, and the question before Colombo now is how it can protect its economic interests while retaining the freedom to provide basic humanitarian assistance to friendly nations.
Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath has tried to distance the government from any private suppliers who might be supplying the stranded Iranian ships. Speaking to the Sunday Times, Herath said that the authorities had identified 15 Iranian vessels among 47 foreign ships outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters. He confirmed that Iran had requested essential supplies for the stranded ships but said that the government had provided nothing and did not intend to do so.
Herath described provisioning the ships as a private business. Companies could make their own decisions, he said, after considering the possibility of U.S. secondary sanctions. Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo told local media that U.S. sanctions apply globally and that these are not threats targeted at one country.
Colombo’s caution has an obvious economic explanation. The Export Development Board’s report for the first six months of 2026 puts the United States’ share of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports at approximately 22 percent. The European Union accounts for 25.5 percent, with Britain providing another substantial market. These figures explain why Sri Lankan policymakers worry about disputes with Western governments.
Yet accepting every U.S. demand also carries costs.
If Colombo does not provide drinking water to hundreds of stranded Iranians due to the fear of economic punishment, it invites further U.S. interference in decisions that should be its own. Officials urging a firmer response recognize that Sri Lanka must sometimes express disagreement to preserve any freedom of action.
In the past, Sri Lanka has indicated that it is willing to risk U.S. ire on humanitarian grounds.
After an American submarine sank an Iranian naval frigate, IRIS Dena, off the Sri Lankan coast in March, Sri Lanka rescued survivors. Colombo subsequently took custody of IRIS Bushehr, brought its sailors ashore and repatriated over 230 Iranians to safety.
India’s recent conduct complicates the decisions before Colombo. New Delhi presents itself as a regional security provider and has had a longstanding relationship with Tehran. Smaller neighbors expect India to take charge when external powers take military action in its backyard. However, when the U.S. sank IRIS Dena, India was nowhere to be found. Sri Lanka had to do the heavy lifting without any military support or diplomatic cover from India.
In recent years, India has grown closer to the United States and Israel. On the other hand, Sri Lanka has taken a strong pro-Palestinian stance and refused to sponsor a Bahrain-led United Nations Security Council resolution against Iran in March 2026.
However, these pressures must not let Sri Lanka diminish its sovereignty. Economic dependence on the West makes exercising its sovereignty difficult, but surrendering its foreign policy decision-making to Washington now would gradually reduce the matters over which Sri Lanka exercises meaningful control.
Sri Lanka cannot afford a reckless confrontation with the United States. Its government must consider the Sri Lankan livelihoods that depend on Western markets. But protecting those livelihoods also requires judging which risks the country can bear. Treating every American objection as a veto would leave Colombo with little foreign policy of its own. Fear of U.S. pressure has already constrained Sri Lanka’s willingness to pursue Russian oil and nuclear energy agreements or certain investments with China.
The government should convey its objections to American officials and allow willing private suppliers to deliver essential provisions to the stranded Iranian vessels. It should explain the risks to the public and defend its decision to prevent a humanitarian emergency.
Sri Lanka took a calculated risk when it rescued Iranian sailors in March. It must now show the same willingness to act before hunger and thirst endanger lives. Dependence on Western markets cannot become a justification for abandoning people at sea.

Former American Idol singer Caleb Flynn sentenced to life in prison for wife’s murder

OHIO – A former music pastor who once auditioned for American Idol was sentenced on Oct 5 to life in prison without possibility of parole for fatally shooting his wife in their Ohio home in February.
Before a judge handed down the sentence, the former pastor, Caleb Flynn, stood in court and maintained his innocence. During the hearing, which was live-streamed by Court TV, he acknowledged lying about “a lot of things”.
“But as I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife,” Flynn, 40, said.
A jury in Ohio convicted Flynn last week of aggravated murder and other charges in the killing of his wife, Ashley, who was shot twice in their home in Tipp City, Ohio, about 24km north of Dayton, on Feb 16. After the shooting, prosecutors said, Flynn staged the scene to make it appear as if an intruder had killed her.
The verdict came after a closely watched nine-day trial, in which prosecutors aired details of Flynn’s affair with a woman he met when she was a 20-year-old intern at his church.
Jurors listened to readings of their text messages and playbacks of the love songs that prosecutors said Flynn created for her using artificial intelligence.
Judge Jeannine Pratt said Flynn had used his faith to manipulate the lives of others. He could have separated from his wife, she said, instead of killing her in her own home while their two daughters were sleeping.
“But instead, through your greed, your selfishness, your lust and your cruelty, you chose to take Ashley’s life,” she said.
L. Patrick Mulligan, a lawyer for Flynn, has said he plans to appeal the verdict.
Flynn appeared briefly in the 12th season of American Idol in 2013, telling viewers in an interview segment that he loved his wife. He auditioned for judges Mariah Carey, Randy Jackson and Nicki Minaj, but did not advance to the main competition, Associated Press reported.
Flynn cried during most of the sentencing hearing, especially when letters from his daughters, who are 10 and 12, were read aloud by other relatives.
“What did she ever do to make you hate her so much?” one daughter asked in her letter.
“By the way,” the other daughter’s letter said, “Ashley Flynn was the best thing that ever happened to you.” NYTIMES

By beating Norway 2-1, Portugal reached the Nations League quarter-finals and a new squad list is expected. The question everyone asks is: and Cristiano Ronaldo?
