Jorge Jesus added that if Cristiano is still playing and wants to be in the national team, he sees no reason why he should not be, but that it is not his decision alone. The coach insisted he bore no resentment and said it had all been "a misunderstanding".
A few minutes later, at the press conference, he was again asked whether he was considering a return for Cristiano either to "say goodbye" or to "compete". Jorge Jesus stressed that Cristiano Ronaldo, "if he is still playing for Al Nassr, will be eligible for selection" and that if "he wants to return to the national team", the door will be open.
Jesus played down the fact that he sent Cristiano Ronaldo to warm up against Norway without bringing him on, saying that "it happens to every player", but admitted that with Ronaldo it was "different", perhaps because he is a "symbol".
He also recalled a conversation he had with Cristiano Ronaldo before this call-up, when he told him that a player like him "could not end his time with the national team by losing a World Cup and in tears", and said he agreed with Bruno Fernandes, the Portugal midfielder, who at Saturday’s press conference had said the captain deserved to finish "on a day of celebration".
Confronted with claims that Cristiano Ronaldo left the camp because a public apology at the press conference had been "pre-agreed" but never happened, as revealed by Edu Aguirre on the Spanish sports show El Chiringuito, Jorge Jesus angrily said it was "a lie" and that he did not have to apologise to anyone.
The player has not yet responded to the coach’s latest statements and has remained more discreet on social media. His last post, four days ago, confirmed that he had left the national team camp.
The next set of fixtures will be in November, first against Denmark at the Braga Stadium and then against Wales in Cardiff.
"We are talking about the greatest player of all time"
The president of the Portuguese Football Federation, Pedro Proença, also played down the situation, calling it a "misunderstanding" and offering fulsome praise for the captain.
"We are talking about the greatest player of all time, a player who has devoted more than two decades to Portuguese football. He will always be part of this team, as long as he is technically able to play. Cristiano knows that. He knows that is how we feel," he told RTP.
Pedro Proença went on to say that Cristiano Ronaldo could have ended his career after the World Cup but, "because of the love he has for his national team", chose not to.
"We will have time and calm to sit down together in the coming weeks and resolve this misunderstanding," the official concluded.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 137 drones, nearly every third jet-powered - how many destroyed
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 6, Russia launched 137 drones at Ukraine, including 49 jet-powered ones. Hits were recorded at 17 locations.
Russia launched 137 drones at Ukraine during the night of October 6, 49 of them jet-powered. Of these, 114 were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this with reference to data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia struck with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 6 (from 18:00 on October 5), the enemy attacked with:
-   137 Shahed-type attack UAVs (49 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, “Banderol”/“Dan-T” drones, and “Parody”-type decoy drones; 
-  from the following areas: Orel, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske; and from the waters of the Sea of Azov. 
How many were destroyed by air defense and how many hit their targets
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 114 enemy Shahed- and Gerbera-type UAVs and drones of other types
Hits by the enemy’s air attack weapons were recorded at 17 locations, while the debris of downed targets fell at 4 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs remain in the airspace.

Could teenage fitness shape your mental health decades later? New research suggests it might
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:10:07 UTC
14:10:07 KST

Being fit as a teenager may help protect against depression in adulthood, a new study suggests.
Exercise has long been linked to better mental health. But could how fit you are as a child or teenager predict your wellbeing years later?
Teenagers with better aerobic fitness have a lower risk of developing depression later in life, according to a new study.
Researchers in Australia analysed more than 1,000 people from a nationwide cohort originally surveyed in 1985 and followed for over three decades to track mental health outcomes through diagnostic interviews.
Participants’ fitness was measured in childhood through physical tests including a 1.6-kilometre run to assess cardiorespiratory fitness and a standing long jump to assess muscular power. A smaller group also completed cycling and handgrip strength tests.
The study, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, found that young people with faster running speeds — indicating superior cardiovascular fitness — had a 15% lower relative risk of developing depression later in adult life.
The average run time was about 8 minutes and 27 seconds, and running roughly 1 minute and 15 seconds faster than average was associated with this reduced depression risk.
The protective benefit of cardiorespiratory fitness was strongest five to ten years after the first tests, when participants were closest to childhood, and gradually attenuated over time. However, the associations persisted across the full 34-year follow-up.
Across all cardiorespiratory fitness measures, the authors noted that the protective effect was consistently stronger in females than in males. Women were also more likely to suffer from depression during their lives.
“While we cannot say a lack of fitness during childhood causes depression in adults, the findings suggest that childhood fitness may have benefits beyond physical health,” said Kyle Smith, the study’s lead author.
“There are many contributing factors to depression, meaning no single factor explains risk on its own. Fitness may be one piece of the puzzle.”
The number of people living with mental health conditions has nearly doubled over the past 30 years, driven mainly by sharp rises in anxiety and depression worldwide. Globally, about 322 million adults, one in 20 people, live with depression.
As rates continue to climb, researchers are focusing on identifying lifestyle factors that can help prevent or delay the condition.
“Importantly, fitness is something we can change; it may be an important target for improving long-term mental health,” said Grant Tomkinson, a researcher at Adelaide University.

Artemis II, satellite constellations and space geopolitics to headline Day 2 of global space congress in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:04:16 UTC
14:04:16 KST

Beril Canakci
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The results of NASA’s Artemis II mission, the future of large satellite constellations and the growing intersection of commercial space and geopolitics will be among the main topics Tuesday as the 77th International Astronautical Congress enters its second day in Antalya, Türkiye.
IAC 2026, which runs from Oct. 5-9, is organized by the International Astronautical Federation and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, with SAHA Istanbul as co-host. It marks the first time that Türkiye is hosting the congress.
At 11.45 am (0845GMT), NASA Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons will join an industry panel on the results of Artemis II.
Artemis II carried four astronauts around the Moon in April, marking the first crewed lunar flyby in more than 50 years. The mission was designed to test systems needed for future crewed missions, including those that will take astronauts to the lunar surface.
The discussion comes a day after NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson told Anadolu that the “civilian space race” between the United States and China was “closer than we would like right now.”
"But we're going to be confident, and we have some exciting news to announce very soon," Anderson said, without providing details.
The crowded orbital environment will be another major focus Tuesday.
Michael Nicolls, SpaceX's senior vice president of Starlink engineering, is scheduled to discuss the sustainability and safety of large satellite constellations in an evening highlight lecture.
The session will address the challenges of operating large numbers of satellites in low-Earth orbit as satellite networks continue to expand.
Earlier in the afternoon, space industry leaders will examine the increasingly close relationship between commercial space and national interests.
The “Geopolitics vs. Innovation” plenary will look at how companies operating Earth-observation fleets, in-space infrastructure and other commercial systems are balancing global markets with growing demands from governments and security institutions.
The morning program will open with a plenary on the transition from national space programs toward a broader global space ecosystem, including lunar exploration, satellite infrastructure and commercial space activity.
The session, titled “Bridging Eras: From Silk Road Astronomy to Lunar Exploration,” will feature Axiom Space Chief Astronaut Michael Lopez-Alegria alongside representatives of the Turkish Space Agency, ASELSAN, Fergani Space and the TUBITAK Space Technologies Research Institute.
The heads of space agencies from established and emerging space nations will also gather Tuesday for the third IAF Global Space Leaders Summit.

Spain's housing crisis bursts into the spotlight at snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:03:57 UTC
14:03:57 KST

Spain's housing crisis bursts into the spotlight at snap election
MADRID, Oct 6 - Spain's snap election will revolve around an issue which has topped voters' list of concerns for three years straight but, until a fortnight ago, failed to dominate the political debate: housing.
It was the attempted eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in central Madrid last month after her building was bought by a real estate firm that upended the country's politics. Her case triggered nationwide protests and catapulted the issue to the top of the agenda, even overshadowing immigration which had dominated headlines for weeks following a mass migrant crossing in Ceuta.
Spain's housing shortage shares patterns with others across Europe: complex bureaucracy and labour shortages stalling supply, proliferating short-term rentals and high demand in urban centres pushing up prices, and rural areas hollowing out.
From Ireland's 2024 election to Berlin's recent mayoral race, the topic has particularly galvanised young voters across the region tired of spending a rising proportion of their incomes on rent.
Yet how to resolve the crisis in Spain is a matter of bitter debate.
'TRUST US TO FIX IT'
Housing plans proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist government in Parliament last Friday were struck down by rightwing MPs who argued the measures - ranging from rent caps to limits on purchasing real estate for corporate entities - would worsen the problem by choking supply.
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the centre-right opposition People's Party, is pledging instead to build 250,000 new homes a year in projects creating 600,000 more jobs.
"If Spaniards give me their trust, my priority, my success, will be housing policy," said Feijoo, whose party leads voting intention in September polls with around 33% support to the Socialist PSOE's 26%.
Feijoo also wants to speed up urban planning to free up land for development and provide stronger mortgage and rental guarantees for young people.
But some are sceptical about his promises. Marta, a 28-year-old Madrid resident and one of tens of thousands of protesters who took to the streets to voice discontent at the decree being struck down, hopes a successful election will strengthen the left's mandate to fix the issue.
"If we leave this issue in the hands of the right, it's going to get much worse," she said.
'PASSING THE BUCK'
Spain's regionalised structure often stands in the way. Central governments can set housing legislation and devise nationwide plans for incentives and subsidies, but their implementation, and wider urban planning, is largely devolved to regional governments and municipalities.
All types of instruments - from rent controls proposed by the Socialists to eased planning permissions proposed by conservatives - have been struck down, blocked, or simply not implemented since the Socialists took power in 2018.
Two decades on from a housing bubble and subsequent market collapse that scarred its economy, Spain's has flipped from a housing glut to a major deficit, estimated by its central bank at 750,000 homes and likely to reach a million by 2028.
A steady recovery in demand, boosted by ultra-low interest rates and rising immigration, was not matched by new supply in the areas needing it most, as developers and lenders scarred by the crisis and lacking workers were loath to resume building.
Though 73% of Spaniards own their homes, over half of 18-34 year olds now live with their parents or depend on them for living costs. House prices rose at three times the rate of wages last year, official statistics show, pushing more people to rent.
At just 1.7% by European Commission calculations, its social housing stock is among the lowest in the EU.
"Maricarmen was the tip of the iceberg. This situation has gone on forever, and all parties, the government and the regions, are to blame for passing the buck," said 40-year-old Alex Dominguez, a Madrid native living with his ex-girlfriend Marta because neither has found an affordable alternative since their breakup.
'VULTURE FUNDS'
The Tenants' Union driving protests has called for a crackdown on "vulture funds", corporate investors it said were driving up prices and forcing evictions.
The union has successfully intervened in several cases where properties were bought by institutional investors, negotiating compensation or preventing evictions like Maricarmen's.
But Jorge Galindo, director of the Centre for Economic Policy EsadeEcPol, argued that aggressive government action against private investors would chill construction projects.
"The (government) decrees create a tradeoff between protecting those already in rent and facilitating supply for those who haven't yet found a place to live," Galindo said.
Land registry data also shows institutional ownership outside densely populated cities like Madrid is minimal.
Just 4.4% of homes nationwide are owned by companies and 4.3% of landlords have 11 or more properties on the market, an amount that subjects them to stricter regulations.
Some 40% of homes for rent belong to individual landlords with just one property on the market who supplement wages with rental income, according to the Bank of Spain.
Political analyst Cristina Monge said that meant successful government policies had to balance the interests of homeowners who make up three-quarters of the populace and renters, a smaller but growing and more vulnerable group.
"Property owners see their own children struggling to access housing - not just to buy, but even to rent," she said. "That is what makes housing policy so complex now; if we were a country with a higher percentage of renters, the policies required might be simpler to devise."
Still, for some of the protesters who marched in Madrid, radical steps are needed.
"We need a bit of humanity in how we deal with this," said Marta, Alex's ex-girlfriend. "Housing is a right." REUTERS

Cricket: Smriti Mandhana takes over captaincy as Kaur steps down
Harmanpreet Kaur's vice-captain, top-order batter Smriti Mandhana, will take over the captaincy of India's women's cricket teams.
The 30-year-old was the obvious successor in waiting, after 13 years in the India setup and as a key contributor to the team's scoring with impressive averages and run-rates at all levels.
She had already captained India in 18 T20 games and four one-day internationals (ODIs) and has captained the Royal Challengers Bengaluru to two Women's Premier League titles.
"To be given the responsibility of leading India is a very specialy honor ... the opportunity to lead the team is something I will value deeply," she said. "I would also like to acknowledge Harmanpreet and the contribution she has made as captain over the years. She has led the team with great commitment and has been an important part of our journey."
Left-handed opening batter Mandhana became the all-time leading run-scorer in Indian women's international cricket during the Asian Cup last month, when she surpassed Mithali Raj's old record and surpassed 10,880 runs. She averages more than 50 in Test matches and almost 50 in ODIs, with 18 career centuries across all international formats.
Earthquake strikes in Uttarakhand near border to Tibet
A fairly large earthquake has struck in Uttarakhand state, not far from the border with the autonomous Chinese region of Tibet or Xizang in the Himalayas.
Preliminary measurements from the US Geological Survey put the magnitude at 5.1. It struck at a depth of around 10 kilometers (roughly 6 miles).
Tremors were also felt in the capital, Delhi, well to the west of the epicenter. There were no preliminary reports on possible damage from the region.
Police break up opposition protest
Police broke up the opposition sit-in in Delhi and briefly detained Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi as Tuesday's demonstrations progressed.
Delhi police said Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, herself a lawmaker, and others were detained in accordance with the law to maintain peace and in the interest of public safety.
Congress said that Gandhi was later released.
Gandhi had at one point joined the people sitting on mattresses inside the compound of the state broadcaster's door, next to the headquarters of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
"We only want to go to the election commissioners, ask them questions, and tell them you have stolen votes," he said.
The commission later said it received a request to meet the lawmakers late on Tuesday, but that the venue they suggested was not in line with ECI protocol. It said it offered to give the lawmakers a copy of their memorandum instead, and they declined.
Opposition leaders dig heels in, detentions reported during protest against election chief
Congress workers and INDIA bloc supporters attempted to breach the gates of the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, leading to scuffles with security personnel, news agency ANI reported.
Some hundred meters away, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other senior opposition lawmakers were holding a sit-in protest at the Akashvani Bhavan complex after being stopped from marching towards the Election Commission's office.

Cricket: Harmanpreet Kaur quits as India women's captain
Harmanpreet Kaur on Tuesday stepped down as the captain of India's women's cricket team in all three international formats.
"This is not an easy decision. It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices, and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life," Kaur said as she announced her decision on social media.
The senior batter's decision to quit comes after she recently led her team to win their second successive Asian Games gold medal.
37-year-old Kaur became the highest-capped player in women's international cricket this year.
The skipper led India in five tests, 51 one-day internationals and 155 T20 internationals.
She also led India to their maiden women's global title at last year's ODI World Cup.
Kaur's announcement comes after a review meeting was held by the Board of Control for Cricket in India on Monday,
In her statement on Tuesday, Kaur indicated that she would continue to play cricket.
"Captaincy may end today, but my love for Indian cricket never will." she said.
What is the controversy surrounding India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
Over the last week, mass protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar have been launched by India's opposition parties and also the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth-led movement.
The outcry comes after The Indian Express newspaper last month reported divisions in India's poll body over the revision of voter lists.
Kumar heads the three-member Election Commission which is overseeing the voter roll revisions.
The Indian Express reported that two of his fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
Concerns emerged over the Election Commission's neutrality following the report.
Opposition leaders and critics say that those struck off the lists in the voter roll revisions include a huge number of minority voters.
They have accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains, questioning the body's independence.
"The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government. We are fighting to save our democracy," Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge, told the media ahead of the opposition march on Tuesday.
The Election Commission of India rejects allegations of wrongdoing and says the exercise removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Kumar became the CEC in 2025 after being chosen by a selection panel led by Modi.
Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, who was also a part of the panel, had opposed Kumar's appointment.
On Monday, India's top court issued notices to the Election Commission of India, the Modi government, Kumar and the other two election commissioners, seeking their response to a batch of petitions against the CEC over the alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.
If "there are decisions against the law ... We will take care of it," the Supreme Court said.

Dramatic visuals emerged from the opposition lawmakers' protest demanding the resignation of the country's chief election commissioner on Tuesday as Congress' Rahul Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra tried to breach the security barricades.

Akashvani Bhavan is the headquarters of India's state-owned public radio, the All India Radio (AIR).
Visuals on news agency ANI show the Gandhi siblings staging an apparent sit-in under a tree inside the Akashvani Bhavan premises.
BJP hits out at INDIA bloc over protest, trains guns on Rahul Gandhi

Leaders and MPs from India's opposition parties are set to carry out a protest march to the Election Commission of India's (ECI) headquarters in New Delhi on Tuesday as they call for the sacking of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar following voter-list changes.
Security arrangements have been beefed up around the national poll body's headquarters, media reported Tuesday morning.
The INDIA bloc — the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties — announced the march last week as part of a broader 'Save Democracy' campaign under which its leaders have been holding demonstrations since October 2 over alleged irregularities made by the ECI.
The opposition is demanding the removal of Kumar, who is facing allegations of taking unilateral action in connection with mass culling of names from registered voter lists.
Critics say the action, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by removing their names from voter lists and that the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The ECI and the BJP reject the allegations.
Around 130 million names have been removed from electoral rolls since the changes began last year.
The opposition march on Tuesday will begin from Parliament House.
INDIA bloc leaders are later also expected to meet President Droupadi Murmu to raise concerns over the SIR exercise, reports said.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's Studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily offering of all the biggest headlines from India.
Demands for the ouster of India's top poll official, Gyanesh Kumar, following contentious changes to voter rolls are set to reach the Election Commission of India's doorstep — quite literally — with opposition leaders and MPs planning a protest march to the election body's headquarters in New Delhi Tuesday.
Meanwhile, another protest seeking Kumar's resignation looms as India's 'cockroach' protesters have announced a return to Jantar Mantar — the same site in the heart of the Indian capital from where the online satirical movement was propelled to the mainstream and forced India's education minister to step down. The Cockroach Janta Party's protest is slated for October 10.
And amid all the pressure that is mounting in the country over allegations of widespread voter-list manipulation, by-elections are underway in three states and one Union Territory.

Simpler itineraries, longer stays: How travellers embrace doing less while on holiday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:43 UTC
14:00:43 KST

From slower, less-planned breaks to AI scepticism and the rise of nearby escapes, travellers are expected to prioritise deeper and more meaningful experiences in 2027.
With the arrival of autumn comes a flurry of new travel trend reports and predictions for the coming year.
The latest body to make its predictions is UK-based travel and tourism marketing brand Lemongrass, which has revealed its picks of the top trends for 2027.
Experts at the company believe that a lot of travel undertaken next year will revolve around the “anti-optimised” holiday, which means that travellers will be choosing to do less and spend longer in a destination, rather than rush about and tick off everything on a perfunctory list.
The Lemongrass travel trend report has also revealed that travellers are also moving away from bucket lists, biohacking and AI-generated itineraries and are instead plumping for deeper, slower and more emotional experiences.
“For years, travel has been caught up in the language of optimisation – more destinations, more experiences, more personalisation and more efficiency,” said Mirjam Peternek McCartney, CEO and Founder of Lemongrass Marketing. “But our 2027 trends suggest that travellers are beginning to ask a much more human question: how do I want to feel?
“This isn’t a rejection of technology, luxury or ambition. It’s a recalibration. People want travel that gives something back – whether that means feeling calmer, understanding a place more deeply, connecting with other people, or simply having the freedom to enjoy a moment without having to maximise it.”
Here are some of the findings from the report.
The anti-optimised holiday and other insights
Lemongrass says "anti-optimised holidays" – that is, cramming every minute of a trip with activities – could be on the way out.
Travellers are increasingly looking for trips that feel less like a checklist and more like a proper break – with fewer destinations, simpler itineraries, longer stays and plenty of time to simply see where the day takes them.
The new meaning of having a luxurious holiday could just be having nowhere to be.
Nervous system design
Wellness is moving beyond spa treatments, health checks and the latest biohacking trends.
Increasingly, hotels and destinations are looking at the whole environment, from lighting and sound levels to access to nature, food, movement and opportunities to connect with other people.
Rather than adding more treatments to an itinerary, the focus is shifting towards creating spaces that naturally help guests slow down, rest and recover and, most importantly, leave feeling better.
From bucket list to depth list
AI can increasingly give travellers a pretty good idea of what to expect before they even set off. As more of the planning process becomes automated, though, there’s growing interest in the things an algorithm can’t quite provide, namely context, curiosity and human insight.
Instead of chasing supposedly hidden gems or ticking off must-see sights, travellers are likely to seek out expert-led tours, cultural trails, literature, history, architecture, workshops and conversations with people who actually live there.
The appeal is less about discovering somewhere first and more about understanding it properly, rather than just working off a checklist.
Epistemic vigilance and the AI trust gap
As AI takes hold of all aspects of travel, knowing what information to trust could become just as important as finding it in the first place.
Travellers are increasingly having to navigate AI-generated content, synthetic images and paid-for recommendations, making first-hand experience and local knowledge more valuable.
That means they’ll also likely want to trust tour operators or travel agents who can say “we’ve been there and seen it first-hand”, rather than an AI programme which is effectively just winging it.
Other travel trends to expect in 2027
Alongside the headline findings, the report also identified 10 other trends which we can expect to see play out in the coming year.
Shifting conversations around masculinity are, apparently, creating a new travel market for men seeking physical, emotional and mental wellbeing. Fitness, nature, mindfulness and outdoor experiences are no longer being used by men just to improve performance, but also to facilitate connection, resilience and meaningful friendship.
Climate change is undoubtedly having an impact on travel, and it’s not just where people go, but how the destinations themselves cope.
In 2027, it seems that travellers won’t want to just escape the heat, but also put value on spots which offer resilient infrastructure, flexible experiences, strong local knowledge and tourism businesses able to respond when conditions change.
That leads into the next trend: citizen science.
Travellers are increasingly moving from observing nature to actively participating in its protection, whether that’s wildlife monitoring, water sampling or recording species. The aim of playing such a role in conservation can mean that tourists achieve a deeper connection with the places they visit.
More tourists will also want to leave places better than they found them, and not just in nature terms. The challenge is making meaningful, locally led conservation and community projects accessible without slipping into traditional voluntourism – and that leads into the new "giving journey" trend.
It’s similar to another trend: journeys “without sacrifice or sermon”.
Sustainable travel is becoming less about compromise and more about the experience. Rail, for example, can offer a more scenic, comfortable and enjoyable way to travel – as well as a lower-impact one. Sustainability is often embraced when it delivers a better experience, rather than making people feel less guilty.
Next up is “earned travel”, or the rejection of trips that are too easy.
Travel has never been more convenient – and that may be exactly why some travellers are starting to seek out the opposite.
From remote landscapes to independent adventures, a bit of effort, uncertainty and spontaneity can make a trip more rewarding. Increasingly, getting there is part of the experience.
At the same time, travellers will be hunting for the next trend, which is the so-called “joy economy”.
With uncertainty and digital overload everywhere, travellers are looking for things that simply make them feel good – from play and surprise to connection and escapism. They're using travel as a form of emotional restoration, and not just something to do.
That ties into the mystic outlands trend, which will see folklore, fantasy and atmospheric landscapes drawing travellers looking to step into another world, not just a destination – whether that means dark skies, ancient forests or places steeped in stories.
More travellers will be asking “who gets to tell the story?” rather than “where are we going?”.
Travellers are increasingly interested in who gets to tell a destination’s story, with female guides, historians, artists, chefs and community leaders bringing different perspectives, especially in areas where the female voice has typically been overlooked.
Finally, according to the report, “near is the new far”.
In 2027, it predicts that travellers will realise they don’t always need to go far to get away. Short-haul trips, rail journeys, staycations and off-season breaks offer an easier escape, with less time, cost and hassle.
Short-haul travel can be cool – and as enjoyable and meaningful as destinations thousands of miles away.

EU mulls tougher restrictions on Russian diplomats as hybrid threats intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

The recent spate of hybrid attacks across Europe has raised questions over the possible involvement of Russian diplomats, prompting member states to consider tighter restrictions and checks.
The movements and actions of Russian diplomats have come under intense scrutiny as the European Union grapples with a succession of hybrid attacks, some of which have been directly attributed to Moscow, that have shaken its collective security.
The topic has emerged as a potential next step in the bloc's sanctions regime, according to senior diplomats with knowledge of the discussions.
Brussels is seeking to turn the page after the contentious removal of two high-profile oligarchs last month, which strained the EU’s united front. Countries are now looking for ways to close ranks and push back against the Kremlin's interference.
Among the options under consideration are tighter restrictions and checks on Russian diplomats in a bid to crack down on state-sponsored hybrid warfare and sabotage.
Last month, Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats accused of "unacceptable" behaviour under the 1961 Vienna Convention. Moscow responded in kind.
Other troubling incidents, including a suspected arson attack at a defence company in Estonia and the discovery of an unexploded drone at Leipzig Airport in Germany, both linked to Russia, have further heightened concerns.
The conversation, which is still in early stages, follows up on the mechanism that the EU introduced last year in its 19th sanctions package.
The system obliges Russian diplomats who are deployed across the bloc to notify their intention to travel to or transit through another member state beyond their host nation "no later than 24 hours" before their intended entry.
It applies to diplomatic and consular agents of all ranks, including ambassadors, the administrative, technical or service staff, and family members.
Though the system has given European authorities greater oversight to monitor the movements of Russian diplomats, it does not, in itself, restrict them.
Member states can apply a stricter procedure to compel Russian diplomats to request an authorisation for transit. If denied, the diplomat cannot travel across. This procedure, however, is optional. So far, only two countries have put it in place.
"As the system has only been in place since January 2026, experience is limited," a spokesperson for the European Commission said.
The notification system was based on the premise that Russian diplomats are "often involved" in activities that spread pro-war narratives and manipulate public opinion. Now, the thinking shifts to their possible role, direct or indirect, in hybrid attacks.
"Russia's actions will not remain unanswered," reads the draft conclusions for next week's summit of EU leaders.
"The European Union and the member states will act resolutely and in a coordinated manner to address these actions, making full use of all tools and mechanisms available.
The debate in Brussels will have to balance the Vienna Convention, which grants extensive rights and protections to diplomatic agents in their day-to-day work. The text is considered one of the greatest successes of international law.
As talks of new sanctions accelerate, the EU is trying to advance a visa ban on former Russian soldiers and tighter rules for Russian tourists.

Turkmenistan grows its arsenal of Chinese air defences as Russia’s role shrinks
Amid regional instability, Central Asian nations look beyond Moscow for arms as the war in Ukraine drains Russian stocks
Turkmenistan has added the FK-2000 missile-and-gun system to its growing arsenal of Chinese-made air defences, highlighting Beijing’s expanding role in the Central Asian weapons market once dominated by Russia.
At least 10 FK-2000 vehicles – along with an array of other Chinese-made military equipment – could be seen in footage of Turkmenistan’s Independence Day parade in Ashgabat on September 27.
Developed by the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation, the FK-2000 is a mobile air defence system combining missiles and twin 30mm (1.1-inch) cannons with on-board radar and electro-optical sensors.
The system is designed to counter aerial threats including aircraft, helicopters, drones and precision-guided weapons.

UK regulator FCA to investigate how it handled Epstein whistleblower who took his own life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

A top UK regulator has launched an investigation into how it handled a whistleblower – who highlighted alleged ties between the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick – after he took his own life.
The British banker Simon Andriesz died late last month aged 57, the campaign group Transparency Task Force, of which he was a member, confirmed over the weekend.
Andriesz had formerly worked as a managing director at BGC Group, the financial brokerage where Lutnick had been chief executive. He had accused the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of failing to hold his former employer to account for alleged wrongdoing, and had been wrongly told he did not qualify for whistleblower protection.
The banker had spent years raising concerns about his former employer: first in regards to accounting irregularities – which he raised internally at BGC in 2016, a year before he was sacked – and then in 2020-21, when he reportedly told the FBI that Lutnick had undeclared business ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Lutnick has since said he had no “personal or professional relationship” with Epstein. He was named Donald Trump’s commerce secretary in late 2024.
Andriesz, who had been living in Cornwall, later unearthed an email chain in the Epstein files that suggested Lutnick and Epstein had discussed the prospects of a startup business they were both involved in, in 2018. Epstein died in jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
However, Andriesz told the BBC’s File on 4 Investigates this summer that authorities in the US and UK had failed to hold BGC and its parent company, Cantor Fitzgerald, properly to account, or protect him from potential retaliation. He also later accused the FCA of mistreating whistleblowers, and raised concerns about the toll that whistleblowing had taken on his family, career and health.
The FCA had also given Andriesz misleading information, saying he would not qualify for whistleblower protection because his identity had become known. The regulator apologised to him and said that further guidance and training would be provided to its whistleblowing team.
The FCA confirmed it had now tasked a new board member to investigate how staff handled Andriesz’s concerns. “We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz’s death,” an FCA spokesperson said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends. Since expressing our condolences, we’d asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future.”
However, the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on investment fraud and fairer financial services is concerned that the FCA is being allowed to “mark its own homework” and called on the regulator to pay an independent party to “forensically and objectively evaluate its handling of whistleblowers”.
The APPG’s chair, the Labour MP John McDonnell, said: “It is vital that this time a truly independent and non-conflicted organisation carries out the work needed. If the FCA refuses to respond positively, the APPG will consider all alternatives, including conducting its own call for evidence from whistleblowers who have interacted with the regulator.”
Lutnick has not been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and has previously said: “I unequivocally condemn the conduct attributed to Jeffrey Epstein and everyone who participated in his illegal activities. The survivors of his crimes deserve our respect and support.”
A BGC spokesperson said: “BGC has long disputed Mr Andriesz’s allegations but does not intend to relitigate these matters at this sad time. BGC is sorry to hear this tragic news and expresses our condolences to Mr Andriesz’s family.”

‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

As fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas.
In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise.
While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate.
Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children.
“You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says.
In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay.
“It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says.
About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, most on the largest island, Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders.
“The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says.
Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry.
“You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says.
Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work.
“Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.”
Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back.
“A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says.
Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage. With almost no public transport, he says he needs to drive to work because of how rural it is. The cost of his commute has meant sacrificing some of the things he likes to do with his girlfriend.
“Me and my girlfriend like to go to restaurants that are a bit of a distance away, around half an hour drive. We’ve not done that in a while. I think it’s safe to say that the cost of fuel will be affecting businesses because they’ll be getting fewer customers,” he says.
As fuel costs rise, islanders have started taking jerry cans to the mainland to stock up on cheaper fuel, even to just save a few pennies a litre, Ryan says. Normally, the cans are used in the winter to stock up when high winds and choppy seas disrupt deliveries to the islands and pumps run dry.
“It’s not often that diesel hits the £2 mark, let along £2.17 or whatever it is now. Whenever people say they’re going to the mainland, they say: ‘We’re going to make sure we will take our jerry cans if we are allowed,’” he says. “Even in Skye, the price of petrol and diesel is about 20p cheaper. So, a lot of people actually take the opportunity when they go down to really stock up on fuel whenever they can.”
But even with the cost of living pressures, Ryan is not considering leaving. He says that people are pulling together in the latest surge of inflation.
“People have a romantic view of the islands as being this quiet paradise where you can really get away from it all. But island life is quite hard, especially when costs are rising so significantly,” he says. “But it’s a nice place with a communal feeling. I think that’s what’s getting people through the situation. Everyone is in it together.”

Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

There’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, it’s him! Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.
And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.
Nigel Farage has been the only one to react with unfettered glee. Reform’s next manifesto is basically now written for him: save Brexit, stop the boats and don’t vote for Restore because it can’t win.
Things are more complicated for the Lib Dems and Greens, who, having pitched themselves as the only real pro-Europeans on the left, are now stuck with trying to take credit for pushing Labour into doing the right thing. But it’s the party currently holding its conference in Birmingham that faces the most interesting dilemma.
Kemi Badenoch doesn’t mention Brexit much these days – only elected after the referendum, she seems to regard the generational Conservative trauma of that period as history now – and it gets only brief mentions in The Right Way, the 95-page personal essay she says would form the bedrock of a Tory government. In his platform speech on Monday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, chose to focus on accusing Burnham of supposedly dragging Britain back to the 1970s, rather than back to 2015. On this they echo much of what’s left of the Tory vote, who are more interested in tax, the costs of doing business, small boats and what exactly Labour has against labradors in pubs than in relitigating the Brexit deal. Yet the Conservatives are still promising to reverse any Labour unravelling of Brexit, regardless of how that affects the economic growth Badenoch simultaneously insists is everything to her.
It makes no intellectual sense, which arguably didn’t bother previous Tory leaders. But it’s a mistake for one pitching herself as a rigorous thinker, approaching power with the same robustly worked-through theory of the world as Thatcher in the 1970s.
Growth is now Badenoch’s rationale for everything, from scrapping the Environment Agency – accused of being a drag on developers, although that’s precisely what some rural Tory voters like about it – to giving parents earning over £100,000 free childcare (on the grounds that, currently, high earners will cut their working hours rather than lose that nursery place). It’s her defence for some potentially unpopular choices, her alpha and omega. Yet by ignoring the ongoing damage Brexit is doing to trade and GDP, Badenoch is chopping her self-professed growth mission off at the knees.
In her 1976 essay The Right Approach, which Badenoch’s treatise consciously echoes, Margaret Thatcher declared that her party “has always been outward-looking, while concerned with the security, the economic interests and the honour of Britain”, and lambasted Labour’s lack of enthusiasm for the then European Community. The context now is obviously different, but Thatcher in 1976 was still a pragmatist arguing for Europe “to concentrate on what is practical and what is attainable”, where Badenoch in 2026 is an ideologue. The Tory brand remains toxic despite its leader’s relative popularity mostly because voters got sick of endless Brexit-related drama consuming Westminster, while none of the practical benefits materialised. There’s no point dangling policies such as free childcare for bankers over the remain-voting former Tory shires without acknowledging all that. But if she can’t bring herself to do so, then Badenoch’s next best bet is to let Burnham rescue her party from a dead end of its own making.
Though they would never have opened this door, in truth it suits the Tories to let Burnham walk through it, while blaming him for whatever goes wrong. If he can construct some mythical EU deal boosting trade and prosperity while remaining acceptable to an electorate convulsed with anxiety about immigration – a big if – then future governments will owe him. If he can’t, Badenoch can just join the chorus of condemnation. But it’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth.
Readers who couldn’t care less about Tory long-term interests, meanwhile, should care that Europe won’t re-enter tortuous Brexit negotiations until it’s clear they could survive a change of government in Britain. If not a referendum, that means at least tacit cross-party acceptance that the country could do better. Badenoch doesn’t even have to say yes to a rethink. All she has to do, for once, is not say no.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:02 UTC
14:00:02 KST

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.
Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.
Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.
The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.
Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.
Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.
“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.
“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”
In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.
Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.
“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”
Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.
“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.
The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.
Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”
Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.
Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.
An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

Jose Pizarro’s recipe for poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:02 UTC
14:00:02 KST

In Spain, vermut is traditionally enjoyed as an aperitif, while pedro ximénez is often poured at the end of a meal, alongside dessert or a piece of cheese, say. In this tart, however, they come together to tell the story of the Spanish table in the form of pudding. We have a wonderful tradition of fortified wines, and while lighter sherries often hog the limelight, vermut and pedro ximénez deserve just as much attention. They’re both made from wine, but each brings something completely different to a dish. Here, vermut, which is infused with herbs and spices, gently perfumes the pears, while PX, with its rich raisin, fig and caramel notes, introduces a flavour that’s impossible to resist.
Poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel
Prep 15 min
Cook 1 hr 50 min
Chill 30 min+
Serves 10-12
750ml bottle red vermut – I like Lustau Vermut Rojo, but any vermut rojo will do, or standard red vermouth
3 tbsp runny honey
1 vanilla pod, split and seeds scraped out
Pared zest of 1 orange
4 just-ripe medium-sized dessert pears (williams or comice, say), peeled
Cream or creme fraiche, to serve
For the pastry
225g plain flour, plus extra for dusting
110g cold unsalted butter
50g caster sugar
2 egg yolks
For the filling
100ml pedro ximénez
2 tbsp caramel sauce (Sainbury’s does a good one), or dulce de leche
1 pinch flaky sea salt
125g unsalted butter, softened
125g caster sugar, plus 2 tbsp extra for the glaze
2 medium eggs
125g ground almonds
1 tbsp plain flour
Put the vermut, honey, vanilla pod and seeds, orange zest and 300ml water in a pan just big enough to hold the pears snugly. Bring to a simmer, then add the pears and leave to poach gently for 20-25 minutes, until glassy-looking and just tender to the tip of a knife. Take off the heat and leave the pears to cool in the liquid.
Meanwhile, in a food processor, pulse the flour, butter and sugar until they resemble breadcrumbs. Add the egg yolks and pulse again briefly to make a dough; if need be, add up to two teaspoons of water to help bring it together. Tip out on to a lightly floured surface, quickly shape into a ball, then press down into a flat disc. Wrap in baking paper and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface, then use it to line a greased deep, fluted 23cm tart tin; the pastry will be very soft, so if it breaks, just press it back together with your fingertips. Return to the fridge to chill again.
In a small pan, bring the PX to a simmer, then reduce until there’s only about two tablespoons of sticky liquid left. Tip into a bowl, blend with the caramel sauce and a pinch of salt, then spread the PX mix all over the base of the tart case, and chill again.
Heat the oven and a baking sheet to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Lift the cooled pears out of the poaching liquid, pat dry, then cut in half lengthways and scoop out the cores. Turn each pear half on to its flat side, then cut a few times across its width without slicing all the way through. Press down gently to fan out the slices, then pat dry again.
Whisk the softened butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy, then work in the eggs, almonds and flour. Spread this evenly over the caramel layer in the tart case, then neatly top with the pear halves pointy ends in, and gently press them into the almond layer.
Bake for 45 minutes on the heated tray, then cover with foil so the pastry doesn’t brown too much and bake for 15 minutes more, until set all the way through.
Meanwhile, put 300ml of the pear poaching liquid in a pan, add two tablespoons of sugar, bring slowly to a boil, then reduce to a glossy, sticky glaze.
Leave the tart to cool for 10 minutes, then remove from its tin and put on a rack. Once it’s just warm, brush the vermut glaze over the top and serve with cream or creme fraiche.

As clocks turn back, Lithuania renews its push to end Europe’s time-change debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

The changing hours are a reminder of a question that Europe has debated for years: Why does the continent still change its clocks twice a year?
In Vilnius, an interactive video screen offers a window into cities around the world, showing them in real time. One city may still be enjoying the afternoon while another is already approaching evening.
At the end of October, Lithuania and the rest of the European Union will once again turn their clocks back one hour, shifting to standard, or winter, time.
For some Lithuanians, the twice-yearly ritual has long been an annoyance.
“I don’t like turning the clocks,” one woman told LRT TV. “It’s like we gain an hour in the autumn, but then, once we get used to it, they change something again. I’d really like them to finally make a decision.”
Another passerby said the time should simply remain fixed.
“There’s no need to turn them back and forth. We need one consistent time – either winter or summer,” he said. “It affects you. Your mood is completely different in the morning and evening.”
Transport Minister Juras Taminskas agrees. He has been trying since the beginning of the year to persuade the Baltic and Nordic countries to agree on ending the practice.
Even his dog, he jokes, does not understand the clock change.
“They used to say cows don’t understand the clock change. Well, my dog doesn’t understand it either, because when you change the time, you have to take him out for a walk at a different time,” Taminskas said. “I’m in favour of not changing the clocks.”
Taminskas hopes to make the issue part of Lithuania’s agenda when it takes over the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union for six months starting in January.
He acknowledges that reaching an agreement could be difficult, particularly with southern European countries.
“Considering the current political situation, when there are so many important issues and challenges, not being able to agree on something as basic as this – an issue that has been dividing people emotionally, psychologically and physically for decades – is, to put it mildly, embarrassing,” he said.
But Žygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor bank, is less optimistic.
“Looking at how difficult it is to reach agreement on other issues in the EU, success is probably unlikely,” he said.
The biggest obstacle, Mauricas said, is not necessarily whether Europe should stop changing its clocks, but which time it should keep.
For Lithuania, that choice presents a particular dilemma.
Summer time would provide more daylight during the evening and, Mauricas said, could be more favourable for people’s health because it would maximise the number of daylight hours when people are awake and active.
But there are also economic considerations. Lithuania, like the other Baltic countries and Finland, are in the Eastern European Time zone (UTC+2), while most of the rest of the EU is one hour behind.
Having the same time as major trading partners can make cross-border business easier. Germany is particularly important for Lithuania, Mauricas said.
But there is hard geography which can be stretched only so much. As it is, Spain and Poland are separated by nearly 3,000 kilometres but operate on the same clock.
“Essentially, that’s completely absurd,” Mauricas said.
The arrangement means Spain sacrifices some morning daylight while Poland gives up some daylight in the evening.
If Lithuania adopted permanent winter time to align with Poland, it would similarly lose brighter evenings.
“Because we are next to Poland, we would also sacrifice our bright evenings if we joined them,” Mauricas said. “But economically, it would probably be more beneficial.”
That could create another source of public frustration, he said.
“If permanent winter time were introduced, believe me, there would be even more complaints,” Mauricas said.
His calculations suggest Lithuania would lose about 40 minutes of daylight if it permanently adopted winter time.
Transport Minister Taminskas says the decision should ultimately be made jointly by the EU member states. He says representatives should vote on which time to retain and accept the outcome of the majority.
Lithuania already has an initial agreement with the Baltic and Nordic countries in favour of permanent summer time, he said. Poland’s position will also be important because neighbouring countries benefit from having a common position.
Previous public opinion surveys in Lithuania have consistently shown support for keeping summer time year-round. The Transport Ministry does not plan to conduct a new survey, however, saying such polls can leave countries stuck in the same arguments.
For now, there is no agreement.
So on the night of October 24-25, Lithuanians will once again turn their clocks back an hour – gaining an extra hour of sleep, but also seeing autumn evenings suddenly getting much darker.

SEOUL, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's imported car sales rose in single digit last month, driven by strong demand for electric vehicles (EVs) and German luxury models, industry data showed Tuesday.
The number of newly imported passenger car registrations here gained 6.3 percent from a year earlier to 34,904 in September, according to the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association.
For the first nine months of this year, 279,729 imported vehicles were sold, up 24.1 percent compared to the same period of last year.
U.S. automaker Tesla took the top spot in terms of automotive sales here among foreign companies by selling 12,372 units.

The number of European models sold here was 17,578 last month, taking up 50.4 percent of the total. U.S., Chinese and Japanese brands recorded the market shares of 36.1 percent, 7.6 percent and 5.9 percent each.
By fuel type, battery-powered EVs accounted for 52.1 percent, followed by hybrid vehicles with 39.0 percent, gasoline vehicles with 8.2 percent and diesel models with 0.7 percent. ■

Leaders visit Pacific atoll Tuvalu at front line of climate change

Leaders visit Pacific atoll Tuvalu at front line of climate change
- Leaders visited Tuvalu to witness the severe impact of climate change, including rising seas and coral death, highlighting the nation's urgent risk of becoming uninhabitable.
- Tuvalu plans to relocate its 10,600 population due to climate threats, while projects like the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project aim to mitigate rising sea levels.
- Australia led the pre-COP gathering but faced criticism from locals over cultural disrespect and its coal export role, amid the urgent call for global climate action.
AI generated
FUNAFUTI, Tuvalu – Over a dozen leaders visited the tiny Pacific atoll nation of Tuvalu on Oct 6 for a first-hand look at a once-vibrant ecosystem wiped out owing to climate change.
The getaway took place on the sidelines of the Pacific “pre-COP” gathering hosted by Fiji and aimed at drawing the world’s attention to life on the front line of global warming.
The meetings are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit known as COP31, to be held in Turkey in November.
The South Pacific is among the regions of the world most vulnerable to global warming – from rising seas jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
Tuvalu is deeply affected, already laying plans to relocate its population of 10,600 if the country is consumed by the ocean.
But only a handful of leaders – mostly from the Pacific – showed up to visit the atoll.
Among them was Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country is head of climate negotiations in 2026, but has faced accusations of hypocrisy given its role as a major coal exporter.
Hundreds of people donning traditional dress, flower tiaras and umbrellas to shield themselves from heavy rain gathered to greet the leaders, who were accompanied by a small media delegation including AFP news agency.
The group then toured the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project, a landmark land reclamation effort that aims to mitigate the impact of rising sea levels.
They also took part in a traditional dialogue session with locals.
Australia has taken a leading role in the pre-COP gathering and defended it as a critical diplomatic event in the face of criticism back home about the cost to taxpayers.
But Albanese drew criticism from a Tuvalu government adviser, who accused him on Oct 6 of disrespect by not wearing a traditional headpiece during an event and for overstepping during the running of the visit.
“Just because we signed the treaty doesn’t mean they can take over our country and our sovereignty,” the aide told AFP on condition of anonymity.
“That’s how it feels.”
Impact of climate change
Tuvalu is one of the world’s least visited countries, and the highest point in the capital Funafuti is just 2m above sea level.
Rising waters have already largely swamped two of Tuvalu’s nine coral atolls, and scientists fear the entire archipelago could be unliveable by the end of the century.
A marine heatwave in 2024 wiped out an estimated 99.9% of the coral that built the remote Tuvalu islands.
“You can swim for hours and hours along the reef in the lagoon, just skeleton after skeleton. It’s all dead,” said marine biologist Austin Bowden-Kerby, who visited in 2025 and documented the devastation.
“The very system that created the islands has died. It wasn’t pollution. It wasn’t overfishing. Just a direct result of climate change.”
Local scientist Rajneel Singh told AFP that climate change was already impacting the food sources that have long sustained Tuvalu’s population.
“Elders used to fish for red snappers and other things,” he said.
“They are no longer frequently found in the catch. And the sizes of the fish have been reduced as well.” AFP

Delhi court grants bail to 17 students, journalists arrested during CEC protest
Unknown

Delhi Police accused of misconduct with female journalist at Jantar Mantar..
NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Monday night granted bail to 17 students and freelance journalists arrested during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, and directed jail authorities to ensure medical treatment for those who sustained injuries.In four separate orders passed between 9 pm and 9:25 pm, Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) Animesh Kumar of Patiala House Court ordered the release of all 17 accused in connection with an FIR registered at Parliament Street police station.The court directed that the accused be released on furnishing a personal bond with one surety of the like amount. It also said they should be released immediately if their custody was not required in any other case.
The court specifically directed the jail superintendent to ensure necessary medical treatment for accused who had sustained injuries, as advised by the medical officer.
Court sets bail conditions for accused
The accused have been directed not to directly or indirectly induce, threaten or influence anyone acquainted with the facts of the case or tamper with evidence. They have also been restrained from committing any offence while on bail.They must provide their correct permanent and residential addresses and active mobile numbers, keep the numbers operational and inform the court of any change in address.
They are also required to appear before the concerned court on every date of hearing and cannot leave the country without prior permission.The court said the investigating agency would be free to seek cancellation of bail if any of the conditions were violated.The FIR was registered under Sections 223(a), 221, 132, 190, 191(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with Section 3 of the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act.Police alleged that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly, obstructed or blocked public space, manhandled police personnel and damaged public property.
Police seek custody, defence cites right to protest
The investigating officer had sought 14 days of judicial custody, arguing that the accused could commit further offences or interfere with the investigation.The defence opposed the plea, arguing that the accused were young and that several were students exercising their democratic right to dissent and protest. Defence counsel also submitted that no individual role had been specified against the accused in the grounds of arrest.The defence pointed out that while police claimed around 50 people were protesting, only 17 had been arrested. It also argued that no CCTV footage of the alleged incident had been produced before the court.The defence further submitted that some of the accused had sustained injuries and their medical examinations had not been conducted immediately after the incident.The court observed that the allegations were serious and noted that a police official had allegedly sustained injuries. However, it said the right to protest peacefully could not be disputed, while assaulting police officials on duty was a serious concern.
The court also noted that, except for the offence under Section 132 of the BNS, the offences invoked were bailable in nature. It further observed that the accused did not appear to be habitual offenders and had their entire careers ahead of them.Considering the facts and circumstances, the court ordered their release on bail subject to the specified conditions.The court directed that the accused be produced before the concerned court on October 6 and ordered that a copy of the bail order be supplied to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi, for information and necessary compliance.

Separatists win Quebec election in test for Canada PM’s national unity strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:38:26 UTC
13:38:26 KST

The separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) won Quebec’s provincial election on Monday but fell short of enough seats to govern alone, returning to power with a promise to hold another referendum on independence from Canada.
The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decade but denies it the majority it sought, forcing the separatists to rely on opposition parties even as they try to revive Quebec’s independence debate.
PQ’s victory could make it tougher for the prime minister, Mark Carney, to maintain national unity against the US president, Donald Trump. Carney, who has stressed the need for a united front to deal with Trump’s tariffs, must now work with a Quebec premier who is determined to break up Canada.
PQ was on track to win nearly 60 seats as the final votes were counted, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority in Quebec’s 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature. A minority government means PQ will need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes.
The result, which was widely expected, reflected voter fatigue with the centre-right Coalition Avenir Quebec government, in office since 2018, analysts said.
Previous PQ governments held failed independence votes in 1980 and 1995 and polls indicate support for the idea of breaking with Canada is at 30%, near record lows.
Plamondon, citing the political uncertainty and economic damage done by the tariffs, says he will not call another referendum until Trump is out of the White House. He also says he will work with Ottawa whenever it suits Quebec’s interests.
But some PQ policies – such as resisting any federal bid to boost immigration levels, vowing to cut Quebec’s ties to the British monarchy and promising to block a proposed high-speed, high-profile rail line linking Quebec with Ontario – could increase tensions with Carney.
Earlier in the day, Carney told reporters he would work with whoever Quebec chose as its next premier.
The Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote on 19 October on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada.
Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said the result should not be viewed as a rejection of Carney, who remains very popular in Quebec.
Still, Béland said a separatist government in Quebec represented a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching elsewhere in Canada.
Quebec, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant policy autonomy.
The province collects its own income tax, has immigration policies favouring French speakers and has laws giving the French language priority over English.
Trump’s tariffs and 51st-state rhetoric have complicated the separatist argument by stirring Canadian nationalism and giving some French-speaking Quebecers another reason to value the protection that comes with remaining part of Canada.
Trump’s tariffs and repeated threats against Canada became a defining issue in the 2025 federal election, helping lift Carney’s Liberals to victory after the party had trailed badly before Trump returned to office.
