Illouz to ‘Post’: Netanyahu must pay political price for October 7 - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:20:06 UTC
13:20:06 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu must be replaced because failing to impose a political price for October 7 would undermine accountability and endanger Israel’s future, former Likud MK and Yisrael Beytenu candidate Dan Illouz said in an interview with The Jerusalem Post.
“If there isn’t a political price to being prime minister when such a disaster happens, then this is something which is dangerous for us as a country,” he said.
For Illouz, the question extends beyond who should lead the next coalition. Allowing Netanyahu to remain in power despite what happened on his watch, he argued, would create political incentives to evade responsibility rather than accept it.
“I think that it’s very important for the next government not to be led by Netanyahu,” he said.
Illouz joined Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu in August and subsequently resigned from the Knesset. He holds the tenth spot on the party’s election slate.
His departure from Likud, he said, reflected a growing divide between the principles that first drew him to the party and the policies he encountered as one of its lawmakers.
Illouz drawn to Likud's commitment to free markets, strong defense
After making aliyah from Canada in 2009 and graduating from McGill University’s law school, Illouz joined Likud before signing a lease. Its commitment to free markets, strong defense and military service for all appealed to him.
Once inside the Knesset, however, he said he repeatedly found himself fighting members of his own party to advance those objectives. He accused Likud politicians of protecting interest groups rather than opening markets and Netanyahu of blocking sovereignty initiatives in the West Bank.
The most pressing rupture concerned military service.
Illouz described friends spending prolonged periods in reserve duty, missing their children’s births and struggling to maintain their careers. Against that backdrop, he argued, integrating haredi men into the military was an urgent practical necessity.
Yet Likud, he said, had worked to preserve its arrangements with the haredi parties instead of delivering meaningful change.
In Yisrael Beytenu, he said, he found the combination of economic liberalism, strong security policies and universal service that had initially attracted him to Likud. He pointed to Liberman’s refusal to join a government in 2019 over the draft dispute as evidence that the party leader had already been tested on the issue.
Illouz’s disillusionment with Netanyahu also centered on the failure to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7.
Initially, he said, he accepted the argument that an inquiry should wait while Israel was fighting an intense war. When Netanyahu subsequently raised the possibility of an alternative mechanism, Illouz waited to see what would emerge.
When no alternative materialized, he said, he concluded that the delay reflected an attempt to avoid responsibility.
Asked whether he supported a state commission of inquiry, his answer was unequivocal: “Definitely.”
Challenged about his previous praise for Israel’s wartime achievements, Illouz said he stood by his assessment of the military’s performance and believed Netanyahu also deserved some credit.
But he distinguished battlefield accomplishments from achieving the government’s stated objectives.
The IDF had dealt major blows to Israel’s enemies, he said, yet Hamas remained in Gaza, Hezbollah retained the ability to rebuild, and Iran’s regime remained in power. In his assessment, those outcomes fell short of the “total victory” Netanyahu had promised.
“But we didn’t deliver total victory,” he said.
Yisrael Beytenu, Illouz align on religion, individual freedom
Alongside security and accountability, Illouz presented his move to Yisrael Beytenu as consistent with his views on religion and individual freedom.
A religious Jew himself, he described his outlook as classical liberalism: support for smaller government and less state intervention in people’s lives.
He distinguished Israel’s Jewish national identity - expressed through its flag, history, and holidays - from imposing religious observance on individuals.
“In general, in every issue when there is religious coercion, I’m against religious coercion,” he said. “As a religious Jew, I think it only hurts religion.”
He backed allowing municipalities to decide whether to operate public transportation on Shabbat, rather than imposing a uniform policy on communities with different identities.
Growing up in Montreal, he said, the availability of public transportation had never interfered with his religious observance.
Illouz confident in Zionist opposition's potential
On coalition arithmetic, Illouz expressed confidence that the Zionist opposition could secure enough seats to form a government, while acknowledging that doing so would require mobilizing voters and persuading the public that change was necessary.
“I really hope that Lieberman is the next prime minister,” he said.
Asked whether he would sit with an Arab party, Illouz answered no, saying his objection concerned recognition of Israel and unequivocal condemnation of Hamas and October 7, rather than Arab identity.
His position on the haredi parties was also firm-and, he acknowledged, represented a change from his earlier belief that negotiations could produce a workable draft agreement.
Illouz said committee discussions had convinced him that proposed compromises were riddled with loopholes that would preserve the status quo.
Instead, he advocated changing the financial incentives surrounding enlistment, including withdrawing state benefits and municipal tax discounts from those who do not enlist.
He argued that meaningful financial consequences would encourage haredi men to serve, while accusing their political representatives of obstructing integration into both the military and the workforce.
Asked what he would reconsider from his time in Likud, Illouz returned to his former confidence in compromise.
“I unfortunately don’t believe that we can get into a compromise with them,” he said

Hundreds of ultra-Orthodox protesters rioted overnight Monday in Modi'in after military police attempted to arrest a draft dodger, storming the building where he lived and clashing with police until security forces ultimately withdrew without taking him into custody.
Footage showed protesters inside the draft dodger's apartment alongside large numbers of police officers. After the failed arrest, the man emerged into the street for a celebratory reception with the rioters, standing on the roof of a vehicle as supporters gathered around him. One protester was filmed handing him sweets.
The protesters had been summoned by the extremist Jerusalem Faction's "Black Color" hotline, which helps ultra-Orthodox draft dodgers evade arrest. Police said during the incident that large forces were operating "to extract the soldiers and restore public order."
After the forces withdrew, the hotline celebrated the outcome. "Following the support of the masses and thanks to the holy public, the police left the yeshiva student's home. Intense dancing at the scene," it said.
The Jerusalem Faction established the hotline last year as the IDF began enforcement efforts against ultra-Orthodox men who failed to report for mandatory military service. Activists distribute its number in ultra-Orthodox communities and have described their strategy openly: "We prevent arrests. Anyone they come to arrest calls the hotline, and we send protesters to him. When protesters arrive, the army leaves."
Moti Leitner, chairman of the Haredi Public Party, condemned the violence. "The place for these savages is behind bars," he said, adding that ultra-Orthodox political leaders Aryeh Deri, Yaakov Asher and Yitzhak Goldknopf should condemn "the violent riot against IDF soldiers and the lawlessness raging in the streets."
The IDF rarely carries out proactive operations to arrest draft dodgers. Nearly all of the dozens currently detained are Breslov Hasidim arrested at Ben Gurion Airport or other border crossings after returning from abroad, including from the annual pilgrimage to Rabbi Nachman's grave in Uman, Ukraine.
The military has largely refrained from such arrests despite a High Court ruling requiring equal enforcement of mandatory military service. Military officials have cited insufficient cooperation from Israel Police, whose assistance is required for military police to operate in civilian areas. Police have rejected that argument, saying enforcement is the responsibility of the Military Police.
Last week, thousands of ultra-Orthodox demonstrators marched in Jerusalem in support of arrested draft dodgers, carrying signs against the IDF, including some calling it the "enemy army." At the end of the march, Rabbi Yehuda Tzadka, head of the Porat Yosef Yeshiva, handed each draft dodger an envelope containing 1,000 shekels, which organizers said came from donations from abroad.
The Modi'in clashes also drew sharp political condemnation. Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of Yashar!, said a country that sends its citizens to fight "cannot accept a reality in which a state within a state exists inside it."
Naftali Bennett, chairman of Beyachad, said Israel was "a moment away from another disaster," describing the incident as one in which soldiers and police "fell into an ambush by hundreds of extremist rioters" and had to negotiate their safe departure.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman said soldiers and police had been attacked while trying to arrest a draft dodger and were forced to leave under heavy police protection. "It is simply intolerable that IDF soldiers are forced to flee under heavy police protection as though they were in Jenin and not Modi'in," he said.

Police braces for nationwide day of protests across French high schools demanding reforms and more resources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:15:36 UTC
13:15:36 KST

Students are demanding the government address issues they view as critical to their education, including upgrading classroom facilities, ensuring schools in less economically affluent areas are not disadvantaged, as well as reforms to the school system and the long hours pupils spend in schools.
After a weekend-long hiatus, high schoolers in France are expected back at the barricades this coming week in their protest movement that is rattling the government of President Emmanuel Macron.
A key question is whether violence on the margins of the demonstrations will worsen, blurring the lines between protest and rioting, and whether Macron's government will ratchet up the already muscular response by police.
According to the interior minister, officers made more than 5,000 arrests last week, 85% of them minors, in scuffled between students and security forces that left hundreds of people injured.
A test of the movement's endurance and appeal will come Tuesday, when the influential CGT labour union is urging workers to demonstrate, too.
Protests first erupted in the Paris capital region in mid-September.
Teachers and students mobilised against a lack of staff at a lycée, or high school, in Creteil, in the southeastern outskirts of the French capital. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, with protests even in high schools of smaller towns.
Around 400 or 500 schools have had to close because of damage or attacks that targeted staff and are expected to remain closed early into this week, according to the education minister. More than 170 pupils and 78 staff members have suffered injuries, he says.
From the outset, students focused on perceived inequalities in the school system, saying that teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement aren’t as good for students in disadvantaged neighbourhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Placards held up by the first protesters in Creteil read “Too many inequalities, we’re disgusted,” “Education is a right, not a privilege,” and “Sorry to bother, it’s for our future,” according to photos posted by Clémence Guetté, the district's lawmaker at the National Assembly.
"The public needs to know that conditions for studying are no longer what they were for us,” said Sophie Bordy, a 50-year-old literature teacher in Paris. "It has deteriorated significantly.”
Pupils elsewhere complained that during summer heat waves, they roast in classrooms without air-conditioning, and they freeze in winter. French media broadcast videos of scampering rats, collapsed ceilings, leaks, broken furniture and other issues filmed in dilapidated schools.
Spending on education is one of the costliest items in the state budget that Macron’s government is proposing for 2027. It earmarked €65.5 billion for schools, more than the €63.4 billion proposed for defence.
Pupils also complain of long hours. In high schools, classes often start at 8 am local time and can last to the early evening. French high schoolers’ compulsory school hours are among the highest in Europe, according to European Union figures.
“I see the teachers more than my family,” read one young girl's placard photographed by French media outlets.
Guetté, the lawmaker who posted photos of herself meeting with the first protesters in Creteil, bullhorn in hand, is a rising star of the far-left France Unbowed party. Other France Unbowed lawmakers and elected officials also quickly identified with the protests, meeting with pupils and backing their demands.
France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon urged party members and supporters to protect pupils from the police, by putting themselves in between the two sides.
Mélenchon has denounced what he called the “savagery” of police officers who have liberally used tear gas and their batons to break up crowds.
Police riot-control projectiles are suspected in some facial injuries that young protesters suffered. Hundreds of police officers have also been injured, according to the interior minister’s office.
Critics of Mélenchon accuse France Unbowed of stoking and manipulating the students for political gain. Mélenchon, a fiery anti-capitalist, says his party supports the movement but isn’t organising it and wants it to be non-violent.
Mélenchon, 75, is making his fourth run for the French presidency in 2027 and is wooing young voters.
They tended to vote less than other age groups in the last presidential election in 2022 but could potentially help Mélenchon qualify for the decisive second-round runoff in May — a success that has always escaped him — if he can mobilise them to turn out.
“What we want is for this country’s young people to emerge from this episode with their heads held high, having won something and learned something, and to remember it when they cast their ballots,” Mélenchon said on Thursday.

Musical residencies: Business is booming, but who pays the most for pop stars playing in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:14:29 UTC
13:14:29 KST

Musical residencies are on the rise in Europe for major pop stars, but costs are increasingly being heaped upon audiences with travel, accommodation and extras pushing up ticket prices, according to Spanish consumer rights group FACUA.
For decades, Las Vegas made musical residencies part of its identity. Instead of taking a show from city to city, major artists would stage the same production in a single venue for weeks or even months, and it was the audience who travelled to see it. Europe is now beginning to experiment with a similar formula.
Madrid is one of the most visible examples of this transformation. Shakira has headlined a 12-date residency in a temporary venue, the Shakira Stadium, set up at Iberdrola Music in Villaverde. Bad Bunny has concentrated ten concerts at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano as part of his tour, while Dani Martín has become the first artist to develop a residency at Madrid’s Movistar Arena.
The phenomenon goes beyond Spanish and Latin American performers. Other international stars such as Céline Dion, Adele and Ariana Grande have also been linked, in different ways, to formats that group several performances in the same European city. The result is a major change in the relationship between artist, city and audience.
For Rubén Sánchez, secretary-general of consumer rights group FACUA, this formula "does not benefit the public". He believes that concentrating performances allows the industry to cut costs by using the same venue for longer, while forcing many spectators to take on additional expenses.
"It is not the same for all the shows to be held in Madrid as for there to be a tour of different cities in Spain," Sánchez explains. On top of the ticket price can come transport, accommodation, food and other costs linked to the trip.
More dates, but also more expenses
Residencies can increase the number of tickets available by offering several chances to see the same artist. However, for those who live far from the chosen city, the real cost of attending can be considerably higher.
Sánchez believes it will be the public’s response that ultimately determines the future of the model. If fans are willing to travel and absorb those extra costs, he thinks it is likely that more residencies will appear. If there is a backlash that translates into lower ticket sales, the industry may reconsider its strategy.
"The success or failure of the new model will depend on the mass reaction of users," he says.
The issue of the final price
FACUA also warns of another problem linked to ticket sales: the lack of clarity over how much consumers end up paying. Sánchez is particularly critical of the so-called "booking fees" added during the purchasing process. For FACUA, the advertised price should include all compulsory costs from the outset.
"From the very first minute, from the very first screen, from the first advert, they have to say what the ticket price is," he insists. On top of that comes the resale market. FACUA argues that resale should only be allowed on a non-profit basis, for instance when a consumer who cannot go sells their ticket to someone else. The organisation is calling for tighter regulation of resale aimed at making a profit.
The consumer will have the final say
The model emulates Las Vegas because it turns the concert into a destination. For host cities, thousands of fans can generate business for hotels, restaurants, transport and shops. For consumers, however, it means shouldering a larger share of the cost and the logistics.
Sánchez believes it is still too early to know whether residencies will become established in Europe. The key will be whether audiences accept this new equation: more chances to see a major artist, but also a greater likelihood of having to travel and spend more to do so.

Climate damage already ‘locked in’ – but these 10 insights show our future is still being decided
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:14:02 UTC
13:14:02 KST

From rising sea levels to food systems fuelling climate change – experts have laid out 10 insights that require urgent action.
Past emissions have already “locked in” future climate impacts – but the scale of this damage still depends on what action we take right now, according to a major new study.
The 10 New Insights In Climate Science report is produced by more than 70 scientists from nearly 30 countries and aims to translate complex research into accessible, concise insights to “inform high-stakes decisions”.
Published today (6 October) it warns that the overshooting of 1.5°C, as set out in the legally binding Paris Agreement, carries “rapidly escalating risks of irreversible impacts” for our oceans, glaciers and permafrost – and that the economic and social costs of doing so are greater than previously understood.
10 insights to prevent further climate damage
“The evidence is unequivocal," says Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam
Institute for Climate Impact Research, co-chair of The Earth League and a member of the report’s editorial board.
“1.5°C is a limit that we cross at our own risk. Beyond it, the risks of cascading and potentially irreversible climate impacts increase, with every additional tenth of a degree making them more severe.”
The 10 New Insights highlights, created by Future Earth, The Earth League and the World Climate Research Programme, point to a “narrowing window for action” but one that is still open, showing us what is already locked in, what can still be avoided, and where policy can have the greatest effect.
Ocean heat uptake clouds long-term outlook
The ocean continues to absorb record amounts of heat due to human-caused climate change – locking in further warming for years to come.
In August, global sea surface temperatures reached 21.1°C – the hottest ever recorded. Experts warned last year that the planet’s ocean acidification - where the water’s pH is lowered due to CO₂ absorption - entered the danger zone for the first time.
The new report says deep cuts to greenhouse gas emissions are “urgently needed” to prevent further long-term heat accumulation.
“The ocean has been our planet’s shock absorber,” says Wendy Broadgate, Global Hub Director at Future Earth and a member of the report’s editorial board.
“Because heat takes decades to penetrate ocean depths, today's emissions effectively lock in further warming and sea level rise. Deep, rapid emissions cuts are the only way to limit these risks.”
Sea levels keep rising
Melting glaciers and ice sheets are driving rising seas, putting more people at risk of severe flooding.
The report warns that some sea-level rise is already irreversible due to the impact of past emissions, but the magnitude of this still depends on how quickly the world acts to cut greenhouse gases.
Freshwater sources are getting scarce
Water gaps are widening as continental drying – the long-term, large-scale decline in freshwater availability and water storage – accelerates. According to the UN, By 2030, one-in-two people are expected to face severe water shortages.
“Climate change and growing water use are causing the rapid loss of freshwater across continents, threatening water security, ecosystems, and food production,” the report says.
“The consequences of inaction extend from threats to local livelihoods to cascading impacts across the Earth system.”
Governments are being encouraged to develop holistic water management plans, known as Integrated Water Resource Management, that take into account the entire water cycle: from source to distribution, treatment, reuse and return to the environment.
Nature-based solutions such as restoring wetlands, rivers and forests can also help capture fresh water that remains on land, rather than letting it dry up or run straight into the ocean.
Impacts of overshooting 1.5C
A recent report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) warned that global temperature rise will exceed 1.5°C, likely within the next few years. This would accelerate much of the environmental degradation the natural world is already experiencing, from shrinking ice sheets to rising sea levels and “unprecedented dieback” of coral reefs and rainforests.
The UNEP says that there are “no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C” and that governments must focus on making the overshoot as small and short as possible.
Food systems still fuel climate change
The report says that transforming food systems, particularly through more plant-rich diets, can deliver major benefits for climate, biodiversity and health, but they must be done “carefully and fairly”.
Globally, food and agriculture contribute one-third of total greenhouse gas emissions, second only to burning fossil fuels – and meat has been identified as the main culprit.
In fact, animal-sourced foods make up between 81 and 86 per cent of total greenhouse gas emissions from EU food production, despite only supplying an estimated 32 per cent of calories and 64 per cent of protein.
According to the carbon footprint calculator CO2 Everything, one 100g serving of beef is equivalent to 78.7 km of driving, releasing 15.5 kg CO2 equivalent.
Understanding the ‘social cost’ of carbon
Experts warn that the economic damages caused by carbon emissions are "substantially higher” than previously estimated – adding that every extra tonne of CO2 carries “additional risk”.
“Using more realistic, up-to-date climate models reveal a social cost of carbon up to four times higher,” the report says.
Strengthening claims for compensation
Advances in science have made it possible to trace climate impacts back to the emissions that caused them.
That means scientists can now link a single company or major emitter to warming – and perhaps even to specific losses or damages.
Moving forward, this extra evidence could strengthen climate litigation and demands for compensation.
‘Climate clubs’ can help industries clean up their act
‘Climate clubs’ made up of countries working together on climate and trade policies can create a collective force to cut down on carbon emissions.
These so-called clubs can rally behind carbon border taxes that prevent companies from off-shoring to places with weaker climate policies, for example – a problem known as ‘carbon leakage’.
But there’s a caveat. While climate clubs can accelerate industrial decarbonisation, they can also have a punitive effect on developing countries that lack the tools, money or technology to cut emissions.
That’s why the authors suggest that wealthier nations may need to combine tougher rules with technical or financial support for other economies.
Climate obstruction is getting harder to spot
Progress is being derailed by more than just denialism.
The report says that carbon-heavy industries are holding back effective policy not just by denying climate change exists anymore. Lobbying efforts now also include a bevy of subtler tactics, from greenwashing to the digital spread of disinformation.
To combat this more deceptive form of climate obfuscation, the report calls for greater transparency in lobbying and political donations, stronger rules against making misleading environmental claims and coordinated action against disinformation.
Conflict creates unequal energy transitions
Wars, trade disputes and fierce competition over energy sources are complicating the global push to decarbonise.
Energy security concerns, like those caused by the war on Iran and the war in Ukraine, have not been met with one universal response. While many wealthy countries have invested in renewables as a buffer against shocks in the oil and gas markets, others have doubled down on fossil fuel production or sought new sources overseas.
The report explains that global instability could make the energy transition more unequal than it already is.
Some blocs of nations could wall off neutral or politically unstable nations, ultimately slowing the global efforts to transition away from fossil fuels. And since more often than not, the most vulnerable suffer from price spikes, the authors add that there is valid reason to be concerned about climate justice in the future.

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:12:00 UTC
13:12:00 KST

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
PARIS – Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 in November but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Nino pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to new highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary “electrification” pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
“In many ways, the defining contexts for this year’s climate summit will be heat and Hormuz,” said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting Nov 9, said the extreme events in 2026 “show climate change is not a future challenge”. He said: “It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising.”
A “pre-COP” meeting began on Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders’ retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Stalemate
Unlike recent COPs – where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels – the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items. There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
“Much of the Antalya summit will be a ‘roll up the sleeves’ effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year,” Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels – the leading cause of climate change. Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At the summit in 2025, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
“Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment,” Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5 deg C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere. Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phase-out conference without UN involvement in 2026. France, the Netherlands and Germany have published “road maps” with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations. “No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward,” he said.
Pressure
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace. “Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail,” said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an “action agenda” alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% today to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put “a huge amount of pressure” on Western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it,” Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. AFP

Trump appears to say Iran should be allowed to ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Diyar Guldogan
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
US President Donald Trump appeared to suggest Monday that Iran should be allowed to “take out” California’s two largest cities while discussing war-related price increases.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, he argued that Americans should accept higher prices as a cost of maintaining national and global security.
“And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial,” he said.
“It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."
Trump then referred to the possibility of an Iranian attack on an American city.
“They can take out a city,” he said. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”
He said the war was “essentially almost over with” while acknowledging that it could continue for a longer period.
The president also discussed Iran's ability to withstand economic pressure, saying Iranian leaders have described themselves as having a “big threshold for pain.”
“They need it, let me tell you,” he said.
Trump predicted that the conflict would eventually end “one way or the other” before returning to the economic consequences Americans are facing.
"But it's going to end very soon, and it'll end one way or the other," he said, adding prices are going to come down "very sharply."
California Governor Gavin Newsom criticized Trump's remarks.
"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous," Newsom said on the US social media platform X.

Why Russia Wants Western Embassies Out of Kyiv – and Why They’re Staying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:10:35 UTC
13:10:35 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed months of Russian warnings for foreign diplomats to leave Kyiv, making clear that Moscow will not decide whether Washington maintains its presence in the Ukrainian capital.
“Look, we have an embassy presence there, and we’ll make the determination about whether it’s safe for them to be there or not,” Rubio told reporters Sunday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They’ve been warning diplomats to leave for months, and I don’t think it’s a surprise to anyone that Kyiv is under attack. I think that’s well understood.”
Rubio said the State Department assesses the security of every US diplomatic mission daily and would change its posture if Washington believed conditions required it.
“We haven’t done that up to this point there,” he said.
The remarks were the latest Western rejection of a sustained Russian effort to warn – and increasingly pressure – foreign governments to pull their diplomatic missions out of Kyiv.
For Moscow, however, the issue goes well beyond embassy security.
An exodus of Western diplomats from the Ukrainian capital would hand the Kremlin a powerful symbolic victory: the image of Ukraine’s allies abandoning Kyiv under Russian military pressure, four years after Moscow failed to capture the city.
Europe says it is staying
Rubio’s comments followed a coordinated response from European governments rejecting Russia’s latest warnings.
Russian Drones Sink Turkish-Owned Grain Ship as Ankara Pushes Black Sea Security Deal
Germany, Italy, Spain and Sweden publicly declared that their embassies would remain in Kyiv, joining France, Poland, Estonia and the European Union in reaffirming their diplomatic presence.
“We are staying in Kyiv,” the embassies said in coordinated messages.
Kyiv Post previously reported that the statements came after Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel that remaining in the Ukrainian capital represented a “mortal danger” as Moscow threatened further large-scale strikes.
The embassies called on Russia to respect the Vienna Convention and international humanitarian law rather than attempt to intimidate diplomatic missions.
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová went further, saying none of the 25 EU member states maintaining embassies in Kyiv was preparing to leave.
“I am not aware of any embassy that is leaving – and certainly not embassies of EU countries,” Mathernová said.
The EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission also remain operational in Kyiv.
The European Commission separately said Russia’s threats would neither reduce EU support for Ukraine nor alter the bloc’s diplomatic presence.
Poland likewise rejected any suggestion it was preparing to withdraw its mission, describing Moscow’s warnings as an effort to intimidate European governments and weaken their backing for Ukraine.
Moscow has been sending the message for months
The current confrontation did not begin with Russia’s October warning.
Kyiv Post reported in May that Rubio had already addressed Russian warnings about the security of diplomatic facilities in Kyiv after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov conveyed a message from Vladimir Putin to the Trump administration.
At the time, Rubio said Russia had not directly ordered the United States to evacuate its embassy, but had issued broader warnings about the danger facing diplomatic facilities in the capital.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Moscow of responding to US peace efforts with threats against Kyiv, calling the warning a “brazen provocation.”
Days later, another controversy erupted when reports suggested the US Embassy had left Kyiv.
Kyiv Post reported that the embassy publicly denied the claim.
“The US Embassy is open. There are no changes to our operations and reports otherwise are false,” the mission said at the time.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry also rejected reports of an American evacuation.
Why an embassy withdrawal would matter to Moscow
Embassies are not merely administrative offices. Their presence in a wartime capital is an unmistakable political signal.
Foreign diplomats meet Ukrainian officials, coordinate military and economic assistance, host visiting delegations and maintain direct communications between Kyiv and allied governments.
Their continued presence also says something more basic: foreign governments continue to recognize Kyiv as a functioning capital whose government remains firmly in control.
That symbolism has carried particular weight since the opening weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Before Russian troops crossed the border in February 2022, the US and a number of other countries temporarily moved diplomats away from Kyiv as Western intelligence warned that Russian forces could rapidly reach the capital.
Russia then attempted to seize Kyiv.
It failed.
As Ukrainian forces pushed Russian troops out of the Kyiv region, Western officials began returning.
On May 18, 2022, the US formally reopened its embassy in Kyiv and raised the American flag over the mission again. Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken explicitly connected the reopening to Ukraine’s successful defense of its capital.
“The Ukrainian people, with our security assistance, have defended their homeland,” he said as the embassy resumed operations.
The return of diplomats became one of the clearest visual markers of Russia’s defeat around Kyiv. A mass departure now would carry the opposite symbolism.
Making Kyiv appear unlivable
Russia’s latest diplomatic warnings coincide with an intensified campaign against the Ukrainian capital. Moscow has struck transport infrastructure, residential areas and other targets while openly promising additional large-scale attacks.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has described Russia’s evolving strategy as an effort to make Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult to live in by systematically attacking the infrastructure required to sustain them.
Four years after failing to seize Kyiv, Moscow is again trying to isolate the capital through missiles, drones and threats.
It has failed again.

Jim Bakker, televangelist whose Christian TV empire collapsed in scandal, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:09:12 UTC
13:09:12 KST

American televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar evangelical television empire before sex and financial scandals brought down his ministry and sent him to prison for fraud, died Monday at 86, his family said.
Bakker became one of the most recognizable faces in American religious broadcasting alongside his then-wife, Tammy Faye Bakker. The couple rose to national fame through “The PTL Club,” a Christian television program launched in the 1970s that grew into a sprawling religious and business enterprise.
Their ministry eventually included a satellite television network and Heritage USA, a vast Christian theme park and resort in South Carolina that became one of the most prominent symbols of the Bakkers’ success. Their increasingly lavish lifestyle, financed as the ministry solicited donations from viewers, also drew mounting scrutiny.
The empire began to unravel in 1987 after revelations emerged about a payment connected to church secretary Jessica Hahn, who accused Bakker of sexual assault. Bakker denied raping her. The scandal forced him to step down from PTL, while investigations into the ministry’s finances exposed much broader allegations of financial misconduct.
In 1989, a federal jury convicted Bakker on 24 counts of fraud and conspiracy stemming from his fundraising operation. Prosecutors accused PTL of selling more than 150,000 “lifetime partnerships” promising lodging at Heritage USA while failing to build enough accommodation to fulfill those commitments.
Bakker was initially sentenced to 45 years in prison and fined $500,000. An appeals court later ordered a new sentencing hearing, and his prison term was reduced to eight years. He ultimately served nearly five years before being paroled in 1994.
Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992 while he was in prison. She later remarried and remained a prominent cultural figure until her death from cancer in 2007. Bakker married Lori Beth Graham in 1998.
Despite the spectacular collapse of his first ministry, Bakker eventually returned to television, launching “The Jim Bakker Show” in 2003 and once again building an audience around evangelical Christianity, prophecy and apocalyptic themes. His later career ensured that he remained a controversial presence in American religious broadcasting decades after the scandal that had appeared to end it.
Announcing his death, Lori Bakker said her husband had “finished his race with faith” after dedicating decades of his life to Christian ministry. His son, Jay Bakker, also confirmed his death.

Yemen hits Saudi airports, Aramco in 3 operations

Yemen's armed forces said they carried out three special operations with numerous ballistic and cruise missiles and drones against targets in Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh's King Khalid airport, the Aramco refinery in Rabigh, and Abha airport.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the first operation targeted King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, disrupting flights there. The second operation targeted the Aramco refinery in Rabigh, causing a fire at the site. The third operation targeted Abha airport, Khamis Mushait base, the Akfa camp in the Asir region, and other sensitive positions in Najran and Jizan.
Saree said the operations were carried out in response to "Saudi aggression" against Yemen, which over the past 24 hours included 60 airstrikes and missile attacks. He said the Saudi attacks targeted Sanaa and the provinces of Jawf, Taiz, Hajjah, Saada and Marib, leading to the martyrdom and injury of civilians, including women and children. He said the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the escalation began has reached 1,576.
Saree warned all global airlines using Saudi airspace about continuing their flights. He said Saudi airspace, with the exception of the holy airspace of Mecca and Medina, would be a scene of their operations. He said Yemeni forces bear no responsibility for the consequences of ignoring this warning.
Saree said Yemeni forces possess capabilities and means that enable them to confront this escalation. He said they are prepared for such a day and the battlefield will determine the outcome.

S. Korea's September foreign reserves fall to 440.56 bln USD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:01:48 CST
13:01:48 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's September foreign exchange reserves fell for the first time in four months, driven by reducing foreign currency deposits by financial institutions and asset entrustment for the U.S. strategic investments, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The total reserves sank 1.72 billion U.S. dollars from a month earlier to 440.56 billion dollars at the end of September, marking the first decrease since May, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The downturn was attributed to a decline in foreign currency deposits by financial institutions and asset entrustment to the Korea-U.S. Strategic Investment Corporation, a temporary state-run agency to manage South Korea's strategic investments in the United States worth 350 billion dollars.
A reduction in the U.S.-dollar-converted value of non-dollar assets also contributed to the sliding reserves. The dollar index, which gauges the U.S. dollar value versus six major peers, went up 1.7 percent last month.
By asset type, securities made up the largest share at 386.03 billion dollars, accounting for 87.6 percent of the total reserves.
Deposits amounted to 29.95 billion dollars, followed by special drawing rights with 15.48 billion dollars, gold holdings with 4.79 billion dollars and the country's IMF reserve position with 4.30 billion dollars. ■

Feature: A growing passion for Chinese language takes root in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
12:01:44 CST
13:01:44 KST

ASTANA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- At a light-rail station, passengers can buy tickets with a tap of the screen, with instructions available in Chinese, Kazakh, Russian and English. Outside, a ride-hailing driver greets passengers in halting Chinese. At restaurants, Chinese-language menus are becoming increasingly common.
Across Central Asia, Chinese is becoming an increasingly familiar part of everyday life, reflecting a growing interest in the language across the region.
In a classroom at the Confucius Institute at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, students spend the evening repeating Chinese phrases and answering questions.
After a day's work, 26-year-old Aiym Naurzbayeva joins more than 100 local learners for evening Chinese classes.
Naurzbayeva works for a local logistics company, where she regularly deals with Chinese business partners. The experience has shown her the opportunities that speaking Chinese can open up. She started learning the language in September.
"I hope to study in China next year and, after completing my studies, return and continue working in Kazakhstan-China cooperation," she said.
The Confucius Institute was jointly established by Lanzhou University and Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. Deng Hong, the institute's Chinese director, said interest in learning Chinese has continued to grow in recent years, with students ranging in age from 7 to 70.
The institute is also a center for Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi (HSK), or Chinese Proficiency Test, serving more than 2,000 test takers each year. The number of applicants has continued to rise.
A similar trend can be seen in Tajikistan. Sun Jing, Chinese director of the Confucius Institute at Tajik National University, said the institute enrolls students twice a year, admitting more than 1,000 students each time. But the number of applicants exceeds 1,500 each time.
"Some parents travel long distances to bring their children to learn Chinese," she said.
Beyond Confucius Institutes, Chinese language learning is becoming increasingly diverse in Central Asia, with private language schools and individual tutoring growing in popularity.
In Astana, a search for "Chinese language courses" on a local lifestyle services platform yielded listings for 136 Chinese-language training institutions. Other major cities in the region also have dozens or even hundreds of similar institutions.
At the "Laoshi" Educational Center in Almaty, classrooms were filled with children, students and working adults studying together.
Tatyana Kaukenova, director of the center, said more local people are choosing to learn Chinese as economic, trade, logistics and technological ties between Kazakhstan and China deepen.
The center now offers classes at different levels. Kaukenova and her colleagues have also developed customized teaching materials incorporating Kazakhstan's local culture and traditions to help students learn and use Chinese more effectively.
Private tutoring has also emerged as a new trend. Roza, who completed her studies at the Confucius Institute at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, now works as a private Chinese tutor and teaches 15 teenagers.
"Chinese culture is fascinating, and the Chinese language has opened a window for us to observe China," she said.
The growing interest in Chinese across Central Asia is no coincidence. Growing economic and trade ties, cultural exchanges and more favorable policies have helped make Chinese more than just a classroom language, opening doors to new opportunities for young people across the region.
Baikazak Sultanbekov, a Kyrgyz student at Jalal-Abad State University, has been learning Chinese for more than two years. Since Aug. 20, Kyrgyz citizens have been eligible for a 240-hour visa-free transit program and a 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan, China's southernmost province.
"I was very happy when I heard the news. It means my dream of seeing the sea in Hainan may soon become a reality," he said.
"All my family fully supports me in learning Chinese," said 17-year-old Muslima, who studies at the Confucius Institute at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies in Uzbekistan.
During a study trip to Xi'an in 2025, she was deeply impressed by the city's historical sites and culture, sparking a strong interest in Chinese culture.
"I really want to see more of China," she said.
Gulnar Shaimergenova, director of the China Studies Center in Astana, Kazakhstan, said China's leading position in high-tech industries such as scientific and technological innovation and the digital economy has increased demand for bilingual talent in fields including artificial intelligence and financial technology, continuously driving demand for Chinese-language learning in the region.
Across Central Asia, Chinese is increasingly becoming a bridge between people, cultures and opportunities. With every new phrase learned and every conversation held in Chinese, ties between the people of the region and China are becoming more tangible. ■

Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:01:01 UTC
13:01:01 KST

Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.
The number of people under 50 diagnosed with prostate cancer in England has quadrupled since 2001, while early onset bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses more than doubled.
Analysis of English, US and Dutch cancer data by World Cancer Research Fund identified “significant increases” in early onset cancers for seven cancer types in England, five types in the US and four in the Netherlands.
Although cancer has been increasing across all age groups globally, the rate rise in early onset cases is greater than other ages.
Experts said the figures reflected the growing global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as growing awareness of cancer and earlier diagnosis.
Cancer among the under 50s is still uncommon, with the median age at diagnosis above 60, but the trend is worrying, the authors noted.
Commenting on the findings, Mark Lawler, professor of digital health and the chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, called the problem “a ticking timebomb that we need to [defuse] as quickly as possible, otherwise the numbers will undoubtedly continue to grow”.
He went on: “The overall trend is also particularly worrying as it comes on the backdrop of lifestyle factors contributing to thousands of deaths.”
In England, of the 12 tumour types studied, incidence rates of prostate cancer among men under 50 jumped from one in every 100,000 people in 2001 to 3.6 in every 100,000 in 2023. Over the same period, rates of bowel cancer among the under 50s leapt from 3.9 in 100,000 people in 2001 to 8.4 in 100,000 in 2023, while early onset uterine and kidney cancers also doubled to 3.9 and 3 per 100,000 people respectively.
The rate of breast cancer among the under 50s increased, albeit less sharply, from 42 to 47.5 per 100,000 in 2023, while there were also increases in the incidence of early onset pancreatic and liver cancers.
In the US, analysis of official data since 2000 found that among patients under 50, incidence rates of kidney cancer more than doubled from 2.5 in 100,000 people in 2000 to 5.3 in 2023, while bowel, uterine and pancreatic cancers all increased by more than 50% and breast cancer by about 20%.
For the Netherlands, the researchers found significant increases in early onset bowel, kidney, liver and cervical cancers.
In contrast, rates of lung cancer among the under 50s declined in all three countries, reflecting continuing declines in smoking in those countries.
Dr Giota Mitrou, the executive director of research and policy at the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), called the trajectory “concerning”, and added: “Behind every figure is a person facing cancer earlier than they, their family and often their doctor would expect. While cancer is still much more common in older adults, these changing patterns among younger generations need to be treated as a serious research and cancer prevention priority.”
WCRF said risk factors such as growing obesity levels, poor diet, insufficient exercise, alcohol consumption, smoking and environmental exposures (such as pollutants, chemicals, plastics, water and air pollution) could be contributing to the trend. About 40% of cancers are linked to these kinds of modifiable risks. However, greater awareness of cancer symptoms also means that people are more likely to be diagnosed earlier.
“While we don’t completely understand why more cancers are occurring in people under 50 years of age, it is likely that risk factors related to cancer – for example, overweight and obesity, diet, alcohol, consumption and smoking – play a role,” said Dr Vanessa Gordon-Dseagu, research translation manager at WCRF.
“At the same time, the public are increasingly aware of the risk factors relating to cancer and the signs and symptoms of the disease to look out for, so are more likely to seek out healthcare when they experience them.”
While more cancers are being diagnosed at an earlier stage, “increased diagnosis does not explain the whole story and more research is needed to understand early-onset cancers” she added.
King’s College London has announced a new trial of 250,000 people, funded by Cancer Research UK, to investigate the increase in bowel cancer cases among younger adults.
The study will seek a clearer understanding of the balance between worsening risk factors and better detection in the rise.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “These findings underline why early diagnosis is at the heart of our national cancer plan. To help catch cancer sooner, we’re investing in new technologies to speed up diagnosis, expanding genetic testing, and supporting research to better understand the causes of cancer and who may be most at risk.
We’re also prioritising research into less-survivable and rarer cancers, and our ambition is for three-quarters of people diagnosed by 2035 to be cancer-free or living well with cancer, saving 320,000 lives.
“Our newly announced national cancer board has a specific representative for children and young people, as we’re aware of the devastating impact of getting cancer at an earlier stage of life.”
