OpenAI to reiterate apology to Australia over Medicare hack as inquiry told artists risk becoming ‘roadkill’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:53:48 UTC
09:53:48 KST

OpenAI has used an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry on AI to apologise again to Australia about the hack on Medicare last month, as media and entertainment organisations argued weakening copyright law for AI model training would leave artists as “roadkill”.
Meanwhile Anthropic told the inquiry it was not seeking to dictate copyright law on model training, but the current rules made it “impossible” to train AI in Australia.
Tuesday morning’s hearing of the joint parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence largely focused on copyright licensing for AI training in Australia, amid concerns companies such as Anthropic were pushing the Australian government to adopt an opt-out model, requiring rights holders to specifically opt out of allowing AI to train on their content.
Anthropic’s special envoy, the former US ambassador to Australia Jeffrey Bleich, told the committee that Anthropic had “never tried to dictate to Australia” on copyright.
“We’ve just shared information about how the training works, and then discussed what its implications would be with respect to our capacity to operate here,” he said.
Anthropic suggests current Australian laws mean AI companies need to obtain a licence for the use of every piece of content on the internet as training material. Bleich said this was “technically impossible”.
Anthropic was keen to explore what the Australian government wants to do to incentivise training in Australia, and Bleich said Australia could shape frontier models if they were trained here, otherwise it would ultimately rely on models trained elsewhere.
OpenAI apologised for its AI agents attacking a number of Australian government websites in June. The multibillion-dollar company notified the government via an email to a public-facing address three months after the breach.
“I want to begin with an apology. During internal training and evaluation, our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to. That should not have happened. We also should have handled our response better,” OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, told the committee on Tuesday afternoon.
“We are sorry, and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people. We are committed to doing that work.”
Following the revelation of a separate hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service last week, Kwon told the committee OpenAI was reviewing logs of AI agent training dating back to November 2025, which identified the latest hack activity taking place in June.
He promised that should more incidents be identified, government agencies would be notified “very, very quickly”.
OpenAI representatives, while apologetic, downplayed the agent activity on Australian government websites as not “not super sophisticated” compared with the Hugging Face attack. The independent senator David Pocock questioned why the company didn’t contact ministers, instead sending an email “to some arbitrary department email” after the Medicare incident.
“I think that on retrospect, we should have done what you were suggesting … I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation, and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties – but it’s not good enough,” Kwan said.
Anthropic’s head of safeguards, Dave Orr, told the committee the company had reviewed hundreds of millions of transcripts of its models and had not found any cases in which it interacted with Australian government systems in an unauthorised way.
He could not say whether Anthropic’s customers may have used the models on Australian government systems, given the company’s “zero data retention” policy.
‘Artists will become roadkill’
Annabelle Herd, the chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), told the committee that “Australia’s artists will be the roadkill in the rush” to make deals with AI companies, and said Aria was not against AI frontier model training being done in Australia but it should be done on “our terms”.
“There is nothing less sovereign than rewriting our laws to suit foreign company commercial interests, done the way that big AI is proposing,” she said. “It will devastate the music industry and make Australia a pariah for rights holders globally.”
She said Anthropic and OpenAI were “asking the government for a free ride” and the creative sector was calling on the government not to cave in to their demands.
The ABC told the committee Australia’s existing copyright regime was “completely adequate”.
The ABC’s head of content and legal operations, Kate Gilchrist, said an opt-out system as proposed by AI companies would place burdens and costs on rights holders, as it would require ongoing surveillance to see whether copyright material was being used.
She said for the ABC, it would mean ensuring every site on which the ABC publishes material had opted out.
“We cannot scour the internet and ensure we are opting out on all of those different sites of publication. It simply does not work,” she said.
Gilchrist said she suspected ABC content had been scraped already.
The union representing the entertainment and news sector, the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), has called for an equitable remuneration scheme that would put fees on companies across the AI technology stack.
“Revenue would support two things: direct payments to creative and media workers whose work contributes to AI systems. And secondly, a cultural fund supporting Australian live entertainment, screen music, public interest journalism and cultural activity,” the MEAA’s acting chief executive, Adam Portelli, said.
The committee is holding hearings from Tuesday to Friday this week.

Breaking Down the Emotional Ending of Four Hands, Two Sonatas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:43:46 UTC
09:43:46 KST

When Four Hands, Two Sonatas launched in late August, the Korean drama presented as a traditional coming-of-age melodrama about two, piano-obsessed teens at a hyper-competitive arts high school. In his first role following his military service, Song Kang (Sweet Home) stars as Kang Pi-o, the perfectionist grandson of a renowned maestro whose mother pushes him to be the very best. And in his last role filmed before he enlisted, Lee Jun-young (When Life Gives You Tangerines) plays Choi Jeong-yo, a scholarship student and musical prodigy who worries more about keeping his alcoholic stepdad safe from loan sharks than finishing first in prestigious contests. When the two are paired together to play “four hands,” or a piano duet on the same instrument, their different backgrounds and priorities put them at odds. However, their love for music wins out, and the two develop a life-changing friendship.
As the 12-episode series progresses, and the story jumps nine years into Pi-o and Jeong-yo’s adulthood, Four Hands, Two Sonatas morphs from a coming-of-age story into a psychological thriller in which trauma, misunderstandings, and obsession combine to place the future of these talented musicians in question. Through it all, Pi-o and Jeong-yo’s intense, often tender relationship serves as a throughline, bringing many viewers to question if the Netflix series qualifies as a boys’ love (aka BL) drama. Let’s discuss how Four Hands, Two Sonatas’ ending answers some of these questions.
Who ordered Jeong-yo’s abduction?
The first chapter of Four Hands, Two Sonatas’ story comes to a head in the Czech Republic, where teenaged Pi-o and Jeong-yo are among a handful of teenage musicians from around the world who are competing in the Prague Harmonie International Competition. After years of cruel dismissal from his grandfather, Kang Seung-woon (Jung Jin-young), and relentless pressure from his mother, Kang Ji-hye (Yoon Se-ah), Pi-o doubts his talent. He has decided that if he does not win this competition, he will quit piano forever. He begs Jeong-yo to compete because he wants to prove, once and for all, that he can beat his best friend. Jeong-yo, who wants Pi-o to be happy, agrees to enter the competition.
Meanwhile, Ji-hye does not think that her son can beat Jeong-yo. Not only does Jeong-yo have an emotional connection to his music performance that Pi-o struggles to find himself, but Pi-o has injured his pinky in the leadup to the final performance, thanks to his obsessive practicing. Faced with the possibility of her son giving up piano forever, Ji-hye decides to hire two men to abduct Jeong-yo, ensuring that he cannot compete in the final performance. However, the abduction goes wrong, and Jeong-yo is shot in his attempt to escape. Not only does he not show up for the final performance, but he disappears completely and is presumed dead. Pi-o wins the competition, but is devastated at the disappearance of his friend.
The nine-year time jump
Nine years later, Pi-o is an internationally renowned solo pianist, having used his victory at the Prague Harmonie International Competition to launch a career. But he has never been able to move on from the disappearance of his friend. He has hired a private investigator to continue searching for Jeong-yo and spends his free time following up on leads. Eventually, he has a meeting with one of the men who abducted Jeong-yo. The man claims Jeong-yo is dead, but he won’t give Pi-o any additional information unless he pays him $1.3 million. Pi-o goes to get the money, but the man is killed by a fellow gang member before he can tell Pi-o the whole story.
Pi-o grieves the death of his friend, unable to get out of bed for days. He stops making music and decides to spend time in Europe. While attending a conducting competition in Brno on a whim, he sees Jeong-yo on stage. He is alive, going by the name Luca Domenico. However, when Pi-o approaches Jeong-yo, the man claims to not know him, revealing that he has amnesia and cannot remember anything prior to an accident nine years earlier.
Jeong-yo’s skills as a musician make international waves. He is recognized as the teen prodigy who went missing a decade prior, and his return as an up-and-coming conductor is heralded. Hankook Symphony Orchestra, which is run by Pi-o’s grandfather, invites Jeong-yo to be a guest conductor.
Jeong-yo’s quest for revenge
At first, Jeong-yo’s return to Seoul and Pi-o's life goes relatively well. Jeong-yo, who can no longer play the piano due to nerve damage from when he was shot, wants to work with Pi-o. He brings his friend on as a soloist for his debut with the orchestra, and the performance is a success. Then, he asks Pi-o to be the soloist for the debut of his first original work, a concerto titled “Nemesis.” Pi-o recognizes it as a piece of music, originally titled “Nocturne,” Jeong-yo first started working on as a teenager. This calls into question Jeong-yo’s claims that he has amnesia.
Meanwhile, Pi-o discovers through his private investigator that his mother was the one behind Jeong-yo’s abduction. He desperately wants to confess to his friend. However, Ji-hye says she would rather die than confess, threatening to kill herself if Pi-o tells anyone. Pi-o is forced to keep his mother’s secret, and agrees to be the soloist in Jeong-yo’s debut of “Nemesis.” During the preparation process, Jeong-yo becomes increasingly cruel and emotionally abusive toward Pi-o.
When Pi-o confronts Jeong-yo about lying about his amnesia, Jeong-yo comes clean. He makes it clear to Pi-o that he has returned to get revenge. He believes Pi-o was the one who arranged his abduction, and blames him for his inability to play the piano. Pi-o, who feels immense guilt about what happened to Jeong-yo and wants to protect his mother, goes along with the lie that he was the one responsible for Jeong-yo’s life-changing injuries.
In the following weeks, Pi-o barely fights back as Jeong-yo pushes him to practice “Nemesis” past the point of mental and physical exhaustion. During a pre-performance recording of the piece, Jeong-yo forces dozens of takes and eventually canceling the recording, claiming that it is Pi-o’s limitations as a pianist that have caused the delay. Pi-o, who signed a terrible contract at Jeong-yo’s urging, is forced to pay the penalties for the delayed recording. Jeong-yo drops him from the “Nemesis” performance, and Pi-o’s agency plans to cancel his contract.
The “Nemesis” performance
The traumatized Jeong-yo finds neither peace nor triumph in revenge. He still cares about Pi-o, and he cares about “Nemesis.” The concerto, from its beginnings as “Nocturne” to its current incarnation, was inspired by his relationship with Pi-o, and no one else can do it justice. Pi-o, who still feels responsible for Jeong-yo’s suffering, wants to do the solo. The music, and his feelings for Jeong-yo, have allowed him to unlock a new, more emotionally connected level of his performance. He convinces Jeong-yo to let him do the piece by playing it once again for his friend-turned-nemesis. The performance is a resounding success, and Jeong-yo tells Pi-o: “The piece was meant entirely for you.”
Rather than revel in the success, Pi-o chooses the moment to make a public confession. To the gathered audience, he claims that he was the one responsible for Jeong-yo’s abduction years prior. The police arrest him for the crime. Jeong-yo, who is confused by the many emotions he feels for Pi-o, is furious that the man’s judgement and punishment has been taken out of his control. For Pi-o, this is the only way he can protect both his mother and Jeong-yo.
Ji-hye’s punishment
Ji-hye is devastated at the arrest of her son, and furiously tries to confess to the crime herself. Initially, neither the police nor Jeong-yo believe her. Her confessions look like maternal desperation rather than the truth. However, when Pi-o’s private investigator gives Jeong-yo a recording of their conversation with one of Jeong-yo’s abductors, the truth wins out. On the audio recording, Jeong-yo hears how desperate Pi-o was to find him, and how devastated he was at the news of his death. He realizes that he has been punishing Pi-o for a crime that he did not commit.
Ji-hye is sent to jail for her crime, and is therefore unable to be with her father when he dies from a heart condition shortly after. Seung-woon requests Pi-o and Jeong-yo visit his hospital bedside. He apologizes to both of them for the pain he caused. It was his stubborn disapproval of Pi-o that led Ji-hye to take such drastic actions. Seung-woon had never forgiven Ji-hye for ruining her chances at becoming a professional ballerina by getting pregnant with Pi-o. Seung-woon, who loved music above all else, wants to listen to Pi-o’s performance of “Moonlight Sonata” as he dies. Pi-o plays the recording for him, finally winning his grandfather’s approval.
A final, four hands performance
Pi-o once told Jeong-yo that he was only happy when he was playing music, so when Jeong-yo learns that Pi-o has sold his piano and intends never to play again, he decides he will not let that stand. He buys Jeong-yo’s piano and brings it to the musical instrument market where Jeong-yo learned to play as a boy. He tells Pi-o that he has regained control of his hand and can play again. The two play four hands together again, and are happy. Later that night, by the Han River, Pi-o asks Jeong-yo to make music with him; it’s all he’s ever really wanted to do. Jeong-yo gently refuses.
The next day, Jeong-yo disappears from Seoul. He has resigned from the Hankook Symphony Orchestra and left Pi-o a note. In it, he tells his Pi-o that he has been “his light and hope,” and that, even when he was seeking revenge, he dreamt about them playing duets together. Jeong-yo says he has left to use his music to comfort others.
Pi-o grieves the loss of his friend again, but uses Jeong-yo’s stated mission to drive his own choices. Rather than performing the most technically complex compositions on a classical music stage, he starts performing simpler songs in small, rural towns and in hospitals; he hopes his surprise pop-up concerts bring comfort to those who hear his music.
Does Four Hands, Two Sonatas have a happy ending?
Yes, against all odds, Four Hands, Two Sonatas has a happy ending—though it is not without its complexities. Three years pass before Pi-o and Jeong-yo see one another again. One day, after Pi-o performs at a hospital, a doctor approaches him to ask how Jeong-yo is doing. The doctor informs Pi-o that he had given Jeong-yo a shot three years prior that temporarily granted him use of his injured hand but at the risk of losing all function forever. Pi-o realizes that Jeong-yo lied to him when he told him that he could play again. Jeong-yo wanted to absolve Pi-o of his misplaced guilt, so he tricked his friend into thinking he could play again. His subsequent disappearance preserved the lie.
For the first time in three years, Pi-o posts a video recording of his performance. Though the video does not show his face, he knows Jeong-yo will recognize his interpretation of “Nemesis.” The viral beacon works. Pi-o receives an unsigned postcard from the Czech Republic offering some friendly critiques. Pi-o immediately packs his bags, and finds the church on the front of the postcard. Jeong-yo is conducting a choir of children inside of the church. He is wearing a religious robe, and has seemingly been dedicating his time to atonement rather than glory or revenge. When Jeong-yo turns around to see Pi-o, the two lock eyes and smile at one another. Four Hands, Two Sonatas ends with Jeong-yo and Pi-o together again, seemingly free of the pressures and misunderstandings that plagued them for so long.
The story’s happy ending comes more than just in the form of a resolution of Jeong-yo and Pi-o’s relationship. The drama also makes a determination about the function of art in our society as something beyond the technical. In the age of AI, Four Hands, Two Sonatas argues that art can and should be made by flawed humans, and that the measure of a musical performance is not determined by how technically perfect it was but also in how it made both the performer and the audience feel.
Is Four Hands, Two Sonatas a BL drama?
As soon as the trailer for Four Hands, Two Sonatas dropped, viewers began wondering if the K-drama might be a queer romance. The initial assumption was that it was not. Though South Korea has begun to produce BL dramas, including 2020’s Where Your Eyes Linger and 2022’s Semantic Error, these series are not mainstream. Four Hands, Two Sonatas is a primetime drama broadcast on tvN, one of Korea’s mainstream pay TV networks, with some of its most high-profile TV actors. In a country where the law does not recognize same-sex marriage nor protect against discrimination based on sexual orientation, there has yet to be a mainstream queer romance. When Love in the Big City, a slice-of-life drama centering a gay protagonist was released in 2024, it was met with homophobic outcries from anti-LGBTQ groups within Korea, accusing the drama of "glorifying and promoting homosexuality.”
However, BL fans who dismissed the possibility of a queer love story may want to give Four Hands, Two Sonatas a chance. Though the drama never explicitly represents Pi-o and Jeong-yo’s relationship as romantic, it also never explicitly undermines the possibility, as is often the case with dramas featuring an intense emotional connection between two men. Pi-o does not end up with longtime friend and occasional girlfriend Jae-in (Jang Gyu-ri). Jae-in is open about her romantic feelings for Pi-o throughout the series, and the two begin to date only when Pi-o believes that Jeong-yo is dead. Pi-o’s feeling for Jae-in are treated as real—he cries when he breaks up with her during Jeong-yo’s period of emotional torture—but he always chooses Jeong-yo as his companion whenever he is an option, including in the finale.
The exact nature of the relationship between the two men is left open for interpretation, and has been publicly commented on by some involved in the production. When asked about the BL interpretation by Korean outlet Star News, Jang said: “When I first read the script, I knew that Jeong-yo and Pi-o were deeply intertwined through music. The work belongs to the viewers, so I respect everything.” Director Park Hyeon-seok’s statements on the subject were similarly open. "It is an immeasurable happiness and a source of gratitude for the entire production team that viewers enjoy the drama from their own diverse perspectives," Park told Korean media. "I am simply grateful that they fill the gaps between the writer's text and the visualized scenes with rich interpretations."
Speaking about his intentions for the script, writer Shin Yi-won said the story began with the question “What if Mozart and Salieri were best friends?” though he also drew inspiration for Pi-o and Jeong-yo from the toxic love between Heathcliff and Catherine in Wuthering Heights. Court composer Antonio Salieri and musical prodigy Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart were contemporaries in 18th century Europe, and their professional rivalry has sometimes been framed as a love-hate relationship in modern media retellings of their lives, including in Peter Shaffer’s 1979 play Amadeus and its 1984 film adaptation. "I am a case of someone who attended an arts high school filled with geniuses, consumed by an inferiority complex while thinking of myself as Salieri,” Shin said. “However, a professor in college told me, 'Art is not done with mere petty talent. To move people with true art, pour your entire life into it.'” Whatever else Four Hands, Two Sonatas may be, the series is deeply devoted to imparting this artistic message.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people at a military base in 2009, the Pentagon said on Oct 5.
Hasan’s execution for the attack at Fort Hood in Texas – which also wounded more than two dozen people – will be the first carried out by the US military since 1961.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by US Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan”, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on social media platform X.
“The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgment day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the Al-Qaeda inspired mass shooting at Fort Hood.
He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial, but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.
Hasan, a US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on Nov 5, 2009, at a medical facility in the sprawling Fort Hood base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones.
Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is partially paralysed.
The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
While mass shootings in the United States are common, they are rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.
A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group”.
Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital, before being shot dead by officers. AFP

FT: Hungary may lift veto on next stage of Ukraine's EU accession talks this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:41:00 UTC

FT: Hungary may lift veto on next stage of Ukraine's EU accession talks this week
The Financial Times stated this, citing two officials, Ukrinform reports.
According to the officials, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has instructed Hungarian diplomats not to block the sending of letters to Ukraine and Moldova concerning the possible opening of the next two negotiating clusters during working meetings this week. The clusters cover issues related to the internal market and competitiveness.
According to the officials, this is a procedural but symbolically important step forward.
At the same time, Hungary's final political support for opening the clusters will depend on whether the Verkhovna Rada adopts a law on October 12 expanding the educational rights of national minorities. The rights of Hungary's minority in Ukraine have long been one of Budapest's key concerns. The draft law was developed taking into account proposals and comments from the Hungarian side.
Adoption of the bill would allow the formal political process on opening the negotiations to begin before the EU leaders' summit in Brussels, which will take place in ten days, the officials said.
An EU official familiar with the negotiations with Budapest said that Ukraine's path toward accession was taking clearer shape, with the process and realism being respected.
If agreement is reached on these two clusters, only two will remain unresolved — those concerning "green" policies, agriculture and cohesion. The European Commission hopes to reach agreements on them with both Ukraine and Moldova by the end of the year.
All 33 negotiating chapters, grouped into six clusters, require the unanimous approval of all 27 EU member states in order to be closed after the European Commission determines that the candidate country's legislation meets EU standards.
Two additional chapters, concerning the institutional integration of a new member into the EU and the resolution of outstanding issues, are considered at the final stage of the accession negotiations.
EU countries agreed to begin negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova on the "Fundamentals" and "External Relations" clusters in June and July, respectively.
As Ukrinform reported, a bill titled "On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine on Ensuring the Educational Rights of Indigenous Peoples of Ukraine and Persons Belonging to National Minorities (Communities) of Ukraine" has been registered in the Verkhovna Rada.
Serhii Babak, chairman of the Verkhovna Rada's Education Committee, said the issue has long been relevant not only to education policy but also to Ukraine's negotiations with the European Union, since protecting the rights of national minorities is part of Ukraine's commitments under Cluster 1, "Fundamentals of the Accession Process," and implementation of the relevant Action Plan is one of the conditions for further progress in Ukraine's EU membership negotiations.

Bestselling British author, former politician jailed for perjury, Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:29:39 UTC
09:29:39 KST

Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday.
Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers like his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less and 1979's Kane & Abel. His final novel, Adam and Eve, is due to be published on Tuesday.
Kate Elton, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor, said in a statement: "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers - and a true friend."
Archer was also a prominent Conservative politician, who briefly served as a lawmaker before becoming a senior party official under then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.
But he was as well-known for his very public downfall.
Archer convicted of perjury after libel lawsuit
In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 in damages. The case returned to the public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London's first elected mayor in 1999. A former friend accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He served two years, during which time he wrote A Prison Diary.
The trial of Archer's libel case, which was heard in front of a jury, became notorious for the judge's summing up of evidence given by Archer's wife Mary.
"Remember Mary Archer in the witness box," the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. "Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?"
And, of Archer, he added: "Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?"
Archer's reputation as one of the most colorful figures in British public life did no harm to his literary career. His books were sold in 119 countries, HarperCollins said. He spent a total of five-and-a-half years on the New York Times bestseller lists.
He was due to speak about his final novel this weekend at the Cheltenham Literature Festival and had recently appeared on radio shows to promote the book.
HarperCollins said he had died suddenly and peacefully, "between writing sessions."

====================================================================================================

China’s AI Governance Push and the Race to Shape Global AI Rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:28:00 UTC
09:28:00 KST

On September 12, China’s National Data Administration (NDA) announced that it would develop standards for embodied artificial intelligence (AI) data. The announcement followed a September 10 meeting chaired by NDA head Liu Liehong, where seven key digital companies called for shared public data infrastructure for smart physical machinery and robotics, along with unified data standards. The participants included the startups ModelBest, Infinigence AI, and X Square Robot.
While much remains to be seen regarding raw AI development and emerging technologies in general, this announcement is an indicator of a broader trend, with China increasingly building a centralized and coordinated framework for governing how AI is developed and deployed. This is critical because establishing usable rules around AI has significant implications, potentially becoming nearly as vital as the ability to develop the underlying AI models themselves. As a result, safety and governance are becoming strategic components of the global competition over AI.
The AI Arms Race
AI governance is a critical front in the broader arena of non-kinetic competition between China and the United States. Instead of direct armed conflict, some have described a new “Silent Cold War,” which focuses on topics like AI, semiconductor chips, and foreign investment. AI is especially important because of its dual-use nature, with its capabilities ranging from advising a fifth-grade child on her homework to providing a 99 percent facial verification match on a suspected human trafficker at a border crossing.
China’s history of increased AI model exportation, which could result in increased information influence, has been detailed as one of the implications originating from the AI arms race between the U.S. and China. This is particularly important for countries in the Global South, due to the influx of Chinese infrastructure designed to support AI, with many of these efforts being made as part of the Belt and Road and Digital Silk Road Initiatives.
If Chinese firms become major providers of AI models and their corresponding cloud services, data centers, and energy grids, then China may also gain influence over technical standards, data practices, content controls, and what defines responsible AI in the first place.
This makes AI governance a regulatory issue that must be tackled at an international level rather than at a regional or domestic level. For developing countries deciding which AI systems to adopt, governance frameworks can be a key driver for these nations, with a country selecting an AI provider simultaneously adopting the same standards for data management, content moderation, privacy, and system oversight.
AI Governance
Consequently, AI governance has become a key frontier topic that must be top-of-mind for policymakers worldwide. AI has and is already being leveraged for nefarious purposes, ranging from human-driven prompts promoting deepfakes and impersonation to AI-generated misinformation.
Most recently, U.S.-based Claude maker Anthropic and ChatGPT’s OpenAI faced significant backlash due to key AI safety concerns, with both AI makers disclosing that their own models went rogue in their own capacities. This was compounded by the resignation of a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher around the same period, with this researcher openly citing these same elements as the reason for his resignation.
Therefore, the core regulatory dilemma has become how to regulate AI while still enabling innovation. The U.S. has often approached this challenge through things like voluntary commitments, state-level laws, and a smattering of sector-specific rules. This approach prioritizes flexibility, but at the cost of fragmentation.
For example, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology released an AI Risk Management Framework in early 2023, with this currently being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan released in early 2025. However, this framework remains entirely voluntary. Fragmentation in America’s governance space has remained significant, with some states like Colorado, New York, and California issuing AI-specific legislation, while the vast majority of other states have not.
China’s Efforts
In stark contrast to America’s fragmented approach, China’s top-down approach has resulted in the creation of a multi-layered regulatory system that covers different parts of the AI lifecycle. This model gives specific regulators concrete levers over AI deployments, even as AI development continues to advance at a blistering pace.
The National Data Administration’s approach is the most recent epitome of this approach. It is focusing on developing standards for the data used to train AI for physical machinery and robotics, while also establishing common standards. This is significant because embodied AI depends heavily on data collected in the physical world. Establishing common approaches to collecting, organizing, and evaluating this data could become an important part of building an AI-enabled domestic robotics ecosystem.
China has pursued similar governance measures in other efforts in AI. On July 15, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), China’s top internet regulator, brought its Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services into effect. This law specifically regulates AI systems that simulate human personality traits, with the CAC introducing prohibited content, rules for minors, and highlighting necessary safety assessments for compliance, among others.
Additionally, on May 8, the CAC, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology jointly released the Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of Intelligent Agents. This marked China’s first comprehensive national policy framework specific to agentic AI, introducing tiered risk governance, priority scenarios, and “off-switches” for exigent circumstances.
The rapid and cohesive pace of this legislation highlights China’s desire to govern AI in a more stringent and systematic manner. Chinese regulators are already connecting policy, technical standards, data infrastructure, and implementation. These efforts could increase the amount of Chinese-built AI systems used on a worldwide scale, particularly as Beijing increasingly positions its systems as usable and trusted due to its leadership in AI governance.
For many, the AI race seems to be determined by who will create the fastest and most advanced AI system. However, China is demonstrating that this race is instead being decided by which country creates an environment in which AI can be trusted, deployed, and adopted at scale.
China’s growing advantage is increasingly visible in its ability to connect regulations, policies, technical standards, and enforcement. As Chinese AI systems and infrastructure become more prevalent internationally, establishing clear governance practices could enable China increased influence over how AI is regulated and deployed on an international level. If America continues to rely on its fragmented and voluntary approach, it risks enabling China to play a larger role in setting the rules that shape the future of the world’s AI economy.

Man sentenced to life for attempted knife attack at Israeli Embassy in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:19:57 UTC
09:19:57 KST

A London court on Monday sentenced Abdullah Albadri, a 34-year-old Kuwaiti, to life in prison with a minimum term of 20 years after he was convicted of attempting to carry out an attack at the Israeli Embassy in the city. He was arrested on April 28, 2025, after a diplomatic security team caught him and pulled him down from the embassy fence. He was carrying two 10-centimeter (4-inch) knives.
The investigation and trial revealed that Albadri, who had arrived in Britain in a small boat 16 days earlier after first entering the country illegally four years before, was driven to carry out the attack by the deaths of Palestinians in Gaza. On the day of the incident, he arrived at the site, saluted police officers and then began climbing the perimeter fence. During questioning, he asked officers why they were stopping him from "committing a crime" and said he wanted to "do something to stop the war."
Prosecutor Catherine Pattison argued that Albadri had planned an act in which he expected to sacrifice his life, noting that people emerging from the embassy at the time would have been unable to defend themselves. Defense attorney Chris Henley, however, argued that his plan could not have succeeded and that he had acted in a theatrical and extreme manner intended to attract attention after struggling to arrange housing. Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, praised the officers' response, which prevented a breach of the security perimeter, and said the severity of the sentence reflected the danger he posed and his lack of remorse.
Albadri's trial began in April, nearly a year after the incident. During the proceedings, the jury was told that he had entered Britain not once but twice aboard boats that sailed from the French coast, the main route used by migrants entering Britain illegally in recent years and one that the Labour government has faced mounting criticism for failing to shut down.
Albadri entered Britain by boat — twice
The investigation found that Albadri first arrived in Britain by boat from France on Aug. 5, 2021. In November 2023, however, he left Britain after withdrawing his application for a residence permit for reasons that remain unclear. On April 12, 2025, he returned to Britain, again aboard a small boat from France, and applied for asylum. He claimed he had been forced to leave Kuwait because he feared for his safety and that of his family, saying he was a human rights activist who had been arrested there. Like many other asylum-seekers, he was temporarily housed at the Crowne Plaza hotel in Hampshire.
In the days immediately after returning to Britain, Albadri was in contact with several organizations that assist asylum-seekers and met with members of London’s Kuwaiti community. But on April 24, his asylum application was rejected, after which he apparently began taking concrete steps toward carrying out the attack. An examination of his phone showed that on the same day he searched for the location of the Israeli Embassy and for information on Islamic law regarding suicide.
The attempted attack took place four days later, on April 28. At 3:30 p.m., he sent his mother a photograph of a farewell letter he had written. A knife with a red-and-white handle could be seen next to it in the photograph. The letter ended with the words: "I will not reverse my decision to go forth for the sake of Allah, to go forth for Him and confront the enemies in support of the religion of Almighty Allah."
Pattison, the prosecutor in the case, said the letter, which was found on his body after his arrest, was a farewell note written in preparation for becoming a martyr.

New York declares measles emergency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:19:43 UTC
09:19:43 KST

New York declares measles emergency
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has declared a statewide disaster emergency over a rapidly growing measles outbreak, expanding authorities to vaccinate and test residents as cases surge across the northeastern US.
The emergency, announced on Monday, is the first declaration of the kind by a US state since measles cases began rising sharply nationwide in 2025. New York has recorded 108 confirmed cases this year through October 3, with the majority reported in rural communities among populations with low immunization rates.
“After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease.”
The executive order is scheduled to remain in force through November 4, the day after the midterm election, and expands the number of healthcare workers permitted to administer measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines and conduct testing. Pharmacists will be allowed to vaccinate children as young as two, while registered nurses will be able to order tests for suspected cases.
The declaration comes as neighboring Pennsylvania battles the first US measles outbreak in 35 years to surpass 1,000 cases, with nearly 200 hospitalizations and five measles-associated deaths.
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic, previously questioned Pennsylvania’s reporting of its first measles-associated deaths and suggested they may have been “fabricated.” State health officials rejected the criticism.
Nationwide, the US is battling its worst measles resurgence since 1991. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded 3,887 confirmed cases as of October 1, compared with 2,289 during all of 2025.
Measles was officially declared eliminated in the country in 2000, meaning there was no continuous domestic transmission for at least 12 months, although imported cases and localized outbreaks continued to occur.
Measles is among the world’s most contagious diseases and spreads through airborne respiratory particles. The virus can remain infectious in a room for up to two hours after an infected person leaves.
A vaccination rate of around 95% is required to prevent sustained measles outbreaks, but vaccination rates have declined in parts of the US and elsewhere, with health experts attributing the trend to misinformation spread during the Covid-19 pandemic and protests against vaccine mandates.

Moroccan journalists recount years of surveillance amid new Amnesty claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:13:16 UTC
09:13:16 KST

Moroccan journalists recount years of surveillance amid new Amnesty claim
Amnesty cites a whistleblower’s account of how Morocco allegedly uses surveillance to silence journalists.
Rabat, Morocco – “I was surveilled not because of a specific article. I was investigating land dispossession in Morocco. I then learned I was a Pegasus target,” Omar Radi, a journalist and human rights defender, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mobile surveillance tool developed by Israeli company NSO Group.
The findings emerged in June 2020, when Amnesty International Security Lab examined his phone. Radi, now based in Germany, said he had spent two years, from 2018 to 2020, noticing signs including his phone’s battery draining quickly, its temperature rising and the network slowing down.
The physical surveillance, he said, was barely discreet.
“They came every day to get a daily report from the parking attendants in my street, the shops I used to go to, and my friends,” he said. “I would sometimes turn around and walk towards the people following me to take photographs, but they ran quickly and hid their faces.”
His case is among four detailed in a new Amnesty International report, We Start With the Verdict: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, produced with 14 media organisations and coordinated by the international network of journalists Forbidden Stories.
The other three are Fouad Abdelmoumni, a veteran activist; Abdessadak El Bouchattaoui, a human rights lawyer; and Hicham Mansouri, a journalist in exile who had been imprisoned in 2015 on charges of adultery and sexual exploitation, which Amnesty describes as trumped-up.
The report draws on interviews with a whistleblower using the pseudonym Safir, a former employee of Morocco’s General Directorate for Territorial Surveillance (DGST). Amnesty said it corroborated key parts of Safir’s testimony with independent sources, technical evidence and interviews with 10 people identified as surveillance targets, including Radi.
“The Amnesty report connected many dots as to what I was living and feeling while I was under tight surveillance,” Radi said.
“It explains the extraordinary aspect of my police interrogations and my trial, where many of my rights weren’t respected, because even the judicial police and the judges were under monitoring,” he added.
Amnesty identifies the DGST as the agency behind the deployment of Pegasus spyware in Morocco and documents what it describes as abuses of the spyware against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021.
Morocco denies surveillance
Morocco has previously rejected Amnesty’s allegations that its authorities used Pegasus to target journalists, activists and other critics.
In statements issued in 2020 and 2022, Moroccan authorities challenged Amnesty to provide material evidence supporting its claims.
Amnesty said it wrote to Moroccan authorities four weeks before publishing its latest report and invited them to respond, but received no response.
Al Jazeera also sought comment from Moroccan officials but had not received a response at the time of publication.
Moroccan media have also challenged the latest report. Le360 cited arguments that the presence of a phone number in Pegasus targeting records does not, by itself, prove that a device was infected or establish who ordered an alleged attack.
The outlet also argued that Amnesty had not provided the conclusive technical and material evidence Moroccan authorities had demanded.
The report says Morocco’s Pegasus operations were fully active by October 2017, pointing to the case of human rights lawyer El Bouchattaoui, whose number was entered into the system in September 2017 and selected for targeting weeks before he received an infection link by text message.
Amnesty said its analysis of Pegasus records matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers to individuals identified as potential targets between September and December 2017. Of those, 65 were identifiable as civil society members, including 34 human rights defenders, 22 journalists and media workers, five lawyers and four academics.
According to Amnesty, Safir described a surveillance apparatus that combined digital and physical methods. Targeted individuals were secretly filmed and recorded in detention, offices, cars, cafes and even bedrooms, he said.
Phone shops, he added, were coopted to sell targets devices infected with spyware. Neighbours of human rights defenders, he said, were recruited as informants to file daily reports on their movements.
Safir also described the use of remote control systems (RCS) at internet cafes. Field agents would identify which cafe a target was visiting, he said, giving the DGST access to activity on machines it had already infected and allowing an operator to track calls, read messages, access photographs and record audio.
The report says similar tactics were used against activist Abdelmoumni, who was secretly filmed at home with his fiancee in 2021. Abdelmoumni said he believed the footage was captured through a hidden camera in an air-conditioning unit, based on the recording’s angle.
Safir described the episode as a “textbook case” of a DGST surveillance and cleanup operation designed to leave no trace.
Journalists describe pressure and intimidation
Taoufik Bouachrine, one of Morocco’s best-known journalists and host of the Talk on Politics podcast, was not named in Amnesty’s report but described a similar pattern.
“In Morocco, as in all Arab countries, inventive methods are used to silence journalists and deter them from investigative journalism, particularly when it concerns the unlawful exercise of power, financial corruption, and the intertwining of political authority and money,” he told Al Jazeera.
The first method, he said, is fabricating criminal cases against journalists, “often involving allegations of sexual misconduct in a conservative society that amount to a journalist’s moral execution”.
The second, he said, is a smear campaign run through armies of online trolls and operatives who target journalists and their families.
Bouachrine, 57, was arrested in 2018 on charges of rape and human trafficking and sentenced to 15 years in prison. He has denied the charges, saying his prosecution was tied to his journalism.
The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Bouachrine’s detention arbitrary and said he had been subjected to judicial harassment. The European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for his release, along with other journalists tried on similar charges.
He served more than six years before being released under a royal pardon. By then, Akhbar Al-Youm, the newspaper he founded, had already closed. Bouachrine said authorities had cut off its advertising revenue.
“This is another method of destroying investigative journalism,” he added, “turning off the advertising tap and leaving a newspaper to die slowly.”

US nuke test detection experiment bid to assert its hegemony: Ex-nuclear chief

MUMBAI: Former chief of Atomic Energy Commission of India, Anil Kakodkar, who played a key role in the Pokhran nuclear weapons tests, said the main aim of the US conducting what is called a non-proliferation experiment last week was to assert its global nuclear hegemony and prevent other nations from conducting atomic tests.On Sept 30, the US conducted an experiment which will enable it to detect whether countries are carrying out low-yield nuclear explosions.Kakodkar told TOI, “The US is attempting to get more sensitivity in terms of nuclear tests detection. Police clash with Kosovo protesters over bid to curb Hague war crimes court

2026-10-06

Police clash with Kosovo protesters over bid to curb Hague war crimes court
The political dispute over the court has become a factor in negotiations to hold a new presidential election.
Police have clashed with protesters outside Kosovo’s Parliament over plans to limit the powers of a Hague-based war crimes court.
The violence broke out on Monday evening after Parliament ended its session without passing the proposed changes, which concerned the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a court dedicated to crimes committed during the Kosovo War from 1998 to 2000.
Founded in 2015, the court is an independent part of Kosovo’s judicial system, based in The Hague and staffed internationally.
Critics, however, have accused the court’s verdicts of being overly punitive. The amendments before Parliament would limit sentences to 15 years, allow sentences to be served in Kosovo and permit appeals to the self-declared republic’s Supreme Court.
The changes passed a first reading earlier on Monday, but Parliament adjourned before a second vote could be held.
Several hundred protesters had gathered outside the Parliament building in Pristina, including supporters and veterans of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), the ethnic Albanian rebel force that fought Serbian troops in the war.
Some tried to block lawmakers from leaving after the session ended. Police used tear gas and water cannons in an attempt to disperse the protesters, some of whom threw flares and firecrackers.
Naser Syla, the emergency director at a hospital in Pristina, told The Associated Press news agency that 12 people were injured, including 11 civilians.
The legislation follows the September 16 convictions of former President Hashim Thaci and three other former KLA commanders for war crimes.
Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison. His co-defendants received prison terms ranging from 13 to 25 years. They have all denied the charges.
The rulings prompted weeks of protests and were unanimously condemned by Kosovo’s Parliament in late September.
The question of reforming the court has also become tied to the political battle over Kosovo’s presidency.
Kosovo’s Constitutional Court has ruled that the self-declared republic has until October 6 to elect a president. If lawmakers fail to do so, Parliament will be dissolved, and Kosovo will face another early election.
The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), the largest opposition party and sponsor of the bill, has hinged its support for electing a president to the successful passage of the changes.
Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s governing Vetevendosje party, or the Self-Determination Movement, wants the presidential vote to take place first.
Kurti backed allowing the bill to proceed but told Parliament on Monday that the changes had been rushed.
He has also said the appeals process should be used to challenge the controversial September convictions.
Kosovo created the Specialist Chambers under pressure from Western allies to prosecute alleged crimes by KLA members.
It was based outside Kosovo partly due to concerns about political pressure and threats to witnesses.
The court remains deeply contentious in Kosovo, where many people regard the KLA as the force that fought Serbian repression and led the self-declared republic towards declaring independence.
The 1998-99 war killed about 13,000 people, most of them ethnic Albanians, and forced about one million Kosovo Albanians from their homes.
The conflict ended after a 78-day NATO bombing campaign against Serbian forces. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but Belgrade does not recognise its sovereignty.

Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence uncovered a sanctions evasion scheme by Russian agricultural tycoons in the EU
Kyiv • UNN
According to intelligence, the Dolgov brothers may be using the Lithuanian company UAB Dognus to circumvent sanctions. Their agricultural holding company earns money in the EU and finances the Russian Federation’s war.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine (HUR) has uncovered another sanctions-evasion scheme used by Russian agricultural magnates from the Kaliningrad region. UNN reports this with reference to the HUR statement.
Details
It is noted that Aleksandr and Dmitry Dolgov use their profits to finance Russia’s genocidal aggression against Ukraine.
The Dolgov brothers are the founders and owners of DolgovGroup, the largest agricultural enterprise in the Kaliningrad exclave. The company cultivates more than 50% of the region’s land and is engaged in crop production, animal husbandry, processing, and the sale of agricultural products. Every year, the Dolgovs’ business produces more than 300,000 tonnes of grain. The holding has grain elevator capacity of 240,000 tonnes and its own railway fleet for transporting grain crops and vegetable oils
It is indicated that, in addition to wheat, the brothers export corn, rapeseed, barley, rye, and rapeseed oil.
At the same time, DolgovGroup is not under sanctions, earns money on the European market, and helps sponsor Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine — both through taxes paid to the budget of the aggressor state, Russia, and through systematic financial and material support for units of the Russian occupation forces
Background
In 2012, the Dolgov brothers became co-founders of the Lithuanian company UAB Dognus. Despite the formal change of owners in 2016–2018, there is a high probability that the Dolgovs in fact retained control over this entity. Dognus carried out extensive trading operations with enterprises linked to DolgovGroup, including the purchase of Russian grain.
After the start of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, UAB Dognus sharply increased its operations. Thus, in 2022, the company’s assets grew from €7.48 million to €42.96 million, cash holdings rose from €86.7 thousand to €23.21 million, and revenue reached €55.1 million.
Dognus’s cross-border activity also increased significantly: of the 708 import-export operations carried out in 2018–2023, 674 took place between January 1, 2022, and January 17, 2023.
According to Ukraine’s military intelligence, the Dolgov brothers may be using UAB Dognus as a shadow European company to circumvent sanctions restrictions and accumulate financial resources in an EU jurisdiction.

Trump officials pursue record number of cases to strip US citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
00:02:23 UTC
09:02:23 KST

Attorney General announces record number of cases to strip US citizenship
Top officials have sought to expand the use of rarely invoked laws that can strip naturalised Americans of citizenship.
The United States Department of Justice has filed 40 new cases seeking to strip naturalised Americans of their citizenship over alleged crimes they have committed.
In a statement on Monday, federal prosecutors said they were targeting individuals accused of “serious offenses”, including money laundering, child sexual abuse, visa fraud and tax evasion.
The statement touted the 40 cases as the largest volume of denaturalisation petitions submitted in such a short period under President Donald Trump. The petitions were filed from late August through early October.
“Today’s announcement marks the largest denaturalization effort in modern history,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, the Department of Justice will continue to employ the denaturalization process to maintain our national security and protect the American people.”
The 40 citizens targeted in Monday’s announcement include people from a range of countries, including Mexico, Pakistan, China and Sierra Leone.
They are accused of concealing criminal acts and other facts about themselves as they sought to obtain citizenship. Their criminal convictions largely came after they took their oaths of citizenship.
Two people on the list are also accused of engaging in espionage on behalf of China. Committing these crimes before they became citizens, the Department of Justice alleges, meant these individuals lacked “good moral character” and should have been denied citizenship.
Expanded use of denaturalisation law
The laws to denaturalise US citizens have been used for decades, but historically, they have been reserved for serious crimes.
After World War II, for instance, the US government moved to denaturalise dozens of citizens accused of concealing involvement in the Holocaust or engaging in war crimes.
Notable cases include that of Emma Goldman, a Lithuanian-born anarchist and women’s rights activist who was jailed in 1917 for her antiwar activities, before being denaturalised and deported to the Soviet Union.
But the practice has become much less frequent since the end of the Cold War.
Top officials in the Trump administration, however, have sought to expand denaturalisation as part of a push to conduct the largest deportation operation in US history.
Under US law, prosecutors can ask courts to strip citizenship from those born outside the country if they wilfully concealed a “material fact” during their citizenship application that would have otherwise disqualified them.
But Trump’s efforts to widen denaturalisation proceedings have received pushback from human rights groups, which argue they could leave people stateless.
Critics have also warned that Trump has sought to leverage denaturalisation against specific groups he perceives to be political rivals or enemies.
Last year, for instance, the Trump administration indicated it would seek to denaturalise large numbers of Somali Americans after allegations emerged in Minnesota of daycare fraud involving the Somali diaspora.
“Send them back from where they came, Somalia, perhaps the worst, and most corrupt, country on earth,” Trump wrote at the time.
Members of Trump’s Republican Party, notably Representative Andy Ogles, have also floated the possibility of yanking citizenship from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was born in Uganda. Trump himself has falsely suggested Mamdani may be in the country illegally.
At one point, Trump even floated the idea of withdrawing citizenship from tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, a close ally and adviser to his second administration, after the two men had a falling-out in 2025.
Trump has also pushed to do away with birthright citizenship, which is granted to virtually all children born in the US. The few exceptions include the babies of diplomats and foreign military forces.
Birthright citizenship is protected under the US Constitution and cannot be taken away the way naturalised citizenship can.
In June, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s efforts to dismantle birthright citizenship, but legal battles continue after the president issued a second executive order also seeking to restrict how birthright citizenship is applied.

New York state declares measles disaster amid resurgence of disease in US
The US had largely eliminated measles by 2000 but has seen several outbreaks amid declining vaccination rates.
New York state has declared a disaster emergency over an outbreak of measles, as cases of the disease that had once been all but eliminated in the United States continue to rise.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said on Monday that she was temporarily expanding the ability of health professionals to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement, adding that New York has recorded 108 cases of measles this year, as of October 3. The declaration will remain in effect through November 4.
Hochul’s announcement marks the first such declaration since measles cases began to tick up in 2025. She said that seven cases were recorded in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.
Hochul’s declaration says 92 cases have been recorded since July 15 in a handful of rural communities with insufficient vaccination rates.
Officials in neighbouring Pennsylvania also announced that the state has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, the largest outbreak in the US in the last three decades. Outbreaks have also been recorded in Texas, Utah, Ohio and South Carolina.
Health experts attribute the resurgence to a decline in vaccination rates below the 95 percent rate they say is necessary to prevent outbreaks.
Critics say the decline has been spurred by an anti-vaccination movement that has surged in popularity and gained advocates inside the administration of President Donald Trump, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
The US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles by 2000, with the last outbreak of more than 1,000 cases occurring over several years in New York City in the early 1990s.
International officials from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) are set to meet in November to determine whether the US and Mexico will retain their measles-free status, or whether the public health designations will be updated.
“PAHO reiterates the importance of maintaining high and homogeneous vaccination coverage, strengthening epidemiological surveillance, and ensuring timely outbreak response, as essential pillars to halt transmission and sustain measles elimination in the countries of the Americas,” the organisation said in a previous statement.

In brief
- A Greens-aligned think tank wants the government to run supermarkets.
- The proposal's promised savings come with a significant initial catch.
A government-owned supermarket chain would sell groceries more than 20 per cent cheaper on average, under a plan hatched by a minor party.
A Greens-affiliated think tank has floated the idea of the federal government buying up 200 Coles and Woolworths stores and opening more than 400 extra shopfronts, and the party's freshly minted leader has given it the nod.
The average four-person household would save $60 a week, or $3,134 a year, according to the Green Institute's report, proposing to offer eggs, milk, fruit, vegetables, meat and cheese at about two-thirds of their current price.
The plan would cost $25.1 billion over five years, making it one of the top 10 most expensive government programs — more expensive than the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
"For half the cost of a single AUKUS submarine we could establish a national network of publicly owned supermarkets that would save families thousands of dollars on their groceries," ex-Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather said on Tuesday.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It's common sense that if you want more affordable prices on essentials, then you need to cut out the profit with public ownership."
After the hefty initial bill, the stores would be self-funded, according to the report.
It's a carbon copy of a policy spearheaded by wildly popular New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is piloting five city-owned grocery stores with the same objective.
It's the second time the Greens have looked to Mamdani's policies, after the party's Victorian arm proposed creating a community safety and crime prevention office combining outreach, mental health, addiction and homelessness services with policing.
More than 80 per cent of Australian voters, including a majority of One Nation supporters, somewhat or strongly support the idea of rolling out state supermarkets to cut the price of groceries, according to YouGov polling commissioned alongside the Green Institute report.
However, just 37 per cent of voters were in the "strongly support" column, and those canvassed were not given details about the policy's costings.
David Shoebridge, who on Wednesday took over as Greens leader after Larissa Waters stepped down due to ill health, has said the policy merits discussion.
The NSW senator is under pressure to turn the party's languishing popularity around as One Nation surges and progressive movements gain traction overseas.
While populist left leaders like Mamdani and the UK's Zack Polanski make good headway in the polls, the Greens have barely moved from the 12 per cent vote share they scraped together at the 2025 federal election.
Chandler-Mather, the former Greens politician leading the public grocery store policy, lost his Brisbane seat at the time, along with two of his lower-house colleagues, including the party's then-leader Adam Bandt.

Myanmar’s military has launched airstrikes on camps for internally displaced people in Rakhine State, killing at least eight people and leaving more injured, according to a local ethnic rebel organization.

One civilian was killed and two injured in the attack, it added.
This came after six were killed in an air attack on a separate displacement camp in the township on Sunday night, the AA claimed. Several more were injured in the attack, which also destroyed buildings.
The two attacks were also confirmed by the Ponnagyun Youth Association, which told Reuters that everyone killed or injured was a “displaced civilian.”
“Attacking these civilian targets with aircraft was a deliberative move,” Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and aid worker, told The Irrawaddy, adding that the camps were located far from the active combat zone in Rakhine State.

This includes the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021 over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.

The air strike was also condemned by U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk.
While Myanmar’s military has recently succeeded in halting the loss of territory to ethnic armed groups and other resistance factions, nearly 3.8 million people remain displaced across the country, according to the United Nations, and the central state’s hold on much of the country remains either loose or non-existent.
With the failure of a recent military offensive aimed at seizing territory around Sittwe, the Myanmar armed forces will likely compensate by relying ever more heavily on the use of air power in Rakhine State.

interlocking biodegradable modules weave regenerative pavilion into gavarres landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:55:33 UTC
08:55:33 KST

interlocking biodegradable modules weave regenerative pavilion into gavarres landscape
woven is a temporary architectural pavilion that explores nature’s continuous cycle of transformation, decay, and regeneration.
wood and biodegradable 3D printed modules form woven pavilion
Woven is a temporary architectural pavilion by Atelier DARN that explores cycles of transformation, decay, and regeneration through a structure made entirely from nature-based materials.
Located in Les Gavarres landscape, in Girona, Spain, the pavilion combines wood with a biodegradable filament made from miscanthus to 3D print around 700 modular pieces. The components interlock into a woven structure that rises from the forest floor toward the surrounding trees, with no glue, rope, or synthetic materials used in the assembly.
pavilion’s cross-shaped module system grows and decomposes
For the structure, Atelier DARN’s design team draws on the growth of climbing plants and vines, relying on the surrounding vegetation and landscape for support. As vegetation gradually covers the pavilion, the structure is intended to blend into its surroundings before weathering and decomposing. Architecture is treated as a changing process that can eventually become part of the landscape.
The individual modules reference Catalan architecture through their cross-shaped section, inspired by the columns of the Barcelona Pavilion. The four-directional geometry allows the pieces to connect and extend into the larger woven structure.
project info:
name: Woven
architect: Atelier DARN | @atelier_darn

Sudan’s army-aligned force announces capture of Bir Sleiba in West Darfur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:55:24 UTC
08:55:24 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Serdar Dincel
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Sudan’s Joint Force of Armed Movements said Monday that the army and its forces had taken control of the Bir Sleiba area in Sudan's West Darfur State following clashes with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The Joint Force, an armed coalition that fights alongside the national army against the RSF, consists of movements in Darfur that signed a peace agreement with the Sudanese government in Juba in 2020.
The main groups include the Justice and Equality Movement led by Jibril Ibrahim and the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Darfur regional governor Minni Minnawi.
In a statement, the force said its troops and army forces engaged in “fierce field battles” Monday morning along the Bir Sleiba and Abu Suruj fronts against the RSF.
The force said its units “destroyed seven RSF combat vehicles, killed a large number of its members, liberated Bir Sleiba and tightened their deployment in the area.”
Army and Joint Force personnel also posted videos on social media announcing that they have taken control of Bir Sleiba.
Bir Sleiba is strategically important as it lies along the northern route leading to El Geneina, the capital of West Darfur State, and contains a network of vital roads.
The RSF has not commented on the reported developments.
In August, Bir Sleiba witnessed heavy fighting between the army and Joint Forces on one side and the RSF on the other, resulting in the displacement of thousands of people from the area, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Of Sudan’s 18 states, the RSF controls the five Darfur states in the west, except for parts of North Darfur and West Darfur that remain under army control.
The army controls most of the remaining 13 states, including the capital Khartoum.
The humanitarian crisis in Sudan has worsened amid a war between the army and the RSF that erupted in April 2023 over a dispute concerning the integration of the military institutions.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced 13 million.

Since October 2023, Israel has expanded its wars across the region, invading southern Lebanon and entering direct armed conflict against Iran in late February alongside the United States.

Egypt’s Sisi rejects any threat to Nile water rights

Hussien Elkabany and Rania Abushamala
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi rejected any infringement on Egypt’s share of Nile waters, attempts to displace Palestinians or moves to circumvent implementation of the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
Sisi spoke Monday while chairing a meeting of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces at the Strategic Command headquarters in the New Administrative Capital east of Cairo, according to a presidential statement.
The meeting formed part of celebrations marking the 53rd anniversary of Egypt’s October 1973 war against Israel.
“The Nile is the very lifeline of Egypt and the cornerstone of its existence across millennia,” he said.
“Egypt’s water share is an established historical and non-negotiable legal right that admits of no compromise or infringement.”
He said Egypt remains committed to cooperation and joint development with fellow Nile Basin countries but would not allow any measures that undermine its water security.
Egypt “shall continue to defend its rights by all means sanctioned under international law,” he added.
Egypt and Sudan, the two downstream Nile countries, are locked in a dispute with upstream Ethiopia over its dam and the absence of a binding agreement governing its filling and operation. Cairo fears the project could affect its annual water allocation of 55.5 billion cubic meters.
Turning to Palestine, Sisi reiterated Egypt’s “categorical rejection of any attempts aimed at displacing the Palestinian people from their land.”
He also called for full implementation of US President Donald Trump’s Gaza ceasefire plan, warning against circumventing or disregarding it.
Sisi stressed the importance of establishing an independent Palestinian state in accordance with international resolutions, describing it as the only guarantee of a just and lasting peace and stability in the Middle East.
He cited Egypt’s peace agreement with Israel as evidence that prolonged conflict can give way to coexistence.
Egypt and Israel fought wars over decades before the courage and foresight of their political leadership, supported by US mediation, opened the door to peace and ended hostilities, he said.
“Peace is by no means an unattainable aspiration but a viable choice capable of resolving conflicts and fostering peaceful coexistence among peoples,” Sisi added.
Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in Washington, DC on March 26, 1979, following the 1978 Camp David Accords.
Addressing regional developments, Sisi said the Middle East faces crises and turmoil, while rapid global changes and unprecedented challenges have destabilized countries and displaced millions.
He warned that challenges to Egypt’s stability persist but said the country’s institutions and the cohesion of its people enable it to protect its national security.
He reaffirmed Egypt’s support for the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Arab countries and the protection of their national institutions.
“The security of the Arab Gulf States is an integral and inseparable part of Egypt’s national security,” he said, renewing Egypt’s condemnation of attacks targeting Arab countries.
He also stressed the need to preserve freedom of navigation through international maritime routes.
Egypt’s armed forces remain ready to defend the country, its resources and national security “at all times and under all circumstances,” Sisi said.
