Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:50:12 UTC
08:50:12 KST

Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.
“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Seoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.
But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.
While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.
The largest carrier, the sanctioned Layla, made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.
Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria, which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.
The third sanctioned tanker, the Chongchon, never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I, at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.
The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.
According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions, and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.
In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.
Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.
In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.
On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.
When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
It said it had expanded its export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.
The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.
The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.
A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”

Explainer: Why Spanish PM calls early election and what comes next?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
07:49:38 CST
08:49:38 KST

MADRID, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- With about 10 months remaining before Spain's next general election, the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced on Monday that he would dissolve the parliament and an early general election will be held on Nov. 29.
The announcement came after the parliament's rejection on Friday of two government decrees aimed at easing the housing crisis, amid widespread protests over soaring housing costs.
Analysts believe that an early election could give Sanchez an opportunity to seek a broader progressive majority that he says is needed to pursue pending reforms, particularly on housing and inequality. Yet the decision also comes as the left is faced with an unfavorable polling result and fragile parliamentary position, making the election a high-risk test for both Sanchez and the camp led by him.
HOUSING CRISIS AS TRIGGER
Spain's housing crisis was considered as an immediate trigger for Sanchez's decision to call an early election. Over the past several years, soaring rents and home prices have made it increasingly difficult for young people and low-income households to find affordable places to live, turning housing into one of Spain's most high-profile social issues.
Public anger intensified after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from the Madrid home she had rented for years, sparking protests in cities across the country.
In response, the Spanish government introduced two emergency decrees on housing last week, aiming to strengthen protections for vulnerable tenants against eviction, curb speculative home purchases and provide greater security for long-term rental contracts.
However, the Congress rejected both decrees on Friday. The People's Party(PP), Vox and the conservative Catalan party Junts per Catalunya voted against them. The rejection highlighted the fragile parliamentary position of the coalition government led by Sanchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), which has relied on support from smaller and regional parties to pass legislation.
BID FOR BROADER PROGRESSIVE MAJORITY
In his address on Monday, Sanchez acknowledged that a part of Spain's social groups was dissatisfied and angry to see their interests "trampled upon in Parliament for the benefits of a few." He admitted that his government had made mistakes and had not achieved everything it had set out to do, citing unresolved problems on inequality, public services and access to housing.
"In order to do more, we need to renew and expand people's support," Sanchez said, calling for "a much broader, progressive majority" in parliament to carry out pending reforms and continue transforming Spain.
Analysts believe that Sanchez made the decision under pressure, trying to garner supports for the camp led by him.
Pablo Simon, a political scientist who authored a recent study by Carlos III University of Madrid, told local media that housing offered a policy frame more favorable to the left, allowing the government to regain the initiative and giving smaller left-wing parties a shared political banner.
Zhu Rui, secretary-general of the Centre for Spain Studies of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told Xinhua in an interview that calling an early election was "a proactive move made under pressure."
In his address, Sanchez presented the election as a choice over the country's political direction. He asked voters whether they wanted Spain to join "that far-right wave" or remain "a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility".
Zhu said the shortened campaign gives Sanchez an opportunity to mobilize young people, tenants and urban voters, while increasing pressure on the smaller left-wing parties to coordinate more closely. The housing issue gives those parties a shared and urgent social concern around which they can coordinate their campaigns and reconnect with voters.
UNCERTAIN ELECTORAL PROSPECT
The formal electoral process is set to begin on Tuesday, when the royal decree dissolving the parliament and calling the election is due to be published in Spain's Official State Gazette. The Congress and the Senate will then be dissolved and the countdown to the Nov. 29 election will be started.
A 40dB poll for Spanish media outlets El Pais and Cadena SER, conducted between Sept. 25 and 28, put the support for the People's Party at 31.6 percent, the PSOE at 27.4 percent and Vox at 18.4 percent. The smaller left-wing parties were also weak, having a combined 8.3 percent.
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the main opposition People's Party, has placed housing at the center of his campaign, promising to increase homebuilding and cut taxes.
But the PP's path to power may depend on Vox, a far-right party whose support could be necessary for a parliamentary majority. Experts said that the prospect raises a key question for the campaign: whether a PP-led government would rely on Vox only for parliamentary backing or bring the party into the government.
Spain's proportional parliamentary system means that finishing first will not automatically translate into power. Current polling suggests that no party is on course to secure the 176 seats needed to govern alone. The People's Party could need Vox while Sanchez would need a more unified left and support from regional parties to retain office.
Nic Lawley, a special adviser at Chatham House, said that Sanchez's decision had set in motion one of a series of highly polarized elections across Europe. He said Sanchez's prospects would depend heavily on whether he could rally Spain's fragmented left, whose smaller parties are disadvantaged by the country's provincial electoral system unless they coordinate effectively. ■

The earliest known plague outbreak happened in what is now Russia 5,500 years ago. Scientists found the evidence in ancient teeth.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:47:42 UTC
08:47:42 KST

The earliest known plague outbreak happened in what is now Russia 5,500 years ago. Scientists found the evidence in ancient teeth.
About 5,500 years ago, several dozen hunter-gatherers died near Lake Baikal. DNA from the bacterium that causes plague survived in their teeth. Science journalist Ilya Kabanov, who runs the Telegram channel Laiflong Muki, explains how a study of ancient burial grounds became something of a detective story — and why the discovery changes our understanding of the history of epidemics.
An archaeological detective story: How researchers found hunters who died mysteriously near Lake Baikal — and picked up the trail of plague
About 5,500 years ago, small groups of hunter-gatherers roamed along the Angara River in the Lake Baikal region, an area rich in deer, moose, fish, and marmots. They did not build cities, farm, or keep domestic animals other than dogs. Still, scientists know quite a bit about their way of life from studies of burial grounds. These ancient Siberians used bows and arrows, for example. They also knew how to fire pottery.
The burial grounds along the Angara were far apart, sometimes as much as 340 kilometers (about 210 miles). Yet the people buried in them shared recent ancestors. Traveling along the riverbanks or by water probably helped them stay in contact. Their genomes also show almost no evidence of inbreeding, suggesting they usually found partners outside their close circle of relatives. Their burial practices varied: At one burial ground, bodies were usually laid parallel to the river; at others, perpendicular to it.
For archaeologists, including specialists at Irkutsk State University and the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Ethnology and Anthropology, burial grounds are a major source of information about the region’s hunter-gatherers. Bones, the positioning of bodies, grave goods, radiocarbon dates, and ancient DNA can reveal diets, family relationships, and sometimes the circumstances of death. In a recent paper in Nature, an international team led by Eske Willerslev, including researchers from Russia, examined the remains of 46 people from four burial sites: Ust-Ida-1, Shumilikha, Bratsky Kamen, and Serovo.
As is often the case with Willerslev’s studies — one of which Meduza covered in an article about why mammoths went extinct — the new research reads like the plot of a true-crime podcast. There is a crime scene with human remains. Many of the people died within a short period, and an unusually large number of the victims were children and adolescents. Some graves contain relatives. Yet the bones show no signs of violence.
To investigate the mystery, the archaeologists brought in geneticists, who examined the ancient people’s teeth. If an infection entered the bloodstream shortly before death, traces of it can survive in dental tissue. The researchers screened ancient DNA for pathogens and found Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, in 18 of the 46 people. At Ust-Ida, the largest burial ground studied, they found traces of plague in a third of those buried there (11 of 31). They also recovered a well-preserved plague genome from Shumilikha and several less complete ones from Bratsky Kamen and Serovo.
The presence of plague DNA in a body does not, by itself, prove that plague caused the person’s death. Someone could have been infected but died of another disease. In this case, however, too many clues lined up: closely clustered burial dates, infected people buried together, family relationships among the dead, unusually high child mortality, and no other obvious cause of death. The paper’s authors concluded that the infections were part of a disease outbreak in small hunter-gatherer communities rather than isolated cases.
The researchers suggest that people in the first phase of the outbreak may have died within a few decades — possibly much sooner. The bacterial genomes recovered from them were very similar, most likely indicating that the infections occurred during a single phase of the outbreak.
The archaeological evidence fits the genetic findings. Ust-Ida has an unusually large number of shared graves, with no evidence that they were reopened later to add more bodies. This suggests the deaths occurred at nearly the same time.
Another clue is the age of those who died. At Ust-Ida and Bratsky Kamen, child mortality was especially high, peaking at roughly 7.5 to 11 years of age. This pattern is unusual for other burial grounds in the Lake Baikal region from that period.
One grave at Bratsky Kamen, for example, held three girls roughly 4 to 9 years old. Two were most likely related, possibly cousins; the third may have belonged to the same maternal line. The researchers found Yersinia pestis DNA in all three. The paper’s authors see this as evidence that the infection spread within a family.
There is a similar pattern at Ust-Ida-1. One grave held an aunt and nephew, both of whom tested positive for plague. In other cases examined by Willerslev’s team, brothers, sisters, and other close relatives were buried together or in neighboring graves. The researchers could not confidently identify the bacterium in all of them, but that is to be expected with ancient DNA: A negative result does not always mean there was no infection.
The authors found no other obvious causes of death. The bones showed no signs of injuries that could explain such high mortality. In one case, they found traces of brucellosis, but they believe that infection was not fatal. Together, the clues make a fairly strong case for plague.
“We have found the earliest evidence of mass mortality caused by plague,” Eske Willerslev said at a press conference, explaining the significance of the discovery. “Plague is an important part of human history and has been with our species for a long time. By studying its origins and evolution, we gain a better understanding of our own history.”
Different ‘diagnoses’: Why the ‘Baikal’ plague is not quite the same disease that killed millions in medieval Europe
The strain found near Lake Baikal lacked the ymt gene, which helps the bacterium survive in a flea’s digestive tract and allows it to spread efficiently through flea bites. A strain with this gene emerged later. That means the infection spread differently around Lake Baikal 5,500 years ago.
Where did the infection come from? Marmots are the prime “suspects.” Today, natural plague hotspots in Central and Northeast Asia are often associated with marmots and other rodents. People could have become infected after hunting these animals, butchering their carcasses, or eating their meat raw or undercooked. Contact with wild animals was an ordinary part of life for the region’s hunter-gatherers, so transmission from animals to humans seems plausible.
The precise route of transmission, however, remains unknown. After the first infection, the disease may have spread between people through respiratory droplets. Family relationships among the dead and shared graves also point to that possibility.
Scientists do not yet know why children were especially vulnerable. It may have had to do with differences in their immune responses. Or adults may have encountered a similar infection before and had some protection. There may also have been behavioral reasons. But there is no direct evidence for these explanations.
Historical significance: How plague in ancient hunter-gatherers challenges a theory about the origins of human infections
The new study is significant for the debate over the origins of epidemics. They are often explained by the shift to farming and herding: People began living closer together, keeping domestic animals, and establishing permanent settlements. These changes created opportunities for infections to spread. But the Baikal discovery shows that this hypothesis does not explain everything.
The people of Ust-Ida, Shumilikha, Bratsky Kamen, and Serovo were not farmers. Local groups remained hunter-gatherers. They had pottery, bows, stone tools, and elaborate burial traditions, but no domesticated plants or animals other than dogs. Yet plague was already present. A natural reservoir, contact with wild animals, and small groups of relatives were enough for an outbreak.
Hunter-gatherer societies are usually considered unlikely settings for early epidemics: They are mobile, live in small groups, and do not depend on a single resource. That makes the discovery near Lake Baikal all the more significant.
Speaking to journalists, Eske Willerslev said that as a child he had dreamed of becoming a hunter-gatherer and imagined it as a very romantic life. After this study, he said, he no longer wanted to. There is some truth in the joke: Hunter-gatherers’ lives were more complicated and dangerous than we tend to imagine.

Aysu Bicer
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
RAF Fairford, a Royal Air Force installation in Gloucestershire that hosts US Air Force operations, remains safe after the United States withdrew its bombers, Downing Street said Monday.
The Pentagon confirmed Sunday that US bombers, believed to include about a dozen B-1 aircraft, had been moved from RAF Fairford back to their home stations in the continental United States.
US media reported that the bombers were withdrawn following a threat against the base.
The move came after police were alerted on Sept. 27 to three "suspicious vehicles" near RAF Fairford in western England.
A No.10 spokesperson told the BBC that he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations" but said the base was safe.
The spokesperson also referred to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, when he "praised our police, defense and security services" in relation to the incident at the base.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that he would not directly link last week's incident to the decision to withdraw the bombers from RAF Fairford.
"It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out," Rubio said.
He added that the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very cooperative since the incident.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences in connection with the incident and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
According to a report by the BBC, the decision was a military rather than political one taken at an operational level and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

Brazil markets’ Bolsonaro rally sends stock exchange to record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:45:00 UTC
08:45:00 KST

Brazil markets’ Bolsonaro rally sends stock exchange to record high
SAO PAULO/BRASILIA – Brazil’s main stock exchange surged to a record high on Oct 5 as the country’s markets cheered on right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s better-than-expected finish in the first round of the Oct 4 presidential election.
Brazil’s Bovespa index settled at 206,911.89 points, a new closing record, after a 7.7% jump, the largest since March 24, 2020.
The eldest son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the votes cast on Oct 4 and will face leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured about 45% of the vote, in a run-off on Oct 25. Polls had forecast Lula would lead the first round of voting by around three percentage points.
Investors cheered on Oct 5 as Flavio Bolsonaro’s strong showing was matched by gains for his allies in Congress. Analysts say a friendlier legislature would make it easier for him, if elected, to push through a pro-business agenda of tighter public spending, privatizations and tax cuts.
In Washington, US President Donald Trump joined the celebration, calling his first-place finish a “very, very big victory” and predicting a close run-off.
“Brazil wants change,” Bolsonaro said on Oct 4, heralding the “end of the era of (Lula’s) Workers’ Party”.
Reuters reported on Oct 5 that Lula is considering tapping Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin to be his next finance minister if re-elected, in a bid to bolster the government’s fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters in the wake of Bolsonaro’s first-round success.
Retailer Magazine Luiza, conglomerate Cosan and stock exchange operator B3 were among the main gainers, with each jumping more than 20%, while oil company Petrobras rose just over 8% and lender Bradesco was up over 13%.
The benchmark index had its best daily performance since March 2020, when markets faced extreme volatility at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
US-traded shares of Brazilian companies also soared, with brokerage XP up 33%, digital lender Nu Holdings up 13%, and fintech firms StoneCo and PagBank each up more than 20%.
The cost of buying insurance on Brazilian government debt through credit default swaps fell 20 basis points as traders bet on an improvement in the country’s finances.
J.P. Morgan upgraded Brazil’s equities to “overweight” on Oct 5, saying a more favourable political backdrop after recent election developments had improved the outlook for the region’s largest market and could drive a period of outperformance.
The Oct 4 vote sent the country’s currency strengthening 4.1% to around 5 per dollar, putting it on track for its biggest one-day gain in four years since the elder Bolsonaro performed better than expected against Lula in the first round of the 2022 election.
He lost to Lula in the second round of that election and was subsequently convicted of trying to carry out a coup to overturn the result. The former president was sentenced to about 27 years in prison and is currently under house arrest.
Brazil’s international debt also rallied on Oct 5, while broader fixed-income markets were jittery. The 2056 bond was up 1.4 cents on the dollar to bid at 93.5 cents, Tradeweb data showed.
‘The market wants change’
Bolsonaro has pitched himself as a “more centred” version of his father to investors concerned about Brazil’s burgeoning fiscal pressures.
“It remains to be seen whether the senator would ultimately prove more fiscally responsible than Lula would be in a fourth non-consecutive presidential term. However, markets are likely to give him the benefit of the doubt,” said Thierry Larose, portfolio manager at Vontobel.
If he is elected, Bolsonaro would enjoy some room to manoeuvre with Congress after his Liberal Party emerged as the biggest winner in congressional races on Oct 4.
His Liberal Party increased its representation in the Senate from 15 to 28 seats, the strongest result for a party since Brazil’s constitution was enacted in the late 1980s, following the country’s return to democracy.
It also is projected to secure 121 seats in the 513-seat lower house, up from its current 98 seats.
“The likelihood of advancing reforms is much greater,” said Pedro Paulo Silveira, an analyst at Terra Investimentos. He noted that during the previous Bolsonaro government, reforms often depended on costly political bargaining or stalled altogether.
Analysts also expect the real to continue strengthening into 2027. Societe Generale forecast that it would move to 5.10 by the end of 2026, with scope to move below 5.00 in the first half of 2027. Morgan Stanley forecast the real could strengthen past 4.90 and toward 4.50 in the first quarter of next year.
“The market wants change, it wants reform, it doesn’t want a high public deficit; with the current government, all of this will continue,” said Pedro Galdi, investment analyst at the AGF Investments platform.
Bolsonaro’s strong showing is likely to boost market confidence in the near term, said Bryan Harris, a managing partner at Sabio.
“The market will be looking for clear signals from Bolsonaro that he is serious about tackling the country’s problems,” Harris said.
Heading into the Oct 4 vote, most private polls, which largely underestimated the younger Bolsonaro’s strength, had shown the 45-year-old senator and Lula, who will turn 81 later this month, about even in a run-off vote. REUTERS

North Melbourne has its new senior coach, with Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham the unanimous choice of the selection panel.
Graham succeeds Alastair Clarkson who was sacked in early September with a year left to run on his contract.
Graham describes himself as a "systems-based and relationships-based coach".
North Melbourne has named Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham as the new coach for the AFL side.
A statement from club president Sonja Hood on Tuesday said Graham was the new senior coach, succeeding four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson, who was sacked by the Kangaroos earlier this year.
Graham spent five seasons at the Dockers as an assistant to Justin Longmuir.
The Kangaroos finished the 2026 season — Clarkson's fourth season in charge — in 14th spot with nine wins.
Loading Twitter content
Speaking at his first press conference, Graham thanked the club for having faith in him.
Having missed out on a number of coaching opportunities before landing the North Melbourne job, he said he was nervous and proud to take charge of the Kangaroos.
"This opportunity came up, things happen for a reason. I feel I belong here already," he said.
"There's no ceiling on where we want to get to. There's clearly some talent on this list, but there's also some work to do."
Graham described himself as a "systems-based and relationships-based coach".
"People don't care how much you know, until they know how much you care."
Club CEO Jen Watt confirmed the panel tasked with finding the new coach had unanimously picked Grham.
Earlier, in the club statement, Hood told members Graham had "the resilience to handle the relentless toils of the football environment, carrying the exact kind of grit we value at North Melbourne.
"As a coach, Jaymie is a process-driven leader with a quiet, grounded presence, sharp attention to detail, and a clear football vision," she said.
"Outside of his exceptional character, he joins us with a proven skill set. He played a key role in West Coast's 2018 premiership success, and more recently he was the line coach for one of the competition's best forward lines at Fremantle as part of a high-performing program.
"He is widely respected across the industry as a developer of talent and a connector of people — someone who builds strong player relationships instantly and earns respect through his actions."
The announcement marks a change in direction, with a young untested AFL senior coach — who has been a caretaker or interim coach for three games in total at West Coast and Fremantle, after a period in charge of East Perth in the WAFL — after the end of the Clarkson era.
The Kangaroos were criticised for the tone of their press conference in early September announcing Clarkson's departure.
At the time, Hood said Clarkson's replacement needed to be "a coach who can coach for the modern game".
"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club," she said.
Football manager Todd Viney said in the press conference there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan".
Fremantle paid tribute to Graham in a statement, wishing him well for his new role and thanking him for his "five outstanding seasons" at the club.
"Jaymie has had a significant impact not only on our player group — but the entire football department and broader club," Fremantle executive general manager of football Joe Brierty said.
"It is well documented that Jaymie has had ambitions of becoming a senior coach in his own right one day, and we couldn't be prouder or happier for him to take an opportunity he's worked so hard for."

UN chief calls for Gaza ceasefire ahead of Oct 7 anniversary
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.
- Guterres condemned the Hamas attack and acknowledged heavy casualties on both Israeli and Palestinian sides, urging respect for international law and humanitarian aid.
- Tensions remain high with Israel refusing to withdraw troops until Hamas disarms, while Hamas seeks gradual disarmament; ongoing conflicts involve Lebanon and Iran as well.
AI generated
United Nations – United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Oct 5 called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
“It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law,” Guterres said in a statement, calling for a “political path to lasting peace across the whole region”.
“Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity and aspirations fulfilled,” Guterres said.
The UN chief acknowledged Israel’s casualties in the statement, calling the Hamas attack “abhorrent” for “killing more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals” and taking hostage another 251 people.
Guterres also said Palestinians in Gaza have faced a “massive loss of life, displacement and destruction”, without specifying their death toll.
“Their suffering, too, demands an end, now,” Guterres said.
Israel’s years-long military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry, which is under Hamas’ authority and whose figures are deemed reliable by the UN.
Guterres acknowledged that a brief ceasefire, announced by US President Donald Trump in October 2025, “brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace”.
Israel, which still controls most of Gaza, refuses to withdraw its soldiers until Hamas’ disarmament has been verified.
Hamas, for its part, has advocated for gradual disarmament rather than immediate and unilateral surrender of its arsenal.
Since the 2023 attacks, Israel has waged military attacks on several fronts, notably invading southern Lebanon to confront Hezbollah, the Islamist movement backed by Tehran, and launching war against Iran in late February alongside the US. AFP

Yemen's Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
Iran-backed Houthis on Monday said they had struck Riyadh's international airport, an Aramco refinery and several other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.
Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit "military targets" belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.
Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on Monday evening as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom's south.
The government announced on Sunday the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory, home to most of Yemen's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Last month the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen's deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen's civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Monday, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other's aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed "to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.
Global oil system 'straining'
Houthi attacks have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.
A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom's exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world's largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were "scarily thin" owing to the war.
"The system is already straining," Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mocha fighting
Yemeni military sources said Monday that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mocha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port's recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
Yemen's civil war broke out in 2014, with the Saudis intervening the following March, but fighting was paused by a 2022 ceasefire that held until July of this year.

Ukraine's EU Accession: Kos hopes two more clusters to open next week

- The PQ gained power despite only about 30% vote share, helped by federalist vote-splitting; leader Paul Saint-Pierre Plamondon plans no referendum before 2029 to ensure calm debate.
- PQ's leader also aims to reduce ties with the British monarchy, a move supported by many Quebecers who feel little attachment to the crown, signalling a shift in provincial identity.
AI generated
MONTREAL – Separatists won provincial elections in Quebec on Oct 5, with a promise to hold a vote on leaving Canada after US President Donald Trump leaves office, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity to confront the United States.
But the Parti Quebecois (PQ) fell short of a majority government in Canada’s French-speaking province, offering some solace for the federalist camp.
The PQ win still upends Canada’s political landscape as the country confronts a trade war and annexation threats levelled by the United States.
It also comes just two weeks before Canada’s oil-producing province of Alberta, an economic powerhouse, holds a separate vote on whether it wants to begin the process of leaving Canada.
The results make PQ leader Paul Saint-Pierre Plamondon, a 49-year-old lawyer known by his initials as PSPP, Quebec’s next premier.
At a jubilant victory party in Montreal, he invoked “the courageous struggle” francophones have endured in a part of the world increasingly dominated by English speakers.
That struggle “will find meaning when (francophones) obtain their own country,” he said.
“We deserve it,” he added, calling a referendum a chance “to decide what our national future will be”.
Independence after Trump?
Carney congratulated PSPP, saying that “building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada”.
The Canadian Prime Minister is popular in Quebec, and the separatist win was not seen as a repudiation of his stance towards Trump, whose trade war and annexation threats have infuriated Canadians.
Instead, the PQ’s rise after more than a decade in opposition has been tied to frustration over affordability and an enduring desire to protect the French language in an increasingly anglophone country.
Surveys suggest that only about 30% of Quebecers want independence, but PSPP has maintained he will call a referendum on leaving Canada, just not while Trump is in office.
He has said a decision on Quebec’s independence “requires conditions that allow for an informed and calm debate”.
That should not be “hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president”, he added, ruling out a referendum until at least 2029.
Quebec has held two previous votes on leaving Canada. Federalists won comfortably in 1980, but the 1995 result was excruciatingly close, with just 50.58% voting to stay in Canada.
First-time voter Alexia Gomez, 19, invoked tensions with the United States when she told AFP she opposed an independence referendum.
“If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable,” she said.
Lydie Periard, a 22-year-old student, said she was “very worried” by the PQ’s victory, condemning what she termed the party’s “populist” stance on immigration.
The PQ has backed immigration cuts, particularly for non-French speakers.
The PQ replaces a party, known as the Coalition for Quebec’s Future (CAQ), that advocated strongly for the province’s distinctive culture within Canada, without supporting separatism.
Lacking a majority, the PQ will struggle to advance its separatist agenda.
The two largest opposition parties after Monday’s vote, the Liberals and Conservatives, both declared they would never back a referendum on independence.
‘Abolish the monarchy?’
PSPP may not have majority backing for an independent Quebec, but his plans to target the British monarchy appear far more popular.
Canada is part of the British Commonwealth. King Charles III, Canada’s head of state, is represented in Ottawa by the governor general. Lieutenant governors represent the monarchy in the provinces, including Quebec.
In a 2025 Leger poll, 87% of Quebecers said they felt no attachment to the British monarchy, and only 31% expressed a favourable view of King Charles.
PSPP has said his government could cut off funds for the lieutenant-governor, calling it a “masquerade that wastes money”. AFP

What is celebrated on October 6 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:29:43 EEST
08:29:43 KST

What is celebrated on October 6 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 6 marks Instagram’s anniversary and the International Geodiversity Day. The Apostle Thomas and people with cerebral palsy are also honored.
On October 6, the world observes Instagram’s Birthday and International Geodiversity Day, reports UNN.
World Cerebral Palsy Day
A global medical initiative launched in 2012 by the Alliance of Organizations Supporting People with Cerebral Palsy. The day was established to draw public attention to the more than 17 million people worldwide living with this neurological disorder, as well as to their families.
This day emphasizes the need for early diagnosis, access to rehabilitation services, and the development of inclusive education, creating conditions for people with cerebral palsy to lead full lives in all spheres of society.
Instagram’s Birthday
An unofficial but widely observed date commemorating the launch of the Instagram app, created by developers Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger in 2010.
The app, originally conceived exclusively as a photo-sharing platform, revolutionized the digital space, becoming one of the most influential social networks of the modern era, with an audience of billions.
International Geodiversity Day
An official international observance under the auspices of UNESCO, proclaimed in 2021 with the support of the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS). The event is dedicated to geodiversity—the nonliving natural foundation of our planet. It includes minerals, rocks, fossils, and soils.
The date is intended to highlight the role of geological sciences in developing sustainable technologies, studying hazardous natural phenomena, and preserving unique geological sites.
The Commemoration Day of Saint Apostle Thomas
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Apostle Thomas, one of the twelve closest disciples of Jesus Christ. In the Gospel tradition, he is known as “Doubting Thomas” because of his doubt about the Savior’s Resurrection, which disappeared after Christ personally appeared to him and allowed him to touch His wounds.
After the Descent of the Holy Spirit, Apostle Thomas set out to preach Christianity to the Parthians, Medes, and Indians, where he founded the first Christian communities on the Indian subcontinent and suffered martyrdom.
According to the old calendar, believers observe the Conception of the Honorable and Glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist of the Lord John. This major feast commemorates the event when the Archangel Gabriel announced to the righteous priest Zechariah in the Temple of Jerusalem the future birth of a son to his childless wife Elizabeth, who would become the forerunner of the Savior.

Protesters clash with police over Kosovo war crimes court law

Protesters clash with police over Kosovo war crimes court law
PRISTINA, Oct 5 - Protesters clashed with police outside Kosovo's government and parliament buildings on Monday, calling for lawmakers to pass legislation that would limit the powers of a Kosovo war crimes court in The Hague.
The protest came weeks after the court sentenced former President Hashim Thaci and three others to a combined 81 years in prison for war crimes.
Police fired tear gas and used water cannon to disperse demonstrators who threw firecrackers and stones at officers guarding parliament and government buildings in central Pristina.
At least 17 people were injured, including six police officers, police said. Three protesters were detained.
Earlier in the day, lawmakers approved the first reading of amendments to a law that established the Kosovo war crimes court in The Hague. Demonstrators later blocked parliament, preventing lawmakers from leaving and demanding a second vote which is needed to pass the legislation.
The clash underscores deep anger in Kosovo over the court's conviction of former fighters who are considered heroes and highlights growing divisions in parliament in one of Europe's poorest nations.
The amendments to the Specialist Chambers law would cap prison sentences at 15 years, allow defendants to appeal to Kosovo's Supreme Court, permit sentences to be served in Kosovo and enable the country's president to grant amnesty to convicted individuals.
The proposed changes faced skepticism from Prime Minister Albin Kurti.
"We consider these moves to amend the law on the Specialist Chambers rushed and insufficiently analysed and thought through," Kurti told parliament.
Despite backing the first vote, Kurti and his party declined to support the second vote on the same day for the amendments presented by Thaci's former party, the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK).
Kosovo established the Specialist Chambers in The Hague in 2015 under international pressure to prosecute former ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) fighters for alleged crimes committed during and after Kosovo's 1998-99 war with Serbia.
The court last month found Thaci, 58, guilty of war crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention, sentencing him to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as a senior commander of the KLA during the conflict.
Thaci and the three co-defendants have appealed the verdict. REUTERS

Australian soldier dies during training exercise in the Northern Territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:19:26 UTC
08:19:26 KST

in brief
- An Australian soldier has been killed during a routine training exercise, the Department of Defence has announced.
- Five others were also injured at the Northern Territory military facility used for joint live-fire exercises.
An Australian Defence Force member who died in a military training accident is being remembered as a mate who "would give you the shirt off his back".
A father of two young children, Corporal Brendan Hannam was killed during an exercise at the Mount Bundey training area in the Northern Territory on Monday evening.
The 28-year-old was survived by a partner and two young children, Chief of Army Lieutenant General Susan Coyle said.
"It is with deep and profound sadness that I can confirm we lost one of our soldiers yesterday," she told media on Tuesday.
Hannam was described as a "much-beloved junior leader".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"He has served and sacrificed on two operational tours to Afghanistan in 2019 ... and also he trained Ukrainians with the British armed forces," Coyle said.
"His mates tell me he would give the shirt off his back ... and the thing he'll be most remembered for is the love and support he had for his partner and his kids."
Hannam was a member of the 5th/7th Army Battalion based in the NT.
He was a passenger in a troop-carrying vehicle when the incident occurred.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the nation's thoughts were with the family and friends of the killed soldier and his injured colleagues.
"There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country's name," he said in a statement.
"This sad incident is a terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation's uniform."
Federal Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh also extended his condolences to the fallen soldier's family.
"We also have been making sure our training systems are fit for purpose and the training is conducted in the safest way possible," he told the ABC.
It was recognised there were unique circumstances when it came to defence force training and there were high levels of risk, he said.
Five others injured
Five other soldiers were injured in the incident at the training area roughly 130km south-east of the capital Darwin.
In a statement on Tuesday morning, Defence announced an incident had taken place on Monday.
"Defence can confirm an Australian Army soldier has died during a training exercise at the Mount Bundey Training Area on 5 October 2026," the statement read.
"Five other Australian Army soldiers were injured," it added.
The statement confirmed that the next of kin of the deceased soldier had been notified and also requested privacy for its members and their families at this time.
Northern Territory emergency services were notified at around 4:30pm on Monday after reports of a vehicle accident.
NT Chief Minister Lia Finocciaro said two evacuations were made by helicopter to Royal Darwin Hospital at around 9:30 on Monday night, while another three were carried out by plane.
Incident occurred at regularly used joint training facility
The Mount Bundey Training Area is a major military facility used for joint live-fire exercises. The former cattle station spans 117,000 hectares south of the Arnhem Highway.
The Australian Defence Force frequently holds joint training exercises at the testing area with the United States military and the Singaporean armed forces.
NT Police commissioner Martin Dole confirmed that police resources had been sent to the training facility to assist with Defence investigations.
Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh told SBS News that a review of training safety procedures would need to be conducted.
"We need to make sure that our forces are trained to be able to confront the circumstances that they may have to, which are obviously quite unique," he said.
"Of course, whenever there's a loss of life, there's investigation into what has occurred and whether there needs to be any improvements in safety."
In 2017, Private Jason Challis was killed during a live-fire exercise at Mount Bundey. His death led to a temporary pause on ADF live-fire combat training exercises and a long-running coronial inquest into safety protocols.
In July 2023, an army helicopter crashed into the ocean near the Whitsundays, killing all four crew members on board.
In May of this year, Warrant Officer Lachlan Muddle died during parachute training at the Jervis Bay Airfield.
Update: This story has been updated to correctly reflect the date of the Whitsundays crash.

POLITICO Blocked From Traveling With Trump on Air Force One Amid Battle Over Media Access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:18:50 UTC
08:18:50 KST

The White House on Monday blocked POLITICO from boarding Air Force One and carrying out its print pool duties, marking the latest escalation in an ongoing battle over media outlets’ access to President Donald Trump.
“The White House has blocked today's print pooler, Politico, from traveling on Air Force One,” Washington Post reporter Katherine Doyle wrote in a White House pool report Monday afternoon.
Doyle added that “since [the White House] was unable to find a replacement, there is no primary print pooler on this trip,” and noted that she would be making reports as “the secondary pooler” as Trump travels to Nebraska for a campaign rally ahead of the midterms.
CBS, the designated representative for the TV pool on Monday, is also sharing its notes with news organizations during the trip. “Neither news organization is replacing Politico,” Josh Gross of CBS News emphasized in an email.
“Many outlets including POLITICO are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House official tells TIME. The official adds that Trump is “the most accessible President in American history,” and says that he will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”
A spokesperson for POLITICO confirmed to TIME that the outlet was blocked from Monday's out-of-town travel pool.
In the White House pool system, a rotating group of journalists accompanies the President to various events and shares updates with the wider press corps to enable news organizations to widely provide coverage despite the often limited space at event venues or on board Air Force One.
But that pool coverage of Trump has been complicated by the President’s most recent efforts to punish media organizations whose coverage he objects to.
POLITICO is one of three outlets, also including CNN and MS NOW, that Trump announced that he was banning from the White House on Sept. 18, claiming that they were repeatedly publishing “FAKE NEWS.” A day after his announcement, journalists from the outlets were turned away from the White House gates and their press badges were taken away.
Within days, the three outlets proceeded to sue the Trump Administration, arguing that the ban violated the First Amendment and their Fifth Amendment right to due process. In solidarity with the impacted outlets, the five broadcast networks that comprise the White House TV pool, which records and shares video footage of the President on a rotating basis, also temporarily suspended their coverage of Trump.
A federal judge on Sept. 24 issued a temporary restraining order against Trump’s ban, in effect for 14 days, and ordered the President to immediately restore the affected outlets’ access, finding that the ban “likely violated” their “constitutional due process rights.” Following that order, journalists from the three outlets were once again allowed to access the White House grounds.
But access to carry out pool duties has remained a point of contention. The White House previously blocked CNN from Air Force One, preventing the network from carrying out its scheduled TV pool duties.
POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW, in response to CNN being prevented from traveling on the President’s plane and fulfilling its pool duties, previously requested that a federal judge block Trump’s ban on the outlets until their case against him was resolved, arguing that he had violated the previously implemented restraining order and had “persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban.”
“The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity,” the outlets’ lawyers wrote in a filing last week.
Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the U.S. District Court in Washington, who granted the temporary restraining order against the ban, is scheduled to hold a hearing over the outlets’ request to extend against Trump on Thursday.
The TV press pool has meanwhile resumed coverage of Trump after journalists from the outlets targeted in the ban were allowed back onto the White House grounds. But people familiar with the situation previously told TIME after CNN was blocked from traveling on Air Force One that decisions about TV pool coverage of the President would be made on a day-by-day basis amid the ongoing uncertainty over the network’s access to perform its pool duties.

The idea of an informal meeting with SC judges on simultaneous polls was first mooted by DMK MP and senior advocate P Wilson

Sources said the idea to meet SC judges was first mooted by DMK MP P Wilson, a senior advocate, and was informally deliberated within the committee before it took this up with the SC.The meeting was fixed for October 6 but the SC secretary general last week informed the committee of the cancellation."They (senior SC judges) are of the opinion that as the proposed amendment might become a subject matter of judicial review before the Supreme Court, it may not be expedient or desirable to discuss the issue on the administrative side. The proposed meeting is accordingly cancelled," the secretary general said.Chaudhary said an email was sent to the Parliament secretariat by SC officials on September 22, stating that a meeting had been fixed on October 6 at 4.30 pm and the law ministry also sent the relevant material to the court.
"After about eight or nine days, some issues were raised publicly. Later, SC cancelled the meeting. If SC felt it was not appropriate, there was no need to pursue the matter. There was no need to create or give further publicity to the issue."
Sources said, on September 18, the Lok Sabha secretariat first wrote to the SC secretary general, conveying the committee's desire to undertake a "local study visit" for "informal discussions" with the CJI and other judges on simultaneous elections.Wilson, through a seven-page letter to the committee, defended the proposal and said in the spirit of broad-based consultation, he had suggested that the panel hear the views of the CJI and other judges. "Unfortunately, due to political objections surrounding this meeting, it was decided to call off the meeting because of unnecessary and unfortunate circumstances caused by vested interests," he said. Opposition MPs, including senior advocate Kapil Sibal, had slammed the proposed meeting.

French teen has hand blown off by police grenade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:10:34 UTC
08:10:34 KST

French teen has hand blown off by police grenade
A 15-year-old school student had his hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade during a protest in the French city of Lens. The incident comes amid a nationwide wave of unrest and street violence that has gripped France since late September.
Demonstrators demand increased funding for public schools and better learning conditions, including more teachers, smaller classes, and repairs to dilapidated buildings.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Francois-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of the northern Pas-de-Calais department, reported that the teenager’s “hand was torn off,” apparently by a police grenade, during a protest outside Behal high school in Lens earlier in the day.
“There was no hand left, not even his wrist, there was nothing there,” one student told BFMTV, describing the gruesome scene. The boy was rushed to a hospital in Lille and is in non-life-threatening condition, according to officials.
Lauch stated that violence erupted after an estimated 200 students began hurling objects at police officers who were deployed to the school to lift a blockade imposed by protesters.
Police sources told AFP that the victim picked up the grenade, apparently intending to throw it back at the officers. An eyewitness account by a fellow protester, however, suggested that the teenager was instead hit by the grenade. The local prosecutor said investigators have yet to establish what happened. The General Inspectorate of the National Police has launched an investigation.
French police have several types of non-lethal explosive crowd-control devices in their arsenal, including grenades capable of dispersing rubber pellets and the GM2L tear-gas and stun grenade. The type involved in the Lens incident has not been officially established, although French media reports that witness accounts and footage appear consistent with a GM2L.
Amid escalating street violence across France, Marine Tondelier, the national secretary of the Ecologists party, called for reform of police crowd-control protocols. Jean-Luc Melenchon, the founder of the left-wing France Unbowed party, wrote on X on Monday that the “escalation of police tactics is out of control,” eclipsing even the May 1968 demonstrations.
“Acts of disgraceful violence, abuses of power, and provocations are multiplying without limit or restraint,” Melenchon said.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office accused France Unbowed and “its far-left proxies” of orchestrating the unrest – which the party has denied.
According to the French authorities, more than 5,060 people have been arrested since late September. Around 650 police officers, 78 education staff, and at least 190 students have also been injured in the unrest.
French police have repeatedly been accused of using excessive force when confronting protesters. In 2018-2019, at the height of the Yellow Vest demonstrations, at least 20 protesters lost an eye, while others had theirs hands partially or entirely blown off after being hit by 40 mm rubber projectiles and explosive grenades.
In March 2019, then-UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Michelle Bachelet called for a comprehensive investigation into reports of excessive use of force by French police.

‘Microbes have gotten smarter’: Trump reacts to mysterious Siberia plague lab death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:08:54 UTC
08:08:54 KST

The death of Daria Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia, continues to reverberate around the world and reached the White House on Monday evening. President Donald Trump was asked by reporters what Washington planned to do in light of the risk that pneumonic plague could reach the United States from Russia.
We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it,” he replied. “We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can.”
Trump spoke to reporters on the South Lawn before boarding the presidential helicopter on his way to a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska. He described the incident as “a big problem for Russia,” adding: “Well, I hate to see them having it. It's a rough disease”
The president also offered his own explanation for the danger: “We used to be able to control [the disease], but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. The germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore.”
The U.S. State Department, however, said earlier in a statement that “plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland before departing for Iceland: “I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it.”
Based on information provided by the Russians, he said, it appears that a laboratory employee was infected.
“There’s very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia, obviously.  But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” Rubio added.
The State Department said it was closely monitoring the situation together with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It noted that many details remain unverified and called on Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and transparently.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), plague has a high fatality rate but can be readily treated with antibiotics when diagnosed early.
WHO said it was in contact with Russian health authorities to verify the incident and its circumstances and to determine what laboratory tests were being conducted and their results. The organization said it was aware of reports that the employee died of severe pneumonia, but that the cause of death had not yet been officially confirmed and, according to the information provided, laboratory testing was still underway.
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” WHO said, adding that it would update its risk assessment as more information became available.
The European Commission also said it was monitoring the case closely and was in contact with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
Kremlin: ‘Don’t listen to rumors’
Publicly, Moscow is seeking to present a relatively calm picture. In the Kremlin’s only response to the case, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday: “We should rely on the official statements from Rospotrebnadzor and not listen to various rumors and speculation.”
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s public health authority, said samples taken from Shipilova contained no microorganisms connected to her work. It said no accident involving pathogens had occurred at the institute and that the epidemiological situation in the region was stable.
Irkutsk Oblast Gov. Igor Kobzev said a special expert commission had determined the cause of death to be “pneumonia of unknown origin,” adding: “The situation remains under our control and the control of specialists.”
“Things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well as they used to.” U.S. President Donald Trump
On the ground, however, restrictions remain in place. More than 60 institute employees have been isolated inside the building since Friday. In Irkutsk, three municipal hospitals, the Ivano-Matreninskaya Children’s Hospital and the city maternity hospital are under quarantine, with no explanation given.
Maxim Modin, head of the Shelekhov district in Irkutsk Oblast, where the institute is located, said no infectious diseases had been reported among institute employees over the past 10 days and that everyone who recently came into contact with Shipilova was being tested.
The institute itself declined to respond to a request for comment from CNN. At the Irkutsk aluminum plant in Shelekhov, near the laboratory, employees were instructed to wear masks. Plant director Artyom Fominikh said “conflicting reports” were circulating and urged people to remain calm.
Central Asian countries also did not wait for further clarification. Kazakhstan’s Health Ministry assessed the risk as “very low” but introduced sanitary and quarantine controls at border crossings. Uzbekistan said it had increased authorities’ preparedness to deal with particularly dangerous infectious diseases.
Kyrgyzstan, which has no land border with Russia and lies about 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from Irkutsk, announced Monday that it was introducing quarantine controls at its border crossings.
Prof. Tal Brosh-Nissimov is the Head of the Infectious Diseases Unit at Samson Assuta Ashdod University Hospital, spoke with ynet this week about the possibility that Shipilova was infected in a laboratory accident.
“Let’s assume what’s being reported is true. I have no idea what the safety level is there or what their procedures are. When people work in laboratories with dangerous bacteria, accidents happen and people are exposed. The description of what happened to this woman is consistent with exposure to the plague bacterium,” he said.
According to Brosh, the key to understanding this scenario is how the bacterium entered the body.
“If a test tube containing the plague bacterium broke and an aerosol was released from the tube — meaning droplets were dispersed into the air — you can develop pneumonic plague if you inhale the bacterium,” he explained.
“There are several forms of plague. The most severe, the deadliest and the most contagious is pneumonic plague. It is an extremely fast-moving and aggressive disease, and the description of her condition deteriorating within days is consistent with it. It’s not certain, but it fits. It progresses very quickly and causes extremely severe pneumonia.
“Plague can be treated, but treatment has to begin very quickly. It does not respond well to late treatment.”

Spain’s Leader Is Betting His Government on the Housing Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:02:23 UTC
08:02:23 KST

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain called for early elections on Monday after Parliament last week rejected two key housing decrees amid widespread protests over rising rents and housing scarcity. The elections, originally scheduled to take place next summer, will now be held on Nov. 29.
One of the decrees was a relief package aiming to extend eviction protections for vulnerable households, regulate rentals, and offer tax relief and assistance for renters, landlords, and first-time homebuyers, while the other aimed to offer greater stability for renters by establishing automatic renewals.
The rejected measures came from Sánchez’s governing coalition, comprising his Socialist Party, PSOE, and the left-wing alliance Sumar. The coalition lacks a majority in Parliament and must rely on other parties to pass legislation. That dependence leaves the government vulnerable when those parties withhold their support—which is what played out with the two housing measures on Oct. 2.
In calling early elections, Sánchez is hoping voters will give his coalition enough support in Parliament to advance its housing agenda—but risks handing his opponents the majority instead.
“To do more, we need to renew and expand the people’s support,” Sánchez said in a statement on Monday.
But he faces a central challenge: persuading voters to blame the parties that blocked his proposals, rather than his government, for the lack of relief.
Various parties have offered differing explanations for why they rejected the decrees.
Junts—a Catalan pro-independence party—said in a statement Oct. 1 that many of the proposed measures would reduce the supply of rental homes and drive up prices, making housing even harder to access for people with lower incomes. Juan Bravo, housing spokesman for the conservative PP party, said on Oct. 2 that the government was proposing significant market interventions without adequately addressing the shortage of homes through construction.
Sergio Nasarre Aznar, a professor of civil law at Universitat Rovira i Virgili, agrees with some of the points the parties have made in opposing the decrees, telling TIME that “what Pedro Sánchez is proposing will cause a serious breakdown of the housing market”—making it even more difficult to access housing.
He also argues that the measures could make housing harder to access by increasing legal uncertainty. He warns of “the threat of future court rulings annulling some of the measures.”
Sánchez’s opponents are also choosing to emphasize other issues, including immigration: Vox leader Santiago Abascal, for instance, has made tougher migration policies a condition of supporting a future government with the conservative PP.
The move is also a gamble because Sánchez’s party may need to overcome blowback over corruption scandals, its handling of migration, and repeated difficulty securing support in Parliament.
Pablo Simón, a political scientist with the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, tells TIME that focusing on housing could help Sánchez move beyond those difficulties and engage progressive voters.
“After months dominated by corruption scandals, parliamentary weakness, and government fatigue, housing gives Sánchez an issue around which he believes he may be able to mobilize key parts of the progressive electorate again,” he says, “particularly younger voters, renters and voters in large cities.”
How did housing become the breaking point?
Spain’s housing supply has struggled to keep pace with demand in recent years, and an increasingly unaffordable market has become a growing pressure point, with the Bank of Spain showing an estimated housing shortfall of 750,000 homes accumulating from 2021 to 2025.
The Spanish Youth Council’s 2025 report showed an average monthly rent of €1,176, the equivalent of roughly $1,317, which then represented 98.7% of a young person’s average salary in Spain.
But public outrage came to a head in September when an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid after occupying the unit for decades. Thousands of protestors took to the streets.
Simón believes that the Prime Minister sees their fury as an opportunity.
“Sánchez is taking advantage of what is probably the best window of opportunity available to minimize PSOE losses,” he says. “If he manages to make the campaign revolve around this issue, he could hope to close the gap with the PP and, in the most favourable scenario for him, even compete to finish as the largest party.”
That does not mean Sánchez expects to win an outright majority, Simón cautions.
And he further questions if housing can become a decisive voting issue.
“It is clearly one of Spain's most important social problems and has a strong capacity to generate political mobilization, but that does not necessarily mean it will determine how people vote,” he says.
What is at stake in the election?
With a snap election, Sánchez is gambling that the housing issue will remobilize the left and give his coalition more seats in Parliament to advance its proposals.
But even if the Prime Minister succeeds in putting housing at the center of the campaign, Simón says, “that does not automatically mean that the PSOE will be the party that benefits electorally from it.”
The PP, Vox and Junts could still hold enough seats between them to block Sánchez’s housing proposals, he says, noting that far-right Vox is “growing strongly.”
Politico polling from Sept. 26 shows Sánchez entering the election campaign at a disadvantage, with PP at 34% of the vote share next to PSOE’s 26%. Vox follows at 18%, while Sumar holds some 5%. Those figures predate the election announcement and do not directly predict parliamentary seats.
“It is widely assumed that the right-wing bloc will secure an absolute majority,” Simón says, “so the main question is not whether Sánchez can remain in government, but how much he can limit the scale of the defeat.”
A defeat for Sánchez could have consequences beyond its borders. A government led by the conservative PP, potentially with far-right Vox, would reinforce Europe’s shift to the right, alongside conservative-led Germany and far-right-led Italy. It could also remove a prominent progressive voice from European debates over immigration, defense spending, and relations with Israel.
If Sánchez secures the greater parliamentary support he’s seeking, meanwhile, it would not guarantee relief from rising housing costs.
Previous efforts illustrate the difficulties. Spain’s 2023 housing law enabled rent limits in designated high-pressure areas, but implementation has varied by region. Attempts to tighten rules on temporary rentals have also encountered parliamentary resistance. A subsequent rental-regulation proposal advanced in December 2024, showing that negotiations could overcome some divisions. But support for debating the legislation did not mean agreement on its substance.
At the same time, expanding public housing requires years of investment and cooperation between national and regional authorities. A new parliamentary majority would not, on its own, remove those obstacles. And Simón says it remains unclear which party can claim ownership of the housing issue.
“Voters assign responsibility to different levels of government, and there is no broad consensus on the appropriate solutions,” he explains.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative PP, said on Monday that he believes Sánchez called the election out of fear—but he supports the decision.
"These are not elections like the previous ones: This is about Spain defeating Sánchez and what he represents,” he said.
He acknowledged the housing crisis has yet to be addressed, claiming that “the cost of living is unbearable” in Spain and that “housing is out of reach.”
Vox leader Abascal commented on Monday that focusing on “national priority, deregulation, and remigration” would be the conditions for a potential governing alliance with the PP.
What is the process of calling for a snap election in Spain?
Following Sánchez’s announcement, elections are set to take place Nov. 29. The call for early elections is fairly common and reflects a core element of Spain’s electoral process.
Spain’s Constitution allows the prime minister, after consulting the Cabinet, to seek the early dissolution of Parliament and a new election. The king formally issues the decree; however, this action is a formality.
Sánchez’s office said Monday that King Felipe VI’s election decree would be published Tuesday.
The previous election was July 23, 2023, and parliamentary terms normally last four years, meaning that the latest possible date to hold elections would have been Aug. 22, 2027.
No official date had been set when Sánchez called to move up the timeline by as many as nine months.
Sánchez has called early elections before: in 2019, after Parliament rejected his budget, and in 2023, after his party suffered losses in local and regional elections. The PP won the most seats in the July 2023 vote, but Sánchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to remain Prime Minister.

Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Oct 5 that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mokha fighting
Yemeni military sources said on Oct 5 that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mokha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port’s recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
